advanced-concepts.definition_short: Concepts that rest on other concepts rather than directly on the board — over 30 of them.
advanced-concepts.definition_long:
The tier where a concept can no longer be explained from the position alone, because it is about the relationship between other ideas.

WHAT PUTS A CONCEPT HERE is a dependency rather than a difficulty. The transformation of an advantage presupposes that you can already identify advantages and know they differ in durability. Prophylaxis presupposes that you can read the opponent's plan. Knight endgames presuppose pawn endgames — that is Botvinnik's formula and it is a dependency stated outright. Piece coordination presupposes piece activity and then says something about the whole army instead of a piece.

THESE ARE ALSO THE CONCEPTS THIS SYSTEM DETECTS WORST, and the two facts are the same fact. A concept that rests on board features can be detected from board features; a concept that rests on other concepts needs those resolved first, and the errors compound. Piece coordination is the clearest case and its own record forbids using it as a fallback label.

DIFFICULTY IN THIS BASE IS ABOUT THE CONCEPT, NOT THE PLAYER. It records how much other machinery a concept needs before it can be stated truthfully, which is why some famous ideas sit high and some obscure ones sit low. A fork is a beginner concept because it can be stated completely in one sentence; the Vancura position is an expert one not because it is hard to play but because stating it correctly requires the rook-ending context in which Tarrasch's rule fails.

IT IS ALSO WHAT DRIVES LEVEL ADAPTATION. Every concept carries explanations.by_level with wording for beginner, intermediate, advanced and master, and the API selects among them. The difficulty field says where a concept BELONGS; the by_level wording says how to say it to whoever is asking. The two are deliberately separate, because an advanced concept still has to be explicable to a beginner who has just met it on the board.

back-rank-mate.knowledge_type_note: A named mating pattern (D). The derived 'back-rank weakness' is a standing positional feature rather than a one-move tactic, and the two should not be conflated in an explanation.
back-rank-mate.definition_short: A rook or queen mates on the back rank because the king's own pawns block every escape square.
back-rank-mate.definition_long:
The castled king sits behind three unmoved pawns. A heavy piece arriving on the back rank gives check, and the king has nowhere to go because its own pawns occupy the only flight squares. The standard prophylactic is to make LUFT — advancing a pawn (usually h2-h3 or h7-h6) to open an escape square.

The back rank is more often a weakness to be exploited indirectly than a mate to be played immediately: it makes defenders of the back rank overloaded, so deflecting or removing them wins material even when mate never actually occurs.

history.notes: Descriptive pattern name of long, largely anonymous usage.

preconditions: The enemy king is on its back rank
Its escape squares on the second rank are occupied by its own pawns
A friendly rook or queen can reach the back rank with check
indicators_for: No luft has been made
The back rank is defended by exactly one piece, which can be deflected or is overloaded
indicators_against: A pawn has moved to create luft
A second defender covers the back rank
The checking square is defended
The king can capture the checking piece

exceptions: Luft defeats it outright: one pawn move can turn mate into nothing.
A defended back rank is not weak; count defenders before claiming the pattern.
limitations: The pattern is easy to detect but easy to over-report — most back ranks that look weak are adequately defended.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

CORRECTED 2026-09-02, and the correction is to the ARGUMENT rather than to the conclusion. An earlier note here said this record's four indicators_against are unreachable because the detector reports only completed mate, `!theirMoves.length && inCheck(after, them)`. That is the test the `mate` tag uses and it is NOT the test this concept uses. findMotifs() has a separate `backRank` block: it checks that all three squares in front of the king are occupied by the king's own men, then hands the move back to the attacker and looks for a rook or queen move to the home rank that the move generator says is mate. So the report is a verified THREAT, not a completed mate. All four indicators_against are still unreachable, and now for the right reason. "A pawn has moved to create luft" makes the boxed-in test fail, because that test requires all three front squares to hold the king's own men. "A second defender covers the back rank" and "The checking square is defended" and "The king can capture the checking piece" all leave the reply list non-empty after the rook lands, so `!legalMoves(nx, them).length` is false and no mate is found. Four conditions, one mechanism, and the mechanism is the move generator rather than a guard.

The report is a threat and one sentence used to state it as a fact. `explanations.by_level.intermediate` said 'the back rank is not adequately defended', which on 3r2k1/5ppp/8/3n4/8/8/5PPP/3R2K1 after Rxd5 is simply false - the rook on d8 defends it and Black is to move. The detector's own sentence was correct and conditional ('a rook or queen landing there is mate'), `by_depth.normal` and `by_depth.deep` were correct and conditional, and one level of one wording was not. It is conditional now. This is the third of the three answers a stated condition can get - build it, argue it cannot be built, or say it in the sentence - and here the sentence was the thing that was wrong.

examples.note: The Opera Game, 17.Rd8 mate - the position the previous four moves were spent arranging. The black king is on e8 with the f8 bishop beside it and the knight just deflected to b8; the rook arrives on the eighth and there is no square. It is not the castled back-rank mate of the diagrams, and that is why it is worth having: the pattern is a king boxed on its home rank by its OWN men, and here the men are a bishop that never moved and a knight that was forced back, rather than three pawns in front of a castled king. PROVENANCE, stated plainly. The game is famous and the move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js - 33 plies, every one legal, which is what makes the FEN trustworthy rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and NOT the human-grounded one: it is evidence that the concept occurs in master play, and not evidence that a person named it here. The validation ladder already draws that line for eleven other concepts and it is drawn again here.
examples.game: Morphy-Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 (the Opera Game)

engine.verdict_note: Re8+ is no longer mate in 1 but mate in 30, and is no longer even the best move (h3 is mate in 28). A single tempo of luft converts a mate in 1 into a mate in 30. Exact quantification of the standard antidote, and a hard demonstration that the pattern must be re-checked against escape squares before it is reported.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-back-rank-threat-the-defender-answers`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: After Rxd5 the black king sits behind three unmoved pawns with no luft, and a rook landing on the eighth rank would be mate. The detector verifies that with the move generator rather than assuming it. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second indicator_against: "A second defender covers the back rank." The rook on d8 covers it, and Black is to move — the mate exists only if White is handed a free move, which is exactly how the detector asks the question. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: THE ANSWER IS THE SENTENCE, and one sentence was wrong. The detector's own text is conditional and correct — 'the king is shut in on its own back rank by its own pieces, and a rook or queen landing there is mate' — and so are by_depth.normal and by_depth.deep. But `explanations.by_level.intermediate` said 'the back rank is not adequately defended', which is false here: it is defended, by the rook that is about to capture. That level now reads 'unless a defender covers it, and the standing weakness is that whatever covers it can then be deflected', which is both true of this position and the actual content of the concept. The concept is still reported, correctly: the back-rank weakness is real and permanent, and the deflection theme is what it is for.

ambiguous_examples.note: BOTH back ranks are weak. Neither king has moved a pawn, both are boxed in by their own men, and a rook or queen arriving on either eighth or first rank would be mate. Neither side can arrange it, and the engine says 0.00. This is the standing weakness the record's deep explanation calls the more valuable half - 'more often than the mate itself, the value is the standing WEAKNESS' - present twice over and worth nothing to anybody, because the same feature on both sides cancels. Filed as ambiguous rather than negative: the pattern is genuinely on the board for both players, correctly, and a report of it tells a reader nothing about who stands better.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 24, settled at depth 18, and the engine's own first move is g3 - making luft, which is the antidote the record names. It spends a tempo on it in a dead position, which is a fair comment on how much the weakness is worth here.

by_level.beginner: The king is trapped on the back row by its own pawns, so a rook or queen arriving there is checkmate.
by_level.intermediate: Back-rank mate. The king's pawns block every escape square, so a rook or queen reaching the back rank is mate - unless a defender covers it, and the standing weakness is that whatever covers it can then be deflected.
by_level.advanced: Back-rank pattern. Often the real value is the standing weakness: it overloads whatever defends the rank.

by_depth.short: The king is boxed in by its own pawns on the back rank.
by_depth.normal: A back-rank mate: the king's own f, g and h pawns block every escape square, so a rook or queen arriving on the back rank is mate — provided the rank is not adequately defended.
by_depth.deep: The castled king sits behind three unmoved pawns, and a heavy piece arriving on the back rank gives a check it cannot escape. The standard antidote is luft, and the cost of omitting it is exact: in a controlled test, moving one pawn from h7 to h6 turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty. More often than the mate itself, the value is the standing WEAKNESS — a back rank that must be guarded overloads whatever guards it, so deflecting that defender wins material even when mate never occurs.

backward-pawn.knowledge_type_note: Names a structural feature. Whether it is a WEAKNESS is a separate judgement and is not part of the definition.

attributions.note: Part of the pawn-weakness doctrine Steinitz introduced; Britannica lists backward pawns among the structural weaknesses his theory named. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: this is the conventional ascription, taken from a secondary source, and no primary text was consulted for it during this research.

history.notes: Attribution is weak. Britannica associates the classification of pawn weaknesses with Steinitz, but no source consulted gives a first use of 'backward pawn' specifically. Recorded low rather than guessed at.

backward-pawn.engine_era_note: Engines carry backward-pawn penalties, but modern practice is markedly more relaxed about accepting one in return for activity or space than classical teaching was. The square in front is generally valued more highly than the pawn.

preconditions: A pawn is on a lower rank than all friendly pawns on adjacent files
It cannot advance safely — the square ahead is controlled by an enemy pawn or piece
indicators_for: It stands on a file that is half-open for the opponent
The square in front of it is controlled by an enemy pawn and can be occupied by a piece
It cannot be defended by a pawn and needs pieces to hold it
The position is simplifying, so fewer pieces are available to defend it
indicators_against: It can advance at a moment of its choosing, so the defect is temporary
No enemy rook can reach the file
It is compensated by space or by the activity its structure enables
The square in front is covered by a piece the opponent cannot dislodge
false_positive_traps: A pawn that is merely behind its neighbours but CAN advance safely is not backward in the operative sense.
A backward pawn on a closed file that nothing can attack is a description, not a weakness.
Reporting the pawn and not the square in front of it usually misses the more important half.
A pawn with no friendly pawn on either adjacent file is ISOLATED, not backward, and reporting both names for one pawn promises the reader a hole in front of it that the isolated case does not create.

A pawn whose advance square is occupied by an enemy pawn is RAMMED. It cannot advance, but not for the reason the concept is about, and the square in front of it is not a hole - an enemy pawn is standing on it.

typical_plans: Fix it by preventing the freeing advance, then attack it with rooks on the half-open file
Occupy the square in front of it with a knight
As the defender: prepare and execute the freeing pawn break, or exchange into a position where it cannot be attacked
typical_pawn_structures: Sicilian structures with a backward d-pawn on a half-open d-file
The result of a minority attack, which aims to leave a backward pawn behind
typical_piece_arrangements: Enemy rooks doubled on the half-open file, knight on the square in front
strategic_consequences: Fixes the defender's pieces to passive defence
The square in front becomes a permanent outpost

exceptions: Not a weakness if it cannot be attacked, or if the freeing break is always available.
Accepting one for space or activity is routine modern practice.
The square in front is often the real asset; winning the pawn can be the lesser goal.
limitations: The geometric test is mechanical; 'cannot advance safely' requires evaluating the square ahead, which is position-dependent.

FIXED 2026-09-01, found by Wade-Korchnoi 1960: the detector reported a pawn with NO friendly pawn on either adjacent file as backward, because the 'is it behind its neighbours' test returns false both when the neighbours are all advanced and when there are none. A pawn with no neighbours is isolated. It also reported a pawn whose advance square is OCCUPIED by an enemy pawn, which is rammed rather than backward and creates no hole in front of it.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the second trap - 'a backward pawn on a closed file that nothing can attack is a description, not a weakness' - had never been built. The file must now be half-open for the opponent, so a rook can actually come down it. 1.9% -> 1.3%: 10 of the 15 backward pawns on the 788 shipped positions stand on such a file and the other five were descriptions. The first trap is Layer 3's and was already built there - the advance square has to be controlled by an enemy pawn, which is what makes advancing unsafe by definition.
misconceptions: That every backward pawn is a weakness.
That the pawn is the target. The square in front of it is usually worth more.

by_level.beginner: That pawn has fallen behind the pawns next to it and cannot move up safely, so it has to be defended by pieces.
by_level.intermediate: A backward pawn on {square}. It cannot advance, it sits on a file their rooks can use, and the square in front of it is a hole for your knight.
by_level.advanced: Backward on a half-open file. Fix the freeing break first, then decide whether the target is the pawn or the square in front of it — usually the square.
by_level.master: Two assets, not one: a fixed target on a half-open file, and a permanent outpost on the square ahead. Weigh both against whatever space or activity was received for it.

by_depth.short: {square} cannot advance and cannot be defended by a pawn.
by_depth.normal: A backward pawn: it has fallen behind its neighbours and cannot safely advance, so it must be defended by pieces. It usually stands on a file that is half-open for the opponent, and the square in front of it is a hole.
by_depth.deep: Defined as a pawn behind all friendly pawns on the adjacent files that cannot be safely advanced. The inability to advance is the operative half, because it means the defect is permanent. It produces two assets for the opponent: the pawn as a fixed target on a half-open file, and the square in front as an outpost no pawn can contest. The second is usually worth more, and it is exactly the mechanism behind Nimzowitsch's outpost — provoke the pawn move that leaves a backward pawn, and the square appears with it. Modern practice accepts backward pawns far more readily than classical teaching did, when space or activity is received in return.

explanations.lesson: When you see a backward pawn, look at the square in front of it before you look at the pawn.

beginner_words: a pawn that has been left behind

backward-pawn.definition_short: A pawn behind all friendly pawns on the adjacent files, which cannot safely advance — usually standing on a half-open file where enemy rooks can attack it.
backward-pawn.definition_long:
Wikipedia's definition is the standard one: 'a pawn that is behind all pawns of the same colour on the adjacent files and cannot be safely advanced.' Both halves matter. Being behind its neighbours is the geometry; being unable to advance safely is what makes it a problem, because it means the defect cannot be repaired.

Two consequences follow and they are what make the concept useful:

  1. The pawn itself is a fixed target, and it usually sits on a HALF-OPEN FILE for the opponent, so rooks and queens can pile onto it from a distance.
  2. The square DIRECTLY IN FRONT of it is a hole. That square is often worth more than the pawn, because a piece placed there cannot be challenged by a pawn — which is exactly the outpost condition.

This is why backward pawns and outposts are usually discussed together: creating a backward pawn in the opponent's camp creates the square in front of it at the same time. Nimzowitsch's outpost mechanism is precisely this — provoking the pawn advance that leaves a backward pawn behind it.

It is not automatically a weakness. A backward pawn that cannot be attacked, or that is compensated by space or activity, is a feature of the structure rather than a defect.

preconditions: A bishop's own pawns predominantly occupy the colour it moves on

The position is closed, so the pawn structure will not change

The structure is fluid and about to change
It can be traded for the opponent's good bishop

A bad bishop that is the sole guardian of a weak colour complex is a load-bearing defender, not a liability.

typical_plans: Break with a pawn move that relocates pawns off the bishop's colour
Trade the bad bishop, ideally for the opponent's good one
Reroute it outside the pawn chain and give it a job there
Against one: fix the opponent's pawns on the bishop's colour so the defect is permanent

Closed centres where the pawns are fixed
typical_piece_arrangements: Bishop shut inside its own chain with no exit square
strategic_consequences: One of the largest static imbalances available, and durable into the endgame
Drives the classic technique of simplifying into an endgame with the better bishop

exceptions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.
If the structure can change, the badness is temporary.

Sources for the historical attributions are weak; see history.notes.

by_level.beginner: Your own pawns are sitting on the same colour squares as your bishop, so they are in its way.
by_level.intermediate: A bad bishop: its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Before writing it off, check whether it can get outside the chain — a bad bishop with an open diagonal is a real piece.
by_level.advanced: Structurally bad. Suba's distinction applies: badness is about the pawns, passivity is about the work it does, and an active bad bishop outside the chain is often fine.
by_level.master: Fix the opponent's pawns on their bishop's colour to make it permanent. And check whether the bad bishop is the sole guardian of a complex before proposing a trade.

by_depth.short: Its own pawns are on the bishop's colour, blocking it.
by_depth.normal: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
by_depth.deep: A bishop's scope is decided by its own pawn structure, since its colour is fixed forever. Pawns on the bishop's colour block it and leave the other colour unguarded; pawns on the opposite colour give the pair full coverage. Formalised by Steinitz and hardened into a rule by Tarrasch. The essential corrective is Suba's 'active bad bishop': a structurally bad bishop that has got outside its own chain can be an excellent piece, because bad is structural and passive is functional. The French ...Bd7-a4 is the standard case — still bad by definition, and cutting the queenside in half.

explanations.lesson: Count the pawns on your bishop's colour to see if it is bad. Then look at what it is actually doing, because those are different questions.

bad-bishop.definition_short: A bishop whose own pawns sit on the colour it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside.
bad-bishop.definition_long:
A bishop moves on one colour forever, so its scope is decided by where its OWN pawns sit. Pawns on the bishop's colour block it from the inside and, worse, leave the other colour uncovered — so the weak squares stay weak and the bishop cannot use them. Pawns on the opposite colour give full-board coverage: pawns hold one colour, bishop holds the other.

The archetype is the French Defence light-squared bishop, buried behind d5, e6 and f7.

THE CRITICAL QUALIFICATION, and the reason this concept is so often misapplied: badness is STRUCTURAL, not positional. Mihail Suba's 'active bad bishop' names the case — a structurally bad bishop that has got OUTSIDE its own pawn chain and is doing real work. The French ...Bd7-a4 is the standard illustration: the bishop is still bad by Steinitz's definition, since its own pawns still block its diagonals, and it is nevertheless an excellent piece. As the distinction is usually put: 'bad' is structural, 'passive' is functional, and they are not the same thing.

The three standard cures are a pawn break that moves the offending pawns off the bishop's colour, trading the bad bishop for the opponent's good one, and rerouting it outside the chain.

battery.knowledge_type_note: Type D by association, but it is really a configuration that enables motifs rather than a motif that wins material. Flagged so an explanation does not claim a battery is itself the reason a move is good.
battery.definition_short: Two or more line pieces stacked on the same file, rank or diagonal, so their force is combined.
battery.definition_long:
Two rooks on a file, a queen behind a rook, a queen behind a bishop on a diagonal. The front piece can capture on a defended square because the rear piece recaptures, and the pair controls the line far more strongly than either alone.

A battery is also the precondition for a discovered attack: put a piece of your own in front of the rear piece and moving it discovers. The queen-plus-bishop diagonal battery aimed at h7 is the standard attacking configuration; three heavy pieces on one file is sometimes called Alekhine's gun.

Recorded as a piece configuration rather than a tactic: a battery does not by itself do anything, it enables things.

history.notes: Descriptive pattern name of long, largely anonymous usage.

preconditions: Two or more friendly line pieces share a file, rank or diagonal with nothing between them
indicators_for: The line points at the enemy king or a weak square
The front piece can capture on a defended square, backed by the rear piece
indicators_against: The line is blocked further along and cannot be opened
The rear piece is more valuable and becomes a target itself
false_positive_traps: Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

exceptions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
limitations: A battery is potential, not achievement. Do not report it as the reason for a move unless the position shows what it actually enables.

Fires on 24.4% of the 788 shipped positions. A first version asked only for two aligned line pieces with one empty square beyond them and fired on 43%, because two rooks stacked behind their own pawns satisfy the geometry and combine nothing. The line must now arrive somewhere: at an enemy man, or into the enemy half.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the second indicator_against - 'the rear piece is more valuable and becomes a target itself' - is now said rather than suppressed, because the geometry is there either way and which piece stands in front is exactly what a learner needs told. A queen in front of a rook is not a battery aimed at the enemy, it is a queen that has to move first every time the line is touched. Building it exposed a bug in the matcher's own bookkeeping: the scan walks from one piece along a direction to the other, so the SECOND piece found is the one nearer the target, and reading them the other way round would have told a reader the queen was in front when the rook was.

examples.note: The Opera Game, Morphy against the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858, at move 14. The battery this base reports is BLACK'S, and it is the expensive kind: 'Black has two long-range pieces stacked on one line, on f8 and e7, and the line runs on to the enemy half - but the queen is in front of the bishop, which is the expensive way round: the front piece has to move first every time the line is touched.' Three moves later Black is mated. That is why this is the right master example rather than a picture of a good battery: the record's trap is that two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere, and here a real battery on a real diagonal arrives nowhere and belongs to the losing side. PROVENANCE. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js, which refuses a wrong list rather than guessing, so the FEN is verified rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

Registered false-positive case `rooks-doubled-behind-a-rammed-pawn`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Two rooks stand one behind the other on the d-file — the exact geometry of a battery. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own trap: "Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions." Here the d-file dead-ends at White's own d4 pawn, which is rammed against d5 and cannot move. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The system does not make the claim: the API reports nothing at all here, because the battery matcher requires the line to arrive at a target and this one arrives at White's own pawn. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 agrees about what the doubled rooks are worth on that file — the position is mate in 5 and the best move is Ra1, which takes the front rook OFF the d-file. The engine's plan is to abandon the battery, which is the strongest possible statement that the geometry was not doing anything.

by_level.beginner: Two pieces are lined up on the same line, so they work together — the one in front can take, and the one behind takes back.
by_level.intermediate: A battery on the {line}. It doubles the pressure and sets up a discovery if the front piece moves.
by_level.advanced: Battery. Check the ordering — the cheaper piece generally belongs in front.

by_depth.short: Two line pieces stacked on one line, so their force is combined.
by_depth.normal: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
by_depth.deep: The geometry is trivial to detect and means nothing on its own — the bare pattern fires on nearly half of all positions. What makes a battery worth naming is that the line ARRIVES somewhere: two rooks stacked behind their own rammed pawn combine nothing. The order also matters and is often got backwards. Queen in front of rook or bishop is the expensive way round, because the front piece has to move first every time the line is touched, and the most valuable piece is the one that should not be exposed. This base's master example is Black's queen-in-front battery in the Opera Game, three moves before Black is mated.

explanations.hedge: A battery enables tactics rather than being one; say what it actually threatens here.

preconditions: An explanation is about to assert a rule
false_positive_traps: The index records beliefs that are FALSE AS STATED, not beliefs that are always wrong. Doubled pawns are frequently a real weakness; the misconception is that they are one by definition.
This record must not be used to contradict a rule in a position where the rule holds. It exists to prevent unconditional assertion, not to invert it.

Prefer describing what is true of this position over invoking a general rule

exceptions: The rules behind these misconceptions are mostly sound in their conditional form; the index targets the unconditional statement, not the underlying idea.
limitations: The index reflects only what this base has researched. Absence from it is not evidence that a belief is correct.

by_level.beginner: Many chess 'rules' are only true most of the time, and the exceptions are common.
by_level.intermediate: A misconception is usually a real rule with its condition stripped off in retelling.
by_level.advanced: The surface features you were taught to distrust are the ones most likely to be innocent in a given position.
by_level.master: Several of these are now settled by measurement rather than opinion, which is a different kind of claim.

by_depth.short: Common chess beliefs that are false as stated.
by_depth.normal: The false beliefs this base has recorded - 210 of them - together with the exceptions, detector traps and banned phrasings that go with them, compiled into a single index an explanation layer can query.
by_depth.deep: Chess teaching travels as short rules, and short rules lose their conditions on the way. What is left is a stock of confident false beliefs that sound exactly like chess teaching, which makes them the most dangerous thing an explanation system can reproduce. Collected in one place, they nearly all have the same shape: a true statement with its condition removed. Doubled pawns are weak, do not move a piece twice, the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, improve your worst piece - each is sound conditionally and false as stated, and several are now disproved here by controlled measurement or tablebase proof rather than by argument.

explanations.lesson: Never assert a rule in a position that is one of its exceptions. Say what is true here instead.

beginner-misconceptions.definition_short: The false beliefs this knowledge base has recorded and, where possible, disproved - over 250 of them.
beginner-misconceptions.definition_long:
Most chess teaching is transmitted as short rules, and short rules lose their conditions in transmission. The result is a stock of confident false beliefs that a system explaining moves must actively avoid reproducing, because they are exactly the phrasings that sound most like chess teaching.

THIS BASE CARRIES 210 recorded misconceptions, 254 exceptions, 222 false-positive traps and 125 banned phrasings, compiled by tools/build_index.py into state/warnings_index.json. That file is the retrieval surface: it answers 'what must I not say about this?' without the caller needing to know which concept holds the warning.

THE RECURRING SHAPE, visible once they are collected in one place, is that the misconception is almost always a TRUE STATEMENT WITH ITS CONDITION REMOVED:
- 'Doubled pawns are weak' — measured here, inflicting them cost the inflicting side 0.34 while the side accepting them was exactly equal.
- 'Do not move the same piece twice in the opening' — the best move in the Ruy Lopez does exactly that, by a margin of 0.34.
- 'Put the rook behind the passed pawn' — proven here to turn a drawn position into a loss in 63.
- 'Improve your worst piece' — both original formulations are conditional and the condition is what decides.
- 'A check forces a reply, so checks are strong' — one proven position holds a check that draws and a check that loses.

THE PRACTICAL RULE that follows, and the reason this record exists: an explanation must never assert a rule in a position that is one of its exceptions. Naming a pattern is not the same as diagnosing a fault, and the surface features people are taught to distrust — doubled pawns, isolated pawns, an exposed king, a piece moved twice — are the ones most likely to be innocent in any given position.

bishop-pair.knowledge_type_note: A concept with an unusually precise measured value, but still conditional on the position being or becoming open.

attributions.note: Steinitz taught the superiority of the two bishops at a time when the bishop-versus-knight question was still disputed. Reported by a publisher's summary of The Modern Chess Instructor; ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED against the passage itself.
Quantified it statistically at about half a pawn, which is the figure engines use.

history.notes: The concept is old and the modern contribution is measurement rather than discovery.

development.change: The two bishops taught as clearly superior, against the prevailing uncertainty.
Tarrasch's high valuation of the unobstructed bishop attacked; bishop-for-knight trades rehabilitated.
Quantified at about half a pawn and built into engine material tables.

bishop-pair.engine_era_note: Confirmed and quantified rather than revised. Engines carry an explicit bishop-pair bonus of roughly half a pawn, which is one of the few positional concepts with a number attached that both statistics and engines agree on.

preconditions: One side has both bishops and the other does not
indicators_for: The position is open or can be opened
The opponent's knights have no stable advanced squares
Play on both wings, where the bishops' range tells
An endgame, where the pair is at its strongest
indicators_against: A locked pawn structure with no way to open it
The opponent has a knight on a secure outpost
One of the bishops is shut in by its own pawns
The opponent can force the trade of one bishop
false_positive_traps: Detecting two bishops is trivial and says nothing about whether they are worth anything. In a locked position the pair can be worth less than a well-placed knight.
Half a pawn is an AVERAGE over many games and can be arbitrarily wrong in one position.
A bishop pair where one bishop is shut in by its own pawns is not really a pair.

typical_plans: Open the position; avoid trading either bishop
Play on both wings so the range advantage tells
Against the pair: keep the position closed, or spend a tempo to trade one bishop off
typical_moves: A pawn break to open lines for the bishops
...Bxc3 or Bxf6 to break up the opponent's pair
typical_pawn_structures: Open or semi-open centres
Positions with pawns on both wings
typical_piece_arrangements: Bishops on adjacent long diagonals raking the board
tactical_consequences: Two bishops generate mating patterns against a castled king that a bishop and knight cannot
strategic_consequences: Grows in value as the position simplifies and opens
Compensates measurably in other imbalances — about 0.6 pawns' worth in exchange-down positions

exceptions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.
Modern practice trades bishop for knight far more readily than Tarrasch would have, sometimes for minimal compensation.
limitations: The half-pawn figure is a statistical average, not a property of any position.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the third false-positive trap - 'a bishop pair where one bishop is shut in by its own pawns is not really a pair' - was written down and not built, and it is the only one of the three that CAN be built. It is now decided by the same test `bad-bishop` uses, in one shared function, and it DOWNGRADES rather than suppresses: 23 of the 178 positions on the shipped corpus where a pair exists are reported at low confidence, with a sentence naming the buried bishop instead of the record's usual advice to avoid trading either one. Suppressing outright was tried first and produced a false negative on this base's own annotated bishop-pair position, Havasi-Capablanca 1929 - where the annotation is precisely that Capablanca showed the pair to be overrated, so the concept has to be REPORTED to be argued with. The direction matters for a second reason: bad-bishop's record says its conclusion 'is frequently wrong' and it reports at low confidence for that reason, so letting it veto a certainty would be the wrong way round. The other two traps are about magnitude ('half a pawn is an AVERAGE') and are not mechanical.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the other two indicators_against are now built, and both DOWNGRADE rather than suppress, for the same reason the buried-bishop guard does - the pair is a fact. 'A locked pawn structure with no way to open it' needs both halves and has neither a threshold nor a judgement in it: at least three of our pawns nose to nose with an enemy pawn, and no pawn advance of ours that arrives in contact with an enemy pawn and survives. A share-of-rammed-pawns threshold was tried first and rejected, because it needs a number nobody can defend while 'no way to open it' is a question the board answers. 'The opponent has a knight on a secure outpost' is read straight off the outpost detector. Of the 178 positions on the shipped corpus where one side holds the pair and the other does not, 5 are locked and 14 face a knight on an outpost. The firing rate is unchanged at 22.6% and saying it moved would be the wrong claim about a change that alters confidence and wording.
misconceptions: That two bishops are always better than bishop and knight. It depends on whether the position is open.
That the pair's value is just two bishops' values added. The synergy is the point, and it is measurable.
That giving up a bishop for a knight is an error. Modern practice does it routinely.

by_level.beginner: Each bishop can only use half the squares. Having both means you cover everything, so the pair is worth more than two separate bishops.
by_level.intermediate: The bishop pair, worth about half a pawn. Open the position to use it, and avoid trading either one — losing one destroys the pair entirely.
by_level.advanced: Kaufman's figure: unpaired bishop 3.5, pair 7.5. It is conditional on open lines, and worth little in a locked structure.
by_level.master: Weigh it against the structure. It is also the quantity that makes an exchange sacrifice affordable — with the pair, 1.15 pawns levels an exchange rather than 1.75.

by_depth.short: Both bishops cover both colours — worth about half a pawn extra.
by_depth.normal: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
by_depth.deep: Its value is synergy, and unusually for a positional concept the size is measured rather than argued: Kaufman puts an unpaired bishop at 3.5 and the pair at 7.5, and database outcomes confirm the effect. It is conditional — bishops need diagonals, so the pair can be worth nothing in a locked structure where a knight hopping over the pawns is the better piece. Hence the plans on both sides: open the position and keep both, or close it and trade one off, since trading ONE destroys the pair entirely. It also shows up in other imbalances: down the exchange but holding the pair, about 1.15 pawns levels the position against 1.75 without it.

explanations.lesson: The bishop pair is worth about half a pawn — but only if you can open the position. In a locked structure, a knight with a secure square may be the better piece.

bishop-pair.definition_short: Having both bishops when the opponent does not. Worth roughly half a pawn on average, because together they cover both colour complexes.
bishop-pair.definition_long:
A single bishop is permanently blind to half the board. Two bishops between them cover everything, which is why the pair is worth measurably more than the sum of its parts.

The size is known rather than guessed. Kaufman's statistical values put an unpaired bishop at 3.5 and the PAIR at 7.5 — half a pawn of pure synergy — and database outcome studies confirm the effect, with the side holding the pair winning 41-46% against 30-32%.

It is conditional on the position. Bishops need open diagonals, so the pair is strongest in open positions and can be worth nothing in a locked one, where a knight that can hop over the structure may be the better piece. Hence the standard plans on both sides: the holder opens the position and avoids trading either bishop, and the opponent keeps it closed or trades one bishop off — trading one is what destroys the pair, and it is worth a tempo or a small concession to do it.

Its practical weight also shows up in other imbalances: a side down the exchange but holding the bishop pair needs only about 1.15 pawns of further compensation to be level, against 1.75 without it.

blindfold-interference.knowledge_type_note: Experimental findings about when a held position degrades, with a measured time course.

attributions.note: Established the interference time course by dictating games under concurrent tasks.
Isolated novelty rather than mere presence of irrelevant information as the disruptive factor.

history.notes: Saariluoma's experiments are known here through Campitelli & Gobet's review rather than from the original papers.

blindfold-interference.engine_era_note: Not applicable; a claim about human cognition.

preconditions: A player is holding a position without sight of it
false_positive_traps: A fact about the player and the interface, not about the position or any move.
The finding is specifically about visual and attention-demanding interference during encoding. Generalising it to 'distraction is bad' loses the whole result, which is that timing decides.

strategic_consequences: A stable display matters more than a minimal one, because change is what interferes

exceptions: Interference after a position is encoded is comparatively harmless, which is the opposite of what the folklore suggests.
Static irrelevant information is tolerated by masters; only changing information disrupts.
limitations: The experiments used dictated games at fixed rates, which is not the same as playing.
The findings concern masters and medium-strength players; weaker players may be more fragile throughout.

by_level.beginner: It is hardest to hold the position while you are taking a move in. Once it is settled, distraction matters less.
by_level.intermediate: Interference bites during encoding, not after. Changing surroundings hurt; static ones do not.
by_level.advanced: Visuo-spatial working memory is essential early and much less so later - once information is matched to stored patterns it is comparatively safe.
by_level.master: Novelty is what the mind's eye uses to separate figure from ground, which is why changing irrelevant information is the disruptive kind.

by_depth.short: Distraction hurts while you are taking a move in, much less afterwards.
by_depth.normal: What disrupts a mentally held position is more specific than general distraction: visual or attention-demanding tasks hurt badly while a position is being encoded and little once it is stored, and irrelevant surroundings interfere only when they change.
by_depth.deep: The research characterises failure more precisely than folklore does. The time course is the central finding: visuo-spatial working memory is essential during early encoding and much less so afterwards, because once incoming information has been matched to structures in long-term memory it is comparatively safe - the matching is the fragile part. Novelty rather than clutter is what breaks it, since irrelevant background affects masters only when it changes during presentation, the mind's eye apparently using novelty to separate figure from ground. Similar concurrent games interfere with each other, and transposing the board's halves badly impairs recall - further evidence that the representation is matched against stored patterns rather than read off an image.

explanations.lesson: The vulnerable moment is while the move is going in. A stable display is worth more than a sparse one.

blindfold-interference.definition_short: What disrupts a mentally held position: visual-spatial distraction during encoding, changing irrelevant surroundings, and similarity between concurrent games.
blindfold-interference.definition_long:
How a blindfold representation fails, which the research characterises more precisely than the folklore does.

THE TIME COURSE IS THE KEY FINDING. Visuo-spatial working memory is essential during the EARLY stages of encoding a position and much less so afterwards. A distracting visual or attention-demanding task hurts badly when it coincides with a game being presented, and hurts little when it comes after the position is already stored. The explanation offered is that once the incoming information has been matched to structures in long-term memory it is comparatively safe; it is the matching that is fragile.

NOVELTY, NOT CLUTTER, is what breaks concentration. Irrelevant background information affects masters only when it CHANGES during presentation of the game. A static irrelevant position alongside is tolerated. The interpretation is that the mind's eye uses novelty to separate figure from ground, so changing surroundings compete for exactly that mechanism.

SIMILARITY BETWEEN GAMES. Fine, describing his own simultaneous blindfold play, noted interference between games that resembled one another — a hazard specific to playing several at once, and a reason blindfold simultaneous players sometimes deliberately steer games apart.

TRANSPOSING THE BOARD'S HALVES badly impairs recall, which is further evidence that the representation is matched against stored patterns rather than read off an image: an image would not care.

FOR A BLINDFOLD PROGRAM the practical reading is that a changing visual interface during the moment a player is taking in a move is the costly kind of distraction, and that a stable display is worth more than a sparse one.

blindfold-representation.knowledge_type_note: An experimental finding from cognitive psychology, replicated across several laboratories and a century of work. It is not a chess principle and carries no exceptions in the way a chess heuristic does.

attributions.note: The first scientific study of chess memory, and the origin of the abstract-representation finding.

attributions.person: William G. Chase and Herbert A. Simon
attributions.note: Supplied the chunking model and the measured chunk relations that explain what is stored instead of an image.

history.notes: Unusually well-evidenced for anything in this base: a documented reversal by the original investigator against his own stated hypothesis, followed by a century of confirmation from independent laboratories. Binet's monograph was consulted through Gobet's and Campitelli & Gobet's summaries rather than in the original French.

development.note: Binet's questionnaire study; hypothesis of concrete visual imagery abandoned.
De Groot shows masters do not search more widely but generate better candidate moves.
Fine's introspective account as a world-class player, emphasising hierarchical organisation and key statements summarising a position.
Chase and Simon's chunking model, with the mind's eye as an internal visuo-spatial store.
Saariluoma and Kalakoski's experiments: dots for pieces, auditory versus visual presentation, the functional figure.
Gobet and Simon's template theory, applied to blindfold chess by Campitelli and Gobet.

blindfold-representation.engine_era_note: Not affected by engine analysis; this is a claim about human cognition.

preconditions: A player is playing or calculating without sight of the position
false_positive_traps: This is a fact about the player, not about the position. It must never be attached to a move as though it explained one.
It describes SKILLED players. A beginner attempting blindfold play may well be trying to hold a literal picture, which is part of why it is so hard for them.

strategic_consequences: Explanations for blindfold players should name relations between pieces rather than appeal to a mental picture

exceptions: Individual players differ in how much visual quality they report, and Fine noted that a blank board helped some players and hindered him.
The finding concerns skilled players; it does not describe how a novice attempts the task.
limitations: Binet's monograph and Fine's paper were consulted through summaries rather than in the original.
This is evidence about representation, not a recipe for acquiring it.

misconceptions: That blindfold players hold a photographic image of the board. This was the hypothesis the first study set out to confirm and had to abandon.
That blindfold chess is a feat of raw memory. Masters have no advantage at all on randomly arranged positions; the advantage is in meaningful structure.
That it requires an exceptional gift. The evidence points at accumulated chess knowledge rather than unusual memory.

by_level.beginner: Blindfold players do not picture the board like a photograph. They remember where the pieces are and what they are doing.
by_level.intermediate: The mental representation is abstract. What is stored is relations - what attacks what, what defends what - not an image.
by_level.advanced: Binet set out in 1894 to prove blindfold players use vivid visual imagery and found the opposite: fuzzy board limits, blurry pieces, and detail abstracted away for economy.
by_level.master: Representation is organised by functional relevance rather than uniformly, which is why significant regions of a position are recalled far better than insignificant ones.

by_depth.short: Blindfold players hold relations, not a picture.
by_depth.normal: Skilled blindfold players do not maintain a visual image of the board. Their representation is abstract - the board's limits are reported as fuzzy and the pieces as blurry - and what is actually held is where the pieces are and how they bear on each other.
by_depth.deep: The consistent finding of over a century of research, and one that began with its investigator being proved wrong: Binet expected to confirm vivid visual imagery in 1894 and had to conclude the opposite, that irrelevant features such as piece colour and shape are abstracted away for economy. The confirmations are varied and strong - replacing pieces with plain dots barely affects recall, presentation by ear works as well as by eye, and functionally significant regions are remembered far better than insignificant ones, which is not how a picture behaves. What is stored is relational: groups of pieces bound by attack, defence, proximity, and common colour or type. For a blindfold program the consequence is direct - explanations should say what bears on what, not ask the player to picture a scene.

explanations.lesson: Describe a blindfold position in terms of what attacks and defends what. That is how the player is actually holding it.

blindfold-representation.definition_short: Blindfold players do not see a picture of the board. Their representation is abstract and functional, and this has been the consistent experimental finding since 1894.
blindfold-representation.definition_long:
The single most important fact about blindfold chess, and the one almost everyone gets wrong — including the researcher who first investigated it.

BINET'S REVERSAL. In 1894 Alfred Binet sent questionnaires to the leading blindfold players of the day, expecting to confirm that they used a concrete visual image of the board and pieces. The replies forced him to abandon that hypothesis. Strong players reported that although they had some feeling of seeing a board, its limits were FUZZY, the pieces had uncertain shapes and blurry colours, and the sensory detail was simply absent. Binet concluded that uncritical features are abstracted away for economy, so that attention goes to what matters, and he shifted his explanation from visualisation to memory. He named three necessary abilities: erudition, imagination and memory, distinguishing a memory of IDEAS from a memory of SENSATIONS.

THE EXPERIMENTAL CONFIRMATIONS are strong and varied. Replacing the chess pieces with plain dots barely affects recall, for masters and intermediate players alike — the identity of the symbol is not what is stored. Presenting a game by ear works as well as presenting it by eye. And functionally significant regions of a position are recalled far better than insignificant ones, which means the representation is organised by relevance rather than uniformly, like a picture would be.

WHAT IS STORED INSTEAD is relational: which piece is where, and how the pieces bear on each other. Chase and Simon measured the relations that bind pieces together in memory — attack, defence, proximity, common colour and common type — and it is groups of that kind, not images, that a player holds.

THE DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROGRAM, which is a blindfold game, is that explanations addressed to a blindfold player should use functional and relational language rather than pictorial language. Telling a player what attacks what matches how they are actually holding the position; asking them to picture a scene does not.

blockade.knowledge_type_note: A strategic method with a concrete, checkable object: a piece placed in front of a pawn to stop it.

attributions.note: Verified in the primary text. He is explicit that masters already blockaded by custom and that his contribution was the theoretical rationale: 'It is customary, at least in master practice, to block the enemy pawn. But to my knowledge no attempt has so far been made to provide a theoretical rationale.'

history.notes: Well founded, and notable for what he does NOT claim: he says explicitly that the practice predates him and only the justification is his. That is a more careful self-attribution than he is usually given credit for.

development.change: Blockading is customary in master practice without a stated rationale.
The rationale is supplied, along with the requirements on the blockading piece.

blockade.engine_era_note: Uncontroversial and confirmed. The specific claim that a knight is the best blockader and a queen the worst is borne out by any engine evaluation of the same position with the blockading piece swapped.

preconditions: An enemy passed or advancing pawn
A friendly piece on the square directly in front of it
indicators_for: The blockader is a knight
The blockading square cannot be attacked by an enemy pawn
The blockader still makes threats from the square
The blockade is supported from behind
indicators_against: The blockader is a queen or rook, which is expensive and evictable
The blockading piece is needed elsewhere
The pawn can be supported and the blockade broken by an advance of its neighbours
false_positive_traps: A piece standing in front of a pawn is not necessarily blockading it usefully. The test is whether the piece keeps its powers there — a queen on a blockading square is doing a knight's chore.
A blockade becomes a weakness when it ties down a piece needed elsewhere, which is the standard cost and is easy to omit.
A pawn stopped by an enemy PAWN is a ram, not a blockade, and no piece is being spent.

typical_plans: Blockade with a knight, support it, and then attack the pawn
Restrain, blockade, destroy — in that order
Against a blockade: advance the neighbouring pawns to challenge the square
typical_moves: Nd4 or Nd5 in front of an isolated queen's pawn
typical_pawn_structures: Isolated queen's pawn — the square in front is the standard blockade square
Passed pawns of any kind
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight in front of the pawn, supported from behind
tactical_consequences: A blockaded pawn cannot generate promotion threats, so the tactics that depend on it disappear
strategic_consequences: Converts a passed pawn from an asset into a fixed target
The blockading square is by construction a square no pawn can attack, so it is also an outpost

exceptions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.
The pawn must not be allowed too far forward before the blockade is established — Nimzowitsch's own caveat.
limitations: Detecting a piece in front of a pawn is mechanical; judging whether the blockade is worth its cost is not.

by_level.beginner: Put a piece right in front of their pawn so it cannot move. A knight is best at this — it still does its job from there.
by_level.intermediate: Blockade the pawn. Choose the blockader carefully: a knight loses nothing standing there, a queen loses almost everything.
by_level.advanced: Nimzowitsch's three requirements: effectiveness as a blocker, threats from the square, and elasticity. The blockading square is also a hole by construction, so it doubles as an outpost.
by_level.master: Restrain, blockade, destroy, in that order — and weigh the tying-down cost, which he states explicitly.

by_depth.short: A piece in front of the pawn stops it dead.
by_depth.normal: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch supplied the rationale for something masters already did by custom, and said so — his claim was the theory, not the practice. He sets three requirements on a blockading piece: effectiveness as a blocker, the threats it makes from the square, and elasticity to leave when needed. The third decides which piece should do it. He also notes that the blockading square tends to become a good square, because the pawn it blocks can never attack it — which makes blockade and outpost the same geometry from two sides. All of it sits inside the formula his primary text states verbatim: first restrain, then blockade, and finally destroy.

explanations.lesson: Stop a passed pawn with a knight if you can. And remember the blockade costs you a piece's freedom — make sure the pawn was worth it.

blockade.definition_short: Stopping an enemy pawn by placing a piece directly in front of it — ideally a knight, which loses nothing by standing there.
blockade.definition_long:
A piece parked immediately in front of an enemy pawn stops it dead. Nimzowitsch devoted a chapter to justifying what masters had done by instinct, and his framing survives intact.

He sets out what a blockading piece must offer: basic effectiveness as a blocker, the threats it can make FROM the blockading square, and elasticity — the ability to leave when needed. That third requirement is what decides which piece should do the job. A knight blockades ideally because it loses none of its power standing in front of a pawn and still radiates over squares beyond it. A queen is the worst blockader, because any minor piece attacking her forces the post to be abandoned.

He also notes the blockading square tends to BECOME a good square: because the pawn in front of it can never attack it, the blockade square is by construction a hole. That is why the blockade and the outpost are the same geometry seen from two sides.

The blockade sits inside his larger formula, which is in the primary text verbatim: 'First restrain, then blockade and finally destroy!' — restrain the pawn from advancing, blockade it so it cannot, then win it.

board-geometry.knowledge_type_note: Geometric facts about the board and the pieces' movement. They are true by construction, not by evidence, though this base has verified the one that people most often get wrong.

history.notes: Anonymous elementary knowledge; the rule of the square has no traced coinage.

board-geometry.engine_era_note: Unaffected. These are consequences of the rules and cannot be revised by analysis.

preconditions: A board
recognition.detector: isLight / legalMoves in lib/features.js and blind-chess.html
false_positive_traps: The rule of the square must be applied with the side to move in hand. This base holds a tablebase-proven pair where the identical position is a draw or a mate in 23 depending only on whose turn it is.
The rule of the square assumes a clear path: another pawn, or a king in the way, breaks it.
Colour-boundedness is a fact about bishops, not a claim that a bishop is limited — it is also why the pair is worth more than two of anything else.

typical_plans: Count whether a king is inside the square before racing
Use the free diagonal to approach two targets at once
Check the promotion square's colour against your bishop
tactical_consequences: A knight can never attack a piece that defends it
strategic_consequences: Colour complexes are permanent; a colour weakness cannot be repaired by a bishop that does not travel on it

exceptions: The rule of the square fails if the pawn's path is blocked, if it can be supported by its own king, or if the defending king's route is obstructed.
limitations: These are geometric facts and settle nothing evaluative on their own.
misconceptions: That the rule of the square is about distance. It is about the square, and about whose move it is.
That a knight can lose a tempo. It cannot: every knight move changes square colour, so returning takes an even number of moves.

by_level.beginner: A bishop never changes colour. A knight changes colour every move. And a king reaches a1 to h8 in seven moves, the same as a1 to a8.
by_level.intermediate: To see if a king catches a passed pawn, draw the square from the pawn to its promotion square — but check whose move it is first.
by_level.advanced: A knight needs an even number of moves to return to its square, so it can never gain a single tempo on a fixed target.
by_level.master: Colour complexes are permanent, and almost every proven draw a piece down in this base is a consequence of colour-boundedness.

by_depth.short: Bishops keep their colour, knights change it every move, and the king's diagonal is free.
by_depth.normal: The geometric facts: a bishop never leaves its starting colour, a knight changes square colour with every move (so it needs an even number of moves to come back), and a king crosses diagonally at no extra cost. The rule of the square follows from that last one — a king catches a passed pawn if it can step into the square between the pawn and its promotion square.
by_depth.deep: Consequences of how the pieces move, which a blindfold player must hold rather than look at. Colour-boundedness makes a single bishop a half-board piece and is behind every wrong-rook-pawn and opposite-coloured-bishop draw in this base. The knight's colour change means it can never gain a single tempo on a fixed target, and can never attack a piece that defends it. And the king's diagonal costing no more than its straight line gives the rule of the square — which carries a trap worth proving rather than asserting: with a white pawn on h5 and a black king on d5, the position is a draw with Black to move and a win in 23 with White to move. Same board, opposite results.

explanations.lesson: Count the square, then check whose move it is. The turn is worth a file.

board-geometry.definition_short: The fixed geometric facts of the board — colour-boundedness, the knight's colour change, and the fact that a king's diagonal path costs no more than a straight one.
board-geometry.definition_long:
Facts that follow from how the pieces move, and that a blindfold player has to hold rather than look at.

COLOUR-BOUNDEDNESS. A bishop never leaves the colour it starts on, which is why the bishop pair covers the whole board and a single bishop covers half of it. Every fortress, every wrong-rook-pawn draw and every opposite-coloured-bishop draw in this base is a consequence of this one fact.

THE KNIGHT ALWAYS CHANGES COLOUR. Every knight move goes from a light square to a dark one or back, so a knight needs an EVEN number of moves to return to its square and can never gain a single tempo on a fixed target. It also means a knight cannot attack a piece that is defending it, and — the practical corollary — that only another knight can attack a knight back without moving away.

THE KING'S DIAGONAL IS FREE. Because the king moves one square in any direction, going from a1 to h8 costs seven moves, exactly as going from a1 to a8 does. A king can therefore approach a target and do something else on the way at no cost, which is the mechanism behind many king-and-pawn endings that look like they must be lost.

THE RULE OF THE SQUARE follows from that: a king catches a passed pawn if it can step into the square whose corners are the pawn and its promotion square. It is the most useful geometric shortcut in chess and it carries a trap this base has proven. The rule depends on WHOSE MOVE IT IS. With a white pawn on h5 and a black king on d5, the position is a DRAW with Black to move and a WIN FOR WHITE IN 23 with White to move — the same position, the same square, opposite results, because the side to move effectively widens the square by a file.

board-vision.definition_short: Fluent knowledge of the board itself — where each square is, what colour it is, and how pieces travel between squares — held without needing to look.
board-vision.definition_long:
The foundation layer beneath blindfold play. Before a player can hold a POSITION without sight of the board, they need the BOARD without sight of it: which squares are light and which dark, which squares a knight on a given square reaches, which diagonal connects two squares.

THE STANDARD DRILL PROGRESSION is consistent across instructional sources: name the colour of a named square; trace a piece's route between two squares; follow a knight's path without a board; reconstruct a small position from brief exposure; then play out simple endgames unseen before attempting whole games. The KNIGHT'S TOUR — visiting all sixty-four squares in sixty-three legal knight moves — is the most-recommended single exercise, and it is very old; Murray traced tours to al-Adli ar-Rumi around 840 AD.

WHY IT PLAUSIBLY MATTERS is consistent with the research on representation. If what a blindfold player holds is relational rather than pictorial, then fluency in the relations — this square is dark, that knight reaches these squares — is exactly the substrate the representation is built on, and effort spent computing it is effort not spent on the position.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is that these drills improve playing strength. That claim is made confidently by instructional sources and this base has found no controlled study supporting it. The honest statement is that the drills train the specific skills they exercise, and that those skills are prerequisites for blindfold play.

building-a-bridge.knowledge_type_note: A specific winning procedure with a proven result in the position it applies to; not a heuristic.

attributions.note: Credited with describing the manoeuvre as 'building a bridge'. Second-hand attribution; not located in the My System text consulted for this project.

history.notes: The technique is much older than the name; only the name is attributed, and that at second hand.

building-a-bridge.engine_era_note: Tablebase-confirmed. Notably, the tablebase's own best move in the Lucena position is the bridge's first move, so the human procedure is also the objectively fastest.

preconditions: A Lucena position: rook and non-rook pawn on the seventh, attacking king in front, defending king cut off
indicators_for: The rook can reach the fourth rank
The defender's only resource is side checks
indicators_against: The pawn is a rook pawn
The defending rook prevents access to the bridge rank
The enemy king has not yet been driven back — interposing early allows perpetual check or stalemate
false_positive_traps: Interposing before the enemy king is driven back is the standard error and can allow perpetual check or a stalemate trick.
The fifth rank is the wrong bridge rank in general, and there is a known line where building there loses the rook to a capture and draws.

typical_plans: Rear check to drive the king back, rook to the fourth, king out under the shield
typical_moves: Rd1+ then Rd4!
Rb4 interposing against the checks
typical_piece_arrangements: Rook on the fourth rank as a shield
tactical_consequences: Ends the defender's checking resource
strategic_consequences: The standard conversion of a rook ending a pawn up

exceptions: Does not work with a rook pawn in general.
Fails if the defending rook denies the bridge rank, though other wins usually exist.
limitations: Applies to one specific position type; it is a procedure, not a principle.
misconceptions: That any rook move on the fourth rank builds a bridge. The order matters — drive the king back first.

examples.note: The Lucena position, which is where the technique lives. The bridge is the answer to one problem: the pawn cannot promote while the black rook checks from behind, and the white king cannot escape the checks by itself. The rook goes to the fourth rank, the king walks out, and the rook interposes on the fourth to end the checking - that is the bridge. Filed separately from `lucena-position` on purpose: the position is a named theoretical position, the bridge is the method, and this base keeps a method and the place it is used as two records.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 25 by the engine, and its first move is Rd1+ - the check that drives the king across and begins the bridge.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 15, mate in 41, and the tablebase's own first move is Rd1+. A technique is a claim that a position is winnable BY A METHOD, and the proof that it is winnable at all is the half a tablebase can supply. Read against `lucena-position`'s counterexample - the same method with a rook pawn, a proven DRAW - which is what makes this a claim about the method rather than about the material.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `the-bridge-needs-a-file-on-each-side`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A pawn one square from queening, the king in front of it, the enemy rook checking from behind, and a rook ready to come to the fourth rank. Every ingredient of the bridge is on the board. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The bridge is built by putting the rook on the fourth rank and then interposing it on the file BESIDE the pawn once the king walks out. A rook pawn has no file on one side, so there is nowhere to interpose and nowhere for the king to walk to. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0. This record's positive example is the same position with a knight pawn and is a PROVEN WIN in 41 whose first move is Rd1+ — the check that starts the bridge. The two boards differ by the file of one pawn and the file of one rook. A technique record is a claim that a position is winnable BY A METHOD, so the pair it needs is one where the method is unavailable rather than one where the material is different, and this is that pair.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, against this record's positive example - the same position with a knight pawn - at a PROVEN WIN in 41. The two boards differ by the file of one pawn.

by_level.beginner: Their rook keeps checking your king. Put your rook in the way so the checks stop, then walk your king out and promote.
by_level.intermediate: Building a bridge. Check their king back first, then put your rook on the fourth rank — it will block the side checks when they come.
by_level.advanced: The Lucena win. The fourth rank is chosen so the rook is far enough to shield and close enough for the king to step under.
by_level.master: Order matters: rear check, rook to the fourth, then walk. Interposing early invites perpetual check or a stalemate resource.

by_depth.short: Use the rook as a shield so the king can walk out.
by_depth.normal: Building a bridge: the defender's only resource is checking your king from the side, so you place your rook on the fourth rank where it can interpose, and the king walks out behind it while the pawn promotes.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch's name for the Lucena winning method, also called the umbrella technique. The procedure is a rear check to drive the defending king back, the rook to the fourth rank, then the king advancing while the defender checks, and the rook interposing at the right moment. The fourth rank is chosen deliberately — far enough to shield, close enough for the king to step under it. A bridge on the fifth is possible but inferior, and there is a known trap where building it prematurely loses the rook. Two conditions: drive the king back first, and it does not work with a rook pawn.

explanations.lesson: When their rook can check yours forever, stop trying to run from the checks and put your rook in the way instead.

beginner_words: block the checks with your rook

building-a-bridge.definition_short: The winning method in the Lucena position: interpose your rook on the fourth rank so it shields your king from side checks while the pawn promotes.
building-a-bridge.definition_long:
The defender's resource in a rook-and-pawn ending is checking the attacking king from the side indefinitely. Building a bridge removes it. The rook is placed on the fourth rank, and when the checks come the rook interposes on the checking line, blocking permanently — the king walks out under the shield and the pawn queens. Nimzowitsch named the manoeuvre; it is also called the umbrella technique, for obvious reasons.

The procedure: drive the defending king back with a rook check from the rear; drop the rook to the fourth rank; advance the king while the defender checks from the side; interpose the rook at the right moment.

The fourth rank is not arbitrary — far enough to shield the checks, close enough for the king to step under it. A bridge can also be built on the fifth, but it is worse, and there is a known trap where building on the fifth prematurely allows the defender to capture the rook and draw. Two other conditions: the enemy king must be pushed back FIRST, since interposing too early allows perpetual checks or stalemate tricks, and the method does not work with a rook pawn.

calculation.knowledge_type_note: A description of a skill and the advice attached to it, not a claim about positions.

attributions.note: The first systematic published attempt to describe how strong players calculate, whatever the standing of his particular prescription.
Established empirically that masters do not search more widely but generate better candidates.

history.notes: No coinage; the term is ordinary. The named contributions are to method rather than to vocabulary.

calculation.engine_era_note: Engines calculate in the way Kotov described and humans cannot, which sharpened rather than replaced the human advice: since exhaustive search is not available, everything depends on pruning well. Engine checking has also made it possible to audit published human analysis, generally unkindly.

preconditions: A position where concrete lines decide the choice of move
indicators_for: Forcing moves are available
Material or the king is at stake in the short term
indicators_against: A quiet position where no forcing line changes anything
false_positive_traps: A description of how a player thinks, not a feature of the position. It cannot be offered as the reason a move is good.
That a move requires calculation is not evidence that it is correct.

typical_plans: Examine checks, captures and threats before quiet moves
Scan shallowly to prune, then go deep on the line the position turns on
Evaluate the position at the end of each line rather than only counting material
Blunder-check the chosen move before playing it

exceptions: Many positions are decided by judgement and require almost no calculation.
In defence the emphasis shifts: pare the candidates down harder and examine the most critical first, since there is little point exploring suspect lines.
limitations: Exhaustive search is not available to a human at any level, so all human method is pruning.
This system cannot observe a player's calculation and so cannot assess it.
