by_level.beginner: Working out what happens: if I go there, they go there, then what? Start with checks and captures.
by_level.intermediate: Calculation. Look at forcing moves first, scan widely before going deep, and check the position at the end of the line.
by_level.advanced: All human calculation is pruning - the tree is far too big otherwise. The skill is which moves get looked at, not how many.
by_level.master: New ideas at the start of a variation are worth more than refinements at the end of it.

by_depth.short: Working out concrete lines and judging where they end.
by_depth.normal: Calculation: working out sequences of moves and evaluating the positions they lead to. Forcing moves - checks, captures and threats - come first, because they restrict the replies and so cost least to calculate.
by_depth.deep: The concrete half of chess thinking, and one governed everywhere by a limit worth stating plainly: with five plausible replies at each turn a tree has over fifteen thousand leaves after three moves each, which is nothing to a machine and impossible for a person. Every human method is therefore about pruning, and de Groot's finding is the evidence - masters do not search more widely than weaker players and may search less, differing in which moves they look at rather than how many. The advice the sources agree on follows from that: forcing moves first, breadth before depth, stop when further depth stops paying since ideas at the start of a line matter more than refinements at the end, evaluate at the leaves, and look again before committing.

explanations.hedge: Guidance about how to think, drawn from grandmaster testimony rather than controlled experiment. The ordering advice - forcing moves first, breadth before depth - is consistent across authors who disagree about much else, but how any individual should calculate depends on the position and on the player.
explanations.lesson: You cannot search the tree. You can only choose well what to look at.

beginner_words: if I go here, they go there

calculation.definition_short: Working out concrete sequences of moves and judging the positions they reach.
calculation.definition_long:
The concrete half of chess thinking, as against the judgement that decides what is worth calculating. The two are not rivals; calculation without judgement has nothing to aim at, and judgement without calculation is unverified.

THE ADVICE THE SOURCES AGREE ON, across authors who disagree about much else:
- FORCING MOVES FIRST. Checks, captures and threats restrict the opponent's replies, so they are cheapest to calculate and most likely to be decisive. Dvoretsky puts examining the most forcing line first; Tisdall recommends starting with the most direct.
- BREADTH BEFORE DEPTH. A shallow scan eliminates the clearly deficient far more cheaply than a full analysis of each. Nunn's objection to the alternative is that twenty minutes can be spent reaching a verdict a quick look would have reached immediately.
- DON'T CALCULATE FURTHER THAN YOU NEED. Dvoretsky's formulation is that new ideas at the START of a variation matter a good deal more than refinements at the end of it.
- KEEP ASSESSING. A variation is only worth what the position at its end is worth, so calculation without evaluation at the leaves produces nothing.
- LOOK AGAIN WITH FRESH EYES, and blunder-check before playing.

THE HUMAN LIMIT is the thing worth being honest about. A tree with five plausible replies at each turn has over fifteen thousand leaves after three moves each. That is nothing to a machine and impossible for a person, which is why every human method is fundamentally about PRUNING, and why de Groot's finding matters so much: masters do not search more widely than weaker players, and may search less. The difference is in which moves get looked at, not how many.

FOR A BLINDFOLD PLAYER the cost structure changes. Calculation and holding the position compete for the same limited resource, so the depth reachable without sight of the board is markedly shorter, and the research on interference suggests the vulnerable moment is while new information is being taken in.

candidate-moves.knowledge_type_note: A thinking technique, not a property of positions. Its first half is close to universally endorsed and its second half is close to universally rejected, which is why the two are kept apart here.

attributions.note: Introduced the candidate-moves technique and the tree of analysis in Think Like a Grandmaster. The book was written in the early 1950s; 1971 is the widely cited English edition.
Revised the technique, keeping the candidate list and rejecting the one-pass rule.
The principal critique of the tree of analysis, on efficiency and on the interaction between lines.

history.notes: Attribution to Kotov is secure and uncontested across every source consulted. The date carries a caveat: the book was written in the early 1950s and the commonly cited 1971 date is the English edition. Kotov's book was consulted only through secondary accounts.

development.note: Kotov formulates candidates plus the one-pass tree as a single method.
Tisdall, Nunn and Dvoretsky each reject the one-pass rule while keeping candidate generation.
Leitao shows Kotov's own worked analysis violating his method; the Chessable survey finds the revised form is the consensus.

candidate-moves.engine_era_note: The revision came mainly from human authors rather than from engines, and largely before engines dominated preparation. What engines added was the ability to check Kotov's own published analysis, which turned out to contain both missed candidates and a miscalculation - Leitao is careful to note that Kotov had no such tool available.

preconditions: A player choosing a move in a position with several plausible options
false_positive_traps: This is a technique for the player, not a property of the position, and must never be presented as an explanation of why a move is good.
The one-pass tree must not be taught as current best practice. Nunn, Dvoretsky, Tisdall and Leitao all reject it, and this base records the rejection as the consensus.

Some strong moves are unreachable by candidate generation at all. Nunn's example is a move that 'makes absolutely no sense except as part of the whole tactical operation' and so never enters a candidate list.

typical_plans: List the candidates before calculating anything
Include the opponent's candidate replies, not only your own moves
Scan shallowly to eliminate the clearly deficient, then go deep on the critical line
Re-examine the position with fresh eyes after analysing

exceptions: Positions with one forced line need no list; the tree is a single branch.
Nunn's goal-seeking case: moves that only make sense as part of a larger operation will not appear in any candidate list, and must be found another way.
Tisdall argues the candidate list should not be the primary task at all, and that leaning on an instinctive first choice engages intuition and starts the abstract assessment.
limitations: The evidence is grandmaster testimony and argument, not controlled experiment. The Chessable survey notes there was no prior scientific research on candidate moves specifically.
This system cannot observe a player's thinking and so cannot tell whether the technique is being used.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE. This record does have a positive - Reti-Capablanca move 18, where a world champion chose the worse of two candidates and the annotator calls the other 'obvious' - and an ambiguous one would have to be a position where it is unclear whether the concept applies. It is not clear what that would look like: enumerating candidates applies to every position without exception, so the concept is never in doubt and never informative on its own. That is a property of the concept rather than a gap in the evidence, and it is written here instead of being filled with a position that would not test anything.

NO REGISTERED FALSE-POSITIVE CASE, and a FEN is not the right instrument for one here. A case in tests/false_positive_cases.json is a POSITION where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is not, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This record's `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`: what it describes is something a player does rather than something a board contains, so there is no surface pattern for a position to carry and nothing for the system to decline. The conditions this record states are read and answered in `limitations` and in the trap audit instead. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item.
misconceptions: That Kotov's tree describes how strong players actually think. It does not, on the testimony of several grandmasters including one who checked Kotov's own analysis.
That revisiting a line is a lack of discipline. It is how the comparison between lines is made, and the ideas found in one line frequently belong in another.
That a longer candidate list is better. Breadth is for generating; the work is done by going deep on the critical one.

conflicts.resolution: Breadth and depth compete for the same clock. The resolution the sources converge on is sequencing rather than balance: be broad and shallow first to prune, then deep on the one line the position turns on.

examples.note: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924, move 18 - a position defined by having exactly two candidates and a world champion choosing the worse one. Keene: 'It is a mystery why Capablanca did not play the obvious 18...Ne6, fighting more directly for control of the centre.' Both moves develop the same knight; the difference is what they bear on. That is what makes this a candidate-moves example rather than a center-control one: the record is about ENUMERATING the moves worth looking at before comparing them, and the annotator's word for the move that was not played is 'obvious', which is the failure mode the record names.
examples.attributed_by: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia - corpus entry reti-capablanca-1924-18Ne6-center-control

engine.verdict_note: The engine's first choice is 18...Ne6, the move Keene says should have been played, at +0.80 on a multipv-3 search recorded in the corpus entry. Both candidates are legal, natural developing moves; the engine separates them and so did the annotator, independently and in the same direction.

by_level.beginner: Before you calculate, make a short list of the moves worth calculating - and do not just analyse the first one you thought of.
by_level.intermediate: Candidate moves. Your move can never be better than your list, so build the list first, and include your opponent's replies.
by_level.advanced: Generate, prune shallowly, then go deep on the critical line. Jumping between lines is how comparison works, whatever Kotov said.
by_level.master: Note the limit: moves that only make sense as part of a whole operation never enter a candidate list, and need goal-seeking instead.

by_depth.short: List the moves worth calculating before calculating.
by_depth.normal: Candidate moves: the short list of moves worth analysing, drawn up deliberately before any line is calculated deeply. The reason is simple - a move that never makes the list will never be played, however well the rest is analysed.
by_depth.deep: The most widely taught thinking technique in chess, and one where the sources agree on the idea and reject the original method. The idea is undisputed: fix the shortlist before calculating, extend it to subsequent moves and to the opponent's replies, and accept that the move played can never be better than the list it came from. The method is not: Kotov prescribed examining each branch exactly once and never returning, and Nunn, Dvoretsky, Tisdall and Leitao all reject it - as inefficient, and more seriously as blind to the interaction between lines, since an idea found in one variation often belongs in another and may even change the list. What survives is the structure rather than the discipline: generate, prune, deep-dive, verify.

explanations.hedge: The candidate-list idea is consensus; Kotov's one-pass tree is rejected by essentially every later authority, and this base follows the rejection.
explanations.lesson: Your move can only be as good as your list. Build the list first - then feel free to jump between lines.

avoid: never go back in a variation

candidate-moves.definition_short: The short list of moves worth calculating, drawn up deliberately before any line is analysed deeply.
candidate-moves.definition_long:
The most widely taught thinking technique in chess, and one where the sources agree on the idea and disagree sharply on the method.

THE IDEA, which nobody disputes: before calculating, fix a list of the moves worth calculating — typically two to four — rather than analysing whichever move occurred to you first. The justification is unanswerable. The quality of the move played can never exceed the quality of the list, because a move that never entered the shortlist will not be found however well the shortlist is analysed. Dvoretsky adds the extensions that matter most in practice: draw up candidates not only for your first move but for subsequent ones, and not only for yourself but FOR YOUR OPPONENT. This is also where de Groot's finding lands — masters do not search more widely than weaker players and may search less, but they generate the right moves to look at.

THE METHOD, which almost every later authority rejects: Kotov's tree of analysis prescribed examining each branch exactly ONCE, in order, never returning to a line already analysed. The objections converge. Nunn calls it extremely inefficient, since twenty minutes may be spent reaching a negative verdict a quick scan would have reached at once, and — the deeper point — it ignores the interaction between lines, because an idea discovered in one variation often applies in another, and may even change the candidate list itself. Dvoretsky: going down each branch once 'seems dubious', because we are not surveying possibilities but hunting for the strongest moves, and those do not always arrive on schedule. Leitao states flatly that no grandmaster calculates this way, and demonstrates it the hard way: Kotov's own showcase analysis misses candidate moves and its main line contains a miscalculation.

WHAT SURVIVES is the structure rather than the discipline: generate candidates, prune shallowly, go deep on the critical one, verify. The jumping between lines that Kotov forbade turns out to be how comparison works.

castling.definition_short: A single move of king and rook: the king moves two squares towards the rook, and that rook jumps to the square the king crossed.
castling.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 3.8.2: 'a move of the king and either rook of the same colour along the player's first rank, counting as a single move of the king and executed as follows: the king is transferred from its original square two squares towards the rook on its original square, then that rook is transferred to the square the king has just crossed.'

Art. 3.8.2.1 — the right is LOST permanently if the king has already moved, or with a rook that has already moved. Art. 3.8.2.2 — castling is prevented TEMPORARILY if the king's square, the square it crosses, or the square it lands on is attacked, or if any piece stands between king and rook.

The lost/prevented distinction is the part implementations most often get wrong. Moving the king and returning it does not restore the right; a check that passes does restore the possibility.

history.notes: Historical development of castling not yet researched for this record.

preconditions: King and the chosen rook are both on their original squares and neither has moved
No piece stands between them
The king is not in check, does not cross an attacked square, and does not land on one
indicators_for: Castling rights flag still set for that side and that rook
indicators_against: King or that rook has moved at any earlier point
King is currently in check
The crossed or destination square is attacked

exceptions: The ROOK may be attacked, and in queenside castling the b1/b8 square the rook crosses may be attacked — only the king's three squares matter.
Rights once lost never return, even if the piece goes back to its original square.
limitations: Affects position identity for repetition: Art. 9.2.3.2 — positions are not the same if a king had castling rights with a rook that has not moved but forfeited them after moving.
Reported for the MOVE, not for the rights. Almost every opening position has castling rights, and a concept true of almost every position is not news; a king moving two squares is.

by_level.beginner: Castling moves your king two squares towards a rook and hops that rook over to the other side — it tucks the king away and brings the rook into play in one move.
by_level.intermediate: Castling is legal only if neither piece has moved, the squares between are empty, and the king is not in, through, or into check. Note the rook may be attacked.
by_level.advanced: Art. 3.8.2. Distinguish rights lost permanently (3.8.2.1) from castling prevented temporarily (3.8.2.2); the latter can be restored.

by_depth.short: King two squares towards a rook; that rook jumps to the square the king crossed.
by_depth.normal: Castling: a single move of king and rook together. It is legal only when neither piece has moved before, nothing stands between them, the king is not in check, and neither the square it crosses nor the square it lands on is attacked.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 3.8.2, and the distinction the article draws is the one people lose: rights lost PERMANENTLY when the king or that rook has moved (3.8.2.1), against castling prevented TEMPORARILY by check or by an attacked square (3.8.2.2), which can be restored a move later. This base does not re-implement any of it — legalMoves() decides castling in a game and decides it here, which is why the three conditions this record states need no separate guard.

center-control.knowledge_type_note: A strategic principle rather than a rule, and one whose CONTENT was the subject of the most famous disagreement in chess theory. What is agreed is that the centre matters; what was disputed is what to do about it.

attributions.note: The centre as a goal dates back to Philidor per Britannica. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED against a primary text.
First master to teach the centre's importance systematically. Second-hand.
Hardened Steinitz's ideas into the dogmatic form the hypermoderns attacked; called 'the father of Classical dogma'.
Reframed the question as control versus occupation.

history.notes: The history is well attested in outline across three sources; no primary texts consulted, and the Philidor attribution in particular is a summary claim.
competing_claims: Classical: the centre should be occupied by pawns.
Hypermodern: the centre should be controlled by pieces, and occupation invites a target.
Modern synthesis: both are conditional on support and timing; the schools are complementary.

development.change: Central pawn occupation becomes doctrine.
Control distinguished from occupation; the pawn centre reframed as a potential target.
Both subordinated to the initiative; structures earlier called bad are accepted for dynamic play.
Treated as complementary; textbooks present hypermodernism as an extension of classical theory.

center-control.engine_era_note: Engines vindicate neither school and both. They are entirely comfortable ceding the centre for concrete compensation and entirely comfortable building a pawn centre when it can be supported — which is the synthesis stated computationally. What they do not support is either position held as a rule.

preconditions: The four central squares are contested
indicators_for: Pawns occupying central squares WITH pieces supporting them
Pieces attacking central squares from a distance, especially fianchettoed bishops
The opponent cannot advance in the centre without loosening something
You can switch wings faster than the opponent
indicators_against: A pawn centre that cannot advance and cannot be defended — a target, not an asset
Central occupation achieved at the cost of development
Central squares occupied by pieces that can be evicted with a pawn move
recognition.detector: lib/features.js: centralSquareControl(); lib/matchers.js: center-control (a structural arm and a move-based one)
false_positive_traps: Counting pawns on central squares measures occupation, not control. A fianchettoed bishop controls e4 without standing anywhere near it.
A big pawn centre is not automatically an advantage. Whether it is an asset or a target is a question of timing and support, and that cannot be read off the structure.
Central pieces are only strong while they cannot be kicked; a piece on a central square a pawn can attack is visiting.

A rook or queen whose line to a central square runs through one of its own men counts as an attacker and should not be read as a piece fighting for the square. The move-based arm measures pawns and minors for this reason.

typical_plans: Occupy with pawns and support them before expanding
Or influence from the flanks, invite the advance, and undermine it with a break
Control the centre before starting a wing attack
Meet a wing attack with a central counter-blow
typical_moves: e4 and d4 (classical)
Nf3, g3 and Bg2 (hypermodern)
...c5 and ...e5 undermining breaks
typical_pawn_structures: Broad pawn centre
Fianchetto structures conceding it
Closed and fixed centres
typical_piece_arrangements: Fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal
Knights on f3/c3 supporting central squares
tactical_consequences: A central break is the standard refutation of a premature wing attack
strategic_consequences: Determines whose wing attack is viable
A centre that is fixed makes flank play safe; a fluid one makes it dangerous

exceptions: Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.
In the endgame the logic inverts: the centre matters for king activity rather than for restriction.
limitations: The single most contested concept in the base: two respected schools gave opposite prescriptions and the resolution is 'it depends on support and timing', which is true and not very operational.

The detector measures control as ATTACKERS of d4/e4/d5/e5 and cannot tell WHICH central squares matter in a given structure. Measured against Reti-Capablanca 1924: it reports center-control for both 18...Ne6 - the move Keene names as fighting for the centre and the move Stockfish puts 0.39 clear - and 18...N6d7, the move actually played, which neither likes. Both raise Black's pawn-and-minor control by one, because moving the f6 knight unblocks the g7 bishop onto d4 and e5. The count is real and it is not doing the discriminating work the annotation does.

The RAW attacker count is worse than useless for a move: on 18...Ne6 it FALLS, from 7 to 6, because the arriving knight blocks a rook that was x-raying its own bishop. The move-based arm therefore measures pawns and minor pieces only, and this is recorded because it is the kind of thing that gets 'simplified' back.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the second trap - 'a big pawn centre is not automatically an advantage. Whether it is an asset or a target is a question of timing and support, and that cannot be read off the structure' - is honoured by never measuring occupation. The matcher counts ATTACKERS of the four central squares and says so; a big pawn centre with nothing behind it produces no report at all, because pawns standing on squares are not the measure.

MEASURED 2026-09-02 against the three unread indicators_against. 'Central squares occupied by pieces that can be evicted with a pawn move' is built and said out loud - `visiting` names them in the sentence. 'A pawn centre that cannot advance and cannot be defended - a target, not an asset' cannot arise as a false positive here, because this matcher never measures occupation: it counts ATTACKERS of the four central squares, so a pawn centre with nothing behind it produces no report at all. 'Central occupation achieved at the cost of development' is a judgement about the whole position and is not attempted.
misconceptions: That controlling the centre means putting pawns there.
That the hypermoderns thought the centre was unimportant — they thought it was too important to commit to early.
That one school won. Textbooks treat hypermodernism as an extension of classical theory, not a replacement.

conflicts.resolution: Not opposed but ordered: a wing attack is viable in proportion to central control. With a fixed or controlled centre the flank attack is safe; with a fluid centre the defender's central break refutes it. Establish the centre first.

by_level.beginner: Pieces in the middle of the board reach more squares. Fight for the centre — either by putting pawns there or by aiming pieces at it.
by_level.intermediate: Centre control. Note that controlling is not the same as occupying: a bishop on the long diagonal controls e4 without going near it, and a pawn there can be attacked.
by_level.advanced: Two schools gave opposite prescriptions and both were conditionally right. A pawn centre is an asset when supported and expanded on time, and a target when static.
by_level.master: Identify which kind of centre is on the board before choosing a plan, and remember the corollary: a wing attack is only as sound as your control of the middle.

by_depth.short: Whoever controls the middle can do more.
by_depth.normal: Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.
by_depth.deep: The most contested idea in chess theory. The classical school, from Steinitz and codified by Tarrasch, held that the centre should be occupied by pawns. The hypermoderns of the 1920s replied that occupation and control are different — a fianchettoed bishop influences central squares without committing to them, and a pawn centre you have committed to can be shot at. The modern position treats these as complementary rather than rival: a big pawn centre is simultaneously an asset and a liability, and which it becomes is a question of support and timing. Ceding the centre on principle against an opponent who supports theirs properly simply loses. One corollary survives both schools intact — a wing attack succeeds in proportion to your control of the centre.

explanations.lesson: Ask what kind of centre is on the board before you choose a plan, and never start a flank attack while your opponent can hit back in the middle.

beginner_words: pieces reach further from the centre
avoid: always occupy the centre with pawns

center-control.definition_short: Influence over the four central squares — which can be achieved by occupying them with pawns or by attacking them from a distance with pieces.
center-control.definition_long:
Pieces in the centre reach more squares, and a side that controls it can switch wings faster than an opponent who does not. Both are uncontroversial. What was fought over for a generation is whether control requires OCCUPATION.

THE CLASSICAL POSITION, from Steinitz and hardened into rules by Tarrasch: occupy the centre with pawns, ideally e4 and d4, and develop behind them. A pawn centre grants space, restricts the opponent and supports an attack.

THE HYPERMODERN REPLY, from the 1920s: occupation and control are different things. A fianchettoed bishop influences central squares from the flank WITHOUT committing to them, and a pawn centre you have committed to is a pawn centre your opponent can shoot at. So invite the occupation, then undermine it.

THE SYNTHESIS is not a compromise but a recognition that both are conditional. A large pawn centre is an asset and a liability at once, and which it turns out to be is a question of TIMING: supported properly and expanded at the right moment it crushes, and left static it becomes a fixed target. Equally, ceding the centre on principle against an opponent who supports it properly simply loses to the space advantage you invited. The honest summary found in the sources is that hypermodern play is 'correct as a correction and false as a dogma' — and modern textbooks accordingly present hypermodernism as an EXTENSION of classical theory rather than a replacement for it.

A standing corollary that survives both schools: a wing attack succeeds in proportion to your control of the centre. An attack on the flank launched while the opponent can strike back in the middle tends to rebound.

check.definition_short: A king is in check when it is attacked by one or more enemy pieces.
check.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 3.9.1: 'The king is said to be in check if it is attacked by one or more of the opponent's pieces, even if such pieces are constrained from moving to the square occupied by the king because they would then leave or place their own king in check.'

The trailing clause matters and is routinely misunderstood: a PINNED piece still gives check. Art. 3.9.2: 'No piece can be moved that will either expose the king of the same colour to check or leave that king in check.' There is no rule requiring check to be announced, and no rule making it compulsory to escape by any particular means.

preconditions: A king stands on a square attacked by an enemy piece
false_positive_traps: A check being available is not a reason to play it. Proven case: Ra7+ draws and Rg8+ loses in the same position.

exceptions: A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.
limitations: Check is not a threat to be evaluated; it is a state. Being in check is not itself bad, and giving check is not itself good.
Fires on 8.4% of the 788 shipped positions with the solution move supplied.

by_level.beginner: Your king is under attack. You must deal with it this move — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker.
by_level.intermediate: Check. Only three replies exist: move the king, interpose, or capture the checking piece. Against a double check only the king move is available.
by_level.advanced: Art. 3.9.1. Note that a pinned piece still gives check.

by_depth.short: The king is attacked and the attack must be answered this move.
by_depth.normal: Check: the king is attacked, and the side to move has exactly three ways to answer — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker. Nothing else is legal, which is why a check is the most forcing move there is.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 3.9.1. Check is decidable rather than judged: the move generator either produces a legal reply or it does not, and this base never second-guesses it. Two consequences are routinely missed. A PINNED piece still gives check, because the pin is about a line to its own king and not about what it attacks. And forcing is not the same as good: this base holds a proven position, the Vancura, where one check draws and another loses by force, sixty-seven moves apart in result.

checkmate.knowledge_type_note: Official rule, and the game's objective.
checkmate.definition_short: The king is in check and no legal move removes the check. The game ends immediately.
checkmate.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 5.1.1: 'The game is won by the player who has checkmated his/her opponent's king. This immediately ends the game, provided that the move producing the checkmate position was in accordance with Article 3 and Articles 4.2 – 4.7.'

Checkmate takes precedence over the automatic-draw provisions: Art. 9.6.2 ends with 'If the last move resulted in checkmate, that shall take precedence' — so a move that both completes 75 moves without capture or pawn move AND delivers mate is a win, not a draw.

preconditions: The side to move is in check
The side to move has no legal move

by_level.beginner: The king is attacked and there is no way out. The game is over.
by_level.intermediate: Checkmate ends the game immediately.
by_level.advanced: Art. 5.1.1. Mate takes precedence over the automatic draw in Art. 9.6.2.

by_depth.short: The king is in check and no legal move removes it. The game ends at once.
by_depth.normal: Checkmate: the king is attacked and every legal reply still leaves it attacked, so there are no legal moves at all. The game ends immediately — there is no claim to make and no agreement to reach.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 5.1.1. The test is the conjunction of two things the move generator answers directly: the king is in check, and the list of legal moves is empty. Neither half alone is mate — the same empty list without check is stalemate and a draw, and this base's two examples are built one square apart to make that visible. Mate also takes precedence over the automatic draw of Art. 9.6.2, so a move that reaches the 75-move limit AND mates is mate.

chess-terminology.knowledge_type_note: A meta-record about how this base handles naming, and why the distinction between a name and a description is enforced structurally.

history.notes: A meta-record about this base's own practice; no external history.

chess-terminology.engine_era_note: Engines name nothing, which is precisely why the naming problem is the human half of the work and cannot be delegated.

preconditions: A concept is about to be named for a reader
false_positive_traps: A descriptive phrase must never be presented as an established term. The schema records which is which precisely so this cannot happen by accident.

Prefer describing what is happening over naming it wrongly

limitations: Name status is a judgement from the sources consulted, and a term rated descriptive here may be standard in a literature this base has not read.
The base's research is English-language, which will under-represent terms established elsewhere.

NO REGISTERED FALSE-POSITIVE CASE, because this record is about the BASE rather than about boards. It is an index over other concepts, and the conditions it states are conditions on how this system names and files things - not patterns a position can exhibit. A false-positive case here would have to be a mis-filed concept rather than a mistaken reading of a board, and that is what tools/audit.py and tools/validate_kb.py check, on every record, on every run. misconceptions: That every chess idea has a name. Many do not, and inventing one is worse than describing the idea.
That a term appearing in many articles makes it established. Several widely repeated terms have no canonical definition behind them.

by_level.beginner: Some chess ideas have proper names and some do not — and using the wrong name is worse than using none.
by_level.intermediate: Every concept here records whether its name is established, common, contested, or just our description.
by_level.advanced: Research names concepts and the engine validates moves; neither does the other's job, and no concept is created because a detector wanted a label.
by_level.master: Five motifs are deliberately unclaimed because every cheap test for them fires where they are not true.

by_depth.short: Whether a term is a real chess name or just a description.
by_depth.normal: Chess vocabulary is inconsistent and full of terms that sound official and are not. Every concept here declares whether its name is established, common usage, contested, or a description of this base's own — because the label is what a learner is being taught to see, and a wrong one teaches a category that does not exist.
by_depth.deep: The naming problem is the human half of this work and cannot be delegated, since engines name nothing. So name status is a structural field rather than a note: established, common usage, descriptive phrase, or contested. The rule that follows is that no concept is ever created because a detector needed a label — the standing example is a puzzle-pipeline tag meaning 'a quiet move with no motif', which is not a chess term and gets no record. Five motifs are deliberately unclaimed for the same reason: every cheap test for deflection, decoy, overloading, interference and double attack fires where they are not true, and a wrong label is worse than a missing one.

explanations.lesson: If you cannot name it correctly, describe it. A wrong name teaches a category that does not exist.

chess-terminology.definition_short: The difference between a recognised chess NAME and a description of what is happening — and the rule that this system never invents the former.
chess-terminology.definition_long:
Chess vocabulary is inconsistent, unevenly attested, and full of terms that sound official and are not. That matters here more than it would in a book, because the label is the thing a learner is being taught to see: a wrong name is worse than no name, since it teaches a category that does not exist.

SO EVERY CONCEPT DECLARES ITS NAME STATUS, and the values are enforced by the schema:
- ESTABLISHED-NAME — sources support this as a recognised term (fork, zugzwang, Lucena position).
- COMMON-USAGE — widely used, without a canonical definition behind it.
- DESCRIPTIVE-PHRASE — this base's own words for something real that has no agreed name. It must never be presented to a reader as established terminology.
- CONTESTED — sources disagree about the name or about what it covers.

THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS: research names concepts; the engine validates moves; and neither may be used for the other's job. A concept is never created because a detector needed a label. The clearest instance is the puzzle generator's tag `positionalTactic`, which is not a chess term at all but the pipeline's word for 'a quiet move with no motif tag'. This base explicitly refuses to create a concept for it and instead maps such moves onto the things they actually are — prophylaxis, restriction, improving the worst piece.

AND FIVE MOTIFS ARE DELIBERATELY UNCLAIMED: deflection, decoy, overloading, interference and double attack. Every cheap test for them fires where they are not true, and a wrong label is worse than a missing one because the label is precisely what the player is learning to recognise. The puzzle generator reached the same conclusion independently, which is the closest thing to corroboration available.

NAMES ALSO DRIFT AND MISATTRIBUTE. The Lucena position is not in Lucena's book; 'the best way to refute a gambit is to accept it' drifts between 'gambit' and 'sacrifice' across sources and may not be Steinitz's; the worst-piece rule carries four different names. Each is recorded with its trail rather than tidied.

chunking.knowledge_type_note: An experimental result about human memory, with a measured mechanism.

attributions.person: William G. Chase and Herbert A. Simon
attributions.note: Proposed the chunking theory of chess memory and measured the chunk relations.

attributions.person: Fernand Gobet and Herbert A. Simon
attributions.note: Template theory, revising chunking to account for faster encoding into long-term memory and for higher-level knowledge structures.

history.notes: The random-position control is due to Chase and Simon (1973); the underlying recall finding is de Groot's (1946/1965). Chase and Simon credit Hans Berliner as a subject. The chunking account rests in turn on Miller's short-term memory limit.

development.note: De Groot's recall task: masters reconstruct positions almost perfectly after five seconds.
Chase and Simon add the random-position control, isolating meaning as the variable.
Chunking criticised for underestimating encoding speed into long-term memory and for saying little about high-level structures; template theory follows.

chunking.engine_era_note: Not affected by engine analysis; a claim about human cognition.

preconditions: A human player is recalling or holding a position
false_positive_traps: A fact about players, not positions. It cannot be reported as a feature of a move.
Chunking explains recall of MEANINGFUL positions only. The master advantage is zero on random arrangements, and claiming otherwise inverts the central finding.

strategic_consequences: Grouping pieces by attack, defence, proximity or type is how a position should be described to someone holding it in memory

exceptions: The advantage does not extend to randomly arranged positions, which is the finding that makes the theory testable.
Chunking alone underestimates how fast experts encode into long-term memory, which is why template theory was needed.
limitations: The theory describes recall and recognition; it is a weaker account of planning and high-level reasoning.
Chunk counts and sizes are estimates from small numbers of subjects.

NO REGISTERED FALSE-POSITIVE CASE, and a FEN is not the right instrument for one here. A case in tests/false_positive_cases.json is a POSITION where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is not, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This record's `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`: what it describes is something a player does rather than something a board contains, so there is no surface pattern for a position to carry and nothing for the system to decline. The conditions this record states are read and answered in `limitations` and in the trap audit instead. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item.
misconceptions: That masters have better memories. On random positions they do not.
That a chunk is a fixed opening pattern. It is any group of pieces bound by chess relations.

by_level.beginner: Strong players remember a position as a few groups of pieces that belong together, not as thirty separate pieces.
by_level.intermediate: Chunking. It is why a master recalls a real position almost perfectly but does no better than a beginner on a random one.
by_level.advanced: About five chunks in short-term memory, each holding four or five pieces bound by attack, defence, proximity, or common colour and type.
by_level.master: Recurring chunks become templates with a stable core and variable slots, which is what makes several boards at once tractable.

by_depth.short: Positions are remembered as a few groups, not many pieces.
by_depth.normal: Chunking: skilled players store a position as a small number of groups of related pieces rather than as individual pieces. This is why a master reconstructs a real position almost perfectly after five seconds and does no better than a novice when the same pieces are scattered at random.
by_depth.deep: The mechanism behind chess memory, established by a genuinely controlled experiment: de Groot showed masters reconstruct positions after five seconds, and Chase and Simon added the control that isolates the cause - the same pieces arranged randomly, on which the master advantage disappears completely. Masters are therefore under the same memory limits as everyone else, and the arithmetic follows: about five chunks holding twenty or more pieces means four or five pieces per chunk, bound by attack, defence, proximity, common colour and common type. The blindfold evidence sharpens it further, since dictated games are recalled almost perfectly when the moves are legal - even when random - and collapse only when they are illegal.

explanations.lesson: Meaning is what makes a position memorable. Scatter the same pieces at random and expertise buys nothing.

beginner_words: groups of pieces that belong together

chunking.definition_short: Skilled players store positions as a few groups of related pieces rather than as many individual pieces, which is why expertise does not transfer to random positions.
chunking.definition_long:
The mechanism behind chess memory, and the reason blindfold play is possible at all.

THE CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT that established it is a model of the method this base tries to follow. De Groot found masters could reconstruct a position almost perfectly after five seconds' viewing, while weaker players managed a few pieces. That alone does not distinguish chess skill from general memory, so Chase and Simon added the control: the SAME pieces arranged RANDOMLY. On random positions the master's advantage disappears entirely. One variable changed — whether the arrangement was meaningful — and the effect vanished with it. Masters are bound by the same short-term memory limits as everyone else.

THE ARITHMETIC. If a player holds around five chunks in short-term memory yet reconstructs twenty or more pieces, each chunk must carry four or five pieces in a single relational structure. Chase and Simon measured which relations bind pieces into a chunk: ATTACK, DEFENCE, PROXIMITY, COMMON COLOUR and COMMON TYPE. There was also evidence of more abstract grouping, notably pieces converging on the enemy king being held together as one attacking unit.

THE BLINDFOLD EVIDENCE. When games are dictated move by move, masters recall almost perfectly if the moves come from a real game — and also if the moves are random but LEGAL. Performance collapses only when the moves are illegal. Legality, not familiarity, is doing much of the work: illegal sequences cannot be absorbed into the structures a player already has.

TEMPLATE THEORY refined this. Frequently recurring chunks develop into templates with a stable core and variable slots, which is why the opening position and familiar opening positions are held so cheaply, and why templates can be linked to one another and to moves.

classical-school.knowledge_type_note: A historical school. Its claims were teaching principles of their era; several were later shown to be overstated, and the record hedges accordingly.

attributions.note: The first systematic positional theory, set out in The Modern Chess Instructor. Well attested; the primary text has been consulted for the 'hole' passage.
Codified Steinitz's ideas into rules; described as 'the father of Classical dogma'. Second-hand.
Summarised Steinitz's theory in three principles in a newspaper article; quoted by Winter.

history.notes: Better founded than most historical entries here, because Steinitz's own text was consulted directly for this project's `hole` record and Winter's Chess Notes were used for the Lasker summary. The Tarrasch half is second-hand.

development.change: Games decided by sacrificial attack; positional features not systematically evaluated.
Positional theory established: weak points, accumulation, attack only with an advantage.
Codified into rules — the form the hypermoderns attacked.
The dogmatic form is corrected; the evaluation framework survives and remains the basis of positional chess.

classical-school.engine_era_note: Steinitz's evaluative framework is essentially what engine evaluation functions encode — pawn structure, square control, king safety, piece quality. Tarrasch's dogmatic form does not survive: engines accept doubled pawns, cede the centre, and trade good bishops for knights whenever concrete play justifies it.

preconditions: A plan built on accumulating durable positional features rather than on immediate tactics
indicators_for: Play directed at fixed weaknesses
Central pawn occupation with pieces developed behind it
Refusal to attack before an advantage exists
indicators_against: The plan depends on a concrete tactical justification rather than a static feature
false_positive_traps: Do not conflate Steinitz with Tarrasch. Steinitz's evaluation framework survived; Tarrasch's dogmatic rules did not, and the hypermodern attack was aimed at the second.
The school was called 'Modern' in its own time, which makes contemporary quotations easy to misread.

typical_plans: Identify the opponent's durable weaknesses and play against them
Accumulate small advantages rather than seeking a knockout
Occupy the centre and develop behind it
typical_moves: 1.e4 and 1.d4 with quick development
typical_pawn_structures: Broad supported pawn centre
strategic_consequences: Provides the evaluative vocabulary nearly all later theory is written in

exceptions: Tarrasch's dogmatic form is widely and correctly broken; the underlying evaluation framework is not.
'Do not attack without an advantage' remains sound, but 'advantage' turned out to include dynamic factors the classical school undervalued.
limitations: A historical school, so it is context for other concepts rather than a technique to apply.
misconceptions: That the classical school was refuted. Its evaluation framework is the basis of modern positional chess and of engine evaluation.
That Steinitz and Tarrasch held the same views with the same rigidity.
That 'classical' was what they called themselves — they were the Modern school.

examples.note: Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz 1908, 9.Nxc6 - the doctrine's two halves in one move. EVALUATION: the trade hands Black a doubled isolated c-pawn beside an already weak d-pawn, which are durable static features of exactly the kind Steinitz taught to identify. TIMING: nothing is attacked for another fifteen moves; Rubinstein manoeuvres until the second weakness is fixed, which is the 'you may only attack when you have earned the right' half. The annotation is quoted in the corpus: 'The critical moment comes at move 9 when Rubinstein plays 9.Nxc6!, trading the knight to give Black a doubled, isolated c-pawn. Black now has two problems.' This base already carries this game as the canonical `two-weaknesses` position; it is filed here for the method rather than for the motif.
examples.attributed_by: corpus entry rubinstein-salwe-1908-9Nxc6-two-weaknesses

engine.verdict_note: +0.50, and the engine's own first move IS 9.Nxc6. A classical accumulation is worth about half a pawn at the moment it is created, which is the honest size of the thing: the doctrine is about what is durable, not about what is decisive, and the game took another forty moves.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `the-classical-prescription-followed-exactly`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White has four pawns abreast in the centre on c4, d4, e5 and f4 and has spent every move building them. Occupy the centre with pawns is the classical instruction, followed to the letter. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The doctrine has two halves and this is only the first. Steinitz's other half is TIMING — you may attack, or commit, only when you have earned the right — and White has developed one piece. This record's own definition says both halves 'are still the base of the game'; a pawn centre built ahead of the pieces is the first half practised without the second. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Letelier-Fischer, Leipzig 1960. The API reports `center-control` for White — which is true, White does control more of it — and does not report the classical school, which has no matcher and should not. Stockfish 18 at depth 24: -0.10, level, with the centre complete and nothing gained; Fischer answered with ...d6 and ...f6 and won in twenty-three. The annotation names the mechanism: 'when central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target'. The same position is `historical-principles`' positive example, a rule caught losing its condition, and `pawn-storm`'s counterexample.

ambiguous_examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein, Berlin 1928, 15...d4 - Rubinstein voluntarily accepting an isolated queen pawn, 'confident that its central control is worth the long-term weakness'. This is the classical doctrine arguing with itself. Steinitz's evaluation half says a durable structural weakness is an asset for the opponent and should be avoided; the same school's teaching on the centre says central control is worth paying for. One of the greatest classical players chose the second reading against the first, in a game he lost to the most classical player of all. Filed as ambiguous because the doctrine covers the move twice and points opposite ways, and the engine is only partly on Rubinstein's side.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-15d4-static-vs-dynamic

engine.verdict_note: The engine's first choice is a different move at +0.09 - level - and the disagreement is the informative part, which is why the corpus entry files it as partial agreement rather than as support. The isolated pawn Rubinstein took on is neither refuted nor endorsed at depth 22.

by_level.beginner: The idea that chess is won by building up small lasting advantages rather than by attacking straight away.
by_level.intermediate: The classical school: evaluate the position's durable features, accumulate them, and attack only once you have an advantage.
by_level.advanced: Steinitz's framework plus Tarrasch's codification. The first survived, the second was corrected by the hypermoderns.
by_level.master: The vocabulary nearly all later theory is written in. Note the distinction between Steinitz's evaluative claims and Tarrasch's prescriptive ones when reading period sources.

by_depth.short: Build small advantages; attack only when you have earned it.
by_depth.normal: The classical school, from Steinitz and codified by Tarrasch: positions have durable features that can be identified and accumulated, and an attack must be justified by an advantage you already hold.
by_depth.deep: Steinitz was the first player to demonstrate systematic positional understanding, replacing the Romantic style with an evaluative one. Two halves: positions have durable features — weak squares, pawn weaknesses, good and bad bishops — that can be accumulated; and one must not attack without a tangible advantage, but should when one exists. Lasker compressed it to three principles: the initial position is balanced, do not attack without an advantage, attack the weak points. Tarrasch turned this into teachable rules, and it was that dogmatic form the hypermoderns attacked rather than Steinitz himself. The evaluation framework survived intact and is the basis of most positional vocabulary — and, recognisably, of engine evaluation functions.

explanations.hedge: A historical school. Its evaluative framework survives essentially unchanged, but its prescriptive form — particularly Tarrasch's — has well-known exceptions and should not be quoted as law.
explanations.lesson: Steinitz's question is still the right one to start with: what are the durable features of this position, and which of them can I play against?

classical-school.definition_short: Steinitz's positional doctrine, codified by Tarrasch: accumulate small static advantages, occupy the centre with pawns, and attack only when you have earned the right.
classical-school.definition_long:
The school that replaced the Romantic style of Anderssen and Blackburne, whose games were decided by sacrificial attack. Steinitz was the first player to demonstrate systematic positional understanding, and his doctrine has two halves that are still the base of the game.

First, EVALUATION: positions have durable features — pawn weaknesses, weak squares, good and bad bishops, holes — which can be identified and accumulated. Second, TIMING: you may not attack without a tangible advantage in position, and if you have one you are more or less obliged to. Lasker summarised the theory in three principles: the initial position is balanced; do not attack without an advantage; attack the weak points.

Steinitz also held the striking view that with best play a draw is the legitimate result — a claim that reads as unremarkable now and was radical then.

Tarrasch codified all this into teachable rules, and that codification is what the hypermoderns attacked. The distinction matters: Steinitz's evaluation framework survived essentially intact and is the basis of most of the concepts in this knowledge base. What was overturned was Tarrasch's DOGMATIC form of it — that the centre must be occupied by pawns, that certain structures are simply bad, that the rules admit few exceptions.

Confusingly, this school was called 'the Modern school' at the time. It is now the classical one.

clearance.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Detection requires reasoning about what the VACATED square enables, so it is heuristic in practice.
clearance.definition_short: Vacating a square or line — often by sacrificing the piece occupying it — so a friendly piece can use it.
clearance.definition_long:
The opposite of interference: instead of blocking an enemy line you clear your own. A piece moves, or is given away, purely to empty a square, file, rank or diagonal that another friendly piece needs. Informant theme c; ECM 'Space Clearance'.

Clearance is usually recognised by the moving piece going somewhere pointless or losing itself — the value is entirely in the vacated square, and normal material reasoning about the moving piece is misleading.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly unit occupies a square or line another friendly unit needs
That unit has a move, possibly a sacrifice, that vacates it
indicators_for: The vacated square gives a decisive check, mate or fork
The clearing move is forcing, so the opponent has no time to reorganise
indicators_against: The vacated square is covered by the defender
The clearance is too slow and the defender consolidates

typical_plans: Look for your own piece standing on the square or line that another piece wants, and price the move that empties it
Count the tempo: a clearance is only sound if the follow-up is forcing, because the vacated square is worth nothing on the opponent's move
In endgames, clear a queening square or the file in front of a passed pawn rather than a diagonal
typical_moves: A minor piece stepping off a long diagonal with check, so the queen behind it arrives with the opponent still answering
A rook giving itself up on the back rank so a pawn can promote
A knight jumping to a square where it is taken, purely to unblock a file
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen and bishop on one diagonal with a friendly piece between them
Doubled rooks with a friendly minor on the file in front
tactical_consequences: The vacating move is usually a sacrifice, so material counting about it is misleading by design
Clearance and interference are the same geometry read from opposite sides: one empties a line of yours, the other fills a line of theirs
strategic_consequences: Rarely a strategic idea. Clearance is almost always a one-move tactical device inside a forced line

exceptions: A clearance sacrifice fails if the follow-up is a tempo too slow — the whole idea depends on forcing continuations.
Clearing a line for a piece that is then driven off achieves nothing; the arriving piece must be able to stay.
A clearance that also opens a line towards your own king is a different move from the one you calculated.
limitations: NO VERIFIED POSITION HAS BEEN BUILT FOR THIS RECORD, and that is recorded rather than filled. Three constructions were tried and thrown away: each needed the vacating move to come WITH TEMPO, and a minimal position with a queen, a blocking piece and a mating square either had no checking square for the blocker to leave on, or was already mate without the clearance. A wrong example of a motif is worse than none, because the label is the thing the reader is learning to see. UPDATE: a verified position now exists - 17...d4 in the position on this record, +6.37 against +0.40 at depth 28 - and it was FOUND rather than constructed. That is the lesson of the three failures: the constructions failed because a clearance needs the vacating move to come with tempo and a hand-built minimal position rarely has one, and a real game has as many as you like if you can state the geometry precisely enough to search for it.

There is deliberately no matcher. Clearance is a claim about what the VACATED square is then used for, which is a property of the continuation and not of the move, and this base does not read continuations at the board.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and the reason is the order of the work rather than a shortage of positions. This record has no POSITIVE example either, and an ambiguous example is a position where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - which cannot be written before there is an agreed instance of the concept being present at all. The four motifs in this base that lack a positive - `clearance`, `decoy`, `deflection`, `interference` - lack it for reasons written on each record, and the ambiguous rung waits on that. Writing one first would be asserting a doubtful instance of something this base has not yet shown a clear instance of. UPDATE: the positive example now exists, so the reason given here - that an ambiguous example cannot be written before there is an agreed instance of the concept being present at all - no longer holds. The ambiguous example is outstanding work, not blocked work.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Alekhine-Nimzowitsch, St Petersburg 1914, 42.Bc4, above. The reason given here was right about the scan and wrong about the games: a concept with no detector cannot be nominated by a scan that reads the API, but the geometry is decidable without one, and tools/mine_master_motifs.js asks it of 2.8 million positions from replayed master games directly.

examples.note:
THE FIRST VERIFIED POSITION ON THIS RECORD. Three earlier constructions were tried by hand and thrown away - the limitation above records why - and this one was not constructed at all. It was found by asking the record's own sentence as a geometric question of every ply of all 788 shipped solutions: does a piece of ours leave a square, land where it is simply lost, give no check, and open a line that one of our own line pieces did not have?

17...d4 is that move. The bishop on e6 looks down the a2-g8 diagonal and its own pawn on d5 is in the way; the pawn steps off and the bishop hits the queen on b3. The pawn cannot be kept - exd4 wins it - and that is the point rather than an objection: the record says clearance is 'usually recognised by the moving piece going somewhere pointless or losing itself, the value is entirely in the vacated square', and normal material reasoning about the pawn is exactly the reasoning that misses the move.

Stockfish 18 at depth 28 with three lines: +6.37 for d4, +0.40 and +0.37 for the next two. A gap of 597 centipawns between winning and level. That number is what makes this a teaching position rather than an illustration - the clearance is not a nicer way to win a won game, it is the whole of the difference between winning and not.

WHAT IT IS NOT. The move is not a discovered check and not a discovered attack: it opens a line for the bishop but the pawn itself is not moving off a line to the king, and the page's own findMotifs() tags nothing here. That distinction is the reason this record exists beside `discovered-attack`, and the reason the scan that found it refuses any candidate whose move gives check.

THE MASTER-GAME RUNG, and a different job from the puzzle position on this record. That one is sharp - the clearance is the whole difference between winning and level. This one is real: Alekhine played it against Nimzowitsch, and it is here because a concept whose only evidence is a puzzle has never been shown to occur in a game.

42.Bc4 takes the bishop off d5 so the rook on d2 looks straight down the file at the rook on d8, and the c6 pawn - one square from queening, with d8 the square that stops it - is what makes the file matter. The bishop is not thrown away here; it goes to c4 where the black rook can take it, and after 42...Rxc4 43.Rd8 the pawn goes through.

Stockfish 18 at depth 30 with three lines is honest about it and so is this note: 42.Bc4 is the THIRD choice at +5.17, behind two quiet king moves at +5.31. All three win. The clearance is not the only road and the card must not say it was - what it is, is the road a world champion took, in a position where the geometry this record describes is exactly what is on the board.

Found by tools/mine_master_motifs.js, which replays every game through the page's own move generator and asks the record's own sentence as a geometric question. 35,648 games replayed, 492 rejected as unplayable and skipped rather than patched.
