counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-line-cleared-to-nowhere`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The rook on d2 steps aside and the rook on d1 behind it is left with a clear file. Vacating a square so a friendly piece can use the line is the concept, word for word. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The line arrives nowhere. The d-file dead-ends at White's own pawn on d4, which is rammed against d5 and cannot move. Clearance is 'usually recognised by the moving piece going somewhere pointless or losing itself — the value is entirely in the vacated square', and here the vacated square is worth nothing, so all that is left is the pointless move. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `worst-placed-piece` at low confidence — the rook does get more scope on a2 — and nothing about clearance, which has no matcher. The same board is `battery`'s registered false-positive case for the same underlying reason: two line pieces on a file that arrives at their own rammed pawn combine nothing, whether they stay stacked or unstack. Stockfish at depth 26 in that entry plays Ra1, taking the front rook OFF the file, which is the engine agreeing that the file is worthless from the other direction.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 5, and the engine's own first move takes the front rook OFF the d-file. That is the strongest available statement that the file was worth nothing: the vacated square a clearance would create is on a line that dead-ends at White's own rammed pawn, and the engine abandons the line rather than clearing it.

by_level.beginner: This gets a piece out of the way so another one can use the square.
by_level.intermediate: Clearance: the point is the square that is emptied, not the piece that moves.
by_level.advanced: Clearance / space clearance (Informant theme c). Judge the moving piece by the square it vacates, not by where it lands.

by_depth.short: Getting a piece out of the way so another can use the square or line.
by_depth.normal: Clearance: a piece moves, or is given away, purely to empty a square, file, rank or diagonal that a friendly piece needs. The moving piece often goes somewhere pointless or loses itself — the value is entirely in what it vacated.
by_depth.deep: The opposite of interference: instead of blocking an enemy line you clear your own. Informant theme c. Normal material reasoning about the moving piece is misleading by design, which is why the motif is hard to see and easy to misdescribe. Two conditions decide whether it works. The vacating move must come WITH TEMPO — a check or a capture — because a vacated square is worth nothing on the opponent's move; and the arriving piece must be able to stay, since clearing a line for a piece that is then driven off achieves nothing.

compensation.knowledge_type_note: A claim about a position's balance that is directly measurable, since an evaluation already nets material against everything else.

history.notes: General evaluative vocabulary with no single coinage traced. The three-tempi-per-pawn yardstick is described by its own sources as something that 'used to be said', with Wikipedia adding that it is unclear how useful the maxim is - so it is recorded as folklore of uncertain provenance rather than as a result.

compensation.engine_era_note: The concept became directly measurable. Where compensation was once a matter of judgement expressed in symbols, an evaluation now states the net balance, which is what allowed the measurements recorded here. What engines do not supply is the DURABILITY of the compensation, which still has to be reasoned about.

preconditions: One side is materially behind
That side holds identifiable non-material assets
indicators_for: A development lead measured in moves still needed, not moves already made
Open files or diagonals aimed at the enemy king
The enemy king unable to castle
Lasting structural damage in the opponent's camp
The opponent's pieces tied to defending the extra material
indicators_against: The only asset is tempi, and the opponent is close to finishing development
The opponent can return the material to defuse the position
Queens are off and the position has simplified
false_positive_traps: Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse.
Counting developed pieces overstates a development lead. Count the moves each side still needs.
An evaluation near zero while a pawn down means full compensation NOW; it says nothing about whether it survives the next ten moves.

typical_plans: Convert an expiring lead into a permanent asset before it runs out
Force the opponent to spend moves untangling rather than developing
As the defender, return the material at the moment it completes development or forces a trade
typical_pawn_structures: Structures damaged by the capture, such as doubled or isolated pawns
typical_piece_arrangements: Rooks on lines opened by the sacrifice
An enemy king still in the centre
tactical_consequences: Threats force defensive replies, which buys further time and compounds the lead
strategic_consequences: If the compensation expires unused, the material deficit is simply a lost endgame

exceptions: Compensation of the structural kind - the Benko Gambit is the standard case - does not expire and can persist into the endgame, so the deadline reasoning does not apply to it.
Where the material given is more than a pawn, tempo compensation alone is rarely enough.
limitations: An engine evaluation states whether compensation is currently adequate; it does not say how durable it is, which is the question a human most needs answered.
The three-tempi yardstick is folklore hedged by its own sources and should not be used as a calculation.

The written sources for this concept are encyclopedia and club-level instruction rather than primary texts, so the source confidence is medium. The quantitative claims here do not rest on them - they rest on this base's own controlled engine measurements.
misconceptions: That compensation means attacking chances. Structural damage and the bishop pair are compensation too, and they last longer.
That the defender should hold the extra material. The standard technique is to return it at the right moment.
That a gambit's name tells you whether compensation exists. It has to be measured.

conflicts.resolution: These are the two halves of one evaluation and do not really conflict: material counts the deficit, compensation counts what was bought with it, and the engine number is the net. The practical error is treating either half as the answer on its own.

examples.note: The Evans Gambit, used here to show that compensation is a measurable quantity rather than a manner of speaking. Same controlled searchmoves comparison as in the gambit record. (Recorded as constructed-test: the FEN was built from the standard move sequence specifically for this comparison, not taken from a game.)

engine.verdict_note: Full compensation, demonstrated numerically. After 4.b4 White is a pawn down and the position evaluates to exactly 0.00, against +0.28 for the quiet 4.c3. Since an evaluation already nets material against everything else, a pawn deficit scoring level means the non-material assets are worth a full pawn. What White gives up is the opening edge, not the pawn.

examples.note: Two moves later, after 27.Bxe6 fxe6, with the sacrifice accepted. This is what the exchange bought: e6 and d5 permanently in Black's hands, a knight heading for d5 where nothing can drive it off, and a bishop whose counterpart has left the board. The compensation is entirely static — no attack, no tempo, nothing that expires — which is why the game is the standard illustration of the type.

counterexamples.note: The Halloween Gambit, where activity exists but does not amount to compensation. (Recorded as constructed-test: the FEN was built from the standard move sequence specifically for this comparison, not taken from a game.)

engine.verdict_note: Activity without compensation. 4.Nxe5 gives a knight for a pawn and produces a genuinely mobile centre and gain of time against the black knights, yet evaluates at -1.67 against +0.08 for the best move. Direct evidence that visible activity is not the same thing as adequate compensation, which is the trap this concept most needs guarding against.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `active-pieces-are-not-compensation`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 — the Halloween Gambit. White has given a knight for a pawn and has a big centre with tempo, every piece pointing forward, and Black's knight about to be chased twice. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap names this exact opening: "Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse." WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report compensation here. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says +1.71 from Black's side, which is the record's own figure re-measured independently and arriving within four centipawns of it. The activity is real; the compensation is not. Note what the API DOES report — center-control for White — which is true and is the thing that makes the position look compensated.

ambiguous_examples.note: The Evans Gambit accepted, after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bxb4 - a gambit played by Morphy, Chigorin, Fischer and Kasparov, and still unsettled after a hundred and seventy years. White is a pawn down with a tempo, the c3 and d4 squares, and a half-open b-file. The engine says -0.10: full compensation, exactly, and no more. That is the most ambiguous number a gambit can produce, and this record's third trap is precisely about it - 'an evaluation near zero while a pawn down means full compensation NOW; it says nothing about whether it survives the next ten moves.' Read against this record's own false-positive case, the Halloween Gambit at 1.71 worse, where the pieces are just as active and the compensation is not there.

engine.verdict_note: -0.10 at depth 24, a pawn down. Full compensation and not a centipawn more. The whole difficulty of this concept is that the same number would be reported for a position with no compensation and a pawn's worth of luck, and nothing in the evaluation distinguishes them.

by_level.beginner: What you get in return for the material you gave away.
by_level.intermediate: Compensation. Being a pawn down is fine if what you got back is worth a pawn - usually time, open lines, or damage to their position.
by_level.advanced: Ask how long it lasts. Tempi expire, open lines last while the position stays open, and a ruined structure lasts into the endgame.
by_level.master: The evaluation already nets it out; what it will not tell you is the durability, and that is the part worth thinking about.

by_depth.short: What you get back for the material you gave up.
by_depth.normal: Compensation: the non-material assets held in exchange for a material deficit - time, open lines, central control, an exposed enemy king, or damage to the opponent's structure. It is what makes being a pawn down consistent with not being worse.
by_depth.deep: What is received in exchange for material, and its forms differ above all in how long they last. Tempi expire once the opponent completes development, so a lead of that kind must be converted while it exists; open lines persist while the position stays open; structural damage and the bishop pair persist into the endgame, which makes them the most reliable compensation of all. The classical yardstick of three tempi per pawn is hedged by its own sources and understates good compensation, since the free moves are rarely the whole of what is gained; the better count is of moves each side still needs, not moves already made. The quantity is directly measurable, because an evaluation nets material against everything else: a pawn down at 0.00 is fully compensated, as the Evans Gambit measures here, while a piece down at -1.67 is not, however active the pieces look.

explanations.lesson: Ask two questions: is it worth the material now, and how long will it last?

compensation.definition_short: What a player receives in return for material given up.
compensation.definition_long:
The non-material assets held in exchange for a material deficit. Compensation is what makes it coherent to be a pawn down and not worse.

THE FORMS DIFFER IN DURABILITY, and this is the distinction that matters most in practice. TEMPI expire: a development lead is spent once the opponent finishes developing, so it must be converted while it exists. OPEN LINES and DIAGONALS persist as long as the position stays open. STRUCTURAL DAMAGE to the opponent — doubled or isolated pawns, holes — persists into the endgame, which is why compensation of that kind is the most reliable. The BISHOP PAIR is similar. An enemy king permanently stuck in the centre sits between the two.

THE CLASSICAL YARDSTICK is that a pawn is worth about three tempi in open positions. Its sources hedge it heavily and so does this base: the free moves are almost never the whole of what the gambiteer gains, so the count understates good compensation and flatters bad. The useful refinement is to count not the developing moves already made but the moves each side still needs to complete development, because a gambiteer with an initiative may force the opponent to spend moves untangling before they can develop at all.

COMPENSATION IS MEASURABLE, and this base has measured it. An engine evaluation nets material against everything else, so a position a pawn down that evaluates to 0.00 has, by definition, full compensation. The Evans Gambit does exactly that. The corollary is the important one: a position a piece down evaluating at -1.67 has partial compensation and no more, whatever the opening is called.

THE DEADLINE. Compensation of the expiring kind has a shelf life, and the standard defensive technique is built on that fact: accept the material, decline to cling to it, and return it at the moment doing so completes development or forces a favourable trade. Strong defenders return gambit material readily. The practical trigger is when holding the extra pawn costs a second tempo or forces a piece to a passive square.

corresponding-squares.knowledge_type_note: A decidable relationship between squares, not a guideline. Which squares correspond is a fact about the position.

attributions.person: Emanuel Lasker and Gustavus Charles Reichhelm
attributions.note: Composed the study that became the standard hard case for the method. Second-hand attribution.
Their treatise 'L'opposition et cases conjuguées sont réconciliées' is the standard treatment. Second-hand; the book has not been consulted.

history.notes: Both attributions come from a single encyclopedia entry and neither primary work was consulted.

corresponding-squares.engine_era_note: Not that the theory is wrong — it is exactly right — but that tablebases have made it largely unnecessary for analysis. What was once the only way to solve these positions is now a way to UNDERSTAND them, while the answer is looked up. That is a real change in the concept's role rather than in its content.

preconditions: A blocked or semi-blocked position where king penetration decides
Simple opposition gives the wrong answer or no answer
indicators_for: Several pawns fixed, with a small number of entry squares to fight over
The attacking king has more squares in the system than the defender
The position is mutual zugzwang at several points
indicators_against: The position is open enough that king manoeuvring is not decisive
Simple opposition already answers it
Pawn tempi remain, which break the correspondence
false_positive_traps: The framework is only needed where opposition fails. Invoking it where simple opposition answers the question is unhelpful precision.
Correspondences break the moment a pawn tempo becomes available.
This is an expert-level tool. Reporting it to a player who has not yet mastered the opposition explains nothing.

typical_plans: Number the key squares for both kings, then move only to squares whose partner the defender cannot reach
As the defender: shift between your numbered squares, always mirroring
typical_pawn_structures: Fixed pawn chains with one or two entry squares
typical_piece_arrangements: Kings manoeuvring behind blocked pawns
strategic_consequences: Decides blocked king-and-pawn endings that opposition cannot analyse

exceptions: Any spare pawn tempo dissolves the correspondence.
Where opposition suffices, the extra machinery adds nothing.
limitations: Human-only in practice: constructing the correspondence is a manual analytical technique.
Largely superseded as an ANALYTICAL tool by tablebases, though not as an explanatory one.

NO POSITIVE EXAMPLE, and the reason is the same one that makes this concept advanced. A positive would have to be a position where SIMPLE OPPOSITION GIVES THE WRONG ANSWER and the correspondence gives the right one - this record's own first trap is that invoking the framework where opposition answers the question is unhelpful precision. The candidates tried were all positions where opposition answers it, which is why the same board is registered here as a false-positive case instead. Building the positive means finding a blocked multi-pawn position small enough for a tablebase, and the ones tried were either symmetric and drawn both ways or too large for Syzygy at seven pieces. Recorded rather than filled. MEASURED 2026-09-03, and the reason is now a number rather than an impression. An exhaustive tablebase search was run over the shape the technique is FOR - two pawns nose to nose on one file, so neither side has a pawn tempo and the whole game is king moves - asking Syzygy for BOTH side-to-move readings of every position with both kings inside a box around the pawns. It found NINE reciprocal zugzwangs (the enumeration was still running when the count was taken, and every later find has been the same shape). SEVEN of the nine are the two kings two squares apart on one file, which is simple opposition; the other two are trebuchets. So for a single blocked pawn pair the correspondence and the opposition are the same relation, and no position from this family can show what this record needs. A genuine correspondence that opposition gets wrong needs a second pawn making the geometry asymmetric, which means enumerating five-man positions rather than four. That is the next attempt, and it is written down so it is not started from scratch again.
misconceptions: That it is a more complicated version of the opposition. It is the general theory; the opposition is its simplest case.
That it applies broadly. It applies to blocked king-and-pawn endings and almost nowhere else.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `opposition-already-answers-it`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A king-and-pawn ending decided by which king has to move: Black to move loses, White to move draws. That is reciprocal zugzwang, and reciprocal zugzwang is what a pair of corresponding squares IS. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "The framework is only needed where opposition fails. Invoking it where simple opposition answers the question is unhelpful precision." And its second indicator_against: "Simple opposition already answers it." The kings are in direct opposition on one file with one pawn on the board; counting the squares between them gives the right answer, which is the case the general theory exists to handle when it does not. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN both ways: Black to move is a LOSS in 28, and the same board with White to move is a PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0. So the mutual zugzwang is real and the concept that names it here is `opposition`, which the API reports at high confidence, and not this one, which has no matcher. The distinction matters because it is a distinction about the READER rather than about the board — this record's third trap says so outright: 'this is an expert-level tool. Reporting it to a player who has not yet mastered the opposition explains nothing.' The same position is this base's strictest controlled pair and serves `opposition`, `key-square` and `zugzwang`.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 15 against the side to move at depth 26, and Syzygy proves it: a LOSS in 28, against a PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0 for the same board with the other side to move. The reciprocal zugzwang is real, and the concept that names it here is `opposition` rather than this one - which is this record's own first trap, that the general framework is only needed where simple opposition fails.

tablebase.note: PROVEN both ways, which is what a reciprocal-zugzwang claim needs: Black to move is a LOSS in 28, and the same board with White to move is a PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0. The pair of squares is real. What this record adds beyond `opposition` is the general theory for positions where counting squares between the kings gives the wrong answer, and this is not one of those - which is why the same position is also this record's registered false-positive case.

by_level.beginner: Some squares come in pairs: if your king goes to one, theirs has to go to the matching one or you get through.
by_level.intermediate: Corresponding squares — a more general version of the opposition, for blocked positions where counting squares between the kings does not work.
by_level.advanced: Squares of mutual zugzwang. Number them for both sides; if you have more squares in the system than the defender, they run out first.
by_level.master: The general framework the opposition specialises. Note that tablebases have moved it from an analytical necessity to an explanatory one.

by_depth.short: Paired squares — if their king cannot match yours, you break through.
by_depth.normal: Corresponding squares: pairs where one king occupying its square forces the other to occupy the partner. They are squares of mutual zugzwang, and the method is to number them and always answer with the matching number.
by_depth.deep: The general theory of which opposition is the simplest case, and the tool for blocked positions where counting squares between kings misleads. Two squares correspond when occupying one obliges the enemy king to occupy the other; with only one pair they are called mined squares. The practical method is numbering — the defender shifts between numbered squares answering each attacking move with its partner, and loses when the attacker has more squares in the system than they do. The famous hard case is a Lasker and Reichhelm study of 1901, treated in a 1932 book by Halberstadt and Marcel Duchamp.

explanations.lesson: Reach for this only when the opposition gives you the wrong answer. That is the signal that the position has a correspondence structure instead.

beginner_words: if their king cannot copy you
avoid: corresponding squares are just the opposition

corresponding-squares.definition_short: Pairs of squares such that if one king occupies its square, the other king must occupy the partner square to hold — squares of mutual zugzwang.
corresponding-squares.definition_long:
Two squares correspond when a king occupying one obliges the enemy king to occupy the other in order to hold the position. They are squares of RECIPROCAL ZUGZWANG: whoever steps onto their square first, while the opponent can answer on the partner square, is the one in trouble.

It is the GENERAL theory of which the opposition is a special case, and it is what you need when simple opposition misleads — typically in blocked positions with several pawns, where counting squares between kings gives the wrong answer. Where there is only one pair, they are called MINED SQUARES: step on yours and you lose if the opponent can step on theirs.

The method in practice is to number the squares: the defending king shifts between its numbered squares, always answering the attacker's move with the corresponding number. If the attacker has more squares in the system than the defender, the defender eventually cannot answer and the position is broken through.

The most celebrated example is a study by Lasker and Reichhelm from 1901, analysed in the 1932 treatise 'L'opposition et cases conjuguées sont réconciliées' by Vitaly Halberstadt and Marcel Duchamp — the artist.

dead-position.knowledge_type_note: Official rule (A). The commonly used 'insufficient material' shortcut is an implementation convention, not the FIDE rule, and is classified separately.
dead-position.definition_short: A position from which neither player can checkmate by ANY series of legal moves. The game is drawn immediately.
dead-position.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 5.2.2: 'The game is drawn when a position has arisen in which neither player can checkmate the opponent's king with any series of legal moves. The game is said to end in a dead position. This immediately ends the game...'

This is broader and stricter than the 'insufficient material' test most software implements. 'Insufficient material' asks whether the material present could ever mate; a dead position asks whether mate is reachable from THIS position by any legal continuation, which includes blocked positions with plenty of material. Conversely, K+B vs K+B on the same colour is insufficient in the FIDE sense, whereas K+N vs K+N is NOT automatically dead, because a helpmate exists.

Nox Chess should not conflate the two terms when explaining a draw.

preconditions: No sequence of legal moves from this position ends in checkmate
indicators_for: K vs K
K+B vs K
K+N vs K
K+B vs K+B with bishops on the same colour
indicators_against: Any pawn remains on the board
A rook or queen remains on the board
K+N+N vs K — mate is not forcible but is not impossible, so the position is not dead

exceptions: K+N+N vs K is a draw in practice but is NOT a dead position: mate is legally reachable with cooperation, so the game does not end automatically.
A completely blocked position with full material can be a dead position even though material is ample.
limitations: Deciding the general case is hard; engines and servers approximate it with a material test. The approximation is correct in the common cases and wrong at the edges.

examples.note: King and bishop against king. FIDE 5.2.2 calls a position dead when no series of legal moves can lead to checkmate, and this is the textbook instance: with one bishop there is no mating net at all, whatever either side plays. The move generator confirms the position is live in the ordinary sense - 11 legal moves, no check - which is the point: dead-position is not about having no moves, it is about no sequence of moves reaching mate. That is why it is the one official rule in this base whose detectability is recorded as heuristic rather than mechanical.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw over every legal continuation, which is the strongest form the claim can take: FIDE 5.2.2 says no series of legal moves can lead to checkmate, and a tablebase is a statement about every series of legal moves. This is one of the few places in this base where the evidence and the definition are the same shape.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `opposite-bishops-and-a-dead-position`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: King and bishop against king and bishop with nothing else on the board. Neither side can force mate, which is what a dead position sounds like. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: FIDE 5.2.2 asks whether checkmate can be reached by ANY possible series of legal moves, not whether it can be forced. With bishops on opposite colours a helpmate exists, so the position is not dead — the players may agree a draw, and the arbiter does not end the game. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report dead-position here, and the record's own example shows the contrast: K+B vs K, where no series of legal moves reaches mate at all and Syzygy proves the draw over every continuation. The two records are neighbours and the difference between them is exactly this — `insufficient-material` is a software convention and `dead-position` is the Law it approximates, which is why this base keeps them apart and files the first as terminology.

by_level.beginner: Neither side has enough left to deliver checkmate, so the game is a draw.
by_level.intermediate: Dead position: no legal sequence of moves from here could ever produce checkmate, so the game ends drawn at once.
by_level.advanced: Art. 5.2.2. Note this is broader than the 'insufficient material' test implemented by most software.

by_depth.short: No series of legal moves can reach checkmate. Drawn immediately.
by_depth.normal: A dead position: neither player can deliver checkmate by ANY sequence of legal moves, however either side cooperates. The game is drawn at once, without a claim.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 5.2.2, and it is broader than the 'insufficient material' test software implements. The article asks about every possible series of moves, which is a statement of the same shape a tablebase makes — this base's example is king and bishop against king, proven drawn over every continuation. Note what the rule does NOT cover: a completely blocked position with ample material is dead in the ordinary sense and is not dead under 5.2.2, because a helpmate exists. That gap is exactly where the software convention and the Law come apart.

avoid: insufficient material (when the FIDE rule is meant)

decoy.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Informant theme h. Recognition is heuristic — it depends on the follow-up.
decoy.definition_short: Luring an enemy piece ONTO a square where a tactic works against it.
decoy.definition_long:
Usually a sacrifice that the opponent must accept, dragging the king or a piece onto a fork square, a mating square, or a line where a pin or skewer becomes available. Where deflection removes a defender, a decoy positions a victim.

The classic form is a check or capture offered on a square adjacent to a knight fork, or a queen sacrifice that pulls the king onto an open line. Anderssen's 21.Qxd7+ in the Evergreen Game is the textbook instance: the king is pulled to d7, and d7 is the square because that is where a bishop and a rook can check at the same moment.

TWO CONDITIONS decide whether it works, and both are about force rather than about geometry. The sacrifice must be one the opponent CANNOT DECLINE - a decoy that can be ignored is a lost piece - which is why the decoying move is almost always a check or a capture. And the tactic waiting on the square must work at the tempo it arrives at: decoying a king to a square where the follow-up needs one more move than the defender has is the commonest miscalculation in the motif.

DECOY AND DEFLECTION ARE THE SAME SACRIFICE read from opposite ends, and a single move is very often both. This base does not adjudicate the word: `themesOf()` refuses to claim either motif mechanically, because every cheap test for them fires where they are not true, and a wrong label is worse than a missing one when the label is the thing the reader is learning to see.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A forcing offer exists that the opponent must or will accept
Accepting places an enemy unit on a square where a further tactic works
indicators_for: The lured square is a fork square, a mating square, or on a line with another target
The offer is a check, so acceptance is forced
indicators_against: The offer can be declined without cost
The follow-up tactic does not actually exist after the capture
The lured piece can immediately step away with tempo

typical_plans: Find the square where a fork, a mate or a skewer would already work, then look for a way to force an enemy piece onto it
Against a castled king, check on a square adjacent to a knight's forking square
In the endgame, decoy the defending king one square away from the queening square rather than one square towards you
typical_moves: A queen sacrifice on h8 or g8 pulling the king onto a square a knight covers
A check that must be answered by a capture, where the capturing piece lands on a pinned line
A pawn push offering itself so the capturing pawn blocks its own defender
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight two moves from a fork whose forking square is empty
An enemy king on an open rank or file with a heavy piece able to arrive on it
tactical_consequences: The decoying move is almost always a check or a capture, because the victim has to be forced rather than invited

Decoy and deflection are the same sacrifice read differently: deflection removes a defender from a duty, decoy puts a victim on a square. A single move is often both, and this base does not try to choose between them

exceptions: A decoy fails outright if the sacrifice can be declined.
A decoy that lands the enemy king on a square where the follow-up needs one more move than the defender has is not a decoy, it is a lost piece.
Decoying a defender onto a square where it still defends is the commonest miscalculation in this motif.
limitations: Only identifiable by looking at the resulting position, so it cannot be detected from the move alone.

NO VERIFIED POSITION HAS BEEN BUILT FOR THIS RECORD. Four constructions were tried and each failed for the same reason: the Damiano and Anastasia shapes that make a clean decoy need a specific queen-and-knight geometry with the h-file already open, and every minimal version either mated without the decoy or left the sacrificing side simply a queen down. The nearest thing this base holds is shipped puzzle mi-9f06a55404, where Qxf8+ forces Rxf8 and exf8=Q is mate — and it is NOT filed here, because sources are divided on whether that combination is a decoy or a deflection and `themesOf()` refuses to name either. A motif label the base cannot defend is worse than a missing example.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and the reason is the order of the work rather than a shortage of positions. This record has no POSITIVE example either, and an ambiguous example is a position where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - which cannot be written before there is an agreed instance of the concept being present at all. The four motifs in this base that lack a positive - `clearance`, `decoy`, `deflection`, `interference` - lack it for reasons written on each record, and the ambiguous rung waits on that. Writing one first would be asserting a doubtful instance of something this base has not yet shown a clear instance of.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-king-decoyed-to-safety`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Ra8+ forces the black king to move to h7 — a check that must be answered by a king move to a specific square is exactly how a decoy operates. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Nothing is waiting on h7. A decoy lures a piece ONTO a square where a tactic works against it — a fork square, a mating square, a line where a pin or skewer becomes available — and White has a rook and three pawns. The king is forced to a square and the square is safe. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `open-file` and nothing else; `decoy` has no matcher and this record's limitations say why — the motif is 'only identifiable by looking at the resulting position, so it cannot be detected from the move alone'. This case is the cheap version of that: forcing a king to a square is mechanical and trivial to detect, and it is the half of the concept that carries none of the meaning. The position is dead level.

ambiguous_examples.note: Anderssen-Kieseritzky, London 1851 - the Immortal Game, 22.Qf6+. The knight on g8 must take the queen, and 23.Be7 is mate. The move is ONE move and it is two motifs, inseparably: the knight is pulled ONTO f6, which is a decoy, and it is pulled OFF the guard of e7, which is a deflection. Neither reading is secondary and no test distinguishes them, because the same forced capture does both at once. Read as a decoy, the square is f6 and the point is that a knight standing there blocks nothing and defends nothing - the mate arrives on e7 regardless of what the knight now does. That is the weaker of the two readings and it is not wrong. This base carries the position on BOTH records as ambiguous rather than choosing, which is the same decision `themesOf()` makes mechanically - it refuses to claim decoy or deflection at all, because every cheap test for them fires where they are not true and a wrong label is worse than a missing one when the label is what the reader is learning to see. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator: 45 plies, every one legal, ending on Be7 mate.

defensive-principles.knowledge_type_note: The literature genuinely disagrees here, and this record keeps the disagreement rather than choosing a side, because the two camps are answering different questions.

attributions.note: Credited by one source with first indicating that an attack from an equal position can be refuted by correct defence, and with declaring - unfashionably - that all gambits can be defended. Recorded at low confidence: a single club source states it and this base has not corroborated it.
Made correct defence a theoretical proposition rather than a temperament, though Polugaevsky notes he took it to an extreme by deliberately avoiding positive action.
Introduced prophylaxis, whose two tasks he gave as restricting the opponent's possibilities and overprotecting important points. Reuben Fine summarised the method as 'restrict, blockade, destroy'.
The Art of Defence in Chess, which treats defence as a discipline with its own procedures.

history.notes: The Paulsen claim is the interesting one and the least secure: the theory of correct defence is normally credited wholly to Steinitz, and one source consulted here makes Paulsen its progenitor. Recorded rather than adopted.

development.note: Paulsen defends gambits against fashion; Steinitz turns correct defence into theory.
Nimzowitsch adds prophylaxis - defending against a plan before it exists.
Polugaevsky treats defence as a technique with named procedures, and notes that modern success nevertheless rests on offensive play.

defensive-principles.engine_era_note: Engines have raised the standing of defence considerably. They find resources humans give up on, which has established that many 'lost' positions were holdable, and they favour active defence over passive far more strongly than classical teaching did. They have also made the practical-chances argument measurable, since one can now see exactly how narrow a saving line was.

preconditions: The opponent has the initiative or a material or positional advantage
indicators_for: A concrete threat that must be answered
An enemy attack in progress
A worse position with identifiable drawing resources
indicators_against: The position is balanced and no threat exists
false_positive_traps: Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle.
The simplify-versus-complicate advice is genuinely contradictory in the sources and must not be reported as settled. Which applies depends on whether the position is holdable or lost.
A concession that was not forced is not a defensive move. Conceding early and conceding more than necessary are the two ways defences collapse.

typical_plans: Identify the threat before choosing a plan
Exchange the opponent's most dangerous attacking piece
Counterattack, or aim for perpetual check
Steer into an ending known to be drawish, giving material if that is the price
Restrain the opponent's plan rather than meet each threat as it arrives
typical_moves: Exchange sacrifices to remove a key attacker or establish a blockade
Prophylactic pawn moves that pre-empt a break
typical_pawn_structures: Structures leading to opposite-coloured bishops or rook endings
typical_piece_arrangements: A blockade on the colour complex the attacker needs
tactical_consequences: Perpetual check and stalemate are defensive resources, not accidents
strategic_consequences: A successfully defended attack leaves the attacker worse, since the attacking pieces must withdraw and regroup

exceptions: Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it - Polugaevsky gives an example where the outwardly more active move loses.
Against a lost position, objectively bad moves that complicate can be the best practical choice.
Polugaevsky is explicit that modern success rests on offensive play, and that seeking defence contrary to the position's demands is as punishable as any other error.
limitations: The literature disagrees on the central practical question of simplifying versus complicating when worse, and this record does not resolve it beyond distinguishing the two cases.
Practical-chances advice is about opponents' fallibility, which this system cannot assess.
misconceptions: That defence means making passive moves and waiting. It is an active discipline with its own techniques.
That a worse position should be simplified. That is right when the position is holdable and wrong when it is lost.
That attacks succeed because attack is stronger than defence. The classical claim is the reverse: attacks from equal positions should fail, and succeed largely because defence is played badly.

conflicts.resolution: The sharpest live disagreement in this record. Exchanging relieves a cramped or worse position and steers towards drawish endings; keeping pieces on preserves the complexity a stronger opponent might go wrong in. The distinguishing question is not preference but assessment: simplify if the position is worse but holdable, complicate if it is lost. Note also that simplification can convert a proven win into a proven draw, which makes it a defensive weapon rather than merely a concession.

examples.note: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, after 21...Kxh7. Speelman's judgement is that 22.Be3 was the best response and that Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. That is the record's subject exactly: the hardest part of defence is admitting the attack is over and switching to it, and the practical failure is almost never a missed defensive resource - it is the move made while still attacking. The engine agrees with Speelman about the move and about the size of the problem.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-passive-move-is-not-a-defence`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White is much worse and retreats a piece to a square where it defends. Retreating and consolidating is what a worse position seems to call for. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle." Speelman's account of the game says exactly this happened — Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, and the two candidate moves are 234 centipawns apart: 22.Be3, the move Speelman says was best and this record's positive example, scores -1.91, and the retreat 22.Nb3 that was played scores -4.25. Both are bad. That is the point of the pair — the choice is not between saving the game and losing it, it is between the least bad move and a worse one, and the passive move is the worse one. The API reports nothing about defensive principles either way, because the concept has no matcher: what makes a move defensive is what it prevents, and this base does not read intentions.

ambiguous_examples.note: Black is a pawn down with one rook each and a trade available at any moment, and the defender's choice is the one this record says the sources contradict each other about. Trading into a pawn ending is simplification, which the literature recommends to the defender, and a pawn down in a pawn ending is usually lost. Keeping the rooks on is complication, which the literature also recommends to the defender, and rook endings a pawn down are famously drawish. The record's second trap says this outright: 'the simplify-versus-complicate advice is genuinely contradictory in the sources and must not be reported as settled. Which applies depends on whether the position is one the defender can hold.' Filed as ambiguous because the concept covers the decision twice and points both ways, and +1.57 is not large enough to settle it.

by_level.beginner: Before you do anything, ask what your opponent's move threatens. Then meet it with the smallest concession you can.
by_level.intermediate: Defence is active. Trade off their best attacking piece, look for counterplay, and do not make weakening moves until you are forced to.
by_level.advanced: Choose deliberately between passive, active and combinational defence, and consider steering into an ending known to be drawish - giving material if that is the price.
by_level.master: Assess first whether the position is holdable or lost; simplify in the first case and complicate in the second, since they are answers to different questions.

by_depth.short: Find the threat, concede as little as possible, and keep your pieces active.
by_depth.normal: Defensive play has its own principles: identify the threat before anything else, avoid concessions until forced and then make only the minimum, exchange the opponent's most dangerous attacking piece, and look for counterplay rather than waiting.
by_depth.deep: The neglected half of chess, and not the absence of a plan. The most portable idea is minimum concession - a defender must be willing to weaken something, but should not do it until forced and then only as far as the threat requires, since most collapses are a series of concessions none of which was compelled. Defence divides into passive, active and combinational, and the choice is a real decision. The techniques are specific: remove the attack's key piece, counterattack, or steer into an ending known to draw, planning a material loss if that is the price. Where the sources genuinely conflict is simplifying versus complicating when worse, and the resolution is that they answer different questions - simplify a position that is holdable, complicate one that is lost.

explanations.lesson: Ask what is threatened before you ask what you want, and give up only what you are forced to give up.

beginner_words: give up as little as possible

defensive-principles.definition_short: How to play a worse position: concede as little as possible, keep the pieces active, and change the character of the position rather than merely react.
defensive-principles.definition_long:
The neglected half of chess. Defence has its own principles and its own techniques, and it is not the absence of a plan.

THE MINIMUM-CONCESSION RULE is the most portable idea in it. A defender must be prepared to make concessions — a weakening pawn move, a passive piece, returned material — but should avoid conceding until forced, and then concede only the MINIMUM needed to meet the threat. Most defensive collapses are a series of small voluntary concessions, none of which was required.

THE THREE KINDS. Polugaevsky divides defence into PASSIVE, ACTIVE and COMBINATIONAL, and insists the choice between them is a real decision rather than a matter of temperament. He also records the option in between: restraining the opponent's initiative without committing to either.

THE STANDARD TECHNIQUES:
- IDENTIFY THE THREAT FIRST. After the opponent moves, ask what it threatens before asking what you want. This is the one piece of advice on which every source agrees.
- EXCHANGE THE OPPONENT'S BEST ATTACKING PIECE. An attack usually depends on one or two pieces; removing them is worth more than adding a defender.
- COUNTERATTACK. The strongest defensive resource is a threat of your own, and perpetual check saves games that nothing else would.
- STEER FOR A DRAWISH ENDING. Mass exchanges into rook endings or opposite-coloured bishops draw positions that are objectively lost, and the defender may correctly PLAN a material loss to get there, since an extra pawn frequently wins nothing.

THE GENUINE DISAGREEMENT is over whether to simplify or complicate when worse, and the sources conflict outright: club-level teaching says exchange when cramped, while the practical-chances school says keep pieces on and complicate, since a simple position lets a stronger opponent convert without risk. The resolution this base adopts is that they answer different questions. If the position is WORSE BUT HOLDABLE, simplification towards a known drawing structure is correct and is Polugaevsky's method. If it is LOST, simplification is surrender on the instalment plan and complication is the only practical policy. The prior question is which of those you are in.

THE HISTORICAL POINT worth keeping: an attack launched from an equal position should fail against correct defence, and the attacker will be worse for having tried. Attacks succeed in practice largely because defence is played badly.

deflection.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), but recognition is heuristic: it depends on identifying a DUTY, which is a functional judgement rather than a geometric one.
deflection.definition_short: Forcing a defending piece away from the square, line, or duty it must hold.
deflection.definition_long:
The defender's piece is doing a job. Deflection forces it to stop — usually with a capture or a check it cannot decline — and the real target then falls.

Deflection and DECOY are constantly conflated; the useful distinction is one of direction. Deflection pushes a piece AWAY from a duty. A decoy lures a piece TOWARDS a bad square. Chess.com merges them into one theme; Chess Tempo and Chess Informant keep them separate (themes d and h). This record keeps them separate and cross-links them.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: An enemy piece is performing a defensive duty (guarding a square, a piece, or a line)
A forcing move exists that compels that piece to move or be captured
indicators_for: The deflecting move is a check or an offer the defender cannot decline
The duty is sole — no other unit covers it
indicators_against: A second defender covers the same duty
The defender can decline the offer and keep its post
Accepting costs the attacker more than the target is worth

typical_plans: Name the duty before naming the deflection: what is the piece holding, and what happens the moment it stops
Attack the defender with something it must take or must answer, rather than with something it can ignore
In the endgame, deflect the king rather than a piece — a king that must answer a check cannot also stop a pawn
typical_moves: A sacrifice on a square the defender is obliged to capture on
A check that forces the defending piece to interpose
A pawn push attacking the piece that guards a mating square
typical_piece_arrangements: A single piece defending two things at once — deflection and overloading are then the same move seen twice
A back rank guarded by exactly one rook
tactical_consequences: Deflection and decoy are the same sacrifice read from opposite ends: deflection removes a defender from a duty, decoy puts a victim on a square, and one move is very often both
The material given is usually irrelevant to the arithmetic — what matters is whether the duty can be abandoned

exceptions: A deflection fails if the deflected piece can answer the threat and keep its duty, which is the commonest miscalculation in the motif.
Deflecting a defender that has a second defender behind it achieves nothing.
If the opponent can decline, it is not a deflection — the whole idea rests on the reply being forced.
limitations: `themesOf()` refuses to claim deflection at all, and deliberately: every cheap test for it fires where it is not true, and a wrong label is worse than a missing one because the label is the thing the reader is learning to see.

by_depth.normal: Deflection: name the duty first — what is this piece holding, and what happens the moment it stops? Then attack it with something it must take or must answer. The piece leaves, and the thing it was guarding falls.
by_depth.deep: Morphy's 16.Qb8+ in the Opera Game is the standard example: the knight on d7 is the only guard of d8, the queen is offered where the knight must take it, and 17.Rd8 is mate. Three conditions are worth checking before claiming it. The reply must be forced — a deflection that can be declined is not one. desperado.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). A named special case of zwischenzug rather than an independent geometric pattern.
desperado.definition_short: A piece already doomed sells itself as dearly as possible before it is lost.
desperado.definition_long:
When a piece is going to be lost regardless, it takes something on the way out, or forces a concession, instead of being captured for nothing. Common in capture races where both sides have hanging pieces, and in stalemate defences.

Formally a special case of the zwischenzug: the doomed piece acts before the expected recapture. Chess.com classifies it that way explicitly.

EVERYTHING RESTS ON THE FIRST WORD. A piece that can be saved by moving, or by a counter-threat, is not doomed, and the desperado is then simply a blunder - which is why this record's first exception is to verify that before anything else. The verification is a search rather than a static test: 'cannot be saved' is a claim about every legal move the piece has and about what happens after each of them, which is why this base has no matcher for the motif.

THE SIZE OF THE GAIN is not the value of what is taken. It is the difference between taking and not taking, and that difference can be large even when the capture is an even trade: this base's example is a rook that is attacked and undefended, where taking a rook rather than retreating is worth 748 centipawns. In stalemate defences the same device is used to SHED material deliberately, which reads backwards to any material test and is the reason the motif needs a name of its own rather than being filed under 'capture'.

preconditions: A friendly piece cannot be saved
That piece has a capture or forcing move available
indicators_for: Both sides have loose pieces at once
The doomed piece can capture something defended, evening the material count
indicators_against: The piece can actually be saved, in which case desperado logic is simply a blunder

typical_plans: Before conceding a piece, list every capture it can make and every check it can give
In a capture race, count who runs out of desperados first rather than who is ahead now
In a lost position, look for a desperado that reaches stalemate rather than one that wins material
typical_moves: A doomed rook taking a defended pawn on the seventh before being captured
A hanging queen giving itself up for a rook rather than for nothing
A trapped bishop taking the pawn that trapped it
typical_piece_arrangements: Both sides with a hanging piece at once, so the side to move decides the order
A piece attacked with every retreat square covered
tactical_consequences: A desperado inverts normal move ordering: the piece acts before the recapture rather than after, which is why chess.com classifies it as a special case of the zwischenzug
The size of the gain is not the value of what is taken, it is the difference between taking and not taking - which can be several pawns even when the capture is an even trade
strategic_consequences: In stalemate defences a desperado is a way to shed material deliberately, so material counting reads it backwards

exceptions: The whole idea rests on the piece being genuinely unsaveable. Verify that first.
A desperado that gives the opponent a tempo they needed is worse than losing the piece quietly.
If the piece can be saved by a counter-threat rather than by moving, it is not doomed and the desperado is a blunder.
limitations: There is no matcher. 'Cannot be saved' is a claim about every legal move the piece has and about what happens after each, which is a search rather than a static test, and the record's own exception says the first thing to do is verify it.

The example on this record was FOUND rather than constructed, by scanning the 788 shipped puzzles for a solution move where the moving piece could already be won before the move and could still be won on its destination. Fifty positions match that shape. Four hand-built minimal positions were thrown away first: trapping a piece with no escape square needs a cage of enemy men, and every small version left the piece a flight square.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET, and the search that failed is worth recording. Five famous games were replayed through this base's own move generator and scanned position by position with the API - the Opera Game, the Evergreen, the Immortal, the Game of the Century and Legall's Mate, 225 plies between them - and this concept was not reported in any of them. That is not evidence the motif is rare; it is evidence that the five games this base can currently verify do not contain a clean instance of it, and that adding one means adding a game rather than looking harder at these. tools/replay_game.js is the instrument: a move list that is wrong is refused rather than guessed at. RESOLVED: Kramnik-Kuzmin, GMA-Open 1989, 34.Rxh8+, above.

examples.note: Shipped puzzle en-a9ff7ebd22, and it is the record's two preconditions on a real board. THE PIECE CANNOT BE SAVED: the white rook on e1 is attacked down the e-file by the rook on e4 and is defended by nothing - the king on g2 does not reach it and the rook on f2 does not either. IT HAS A CAPTURE AVAILABLE: Rxe4, which is answered by fxe4, so the rook does not survive that either. What makes it a desperado rather than a trade is the alternative: retreating scores -4.93 and taking scores +2.55, a gap of 748 centipawns, because the rook that is going to be lost anyway takes a rook with it and the b7 pawn then decides. Found by scanning all 788 shipped puzzles for a solution move where the moving piece was ALREADY losable before the move and is losable on its destination too - fifty positions match that shape and this is the clearest.

examples.note:
THE MASTER-GAME RUNG, and it earns the record's first word. So it takes a rook on the way out. 34.Rxh8+ Kxh8 and White has had a rook for a rook instead of a rook for nothing.

Stockfish 18 at depth 26 with three lines: −0.54, against −1.89 and −2.14. WHITE IS WORSE IN ALL OF THEM, and that is the right shape for this concept rather than an embarrassment. A desperado is damage limitation - the piece is going, and the question is only what it takes with it. The margin, 135 centipawns, is the value of asking that question instead of retreating.

WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own exception, which it states first: "The whole idea rests on the piece being genuinely unsaveable. Verify that first." The bishop has seven safe squares. by_level.intermediate: A desperado: since the piece cannot be saved, it takes material on its way off the board.
by_level.advanced: Desperado, a special case of zwischenzug. Confirm the piece really is unsaveable before applying the logic.

by_depth.short: A piece that is lost anyway takes something on the way out.
by_depth.normal: A desperado: the piece cannot be saved, so instead of being captured for nothing it makes a capture, or forces a concession, first. The gain is not the value of what it takes — it is the difference between taking and not taking.
by_depth.deep: Formally a special case of the zwischenzug: the doomed piece acts BEFORE the expected recapture. Everything rests on the first word of the definition, and this record's own exception says to verify it first — a piece that can be saved by moving, or by a counter-threat, is not doomed and the desperado is a blunder. The margin can be large even when the capture is an even trade: this base's example is a rook that is attacked and undefended, and taking a rook with it rather than retreating is worth 748 centipawns. discovered-attack.definition_short: One piece moves out of the way, unmasking an attack by a piece behind it.
discovered-attack.definition_long:
A friendly unit steps off a line, revealing an attack by a friendly bishop, rook or queen behind it. Its power is that the MOVING piece is free to make a second threat of its own, so one move produces two attacks — and the moving piece can go somewhere it would otherwise never be allowed to stand, including en prise, because the revealed threat outweighs it.

If the revealed attack hits the king it is a DISCOVERED CHECK, which is far stronger because the defender must answer the check and has no time for the moving piece. If both the moving and the revealed piece attack the king it is a DOUBLE CHECK, and only a king move is legal.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly line piece is behind a friendly unit, aimed at an enemy target
The intervening friendly unit has a move that leaves the line
indicators_for: The revealed attack hits the king or the queen
The moving piece can create its own threat
The moving piece may safely occupy an attacked square because the discovery outweighs it
indicators_against: The revealed line is blocked by another unit further along
The revealed 'attack' hits something defended and not worth taking
The defender can answer both threats with one move

exceptions: A discovery is worthless if the unmasked line hits nothing of value.
In a discovered check the moving piece may stand en prise with impunity — normal safety reasoning does not apply to it.
limitations: Detecting that a line opens is mechanical; judging whether the two threats together are decisive is not.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

Verified 2026-09-02. "The revealed line is blocked by another unit further along" is unreachable rather than unguarded: findMotifs() does not report that a line was opened, it reports a specific unit on a specific square that the revealed piece now attacks, computed from the board after the move. A line blocked before it reaches anything produces no target and no tag. The condition that WAS live on this record - "The revealed 'attack' hits something defended and not worth taking" - was true of 33 of the 788 shipped puzzles and is now guarded by SEE at the motif-mapping site. "The defender can answer both threats with one move" remains unbuilt and needs a search.

examples.note: Legall's Mate, Paris 1750 - 5.Nxe5, and the detector's reading of it is the honest one: 'moving the knight uncovers the queen on d1, which now attacks the bishop on g4'. Both readings are true of the same move, and this base reports the one it can see. The engine's verdict on the whole idea is +2.04, which is a comment on Black's fourth move rather than on the sacrifice - against best defence White simply recaptures on g4 and is two pawns better. by_level.beginner: Moving this piece uncovers an attack from the piece behind it, so you get two attacks in one move.
by_level.intermediate: A discovered attack. The moving piece is free to threaten something else, because the revealed attack does the work.
by_level.advanced: Discovery. If the unmasked line hits the king it is a discovered check, and the moving piece may go anywhere, including en prise.

by_depth.short: A piece moves aside and unmasks an attack from the piece behind it.
by_depth.normal: A discovered attack: two attacks for one move — whatever the moving piece does, and whatever the piece behind it now hits. The moving piece is comparatively free, because the opponent has to deal with the revealed threat.
by_depth.deep: The revealed attack has to be worth something, and that is where the motif is most often overclaimed: a rook unmasked onto a defended pawn is a discovery that wins nothing, and 33 of the 788 puzzles in this repository carried exactly that report before it was guarded. Two other conditions matter. The revealed line must not be blocked further along — a second unit in the way makes the discovery empty. And the defender must not be able to answer both threats with one move. When the revealed line gives CHECK the motif becomes much stronger and gets its own record, because a check cannot be ignored.

discovered-check.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Strictly a sub-case of discovered attack, distinguished because the forced reply changes what the moving piece may do.
discovered-check.definition_short: A discovered attack where the revealed line gives check, so the moving piece is free to do anything.
discovered-check.definition_long:
A friendly unit steps off a line and the piece behind it checks the king. Because the opponent must answer the check immediately, the MOVING piece is effectively unconstrained for one move: it may capture, it may threaten a second target, and it may stand on a square where it is attacked, because there is no time to take it.

That last point is the one that makes discovered checks so hard to see. Ordinary safety reasoning — 'I cannot go there, it is defended' — does not apply to the discovering piece.

history.notes: Descriptive pattern name of long, largely anonymous usage.

preconditions: A friendly line piece is aimed at the enemy king through exactly one friendly blocker
That blocker has a legal move off the line
indicators_for: The moving piece can capture something or create a second threat
The moving piece lands on a square that would otherwise be unsafe
indicators_against: The check is easily blocked or the checking piece captured
The moving piece has no useful destination

exceptions: If the discovered check can be met by a capture of the checking piece, the free move is not free.
limitations: Fires on 1.5% of the 788 shipped positions. Defers to double-check, whose record says more about the same move.

by_level.beginner: Moving this piece gives check from the piece behind it. Your opponent must answer the check, so this piece can go anywhere — even somewhere it could be taken.
by_level.intermediate: Discovered check. The opponent must deal with the check, so the moving piece gets a free move.
by_level.advanced: Discovered check. Suspend normal safety reasoning for the discovering piece; the check buys the tempo.

by_depth.short: Moving a piece uncovers a check, so the moving piece can go anywhere.
by_depth.normal: A discovered check: the piece that moves is not the piece that checks, so the reply must answer the check and the moving piece is free to take, threaten or run wherever it likes. That freedom is the whole value of the motif.
by_depth.deep: It is only free if the check cannot be answered another way. If the defender can interpose or capture the checking piece rather than moving the king, the moving piece is not free at all — the defence deals with the check and keeps its options, and this base withholds the report when the move generator finds such a reply. Byrne-Fischer 1956 is the master example and shows why the motif is worth a name: Fischer plays the same discovered check four times in a row, taking something different each time, in a position where he has already given up his queen.

double-attack.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). The fork/double-attack boundary is a terminological disagreement between sources, recorded rather than resolved.
double-attack.definition_short: Any move that creates two threats at once, whether by one piece or two.
double-attack.definition_long:
The general case of which the fork is the special case. A fork is a double attack by a single piece; a discovered attack is a double attack by two pieces, one moving and one revealed. Chess Informant treats 'Double Attack' as a top-level theme.

Sources disagree on whether 'fork' and 'double attack' are synonyms. Chess.com treats them as one theme; Wikipedia and Chess Tempo keep the distinction that a fork is by one unit. This record follows the narrower usage and records the conflation as an alternate usage rather than an error.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: After the move, two distinct threats exist that cannot both be met
indicators_for: The two threats require different defensive resources
One threat is a check, forcing the reply
indicators_against: A single defensive move parries both
One 'threat' is not real because the target is adequately defended

exceptions: A single move can sometimes answer both threats — an interposition that also defends, or a counter-check.
limitations: 'Threat' is broader than 'attacks a piece' and includes mate threats and positional threats, which makes fully mechanical detection unreliable.

This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled.

examples.note: Constructed. The record's precondition is 'after the move, two distinct threats exist that cannot both be met', and the record's definition is deliberately wide - 'any move that creates two threats at once, whether by one piece or two'. Here it is one piece and the two threats are of different kinds: check to the king on e8 along the eighth rank, and capture of the rook on a8 along the same rank. Black must answer the check, and answering it does not defend the rook. This is why this base treats double-attack as a family that contains the fork rather than as a synonym for it.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The queen on d5 attacks the rook on a8 down the long diagonal and the pawn on f7 down the other. Two enemy units attacked at once by one piece, which is this record's precondition exactly. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The precondition has a second half: 'two distinct threats that CANNOT BOTH BE MET'. Both can. The rook on a8 is defended by the rook on b8 and the pawn on f7 by the king, and a queen taking a defended rook or a defended pawn is not a threat at all — nothing needs answering, so there is nothing for one move to fail to answer. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report a double attack. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says -4.90 for the side making it and retreats the queen to d1. This is the geometric half of the concept without the arithmetic half, and it is the commonest way a reader gets the motif wrong: counting how many enemy pieces a queen touches is easy and says nothing, and what makes the difference is whether taking either one is worth doing.

Two distinct threats that cannot both be met is this record's precondition, satisfied exactly. It is also worth nothing: the tablebase's own move is Qxa7, taking the pawn immediately and without any double attack, and the position is a proven win either way. Filed as ambiguous because the concept applies in full and adds no information - a double attack that wins a pawn in a position already winning by a queen is a true description of a move nobody needs to find.

by_level.beginner: This move makes two threats at once, and only one can be answered.
by_level.intermediate: A double attack: two threats, needing two different answers.
by_level.advanced: Double attack (Informant theme j). Distinguish from a fork proper, which is a double attack by a single unit.

by_depth.short: One move, two threats, and only one can be answered.
by_depth.normal: A double attack: any move that creates two threats at once, whether by one piece or two. The test is not how many enemy units are touched — it is whether both threats are real and whether one move can meet them both.
by_depth.deep: The family that contains the fork rather than a synonym for it: a fork is one piece hitting two targets, and a double attack includes a move that makes one threat while a second piece makes another. Counting how many enemy pieces a queen touches is the easy half and says nothing. Both targets must be worth taking — two defended units both cheaper than the attacker are not threats at all — and the defender must not have a single move that covers both, which is the condition a static scan cannot see. Smyslov-Botvinnik 1954 is the master example and the forking piece there is a pawn, which is the cheapest attacker there is and the condition that makes a double attack work.

double-check.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D) with a hard consequence that follows from the rules — the forced king move is a proven consequence, not a heuristic.
double-check.definition_short: A discovered check where both the moving piece and the revealed piece give check. The king MUST move.
double-check.definition_long:
Two pieces check the king at once. Neither can be captured (capturing one leaves the other checking), and no interposition covers two lines. FIDE leaves only one legal reply: a king move. Wikipedia notes the rare third case where a third piece delivers the second check, possible via an en passant capture.

This is why double check underlies smothered mate and many king hunts: it strips the defender of every resource except moving the king, so the attacker can sacrifice freely.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: After the move, two enemy pieces attack the king simultaneously
indicators_for: The king has few or no flight squares
indicators_against: The king has a safe square, in which case the double check may achieve nothing

tactical_consequences: Only a king move is legal, so material on any other square is irrelevant for one move

exceptions: A double check is not automatically strong: if the king simply steps aside safely, the attacker may have given away material for nothing.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

Verified 2026-09-02, and the answer is a hedge rather than a guard. "The king has a safe square, in which case the double check may achieve nothing" is checkable - the move generator would list the flight squares - but suppressing the report would be wrong, because a double check that is not mate still forces a king move and that is usually its whole point: it is what lets the discovered piece do something the defender cannot answer. The record's own wording says 'may achieve nothing', and a matcher that turned a 'may' into a refusal would be claiming more than the record does. This is the third of the three answers a stated condition can get, and here it is the right one.

That last clause is the whole concept. Black has a queen on f3 and two rooks and none of them can interpose or capture; the king went to d7 one move earlier and must now walk into the mate. by_level.beginner: Two pieces are checking the king at the same time. The king has to move — nothing can block or capture both.
by_level.intermediate: Double check. The only legal reply is a king move, so you can ignore everything else for a move.
by_level.advanced: Double check: no interposition or capture can answer two lines, which is what makes smothered mate work.

by_depth.short: Two pieces check at once, so only a king move is legal.
by_depth.normal: A double check: the moving piece and the piece it unmasked both attack the king. Nothing can block two lines and nothing can capture two attackers, so the king MUST move — no interposition, no capture, no counter-threat.
by_depth.deep: The strongest forcing move in chess, and the reason is arithmetic rather than tactical: every other check leaves the defender three answers and this one leaves a subset of one. Anderssen's 22.Bf5+ in the Evergreen is the master example — Black has a queen and two rooks and not one of them can interpose. The record's own caution is that a double check which is not mate can still achieve nothing if the king has a safe square, so the motif forces a move rather than winning by itself.
