doubled-pawns.knowledge_type_note: Names a structural fact. Whether it is a weakness is a judgement, and the sources disagree sharply enough that the disagreement is part of the record.

attributions.note: Britannica lists doubled pawns among the structural weaknesses named by Steinitz's theory. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: this is the conventional ascription, taken from a secondary source, and no primary text was consulted for it during this research.
The hypermodern challenge to treating them as an objective weakness.

history.notes: A widely repeated Capablanca line — 'I would take doubled pawns if in return I may place my rook on the seventh rank' — is attached to this concept in one source, which itself prefaces it 'Legend has it'. It is NOT verified and must not be quoted as Capablanca's. Recorded here only so a later session does not rediscover it and assume it is sound.
competing_claims: Classical school: doubled pawns are an objective weakness to be avoided.
Hypermodern school: dynamic compensation routinely outweighs the structural defect.

development.change: Treated as a defect to avoid.
Challenged; compensation in activity and files given equal standing.
Engines accept severe pawn defects for activity, which has moved practice towards the hypermodern view without settling it.

doubled-pawns.engine_era_note: The classical assessment is the one engines have most clearly softened. Modern practice takes doubled pawns readily for the bishop pair or an open file. The one drawback engines still price heavily is the crippled majority — doubled pawns in a majority usually cannot make a passer, and that is an endgame fact rather than an opinion.

preconditions: Two or more friendly pawns occupy the same file
indicators_for: They are also isolated, so no pawn can ever defend them
They stand on a half-open file the opponent's rooks can use
They are in a majority, which therefore cannot produce a passer unaided
The square in front of the front pawn can be blockaded by an enemy piece
The position is simplifying towards an endgame
indicators_against: The doubling opened a file that is actually being used
The bishop pair was obtained in the exchange
They increase control of central squares
They create an outpost the opponent cannot contest
They shield the king rather than exposing it
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: doubled pawns are not automatically weak. Detecting them is trivial; concluding weakness from the detection is wrong often enough to be a real hazard.
The compensation is usually invisible to a structure check — the bishop pair and the opened file are elsewhere on the board.
Doubled CENTRAL pawns are frequently an asset, controlling four squares between them.

typical_plans: Against them: blockade the front pawn, double rooks on the file, and simplify
With them: use the opened file, play on the squares they control, and avoid endgames if the majority is crippled
Undouble by advancing and exchanging the front pawn when possible
typical_moves: bxc3 in the Nimzo-Indian, accepting the structure for the bishop pair
typical_pawn_structures: Nimzo-Indian c3/c4 doubled pawns
Doubled isolated pawns — the worst case
Rossolimo and Exchange Ruy structures where doubled pawns are inflicted deliberately
typical_piece_arrangements: Enemy knight blockading in front of the front pawn
strategic_consequences: A majority containing doubled pawns generally cannot make a passer unaided
The half-open file created is often the compensation

exceptions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.
The recapture-towards-the-centre guideline has three standard exceptions: king shelter, a more useful file, and creating a chronic target.
limitations: Recognition is trivial; evaluation is not, and the compensating factors are usually not in the pawn structure at all.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the last two indicators_against are now said as well. 'They create an outpost the opponent cannot contest' is read as a hole the doubled pawns themselves defend, and 'they shield the king rather than exposing it' as a pair standing in front of their own king - the doubled f-pawns after ...gxf6 are the classic case, and a base that lists a structure without them invites exactly the conclusion this record's first trap forbids. All five of this record's indicators are now in the sentence; none of them is a guard, because doubled pawns are a fact.
misconceptions: That doubled pawns are a weakness. They are a concession with a price attached, and the price is often worth paying.
That the Capablanca quotation about doubled pawns and the seventh rank is verified. It is not.
That they matter equally in middlegame and endgame. They mainly bite in the endgame.
That doubled pawns are a weakness. Measured here: inflicting them cost the inflicting side 0.34, and the side that accepted them is exactly equal.

by_level.beginner: Two of your pawns are on the same file. They cannot protect each other, but the trade that put them there often gave you something in return.
by_level.intermediate: Doubled pawns on the {file}-file. Ask what the exchange bought — a file, the bishop pair, central control — before calling them a weakness.
by_level.advanced: Structural concession. The concrete drawback is the crippled majority; the compensation is usually the half-open file or the bishop pair. They bite mainly in the endgame.
by_level.master: Price them by the majority. Doubled pawns in a majority that can no longer produce a passer is a real, permanent, endgame-deciding defect; doubled central pawns with an open file beside them frequently are not.

by_depth.short: Two pawns on the {file}-file — they cannot defend each other.
by_depth.normal: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
by_depth.deep: Two pawns on the same file, normally after a capture. Three real drawbacks: they cannot defend each other, the rear one is blocked, and a majority containing them usually cannot manufacture a passed pawn — which is the one engines still price heavily, because it decides endgames. Against that sit the standard compensations of an opened file, the bishop pair, extra central control and new outposts. This is a genuine disagreement between schools rather than an unsettled definition: the classical view treated them as an objective defect, the hypermoderns held that dynamics outweigh structure, and modern practice has moved towards the second without settling it.

explanations.lesson: Doubled pawns are a price, not a verdict. Ask what was bought with them — and check whether the majority they sit in can still make a passer.

doubled-pawns.definition_short: Two friendly pawns on the same file, usually after a capture. A structural concession that is frequently worth its price.
doubled-pawns.definition_long:
Two pawns of one colour on the same file. They cannot defend each other, because pawns defend diagonally; the rear pawn is blocked by the front one; and a majority containing doubled pawns usually cannot produce a passed pawn without help, which is the most concrete of the drawbacks and the one that decides endgames.

But the capture that doubles them almost always pays for something. The standard compensations: an opened or half-opened file for a rook, the bishop pair, extra control of central squares (doubled c-pawns on c3 and c4 both bear on d4 and d5), and the outposts that the new structure creates. The Nimzo-Indian 4...Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 is the classic bargain — White takes the doubled c-pawns and gets the bishop pair, a half-open b-file and a broader centre.

THIS IS A GENUINE SCHOOL DISAGREEMENT, not vagueness. The classical school (Steinitz, Tarrasch) treated doubled pawns as an objective defect to be avoided. The hypermoderns, Nimzowitsch above all, argued that dynamic factors routinely outweigh static structure. Modern engines side with neither absolutely, and will accept severe pawn defects for activity.

The practical form of the question is almost never 'should I allow doubled pawns' but 'which pawn should I recapture with', and the general answer — recapture towards the centre — has well-known exceptions: not when it tears open your own king's shelter, not when the other capture opens a file you can actually use, and not when it creates a chronic weakness on a file your opponent controls.

early-queen-development.knowledge_type_note: A teaching rule with a real but modest cost, now measured. It is typed rule-of-thumb rather than principle because the penalty is a fraction of a pawn and depends entirely on whether the opponent can actually attack the queen with developing moves.

history.notes: Part of the anonymous standard beginner canon. The underlying idea - that development and time govern the opening - is associated with Morphy, whose style Euwe summarised as rapid development, control of the centre and open lines, but the specific rule about the queen is not traced to him here.

early-queen-development.engine_era_note: Confirmed in direction and quantified in size. Engines consistently prefer minor-piece development to early queen moves in the same position, but by less than the rule's usual phrasing implies. In this base's own test 2.Qh5 - the move beginners are told never to play - is actually evaluated HIGHER than the King's Gambit 2.f4, a respected historical opening.

preconditions: The queen leaves her starting square in the opening
Minor pieces are still largely undeveloped
indicators_for: The opponent can attack the queen with a natural developing move
The queen has no stable square and must move again
The player's other pieces are still at home
indicators_against: No enemy piece can reach the queen with tempo
The queen move creates a real threat that must be answered
The queen move is part of established theory in this opening
The queen recaptures or occupies a square she can hold
false_positive_traps: Many sound openings move the queen early. The Scandinavian's main line brings Black's queen out on move two and is entirely respectable, so the bare fact of an early queen move must never be reported as an error.
The rule is about being attacked with tempo, not about the queen being 'exposed'. If nothing attacks her profitably, there is no penalty.
The measured cost is about 0.68 pawns. Reporting an early queen move in the language of a blunder overstates the evidence.

typical_plans: Develop knights and bishops first and bring the queen out once she has a stable square
typical_moves: Nf3 and Nc3 before Qd2 or Qe2
tactical_consequences: The opponent develops with gain of time while the queen retreats
strategic_consequences: A persistent development deficit, which is what actually costs the evaluation

exceptions: Openings where theory brings the queen out early, such as the Scandinavian after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5. Measured, these do not escape the tempo cost - the Scandinavian concedes about 0.46 more than 1...e5 - they simply accept it as affordable.
Queen moves that create a threat the opponent must answer, which reverses who is gaining tempi.
Positions where no minor piece can attack the queen usefully.
limitations: The penalty is measured in one position (after 1.e4 e5) and one move (2.Qh5). The size of the cost in other openings has not been measured here.
The rule says nothing about queen moves later in the opening, once development is under way.
misconceptions: That an early queen move loses material or the game. In the measured case it costs about two thirds of a pawn.
That the danger is to the queen herself. The queen is rarely trapped; the cost is time.
That the rule is absolute. Several sound openings violate it by design.
That openings which break the rule escape its cost. The Scandinavian pays about 0.46 for its early queen move and is a good opening anyway.

conflicts.resolution: An early queen move that makes a genuine threat gains the initiative and gives tempi rather than losing them. The rule applies only when the opponent can attack the queen with moves that develop; when the queen is the one forcing replies, it is inverted.

examples.note: Anderssen-Kieseritzky, London 1851 - the Immortal Game, before 3...Qh4+. The queen comes out on move three, gives check, and cannot be driven away cheaply because g2-g3 is impossible with the f-pawn gone; White's king is committed to f1 and loses castling. This is the early queen sortie in the most famous game ever played, and the record's own engine_era_note is the right frame for it: engines are far more willing than classical teaching to bring the queen out when concrete lines support it. Here they support it. The engine prefers 3...Nc6 by about a third of a pawn, which is the honest size of the objection - the move is not refuted, it is second best. PROVENANCE. Where no such harassment exists — the Scandinavian after ...Qa5, or 2.Qh5 lines that have concrete point — the objection does not apply. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Tested and only partly as expected, which is why it is recorded as partially resolved. The Scandinavian is a sound opening whose queen comes out on move two, so an early queen move must not be reported as an error - that much holds. But it does NOT escape the tempo cost: White is +0.76 here against +0.30 after 1...e5. The correct statement of the false positive is therefore narrower than first written - the pattern must not be flagged as a mistake, but neither should the base claim such openings pay nothing.

It does bite: White stands at +0.76 here against +0.30 after 1...e5, so Black concedes roughly 0.46 by exactly the mechanism the rule names, and White's best move 3.Nc3 gains the tempo the rule warns about. Filed as ambiguous because the opening is nonetheless entirely sound and played at every level - which makes it evidence that the rule measures a real price rather than evidence that early queen moves are refuted.

by_level.beginner: Bring your knights and bishops out first. If the queen comes out early, your opponent attacks her and develops at the same time.
by_level.intermediate: An early queen sortie usually loses time, because the opponent hits her with moves they wanted to play anyway.
by_level.advanced: The cost is tempo, not danger. It only applies where the opponent can attack her with developing moves - plenty of sound openings move the queen early.
by_level.master: Worth roughly two thirds of a pawn in the standard test case. Directionally right, routinely overstated.

by_depth.short: Develop the minor pieces before the queen.
by_depth.normal: Bringing the queen out early usually costs time: she has to retreat from any piece that attacks her, and if attacking her is a move the opponent wanted to play anyway, they develop while you shuffle.
by_depth.deep: The mechanism is tempo rather than danger. The queen outvalues everything that can attack her, so she must always retreat, and if the attacking move also develops a piece, the exchange of time is one-sided. Measured here: after 1.e4 e5, Stockfish at depth 26 puts 2.Nf3 at +0.30 and 2.Qh5 at -0.38, a swing of 0.68 pawns - real, consistent, and considerably smaller than the rule's usual phrasing suggests. The condition is whether the queen can be attacked with tempo at all; where she cannot, the rule does not apply, which is why sound openings such as the Scandinavian bring the queen out on move two without objection.

explanations.hedge: A rule of thumb with a measured cost of roughly two thirds of a pawn in the standard case; several sound openings break it deliberately.
explanations.lesson: The question is not whether the queen is out early but whether the opponent can attack her with a move they wanted to play anyway.

early-queen-development.definition_short: Developing the queen before the minor pieces usually loses time, because the opponent gains tempi by attacking her with moves they wanted to play anyway.
early-queen-development.definition_long:
The most-repeated rule in beginner instruction, and one of the few whose cost this base has measured directly.

THE MECHANISM is tempo, not danger. The queen is worth more than every piece that can attack her, so she must retreat from any attack. If the attacking move is one the opponent wanted to play in any case — a knight or bishop coming to a natural square — then the attack is free for them and the retreat is not free for you. The opponent develops; you shuffle. Nothing is hanging and nothing is lost, which is why the penalty is a matter of a fraction of a pawn rather than of material.

THE MEASURED COST: in the position after 1.e4 e5, Stockfish 18 at depth 26 evaluates 2.Nf3 at +0.30 and 2.Qh5 at -0.38 — a swing of 0.68 pawns. That is a genuine and consistent penalty, and it is also a good deal smaller than the rule's tone in most primers suggests. An early queen move costs about two thirds of a pawn, not the game.

THE CONDITION is whether the queen can be attacked with tempo, and the standard counterexample turns out to be more interesting than it is usually presented. The Scandinavian brings Black's queen out on move two and is a thoroughly respectable defence - but measured, it PAYS the cost the rule predicts. After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5, White stands at +0.76, against +0.30 for the mainstream 1...e5. Black concedes about 0.46 by the same mechanism the rule describes, and 3.Nc3 hitting the queen is exactly how. The honest conclusion is not that the rule fails here but that the cost is AFFORDABLE: +0.76 is a playable position, and a sound opening may pay a tempo for something it wants. The rule identifies a real price; it does not decide whether the price is worth paying.

en-passant.knowledge_type_note: Official rule, quoted verbatim from the authentic English text.
en-passant.definition_short: A pawn that has just advanced two squares may be captured, on the very next move only, by an enemy pawn beside it, as though it had advanced one square.
en-passant.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 3.7.3.1: 'A pawn occupying a square on the same rank as and on an adjacent file to an opponent's pawn which has just advanced two squares in one move from its original square may capture this opponent's pawn as though the latter had been moved only one square.' Art. 3.7.3.2: 'This capture is only legal on the move following this advance and is called an en passant capture.'

The right expires immediately. It exists so that the two-square first move cannot be used to run a pawn past an enemy pawn that would have been able to capture it had it advanced one square at a time.

history.notes: The modern rule dates from the introduction of the two-square pawn advance in late-medieval Europe, but no origin research has been done for this record yet. Only the current codification is cited.

preconditions: The immediately preceding move was an enemy pawn advancing two squares
A friendly pawn stands on an adjacent file, on the same rank as that pawn
indicators_for: The position's en-passant target square is set
indicators_against: Any other move has intervened since the two-square advance

exceptions: Cannot be deferred: the right is lost if not exercised immediately.
Like any move, it is illegal if it leaves or places one's own king in check.
limitations: Affects repetition claims: see Art. 9.2.3.1 — two positions are not the same if, at the start of the sequence, a pawn could have been captured en passant.
Reported only when the capture is AVAILABLE. A FEN carries an en-passant target square whether or not any pawn can use it, and most that do are the second kind.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

No engine was consulted, because no engine is needed to establish that a legal move exists. A REAL GAME FOR A RULE, which sounds like a small thing and is not. Every other position on this record was constructed to show the rule, and a constructed position can show a rule that never comes up. It is reported at HIGH confidence, which is right: this is not a judgement, it is a legal fact, and the matcher checks that the capture is actually AVAILABLE rather than that the FEN carries a target square - a FEN carries one whether or not anything can use it.

The geometry is identical to the position where exd6 is legal and the difference is one field of the FEN. This record's indicator_against says it: 'any other move has intervened since the two-square advance.' The right to capture en passant exists for exactly one move and this base reads it from the target square rather than from the picture.

Registered false-positive case `an-en-passant-window-that-has-closed`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A white pawn on e5 stands beside a black pawn on d5. That is the picture of an en-passant capture and it is the position the rule is drawn in every textbook. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's only indicator_against: "Any other move has intervened since the two-square advance." The right to capture lasts exactly one move, and the FEN records that in one field. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Two FENs, one character apart. With the en-passant field set to `-`, this base's move generator produces six legal moves and none of them is exd6. With the field set to `d6` it produces seven, and the seventh is exd6. The board is identical in both. This is the sharpest available illustration of the `notation` record's third trap — 'a FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one' — and of why en-passant cannot be read off a diagram.

by_level.beginner: That pawn just jumped two squares past yours, so you may take it as if it had only moved one — but only right now.
by_level.intermediate: En passant: the two-square advance does not let a pawn slip past an adjacent enemy pawn. The capture is available on this move only.
by_level.advanced: En passant capture (Art. 3.7.3). Note it also affects position identity for repetition claims under Art. 9.2.3.1.

by_depth.short: A pawn that just advanced two squares may be taken as though it had advanced one — this move only.
by_depth.normal: En passant: when a pawn advances two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved one square. The right lasts exactly one move and then disappears.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 3.7.3. The one-move window is why the right is part of the POSITION rather than of the board: two identical arrangements of men are different positions if one carries an en-passant target and the other does not, which Art. 9.2.3.1 makes explicit for repetition claims. This base's registered case is two FENs one character apart — with the field set to `-` the move generator gives six legal moves and none of them is the capture; with it set, seven.

endgame-principles.knowledge_type_note: An umbrella record naming the standard principles and pointing at the concepts that hold the detail and the exceptions.

attributions.note: Endgame Strategy sets out the four principles as an organising scheme; he states them as four and this record follows his enumeration.

history.notes: None of the individual principles originates with Shereshevsky - two weaknesses in particular has a longer and disputed history recorded on its own concept - but the grouping into four is his and is quoted from his own preface.

endgame-principles.engine_era_note: The endgame is the phase where engines and tablebases have most changed what can be asserted. Principles that were previously supported by authority alone can now be tested, and several have not survived unchanged.

preconditions: Few pieces remain
Queens usually exchanged
Promotion rather than mate is the governing objective
indicators_for: The king can move without being attacked
Passed pawns or pawn majorities exist
indicators_against: Queens remain and mating attacks are still live
false_positive_traps: The boundary is not sharp. A queenless position with many pieces may still be a middlegame, and treating it as an endgame is how kings get mated.
These are organising ideas, not a substitute for calculation. Every one of them has recorded exceptions, several proven by tablebase in this base.

typical_plans: Activate the king
Create a second weakness and attack on two fronts
Improve every piece before committing
Decide the target arrangement, then find the route to it
typical_pawn_structures: Pawn majorities capable of producing a passed pawn
strategic_consequences: Small advantages that are meaningless in a middlegame become decisive

exceptions: Do not hurry does not apply against a concrete threat or in a race, where a single tempo decides.
Centralisation of the king has documented failures in rook endings, recorded on its own concept.
Simplification, the other common endgame reflex, can convert a proven win into a proven draw - this base holds tablebase proofs of exactly that.
limitations: This is an umbrella record. The detail and the exceptions live on the individual concepts.
Where a position is small enough, principles are unnecessary: the position can simply be solved.
Rests substantially on a single source (Shereshevsky), which is why the source confidence is medium despite that source being a primary text read directly.
misconceptions: That endgames are simple because few pieces remain. They are the most exact phase, which is the opposite of forgiving.
That trading into an endgame is safe when ahead. Which endgame is reached decides, and several are proven draws a piece down.

examples.note: Capablanca-Tartakower, New York 1924, 35.Kg3 - the position every endgame book uses for the first principle of the phase, which is that the king is a fighting piece once the queens are off. Chernev: 'Le roi s'amuse! The King is headed for B6 (f6), a square from which he can assist the White Rook in threats of mate, and also help the passed pawn take those last three steps.' Capablanca gives up three pawns on the way. The point is not that the king is safe; it is that safety has stopped being the question, which is the difference between this phase and the middlegame that the record is about.
examples.attributed_by: Irving Chernev - corpus entry capablanca-tartakower-1924-35Kg3-king-activation

engine.verdict_note: +3.14 at depth 24, and the engine's own first move is 35.Kg3. Three pawns' worth, for a king march that costs three pawns.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `endgame-principles-with-the-queens-on`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A simplified position: no minor pieces, a rook and a queen each, pawns on both wings, and nothing tactical happening. It looks like the point at which endgame technique takes over. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The queens are still on the board, and the first principle on this record — that the king is a fighting piece — is a statement about what becomes true ONCE the queens are off. Walking the king up here loses it. Every other principle on the record inherits the same precondition: king activity, the outside passer, the race, all of them assume no queen is available to punish the king. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing at all here, and `endgame-principles` has no matcher. What makes the case worth registering is that phase is not a property a piece count settles: this position has fewer men than many endgames in this base and is not one. Stockfish 18 at depth 20: 0.00, and its line doubles rooks rather than touching the king. This record's positive example is Capablanca marching his king up the board for three pawns — in a position with no queens.

ambiguous_examples.note: The first principle of the endgame is that the king is a fighting piece, and this record's positive example is Capablanca marching his king up the board at the cost of three pawns. Here the white king is doing the opposite and it is the only reason the position is not lost: it stands on a6 shielding a rook pawn, does nothing, goes nowhere, and holds a draw against a whole queen. Activating it loses at once. Filed as ambiguous rather than negative because the principle is not wrong here so much as silent - 'the king is a fighting piece' is a statement about what the king MAY do once the queens are off, and this position is the case where what it may do is stand still.

by_level.beginner: In the endgame: use your king, make more than one target, and take your time.
by_level.intermediate: Four ideas govern endgames - centralise the king, create a second weakness, do not hurry, and think in target positions rather than move by move.
by_level.advanced: Do not hurry means improve everything improvable first; thinking in schemes means decide the arrangement you want, then find the route.
by_level.master: The one phase where claims can be proven rather than argued, and where several standard rules do not survive being checked.

by_depth.short: Active king, two weaknesses, do not hurry, think in schemes.
by_depth.normal: The ideas that govern endgame play: centralise the king, create a second weakness so a finite defence is stretched past breaking, do not hurry - improve everything before committing - and think in schemes, deciding the arrangement you want to reach rather than calculating move by move.
by_depth.deep: An endgame has arrived when material is limited, the king becomes a fighting piece, and promotion rather than mate is the objective - the second being the real marker. Four principles organise the phase, and the fourth is the least known and most useful: thinking in schemes means choosing the piece arrangement you want and then finding the route, which suits endgames because the piece count is low and the target is often recognisable. What separates this phase from every other is that truth is available - positions of seven pieces or fewer are solved - so claims can be checked rather than argued, and several standard teachings have not survived the check.

explanations.lesson: In the endgame you can often find the truth instead of reasoning towards it. Where you can, do.

endgame-principles.definition_short: The small set of ideas that govern play once queens and most pieces are off: an active king, two weaknesses, not hurrying, and thinking in schemes.
endgame-principles.definition_long:
WHEN AN ENDGAME HAS ARRIVED is itself a judgement rather than a fact, and the working test used in the literature has three parts: material is limited, the king becomes an active fighting piece, and the governing objective shifts from attacking the king to promoting a pawn. The second is the one that really marks the change.

THE FOUR PRINCIPLES, as Shereshevsky sets them out:
1. CENTRALISATION OF THE KING. The king stops hiding and starts working.
2. THE PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES. One weakness can usually be held; a second on the far side of the board stretches a finite defence until it breaks.
3. 'DO NOT HURRY'. Improve everything improvable before committing to a concrete operation. Endgames reward patience because the defender rarely has counterplay to punish it, and a position played out too fast throws away the free improvements.
4. THINKING IN SCHEMES. Decide what arrangement of your pieces you want to reach, then work out how to get there — as against calculating move by move from where you stand. Endgames are peculiarly suited to this because the piece count is low and the target arrangement is often recognisable.

WHAT MAKES ENDGAMES DIFFERENT is that they are the one phase where truth is available. Positions of seven pieces or fewer are solved, so a claim about them can be checked rather than argued, and this base has used that repeatedly — including to disprove a rule of Tarrasch's and to correct a piece of standard teaching about triangulation. Endgame principles are therefore held here to a higher evidential standard than any other part of the taxonomy, because they can be.

THE MATCHING WARNING is that endgames are concrete. Every principle in this list has proven exceptions recorded against it, several of them established by tablebase in this base.

exceptions-to-rules.knowledge_type_note: A meta-record describing how this base handles the relationship between rules and their exceptions, and indexing the exceptions themselves.

history.notes: A meta-record about this base's own method; no external history.

exceptions-to-rules.engine_era_note: The engine era is why a good many of these exceptions are provable rather than arguable. Before tablebases, 'the rook belongs behind the passed pawn' could only be met with a counter-opinion; now it can be met with a proof that the same position is a draw one way and a loss in 63 the other.

preconditions: A principle is being applied to a position
false_positive_traps: An exception existing does not make a rule useless. Most of these rules are correct in the large majority of positions.
The absence of a recorded exception means this base has not found one, not that none exists.

typical_plans: Record the exception with the rule, never separately
Prefer a source's own statement of its condition over a later paraphrase
Where two principles conflict, record the resolution rather than dropping one

exceptions: Official rules of chess and proven results have no exceptions, and are typed so that the test suite does not demand any.
Mechanical tactical motifs have conditions rather than exceptions - a fork either exists on the board or does not.
limitations: Exceptions are only as complete as the research behind them; this base does not claim its lists are exhaustive and says so on individual concepts.
The index does not currently distinguish exceptions proven by measurement from those resting on authority, which is a known gap.

Counts in this record are stated as floors ('over N') rather than exact figures, because the base grows and an exact count written into prose silently becomes false. The live figures are in state/warnings_index.json and state/coverage.json.
misconceptions: That a principle with many exceptions is a bad principle. It may simply be a well-studied one.
That listing exceptions is hedging. It is the part that makes the rule applicable.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Here is a position where the most-quoted rule in rook endings fails: the defending rook is behind the passed pawn, exactly as Tarrasch prescribed, and Black is lost. A recorded exception to a recorded rule. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own first trap: "An exception existing does not make a rule useless. Most of these rules are correct in the large majority of positions." Finding this position does not license reporting the rule as unreliable, and the record exists to hold the two claims apart — 254 exceptions are recorded here precisely so that rules can be applied safely rather than abandoned. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN WIN in 63 for the attacker, with the defending rook obeying the rule. The API reports the position's features and makes no claim about rules at all, which is the only correct behaviour: `exceptions-to-rules` is a record ABOUT this base's other records rather than about boards, and a system that reported it would be reporting on itself. Read against the same position with that rook on f6, active on the sixth — the Vancura defence, a proven draw. One rook move between the rule failing and the rule being irrelevant, and neither of them is the rule being wrong.

by_level.beginner: Chess rules have exceptions, and knowing them is part of knowing the rule.
by_level.intermediate: A principle without its exceptions cannot be applied safely - the exception tells you the condition.
by_level.advanced: Three kinds: conditions the author stated and retelling dropped, proven counterexamples, and conflicts between two sound rules.
by_level.master: The third kind is the hard one, and is why every concept here carries an explicit conflicts list with a written resolution.

by_depth.short: Every principle here records where it fails.
by_depth.normal: A structural commitment of this base: every soft-typed concept must record its exceptions - over 250 so far - and the test suite fails the build if one does not. The exception is where the information is, because it shows the condition under which the rule applies.
by_depth.deep: A rule that holds everywhere tells you nothing about any particular position; what makes a principle usable is knowing its conditions, and conditions are only visible from the cases where the rule breaks. Three kinds are distinguished here. Conditions the original author stated and later retelling dropped - both worst-piece formulations are conditional, and Shereshevsky documents rook endings where his own first principle simply fails. Proven counterexamples, where a tablebase or controlled comparison settles the matter rather than an opinion. And conflicts between two sound principles pointing opposite ways, which is the hardest kind and is recorded structurally, each concept carrying a conflicts list with a written resolution so a caller meeting two applicable concepts has something better than a coin toss.

explanations.lesson: Learn the condition, not the slogan.

beginner_words: when this rule does not apply

exceptions-to-rules.definition_short: Every principle here carries its exceptions - 254 recorded - because a rule without them cannot be applied safely.
exceptions-to-rules.definition_long:
A structural commitment of this knowledge base rather than a chess idea. Every concept typed as a principle, rule of thumb, guideline or positional concept must record where it fails, and the test suite enforces it: a soft-typed concept with no recorded exception fails the build.

THE REASON IS THAT THE EXCEPTION IS WHERE THE INFORMATION IS. A rule that holds everywhere tells you nothing about any particular position; what makes a principle usable is knowing the conditions under which it applies, and those conditions are only visible from the outside — from the cases where it breaks.

THE THREE KINDS this base distinguishes:
1. CONDITIONS THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR STATED and later retelling dropped. Anderssen's and Makogonov's worst-piece rules both carry explicit preconditions; Shereshevsky documents rook endings where his own first principle fails.
2. PROVEN COUNTEREXAMPLES, where a tablebase or a controlled engine comparison settles it. Tarrasch's rook rule, the check that loses, doubled pawns, the piece moved twice.
3. CONFLICTS BETWEEN PRINCIPLES, where two sound rules point opposite ways and the resolution is a further judgement — king safety against king activity, simplify against complicate when worse, material against activity.

THE THIRD KIND IS THE HARDEST and is recorded structurally: concepts carry an explicit conflicts list, each with a written resolution, so that a caller meeting two applicable concepts has something better than a coin toss.

All 254 exceptions are compiled into state/warnings_index.json alongside the misconceptions and detector traps.

exchange-sacrifice.knowledge_type_note: A strategic method: it prescribes converting a specific, small material deficit into a specific kind of asset. Spielmann gave it a chapter of its own, classified by the material given rather than by object, because the trade-off is unusually consistent.

attributions.note: Gave it a chapter of its own, classified by material given rather than by object.
Raised it to a positional art form; devoted a chapter of one of his own books to it.

history.notes: Both attributions are secure as relations but neither is a claim of invention — players gave up the exchange long before either wrote about it. Petrosian's association is with the positional USE, not with the idea.

development.change: Classified as its own category.
Becomes a standing positional method rather than a tactical device.
Neural-network evaluation values the resulting compensation much more highly than classical material-weighted search, endorsing many exchange sacrifices earlier engines rejected.

exchange-sacrifice.engine_era_note: Older engines systematically undervalued exchange sacrifices because a rook outweighs a minor piece in any material table. Neural-network evaluation weighs the compensating factors directly and endorses far more of them. This is one of the clearest cases where engine progress changed an assessment rather than confirming it.

preconditions: A rook is given for a knight or bishop
indicators_for: The captured minor piece was the defender of a colour complex or a key square
The capture permanently damages the enemy pawn structure
The remaining rook has no open file to work on, so the material lost had no role
A knight obtains a square no pawn can challenge
The enemy bishop pair is broken up
indicators_against: Open files exist for the rooks, so a rook is worth more than the table says
The compensation is an attack that can be defused, rather than a static asset
The opponent can return the exchange to liquidate favourably
The position is simplifying and no asset survives
false_positive_traps: THE MAIN ONE: a rook given up inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice, not a positional exchange sacrifice, even though the material given is identical. The engine test on puzzle mi-bb512d9713 in this record is exactly that case — tagged exchangeSacrifice, actually mate in 2.
Detecting 'rook for minor piece' is mechanical; deciding it was POSITIONAL requires that no forced return exists, which the material test cannot see.
In an open position with files for the rooks, the same trade can simply be bad.

typical_plans: Capture the knight defending a colour complex, then occupy it
Take on c3 to double the c-pawns and take the dark squares
Remove the piece blockading a passed pawn
Defensively, give the exchange to eliminate the opponent's most dangerous attacker
typical_moves: ...Rxc3 in Sicilian structures
...Rxe4
Rxf6 destroying the knight that guards the dark squares
typical_pawn_structures: Sicilian structures where ...Rxc3 leaves doubled, fixed c-pawns
Closed positions where the rooks have no files
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight installed on a square no pawn can attack, paid for with the exchange
tactical_consequences: Can also occur inside a forced mating line, where it is a sham sacrifice
strategic_consequences: The material deficit is small enough to be outweighed by one permanent asset
Closed positions reduce a rook's value, which is what makes the trade affordable

exceptions: In open positions with files available, a rook is worth more than the nominal margin and the sacrifice is correspondingly worse.
Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.
An exchange sacrifice inside a forced mate is not a positional sacrifice at all, whatever it is tagged.
limitations: The material pattern is mechanically detectable; its CLASSIFICATION as positional is not.
Confidence is medium: 'rook for minor piece' fires reliably, 'and it was positional' does not.

Fires on 1.0% of the 788 shipped positions with the solution move supplied, and on Reshevsky-Petrosian 1953 at 25...Re6, which is the game this concept is usually taught from. It requires the rook to be winnable where it lands and the cheapest attacker to be a MINOR piece - a rook taken by a rook is a trade. The record's main trap stands and is not detectable: a rook given inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice with identical material.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'in an open position with files for the rooks, the same trade can simply be bad' is not implemented. It could be approximated by counting open files, and was not, because the concept fires on 1.0% of the 788 shipped positions and a threshold fitted to eight cases is a threshold fitted to nothing. Recorded rather than guessed at.

The opponent can return the exchange to liquidate favourably: stated on this record as an indicator_against and NOT built, because giving the exchange back is a move at least two plies out and whether the liquidation is favourable is an evaluation, not a board fact. The two conditions beside it are answered instead: whether there is a STATIC asset is read off the position after the move - doubled pawns, the bishop pair, a passed pawn, a permanent hole - and when there is none the card says the compensation is an attack and that an attack can be defused; and 'the position is simplifying and no asset survives' is read off how much material is left. Neither is a guard, for the reason this record already gives about its first indicator: the exchange WAS given, and refusing to name the move because the position looks unfavourable for it would be judging the move rather than naming it.
misconceptions: That an exchange sacrifice is always positional. It is frequently just a mating combination.
That Petrosian invented it. He popularised its positional use.
That the exchange is worth a fixed amount. Its value depends on whether the rook would have had a file.

examples.note: The position immediately after 25...Re6, the move usually called the first modern positional exchange sacrifice. The rook steps onto a square where White's bishop can take it, and Petrosian is not calculating a combination — Kasparov's judgement is that he sacrificed 'for the sake of quality of position'. His own reasoning, as reported by Watson, was that he disliked his position, foresaw h4 provoking a kingside weakness, and wanted a knight on d5; vacating e7 was the way to get one there. FEN derived by replaying all 81 plies through the page's own move generator.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-rook-given-inside-a-mate`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Rxd5 hands over a rook for a knight. That is the material transaction the concept names, and it is available and correct. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's MAIN trap, in its own words: "a rook given up inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice, not a positional exchange sacrifice, even though the material given is identical." The point of Rxd5 is not a long-term asset — it is that the rook on d8 cannot recapture, because Re8 would then be mate. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report exchange-sacrifice. It reports back-rank-mate, hanging-piece and sacrifice, which between them describe what is actually happening. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says +6.73 and its own line is Rxd5 followed by ...Rb8 — Black DECLINES the recapture and is simply a knight down. This position is `overloading`'s positive example, and the two records reading the same board differently is the point: what the exchange record would have to claim is that a rook was invested in a position, and what happened is that a rook was never taken.

ambiguous_examples.note: Real position from the shipped middlegame ladder (puzzle mi-bb512d9713), tagged `exchangeSacrifice` by the repository's own pipeline. Black plays Re1+ giving the rook, and Bxe1 is forced. Included as the concept's principal FALSE-POSITIVE case.

engine.verdict_note: Re1+ is MATE IN TWO (Re1+ Kf2 Re2#). The material given is a rook for a bishop, so the mechanical 'exchange sacrifice' test fires correctly — but this is a MATING sacrifice, sham in Spielmann's sense, not a positional exchange sacrifice. Recorded as `contradicts` deliberately: it shows the material pattern alone cannot establish the concept, and that using corpus tags as ground truth for 'positional exchange sacrifice' would produce false matches. The alternative Rxe2 loses to mate in 14, so the move is also uniquely correct.

by_level.beginner: This gives a rook for a smaller piece. That normally loses material, but here it buys something worth more.
by_level.intermediate: An exchange sacrifice: rook for a minor piece. First check whether it is forced — if mate or material follows by force, calculate it. If not, name the lasting asset it buys.
by_level.advanced: Rook for minor. The margin is small enough that one permanent asset — a colour complex, a fixed structural wound, an unassailable knight — can outweigh it, especially where the rooks have no open files.
by_level.master: Petrosian's instrument. Price it by what the rook would actually have done: in a closed position with no files, the nominal deficit is not an operative one.

by_depth.short: A rook given for a minor piece, in return for {asset}.
by_depth.normal: An exchange sacrifice — rook for knight or bishop, about a pawn and a half. That margin is small enough to be outweighed by a permanent asset such as {asset}, particularly when the rooks have no open files to work on.
by_depth.deep: The smallest material investment that buys a real positional asset, which is why it is the most common positional sacrifice. Spielmann gave it its own chapter and Petrosian made it a standing method. The critical distinction is one the name hides: an exchange sacrifice can be sham or real. A rook given inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice that happens to cost the exchange; a rook given for a dark-square grip is a positional one. Most software tags both identically. Modern neural-network evaluation endorses far more exchange sacrifices than earlier engines did, because it weighs the compensation directly rather than counting material.

explanations.lesson: Before calling a rook-for-minor trade a positional sacrifice, check whether anything is forced. If mate or material comes back by force, it is a combination, not a positional decision.

beginner_words: giving a rook for a smaller piece
avoid: the exchange is worth 1.5 pawns (as a fixed fact)

exchange-sacrifice.definition_short: Giving a rook for a minor piece — roughly a pawn and a half of material — in return for squares, structure or the neutralisation of the opponent's best piece.
exchange-sacrifice.definition_long:
The smallest material investment that buys a genuine positional asset, which is why it is the most common positional sacrifice and the one strong players make most readily. A rook is worth about a pawn and a half more than a knight or bishop, and that margin is small enough to be outweighed by a permanent square, a wrecked structure, or the removal of a defender.

Spielmann treated it separately from his object-based taxonomy, classifying it by the material given up rather than by aim. Petrosian made it a standing strategic instrument rather than an occasional device, and is the player the idea is now attached to.

IT IS NOT ONE THING. An exchange sacrifice can be sham or real in Spielmann's sense, and the difference matters more here than the name does. A rook given to force mate in two is a MATING sacrifice that happens to cost the exchange; a rook given for a dark-square grip that will still matter in forty moves is a positional sacrifice. Both are tagged the same way by most software, including this repository's puzzle generator, and confusing them is the principal false-positive risk for this concept.

The classic vehicles are ...Rxc3 in Sicilian structures, wrecking the queenside pawns and seizing the dark squares, and ...Rxe4 type captures giving the exchange for a pawn, the bishop pair and a better structure.

fifty-move-rule.knowledge_type_note: Official rule. The tablebase point is a genuine conflict between rule (A) and proven result (B) and is recorded as such.
fifty-move-rule.definition_short: A player to move may CLAIM a draw when the last 50 moves by each player have been made with no pawn move and no capture.
fifty-move-rule.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 9.3: the game is drawn on a correct claim if the player indicates a move that 'will result in the last 50 moves by each player having been made without the movement of any pawn and without any capture' (9.3.1), or if 'the last 50 moves by each player have been completed without the movement of any pawn and without any capture' (9.3.2).

'50 moves by each player' means 100 ply. Any capture or any pawn move resets the count. Like threefold repetition it is a claim, not automatic — Art. 9.6.2 supplies the automatic version at 75.

Historically FIDE granted exceptions for specific endgames later shown by tablebases to need more than 50 moves; those exceptions were removed, so some theoretically won endings are drawn under the current Laws.

history.notes: History of the exception list not yet researched for this record.

preconditions: 100 ply have elapsed with no capture and no pawn move
indicators_against: Any capture or pawn move in that span resets the counter
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: fifty-move-rule, over the halfmove clock

exceptions: Not automatic — it must be claimed.
Some endgames proven winnable by tablebase require more than 50 moves and are therefore drawn under the Laws. The rule and the theoretical truth genuinely diverge here.
limitations: Reported from 80 ply, because a count of 4 is not news and a count of 92 is.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

examples.note: The positive half of the controlled pair, and the tablebase gives it the best possible label: CURSED-WIN. White mates in 21, and the fifty-move rule takes the win away - the position is a theoretical win that the rule converts into a draw. The identical board with the halfmove clock at zero is an ordinary win. Nothing on the board distinguishes them.

tablebase.note: PROVEN: cursed-win, dtz 21. 'Cursed' is Syzygy's word for exactly this - a win that the fifty-move rule spoils. There is no stronger illustration of the concept available, because the tablebase is naming the rule's effect rather than a position's evaluation.

examples.note:
EIGHTY PLY WITH NO CAPTURE AND NO PAWN MOVE, in a game somebody actually played to move 123. The halfmove clock in the FEN is the rule: it counts what the rule counts and it resets on exactly what the rule resets on, which is why this record's indicator_against - 'any capture or pawn move in that span resets the counter' - needs no separate test.

The matcher reports from 80 rather than from 1, because a count of 4 is not news, and a position at 80 is one where a player should be counting. This is what that looks like on a real board: two knights and a pawn, neither side able to force anything, the clock at 80 and twenty ply left.

PROVENANCE. Found by tools/harvest_games.js. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator, which is also what makes the halfmove clock trustworthy - it was computed by playing the game, not copied from a source.

counterexamples.note: The same board on move 99 with the halfmove clock at ZERO instead of 99. Nothing about the pieces has changed and the rule is nowhere near applying: the record's indicator_against - 'any capture or pawn move in that span resets the counter' - is the whole of the difference, and it is carried in one FEN field that a reader looking at a diagram cannot see. Move numbers are not the fifty-move rule; the halfmove clock is.

Registered false-positive case `a-counter-about-to-be-reset`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The halfmove clock reads 96. Two more moves each and either side may claim a draw. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's only indicator_against: "Any capture or pawn move in that span resets the counter." White is in check and has exactly one legal move, Kxg2, which is a capture. The counter goes back to zero on the next ply and the claim never becomes available. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The move generator produces one legal move, h1g2, and it is a capture. The matcher does report fifty-move-rule here — correctly, because what it says is '96 ply have passed with no capture and no pawn move; at 100 either side may claim a draw', which is true and is a statement about the count rather than a prediction. This case is registered to hold that distinction in place: the concept is about a counter, the counter is at 96, and whether it ever reaches 100 is a question about the game and not about the position. A matcher that tried to predict it would be guessing.

by_level.beginner: Fifty moves have gone by for each side with no capture and no pawn move, so a draw can be claimed.
by_level.intermediate: The fifty-move rule. Any capture or pawn move resets the counter, and the draw must be claimed.
by_level.advanced: Art. 9.3. Note the divergence from tablebase truth in long theoretical endings.

by_depth.short: After fifty moves each with no capture and no pawn move, either player may claim a draw.
by_depth.normal: The fifty-move rule: a player to move may CLAIM a draw when the last fifty moves by each side have passed with no capture and no pawn move. It is a claim and not an automatic result — the game continues if nobody makes it.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 9.3. The counter is the halfmove clock in the FEN, and any capture or any pawn move resets it to zero, which is the whole of the rule's second half. Two things are worth keeping separate from it. The seventy-five-move rule at Art. 9.6.2 is automatic and needs no claim. And tablebase truth diverges from both: several theoretical endings are won and need more than fifty moves, so a proven win can be a drawn game.

audit_notes: 2026-09-01: detector field named 'halfmoveClock', which does not exist anywhere in the codebase. The audit's hardcoded whitelist had been accepting it. Repointed at real code, or marked as proposed where nothing implements it.

fivefold-repetition.knowledge_type_note: Official rule; the automatic counterpart to the claimable Art. 9.2.
fivefold-repetition.definition_short: If the same position appears five times, the game is drawn automatically — no claim needed.
fivefold-repetition.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 9.6.1: the game is drawn if 'the same position has appeared, as in 9.2.2 at least five times.' Unlike threefold repetition this needs no claim and no agreement; it happens by force of the Laws. Introduced so that a game cannot continue indefinitely when neither player claims.

THE COUNT IS THE ONLY DIFFERENCE from Art. 9.2, and that is worth stating plainly because the two rules are otherwise identical. Position identity is the same term of art at 9.2.3: the same men on the same squares, the same side to move, the same castling rights, and the same en-passant possibility. Two of those four are invisible on a diagram, which is why this base's example for both rules is a SEQUENCE rather than a position - sixteen plies replayed through the move generator, in which the starting position recurs five times.

WHY IT EXISTS. The threefold claim was being missed in practice, and declined in practice: a player who has not noticed cannot claim, and a player who is winning has no reason to. The fivefold rule makes the outcome independent of both players and of the arbiter's attention. The seventy-five-move rule at Art. 9.6.2 is its counterpart on the other counter, and both were added in the same revision for the same reason.

preconditions: The same position, by the Art. 9.2.3 test, has occurred five times

limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

examples.pgn: 1. Ra2 Kd8 2. Ra1 Ke8 3. Ra2 Kd8 4. Ra1 Ke8 5. Ra2 Kd8 6. Ra1 Ke8 7. Ra2 Kd8 8. Ra1 Ke8
examples.note: The same line as the threefold example, carried to eight moves, and deliberately the same position: the two rules differ only in the count and in who has to speak. Threefold is a CLAIM a player may make; fivefold is automatic and the arbiter ends the game whether anyone notices or not. Replayed through this base's move generator: every move legal, the starting position recurring five times.

counterexamples.note: Constructed, and it is a SEQUENCE because the rule is about history. From r3k2r/8/8/8/8/8/8/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1 both sides move a rook out and back: 1.Rg1 Rg8 2.Rh1 Rh8. Every man is on the square it started on and the position has NOT repeated, because both sides have lost the right to castle kingside - the FEN reads `w Qq - 4 3` where it read `w KQkq - 0 1`. FIDE Art. 9.2.3 includes castling rights in the definition of the same position, so a diagram that looks identical is a different position and no claim exists. This is the exact error the `notation` record's third trap names: a FEN without the castling, en-passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one. The four moves were played through this base's own move generator, which emitted both FENs. The fivefold rule inherits the same definition of identity and therefore the same negative: a board that returns to its starting arrangement five times has still repeated nothing if a castling right was lost on the way.

by_level.beginner: The same position has appeared five times, so the game is automatically a draw.
by_level.intermediate: Fivefold repetition ends the game at once, with no claim required.

by_depth.short: The same position five times ends the game automatically.
by_depth.normal: Fivefold repetition: once the same position has occurred five times, the arbiter declares the game drawn. Unlike the threefold rule, nobody has to claim it and nobody has to notice.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 9.6.1. It differs from Art. 9.2 in the count and in who must speak, and in nothing else — position identity is the same term of art, including the castling and en-passant riders. The pair exists because the threefold claim was being missed or declined in practice; the fivefold rule makes the outcome independent of the players. This base files the two rules on the same replayed line for that reason.
