There is no further research to do, and padding it to match the median would add words without adding knowledge. Short is the correct length here.

validation_na.false_positive_test: N/A rather than missing. A registered false-positive case is a position where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is absent, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This concept is DECIDED BY THE MOVE GENERATOR - the same function that decides it in a game - so there is no judgement to get wrong and no surface pattern that can be present without the thing itself. The nearest genuine risk is a PATTERN NAME attached to a position that is check and not mate, and that risk belongs to `back-rank-mate` and `smothered-mate`, both of which carry a registered case for it.

forcing-moves.knowledge_type_note: A rule about what to look at first, not a claim that forcing moves are good. Its whole value is in ordering the search.

attributions.note: Gives examining the most forcing line first among his rules for calculating variations.

history.notes: Anonymous standard advice with no traceable coinage; the named sources state it rather than originate it.

forcing-moves.engine_era_note: Engines order their search by much the same logic, extending forcing lines further than quiet ones, which is a rare case of human calculation advice and machine implementation converging on the same principle for the same reason.

preconditions: A check, capture or direct threat is available to either side
indicators_for: The opponent's king can be checked
A capture changes the material balance
A threat cannot be met without concession
recognition.detector: legal move generation; findMotifs for threats
false_positive_traps: Forcing is not the same as good, and this is the trap that matters. This base holds a proven position in which one check draws and another loses.
The rule is about search order, not move choice. Reporting 'it is forcing' as a reason a move is strong misuses it entirely.
Applying it only to your own moves is how calculated lines get refuted; the opponent's forcing replies are the ones that overturn analysis.

typical_plans: Examine checks, then captures, then threats, before quiet moves
Check the opponent's forcing replies before committing
Use a forcing sequence to reach a position you can evaluate
typical_moves: Checks
Captures
Direct threats against a piece or square
tactical_consequences: Forcing sequences are where combinations are found, because the opponent's options are constrained
strategic_consequences: A forcing line spends the position's tension and cannot be taken back

exceptions: Quiet positions may contain no useful forcing move at all, and the search then has to be conducted differently.
Nunn's goal-seeking case: some strong moves make no sense except as part of a whole operation and will never appear in a forcing-move scan.
limitations: The rule orders the search and does not evaluate anything.
Detecting checks and captures is mechanical; detecting threats is not, and the threat half is the weakest.
misconceptions: That forcing moves are usually best. They are usually cheapest to check.
That checking first means checking always. A check spends a resource and can be the losing move.

examples.note: Anderssen-Dufresne 1852, before 21.Qxd7+ - the position where the rule about search order is worth everything and worth nothing at the same time. Every move of the finish is a check: Qxd7+ Kxd7, Bf5+ Ke8, Bd7+ Kf8, Bxe7 mate. A player who looks at the forcing moves first finds it, which is the rule working; a player who looks at the forcing moves first in almost any other position finds nothing, which is the rule's second trap - it orders the search and does not choose the move. Black is a rook and a bishop up and threatening mate himself, so nothing but a forced sequence would do. PROVENANCE. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js, which refuses a wrong list rather than guessing, so the FEN is verified rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 4 at depth 20, settled at depth 1, every move of it a check. The limiting case of a forcing line.

examples.note: the side to move has 8 checks and 11 captures available — the forcing moves a search should look at first. The feature was established mechanically from the position by the page's own move generator and lib/features.js. What is NOT claimed is that this feature decides the position. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 4 at depth 22, beginning with Qxf2. A forcing line settled by the engine finding the mate rather than by an evaluation: the concept is about moves that leave the opponent no choice, and a forced mate is the limiting case of one.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `one-check-draws-and-another-loses`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Black has two checks available with the same rook. A check is the most forcing move there is, and the rule says to look at the forcing moves first. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap, and the record names this exact position: "Forcing is not the same as good, and this is the trap that matters. This base holds a proven position in which one check draws and another loses." The Vancura position. ...Rd6+ holds; ...Rf4+ loses. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN, both of them, and this is the claim the record has been making in prose. After ...Rd6+ the position is still a DRAW at dtz 0. After ...Rf4+ it is a WIN FOR WHITE, dtz 21, mate in 67. Two checks by one rook from one square, one holding and one losing by force, and nothing about their forcing-ness distinguishes them. The rule is about search ORDER and not about move choice, which is this record's second trap, and a position where the two most forcing moves available differ by sixty-seven moves of result is the sharpest way to say it.

tablebase.note: PROVEN both ways, and that is the case. From this position ...Rd6+ leaves a DRAW at dtz 0; ...Rf4+ leaves a WIN FOR WHITE at dtz 21, mate in 67. Two checks by one rook from one square, sixty-seven moves of result apart, and nothing about their forcing-ness distinguishes them.

ambiguous_examples.note: Forcing moves are available - the knight on d5 has Ne7+ and Nb6, both forcing, and the rule says to look at them first. Looking at them first is right and playing them is wrong: the engine's choice is Be3, a quiet developing move, at +0.30. This record's second trap says exactly that the rule is 'about search ORDER, not move choice. Reporting it is forcing as a reason a move is strong misuses it entirely.' Filed as ambiguous because the concept is correctly applicable - there really are forcing moves and they really should be examined - and following it produces the wrong move. A search heuristic that is right about what to look at and silent about what to play is the honest description, and it is not one an explanation can lean on.

engine.verdict_note: +0.30 for the quiet move, in a position that offers a check and a capture-threatening knight jump. The forcing moves are real and none of them is best.

by_level.beginner: Look at checks first, then captures, then threats - for both sides.
by_level.intermediate: Forcing moves limit the replies, so they are the cheapest lines to calculate to the end. Start there.
by_level.advanced: It is a search-ordering rule, not a quality judgement, and the opponent's forcing replies matter as much as yours.
by_level.master: Checking first is efficient; checking always spends a resource - a check can be the losing move in a drawn position.

by_depth.short: Look at checks, captures and threats first.
by_depth.normal: Forcing moves - checks, captures and direct threats - sharply restrict the opponent's legal replies, which makes them much cheaper to calculate to a conclusion. That is why they are examined first, for both sides.
by_depth.deep: The organising rule of practical calculation, and one of the few shared by authors who disagree about everything else. The reason is arithmetic rather than optimism: a check may leave two or three legal replies where a quiet move leaves thirty, so since all human calculation is pruning, starting where the tree is narrowest is simply efficient. The order is checks, captures, threats, in decreasing degree of compulsion, and it applies to the opponent's moves as much as your own, since a missed enemy in-between move is what refutes most calculated lines. What it does not do is say anything about quality - this base holds a proven position containing two checks, one of which draws and the other loses.

explanations.hedge: This orders the search; it is not a claim that forcing moves are good, and a forcing move can be the worst move available.
explanations.lesson: Look at them first because they are cheap to check - not because they are likely to be right.

beginner_words: look at the forcing moves first

forcing-moves.definition_short: Moves that sharply limit the opponent's legal replies - checks, captures and direct threats - which is why they are examined first.
forcing-moves.definition_long:
The organising rule of practical calculation, and the one piece of advice shared by authors who disagree about everything else in how to think.

WHY THEY COME FIRST is arithmetic, not optimism. A check may leave two or three legal replies where a quiet move leaves thirty, so a forcing line is far cheaper to calculate to the end. Since all human calculation is pruning, starting where the tree is narrowest is simply efficient. Dvoretsky puts examining the most forcing line first; Tisdall recommends starting with the most direct.

THE ORDER, conventionally: CHECKS, then CAPTURES, then THREATS. Checks are the most forcing because the reply is legally compelled; captures because ignoring one usually costs material; threats because they can sometimes be met in several ways or ignored for a bigger threat.

IT APPLIES TO BOTH SIDES, and this is the half that is usually dropped. The opponent's forcing moves need checking as carefully as your own — a missed enemy zwischenzug is what refutes most calculated lines. The routine survives as the blunder-check before committing to a move.

IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT QUALITY, and this base is strict about it. Forcing is a property of the move's effect on the opponent's options, not evidence about its value. This base holds a tablebase-proven position containing two checks where one draws and the other loses, which settles the point: a forcing move can be the best move and the worst move in the same position. The rule tells you where to look, and nothing more.

IN THIS CODEBASE the underlying detection is already mechanical: checks and captures are generated by the move generator, and the motif detector recognises several kinds of threat.

fork.knowledge_type_note: A tactical motif: a geometric pattern, mechanically detectable, not a guideline. NOTE ON NAMING: 'double attack' was previously listed here as an alias, which the audit flagged as a possible duplicate of the `double-attack` record. They are NOT the same concept in the usage this base follows — a fork is a double attack by ONE piece, while `double-attack` is the general case including discovered attacks. Chess.com merges them; Wikipedia and Chess Tempo do not. The alias has been removed so the distinction is not undermined by the record's own metadata.
fork.definition_short: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
fork.definition_long:
A single piece attacks two or more targets simultaneously. The defender can normally answer only one threat, so material falls. Knights fork most often because no other piece attacks a knight back from a forked square, and because the knight's move is the hardest to see. Pawns fork cheaply: the forked pieces being defended does not help, since the pawn is worth less than either.

Forks are ABSOLUTE when one target is the king — the defender is forced to answer the check and cannot save the other piece or insert a zwischenzug (except a cross-check). Otherwise they are RELATIVE, and the defender may have resources: defending both, counter-attacking, or an in-between move.

Targets need not be pieces. A square, a mate threat, or a follow-up fork can be one prong.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: One piece attacks two or more enemy units after the move
indicators_for: At least one target is undefended, or worth more than the forking piece
One target is the king, making the fork absolute
The forking piece is not itself capturable on its square
indicators_against: The forking piece can simply be captured
Both targets are defended and each is worth less than the forker
The defender has a check or a stronger counter-threat available first

typical_moves: A knight to a square attacking king and rook (the classic Nc7+ / Nf7 pattern)
A pawn advance attacking two pieces on adjacent diagonals
A queen check that also picks up a loose piece
tactical_consequences: Wins material when at least one target cannot be saved
strategic_consequences: Loose pieces invite forks; keeping pieces defended is prophylaxis against them

exceptions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.
limitations: Detecting the geometry is mechanical; deciding whether it WINS material requires resolving the whole capture sequence, so recognition alone is not enough.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

Verified 2026-09-02 by reading blind-chess.html's findMotifs() directly, which is where this concept is detected: the tag arrives from the page and Layer 4 translates it. tools/trap_audit.js reads lib/matchers.js and lib/features.js and cannot see that function, so a condition honoured there reads as unread. This note is the reading. "Both targets are defended and each is worth less than the forker" is ENFORCED, and the line is `if (VAL[p.t] > VAL[moved.t] || !defendersOf(after, i, them).length) hit.push(...)`. A square only joins the fork's target list if the unit on it outranks the forking piece OR has no defender at all; two defended targets both cheaper than the forker leave the list empty and no fork is reported. The remaining indicator_against on this record - "The defender has a check or a stronger counter-threat available first" - is NOT built and is the harder kind: a zwischenzug is not a property of the forking move, and finding one needs a search this base does not run at the board.

examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik, World Championship 1954, game 1, 6.b4 - a pawn fork in a world-championship game, and one recommended in print thirty years earlier. The detector: 'the pawn on b4 forks the bishop on a5 and the pawn on c5.' Botvinnik's own note calls it 'a well-known pawn sacrifice, recommended by Alekhine in the book of the New York international tournament of 1924'. The two readings do not conflict - the fork is the mechanism and the sacrifice is the intention, since Black takes on b4 and White gets the initiative. A PAWN fork is worth having as the master example because the forking piece is the cheapest on the board, which is the condition that makes a fork work at all. PROVENANCE. The position is a corpus entry - a master game with a verified move list and a named annotator - and the annotator named a DIFFERENT concept there. So this grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one: the motif is what this base's own detector reads off the board, and the game is what makes the board real. `attributed_by` is deliberately absent.

engine.verdict_note: +0.53 for the move played against +0.55 for the engine's first choice, at depth 22 with three lines - two centipawns apart, which is agreement in everything but rank. The gambit is sound and is not forced.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. Nc7+ forks Ke8 and Ra8; c7 is unguarded because the black bishop stands on e7.

engine.verdict_note: Nc7+ is best at +7.39, a full 2.21 ahead of the next move (Bd3, +5.18). The engine line is 1.Nc7+ Kd7 2.Nxa8 — the rook simply falls. Confirms the motif when the forking square is safe.

examples.note: Real position from the shipped endgame ladder (puzzle en-154023780e). Black plays Re1+, and the point is that the check means the reply is not free — the rook then promotes on d1. Tagged fork by findMotifs() alongside hangingPiece, promotion and zwischenzug, which is a good illustration that several motifs usually co-occur and that ranking them by explanatory importance is the real problem, not detecting them.

engine.verdict_note: Numbers come from the repository's own puzzle verification pipeline at its verdict depth, NOT from education/tools/sf_analyse.py. Recorded that way deliberately so provenance stays honest. The puzzle's stored `why` says the runner-up (Re4) leaves Black losing, so the move is uniquely correct here.

examples.note: A clean instance: the detector reports fork alongside hangingPiece, for the move Ng3. Two things are verified here and a third is not. VERIFIED: findMotifs() in blind-chess.html reports the motif — and that detector, not this system, is the authority on whether a motif is present. ALSO VERIFIED: Ng3 is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. NOT claimed: that the motif is the whole reason the move wins. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Inherited validation: this position ships as a puzzle, and the generator's standard is that exactly one move is best by at least GAP_MIN at confirmation depth, re-checked deeper by tools/verify_puzzles.js. The move is therefore engine-verified as best without this base running its own search. The motif label comes from findMotifs, not from the engine — the two are independent and both had to agree for this to be recorded.

counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. IDENTICAL to the positive example except the black bishop is on d8 instead of e7, so it guards c7. The fork geometry is unchanged.

engine.verdict_note: Nc7+ collapses to +0.57 and is ranked LAST of the three moves tested, 4.16 behind the best (Bd3, +4.73). The line is 1.Nc7+ Bxc7 — the knight is simply lost. The same geometric pattern swings 6.82 pawns between the two positions purely on whether the forking square is defended. This is the canonical false-match case: geometric detection alone is NOT sufficient to report a fork.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-pawn-fork-the-pawns-simply-eat`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White plays c4-c5, and the pawn on c5 attacks the black pawns on b6 and d6. One piece attacking two enemy units is the definition of a fork, and the detector says so in those words. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first indicator_against: "The forking piece can simply be captured." Both forked units are pawns, both defend the square the forker stands on, and Black moves first. Also the second: "Both targets are defended and each is worth less than the forker" — here they are worth exactly the same and there are two of them. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: THIS WAS A REAL FALSE POSITIVE and it was reported at HIGH confidence, because a motif tag arrived from findMotifs() with no guard between it and the concept. Syzygy proves the move loses: after c5 the position is 5 pieces, a WIN FOR BLACK, dtz 1, mate in 35, and the tablebase's own best reply is dxc5 — the fork is answered by eating the forker. A guard now implements the record's first indicator_against at the motif-mapping site: if SEE says the piece that just moved can be taken at a profit, the fork is not reported. Rate: fork fell from 16.0% to 11.5% of the 788 shipped puzzles, and the canonical royal fork (Nc7+ forking rook and king) still reports at high.

tablebase.note: PROVEN, from the mover's side: after c4-c5 White is LOST, mate in 35, and the tablebase's own reply is dxc5. The fork is answered by eating the forker.

ambiguous_examples.note: Nominated by tools/mine_ambiguous.js on its fourth ground, NOT-THE-MOVE: the concept fires on a legal move that is not the solution of a shipped puzzle. The first three grounds ask about a POSITION and could not reach a move-based or motif concept at all - this concept and eleven others reported NONE until the tool learned to supply a move. What makes the case ambiguous rather than false is that nothing reported is absent: the fork is on the board and the detector is right about it. It is also a move that throws away a winning position: ...c6 wins the bishop on b5 outright and scores +4.18, while the forking move scores +0.28 - level. A fork that costs four pawns of advantage is a fork, and it is not the answer, and both halves of that need to be sayable at once.

engine.verdict_note: The forking move scores +0.28 and the solution ...c6 scores +4.18, both from Black's side at depth 22. Nothing is wrong with the report; the position simply had a much better move in it.

by_level.beginner: This one piece attacks two things at the same time. Your opponent can only save one of them.
by_level.intermediate: A fork. Because it hits {targets} at once and {reason}, the defender cannot cover both.
by_level.advanced: Fork. Note whether it is absolute (a target is the king, so no zwischenzug is available) or relative (the defender may have an in-between resource).

by_depth.short: One piece attacks two things at once.
by_depth.normal: A fork: this piece hits {targets} simultaneously, and only one can be saved. It works because {target} is {undefended / worth more than the forking piece} and the forking square is safe.
by_depth.deep: A single piece attacking two or more targets. It wins material only when at least one target is undefended or outranks the forking piece, and when the forking square itself is safe — those conditions are what separate a fork from a move that merely looks like one. An absolute fork hits the king, so the defender is forced to answer the check and cannot insert a zwischenzug; a relative fork leaves them resources. Targets need not be pieces: a mate threat or a follow-up fork can serve as a prong.

fortress.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept in general, though individual fortresses within tablebase range are proven results. The general concept is not decidable; the specific ones are.
fortress.definition_short: A defensive setup, usually material down, that the stronger side simply cannot break into — the material advantage becomes unconvertible.
fortress.definition_long:
Dvoretsky's definition, as quoted in the sources: 'a situation in which a king, with or without the assistance of pieces or pawns, successfully defends a small territory'. The defender gives up on activity and instead builds a wall the attacker has no way through, so an advantage that would normally win is simply never realised.

Two senses are worth keeping apart. An ELEMENTARY fortress is a theoretically drawn position — a book draw — that passive defence maintains: the wrong rook pawn, king and bishop against king, and similar. The general sense covers constructed positions where the defender is material down and holds anyway, typically by keeping the enemy king out or by blockading on a colour complex the attacker cannot contest.

The commonest vehicles are opposite-coloured bishops, where the defending bishop holds one colour indefinitely, and blocked pawn structures where no entry square exists.

IT IS THE CLEAREST ENGINE BLIND SPOT IN CHESS. A fortress is defined by the ABSENCE of progress rather than by a line, so a search that looks n moves ahead sees the material and reports an advantage that does not exist. This is why tablebase integration is standard practice for endgame analysis, and why an evaluation bar showing +3 in a fortress should be disbelieved rather than explained.

The concept also cuts directly against the principle of two weaknesses: once a fortress is reached, the number of weaknesses stops being the operative variable, because none of them can be converted.

attributions.note: The standard definition quoted throughout the literature is his. ACCESS CAVEAT: taken from a community study quoting him, not from his text.

history.notes: Fortresses are as old as endgame study and no coinage is claimed. Only the standard modern definition is attributable, and that at second hand.

development.change: Fortress ideas appear throughout composed endgame studies long before the term is systematised.
Becomes a recognised evaluation failure mode: search cannot see the absence of progress, so fortresses must be hard-coded or looked up.

fortress.engine_era_note: Revised in an unusual direction: engines are WORSE at this than a knowledgeable human, and knowingly so. A fortress is the absence of a way through, which a bounded search cannot represent, so evaluation functions encode specific fortresses by hand and serious analysis uses tablebases. An explanation should never repeat an engine's evaluation of a suspected fortress without checking it.

preconditions: The defender is material down, or would otherwise be losing
No path exists for the attacker to make progress
indicators_for: The attacking king has no entry square anywhere
The defending bishop covers a colour complex the attacker cannot contest
The pawn structure is blocked and no pawn break exists
The defender has spare waiting moves, so zugzwang cannot be imposed
The position falls into a known elementary case — wrong rook pawn, opposite bishops with a blockade
indicators_against: A pawn break exists that opens a line
The defender will eventually run out of waiting moves — that is zugzwang, not a fortress
The attacker can sacrifice material to break the wall and still be winning
An entry square exists that the defender cannot permanently cover
false_positive_traps: A position that is merely HARD to break is not a fortress. The test is that no progress is possible at all, and that is a strong claim.
Claiming a fortress on the basis of an engine evaluation being stuck is backwards — engines misjudge these in BOTH directions.
A defender with a limited number of waiting moves does not have a fortress; they have a position that loses to zugzwang.
The commonest error is the reverse one: declaring a real fortress lost because the material count says so.

typical_plans: As the defender: identify the entry squares, cover them permanently, and stop trying to be active
As the defender: use opposite-coloured bishops or a blocked structure as the wall
As the attacker: look for a sacrifice that creates an entry square, or a zugzwang the defender cannot answer
As the attacker: avoid liquidating into a known elementary fortress
typical_moves: Passive but permanent piece placement
A sacrifice to break the wall
typical_pawn_structures: Blocked chains with no break available
Pawns fixed on the defending bishop's colour
typical_piece_arrangements: Bishop holding a long diagonal indefinitely
King and minor piece covering all entry squares
tactical_consequences: Justifies material sacrifices that look absurd on a material count
strategic_consequences: Makes a material advantage unconvertible
The standing counterexample to material-based evaluation

exceptions: A fortress that can be broken by a sacrifice was never a fortress.
Many apparent fortresses fail to zugzwang once the defender's waiting moves run out.
Within tablebase range the question is not a judgement at all — look it up.
limitations: Recognition confidence is LOW and the concept is not mechanically detectable, since it is defined by the absence of a continuation.
Engines are unreliable here in both directions, so their evaluation cannot be used as evidence.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled.
misconceptions: That a fortress is any stubborn defence. It is the impossibility of progress.
That the engine bar settles it. This is the clearest case where it does not.
That being material down means losing. A fortress makes the material count irrelevant.

conflicts.resolution: A fortress ends the two-weaknesses method outright. That principle converts an advantage by stretching the defence across targets; a fortress means no target can be converted at all, so the count stops mattering. Where a fortress is available, look for a sacrifice that breaks it rather than for a second weakness.

examples.note: An elementary fortress: the wrong rook pawn. The defending king in the corner cannot be evicted because the bishop cannot cover h8, and the attacking king cannot force it without stalemate. Shared with the `wrong-rook-pawn` record, where the controlled pair lives.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw with an extra bishop and pawn — an elementary fortress in the strict sense.

engine.verdict_note: THE ENGINE IS WRONG HERE AND THE TABLEBASE IS NOT, which is why both numbers are recorded. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says +0.92. Syzygy says draw, dtz 0, 4 pieces, best move Kg6 - proven over every legal continuation. The bishop is light-squared and the queening square h8 is dark, so the defending king cannot be driven out of the corner however long White plays. This is the base's own rule about instruments said out loud: a tablebase gives proof, an engine gives an opinion, and where they disagree inside seven pieces the opinion loses.

examples.note: A blockading fortress with opposite-coloured bishops, two connected pawns down.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw two pawns down; the defending bishop holds the blockade square indefinitely.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 by the engine and PROVEN drawn by Syzygy - 5 pieces, dtz 0, best move d6+. A fortress claim is a claim that no series of moves breaks through, and that is exactly the shape of statement a tablebase makes and an evaluation does not. The two agreeing here is worth less than the tablebase alone; the engine number is recorded because it is what a reader without a tablebase would see.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-fortress-that-is-not-one`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: King, bishop and rook-pawn against a bare king in the corner. This is the picture of the most famous fortress in chess: the defender sits on h8 and cannot be dislodged. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The bishop is the WRONG colour for that fortress, or rather the right one. The drawn version needs a bishop that does not control the queening square; here the bishop is dark-squared and h8 is dark, so the defending king can be driven out and the pawn queens. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN, not evaluated. The API does not report a fortress here. Syzygy: 4 pieces, WIN, dtz 1, mate in 9, best move Kg6+. Read against this record's own positive example, which is the SAME material with the bishop on the other colour and is a proven draw at dtz 0 — one bishop, two colours, mate in nine and a dead draw. That pair is why a fortress claim in this base is only ever made with a proof behind it: the two positions are indistinguishable to any test that counts material.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 9, best move Kg6+. The same material with the bishop on the other colour is a proven draw at dtz 0, and this record's positive example is that position. One bishop, two colours, mate in nine and a dead draw.

ambiguous_examples.note: Rook and bishop against rook, a PROVEN DRAW - and whether it is a FORTRESS is the question. A fortress in this record's sense is a position the stronger side cannot break however long they play, and this qualifies by proof: dtz 0, held over every legal continuation. It also requires the defender to find the right square for fifty moves in a row against an opponent with an extra piece, and the same material one arrangement away is a proven WIN in 15. A defence that is theoretically impregnable and practically famous for being lost is exactly the case the word is used loosely about. Filed as ambiguous because both readings are correct and the record cannot choose between them: this base's other fortress example, king and bishop and a rook pawn, needs no accuracy at all.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 26, settled at depth 13 - and the engine does not always find this in the drawn positions of this ending, which is part of why it is famous.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0. Read against the same five men in `mixed-piece-endgames`' ambiguous example, a PROVEN WIN in 15: one material balance, two results, and whether the drawn one deserves the word fortress is not a question a tablebase answers.

by_level.beginner: They are ahead on material but there is simply no way in. If you set your pieces up so their king can never get through, the extra material does not matter.
by_level.intermediate: A fortress: a wall the stronger side cannot break. Stop trying to be active, work out which squares they need to enter on, and cover them permanently.
by_level.advanced: Progress must be impossible, not merely hard. Check the defender has enough waiting moves to avoid zugzwang, and that no sacrifice opens a line.
by_level.master: The standing counterexample to material evaluation, and the clearest engine blind spot — a bounded search cannot represent the absence of a continuation. Within seven pieces, look it up rather than judging it.

by_depth.short: A wall the stronger side cannot break, whatever the material says.
by_depth.normal: A fortress: the defender, usually material down, sets up a position the attacker cannot penetrate. The material advantage becomes unconvertible — there is no entry square, no pawn break, and no zugzwang available.
by_depth.deep: Dvoretsky's definition is the standard one: a situation in which a king, with or without pieces or pawns, successfully defends a small territory. Elementary fortresses are book draws held by passive defence, like the wrong rook pawn; the general sense covers any constructed wall the attacker cannot breach, most often built on opposite-coloured bishops or a blocked structure. It is the clearest engine blind spot in chess, because a fortress is defined by the absence of a way through and a bounded search cannot represent an absence — which is why engines hard-code specific fortresses and why serious endgame analysis uses tablebases. It also ends the principle of two weaknesses: once the wall holds, the number of targets stops mattering.

explanations.lesson: When you are losing on material, stop looking for activity and start asking whether there is a wall you can build. And when you are winning and cannot make progress, check whether you are looking at one — the evaluation bar will not tell you.

avoid: the engine says +3 so it is winning

open_questions: Read Dvoretsky's definition from the Endgame Manual rather than via a community study.
Build a controlled pair: a fortress and a near-identical position with one entry square available, to demonstrate the boundary.
Collect an example where an engine evaluation is badly wrong and the tablebase corrects it, as a direct demonstration of the blind spot.

gambit.knowledge_type_note: The term itself is definitional. Whether a particular gambit is SOUND is a separate, concrete question that this base answers only with evidence.

attributions.note: Applied the Spanish 'gambito' to chess openings, from the Italian expression dare il gambetto, to put a leg forward in order to trip someone.

history.notes: Murray (A History of Chess, 1913, p.813) quotes Lopez's own derivation at folio 108a from gamba, a leg, with gambitare meaning to set traps. The word first appears in English in Francis Beale's 1656 translation of a Greco manuscript, The Royall Game of Chesse-play, advertised as 'illustrated with almost one hundred Gambetts'; the general metaphorical sense is first recorded in English in 1855. Murray was consulted at second hand through Winter, not read directly.

development.note: Gambit play was the norm and declining one was near-unthinkable socially.

Gambit play declined as defensive technique improved; Exeter names Mieses-Maroczy, Monte Carlo 1902 as illustrating the defensive method that undid the romantic gambits - returning material to complete development.

gambit.engine_era_note: Engines have sorted the historical gambits, and mostly downwards. Two-pawn gambits largely do not survive computer analysis; one-pawn gambits vary from fully compensated to merely playable. The important qualification is that an engine verdict is the CEILING of a gambit's soundness and not its practical value: a line refuted only by a narrow computer defence remains a strong practical weapon, because the refutation has to be found at the board.

preconditions: Material is offered in the opening
It can be declined or accepted
indicators_for: The offer opens a file or diagonal towards the enemy king
The capture costs the opponent tempi and decentralises a piece
The gambiteer's development lead is large after the capture
indicators_against: The material offered is more than a pawn without a forcing follow-up
The opponent can return the material at will to finish developing
The compensation is only tempi, which expire
false_positive_traps: A pawn offered in the opening is not automatically a gambit with compensation. The Halloween Gambit is measured here at 1.75 pawns worse than the best move.
Openings named 'Gambit' are not necessarily gambits - the Queen's Gambit is the standard example, since the pawn cannot be held.
This system has no opening database and cannot identify a named gambit. It can only observe that material was given and ask what came back.
Not detectable by this system: identifying this requires an opening database, which the Education System does not have.

typical_plans: Open lines towards the uncastled enemy king and attack before development completes
Use the tempi gained while the opponent secures and holds the material
Accept, then return the material at the moment it buys development or a favourable trade
tactical_consequences: The defender's extra material is often returned under duress
strategic_consequences: If the attack is neutralised, the gambiteer is simply a pawn down for the endgame

exceptions: Openings called gambits where the material cannot actually be held, such as the Queen's Gambit.
Gambits whose compensation is structural rather than dynamic - the Benko is the standard case, where the pressure on the a- and b-files persists into the endgame instead of expiring.
limitations: Soundness is specific to each gambit and cannot be inferred from the word.
The three measurements here cover three gambits at one depth; they do not license a general claim about gambits as a class.
misconceptions: That a gambit must be accepted. Declining is often entirely satisfactory.
That compensation is automatic. It is a claim to be checked, and one of the three gambits measured here has none.
That gambits are unsound in general. The Evans measures at exactly equal, which is not the same as bad.

examples.note: The Evans Gambit position: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5, White may play 4.b4. Compared under searchmoves against the quiet alternatives in the SAME position, which makes this a controlled test of whether the compensation is real. (Recorded as constructed-test: the FEN was built from the standard move sequence specifically for this comparison, not taken from a game.)

engine.verdict_note: A sound gambit measured. 4.c3 +0.28, 4.d3 +0.24, 4.b4 exactly 0.00. Being a pawn down, the Evans still evaluates to equality, so the compensation recovers essentially the whole pawn; what it costs is White's opening edge of 0.28, not material. This is the clearest evidence in this base that gambit compensation is a real, measurable quantity rather than a figure of speech.

examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik, World Championship match (game 1), Moscow 1954, b4. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Mikhail Botvinnik, annotating his own game (tr. Douglas Griffin). Corpus entry `smyslov-botvinnik-1954-g1-6b4-gambit`. by_level.beginner: Giving up a pawn early on to get your pieces out fast and attack.
by_level.intermediate: A gambit. You pay material for time, open lines or the centre - and whether that is a fair price depends on the gambit.
by_level.advanced: Judge it by what comes back: tempi expire, open lines and structural damage do not.
by_level.master: The engine verdict is the ceiling of soundness and practical results are the floor; a narrow computer refutation is still a good practical weapon.

by_depth.short: Offering material in the opening for activity.
by_depth.normal: A gambit: material, usually a pawn, deliberately offered in the opening in exchange for time, open lines or central control. Whether the compensation is adequate is a separate question for each gambit, not something the word guarantees.
by_depth.deep: A material offer made before the fight starts, in exchange for something that is not material. Soundness is judged on three counts: the time the opponent spends capturing and then holding the material, the activity difference created when their pieces decentralise and lines open, and any lasting structural damage. Measured in this base against the quiet alternatives in each position: the Evans Gambit comes to exactly equal where the quiet move gives +0.28, so a pawn is fully compensated; the King's Gambit concedes 0.91, a real deficit but far from a refutation; the Halloween Gambit, a knight for a pawn, loses 1.75. Compensation is real, it can be complete, and it must be established case by case.

explanations.hedge: The soundness of any particular gambit is a concrete question; the three measured here span the range from fully compensated to plainly insufficient.
explanations.lesson: Ask what came back, and whether it expires. Tempi run out; open lines and ruined structures do not.

beginner_words: giving up a pawn to get ahead in development

gambit.definition_short: An opening in which material, usually a pawn, is deliberately offered for non-material compensation.
gambit.definition_long:
A material offer made in the opening in exchange for something that is not material — time, open lines, central control, or an enemy king that never gets safe.

SOUNDNESS is the whole question, and it is asked in three standard terms: the opponent spends time capturing and then reorganising to hold the material; the captures decentralise their pieces and open lines and diagonals that favour the gambiteer; and accepting may leave lasting structural damage. A gambit is sound when these together are worth what was given.

THE MEASURED SPECTRUM. This base compared three gambits against the quiet alternatives in their own positions, under identical search conditions. The Evans Gambit (a pawn) evaluates to exactly 0.00 where the quiet 4.c3 gives +0.28 — the pawn is fully compensated, and what is surrendered is not material but White's opening edge. The King's Gambit (a pawn) comes to -0.61 against +0.30 for 2.Nf3, a concession of 0.91: a real deficit, but nothing resembling refutation. The Halloween Gambit (a knight for a pawn) evaluates to -1.67 against +0.08, a loss of 1.75. The conclusion the numbers support is narrow and worth stating plainly: compensation is real and measurable, it can be complete, and whether it is adequate has to be established for each gambit rather than assumed from the fact that one was offered.

NOT EVERY MATERIAL OFFER IS A GAMBIT, and not everything named one is. The Queen's Gambit is not a true gambit, since Black cannot hold the pawn profitably. Conversely some genuine pawn sacrifices in the opening carry other names. The nomenclature is inconsistent and is not a guide to the chess.

greek-gift.knowledge_type_note: A named tactical pattern with unusually precise preconditions, which is what makes it worth a record of its own rather than an instance of `sacrifice`. Vukovic states the conditions explicitly, so recognition can be close to mechanical — rare for an attacking idea.
greek-gift.definition_short: Bxh7+ against a castled king, followed by Ng5+ and Qh5 — a bishop given to strip the h-pawn and drag the king out.
greek-gift.definition_long:
The best-known sacrificial pattern in chess. White plays Bxh7+, Kxh7 is usually forced, Ng5+ follows, and the queen arrives on h5. The bishop buys the h-pawn and the king's exposure; the knight and queen do the work.

VUKOVIC'S CONDITIONS, which is why this is a pattern rather than a hope. He states four:

  1. White must have a queen, a bishop and a knight — all three.
  2. The light-squared bishop must be able to reach h7 'in order to force the tempo of the attack', though it need not give check or win a pawn in doing so.
  3. The knight must be 'within easy and safe reach of the square g5'.
  4. The queen must be within reach of h5, 'though in some cases it is enough for it to be able to get to some other square on the h-file'.

The single most common refutation is that condition 3 fails in a specific way: g5 is DEFENDED, so Ng5+ is answered by a capture and White has given a bishop for a pawn. A black bishop on e7, or a queen on the d8-h4 diagonal, does this. Other standard defences are the king walking to g6 rather than back to g8, and a knight reaching f6 in time to cover h5.

It is the reason the Colle System is recommended to players learning attacking chess: the bishop reaches d3 by itself, and from there condition 2 is met almost automatically.

attributions.note: The Art of Attack in Chess gives the conditions under which the sacrifice is sound; the chapter is titled 'The classic bishop sacrifice'.

The name 'Greek gift' is conventionally linked to Greco, the 17th-century Italian player, and separately to the Trojan horse of the Aeneid ('beware of Greeks bearing gifts'). NEITHER derivation has been verified in this research and the two are not compatible. Recorded as an open question rather than repeated as fact.

history.notes: The CONDITIONS are securely Vukovic's. The NAME's origin is not established: two incompatible derivations circulate (Greco the player; the Trojan horse) and neither was verified here. This is precisely the sort of appealing etymology the brief warns against repeating, so it is recorded as uncertain.
competing_claims: Named after Gioachino Greco, who is said to have played or analysed it.
Named from 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts' — the Trojan horse — with no reference to Greco.

greek-gift.engine_era_note: Engines settle any individual instance instantly, which has sharpened rather than overturned the pattern: Vukovic's conditions turn out to be necessary but not sufficient, and borderline cases that were once argued about are now simply checked. The pattern remains sound when the conditions hold and the defensive resources listed are absent.

preconditions: The attacker has queen, light-squared bishop and knight
The bishop can reach h7 (h2 mirrored) with tempo
The knight can reach g5 safely
The queen can reach h5, or another square on the h-file
indicators_for: The defending king has castled kingside with the h-pawn still on h7
g5 is not defended by an enemy piece
No enemy knight can reach f6 to cover h5
The defending king's escape squares on the f-file and g6 are covered or unhelpful
The attacker has a rook that can join on the h-file or via a lift
indicators_against: g5 IS defended — a bishop on e7, or a queen on the d8-h4 diagonal — so Ng5+ is simply met by a capture
A knight can reach f6 covering h5
The king can go to g6 and survive
The h-pawn has already moved, so there is nothing to take with tempo
The attacker lacks one of the three required pieces
false_positive_traps: The pattern is extremely recognisable, which is exactly why it is played in positions where it does not work. Vukovic's conditions are necessary, NOT sufficient.
The commonest single error is not checking whether g5 is defended. The controlled pair in this record isolates that one variable.
Bxh7+ 'looks like' the Greek gift whenever a bishop eyes h7; without the knight and queen in range it is just a lost bishop.

typical_plans: Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+, then Qh5 with mating threats on the h-file
If the king walks to g6, follow with h4-h5+ or Qd3+ depending on the structure
Bring a rook to the h-file or via the third rank as the third attacker
typical_moves: Bxh7+
Ng5+
Qh5
typical_pawn_structures: Black pawns f7-g7-h7 intact with the king on g8
Colle and Queen's-Gambit structures where the bishop sits on d3
typical_piece_arrangements: Bishop on d3, knight on f3, queen on d1 with the d1-h5 route clear
tactical_consequences: Mating attack, or the recovery of material with a decisive king walk
strategic_consequences: A standing reason to keep a defender able to cover g5, and a reason to consider ...h6 before castling into it

exceptions: Vukovic's conditions are necessary but not sufficient. Every instance still has to be calculated.
If g5 is defended, the sacrifice is refuted outright — a bishop for a pawn.
The king walking to g6 rather than retreating is the standard tricky defence and must be checked separately.
The mirrored Black version (...Bxh2+) is the same pattern with the same conditions.
limitations: Recognition of the geometric preconditions is mechanical; soundness is not, and the gap between the two is where players go wrong.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Karpov-Glauser, Zurich simul 1988, 10.Bxh7+, above, found by tools/mine_master_motifs.js. Sixteen candidates in 2.8 million master positions have the shape AND the Ng5+ follow-up actually available; this one has the queen arriving on h5 in the engine's own principal variation.
misconceptions: That Bxh7+ works whenever the bishop can reach h7.
That the name's origin is settled. Two incompatible derivations circulate and neither is verified here.
That Kxh7 is forced. Declining is sometimes better, and that possibility has to be checked too.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. Vukovic's conditions are met: White has queen, light-squared bishop and knight; the bishop reaches h7; g5 is undefended; the queen has the d1-h5 route. Black's bishop sits on c8, blocked behind the d7 knight.

engine.verdict_note: Bxh7+ is best at +6.71, 1.41 clear of the runner-up, and settled from depth 11. Paired with the negative half below, which differs only in the black bishop's square.

examples.note:
THE MASTER-GAME RUNG, and the pattern arrives in the order the record states it. 10.Bxh7+ Kxh7 11.Ng5+ Kg8 12.Qh5 is the engine's own principal variation at depth 30 - the bishop, then the knight, then the queen, which is the definition on this record read straight off the board.

Every precondition holds and can be checked: White has queen, light-squared bishop and knight; the black king has castled kingside with the h-pawn still on h7; g5 is not defended, because Black's dark-squared bishop went to b4 rather than e7 - which is the FIRST indicator_against this record lists, and its absence here is what makes the sacrifice sound; and the knight on d7 is the piece that would have covered h5 from f6, standing one square from the wrong place.

Stockfish 18 at depth 30 with three lines: +6.21, ahead of +4.96 and +4.03. White is better before the sacrifice and much better after it - which is honest about what a Greek gift is. It is not usually a rescue; it is the way an attack that has been earned is cashed.

PROVENANCE. A simultaneous exhibition rather than a tournament game, and that is said rather than hidden: the opposition is weaker than Karpov's usual, which is one reason the pattern appears in its textbook form at all. The move list replayed legally through the page's own move generator, and the position was found by tools/mine_master_motifs.js over 2,822,256 positions from 35,648 replayed games. `attributed_by` is absent - no annotator has been read; this grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

engine.verdict_note: +6.21 at depth 30, best by 125 centipawns, and the principal variation is Bxh7+ Kxh7 Ng5+ Kg8 Qh5 - the record's own three-move pattern, in order.

counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. IDENTICAL material — the same black bishop, relocated from c8 to e7, where it covers g5. Verified with python-chess `attackers`: g5 has no black defender in the positive position and is defended from e7 here. Every other piece and pawn is on the same square.

engine.verdict_note: Bxh7+ collapses from BEST at +6.71 to LAST at +3.77 — a swing of 2.94 pawns, and from 1.41 ahead of the field to 1.59 behind it, on one defender of g5. The concept's central precondition is confirmed. HONEST QUALIFICATION: +3.77 still means White is much better, because White is much better in this constructed position for unrelated reasons — the sacrifice throws away most of an advantage rather than losing outright. Note also that the engine's line after Bxh7+ Kxh7 is Bc1-g5, not Ng5+, so White does recover some compensation; the textbook refutation ...Bxg5 is not what Stockfish plays. Contrast this clean tactical isolation with the three failed attempts to isolate the outpost.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-bishop-eyeing-h7-is-not-a-greek-gift`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A white bishop on d3 bears on h7, the black king is castled short behind an untouched h-pawn, and Bxh7+ is available. That is the picture the pattern is famous for. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's third trap, word for word: "Bxh7+ 'looks like' the Greek gift whenever a bishop eyes h7; without the knight and queen in range it is just a lost bishop." White's only knight is on c3 and cannot reach g5. And the fifth indicator_against fires too — a knight covers the kingside: the black knight on f6 guards h7, so the king does not even have to take. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report greek-gift, because the matcher asks for Vukovic's three pieces rather than for a bishop pointing at h7. Stockfish 18 settles what the move is worth: the position is 0.00 with a normal move and Bxh7+ scores -3.89, and the refutation is not even Kxh7 - the KNIGHT takes on h7. Nearly four pawns, for the most recognisable sacrifice in chess played one piece short. The record's first trap says the pattern's recognisability is exactly why it gets played where it does not work, and this is that sentence with a number.

THE SHAPE WITHOUT THE PATTERN, from a real game, and the harder version of this record's registered false positive. That one is a position where Bxh7+ is bad. This is a position where Bxh7+ is BEST - +3.85 at depth 30 against +1.82 - and is still not a Greek gift.

Black's bishop is on e7, which is the first indicator_against this record lists: g5 is defended, so Ng5+ is met by a capture and the pattern is unavailable. The engine never plays it. Its line is 14.Bxh7+ Kxh7 15.Qc2+ Kg8 16.Rxd8 - the bishop is given to deflect the king so the rook takes the queen, which is a deflection wearing the Greek gift's clothes.

This is the negative that is worth having, because the easy one teaches the wrong lesson. A reader who learns 'Bxh7+ fails when g5 is defended' will disbelieve it the first time they see the sacrifice work anyway. What fails is the CONCEPT, not the move: the three-piece machine this record describes is not running here, and any explanation that names it is describing a mechanism that is not on the board.

Bronstein-Smyslov, USSR Championship 1960, move 20, is the same thing again - bishop on e7, Bxh7+ the engine's first choice at +0.08, and no Ng5+ anywhere in the line. Two of the three candidates put to the engine were this case, which says something about how often the shape occurs without the pattern.

engine.verdict_note: Bxh7+ is BEST here by 203 centipawns and the Greek gift is still absent: the engine's line is Bxh7+ Kxh7 Qc2+ Kg8 Rxd8, a deflection. The move being good is not the same claim as the concept being present, and this record must not be allowed to take credit for the one on the strength of the other.

ambiguous_examples.note: All four of Vukovic's conditions hold. White has the queen, the light-squared bishop and the knight; the bishop reaches h7 with check; the knight reaches g5 safely, because the h-pawn that would cover it has just been captured; and the queen reaches h5 the moment the knight moves. The sacrifice is SOUND - White is still more than two pawns better after it - and it is a mistake, because the quiet 1.Qc2 is worth five. This record's first trap says exactly this and no more: 'Vukovic's conditions are necessary, NOT sufficient.' Filed as ambiguous because the pattern is genuinely present and genuinely playable and is not the move: the conditions tell you the gift is available and nothing about whether to accept the invitation.

engine.verdict_note: +2.06 for the gift against +5.07 for the quiet 1.Qc2, at depth 22 with two lines. The sacrifice keeps a large advantage and throws away three pawns of it - which is the only kind of number that can distinguish 'the conditions are met' from 'the sacrifice is right'.

by_level.beginner: White gives up the bishop to take the pawn in front of the king and drag the king out, then brings the knight and queen in for the attack.
by_level.intermediate: The Greek gift: Bxh7+ Kxh7 Ng5+ and Qh5. Before playing it, check whether anything defends g5 — that is the usual refutation.
by_level.advanced: Vukovic's conditions: queen, bishop and knight present; bishop reaching h7 with tempo; knight safely to g5; queen to h5 or the h-file. Necessary, not sufficient — calculate the Kg6 defence separately.
by_level.master: Check the g5 defenders, whether a knight reaches f6 in time, and the king's walk to g6. The conditions get you to a candidate; only calculation gets you to a move.

by_depth.short: Bxh7+ strips the king's pawn and brings the knight and queen in.
by_depth.normal: The Greek gift sacrifice: Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+, Qh5. It needs the queen, bishop and knight all in range, and it fails if g5 is defended or a knight can reach f6 to cover h5.
by_depth.deep: The classic bishop sacrifice, and the pattern Vukovic gave precise conditions for: the attacker needs a queen, a bishop and a knight; the bishop must reach h7 with tempo; the knight must have safe access to g5; the queen must reach h5 or the h-file. The bishop buys the h-pawn and the king's exposure, and the knight and queen convert it. The commonest refutation is that g5 turns out to be defended — a bishop on e7 or a queen on the d8-h4 diagonal answers Ng5+ with a capture, and the sacrifice is just a lost bishop. The conditions are necessary but not sufficient, so the pattern identifies a candidate and calculation decides it.

explanations.lesson: The Greek gift is the most recognisable sacrifice in chess, which is why it is played in positions where it loses. Check g5 before you check anything else.

hanging-pawns.knowledge_type_note: A structure with a genuinely two-sided assessment, which is why its record is written as a pair of plans rather than as a verdict.

history.notes: Standard structural vocabulary with no traced coinage; the treatment is classical and anonymous.

hanging-pawns.engine_era_note: Engines assess the structure by the piece configuration rather than by the pawns, which is what the classical treatment already said. What they changed is the confidence: the structure is now known to be closer to balanced than the older 'weak by nature' framing implied.

preconditions: Two friendly pawns abreast on adjacent files
No friendly pawn on either flanking file
Both files half-open for the opponent
indicators_for: The pair is on c and d, or on d and e
The opponent has rooks on the two half-open files
The pair can advance together with pieces behind it
indicators_against: A friendly pawn still stands on a flanking file — then it is a chain, not a hanging pair
One of the two has already advanced, which usually ends the structure
recognition.detector: pawnStructure().undefendable in lib/features.js — two abreast on files the opponent has no pawn on
false_positive_traps: Hanging pawns are not automatically weak. The structure is dynamic, and the same pair that loses one game wins the next depending on where the pieces are.
Do not assess them as an isolated pawn. They defend the squares in front of one another and the pair advancing is a genuine threat.
The detector finds the STRUCTURE. Whether it is an asset needs the piece placement, which the detector does not read.

typical_plans: Against them: pressure both until one must advance, then blockade the square it left
With them: activate the pieces first and advance only when the advance gains something
Against them: trade pieces, since fewer defenders makes two pawns harder to hold
With them: avoid trades for the same reason
typical_moves: The pair advancing together
A rook doubling on one of the half-open files
typical_pawn_structures: c5 and d5 against a queenside fianchetto or a rook on c1
Arising from the Queen's Gambit Tartakower, the Alapin Sicilian and the Petrov
typical_piece_arrangements: Rooks on the two half-open files
A blockading knight in front of the advanced pawn
tactical_consequences: The advance of one pawn is often a tactical as well as a positional decision
strategic_consequences: Two targets that only pieces can defend, and two files the opponent's rooks can use

exceptions: Where the pair can advance profitably, they are a space-gaining asset rather than a weakness.
With enough piece activity the structure is fully sound; the 'weak by nature' framing is a starting assessment, not a verdict.
limitations: The detector finds the structure and cannot judge whether it is an asset, which is the whole question.
This base has one master-game example and no counterexample where the pair proved strong; the record is therefore one-sided in its evidence and says so.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'do not assess them as an isolated pawn. They defend the squares in front of one another and the pair advancing is a genuine threat' is honoured by the sentence, which names the PAIR - 'abreast, on half-open files, and no pawn can defend either' - and never reports either pawn as isolated. The two concepts have separate records and separate matchers, and this base has never reported both about one pair.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, and it is a defect rather than a refinement: the matcher's `implements` string has claimed 'no friendly pawn on either flanking file' since the day it was written, and the code never tested it. That is the second `implements` string found overstating in one day. This record says the same thing as an indicator_against - 'a friendly pawn still stands on a flanking file: then it is a chain, not a hanging pair' - and it is the difference between the structure and a phalanx of three. b5-c5-d5 was being reported as hanging pawns on c5 and d5. Built: 7.2% -> 3.4% of the 788 shipped positions, and Fischer-Spassky 1972 game 6, this corpus's annotated instance, is untouched. The other indicator, 'one of the two has already advanced', is the abreast test and was already built.
misconceptions: That hanging pawns are simply weak. They are dynamic, and the assessment turns on the pieces.
That they are two isolated pawns. They defend the squares in front of each other, which an isolani has nobody to do.
That the way to play against them is to attack them. The way is to make one of them move.

conflicts.resolution: This structure is the clearest case of the distinction rather than a conflict with it: statically two permanent targets, dynamically two pawns that can advance and take the centre. Which reading applies is decided by the pieces, not by the pawns.

examples.note: Fischer-Spassky, World Championship 1972, game 6, after 16.Bb5 - the position the structure is named for in the modern literature, with Anthony Levin (Chess.com) and Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase) both naming it outright. The annotation is careful in the way this record needs: 'usually, the side with hanging pawns should place his pieces actively and try to advance the pawns at an appropriate moment. Here, however, Spassky's pieces are passively placed.' The structure alone is not the verdict, which is this record's first trap - 'hanging pawns are not automatically weak. The structure is dynamic, and the same pair that loses one game wins the next depending on where the pieces are.' This base's own Layer 3 reports c5 and d5 independently: two pawns abreast that no pawn can defend, on files the opponent has none.
examples.attributed_by: Anthony Levin (Chess.com, 2022) and Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase, 2022) - corpus entry fischer-spassky-1972-g6-hanging-pawns

engine.verdict_note: DELIBERATELY NOT ENGINE-SCORED, and the corpus entry says so too. The human claim here is about a STRUCTURE rather than about a move, and an evaluation of the position would answer a different question - it would say who stands better, which nobody disputes, and not whether the pawn pair is what makes it so. A number attached here would look like evidence and be none.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-phalanx-of-three-is-not-a-hanging-pair`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Three white pawns stand abreast on c4, d4 and e4 with no friendly pawns beside them — an advanced, unsupported pawn mass on half-open files. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Hanging pawns are a PAIR of adjacent pawns on half-open files with no friendly pawns on the flanking files. Three abreast is a phalanx, which is a different structure with different properties: the outer two support the advance of the middle one, and there is no pair to be attacked as a pair. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: This is a REGRESSION CASE, not a hypothetical. The hanging-pawns matcher's `implements` string quoted the flanking-file condition and the code never tested it, so a phalanx of three was reported as a hanging pair; the rate fell from 7.2% to 3.4% when the condition was actually built. The API is now silent here. Syzygy: 5 pieces, WIN for White, dtz 1, mate in 27 — three connected passers on the fourth rank win, which is the opposite of the liability 'hanging pawns' names, and the clearest possible statement that calling this structure by that name would mislead.

This record's first trap says the structure is dynamic and 'the same pair that loses one game wins the next depending on where the pieces are', and its third says the detector finds the STRUCTURE while whether it is an asset needs the piece placement, which the detector does not read. by_level.beginner: Two pawns side by side with no pawns next to them — no pawn can defend either one.
by_level.intermediate: Hanging pawns. They are strong if you can advance them and weak if you cannot, so activate your pieces before pushing.
by_level.advanced: Against them, do not attack the pawns — force one to advance, then blockade the square it left behind.
by_level.master: A dynamic structure: the same pair is an asset or a liability depending entirely on the piece configuration.

by_depth.short: Two pawns abreast that no pawn can defend.
by_depth.normal: Hanging pawns: two connected pawns on half-open files with no friendly pawns on either side, so only pieces can defend them. They are dynamic — a weapon when they can advance and two targets when they cannot.
by_depth.deep: Two abreast, usually c and d, with the b- and e-pawns gone, so no pawn can ever defend either. That single fact gives the structure its character: pieces must hold them, and whether the pieces are doing that or something better decides everything. The method against them is not to attack the pawns but to make one MOVE — pressure both, and when one advances the pair is broken and the square it left is a permanent hole. Fischer against Spassky in 1972 is the model, pressing c5 and d5 until 20...d4 fixed the structure and handed him c4 and a new target on e6.

explanations.lesson: Do not attack hanging pawns. Make one of them move, then occupy the square it leaves.

beginner_words: two pawns side by side with no neighbours

hanging-pawns.definition_short: Two connected pawns side by side on half-open files, with no friendly pawns left on either neighbouring file to defend them.
hanging-pawns.definition_long:
Two abreast, usually on c and d, with the b- and e-pawns gone. No pawn can ever defend either of them, so pieces must — and that is the whole of the structure's character.

THEY ARE A WEAKNESS AND A WEAPON, and which one depends on the pieces. Advanced together at the right moment they take squares and open lines; left to be attacked they are two targets that only pieces can hold. The standard formulation is that the structure is DYNAMIC — piece play is the major factor — and it is why the same pawns are an asset in one game and a liability in the next.

THE METHOD AGAINST THEM is not to attack the pawns but to make one of them MOVE. Pressure both, and the defender must advance one; the advance breaks the pair, and the square the moving pawn leaves becomes a permanent hole for a blockading piece. Fischer's handling of Spassky in 1972 is the model: he pressured c5 and d5 until 20...d4 came, after which d4 was fixed, c4 was free for his bishop, and e6 was a new weakness.

THE METHOD WITH THEM is the mirror: place the pieces actively FIRST, and advance only when the advance gains something. The annotation of that same game puts the failure precisely — the structure was reached with Black's pieces passively placed, and from there the pawns were only targets.

THEY ARE NOT AN ISOLATED PAWN and should not be assessed as one. An isolated pawn has one neighbour-less file; hanging pawns defend the squares in front of each other and control four squares between them, which is why the pair advancing is a real threat and a lone isolani advancing usually is not.

hanging-piece.knowledge_type_note: Terminology, not a motif. It names a STATE of the board, not a move or a method. The tactics that exploit it (fork, discovered attack) are the motifs; this is the condition that makes them pay.

history.notes: 'En prise' is a French borrowing in English chess writing since at least the nineteenth century; no origin research has been done and no single coiner is claimed. 'Hanging' has no established first use in the sources consulted.

hanging-piece.engine_era_note: Entirely mechanical and unaffected by engine-era revision. Static exchange evaluation is the standard test and is what this codebase uses.

preconditions: An enemy piece is attacked
The exchange sequence on its square wins material for the attacker
indicators_for: The piece has no defender at all
It is attacked more times than it is defended
Its only defender is pinned, overloaded, or would be deflected by the capture
indicators_against: Recapture regains equal or greater material — an even trade is not a hanging piece
Taking it walks into a stronger counter-tactic
It is bait: the capture opens a line or removes a defender the opponent wants gone
The piece was ALREADY winnable before this move, so the move is not what hung it
false_positive_traps: A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange.
A nominal defender that is pinned does not defend. SEE catches this; a naive defender count does not.
Material already loose before the move is not this move's doing — reporting it makes the move look worse than it was.

typical_plans: Take it, after checking the recapture sequence and any counter-tactic
tactical_consequences: Direct material gain
Supplies the second target that makes a fork or discovered attack pay

exceptions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.
limitations: Purely material. It says nothing about whether taking is best.

Verified 2026-09-02 by reading blind-chess.html's findMotifs() directly, which is where this concept is detected: the tag arrives from the page and Layer 4 translates it. tools/trap_audit.js reads lib/matchers.js and lib/features.js and cannot see that function, so a condition honoured there reads as unread. This note is the reading. Four of this record's conditions are ENFORCED there and all four by the same two lines. "Material already loose before the move is not this move's doing - reporting it makes the move look worse than it was" and "The piece was ALREADY winnable before this move, so the move is not what hung it" are one line: `if (see(before, i, attackerColor) > 0) continue;`. "A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange" and "Recapture regains equal or greater material - an even trade is not a hanging piece" are the other: the test is `see(after, i, attackerColor) > 0`, a static exchange evaluation rather than an attacker count, which is also why "A nominal defender that is pinned does not defend. SEE catches this; a naive defender count does not" needs nothing further - the record names the instrument and the instrument is what is used. The two conditions that are NOT built are the two that require reading intentions: "Taking it walks into a stronger counter-tactic" and "It is bait". Neither is decidable without a search, and this base reports at the board.
misconceptions: That a piece with a defender cannot be hanging. It can — if the defender is pinned or overloaded, or if it is attacked twice and defended once.
That every hanging piece should be taken.

ALSO VERIFIED: Nf6 is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. NOT claimed: that the motif is the whole reason the move wins. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

The move is therefore engine-verified as best without this base running its own search. The motif label comes from findMotifs, not from the engine — the two are independent and both had to agree for this to be recorded.

counterexamples.note: The same rook move against the same knight, with a black pawn added on b4 to defend it. Undefended is the whole of what 'hanging' means, and one pawn removes it - the knight is still attacked, still worth three points, and no longer hanging. A base that called this hanging would be teaching a reader to count attackers and stop.

Registered false-positive case `defended-knight-attacked-once`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A black knight on d5 is attacked by a white bishop. An attacked piece looks hanging. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own trap: "A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange." The knight is defended by the c6 pawn, and bishop-takes-knight is answered by pawn-takes-bishop. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN, not evaluated. The API is silent on hanging-piece, because the matcher asks SEE rather than counting attackers. Syzygy settles what the capture is worth: 5 pieces, draw, dtz 0, and the tablebase's own best move is Bxd5 — the capture is available, is best, and changes nothing, which is exactly what 'attacked once and defended' means. A detector that counted attackers would have called this a hanging knight.
