by_level.beginner: That piece can just be taken for free — nothing is defending it.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} on {square} hangs: it is attacked {n} times and defended {m}, so the exchange wins material.
by_level.advanced: Hanging by static exchange evaluation. Check whether the capture is a genuine win or an offer — SEE measures material, not correctness.
by_level.master: En prise. Confirm the defender is real (not pinned or overloaded) and that the capture does not concede a line or a tempo worth more than the material.

by_depth.short: The {piece} on {square} can be taken for free.
by_depth.normal: The {piece} on {square} is hanging — attacked and not adequately defended, so the exchange there wins material.
by_depth.deep: Hanging, or en prise in the older French term. The test is the exchange sequence on the square, not a count of attackers: a defender that is pinned or overloaded does not defend. Distinguish from loose, which means undefended but not yet attacked — that is a future problem rather than a present loss.

explanations.lesson: Before every move, check both sides for pieces that can simply be taken. Below master level this decides more games than every strategic idea combined.

hanging-piece.definition_short: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
hanging-piece.definition_long:
A piece stands where the opponent can take it and come out ahead. In everyday English it 'hangs'; the traditional French term is EN PRISE, literally 'in a position to be taken'.

Three words are used in this area and the distinction between them is worth keeping:

  EN PRISE — attacked and capturable. Strictly this says nothing about defence, though in living usage it means capturing wins material.
  HANGING — the English equivalent, and in practice the stronger claim: attacked AND undefended, or defended too few times.
  LOOSE — undefended but not necessarily attacked YET. Not a loss today; the raw material of tomorrow's tactic. Recorded separately as `loose-piece`.

The hanging/loose line is the one that carries weight, because it separates a mistake that has already happened from a condition that invites one.

IN THIS CODEBASE: `findMotifs()` emits `hangingPiece` using static exchange evaluation — it reports a piece only where `see(after, square, attacker) > 0`, i.e. the exchange on that square actually wins material, and it explicitly skips anything that was already winnable before the move. That is the strict, correct reading, and it is by far the most common theme in the shipped puzzle set (598 of 788 puzzles).

historical-principles.knowledge_type_note: Principles preserved as history: what was taught, when, and what has happened to it since.

attributions.note: The first body of chess principle presented as a theory rather than as advice.
My System, the most influential single statement of positional principle, and the source of several rules this base has had to qualify.

history.notes: A meta-record over this base's historical findings; the individual claims are documented on their own concepts.

development.note: Steinitz turns advice into theory.
Nimzowitsch and the hypermoderns state the positional principles that are still taught.
The Soviet school shifts the deciding method from principle to concrete analysis.
Principles become checkable; some are quantified, a few are disproved, most are qualified.

historical-principles.engine_era_note: The characteristic engine-era finding is not that an old principle is wrong but that it is smaller than it sounds. Most of this base's measurements confirm a rule's direction and shrink its magnitude.

preconditions: A traditional principle is being applied or quoted
recognition.detector: the engine_era_status field, enforced by tools/schema.json
false_positive_traps: An old principle being qualified does not make it worthless; most are right in direction and overstated in strength, which is why they are kept rather than deleted.
Quoting a principle in its popular form usually drops the condition its author attached. Prefer the author's own wording where this base holds it.
That a principle is old is not evidence against it, and that it is modern is not evidence for it.

typical_plans: Quote a principle with the condition its author gave it
State the measured magnitude where this base has one
Record what happened to a principle rather than silently updating it

exceptions: Some principles have survived checking unqualified, particularly the geometric facts and the rules of the game itself.
limitations: This base has measured a small number of principles and qualified those; silence about a principle is not endorsement.
The historical research is English-language and mostly second-hand.
misconceptions: That engines have refuted classical chess strategy. They have mostly measured it and found it directionally right and overstated.
That a principle stated by a world champion has been checked. Several in this base had not been until now.

examples.note: Letelier-Fischer, Leipzig Olympiad 1960, after 7.f4 - a principle caught in the act of losing its condition, which is the first of the three fates this record catalogues. 'Occupy the centre with pawns' is stated in the classical literature without qualification; White has four of them abreast on c4, d4, e5 and f4 and the annotation names the missing condition: 'When central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target for the opponent.' Fischer's answer was ...d6 and ...f6, dissolving the centre, and he won in twenty-three moves. The corpus files the same position under `center-control` as AMBIGUOUS; it is filed here as a positive, because what this record is about is the history of the rule rather than the evaluation of the position.
examples.attributed_by: corpus entry letelier-fischer-1960-7c5-center-control-ambiguous

engine.verdict_note: -0.10 - level. Four pawns on the fourth and fifth ranks in the centre and the position is equal, which is the whole point: the rule was followed to the letter and produced nothing. The engine's own first move is ...dxe5, beginning the dissolution the annotation predicts.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-principle-that-never-needed-qualifying`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The Lucena position — a rule taught since the fifteenth century, stated without conditions, and repeated in every endgame book since. Exactly the profile of a principle this record collects. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record collects principles that have been QUALIFIED, reattributed or disproved, and its own definition names the three fates: losing a condition, losing its author, or being shown false. The Lucena rule has suffered none of them. It is not a rule of thumb at all — it is a proven result, and it is filed in this base as a `named-theoretical-position` for that reason. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN WIN, dtz 15, mate in 41, and the tablebase's own first move is Rd1+ — the first check of the bridge. The API reports `passed-pawn`, `king-activation` and `open-file` and nothing historical. The case exists because this record's subject is the HISTORY of a claim rather than its content, and history is not on a board: what distinguishes a rule that needed qualifying from one that did not is a fact about the literature, and no position can carry it. That is also why the record's detectability is recorded as mechanical only for the narrow purpose of matching named principles by text.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 15, mate in 41, first move Rd1+. A rule taught since the fifteenth century that has never needed a condition attached - which is what disqualifies it from this record.

ambiguous_examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein 1928, 15...d4 - a principle in the middle of being qualified rather than after it. 'Avoid the isolated queen pawn' was taught as law; Rubinstein accepts one voluntarily, 'confident that its central control is worth the long-term weakness', and the modern qualification is exactly that - the pawn is a weakness in the endgame and a source of activity in the middlegame. This record catalogues three fates for an old principle and the first is that it LOSES ITS CONDITION. Filed as ambiguous because the qualification had not been written when the move was played and the move is one of the reasons it was: the position is where the condition came from, so it cannot demonstrate the condition being applied. The engine is only partly on Rubinstein's side, which is the right amount for a rule still being argued about.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-15d4-static-vs-dynamic

engine.verdict_note: The engine's first choice is a different move at +0.09 - level - so the isolated pawn Rubinstein took on is neither refuted nor endorsed at depth 22. A rule caught mid-qualification measures exactly like that.

by_level.beginner: Old chess rules are mostly still useful, but they were stated more strongly than they should have been.
by_level.intermediate: Three things happen to an old principle: it loses its condition, it gets disproved, or it gets measured. The first is much the commonest.
by_level.advanced: The engine era's real contribution has been measurement rather than demolition — the early-queen rule is true and worth about two thirds of a pawn.
by_level.master: A base that deleted every principle an engine has qualified would delete most of chess strategy and would be wrong to.

by_depth.short: Old principles, and what has happened to them since.
by_depth.normal: Principles once taught as law, kept here with their history: most have lost the condition their author attached, a few have been disproved outright, and several have been measured and turn out to be true but smaller than they sound.
by_depth.deep: Chess teaching accumulates rather than corrects, so a rule stated confidently in 1925 is still circulating without the qualification its author gave it. Three things happen to an old principle. It loses its condition, which is much the commonest and is the shape of nearly every misconception in this base. It is disproved, which is rarer - Tarrasch's rook rule is false as stated and this base holds the proof. Or it survives and gets quantified, which is the engine era's real contribution: the early-queen rule costs about 0.68, gambit compensation can be exactly one pawn, and the side to move is worth exactly one file in the rule of the square. The pattern is that the old teaching was usually onto something and stated it too strongly.

explanations.hedge: Preserved as history and as teaching; where this base has measured a principle the measurement is on the concept itself, and silence about one is not endorsement.
explanations.lesson: Old principles are usually right about the direction and wrong about the strength.

historical-principles.definition_short: Principles that were once taught as law and have since been qualified, reattributed, or shown to be false.
historical-principles.definition_long:
Chess teaching accumulates rather than corrects. A rule stated confidently in 1925 is still in circulation in 2026, usually without the qualification its author attached and sometimes after being disproved. This record is where that history is kept, because the qualification is generally the useful part.

THE THREE THINGS THAT HAPPEN TO AN OLD PRINCIPLE:

1. IT LOSES ITS CONDITION. The commonest fate, and the shape of nearly every misconception in this base. Anderssen and Makogonov both stated the worst-piece rule conditionally and the popular form drops the condition. Shereshevsky documented rook endings where his own first principle fails.

2. IT IS DISPROVED. Rarer and more interesting. Tarrasch's rule about the rook behind the passed pawn is false as a general rule, and this base holds the proof: same material, one rook moved, a draw becomes a loss in 63. Kotov's one-pass analysis tree is rejected by every later authority consulted here. Fine's 1941 verdict on the four-against-three knight ending has been downgraded.

3. IT SURVIVES AND GETS QUANTIFIED. The engine era's real contribution to old principles is not demolition but measurement. 'Do not bring the queen out early' is true and costs about 0.68 in the standard case. Gambit compensation is real and the Evans is worth exactly one pawn. The rule of the square is exact, and the side to move is worth exactly one file.

THE PATTERN ACROSS ALL THREE is that the old teaching was usually onto something and stated it too strongly, which is what makes it worth preserving rather than discarding. A base that deleted every principle an engine has qualified would delete most of chess strategy and would be wrong to.

AND THE ENGINE-ERA CAUTION runs the other way too: an engine can say that a move is better than another and cannot say what a principle MEANS, which is why research names concepts and the engine validates moves, and neither does the other's job.

hole.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept, not a rule and not a tactical motif. It names a durable structural feature rather than prescribing a move. Classified separately from `weak-square`, which is the broader modern term — see the note on their overlap below.
hole.definition_short: A square in front of a pawn that can no longer be guarded by a pawn, because the pawns on both adjoining files have advanced past it or been exchanged.
hole.definition_long:
Steinitz's own wording, The Modern Chess Instructor (1889), p. xxxix: "The 'hole' means a square on the third or forth [sic] row in front of a pawn after the two adjoining pawns have been moved or captured." His illustration: after 1.e4 e5 2.c4 White already has holes at d3 and d4, and they are worse while Black's e5 pawn stands, because it restrains the two white pawns that would otherwise repair the damage.

Steinitz also anticipated Nimzowitsch's later emphasis on files: "A hole or weak square are still more troublesome when the opponent is enabled to open the file on which they are situated for his Queens and Rooks." And he located them by phase: most dangerous in the centre or on the kingside before queens come off, but on the queenside in the endgame.

DEFINITIONAL DRIFT. Hooper and Whyld's Oxford Companion (1992) gives 'a square on a player's third rank or beyond that cannot be guarded by a pawn' — which drops Steinitz's requirement that the square be in front of a pawn, and removes his fourth-rank ceiling. Both definitions are in current use and they are not equivalent. This record follows Steinitz for the term's meaning and notes the broader usage.

A hole matters only if the opponent can use it. Romanovsky's refinement is the operative test: a square becomes a real weakness when an enemy piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged threatens to occupy it. An unusable hole is a curiosity.

attributions.note: Steinitz states in The Modern Chess Instructor (1889) that he first used the term in The International Chess Magazine, November 1886, and that he was also the first to point out the disadvantage it describes.
Britannica: 'He originated the term hole'. Lasker's Manual (p.203) also attributes the idea to Steinitz.
Developed the exploitation side as the outpost, tying occupation of such squares to play on open files.

history.notes: Unusually well founded for a chess term: a self-claim in a primary text, an independent attribution by Lasker in his Manual, and Britannica agreeing. Recorded as 'high' rather than certain because the strongest single piece of evidence is Steinitz claiming credit for himself. Edward Winter, reviewing exactly this, notes the attribution is significant but cautions 'This one item is certainly not enough to settle the matter.' The November 1886 International Chess Magazine issue has not been examined directly.

development.change: Term coined; defined as a square on the 3rd or 4th rank in front of a pawn whose adjoining pawns have gone.
The offensive use of such squares is systematised as the outpost, with the open file as the enabling condition.
Refined: a hole is a real weakness only if a piece that cannot be dislodged or exchanged can occupy it.
Broadened to any square on the third rank or beyond that no pawn can guard, dropping Steinitz's 'in front of a pawn' condition.

hole.engine_era_note: Engines do not use the word, but the underlying feature is standard in evaluation functions as pawn-attackable-square and outpost terms. Nothing in engine practice contradicts the concept; what engines do contradict is the assumption that every hole is exploitable, which is Romanovsky's point restated.

preconditions: A square on the third rank or beyond (from its owner's side) that no friendly pawn can ever attack
In Steinitz's stricter sense, the square also lies in front of a pawn, with both adjoining pawns advanced past it or gone
indicators_for: Both adjoining pawns have advanced beyond the square's rank or have been captured
The square is central, or adjacent to the king's shelter
An enemy piece can reach it and be supported there
A file leading to the square is open or half-open for the opponent
indicators_against: A friendly pawn can still advance to attack the square
No enemy piece can reach the square, or reaching it costs more than it gains
An enemy piece that occupies it can be exchanged on favourable terms
The square is on the edge or deep in the opponent's own half, where occupying it achieves nothing
false_positive_traps: Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard. Most of them are irrelevant. Reporting a hole requires that the opponent can actually use it.
A hole that only a queen can occupy is usually not a weakness, because the queen can be driven off by cheaper pieces.
Fianchetto structures leave permanent holes on the long-diagonal colour complex that are nonetheless well covered by the bishop; the hole is real, the weakness is not.

typical_plans: Manoeuvre a knight towards the square by a route the defender cannot contest
Open the file leading to the square, following Steinitz's own observation about files
Exchange the defender that covers the square, especially a fianchettoed bishop
Provoke a further pawn advance to create a second hole on the same colour complex
typical_pawn_structures: After 1.e4 e5 2.c4 — Steinitz's own example, holes at d3 and d4
After a kingside fianchetto is played and the bishop later exchanged, holes on the dark squares around the king
In front of a backward pawn on a half-open file
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight permanently posted on the square, supported by a pawn
tactical_consequences: An unchallengeable piece near the king generates mating threats
strategic_consequences: Holes are permanent: pawns cannot move backwards, so the defect cannot be repaired
Their value increases as the pieces that could cover them are exchanged

exceptions: A hole is only a weakness if it can be occupied usefully. Romanovsky: the square becomes a real weakness when a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged threatens to take it up.
Creating a hole is often the correct price for something else — space, the bishop pair, or a tempo. Steinitz's own example (1.e4 e5 2.c4) is a playable opening, not a mistake.
A hole covered by a well-placed piece is not exploitable while that piece remains; the plan is to exchange the defender first.
limitations: The term's boundaries are not agreed. Steinitz's definition and Hooper & Whyld's are both current and are not equivalent.
Detecting squares no pawn can attack is mechanical; deciding which of them matter is not.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Corzo-Capablanca, Havana 1901, above.
misconceptions: That every square a pawn cannot guard is a hole worth naming. Most are not.
That holes are always bad. They are a structural cost that is frequently worth paying.
That a hole is created by moving a pawn. It is created by moving BOTH adjoining pawns, or by their exchange.

examples.note: Constructed. d5 is a hole in Black's position in the strict sense the record requires: no black pawn can ever attack it, because the c-pawn is gone and the e5 pawn captures towards d4 and f4 rather than backwards. A hole is a property of the PAWNS and survives every piece trade, which is why it is a different concept from the piece standing on it - this base files the square as `hole`, the square-plus-a-friendly-pawn-defending-it as `strong-square`, and the piece parked there as `outpost`, and this one position carries all three descriptions honestly. Material is symmetric down to the pawn count, so the evaluation is about the square.

engine.verdict_note: +0.30 with symmetric material. Small and real. A hole is worth about a third of a pawn here, and the engine's own line trades the knight off it - the square is a standing feature, not a plan.

examples.note:
A HOLE IN WHITE'S CAMP THAT BLACK CAN REACH, from Capablanca's first match. The square is g4. White's f- and h-pawns are the only pawns that could ever cover it: f3 has gone past and h2 is on the second rank behind its own rook, and after f3 the g4 square can never be attacked by a white pawn again.

A HOLE IS NOT A WEAKNESS UNTIL SOMETHING CAN USE IT, which is why the scan asked Layer 3 for REACHABLE holes rather than for holes. `holesFor()` finds squares no enemy pawn can attack; `reachableHoles()` keeps the ones a minor piece can actually get to and survive on. The difference is the whole concept - every position has holes, and most of them are irrelevant.

And it asked for positions with exactly ONE, because a position with four holes is a position where the reader learns nothing about which one matters.

PROVENANCE. Found by reading Layer 3 over 330 replayed master games rather than by asking the API, which never reports this concept because it has no matcher. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-hole-on-the-rim`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Neither side has an a-pawn, so a6 and a3 are squares no pawn can ever attack — the definition of a hole, satisfied twice on the same board. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's fourth indicator_against: "The square is on the edge or deep in the opponent's own half, where occupying it achieves nothing." And its first trap: "Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard. Most of them are irrelevant." WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `outpost` and `weak-square` for d5 and says nothing about a6 or a3. That is the correct set of answers, and the interesting half is what is NOT reported: a naive hole detector finds three holes here and two of them are noise. The record's own trap is that most holes are irrelevant, and this position is that trap with a count attached.

Registered false-positive case `a-fianchetto-hole-the-bishop-covers`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Black has played ...g6 and fianchettoed, so f6 and h6 are permanently weak on the dark squares and no black pawn will ever cover them again. This is the most-taught hole in the openings. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's third trap, in full: "Fianchetto structures leave permanent holes on the long-diagonal colour complex that are nonetheless well covered by the bishop; the hole is real, the weakness is not." The bishop on g7 covers the complex it created. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report a hole here. This is the same trap that `weak-square` was tightened against — the fianchetto guard lives in reachableHoles() in Layer 3 and is quoted in a comment there — and `hole` inherits it, because both concepts read the same Layer 3 output. The case exists so that inheritance is pinned down rather than assumed: a guard in a shared function protects whoever happens to call it, and nothing in the code says which concepts those are.

ambiguous_examples.note: The same board as this record's positive example with White's pawn on e3 instead of e4. The HOLE is unchanged - no black pawn can ever attack d5, the c-pawn is gone and the e5 pawn captures the other way - and everything about what it is worth has changed, because the knight standing on it is now held by a queen rather than by a pawn. This is filed as ambiguous rather than negative on purpose: the hole is genuinely there and reporting it would not be an error, and the engine says -0.17 against +0.30 for the version one pawn further up. A hole is a property of the pawns and its VALUE is a property of everything else, which is the distinction this record's first trap draws - 'most of them are irrelevant'.

engine.verdict_note: -0.17, against +0.30 for the same board with the pawn on e4, and the engine's own first move here is e3-e4. A 47-centipawn swing on one pawn, with the hole identical in both.

by_level.beginner: Your pawns can never go backwards, so a square they have moved past is one they can never guard again. If your opponent can park a piece there, it will sit there for the rest of the game.
by_level.intermediate: A hole on {square}: neither adjoining pawn can ever attack it. It matters here because {piece} can reach it and cannot be driven off.
by_level.advanced: Hole in Steinitz's sense — in front of a pawn, both adjoining pawns gone. Exploitable only on Romanovsky's condition that the occupying piece cannot be dislodged or exchanged.
by_level.master: Structural, permanent, and worth evaluating against what was received for it. The operative questions are which piece can occupy it, whether the defender covering it can be traded, and whether a file can be opened towards it.

by_depth.short: Neither pawn can ever guard {square} again — a permanent hole.
by_depth.normal: The pawns that used to control {square} have gone past it, and pawns cannot move backwards, so the square is weak for good. That matters when a piece can occupy it and cannot be chased away.
by_depth.deep: Steinitz coined 'hole' in 1886 for exactly this: a square in front of a pawn whose adjoining pawns have advanced or been exchanged. He noted they are worst when the opponent can also open the file leading to them, and that they hurt in the centre and near the king in the middlegame but on the queenside in the endgame. Romanovsky added the condition that decides whether it matters at all — a hole is a real weakness only when a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged can occupy it.

explanations.lesson: Before pushing a pawn, look at the square it will never be able to guard again, and ask whether your opponent has a piece that could live there.

beginner_words: a square your pawns can never defend again

open_questions: Examine The International Chess Magazine, November 1886 directly to confirm Steinitz's self-claim.
Construct and engine-test a controlled pair: an exploitable hole versus a structurally identical but unusable one, to validate Romanovsky's condition.
Confirm the Hooper & Whyld wording against the book rather than via secondary quotation.

hypermodern-school.knowledge_type_note: A historical school, so its claims are teaching principles of their time rather than timeless truths. Mandatory hedging applies: several of its positions were corrections to a dogma rather than laws in their own right.

attributions.note: Originated the term 'hypermodern'; his Die hypermoderne Schachpartie appeared in 1924.
Considered the founder and leading practitioner; My System (1925-27) is the school's central text.
Die neuen Ideen im Schachspiel (1922) traced the evolution of chess thinking to the new school.

history.notes: Unusually well dated: three named books with years, an agreed founder, and an agreed coiner of the term. Recorded high because two independent sources agree on all of it, though none of the primary texts beyond My System was consulted.

development.change: Die neuen Ideen im Schachspiel.
The term 'hypermodern' is coined.
My System published in five installments.
The openings are absorbed by everyone, including Capablanca and Tarrasch. The polemic dies down.
Treated as an extension of classical theory rather than a rival to it.

hypermodern-school.engine_era_note: Engines are comfortable with hypermodern structures and have vindicated several specific openings, but they do not support the polemical claim. A pawn centre that can be supported is simply good, and engines build one readily.

preconditions: An opening or plan that declines central occupation in favour of piece pressure
indicators_for: Fianchettoed bishops aimed at the centre
The opponent invited to build a pawn centre
An undermining break prepared against that centre
Restraint and prophylaxis as the plan
indicators_against: The centre is ceded with no undermining break available — that is not hypermodern play, it is passivity
The opponent's centre is properly supported and expanding on schedule
false_positive_traps: A fianchetto is not by itself hypermodern. The school's claim is about the centre, and a fianchetto with no plan against a central pawn mass is just a bishop on a long diagonal.
Ceding the centre without a break is not hypermodern; it is the failure mode the school itself warned about.
Attributing every modern positional idea to hypermodernism. Several were understood by Staunton's generation.

typical_plans: Invite the pawn centre, fix it, then undermine it with a break
Restrain first, blockade, then destroy — Nimzowitsch's formula
Fianchetto and pressure the centre from the flank
typical_moves: 1.Nf3 and 1.c4
...Nf6 and ...g6
...Nf6 against 1.e4 (Alekhine's Defence)
typical_pawn_structures: Opponent's broad pawn centre awaiting an undermining break
typical_piece_arrangements: Bishops on the long diagonals
strategic_consequences: Introduced restraint and prophylaxis as plans in their own right

exceptions: The school's own central claim fails as a rule: cede the centre against proper support and you lose to space.
It did not replace classical theory and was absorbed into it within a decade.
Several of its ideas predate it in nineteenth-century practice.
limitations: A historical school rather than a technique; its content is now distributed across other concepts (outpost, blockade, prophylaxis, overprotection, restraint).
misconceptions: That hypermodernism beat classical theory. Textbooks present it as an extension of it.
That hypermoderns thought the centre unimportant.
That fianchetto equals hypermodern.

examples.note: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924, after 8.d3 - the game the school is usually taught from, and the annotation is the school's own founder describing the system he is playing: Reti in Masters of the Chessboard, 'The move directs pressure against the centre, prevents 1...e5, and keeps open almost all the possibilities for the first player.' White has not one pawn on a central square. His influence over d4, e4 and e5 comes from a bishop on the long diagonal, a knight on f3 and pawns on c4 and d3, which is the ground principle of the record stated as a position. Capablanca is about to occupy the centre with ...e5 and lose. Corpus entry `reti-capablanca-1924-8d3-center-control-ambiguous` reads the same position for `center-control`, where it is ambiguous; here it is not, because what is being illustrated is the METHOD rather than who stands better.
examples.attributed_by: Richard Reti, Masters of the Chessboard - corpus entry reti-capablanca-1924-8d3-center-control-ambiguous

engine.verdict_note: -0.27 from Black's side: the player with NO pawn on a central square is the one very slightly better. That is a small number and it is the right size - the hypermodern claim is that the indirect method is sound, not that it wins, and an example evaluating at +1.5 would be evidence for a different and false proposition.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-fianchetto-with-nothing-behind-it`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Both sides have fianchettoed. Bishops on g2 and g7 on the long diagonals, knights on f3 and f6, no pawn on e4 or e5 — the hypermodern picture, twice. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The ground principle is to control the centre INDIRECTLY with pieces, inviting the opponent to occupy it so the pawns become targets. Neither bishop bears on anything: g2 is blocked by its own knight on f3 and by the d4 pawn beyond it, g7 by its own knight on f6 and the d5 pawn. Nobody is being invited to occupy anything, and the centre is already symmetrically fixed. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing here at all. +0.27 at depth 22, settled at depth 21 — an ordinary symmetrical position. The case is registered because the fianchetto is the most recognisable thing about the school and is the part that carries none of the content: this record's positive example, Reti-Capablanca after 8.d3, has White's bishop on b2 bearing down an OPEN long diagonal at a centre Black is about to occupy. The picture is nearly the same and the idea is absent.

ambiguous_examples.note: Reti-Capablanca 1924, move 18 - the canonical hypermodern game, in which the annotator's advice to the losing side is classical. Keene: 'it is a mystery why Capablanca did not play the obvious 18...Ne6, fighting more directly for control of the centre.' Fighting for the centre is the thing hypermodernism was a reaction against being dogmatic about, and here it is the recommendation, inside the game the school is taught from, given against the player the school beat. Filed as ambiguous because both readings survive: Reti's system won by controlling the centre from a distance, and Capablanca's error was not contesting it directly enough, and those are the same claim about central control read from two schools.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia - corpus entry reti-capablanca-1924-18Ne6-center-control

engine.verdict_note: +0.80, and the engine's first choice is the move Keene recommends. Both candidate knight moves develop and neither occupies a central square; what separates them is how much they contest d4 and c5, which is the hypermodern criterion applied to a classical recommendation.

by_level.beginner: A group of players in the 1920s argued you do not have to put pawns in the middle — you can aim pieces at it from far away and let your opponent's pawns become targets.
by_level.intermediate: Hypermodernism: control the centre with pieces, invite the pawn centre, then undermine it. It is a correction to the older rule, not a replacement for it.
by_level.advanced: The 1920s reaction to Tarrasch's dogma. Its lasting contributions are restraint, prophylaxis, the blockade and the outpost, more than the central polemic itself.
by_level.master: Read it as a set of exceptions rather than a system — Réti said as much. Ceding the centre without a concrete break is the failure mode the school itself identified.

by_depth.short: Control the centre with pieces instead of occupying it with pawns.
by_depth.normal: The hypermodern school, from the 1920s: control the centre from a distance rather than occupying it, and let the opponent's pawn centre become a target. It produced the Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld, King's Indian and Réti, along with restraint, prophylaxis and the blockade.
by_depth.deep: A post-war movement led by Nimzowitsch and Réti, with Tartakower coining the name in 1924. Its target was Tarrasch's dogmatic codification of Steinitz rather than Steinitz himself, and Réti characterised the generation as interested not in rules but in exceptions. Its concrete legacy outlived the polemic — the fianchetto revived as a central weapon, restraint and prophylaxis as plans, the blockade, overprotection, the outpost. What it did not do is win: by the late 1920s its openings had been absorbed by everyone including Capablanca and Tarrasch, and modern textbooks treat it as an addition to classical theory rather than a replacement. Its own limit is honest and well known — cede the centre as a principle against an opponent who supports theirs and expands on time, and you lose to the space you invited.

explanations.hedge: A historical school, not a set of laws. Its central claim was a corrective to a prevailing dogma and fails when applied as a dogma itself: ceding the centre without a concrete plan to undermine it simply concedes space.
explanations.lesson: The hypermodern insight worth keeping is that controlling a square and standing on it are different things. The polemic around it is history.

beginner_words: control the middle from far away

hypermodern-school.definition_short: The 1920s movement holding that the centre should be controlled from a distance with pieces rather than occupied with pawns, and that a committed pawn centre is a target.
hypermodern-school.definition_long:
A school that emerged after the First World War, led by Nimzowitsch and Réti with Tartakower supplying the slogans, and including Breyer, Bogoljubov and Grünfeld — all Central European. Its target was not Steinitz but Tarrasch's dogmatic codification of him.

The ground principle: control the centre indirectly with pieces, inviting the opponent to occupy it with pawns so those pawns become targets. Réti's summary of the generation was that they were interested 'not in rules but in exceptions', and Breyer's joke — 'after the first move 1.e4 White's game is in the last throes' — was the provocation in concentrated form.

It produced a body of concrete ideas that outlived the polemic: the fianchetto revived as a central weapon, restraint and prophylaxis as plans in their own right, the blockade, overprotection, the outpost, the pawn chain, and the openings that carry the names — Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld, Réti, King's Indian, Alekhine's Defence.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED TO IT is the part usually got wrong. It did not win and did not replace classical theory. Modern textbooks describe it as an ADDITION to classical theory, and by the late 1920s its openings had been absorbed by everyone, Capablanca and Tarrasch included. Its own honest limit is that ceding the centre as a principle, against an opponent who supports the resulting mass and expands on time, loses to the space advantage invited — so it is a correction to a dogma rather than a replacement dogma.

Historically it was also less novel than it presented itself: Staunton and other nineteenth-century players understood several of the ideas, and the fianchetto had simply fallen out of fashion after Morphy popularised open centres.

initiative.knowledge_type_note: A dynamic advantage — a positional concept whose defining property is that it EXPIRES. That distinguishes it from static concepts like a weak square, and it is why the same evaluation means different things depending on which kind of advantage produced it.

attributions.note: His enumeration of advantages splits them into permanent and temporary, which is where the initiative's defining property comes from. ACCESS CAVEAT: taken from a community study, not from Steinitz's text.

history.notes: Ordinary chess vocabulary; no coinage claimed. The classification of the initiative as a temporary advantage is conventionally Steinitz's, but the only source consulted for that here is a community study, so confidence is low. Worth verifying against The Modern Chess Instructor, which this project already has access to.

initiative.engine_era_note: Engines evaluate the initiative implicitly and are notably better than humans at telling a real initiative from a series of checks that achieve nothing. The concept is unrevised; what engines correct is the human tendency to overvalue forcing moves.

preconditions: One side is making threats the other must answer
The answering side has no time for a plan of their own
indicators_for: A sequence of forcing moves is available
The opponent's last several moves were all forced or defensive
A lead in development in an open position
The opponent's king is stuck in the centre
indicators_against: The threats can be answered by a move that also improves their position
The position is closed, so threats are hard to generate
The opponent can trade queens or simplify
The forcing moves have run out and nothing has been achieved
false_positive_traps: A series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them.
Having more active pieces is not the same as having the initiative — the test is whether they must answer you.
The initiative is invisible to a static feature scan, so it cannot be detected from the board alone; it is a property of the sequence.

typical_plans: Keep making threats so the opponent never gets a free move
Convert it into something permanent before it expires — material, structure, or a weak square
Sacrifice material to obtain or prolong it
As the defender: return material, trade queens, or find the move that both parries and improves
tactical_consequences: Forcing sequences that end in material or mate
strategic_consequences: Decays if not used — the defining property
The commonest form of compensation for a sacrifice

exceptions: It expires. An initiative that is not converted into something permanent is worth nothing afterwards.
A series of forcing moves is not an initiative if the replies help the opponent.
Black can hold it. It is not White's by right of the first move.
limitations: Recognition confidence LOW, and it is not detectable from a static position at all — it is a property of the sequence of moves, like the zwischenzug.

This base has NO detector for the initiative and will not gain one: the record already states it is invisible to a static feature scan. tools/corpus_check.py therefore scores its corpus entries as 'absent by design' rather than as false negatives, and scores a NEGATIVE example for it as vacuous - nothing could have reported it, so its passing is not evidence about false positives.
misconceptions: That the initiative is the same as being better. A worse position can hold the initiative, and often that is the only reason it survives.
That checks and captures create an initiative. They create forcing moves, which is not the same thing.
That it is White's by right.

conflicts.resolution: Opposed in tempo, not in truth. The two-weaknesses method requires TIME — fix, improve every piece, do not hurry — which is exactly what a player holding the initiative cannot afford to spend. Which applies depends on whether the advantage is dynamic or static: convert an initiative before it expires, accumulate a static edge slowly.

examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik, World Championship match (game 1), Moscow 1954, Qc7. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Mikhail Botvinnik, annotating his own game (tr. Douglas Griffin). Corpus entry `smyslov-botvinnik-1954-g1-20Qc7-initiative`, which carries the full annotation, the alternates the annotator rejected, and the engine's verdict. This is the concept in its defining form and it is why the entry exists. Botvinnik does not claim Black is better; he claims the roles have swapped - from here White answers and Black asks. The move itself does nothing visible: it steps off the b-file, eyes c3, and leaves White's knight on b3 with no good square, so every White move for the next several is a reply. The concept record's own test is

engine.verdict_note: on the move, completely - 20...Qc7 is the engine's first choice at depth 22, ahead of 20...O-O by 0.15. On the assessment, not at all: the engine still gives White about half a pawn from Black's side of the board. That split is the finding, and it is worth more than agreement would have been. Holding the initiative is not the same as standing better, which is exactly what the concept record says and exactly what an engine-labelled corpus would have destroyed by throwing this position away.

counterexamples.note: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924 (round 5), Qe5. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia. Corpus entry `reti-capablanca-1924-27Qe5-initiative-negative`, which carries the full annotation, the alternates the annotator rejected, and the engine's verdict. The surface of an initiative is all here and none of the substance, which is what makes it a negative example. From move 20 Capablanca's queen has been to c4, c5, h5 and now e5, hitting something every time, and White has answered every time - Rxd6, Rad1, Ne3, Nd4, Nc4. Count only 'one side keeps making threats and the other keeps answering' and Black has the initiative. The concept record's actua

The engine's first choice at depth 22 is 27...Rxe3, which is the move Keene says Black had to try, and the game move 27...Qe5 is second and 0.36 worse. Black is lost either way, which is the point: the side with the 'threats' is two pawns down in evaluation. ambiguous_examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik 1954, game 1, after 21.Nc5 - nine moves after this base's positive example from the same game, where the annotator writes that 'the initiative now passes to Black'. It has passed, both sides are still making and answering threats, and the position is level: -0.08 at depth 22. The knight White was obliged to place on c5 'does not stand safely' and is exchanged off fifteen moves later. engine.verdict_note: -0.08 from Black's side at depth 22 with three lines: level, in a position the annotation says the initiative belongs to Black in. The concept and the evaluation are both right and they are not about the same thing.

by_level.beginner: You are the one making threats, so your opponent has to keep answering instead of doing what they want.
by_level.intermediate: You have the initiative. It does not last — turn it into something permanent, like material or a lasting weakness, before it runs out.
by_level.advanced: A dynamic advantage: it decays. The question is what it can be converted into before the opponent consolidates.
by_level.master: Temporary by definition, and therefore in direct tension with slow methods like the two weaknesses. Price the conversion, not the initiative itself.

by_depth.short: You are making the threats; they are answering.
by_depth.normal: The initiative: your opponent has to answer your threats rather than pursue their own plans. It is temporary — one slow move lets them consolidate — so it has to be converted into something permanent while it lasts.
by_depth.deep: The state of setting the problems. Its defining property is that it expires, which puts it firmly on the dynamic side of Steinitz's split between permanent and temporary advantages and produces the standing instruction to use it or lose it. It is built out of tempi — a tempo is one move, the initiative is the sustained state — and it is the commonest compensation for a real sacrifice: when material is given for 'time', this is what is bought. The usual error is mistaking a run of forcing moves for an initiative; if the forced replies improve the opponent's position, the checks are helping them.

explanations.lesson: The initiative is a wasting asset. Ask what you are going to have left when the threats run out — and if the answer is nothing, you did not have an initiative.

avoid: the initiative means you are better

initiative.definition_short: The state of being the one making threats — the opponent must answer rather than pursue their own plans. It is temporary and must be used or lost.
initiative.definition_long:
Whoever is setting the problems has the initiative. The opponent's moves are answers rather than plans, and every tempo spent answering is one they cannot spend improving.

Its defining property is that it is TEMPORARY. Unlike a weak square or a damaged structure, it decays: one slow or decorative move lets the defender consolidate and it is gone. That is what puts it on the dynamic side of Steinitz's division of advantages into permanent and temporary, and it is why the standing instruction attached to it is 'use it or lose it'.

Relation to TEMPO: a tempo is one move; the initiative is the sustained state built from repeatedly gaining them. Relation to a LEAD IN DEVELOPMENT: development is the raw material, the initiative is what it can be converted into if converted quickly.

It is also the most common form of compensation for a sacrifice. When Spielmann's real sacrifice buys 'time', this is what is meant: a sequence of threats the opponent must answer, each one denying them a free move.

The first move gives White a small initial initiative, but it is not White's by right — Black takes it with counterplay, central breaks, or rapid development whenever they create the threats that must be answered.

insufficient-material.knowledge_type_note: Type I, not A. This is the single clearest case in the rules area where a widely used term is a convention rather than the codified rule, and it is the reason the epistemic typing exists.
insufficient-material.definition_short: The common software test for an automatic draw: the material on the board could not force mate. It approximates, but is not identical to, FIDE's 'dead position'.
insufficient-material.definition_long:
'Insufficient material' is not a term in the FIDE Laws. It is the convention chess servers and engines use to implement Art. 5.2.2 automatically, normally covering K vs K, K+B vs K, K+N vs K, and (in most implementations) K+B vs K+B with bishops on the same colour.

It differs from the rule in both directions. It misses dead positions that have ample material but are completely blocked. And implementations disagree at the edges — notably K+N+N vs K, which is drawn in practice but is not a dead position under Art. 5.2.2 because a helpmate exists.

Recorded as terminology (type I) rather than as an official rule, precisely so the Education System does not present a convention as a Law.

history.notes: A software convention with no single origin; not codified by FIDE.

preconditions: Only kings, or a king and a single minor piece, remain for the side in question
indicators_for: K vs K
K+B vs K
K+N vs K
K+B vs K+B same colour squares
indicators_against: Any pawn, rook or queen on the board
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: insufficient-material, over the material counts

exceptions: Implementations differ on K+N+N vs K and on K+B vs K+N; do not state a universal rule.
Blocked positions with full material are dead under the Laws but are not caught by this test.
limitations: Because implementations vary, an explanation should say what THIS program does, not what 'the rules' say.

Reported only when NEITHER side can force mate, which is the position that is drawn rather than merely hard to win. Adding it corrected a test that had asserted the OPPOSITE: three suites required bare kings to license nothing at all, which was a missing detector being asserted as a virtue. The refusal principle they were demonstrating is real and is now demonstrated on two kings and two blocked e-pawns, where nothing researched applies.

examples.note: King and bishop against a bare king: a proven draw, and the positive half of the pair whose other half - the same board with a knight added on d3 - is a forced win in 57.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0: mate cannot be forced, which is what insufficient material means.

examples.note:
KING AND KNIGHT AGAINST KING, reached in a real game and not built to show the rule. That distinction is the whole reason to keep this position: every other example on this record was constructed, and a constructed position can demonstrate a rule that never actually arises over the board.

It is one of the four cases the convention names - bare kings, a lone bishop, a lone knight, two same-coloured bishops - and the matcher tests the four by name rather than by the looser 'at most one minor per side', which admits knight against knight and opposite-coloured bishops, in both of which a helpmate exists and no arbiter declares the game drawn.

PROVENANCE. Found by tools/harvest_games.js. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator.

counterexamples.note: King, bishop and knight against a bare king. Two minor pieces, no pawns, and a position that LOOKS like the drawn minor-piece ending - and it is a forced win in 57. The record's precondition is a single minor piece, and this is the position that shows why the word 'single' is load-bearing rather than decorative. Paired with the same board minus the knight, which is a proven draw.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 57 for White. Mate is not merely possible here, it is forced, so the material is not insufficient by any reading. The paired K+B ending is a proven draw at dtz 0.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `two-knights-facing-each-other`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Two kings and one knight each. Neither side has a pawn, a rook or a queen, and neither has more than one minor piece — this record's precondition, word for word. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The precondition is not the convention. This record's own definition_long names what the convention covers: "K vs K, K+B vs K, K+N vs K, and (in most implementations) K+B vs K+B with bishops on the same colour." Knight against knight is not on that list, and the reason is the one the record gives in the next paragraph about K+N+N vs K: a helpmate exists, so the position is not dead under Art. 5.2.2 and no arbiter declares the game drawn. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: THIS WAS A REAL FALSE POSITIVE and it was reported at the type's ceiling. The matcher tested the precondition per side — no pawn, rook or queen, at most one minor — and that admits two combinations the convention excludes: knight against knight, and bishops of OPPOSITE colours. It now tests the four combinations by name. All four still report: bare kings, a lone bishop, a lone knight, and two bishops of the same colour; and the sentence says which of the four it is, so a reader can check the claim against the board. The distinction matters because this record is filed as TERMINOLOGY rather than as an official rule, precisely so the system does not present a convention as a Law — and a convention that has been widened past what its own definition says is the worst of both.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 24. Knight against knight IS drawn in practice and is NOT covered by the convention, because a helpmate exists and no arbiter ends the game - which is the distinction this record is filed as terminology to preserve. The engine's zero and the convention's silence are two different facts and this position separates them.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `bishops-of-opposite-colours-are-not-insufficient`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: King and bishop against king and bishop. One minor piece each, nothing else on the board, and the two bishops can never attack one another. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Same trap, other half. The convention covers K+B vs K+B only when the bishops are on the SAME colour, because bishops of opposite colours cover disjoint square sets and a helpmate is available. The record's definition_long says 'with bishops on the same colour' and the matcher did not read the qualifier. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API is now silent on insufficient-material here and reports `opposite-coloured-bishops` instead, which is the correct concept for this board and was already firing beside the wrong one. The same position with the black bishop on g8 rather than f8 — both bishops light — still reports insufficient-material, which is the controlled comparison: one bishop, one square, and the difference between a convention that applies and one that does not.

by_level.beginner: There is not enough material left on the board to checkmate, so the game is drawn.
by_level.intermediate: Insufficient material: neither side can force mate with what remains, so the game ends in a draw.
by_level.advanced: The implementation convention for Art. 5.2.2. Note it is narrower than 'dead position' and varies between programs.

by_depth.short: The software convention for an automatic draw: what is left could not force mate.
by_depth.normal: Insufficient material is not a term in the FIDE Laws. It is the convention servers and engines use to implement Art. 5.2.2 automatically, and it covers four cases: king against king, king and bishop against king, king and knight against king, and king and bishop against king and bishop with the bishops on the SAME colour.
by_depth.deep: It differs from the Law in both directions, which is why this base files it as terminology rather than as a rule. It MISSES dead positions with ample material that are completely blocked. And it is narrower than people assume at the edges: knight against knight and bishops of OPPOSITE colours both satisfy 'neither side can force mate' and are not in the convention, because a helpmate exists and no arbiter ends the game. This matcher reported both until it was corrected against the record's own definition.

explanations.hedge: This is how most software implements the rule, not a phrase from the FIDE Laws themselves.

interference.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), mechanically detectable in principle, but rarely spotted because the candidate move looks unnatural.
interference.definition_short: Placing a piece — often as a sacrifice — on the line between an enemy piece and what it defends.
interference.definition_long:
A unit is inserted onto the line a defending bishop, rook or queen needs, cutting the defence. Because the interfering unit is usually en prise, interference is typically a sacrifice; the point is the line, not the material.

It is the rarest of the common motifs, and the hardest to see, because the interfering move goes to a square that looks absurd. Informant theme i; the ECM lists it as 'Interception'.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: An enemy line piece defends a target along a line
A friendly unit can be placed on a square of that line
indicators_for: The interfering unit cannot be captured without abandoning something bigger
Two enemy defenders share the crossing square, so one move cuts both
indicators_against: Capturing the interfering unit restores the defence at no cost
The defender has an alternative route to the target
recognition.detector: proposed, and deliberately unclaimed: every cheap test fires where it is not true (not yet written)

exceptions: Fails if the interposed unit can be captured by a piece that does not itself have a duty.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and the reason is the order of the work rather than a shortage of positions. This record has no POSITIVE example either, and an ambiguous example is a position where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - which cannot be written before there is an agreed instance of the concept being present at all. The four motifs in this base that lack a positive - `clearance`, `decoy`, `deflection`, `interference` - lack it for reasons written on each record, and the ambiguous rung waits on that. Writing one first would be asserting a doubtful instance of something this base has not yet shown a clear instance of. UPDATE: the positive example now exists - 28...Nf5+ in the position above, verified as the only move by 4.43 pawns - so the reason given here no longer holds and the ambiguous example is simply outstanding work rather than blocked work. RESOLVED: Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927 game 13, 39...c4 - the interference on the board, 0.00 at depth 30, and not among the engine's three choices.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED, and by the position that also resolves the ambiguous rung: Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927 game 13, 39...c4. The reason recorded here was right about the scan and wrong about the games - a concept with no detector cannot be nominated by a scan that reads the API, but the geometry is decidable without one, and tools/mine_master_motifs.js asks it of 2.8 million positions from replayed master games directly.

examples.note:
THE FIRST VERIFIED POSITION ON THIS RECORD, and it was found by geometry rather than by a detector, because this concept has no detector and the record said so. The scan asked one question of every ply of all 788 shipped solutions: does our move put a piece, uncaptured and en prise, strictly between an enemy line piece and something that piece was defending, such that the defended man becomes winnable and was not before? Six positions in 788 answer yes and this is the cleanest.

White's rook on f7 is defended only by the rook on f1, down the f-file. 28...Nf5+ puts the knight in the middle of that file. It cannot be ignored - it is check - and it cannot be taken without the line staying shut: 29.Rxf5 exf5 and the f7 rook, now defended by nothing, goes for the exchange after 30.Rxf5 Rxf5 31.Bxf5 Rf8.

Stockfish 18 at depth 30 with three lines: Nf5+ is 0.00 and the next two moves are -4.43 and -4.58. That gap is what makes the position worth keeping. This is not a combination that wins material out of a level position; it is the only move that holds a lost one, and interference is the whole of the reason it holds. A concept whose sole example is a flourish teaches the flourish; one whose example is a rescue teaches the geometry.

PROVENANCE. A shipped puzzle position, not a master game. It grounds the positive-example and engine rungs and NOT the master-game one, and the record's limitation about the master game stands unchanged.

engine.verdict_note: Only move, by 4.43 pawns over the second best at depth 30. The interference is not decoration on a won position - it is the position's only defence.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `an-interposition-that-is-simply-taken`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Nd6 puts a piece on the line between the rook on d8 and the knight it defends on d5. Blocking a defender's line is the definition of interference. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The rook takes it. An interference has to be an obstruction the defender cannot remove, or one whose removal costs more than the target; a knight dropped on a square the defending rook covers is neither. The concept's whole content is that the line stays blocked. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `hanging-piece` at high confidence — which is exactly right about the knight on d6 — and nothing about interference. The numbers make the case sharper than a description could: with a normal move the position is +4.22 for White, because Ne3 attacks the knight on d5 a second time and wins it; the interfering Nd6 scores -4.20. Eight and a half pawns thrown away by a move that satisfies the concept's surface description.

engine.verdict_note: +4.22 for the best move against -4.20 for the interfering Nd6 - eight and a half pawns thrown away by a move that satisfies the concept's surface description. The winning idea is Ne3, attacking the knight on d5 a second time, which is the ordinary way to win a defended piece and needs no motif at all.

ambiguous_examples.note:
THE GEOMETRY WITHOUT THE VERDICT, from a World Championship game between the two players this base quotes more than any others. 39...c4 puts the pawn between White's bishop on d3 and the a6 pawn it defends - the interference is on the board and it is exactly the shape the positive example on this record has.

And it settles nothing. Stockfish 18 at depth 30 with three lines gives 0.00 for all three, and c4 is not among them: the engine's choices are 39...Rh4, 39...Rf3 and 39...Ra1, all drawing. The rook ending is a draw with the interference and a draw without it.

This is what makes it worth keeping rather than a failure to find something better. A reader who has learned interference from the positive example - a knight interposed on f5 that is the only move in a lost position - has learned a pattern that WINS, and the next thing they need is a position where the same pattern is present and wins nothing. The motif is a geometric fact about a line. Whether it is worth anything is a separate question about the position, and this base has no business collapsing the two.

PROVENANCE. Found by the same geometric scan of the shipped puzzle corpus and of replayed master games. The move list replayed legally through the page's own move generator; no annotator read.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 across all three lines at depth 30, and the move that performs the interference is not one of them. The geometry is present and decides nothing.

by_level.beginner: This move stands right in the way of the piece that was defending, cutting it off.
by_level.intermediate: Interference: the {piece} is placed on the defender's line, so the defence is cut even though the piece can be taken.
by_level.advanced: Interference / interception (Informant theme i). Look for a square where two enemy defensive lines cross.

by_depth.short: Putting a piece on the line between a defender and what it defends.
by_depth.normal: Interference: a piece — often a sacrifice — is placed on the line an enemy piece is defending along, cutting the defence. The obstruction has to be one the defender cannot simply remove, or one whose removal costs more than the target.
by_depth.deep: The opposite of clearance: instead of emptying your own line you block theirs. The Nowotny and Plachutta themes are the composed forms, where one interposition cuts two defending lines at once and whichever piece captures blocks the other. Over the board the motif fails in one common way, and it is arithmetic: a piece dropped on a square the defender covers is simply taken, and the line reopens. In this base's registered case the interfering move throws away eight and a half pawns, because the position was already winning by attacking the target a second time instead.

by_level.beginner: Ideas that come with an 'unless' attached.
by_level.intermediate: Concepts that need a condition stated with them — doubled pawns are weak UNLESS the capture bought something.
by_level.advanced: The largest tier and the one misconceptions come from, because the condition is what gets dropped in retelling.

by_depth.short: Concepts that need a condition attached.
by_depth.normal: The tier where an idea can no longer be stated in one sentence without losing its condition — over 50 concepts, the largest group and the one most misconceptions come from.
by_depth.deep: A beginner concept is self-contained: a fork attacks two pieces and that is the whole idea. An intermediate concept needs a condition, and the condition is what gets lost in retelling - doubled pawns are weak unless the capture bought something, an outpost is strong if a pawn defends it, improve your worst piece when nothing more urgent is happening. That is why this is both the largest tier and the most dangerous: nearly every entry in this base's misconception index is an intermediate concept with its condition stripped off.

explanations.lesson: If you can state it without an 'unless', it is probably a beginner concept. If you cannot, do not drop the 'unless'.

intermediate-concepts.definition_short: Concepts that need one layer of context to state truthfully — over 50 of them, the largest tier.
intermediate-concepts.definition_long:
The tier where a concept can no longer be stated in one sentence without losing its condition.

A BEGINNER CONCEPT IS SELF-CONTAINED: a fork attacks two pieces, and that is the whole idea. An INTERMEDIATE CONCEPT NEEDS A CONDITION, and the condition is the part that gets lost in retelling. Doubled pawns are a weakness — unless the capture bought a file, the bishop pair or the centre. An outpost is strong — if a pawn defends it and no enemy pawn can attack it. Improve your worst piece — when nothing more urgent is happening.

THAT IS WHY THIS IS THE LARGEST TIER AND THE MOST DANGEROUS ONE. Nearly every entry in this base's misconception index is an intermediate concept with its condition removed, which is exactly the shape a chess misconception takes.

DIFFICULTY IN THIS BASE IS ABOUT THE CONCEPT, NOT THE PLAYER. It records how much other machinery a concept needs before it can be stated truthfully, which is why some famous ideas sit high and some obscure ones sit low. A fork is a beginner concept because it can be stated completely in one sentence; the Vancura position is an expert one not because it is hard to play but because stating it correctly requires the rook-ending context in which Tarrasch's rule fails.

IT IS ALSO WHAT DRIVES LEVEL ADAPTATION. Every concept carries explanations.by_level with wording for beginner, intermediate, advanced and master, and the API selects among them. The difficulty field says where a concept BELONGS; the by_level wording says how to say it to whoever is asking. The two are deliberately separate, because an advanced concept still has to be explicable to a beginner who has just met it on the board.

isolated-queen-pawn.knowledge_type_note: The textbook case of a feature that is simultaneously a static weakness and a dynamic asset, which is why it is classified as a concept rather than as a weakness.

attributions.note: Britannica records isolated pawns among the weaknesses named by Steinitz, and notes explicitly that they 'may confer middlegame compensation through control of important squares'. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: this is the conventional ascription, taken from a secondary source, and no primary text was consulted for it during this research.
Conventionally associated with an optimistic view of the IQP's dynamic side; not verified in this research.
Winning Pawn Structures is the standard modern treatment of the structure.

history.notes: Notably, Britannica's summary of Steinitz already contains BOTH halves — isolated pawns are a weakness, and they may confer middlegame compensation. The Tarrasch association is conventional and unverified here. Baburin's book has not been read.

development.change: Named as a structural weakness, with the compensation already noted.
Systematic treatment of the structure's plans for both sides.

isolated-queen-pawn.engine_era_note: Engines handle the IQP better than the rules of thumb do, because they simply evaluate the position rather than choosing a side. The received teaching — weakness in the endgame, asset in the middlegame — survives as a description of the tendency; what does not survive is any general verdict on whether the structure is good.

preconditions: A d-pawn with no friendly pawns on the c- or e-files
indicators_for: Minor pieces have been exchanged, so the pawn is a target and little else
The square in front is securely blockaded
The position is heading for an endgame
The half-open files are contested or neutralised
indicators_against: Pieces are still on and the IQP side has the initiative
The c- and e-files are giving the rooks real work
Knights are established on the outposts beside the pawn
Attacking chances against f7 are live
The pawn can advance at a chosen moment to liquidate favourably
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: an isolated pawn is not automatically a weakness. In the middlegame it is frequently the source of the better side's whole game.
The structure is trivially detectable and says almost nothing on its own — the material left on the board decides the evaluation more than the structure does.
Reporting it as a weakness while its owner has the initiative inverts the position.
An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).

typical_plans: With the IQP: keep pieces on, use the c- and e-files, occupy e5 and c5, attack f7, and time the d4-d5 break
Against it: exchange minor pieces, blockade the pawn with a knight, keep a queen and rook to attack it, and steer for an endgame
typical_moves: d4-d5 as the liberating break
Ne5 and Nc5 occupying the outposts
Nd4 as the blockader
typical_pawn_structures: Queen's Gambit and Panov structures with White's d4 isolated
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight blockading on d5 or d4
Rooks on the c- and e-files
tactical_consequences: Sacrifices against f7 and h7 arising from the space and open lines
strategic_consequences: The clearest instance of a static-versus-dynamic race in standard theory

exceptions: The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.
A d4-d5 break at the right moment can dissolve the weakness entirely and leave only the activity.
In some structures the isolated pawn is an asset even in the endgame, if it cramps the opponent and cannot be won.
limitations: Detecting the structure is mechanical; nothing about the evaluation follows from it without counting the remaining pieces.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, on the two traps about interpretation rather than detection: 'the structure is trivially detectable and says almost nothing on its own - the material left on the board decides the evaluation more than the structure does', and 'reporting it as a weakness while its owner has the initiative inverts the position'. Neither is answerable by a static feature, and neither has to be: this base never calls an isolated queen's pawn a weakness. The sentence reports the structure and the wording layer supplies the record's two-sided reading - space and two half-open files in the middlegame, a target in the endgame - and test_explanations.js forbids the word.

A NOTE ON THIS RECORD'S indicators_against, 2026-09-02, because the field means something different here from what it means on a concept that names an asset. All five - 'pieces are still on and the IQP side has the initiative', 'the c- and e-files are giving the rooks real work', 'knights are established on the outposts beside the pawn', 'attacking chances against f7 are live', 'the pawn can advance at a chosen moment to liquidate favourably' - are reasons the isolated pawn is an ASSET rather than a liability. They are not reasons to withhold the concept: the pawn is on the board either way. This base answers them by never calling it a weakness. The matcher reports the structure and the wording layer supplies the record's two-sided reading, and test_explanations.js forbids the word. Building any of them as a guard would suppress a structure that is present.
misconceptions: That an IQP is a weakness. It is a weakness in the endgame and often an asset in the middlegame.
That the correct plan against it is to trade everything. Trading the ATTACKERS leaves nothing to attack it with.
That the pawn is the target. The square in front of it is the more permanent asset.

conflicts.resolution: Not opposed, but they illustrate the same trap from two directions: a structural feature that is trivially detectable and whose value depends entirely on what else is on the board. Report the feature, then the condition that decides it — remaining material for the IQP, mobility for a passer.

by_level.beginner: That pawn has no pawns next to it to defend it, so pieces have to. In return it gives more space and open lines for the rooks.
by_level.intermediate: An IQP. In the middlegame it gives space, two half-open files and outposts on {squares}; in the endgame it is a target. The race is between those two clocks.
by_level.advanced: Static weakness, dynamic asset. With it, keep pieces on and look for the d5 break. Against it, trade minor pieces but keep a queen and rook — trading everything leaves nothing to attack it with.
by_level.master: The evaluation is a function of remaining material more than of structure. Blockade first, exchange the right pieces, and note that d4-d5 at the right moment converts the liability into pure activity.

by_depth.short: An isolated d-pawn: a target later, space and open files now.
by_depth.normal: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
by_depth.deep: The thematic case of static weakness against dynamic compensation, which is why it is taught more than any other structure. The static side: no pawn can defend it, and the square in front is a permanent blockading square. The dynamic side: central space, two half-open files for the rooks, outposts on the squares beside the pawn, and attacking chances against f7. The practical shape is a race — the IQP side must create something before the minor pieces come off, and the other side must trade them and reach an endgame. Note the qualification the blanket rule omits: trade MINOR pieces against an IQP, but keep a queen and a rook, because otherwise nothing remains to attack the pawn with.

explanations.lesson: An isolated pawn is a weakness in an endgame and a source of activity in a middlegame. Before judging it, count what is still on the board.
