isolated-queen-pawn.definition_short: A d-pawn with no friendly pawns on the c- or e-files: a static endgame liability and a middlegame source of space, open files and outposts.
isolated-queen-pawn.definition_long:
An isolated pawn on the d-file. It cannot be defended by a pawn, and the square in front of it is a permanent hole. That is the static side, and it grows more serious with every exchange — which is why the standard rule against it is 'trade pieces and it becomes a target'.

The dynamic side is equally real. The IQP grants a central space advantage, two half-open files (c and e) for the rooks, and outposts on the squares beside the pawn — e5 and c5 for White — which are exactly the squares knights want. Attacking chances against f7 flow from the same source.

It is the most thematic case in chess of static weakness against dynamic compensation, which is why it is taught so heavily; Baburin's Winning Pawn Structures is the standard treatment. The practical shape is a race between two clocks: the IQP side must generate something before the pieces come off, and the other side must trade minor pieces and reach an endgame.

Hence the two rules of thumb that follow, and they are genuinely opposed by design: with the IQP, keep pieces on; against it, trade minor pieces but keep the queen and a rook so the pawn can be attacked.

key-square.knowledge_type_note: Which squares are key is determined by the pawn's position and is computable, not a matter of judgement.

history.notes: No coinage researched. The concept is standard endgame theory of long standing.

key-square.engine_era_note: Computable and confirmed; tablebases make key squares derivable rather than memorised.

preconditions: A king-and-pawn ending where king penetration decides the result
indicators_for: The attacking king can reach a key square by force
The defending king cannot occupy or cover all of them
A route exists around the pawn that the defender cannot mirror
indicators_against: The defending king holds all the key squares
The pawn is a rook pawn, where the key squares are fewer and the draw is common
Pieces remain on the board, so the ending is not decided by king geometry

For a rook pawn the usual rules do not apply and the ending is frequently drawn regardless.
Reaching a key square is the goal; taking the opposition is only one way of getting there and is sometimes the wrong one.

typical_plans: Head for a key square, taking the opposition only when it helps you get there
Approach around the side of the pawn when the direct route is blocked
As the defender: cover the key squares and take the opposition when the attacking king advances
typical_moves: A king move that sidesteps rather than taking the opposition
typical_pawn_structures: King and pawn versus king
Blocked opposing pawns
strategic_consequences: Gives the opposition a purpose and tells you when to ignore it

exceptions: Rook pawns have their own, much more restrictive key squares and are often drawn.
Reaching a key square by the direct route is sometimes impossible while a route around the pawn works.
limitations: Applies to king-and-pawn endings; not a general concept.
misconceptions: That the opposition is the goal. The key square is the goal; the opposition is a means.
That key squares are the same for every pawn. They depend on the pawn's rank and file.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The white king stands on g6, directly in front of and beside its own passed pawn, with the black king shut in the corner. For any other pawn on the board that square is a key square and the position is winning. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: A rook pawn has no key squares in the ordinary sense, because the defending king cannot be driven off the queening square — there is no room on the other side of the pawn to be driven towards. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, and the tablebase's own best move is h6 — which leads nowhere. The API does not report key-square. This is the case that catches a detector built on 'the king is in front of the pawn': the geometry is identical to the winning case and the file is the whole difference. Compare `wrong-rook-pawn`, which is the same fact stated about the bishop instead of the king.

by_level.beginner: If your king can get to one of these squares, the pawn promotes. That is what your king is trying to do.
by_level.intermediate: Key squares. Take the opposition when it gets you to one; if it does not, head for them directly instead.
by_level.advanced: The pawn's rank determines them. Averbakh's point applies: the opposition is a means and this is the end.
by_level.master: Computable from the pawn. In blocked-pawn positions they extend three files either side of the enemy pawn, and the first king to arrive wins one pawn while holding its own.

by_depth.short: Get the king here and the pawn queens.
by_depth.normal: Key squares: if the king reaches one, the result follows by force. For a pawn on the second to fourth rank they are the square two ranks ahead of it and the squares either side.
by_depth.deep: Squares whose occupation by the king forces a gain. In king and pawn versus king they depend only on the pawn's position and are computable. Their real importance is that they give the opposition a purpose — Averbakh's formulation is that the opposition is a means to an end and the end is penetration to a key square, which is what stops opposition-taking being a ritual. In some positions the correct move ignores the opposition entirely and marches for a key square by a route around the pawn.

explanations.lesson: Work out the key squares first. Then the opposition tells you how to get there — or that you should not bother.

beginner_words: the squares that win the game

key-square.definition_short: A square such that if a king reaches it, some gain follows by force — usually the promotion of a pawn or the capture of one.
key-square.definition_long:
Squares whose occupation by the king forces a result. In king and pawn versus king they depend only on where the pawn is and are easy to state: for a pawn on the second to fourth rank there are three key squares, two ranks ahead of the pawn and the squares either side of that; for a pawn on the fifth or sixth rank the squares one rank ahead also become key; for a rook pawn the key squares are different again.

Their importance is that they give the OPPOSITION its purpose. Averbakh's formulation — the opposition is a means to an end, and the end is penetration to a key square — is what stops the opposition being a ritual. If taking the opposition does not lead to a key square, taking it may be pointless; and in some positions the king should ignore the opposition and march for a key square directly.

In blocked-pawn positions the concept generalises: with a pair of pawns facing each other, the key squares extend three files either side of the opponent's pawn, and the first king to reach one wins the opposing pawn while defending its own.

king-activation.knowledge_type_note: Typed a principle rather than a rule because its own principal advocate documents a class of positions where it fails, and this base follows him.

attributions.note: Lists centralisation of the king first among the four basic endgame principles in Endgame Strategy, and documents its failure mode in rook endings.

The standard exemplar of the marching endgame king. Znosko-Borovsky is quoted as contrasting Alekhine's queen with the king as the principal instrument of Capablanca's victories - a quotation this base has not verified at source.

history.notes: The idea long predates Shereshevsky and is not his invention; he is credited with systematising it and, more valuably, with documenting where it breaks. The Znosko-Borovsky quotation reaches this base through an instructional blog and is recorded at low confidence.

king-activation.engine_era_note: Strongly confirmed. Engines value an active king in simplified positions highly and will spend material to activate one, which was the part of Capablanca's method that looked most like intuition and turns out to be calculable.

preconditions: Queens are off or a transition to an endgame is imminent
No mating threats against the king
indicators_for: Weak enemy pawns the king could attack
A passed pawn needing escort or blockade
The enemy king is further from the action
Few enough pieces that mating nets are unlikely
indicators_against: Queens or many pieces remain and the king can be attacked
A rook ending with concrete defensive resources, where the king may be needed at home
The centralising move loses time in a race
The king would step into a check that gains the opponent a tempo
false_positive_traps: The single most important trap is rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate: Shereshevsky found centralisation there to be not merely untimely but sometimes simply wrong, and warns against automatic centralising moves.
A king moving towards the centre is not automatically doing the right thing; the move still has to survive checks. His example has 1...Ke5? losing to 2.Rd5+ while the retreat 1...Kc5! draws.
Centralisation with queens still on is a different matter entirely and this concept does not apply.
Never recommend centralising a king while the opponent has a queen, whatever the piece count says. The phase test in lib/features.js is material-based and can call a queens-on position an endgame.

typical_plans: Bring the king to the centre as the queens come off, before it is needed
Use the king to attack fixed pawn weaknesses
Escort a passed pawn with the king
Blockade an enemy passed pawn with the king, freeing pieces for active work
typical_moves: Kf2-e3-d4 style marches once queens are exchanged
typical_pawn_structures: Fixed pawn weaknesses within a king's reach
typical_piece_arrangements: Simplified positions with few or no minor pieces
tactical_consequences: An exchange sacrifice to install the king on a strong central square can be sound
strategic_consequences: The side whose king arrives first usually wins otherwise level endings

exceptions: Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.
Races, where a centralising move may simply be too slow.
limitations: Whether a particular king move is right remains a concrete question; the principle says where the king belongs, not whether this move gets it there safely.
This base's attempts to build a controlled pair isolating king activity in rook endings FAILED twice - see the concept's audit notes - which is itself consistent with Shereshevsky's finding.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first trap - 'the single most important trap is ROOK ENDINGS... Shereshevsky found centralisation there to be not merely untimely but sometimes simply wrong, and warns against automatic centralising moves' - is now carried in the sentence, which names the rook ending and the warning. Both stronger answers were tried and both are wrong: refusing the concept in rook endings deletes Capablanca-Tartakower 1924, this corpus's own annotated instance and the most famous king march in a rook ending in the literature; and downgrading to low confidence says 'we are not sure the king is off its back rank', which is not the doubt Shereshevsky is expressing. He warns against centralising AUTOMATICALLY. 33 of the 122 positions this fires on are rook endings.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the third trap - 'centralisation with queens still on is a different matter entirely and this concept does not apply' - is enforced by the phase gate rather than by a separate test, and it is the same mechanism as the fourth: phaseOf() returns 'endgame' only when there are NO queens on the board, so a queens-on position never reaches this matcher at all.
misconceptions: That the king should be kept safe in the endgame as it is earlier. The change in the king's role is what defines the phase.
That centralisation is always correct. Its own advocate documents rook endings where it is not.

conflicts.resolution: The same piece, opposite advice, and the phase decides. King safety governs while a mating attack is possible; king activity governs once it is not. The dangerous ground is the transition, and the honest test is whether any enemy force can still generate threats against the king rather than whether the queens happen to be off.

by_level.beginner: Once the queens come off, bring your king towards the middle. It is a fighting piece now.
by_level.intermediate: Centralise the king in the endgame. The side whose king gets to the action first usually wins otherwise level endings.
by_level.advanced: Bring it in anticipation of the ending rather than after it arrives - but be careful in rook endings, which are concrete enough to punish automatic centralising.
by_level.master: Shereshevsky himself reports finding outright incorrect centralisation in rook endings, and attributes it to the king's larger defensive role there.

by_depth.short: In the endgame the king is a fighting piece - bring it to the centre.
by_depth.normal: Centralisation of the king: once queens are off and mating attacks are unlikely, the king becomes an active piece and often the strongest one. by_depth.deep: The change that defines the endgame, and the first of Shereshevsky's four basic principles - stated by him at close to full strength, since centralisation is 'almost never wrong' and 'can only be untimely'. The exception is worth as much as the rule and comes from the same source: Shereshevsky reports being surprised to find centralisation in rook endings that was not merely untimely but wrong, explaining that rook endings are very concrete, full of defensive set-ups and fortresses, and that the king's defensive role there is much larger. king-activation.definition_short: Once queens are off, the king becomes a fighting piece and belongs in the centre rather than in shelter.
king-activation.definition_long:
The change that defines the endgame. In the opening and middlegame the king hides; once the chance of a mating attack recedes, it becomes an active piece and often the strongest one on the board. Shereshevsky lists it first among the four basic principles of endgame play and states the rule at close to full strength: centralisation of the king in the endgame is 'almost never wrong. It can only be untimely.'

THE MECHANISM is that the king is a short-range piece that is finally allowed to move. It attacks weak pawns, escorts passed pawns, blockades enemy ones, and does all of it without costing a piece elsewhere. The side whose king reaches the action first usually wins endings that look level, which is why experienced players bring the king towards the centre in ANTICIPATION of an ending rather than after one has arrived.

THE AUTHOR'S OWN EXCEPTION is the reason this record exists in the form it does, and it is unusually honest testimony. Shereshevsky reports being SURPRISED that in rook endings he could find examples of centralisation that were not merely untimely but outright INCORRECT, and offers a candid explanation: rook endings are very concrete, full of specific defensive set-ups and fortresses, and the king's defensive role there is much more significant than in other endings. His own illustration has the natural 1...Ke5? losing while the illogical 1...Kc5!, stepping the king FURTHER from the enemy passed pawn, draws.

MEASURED HERE: with identical material and only the defending king's square changed, the defence lasted more than twice as long with the king in front of the pawn — mate in 35 against mate in 15. That quantifies the king's defensive value directly, in a position where nothing else differs.

king-attack.knowledge_type_note: A strategic principle with an unusually firm PRECONDITION attached, which is what stops it being merely a rule of thumb. Vukovic's tradition holds that an attack is not a choice of style but a consequence of an existing advantage.

attributions.note: The doctrine that one must not attack without an advantage is his; Lasker summarised his theory as 'Do not attack when you have no tangible advantage in position.'
The Art of Attack in Chess is the standard systematic treatment; focal points and the conditions for the classic bishop sacrifice are his.

history.notes: Attacking the king is as old as chess; what is attributable is the doctrine that it requires justification (Steinitz) and its systematic treatment (Vukovic). Neither is a claim of invention. Vukovic's text has not been read directly — see the source's access caveat.

development.change: Attack treated as the normal way to play; soundness a secondary question.
Attack becomes conditional on an existing advantage rather than a matter of style.
Systematised: preconditions, timing, focal points, pawn-shelter types, named sacrifices.
Defensive resources better understood; the third opposite-castling scenario — attacking while also slowing the opponent — becomes the common treatment.

king-attack.engine_era_note: Engines have raised the bar for what counts as a justified attack, refuting many attacking sacrifices that were played on general grounds, and have made defence look far more resilient than classical writing assumed. The PRECONDITION doctrine survives this well; what does not survive is the romantic assumption that a king with a damaged shelter is losing.

preconditions: More attacking units bear on the king's sector than defending units, or the king's cover is durably weakened
The attacker's own king is safe, or safe enough for the time the operation needs
The centre is closed or under control, so a counter-blow there is not available
indicators_for: A clear focal point — a weak square next to the king that pieces can occupy or sacrifice on
The defender's key defensive piece (often a knight on f6 or a fianchettoed bishop) can be exchanged or driven off
A file or diagonal can be opened towards the king by a pawn break
Opposite-side castling, so pawns can advance without cost
A hook — an advanced enemy pawn that gives the attacker something to attack in order to open a line
indicators_against: The centre is open or can be opened by the defender
Development is unfinished; a missing rook is often the exact tempo the attack lacks
The defender can trade queens, which usually ends the attack
The attacker has no way to bring a third piece to the sector
The king's shelter is intact and there is no sacrifice that breaks it
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: king-attack, implementing all three of the record's preconditions. The repository's `kingAttack` puzzle tag (checks >= 2 or mate) remains a proxy for puzzle classification and is NOT this.
false_positive_traps: Two checks is not an attack. The repository's `kingAttack` tag fires on checks >= 2 or mate, which is a proxy for puzzle classification and NOT a definition of the concept.
An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one. This is a registered false-positive case.
Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow into the lines that open.

typical_plans: Exchange the defender — the f6 knight, the g7 bishop — before striking
Open a file or diagonal with a pawn break, then double heavy pieces on it
Sacrifice on a focal point to strip the shelter, with a follow-up piece already in range
In opposite-side castling, count tempi to contact and start the storm first
Combine the attack with prophylaxis against the opponent's counter-attack

Bxh7+ and Bxh6 sacrifices on the shelter
Rook lifts to the third rank and across

f7-g6-h7 — holes on f6 and h6, but sound while a bishop sits on g7
f7-g7-h6 — h6 is both a target and a hook for g4-g5
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen and bishop battery on b1-h7
Rook on the g- or h-file behind an advancing pawn
Knight reaching g5 or f5

strategic_consequences: An attack that fails usually leaves the attacker structurally worse, especially after a pawn storm

A wing attack can be refuted by a central counter-blow — the standard antidote.
Trading queens usually ends an attack, so the defender's simplest defence is often to seek that trade.
Damaged pawn cover is not decisive by itself. It matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.

The repo's kingAttack tag is a puzzle-classification proxy and should not be read as the concept.

by_level.beginner: White is bringing more pieces near the black king than Black has defending it, and trying to open a line to get at it.
by_level.intermediate: An attack on the king. It works here because {more attackers than defenders / the shelter is weakened} — and note the centre is {closed / controlled}, so there is no counter-blow.
by_level.advanced: The attack is justified by {local superiority / a focal point on {square}}. The critical question is the defender's key defensive piece and whether it can be removed.
by_level.master: Count attackers against defenders in the sector, identify the focal point, and check the centre and the queen trade before committing. The doctrine since Steinitz is that an attack must be earned, not chosen.

by_depth.short: More force is bearing on the king than is defending it.
by_depth.normal: An attack on the king, justified by {reason}. Attacks require a pre-existing advantage — usually more pieces near the king than the defender has, or holes in the pawn cover — and they fail when the centre is open or the defender can trade queens.
by_depth.deep: Vukovic's treatment is the standard one. An attack is a consequence of an advantage rather than a choice of style, a doctrine going back to Steinitz. It is usually best understood as an operation against a specific weak square next to the king — a focal point — rather than against the king in general. The pawn shelter's type matters: f7-g7-h7 intact is the most resistant and normally needs a sacrifice; f7-g6-h7 has holes on f6 and h6 but is sound while a bishop stands on g7, which is why trading that bishop is so often the whole plan. Opposite-side castling turns the game into a race where a tempo decides, and the modern treatment combines attacking with slowing the opponent down rather than pure racing.

explanations.lesson: Before attacking, count: how many of your pieces can reach the king's sector, and how many of theirs defend it? If the answer is not in your favour, improve the position instead — and check the centre first.

beginner_words: opening a line to the king
avoid: attack because the king looks exposed

king-attack.definition_short: A concerted operation against the enemy king, justified only by an existing advantage — usually local superiority in force near the king, or weaknesses in its cover.
king-attack.definition_long:
Not a mood but a consequence. The classical position, following Vukovic, is that an attack must be EARNED: you cannot attack the king without a positional advantage, and attacking without one fails against any competent defence. The advantage usually takes the form of LOCAL SUPERIORITY — more pieces bearing on the king's sector than the defender has defending it, or a pawn majority there — or of durable weaknesses in the king's pawn cover.

FOCAL POINTS. Vukovic's central contribution: 'every focal-point is a weak square in the defender's territory and a potentially strong one for the attacker', especially when adjacent to the king. g7 and h7 (g2 and h2 mirrored) are the classic ones. An attack is usually best understood as an operation against a specific square rather than against the king in general.

PAWN COVER. The three common shelters differ sharply in resilience. f7-g7-h7 unmoved is the most resistant and usually has to be broken by sacrifice. f7-g6-h7 leaves f6 and h6 as holes and invites h4-h5 or f4-f5 to open a file — but is not weak while a bishop sits on g7, which is why exchanging that bishop is so often the whole plan. f7-g7-h6 gives the h6 pawn as a target and a hook for g4-g5.

OPPOSITE-SIDE CASTLING changes the character completely: pawns can be thrown forward without exposing one's own king, and the game becomes a race where a single tempo decides. Franco distinguishes three scenarios — a mutual race, an attack against pure defence, and the modern treatment that combines attacking with prophylaxis on one's own wing.

The standing counter-principle is that a wing attack is answered in the centre. An attack launched while the centre is open, or while one's own development is unfinished, tends to rebound.

king-safety.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept, and the one that overrides the others — not because it is more important in the abstract but because checkmate ends the game, so every other advantage is conditional on it.

attributions.note: King exposure enters positional theory as a durable feature to be evaluated rather than a matter of tactical alertness.

history.notes: No coinage claimed; the term is ordinary. The attribution to Steinitz is for the doctrine of evaluating it, and is weakly sourced here.

development.change: King exposure becomes an evaluable positional factor rather than a purely tactical one.
Quantified explicitly: attack units by piece type, a defined king zone, and a non-linear scoring table.

king-safety.engine_era_note: Not merely reliable but quantified, and the quantification is public. The engine-era refinement worth carrying into explanations is the NON-LINEARITY: danger rises slowly with one or two attackers and then steeply, which is why 'they have a piece near my king' is not a warning and 'they have three' is.

preconditions: A king's exposure is being assessed
indicators_for: Pawn shield intact and unmoved
Few enemy pieces able to reach the king zone
No open file or diagonal pointing at the king
Defenders present, especially a knight on f3/f6
Escape squares available
Queens off the board
indicators_against: Three or more attackers can reach the king zone
Shield pawns advanced or missing, especially with an open file beside the king
A hook the opponent can attack to open a line
King uncastled with the centre open or opening
Key defender exchangeable — the fianchettoed bishop, or the f6 knight
No escape square, so back-rank tactics are live

false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: an exposed king is not automatically losing. With the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often simply an active one — and in the endgame that is the goal.
Castling does not establish safety and failing to castle does not establish danger. A closed centre changes both.
Counting attacking pieces linearly overstates one or two and understates four. The relationship is S-shaped, and it is not worth reporting an attack below three attackers.
A pawn move near the king is not automatically a weakening — h3 in a quiet position is useful luft; the same move against a queenside-castled opponent is a hook.
An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.

typical_plans: Castle by default in open positions; delay only for a stated concrete reason
Leave the shield pawns alone unless there is a specific need
When under attack: trade the strongest attacker, ideally queens; add a defender; close the line; return material; or run the king before the files open
When attacking: count attackers against defenders before calculating
typical_moves: Qe2 or Re1 or Nf1 as quiet defensive additions
h3 as luft — in the right circumstances only
typical_pawn_structures: f2-g2-h2 unmoved — the hardest structure to break
Fianchetto: g3 and Bg2, sound while the bishop lives
h3 or h6 played against an opponent who can storm — a hook
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight on f3/f6 as the best defensive minor piece
Rook on e1/e8 covering entry squares
tactical_consequences: Back-rank mates when there is no escape square
Sacrifices on the shield become sound once attackers outnumber defenders
strategic_consequences: Overrides other advantages, because mate ends the game
Inverts in the endgame, where the king becomes a strong piece

exceptions: An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.
An uncastled king in a closed position can be safer than a castled one.
Castling into an oncoming pawn storm gives the attacker a fixed address; sometimes delaying or castling the other way is correct.
h3 or ...h6 is useful luft in a quiet position and a hook against an opponent who can storm. The same move, opposite meanings.
limitations: Judgement, not measurement, at the human level — though Stockfish's scheme is a usable specification for a detector.
The attacker/defender count is an alarm, not a verdict; it tells you when calculation is worth starting.

The static arm reports EXPOSURE, never danger, and the difference is the whole of the concept's registered false positive. Adams-Kasparov 2005 after 21...Kxh7 is the measured case: Black's king has no pawn in front of it at all and exactly ONE enemy piece bearing on its zone, and Black is winning by two pawns of evaluation. Anything that turns the first fact into a verdict is wrong.
It cannot see the thing that decides such positions, which is who mates first. That is a property of the concrete lines and this base does not calculate.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'castling does not establish safety and failing to castle does not establish danger. A closed centre changes both' is honoured by never testing castling at all. The three arms count attackers and defenders of the king zone and read the shield pawns; the word 'castled' appears nowhere in the matcher, and an uncastled king in a closed position produces no report.

A NOTE ON THIS RECORD'S indicators_against, 2026-09-02: this concept names a SCALE, so they are the conditions under which the king is UNSAFE - which is to say the conditions the matcher fires ON, not guards against firing. 'Three or more attackers can reach the king zone' is the count arm, 'shield pawns advanced or missing' is the bare-shield arm, and 'no escape square, so back-rank tactics are live' is what `luft` reports. Building them as false-positive guards would invert the concept. The distinction is now written into tools/trap_audit.js's artifact so the next reader does not build them backwards.
misconceptions: That castling makes the king safe.
That an exposed king is losing.
That pushing a pawn to chase an enemy piece away from your king is a defensive move. It usually creates a hook and the piece just steps aside.
That material compensates for king danger. It does not — checkmate ends the game regardless.

With same-side castling there is, and the burden of proof sits on the attacker: a wing attack that opens your own king is refuted by a counter-blow in the centre.

by_level.beginner: Your king is safest castled, behind pawns you have not moved, with a piece or two nearby. Moving those pawns makes holes you can never fill again.
by_level.intermediate: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
by_level.advanced: Shield, lines, attacker count, escape squares. Note that danger is non-linear in the attacker count, and that trading queens is the strongest single defensive resource.
by_level.master: Assess by what the opponent can concretely open and how fast. Castling is a means; an uncastled king behind a closed centre may be the safest king on the board, and in the endgame exposure becomes activity.

by_depth.short: The king is {safe / exposed} — {reason}.
by_depth.normal: King safety: the shield is {intact/damaged}, {n} enemy pieces can reach the king's zone against {m} defenders, and {an open file / no open line} points at it. That is what decides whether an attack is possible, not whether the king has castled.
by_depth.deep: Five factors: castled or not, shield integrity, attackers against defenders, open lines, escape squares. The shield is strongest unmoved because it offers no target, and every advance both weakens squares permanently and creates a hook for the opponent to bite on. Engine practice makes the counting explicit — Stockfish weights a minor piece attacking the king zone as 2 units, a rook 3, a queen 5, and looks the sum up in an S-shaped table, with the practical consequence that an attack with fewer than three attackers is not worth evaluating. The concept overrides the others because checkmate ends the game, and it inverts entirely in the endgame, where the exposed king becomes a fighting piece.

explanations.lesson: Count attackers against defenders before you decide whether to worry. And do not push the pawns in front of your own king to chase a piece — the piece steps aside and the hole stays forever.

beginner_words: pawns in front of the king

king-safety.definition_short: How exposed the king is to attack, judged by pawn cover, open lines pointing at it, the count of attackers against defenders, and escape squares.
king-safety.definition_long:
Five things decide it, and they are worth checking in order: is the king castled; is the pawn shield intact; how many enemy pieces can reach the king's zone against how many defenders; do open files or diagonals point at it; does it have escape squares.

THE PAWN SHIELD is the part players damage themselves. Pawns in front of a castled king are strongest unmoved, because an unmoved shield presents no target. Every advance does two things: it permanently weakens the squares the pawn has left, and it creates a HOOK — a fixed pawn the opponent can attack in order to force a file open. Playing g3 weakens f3 and h3 for good and gives ...h5-h4 something to bite on.

CASTLING IS NOT SAFETY. A castled king with a damaged shield and an open file beside it is a target with a known address; an uncastled king in a closed position can be perfectly safe. Castling usually helps, and should be the default in open positions, but it is a means.

ENGINE PRACTICE IS UNUSUALLY EXPLICIT HERE and worth borrowing. Stockfish defines a king zone as the squares the enemy king can reach plus three forward squares, counts a minor piece attacking it as 2 attack units, a rook as 3 and a queen as 5, adds 6 for a safe queen contact check, and looks the total up in an S-shaped table that rises slowly then steeply. The Chess Programming Wiki's practical note is the useful one: it is not worth evaluating a king attack at all with fewer than three attackers. That matches the coaching heuristic that three or more attackers against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.

The strongest single defensive idea is trading queens. In the endgame the whole concept inverts and the king becomes a fighting piece.

knight-endgames.knowledge_type_note: A principle with a named formula behind it, and an explicit admission from the standard reference that a large part of the territory has no operative principles at all.

attributions.note: 'A knight ending is really a pawn ending', quoted as Botvinnik's Formula in Dvoretsky's Endgame Manual.
Endgame Manual, whose knight chapter is the standard modern treatment; the 5th edition's revisions are Karsten Mueller's.
The four-against-three analysis, whose winning verdict modern theory has downgraded.

history.notes: Botvinnik's remark is quoted consistently by two independent sources here, in slightly different wordings, which is normal for a remark rather than a written formulation.

development.note: Fine analyses four-against-three as a win.
The verdict is revised to 'good winning chances'; Mueller's 2019 analysis corrects several long-accepted lines.

knight-endgames.engine_era_note: Knight endings have been substantially rewritten by engines and tablebases. A verdict standing since 1941 has been downgraded, and the standard reference now carries corrections dated 2019 to lines that had been accepted for decades.

preconditions: Knights and pawns only, or nearly so
indicators_for: An outside passed pawn
A king that can be activated
A zugzwang available
false_positive_traps: Botvinnik's formula is a guide to which techniques transfer, not a claim that the ending IS a pawn ending. The knight's ability to fork and check reintroduces tempo, and knight against knight and pawn has no operative principles at all on the standard reference's own account.
A knight cannot lose a tempo, so triangulation and other tempo-losing methods that work with other pieces are unavailable to it.

typical_plans: Activate the king, exactly as in a pawn ending
Create and advance an outside passed pawn
Play for zugzwang
Sacrifice the knight to reach a won pawn ending or clear a promotion path
Blockade an enemy passer with the knight rather than chase it
typical_moves: The deflecting knight sacrifice
typical_pawn_structures: An outside passed pawn
All pawns on one wing, where the knight is at its best
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight in front of an enemy passed pawn
tactical_consequences: Knight forks and checks are the way tempo is won in an otherwise tempo-less ending
strategic_consequences: Pawn-ending judgement transfers, so a knight ending can often be assessed by asking what the pawn ending would be

exceptions: Knight against knight and pawn is explicitly outside the principles: the standard reference says there are none operative for many such positions.
The knight is poor at catching a passed pawn, so the pawn-ending intuition about races does not transfer.
Rook pawns suit the knight badly.
limitations: This base holds no tablebase-verified knight-ending positions yet; the record rests on textual authority.
Fine's downgraded verdict is recorded from the secondary literature and has not been re-derived here.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION. The examples on this record are `tablebase-position`s, and for this family that is the stronger provenance rather than a substitute: the claims here are about what a class of ending can and cannot do, and a proof over every legal continuation settles that where a single game only illustrates it. What a master game would add is evidence that the principle GUIDED a strong player, which is a different claim, and this base has not yet found an annotated position making it for this family. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Karpov-Ponomariov, Zlatoust 1961, above.
misconceptions: That a knight ending is a pawn ending. It is one for the purposes of several techniques and is not one when the knights start forking.
That knights are good blockaders and good chasers. They are excellent at the first and poor at the second.

conflicts.resolution: Triangulation is unavailable to a knight, which cannot lose a single tempo because every move changes square colour. The king must do the tempo-losing in a knight ending, which is one of the concrete ways Botvinnik's formula holds.

examples.note: Constructed, and it is Botvinnik's sentence with a board under it: knight endings are pawn endings. Two pawns against none, knight against knight, and the extra material converts the way it would if the knights were not there - the knight cannot build a fortress, cannot stop two connected pawns on its own, and cannot lose a tempo to gain the opposition. What it takes is a long time, which is the second half of the lesson and is why the proof matters more than the evaluation.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 1, mate in 65, best move e3. Sixty-five moves for two extra pawns and no tactics anywhere in it: the proof is what makes this an example of a PRINCIPLE rather than of a position, because no human calculation reaches the end of that and the principle is what tells you to enter it.

examples.note:
KNIGHTS AND PAWNS ONLY, which is this record's whole precondition, on move 79 of a real game. A white knight on d5 and a black knight on h8, four pawns, two kings, and nothing else.

The record's claim is that these endings behave like pawn endings because a knight cannot lose a tempo, and the position shows exactly the shape that makes that matter: White's h-pawn is one square from queening and the black knight on h8 is the only thing stopping it, while both kings are on the other side of the board.

WHAT IS CLAIMED AND WHAT IS NOT. The category is decided by the material, which is mechanically certain and needs no engine. Whether the position is INTERESTING, or who is better in it, is a different question and this record does not answer it - its own typical_confidence says as much. What the position establishes is that the class of ending this record is about occurs in master play and can be pointed at.

by_depth.deep: Botvinnik's formula is mechanical rather than poetic. A knight changes square colour every move, so it cannot lose a single tempo and cannot triangulate, and the techniques that turn on tempo therefore transfer intact from pawn endings. The knight's own properties modify that: it blockades a passed pawn superbly and chases one badly, it dislikes rook pawns, and it can fork or check to win the tempo the ending otherwise lacks. The characteristic technique is the deflecting sacrifice - giving the knight to reach a won pawn ending. And the principles run out in a place the standard reference names: knight against knight and pawn is called chaotic, with no principles operative for many positions.

knight-endgames.definition_short: Endings with knights and pawns, which behave like pawn endings because a knight cannot lose a tempo.
knight-endgames.definition_long:
BOTVINNIK'S FORMULA is the organising idea: 'a knight ending is really a pawn ending'. The mechanism is precise rather than poetic. A knight changes square colour with every move, so it cannot lose a single tempo and cannot triangulate — and the techniques that depend on tempo therefore transfer intact from pawn endings. The active king, the outside passed pawn, the breakthrough, shouldering and every method of playing for zugzwang all work in knight endings much as they do with pawns alone.

THE KNIGHT'S OWN PROPERTIES modify that. It is poor at chasing a passed pawn and ideal at blockading one, since it controls the squares in front rather than needing to catch up. It has a well-known distaste for rook pawns. And it can fork or check to win a tempo, which is the one way tempo re-enters an ending that otherwise runs on pawn-ending logic.

THE DEFLECTING KNIGHT SACRIFICE is the characteristic technique — giving the knight to reach a pawn ending that is winning, or to remove the piece guarding a promotion path. Dvoretsky calls it 'almost universally employed' in these endings.

WHERE THE PRINCIPLES RUN OUT, and the standard reference says so plainly: knight against knight and pawn is 'quite complex, and rather chaotic', with 'no principles which are operative for many positions' — the evaluation depends entirely on concrete details. That is an unusually direct admission and this record keeps it rather than papering over it.

AND A CLASSIC VERDICT HAS BEEN DOWNGRADED. Fine's 1941 analysis held the four-against-three knight ending to be a win; modern theory revises that to 'good winning chances', because so many of the resulting positions are drawn. Knight endings are also where a player's practical chances of converting an extra pawn with all pawns on one wing are highest, pawn endings excepted.

by_level.beginner: The knight attacks two pieces at once. They cannot both move, and nothing can block a knight.
by_level.intermediate: A knight fork. Check the square the knight lands on is safe first — that is what decides whether it wins anything.
by_level.advanced: The knight attacks the opposite colour to the square it stands on, so a forked piece can never defend itself by attacking back. Nothing interposes either.
by_level.master: Geometry first: get the enemy pieces onto one colour and the knight within range. The forking square's safety is the whole condition.

by_depth.short: The knight hits two things at once.
by_depth.normal: A knight fork: one knight attacks two or more pieces, and neither interposition nor counter-attack defends, because a knight cannot be blocked and attacks the opposite colour to the one it occupies.
by_depth.deep: The most dangerous form of fork, for three reasons rooted in the knight's move. It attacks squares of the opposite colour to the one it stands on, so a forked piece cannot defend itself by attacking back — only another knight can. Its move is the hardest to visualise, so these are the tactics most often missed. And it cannot be blocked, so interposition is never a defence. The classic squares are c7 and f7 against a king and a corner rook. The conditions for it to win material are the fork's general ones and they bite hard: in a controlled test the same Nc7+ is worth +7.39 with the landing square free and +0.57 with one bishop guarding it.

explanations.lesson: When you see a knight fork, check the square it lands on before you check anything else.

avoid: a knight fork always wins material

knight-fork.definition_short: A fork delivered by a knight — the most dangerous kind, because no other piece can be defended against it by standing next to it.
knight-fork.definition_long:
The fork's most common and most dangerous form. Three properties of the knight's move are responsible.

First, the knight attacks squares of the OPPOSITE colour to the one it stands on, so a forked piece can never simply defend itself by attacking the knight back — except another knight. Second, its move is the hardest to visualise, so knight forks are the tactics most often missed. Third, the knight cannot be blocked, so interposition is never a defence.

The archetypal squares are c7 and f7 (c2 and f2 mirrored), where a knight forks the king and a rook in the corner. When king, queen and rook are hit at once, the result is often called a FAMILY FORK; when it is king and queen, a ROYAL FORK. Both names are attested and neither is essential.

The conditions for it to WIN are the fork's general ones, and they matter as much here: the landing square must be safe, and at least one target must be undefended or worth more than the knight. A knight fork on a defended square wins nothing, and this base contains an engine-tested controlled pair demonstrating exactly that — the same Nc7+ swings 6.82 pawns depending on whether one bishop covers the landing square.

knight-vs-bishop.knowledge_type_note: A comparison whose answer is entirely positional. The individual piece values are disputed; only the bishop PAIR has a measured advantage.

attributions.note: Known for preferring the bishop and for the 3.25 versus 3 valuation. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED against Fischer's own writing.
Statistical values put the two pieces equal at 3.5 and locate the advantage in the pair.

history.notes: Disputed as to the VALUES, not the concept. Fischer's preference, Kaufman's parity and Studer's scepticism about the evidence for bishop superiority are all recorded rather than reconciled. What is not disputed is the pair.
competing_claims: Bishop 3.25 versus knight 3 (Fischer, and much popular teaching).
Bishop 3.5 and knight 3.5 — equal — with the pair worth an extra half pawn (Kaufman, statistical).
The claim of individual bishop superiority is unsupported by evidence (Studer).

KNIGHT: closed position, secure outpost, pawns on one side only, queen alongside it, blockading duty

The knight has no square it can reach and hold
The structure is about to change, which can reverse the assessment

Pawns on one side only REVERSES the usual open-position reasoning — the knight is stronger there, which surprises people who have learnt 'bishops are better in the endgame'.
A knight without a stable square is not a knight worth keeping; the outpost is the whole condition.

typical_plans: With the bishop: open the position and create play on both wings
With the knight: close the position and secure an outpost
Studer's rule: with two knights and a bishop, play on your bishop's colour; with two bishops and a knight, play on the colour your opponent's missing bishop covered
typical_pawn_structures: Closed centres favouring the knight
Pawns on both wings favouring the bishop
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight on a protected outpost
Bishop on a long open diagonal
strategic_consequences: Determines whether to open or close the position
The bishop pair is complementary; a knight pair is redundant

exceptions: Pawns on one wing only favours the knight, reversing the usual endgame guidance.
A queen prefers a knight as a partner; a rook prefers a bishop.
A knight with no secure square is worse than almost any bishop.
limitations: The individual values are disputed between reputable sources and this record does not resolve it.
Recognition confidence is low because the answer depends on structure that may change.
misconceptions: That bishops are simply better than knights. Kaufman's data has them equal and a grandmaster says the superiority claim is unevidenced.
That bishops are always better in the endgame. With all the pawns on one wing the knight is stronger.
That two knights are a 'pair'. They are redundant — they want the same squares.

by_level.beginner: Bishops like open positions and pawns on both sides of the board. Knights like closed positions and a safe square in the middle they cannot be chased off.
by_level.intermediate: Knight or bishop? Ask whether the position is open, whether the pawns are on one wing or two, and whether the knight has a square it can hold.
by_level.advanced: The individual values are disputed — Kaufman's data has them equal, with the bonus attaching to the pair. Note the reversal: pawns on one wing only favours the knight.
by_level.master: With two knights and a bishop, play on your bishop's colour; with two bishops and a knight, play on the colour your opponent's missing bishop covered.

by_depth.short: Bishops want open positions; knights want closed ones and an outpost.
by_depth.normal: The commonest imbalance. Bishops are better in open positions and with pawns on both wings; knights are better in closed positions, with a secure outpost, and when all the pawns are on one side.
by_depth.deep: Which piece is better is entirely positional, and the individual values are genuinely disputed — Fischer put the bishop above the knight, Kaufman's statistics put them equal at 3.5 each, and GM Studer says the superiority claim has no evidence behind it. What is agreed and measured is the PAIR, worth about half a pawn, and the reason is complementarity: two bishops cover different colours while two knights compete for the same outposts. A reversal worth remembering is that endgames with pawns on one wing only favour the knight, because the bishop's range buys nothing there and access to both colours matters more.

explanations.lesson: Do not ask which piece is better. Ask which piece has the better future in this pawn structure — and if the pawns are all on one side, expect the knight to win that argument.

knight-vs-bishop.definition_short: Which minor piece is better depends on the structure: bishops want open positions and pawns on both wings, knights want closed positions and a secure outpost.
knight-vs-bishop.definition_long:
The most common imbalance in chess, and the one where 'it depends on the position' is a real answer rather than an evasion.

THE BISHOP is better in open positions, where its range tells; with pawns on BOTH wings, where it can defend on one and attack on the other in a single move; alongside a rook, since rook and bishop coordinate better than rook and knight; and when the knight has no secure central square.

THE KNIGHT is better in closed positions, where it jumps over what blocks a bishop; when it has a stable outpost it cannot be evicted from; with pawns on ONE side only, where the bishop's range buys nothing and the knight's access to both colours matters more; as a blockader; and alongside a queen, since the queen already moves like a bishop and gains more from a knight's different geometry.

THE INDIVIDUAL VALUES ARE DISPUTED and this record does not resolve it. Fischer valued the bishop at 3.25 against a knight's 3. Kaufman's statistical work puts an unpaired bishop and a knight at 3.5 EACH — equal — with the half-pawn bonus attaching to the PAIR rather than to the bishop. GM Studer goes further and says the claim of individual bishop superiority 'is not funded with evidence' and that he knows of no statistic supporting it. What is agreed and measured is that two bishops beat bishop-and-knight or two knights.

A useful asymmetry: the bishop pair is complementary, because the two bishops cover different colours, while a knight 'pair' is redundant, since knights compete for the same outposts. That is why the pair is a named advantage and two knights are not.

Studer's refinement is worth knowing and is rarely taught: with two knights and a bishop, play on the colour of your OWN bishop, which you then control three times over; with two bishops and a knight, play on the colour of the bishop your opponent does NOT have.

loose-piece.engine_era_note: Mechanically detectable and uncontroversial. Engines do not use the word but every evaluation weighs hanging and undefended material.

preconditions: A piece has no friendly defender
It is not currently attacked
indicators_for: Two or more loose pieces on the same side — a double attack probably exists
A loose piece and the king share a line, rank, file or diagonal a queen or knight could hit at once
The position is open, with forcing moves available
indicators_against: The piece is on a square nothing can reach
It can be defended or moved in one tempo the opponent cannot deny
Defending it would cost more than the risk — a loose piece is a risk, not an error
false_positive_traps: Being loose is not being bad. Reporting every undefended piece would flag most positions and teach nothing.
It only matters when a forcing move can reach it. A loose rook in a locked position is not a weakness.

typical_plans: Scan for enemy loose pieces, then hunt for a check or threat hitting two things at once
Prophylactically, keep your own pieces defended in open positions with queens on
typical_moves: A queen check that also attacks an undefended piece on the far wing
tactical_consequences: Supplies the second target for a fork, discovered attack or skewer
strategic_consequences: A camp full of loose pieces is a combination waiting for its trigger

exceptions: Strong players leave pieces loose constantly and correctly, when no forcing move can exploit it.
Spending tempi to defend a piece nothing attacks is a real cost and often the worse choice.
limitations: Says nothing on its own. Its whole value is conditional on forcing moves existing.

The record has two traps and the first is only avoided by honouring the second. A version asking "is there a move after which this undefended piece can be won" fired on 66.8% of the 788 tactical positions and 40.6% of the annotated master corpus, because "undefended and attackable" describes most pieces - which is the first trap, "reporting every undefended piece would flag most positions and teach nothing", reached by ignoring the second, "it only matters when a FORCING move can reach it". Requiring the move to be a check or a capture brings it to 34.9% and 34.4%, and the agreement between two unrelated corpora is the sign that it is now measuring the position rather than the corpus.

A second false positive, found on Lisitsin-Capablanca 1935 in a PURE QUEEN ENDING: the guard asked for a forcing move after which static exchange evaluation says the piece is won, and 52...Qd2+ is a check that also attacks the white queen on b2, so SEE duly reported a queen won - while White answers the check with Qxd2 and Black has won nothing. Every queen in a queen ending is undefended and attackable by the other one, which is this record's first trap exactly. The forcing move must also survive being forcing. Firing rate 34.9% -> 9.1% on the 788 shipped positions, and 34.4% -> 0% on the annotated master corpus.
misconceptions: That every piece should be defended.
That a loose piece is a blunder. It is a standing risk.

by_level.beginner: Nothing is defending that piece. It is safe right now, but it is the kind of thing that gets picked off by a check.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} is loose — undefended, though not attacked yet. Look for a forcing move that hits it and something else at once.
by_level.advanced: Loose, not hanging. It is tactical fuel: any double attack needs a target that is outranked or undefended.
by_level.master: Undefended. Weigh the tempo cost of covering it against the concrete forcing resources available to the opponent.

by_depth.short: The {piece} is undefended.
by_depth.normal: The {piece} is loose — nothing defends it, and nothing attacks it yet. That matters because forks, skewers and discoveries all need an undefended target to pay off.
by_depth.deep: Loose means undefended but not attacked, and it is worth distinguishing from hanging because it describes a risk rather than a loss. Nearly every double-threat device needs a target that is either outranked by the attacker or undefended, so undefended pieces are what combinations are built out of. The commonest concrete pattern is check plus loose piece: a queen reaching a square that gives check and attacks the undefended piece at the same time.

explanations.lesson: Run two scans, not one: what can be taken right now, and what is merely undefended that a check could reach.

loose-piece.definition_short: A piece that is undefended but not currently attacked. Not a loss yet — the raw material of a future tactic.
loose-piece.definition_long:
Undefended, and nobody is attacking it. Nothing is wrong this move. The point of having a word for it is that almost every double-threat device needs an undefended target to pay off: a fork wins material only if a target is outranked or undefended; a discovered attack needs somewhere for the unmasked line to land; a skewer only cashes if the piece behind is loose.

So loose pieces are the precondition for tactics rather than the tactic. The progression is the thing to see: a piece becomes loose innocently, then some forcing move attacks it as a by-product, and now it is hanging with no time to save it. The blunder was usually the earlier quiet decision, not the move that lost the piece.

The most quoted concrete pattern is check plus loose piece: an undefended piece and an enemy queen able to reach a square that checks the king and hits the piece at once.

lpdo.knowledge_type_note: A rule of thumb and explicitly described as one by its sources — 'as usual, this is a rule of thumb which happily may be ignored by a strong player'. It carries mandatory hedging wording. It is NOT a law: strong players leave pieces loose deliberately and correctly.

attributions.note: Two independent sources say 'PROBABLY coined by the English player Mike Cook'. The hedge is theirs and is kept. Cook is the 2300-rated player who lost the 100-game match to Nunn and used the phrase to explain his losses.
Recounted the match in Secrets of Practical Chess, which is how the phrase reached general usage.

history.notes: Popularisation by Nunn is well attested. Coinage by Cook is reported by two sources, both hedged with 'probably', and no primary evidence has been seen. Recorded as medium: this is exactly the 'repeated attribution, no primary evidence' case the confidence scale exists for. Do not write 'Nunn coined LPDO' — he popularised it.
competing_claims: Some sources credit Nunn with the term itself; the better-sourced account credits Cook with the phrase and Nunn with its currency.

lpdo.engine_era_note: Nothing in engine analysis undermines the statistical observation, and engines punish loose material ruthlessly. What engine play does contradict is any strict reading: top engines leave pieces undefended constantly, because they can calculate that no forcing move reaches them. The heuristic is a substitute for calculation, and loses its force exactly to the extent that calculation is available.

preconditions: One or more pieces are undefended
Forcing moves are available in the position
indicators_for: Two or more loose pieces on the same side
An undefended piece on a line the enemy queen or a knight can reach with check
Open position, queens on, several forcing moves available
indicators_against: Closed position where no forcing move reaches the loose piece
The loose piece can be defended or moved with tempo at any time
Defending would cost a tempo the position cannot spare
false_positive_traps: A piece being undefended is not a mistake, and calling it one teaches a habit of pointless defending.

Not every loss of a loose piece is an LPDO instance. A ChessBase reader demonstrated that the article's own headline example was not: the piece did not fall because it was loose but because a square had become a forking square. If the tactic would work against a defended piece too, LPDO is not the explanation.

typical_plans: Scan both sides for undefended units before calculating
Given two loose enemy pieces, look for the move that attacks both
typical_moves: A queen check that also hits an undefended piece
tactical_consequences: Directs the search towards double attacks that actually pay
strategic_consequences: Prophylactically, coordination reduces exposure to tactics

exceptions: Strong players leave pieces loose deliberately, having calculated that nothing reaches them.
Defending everything is a real error in the other direction: it wastes tempi and produces passive pieces.
The heuristic describes a tendency across many games, not a property of any one position.
limitations: A search heuristic, not an evaluation. It suggests where to look; it does not say a move is bad.
Its force decreases as calculation increases.

Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Kramnik-Yakovich, GMA-qual 1989, 18.Bd3, above.
misconceptions: That LPDO means you should defend every piece.
That Nunn coined it — the better-sourced account is that Mike Cook did and Nunn popularised it.
That any lost undefended piece illustrates LPDO. It illustrates it only when being undefended is why the tactic worked.

examples.note:
THE MNEMONIC DOING WHAT IT CLAIMS TO DO. Black's bishop on b6 is loose - no black man defends it and no white man attacks it, which is `loose-piece`'s definition exactly. Nothing is wrong with it and nothing is threatening it. Then 18.Bd3 goes after the knight on e4, and the loose bishop turns out to be why the sequence works: 18...exd4 19.Bxd4 Bxd4 20.Bxe4 Rxe4 21.Rxe4, and every exchange in that line runs through a piece that was undefended when the move was played.

Stockfish 18 at depth 28 with three lines: +1.37 for Bd3, against −1.13 and −1.26 for the next two. **The move is the difference between better and worse — a swing of 250 centipawns — and nothing about it is forcing.**

WHAT THIS RECORD IS AND IS NOT. It is 'a mnemonic for a statistical fact about practical play rather than a rule about correct play', in its own words, so the evidence for it is not a clever move. It is a position where the tactic works BECAUSE a piece was loose, and the search that found it insisted on exactly that: the piece must be undefended and unattacked BEFORE the move, and the move must create a second threat, or the mnemonic is being credited for an ordinary attack on a hanging piece.

PROVENANCE. Found by tools/mine_master_motifs.js over 2,822,256 positions from 35,648 replayed games. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

by_level.beginner: Pieces that nothing is defending tend to get picked off. Before you move, look at which of your pieces are undefended.
by_level.intermediate: LPDO — loose pieces drop off. With {n} undefended pieces here, look for a forcing move that hits two things at once.
by_level.advanced: Nunn's heuristic. Useful as a search filter rather than as an evaluation: undefended units are the natural second target of any double attack.
by_level.master: A statistical regularity about practical play. Weigh it against the tempo cost of defending, and note that it says nothing once the relevant lines are calculated.

by_depth.short: Undefended pieces tend to get lost to tactics.
by_depth.normal: Loose pieces drop off: nearly every double attack needs a target that is undefended, so a camp with several undefended pieces is likely to lose one sooner or later. Use it as a scan, not as a rule to defend everything.
by_depth.deep: Popularised by John Nunn in Secrets of Practical Chess, and probably coined by Mike Cook, the opponent whose losses it explained. The mechanism is that forks, discoveries and skewers all need a second target that is either outranked by the attacker or undefended, and an undefended piece qualifies automatically. Its practical use is as a search heuristic. Its limit is that it is a substitute for calculation, so it loses force wherever calculation is actually done — which is why strong players leave pieces loose without concern.

explanations.hedge: This is a rule of thumb, not a law. Strong players leave pieces undefended deliberately and correctly whenever no forcing move can reach them, and defending everything costs tempi and produces passive pieces.
explanations.lesson: Undefended pieces are what combinations are made of. Scan for them on both sides before you calculate — but do not spend moves defending what nothing can attack.

lpdo.definition_short: Undefended pieces tend to be lost to tactics sooner or later, because almost every double-threat device needs an undefended target.
lpdo.definition_long:
A mnemonic for a statistical fact about practical play rather than a rule about correct play. Forks, discovered attacks, skewers and double attacks all work by creating two problems at once, and an undefended piece is the ideal second problem — it needs no other justification to be worth taking. So a position with several loose pieces is disproportionately likely to lose material to a tactic, whether or not any tactic exists right now.

Its practical value is as a SEARCH HEURISTIC. It converts an open-ended hunt for tactics into a fast scan: list the undefended units on both sides, then look for a forcing move that reaches two of them, or one of them and the king.

It is not advice to defend everything. Defending costs tempi, and a piece that no forcing move can reach is not at risk.

lucena-position.knowledge_type_note: A specific, named position with a proven result. Not a principle — it either is the position or it is not.

attributions.note: MISATTRIBUTION. The position does not appear in his book. The name is universal and should be retained as terminology, but it is not evidence of authorship.
Credited by Salvio, who gives the earliest preserved discussion. Second-hand; Salvio's text not consulted directly.
Il Puttino contains the earliest surviving treatment.
Editor of the sixth Handbuch des Schachspiels, where the erroneous attribution to Lucena appears to have originated.
Named the winning technique 'building a bridge'. Second-hand attribution.

history.notes: An unusually well-documented case of a chess name being wrong: the misattribution, its probable source and its probable cause are all recorded. Confidence is medium rather than high because the whole chain comes from one encyclopedia entry and none of the primary works (Lucena 1497, Salvio 1634, Handbuch 1880, van der Linde 1874) was consulted here. Worth checking against Winter's Chess Notes.
competing_claims: Named for Lucena (1497) — universal, and demonstrably not where the position appears.
Attributed by Salvio (1634) to Scipione Genovino.
Misattribution traced to the Handbuch des Schachspiels, 6th ed. (1880).

lucena-position.engine_era_note: Proven by tablebase. The human method survives because it is the clearest route a person can follow, not because the result was ever in doubt.

preconditions: Rook and pawn against rook
Pawn on the seventh rank and not a rook pawn
Attacking king on the queening square
Defending king cut off by at least one file
indicators_for: The defending rook has checking distance on the far side of the pawn
The attacking rook can reach the fourth rank to build the bridge
indicators_against: The pawn is a rook pawn — a different and usually drawn ending
The defending king is NOT cut off, so it can reach the queening square
The defending rook prevents the rook reaching the bridge rank
The defender has the short-side defence available: at least three files of checking distance with the king on the side with fewer files
false_positive_traps: A rook pawn is NOT a Lucena. The mechanism needs room on both sides of the pawn, and rook-pawn endings are frequently drawn — see the Vancura position.
'King in front of the pawn on the seventh' is not sufficient: the defending king must also be cut off, and the short-side defence must not be available.
The name does not tell you who discovered it, and a record that repeats the attribution as fact is wrong.

typical_plans: Drive the defending king back with a rook check, drop the rook to the fourth rank, walk the king out under the shield
typical_moves: Rd1+ then Rd4! — the bridge
strategic_consequences: The target of conversion in most rook endings a pawn up

exceptions: Does not apply to rook pawns.
Fails if the defending rook can stop the attacking rook reaching the bridge rank — though other wins usually exist.
The short-side defence draws if the defending king is on the side with fewer files and the rook has at least three files of checking distance.
limitations: NO MASTER-GAME POSITION, and the reason is what this record IS. A named theoretical position is a position rather than a moment in a game: it is defined by its own geometry, it is reached from thousands of different games and from none in particular, and its authority is a tablebase rather than an annotator. The examples on this record carry `origin_kind: tablebase-position` for that reason and it is the correct provenance, not a weaker one - a Syzygy result is a statement about every continuation, which is more than any game can be. A famous game that REACHED this position would be a fact about that game and would add nothing to the claim.
misconceptions: That Lucena discovered it. He did not, and the position is absent from his book.
That any rook-and-pawn-on-the-seventh position is a Lucena.
That it works with a rook pawn.

examples.note: Lucena setup: White Kb8 and pawn b7 with the rook free to check, Black Kd7 cut off and the rook on a2 with checking distance. The textbook win is 1.Rd1+ Ke7 2.Rd4! and the bridge.

tablebase.note: PROVEN win, mate in 41. The tablebase's own best move is Rd1+ — exactly the first move of the textbook bridge-building method, which is a pleasing confirmation that the human technique is also the objectively correct one.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 15, mate in 41, best move Rd1+ - the first move of building the bridge. The engine agrees with mate in 25. What the pair establishes is that the win belongs to the position and not to the technique's reputation: the same method with a rook pawn is a proven draw.

counterexamples.note: The Lucena setup moved to the a-file, with the defending king brought to c7: White Ka8, pawn a7, rook f1; Black Kc7, rook a2. Every ingredient of the Lucena position is present - king in front of its own pawn on the seventh, rook free, defending rook checking from behind - and it is a PROVEN DRAW, because on a rook file there is no short side to build the bridge on and the white king cannot come out from in front of its own pawn. The record's own condition is that the pawn must not be a rook pawn; this is what that costs.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0. The paired position - the same men one file to the right, on the b-file - is a proven win in 41. One file is the whole difference.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Ra1, and the engine agrees at 0.00. The negative half: the Lucena method needs a file on each side of the pawn to build the bridge, and a rook pawn has only one. Nothing else differs between the halves.

ambiguous_examples.note: Every characteristic this record lists holds except one: the pawn is a knight pawn on the seventh, the attacking king is on the queening square in its own pawn's way, the defending king is cut off - and the DEFENDING ROOK is on the pawn's own file rather than on the file beyond it. The record states that fifth condition as part of the definition. The position is still a proven win, and it is won by a different first move: Ra1 rather than Rd1+, which is to say NOT by building a bridge. So the name is the whole question. A reader who has learnt the five conditions will not call this the Lucena position; a reader who has learnt 'rook and pawn on the seventh with the king in front' will. Both are right about the chess and only one can be right about the word, and this base does not adjudicate the word.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 7, mate in 39, best move Ra1 - and Ra1 is not the bridge. This record's positive example is a proven win in 41 whose first move IS the bridge's first check, Rd1+. Same material, same result, different technique, and the difference is which file the defending rook stands on.

by_level.beginner: The pawn is one square from queening but the king is in its way. The trick is to use the rook as a shield so the king can step out.
by_level.intermediate: The Lucena position — a forced win. Check the king back, put the rook on the fourth rank, then walk out: the rook blocks the checks.
by_level.advanced: Lucena. Confirm it is not a rook pawn and that the defending king is genuinely cut off before relying on it.
by_level.master: The conversion target of most rook endings a pawn up. Note the short-side defence is the standard way it fails to be a Lucena at all.

by_depth.short: Pawn on the seventh, king in front, rook builds a bridge — a win.
by_depth.normal: The Lucena position: rook and pawn against rook with the pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it and theirs cut off. It wins by building a bridge — check the king away, drop the rook to the fourth rank, then walk your king out behind the shield.
by_depth.deep: The canonical winning position in rook and pawn versus rook, and the one the stronger side aims for while the defender aims for the Philidor. The conditions are exact: not a rook pawn, pawn on the seventh, attacking king on the queening square, defending king cut off by at least a file. The win is Nimzowitsch's 'building a bridge'. A footnote worth knowing: the name is wrong. The position does not appear in Lucena's 1497 book; the earliest surviving discussion is Salvio's of 1634, who credits Scipione Genovino, and the misattribution seems to have entered through an 1880 edition of the Handbuch des Schachspiels.

explanations.lesson: In a rook ending a pawn up, this is what you are steering towards. Check first that your pawn is not a rook pawn — that changes everything.

beginner_words: using the rook as a shield
avoid: any pawn on the seventh is a Lucena

lucena-position.definition_short: Rook and pawn against rook, pawn on the seventh with the attacking king in front of it and the defending king cut off. A forced win by building a bridge.

validation_na.master_game: N/A rather than missing, and the argument is what this record IS. A named theoretical position is a POSITION rather than a moment in a game: it is defined by its own geometry, it is reached from thousands of games and from none in particular, and its authority is a tablebase. The examples here carry `origin_kind: tablebase-position`, which is the stronger provenance and not a weaker one - a Syzygy result is a statement about every legal continuation, and a game is a statement about one. A famous game that happened to REACH this position would be a fact about that game and would add nothing whatever to the claim the record makes.

luft.knowledge_type_note: Terminology for a specific prophylactic move and the square it creates.

history.notes: A German loanword in English chess writing; no coinage researched.

luft.engine_era_note: Engines make luft when it is needed and not otherwise, and are unimpressed by it as a routine move. That matches the conditional reading rather than the habitual one.

preconditions: A castled king with its shield pawns unmoved
A pawn move that creates a flight square
indicators_for: Heavy pieces remain, so back-rank mates are live
The opponent cannot storm the king's wing
The back rank is already defended by only one piece
indicators_against: The opponent has castled on the other wing and can throw pawns forward
The advanced pawn becomes a hook for a specific break
The tempo is needed elsewhere in a sharp position
false_positive_traps: Making luft is not automatically prudent. The same move is a hook against an opponent who can storm, and this is the standard error.
Luft is unnecessary when the back rank is adequately defended or when no heavy pieces remain.

typical_plans: Make luft in a quiet moment, before it is forced
Prefer the pawn move that creates the fewest weaknesses
typical_moves: g3 / ...g6 — more committal, since it weakens two squares
typical_pawn_structures: f2-g2-h2 intact, with h3 the usual choice
tactical_consequences: Removes back-rank mate outright
strategic_consequences: Permanently uncovers the squares the pawn left

exceptions: Against a queenside-castled opponent, luft is a hook and usually a concession.
With no heavy pieces left, back-rank mate is not a threat and luft is a wasted move.
limitations: Trivially detectable; whether it is wise is entirely conditional on the opponent's attacking prospects.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, against this record's two traps. The first - 'making luft is not automatically prudent. The same move is a hook against an opponent who can storm' - IS carried, in the wording rather than in the matcher: the teaching sentence reads 'worth playing when heavy pieces are on and back-rank mates are live - but it also weakens squares permanently, so check they cannot storm that wing.' The second - 'luft is unnecessary when the back rank is adequately defended or when no heavy pieces remain' - is half built and half unbuildable. 'No heavy pieces remain' is enforced: the matcher requires an enemy rook standing on a file that reaches the rank. 'Adequately defended' is not mechanical at any threshold this base could defend: 36 of the 39 side-instances where luft fires on the 788 shipped positions have a friendly rook or queen ON their own back rank, and refusing those would delete the concept - a rook on the back rank is exactly what most back-rank mates happen in spite of.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first indicator_against - 'the opponent has castled on the other wing and can throw pawns forward' - is now concrete rather than general. The wording already carried the caveat in the abstract ('it also weakens squares permanently, so check they cannot storm that wing'); the sentence now says it when the kings are ACTUALLY on opposite wings, which is the standard error this record names.
misconceptions: That making luft is always sensible prophylaxis. It is conditional, and the condition is whether the opponent can attack that wing.
