by_level.beginner: Move one pawn in front of your castled king so the king has somewhere to go if it gets checked on the back row.
by_level.intermediate: Luft. Worth playing when heavy pieces are on and back-rank mates are live — but it also weakens squares permanently, so check they cannot storm that wing.
by_level.advanced: A conditional move. The same h3 is useful prophylaxis in a quiet position and a hook against a queenside-castled opponent.
by_level.master: Measured: in a controlled test one tempo of luft turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty. The cost is the hook, and which dominates is the whole question.

by_depth.short: A pawn move giving the king an escape square.
by_depth.normal: Luft — German for air. Advancing a pawn in front of the castled king gives it a flight square and removes back-rank mates, at the cost of permanently weakening the squares the pawn left.
by_depth.deep: A castled king behind three unmoved pawns has no escape square, which is what makes back-rank mates work. One pawn move fixes it — and in a controlled test in this base, moving a pawn from h7 to h6 turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty. The cost is that the vacated squares are uncovered for good and the advanced pawn becomes a hook the opponent can attack to open a file. So the same move is good or bad on one question: can they realistically storm this wing? In a quiet position it is free; against an opponent castled the other way it is a concession.

explanations.lesson: Make luft when heavy pieces are on and nobody can storm you. Against an opponent castled the other way, that same pawn move is a target.

luft.definition_short: German for 'air': a pawn move in front of the castled king that gives it an escape square and removes back-rank mates.
luft.definition_long:
A castled king behind three unmoved pawns has no escape square, which is what makes back-rank mates possible. Advancing one of them — usually the h-pawn to h3 or h6 — creates a flight square and eliminates the whole family of back-rank tactics at a stroke.

The cost is exactly the cost of any shield-pawn move: the squares the pawn has left are permanently uncovered, and the advanced pawn itself becomes a HOOK the opponent can attack to force a file open.

So the same move is good or bad depending on one question: can the opponent realistically storm your king? In a quiet position, or with queens off, h3 is a free and useful move. Against an opponent castled on the other wing with mobile pawns, the identical move hands them something to bite on with ...g5-g4.

Its value is measurable and large. In a controlled test in this knowledge base, moving one pawn from h7 to h6 turned a mate in one into a mate in thirty.

master-concepts.definition_long:
The tier where a concept cannot be stated correctly without a particular piece of theory in hand, and where getting it slightly wrong makes it false rather than vague.

THE TWO RECORDS AT THIS TIER are both rook endings and both are here for the same reason. The VANCURA POSITION is expert-level not because the moves are hard but because stating it correctly means stating where Tarrasch's rule fails — this base holds the proof that one rook move turns a draw into a loss in 63, and a summary that omits that is worse than no summary. CORRESPONDING SQUARES is expert-level because the concept is a mapping between square pairs, and an approximate account of it is simply wrong.

THE TIER IS DELIBERATELY THIN, and this record says so rather than padding it. Very few concepts genuinely require this much before they can be stated, and marking things master-level to signal importance would defeat the field's purpose. Most of what people call master-level knowledge is concrete rather than conceptual — specific positions, specific lines — and belongs in a tablebase or an opening file rather than in a concept record.

A NOTE ON THE FIELD'S RANGE. The schema allows beginner, novice, intermediate, advanced, expert, master and highly-theoretical. Only four are currently in use; the unused values are kept because a range with gaps is more honest than one retro-fitted to what happens to exist.

DIFFICULTY IN THIS BASE IS ABOUT THE CONCEPT, NOT THE PLAYER. It records how much other machinery a concept needs before it can be stated truthfully, which is why some famous ideas sit high and some obscure ones sit low. A fork is a beginner concept because it can be stated completely in one sentence; the Vancura position is an expert one not because it is hard to play but because stating it correctly requires the rook-ending context in which Tarrasch's rule fails.

IT IS ALSO WHAT DRIVES LEVEL ADAPTATION. Every concept carries explanations.by_level with wording for beginner, intermediate, advanced and master, and the API selects among them. The difficulty field says where a concept BELONGS; the by_level wording says how to say it to whoever is asking. The two are deliberately separate, because an advanced concept still has to be explicable to a beginner who has just met it on the board.

material-imbalance.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept resting on unusually hard statistical evidence, but still a concept: the values are averages over large samples and any individual position may depart from them arbitrarily far.

attributions.note: How to Reassess Your Chess built a whole method on identifying imbalances and letting them dictate the plan. Full text consulted.
Put piece values on a statistical footing; his figures are the basis of modern engine material tables.

history.notes: Piece values are as old as chess writing; what is attributable is the statistical derivation (Kaufman) and the planning framework (Silman). Neither is a claim of originating the concept.
competing_claims: The exchange is worth 2 pawns (conventional).
1.5 pawns (Tarrasch, Mednis, Evans).
1.75 pawns (Kaufman, statistical).
1 pawn (Petrosian) — probably reflecting positions where the bishop pair is also involved.

development.change: Fixed piece values taught as a scale.
'A new appreciation of differences in material' — imbalances taken seriously as strategic content.
Values derived statistically; the bishop pair quantified at about half a pawn.
Outcome studies contradict some received wisdom outright, notably queen versus two rooks.

material-imbalance.engine_era_note: Substantially revised, and in a measurable way. Kaufman's values are what modern engines use, and they differ from the taught scale in every entry — the bishop pair is worth half a pawn on its own, the exchange is 1.75 rather than 2, and values shift with how much material remains. Database outcomes also refute at least one standard claim, since the queen outperforms two rooks in practice.

preconditions: The two sides hold different kinds of material, not merely different amounts
indicators_for: One side has the bishop pair and the other does not
Queen against two rooks, or rook against two minor pieces
The position's character suits one kind of material — open files for rooks, closed structure for knights
indicators_against: Material is symmetrical in kind, in which case simple counting applies
The imbalance is temporary and about to be liquidated
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: the 1/3/3/5/9 count is not an evaluation. Being 'ahead on material' by that scale says very little once the material is of different kinds.
Detecting the imbalance is mechanical and trivial; saying who it favours is not, and depends on open files, king safety and how much else remains.
Statistical values are averages. They tell you what to expect across many games, not what is true in this one.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: a knight against a bishop is not an imbalance by this record's own preferred numbers - Kaufman puts a knight and an UNPAIRED bishop at the same 3.5 - and the matcher fired on every such swap, 42.1% of the 788 shipped positions. It is a third name for a fact `bishop-pair` and `bad-bishop` already report. The exception is the pair itself, which Kaufman does separate (7.5 against 7.0), so two bishops against two knights is still reported. 42.1% -> 35.5%.

typical_plans: Identify the imbalances, then let them choose the plan — Silman's method
With two minor pieces against a rook, keep major pieces on
With a rook against two minor pieces, trade major pieces even if nominally behind
With the bishop pair, open the position; against it, keep it closed or trade a bishop
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen against two rooks — coordination of the rooks is the deciding factor
tactical_consequences: Disconnected rooks against a queen are vulnerable to double attacks
strategic_consequences: The imbalance usually determines the plan more directly than any other feature

exceptions: Values shift with the amount of material: minor pieces are worth more pawns with a full board, rooks more with an empty one.
The redundancy of major pieces reverses the usual exchanging rule for the side with a lone rook against two minors.
Queen against two rooks favours the queen in practice, against the standard teaching.
An exposed king shifts everything towards the queen.
limitations: Statistical values are averages over many games and can be arbitrarily wrong in a single position.
The concept names a condition, not a verdict.

The second trap says it directly: 'detecting the imbalance is mechanical and trivial; saying who it favours is not, and depends on open files, king safety and how much else remains.' Both sides are now named, always, and the sentence calls the point count 'a scale that stops applying here'.

MEASURED 2026-09-02 against the two unread indicators_against. 'Material is symmetrical in kind, in which case simple counting applies' is the precondition itself - the matcher requires two differing piece types or a heavy piece traded against minors, so symmetrical material never reaches it. 'The imbalance is temporary and about to be liquidated' is a claim about the next few moves and is not attempted; the wording compensates by calling the point count 'a scale that stops applying here' rather than by predicting.
misconceptions: That the piece-value scale evaluates positions. It counts material, which is a different thing.
That two rooks beat a queen. The database says the opposite.
That the bishop pair is worth nothing measurable — it is about half a pawn, and that is quantified.
That the side ahead in material should always trade. With a rook against two minors the reverse is true.

by_level.beginner: The two sides have different kinds of pieces rather than different amounts. Counting points does not tell you who is better here.
by_level.intermediate: A material imbalance. Ask what the position suits: open files favour rooks, a closed structure favours knights, an exposed king favours the queen.
by_level.advanced: Use Kaufman's values rather than the taught scale — the bishop pair alone is worth about half a pawn, and the exchange 1.75 rather than 2. Note that values shift as material comes off.
by_level.master: The redundancy of major pieces is the least-known useful rule here: with a rook against two minors, seek major-piece trades even when nominally behind.

by_depth.short: Different kinds of material, so counting points does not settle it.
by_depth.normal: A material imbalance: the sides hold different kinds of material rather than different amounts. The 1/3/3/5/9 scale stops applying, and the question becomes which pieces the position suits.
by_depth.deep: Once material is unbalanced, counting stops being an evaluation. Kaufman's statistical values are the best starting point and are what modern engines use: knight and unpaired bishop 3.5, rook 5.25, queen 10, and the bishop PAIR 7.5 — half a pawn more than two bishops separately. More useful than the numbers are two findings. Values move with the board: fewer pieces means a minor piece is worth fewer pawns, and every pawn trade helps a rook. And major pieces are redundant — a second one adds less than the first, which is why the side with a lone rook against two minors should trade majors even when nominally behind. Database outcomes also contradict the standard teaching that two rooks beat a queen: in practice the queen wins 49% and the rooks 31%.

explanations.lesson: When the material is unbalanced, stop counting and ask what the position wants. Open files want rooks, closed positions want knights, and an exposed king wants a queen.

beginner_words: counting points does not work here
avoid: a rook is worth five points

material-imbalance.definition_short: A position where the two sides hold different KINDS of material — queen against two rooks, rook against two minor pieces, bishop pair against bishop and knight.
material-imbalance.definition_long:
The 1/3/3/5/9 scale is a counting aid for beginners, not an evaluation. Once the two sides hold different kinds of material the scale stops applying and the position has to be judged on what the pieces can actually do.

KAUFMAN'S STATISTICAL VALUES, from a large-sample study and the basis of modern engine values, are the best available starting point: knight 3.5, unpaired bishop 3.5, rook 5.25, queen 10, and — the important one — the bishop PAIR 7.5, which is half a pawn more than two separate bishops. He puts the exchange at 1.75 pawns, against the conventional 2, Tarrasch and Mednis and Evans at 1.5, and Petrosian's claim of just 1.

Two of his findings are more useful than the numbers. First, values move with the board: the fewer pieces remain, the fewer pawns a minor piece is worth, and each pawn trade helps a rook because rooks need open files. Second, the REDUNDANCY OF MAJOR PIECES — a second major piece adds less than the first, since there may only be time to use one on an open line. That is why the side with a rook against two minor pieces should seek major-piece trades even when nominally behind, which reverses the usual rule that the materially superior side trades.

EMPIRICAL OUTCOMES CONTRADICT RECEIVED WISDOM in at least one well-known case. 'Two rooks beat a queen' is standard teaching; over a large database the queen WINS 49% against two rooks and loses 31%. Two minor pieces against a rook is confirmed emphatically in the other direction — a rook facing two bishops loses two games in three. The bishop pair is confirmed.

Silman's framing is the practical one: an imbalance is any significant difference between the two positions, and the imbalances present are what tell you what the plan should be.

middlegame-principles.knowledge_type_note: An umbrella record. The middlegame has no compact principle set of its own, and saying so is part of the content.

attributions.note: The accumulation theory is the closest thing the middlegame has to a governing principle: when to attack and why.

history.notes: No single tradition; the middlegame literature is organised by structure and by example rather than by principle.

middlegame-principles.engine_era_note: The phase engines changed least in principle and most in practice. There is still no compact rule set, but engine analysis has made it possible to check individual judgements, which is what most of this base's measurements are.

preconditions: Development is broadly complete
Queens or several pieces remain
false_positive_traps: The phase boundaries are not sharp, and a queenless position with many pieces is still a middlegame. Treating it as an endgame is how kings get mated.
This is an umbrella record. Attaching it to a move explains nothing; the specific concept under it is what carries content.

typical_plans: Assess, then plan from the assessment rather than from preference
Ask what the opponent intends before pursuing your own idea
Improve the worst-placed piece when nothing is urgent
Act once an advantage is sufficient, since it otherwise dissipates
typical_pawn_structures: The structure decides which plans exist, which is why structures are studied rather than positions
strategic_consequences: Small advantages accumulate here and are converted in the endgame

exceptions: Sharp theoretical positions are played from preparation rather than from principle.
Forcing positions require calculation and the procedure above does not apply.
limitations: Deliberately an umbrella; the content is on the concepts it points at.
This is the phase where this base's coverage is broadest and its confidence lowest.
misconceptions: That the middlegame has principles like the opening does. It has a procedure, and the general rules are exactly what have run out by then.
That a plan should be found before the position is assessed. The plan is supposed to follow from the assessment.

examples.note: Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz 1908, 20.e3 - one quiet pawn move doing four things, which is what a middlegame principle is for. The corpus annotation lists them: 'it gains a tempo by attacking Black's queen, opens a diagonal for the bishop, and improves the worst-placed piece.' This base already files the same move under `worst-placed-piece`, and it is filed here because the record's subject is the ORDER of middlegame thinking - improve the worst piece when nothing is forcing - and this is the move that shows the precondition and the rule together rather than the rule alone.
examples.attributed_by: corpus entry rubinstein-salwe-1908-20e3-improving

engine.verdict_note: +0.34, and the engine's own first move is 20.e3. A third of a pawn: the move is best and it is not decisive, which is the correct size for a principle about accumulating rather than about winning.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-middlegame-principle-with-no-middlegame`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A quiet position with no checks, no captures and nothing hanging — exactly the conditions under which this record's principles apply, and the state in which 'improve the piece doing least' is the standard advice. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: There are no pieces. Every white and black man is a pawn or a king, the structure is rammed shut on every file, and no plan of any kind is available to either side. The principles on this record are about choosing between candidate moves in a position with pieces in it; a position with none is quiet in the way an empty room is quiet. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing at all here, and the same position is registered against `restraint`, `prophylaxis` and `planning` for the same reason — each is a claim about what a move is FOR, and there is nothing for a move to be for. Stockfish 18: 0.00, with both kings walking about on the kingside. Four records now share this board, which makes it the most-reused negative in the base and, for that reason, worth stating plainly: a position where nothing is happening is not evidence that a concept is subtle, it is evidence that the concept needs something to be happening.

ambiguous_examples.note: Two of this record's principles apply and point at different moves. A knight sits on a permanent outpost and the forcing continuation Ne7+ is available, which is one principle - examine the forcing moves. The other is that when nothing is urgent the right move improves the piece doing least, and the piece doing least is the bishop on c1. The engine plays Be3, the quiet move, at +0.30. Filed as ambiguous because both principles are correctly applicable and this record contains no rule for ordering them: what a middlegame principle gives is a list of candidates and not a choice between them, and the position where two of them disagree is the ordinary case rather than the exception.

engine.verdict_note: +0.30 for the quiet developing move, in a position that also offers a check. Both principles name a real move and only one of them names the best one.

by_level.beginner: Once your pieces are out, there is no rule to follow — look at the position and find something to aim at.
by_level.intermediate: Assess, plan from the assessment, check what your opponent wants, and improve your worst piece when nothing is urgent.
by_level.advanced: Steinitz's condition governs timing: do not attack without an advantage, and do act once you have one, because it dissipates.
by_level.master: There is no short list because the position differs every game, which is also why this is where the clock goes.

by_depth.short: The phase where you have to judge rather than follow rules.
by_depth.normal: The middlegame has no compact set of principles, because unlike the opening the position differs every game and unlike the endgame it cannot be solved. What replaces them is a procedure: assess, plan from the assessment, watch the opponent's plan, improve the worst piece, and calculate before committing.
by_depth.deep: The absence of a short list is a fact about the phase rather than a gap. The opening has principles because the starting position is always the same; the endgame has principles and, where it does not, tablebases; the middlegame has neither. What replaces them is a procedure whose every step is a concept in its own right, governed by Steinitz's condition on timing - do not attack without an advantage, and do act once you have one, since it otherwise dissipates. It is also measurably the expensive phase: options grow roughly linearly for twenty moves, and strong players spend less time on openings and endings precisely to spend more here.

explanations.hedge: An umbrella over a procedure rather than a rule set; the middlegame is where this base's coverage is broadest and its confidence lowest.
explanations.lesson: There is no rule to follow here. Assess first, and let the plan come from the assessment.

middlegame-principles.definition_short: The phase where development is finished and the position must be judged and acted on rather than followed.
middlegame-principles.definition_long:
THE MIDDLEGAME HAS NO SHORT LIST, and that is a fact about it rather than a gap here. The opening has principles because the starting position is the same every time. The endgame has principles, and where it does not it has tablebases. The middlegame has neither: it is the phase in which the position is different every game and the general rules have run out.

WHAT REPLACES THEM IS A PROCEDURE, and every part of it is a concept in its own right here: ASSESS the position by its elements, form a PLAN that the assessment actually points at, check the opponent's plan (PROPHYLAXIS), improve the WORST-PLACED PIECE when nothing is urgent, and CALCULATE the forcing lines before committing.

STEINITZ'S CONDITION governs when to act: do not attack without an advantage, because an attack on a balanced position should fail against correct defence and leave the attacker worse for trying — and conversely, once a sufficient advantage exists it MUST be acted on or it dissipates. Lasker put the same thing from the tactical side: no combination without a considerable plus, and no considerable plus without a combination.

THE MEASURED FACT ABOUT THE PHASE, from this base's practical research, is that the middlegame is where strong players spend their clock. Options grow roughly linearly for the first twenty moves, and players above 1900 spend LESS time than weaker ones on openings and endings in order to spend more here. The phase is expensive because the decisions are genuinely harder, and that is measurable rather than impressionistic.

THIS IS ALSO WHERE THIS SYSTEM HAS THE MOST TO OFFER AND THE LEAST CERTAINTY. The shipped explanation layer names a motif in 65% of tactical puzzles and manages 4% on positional ones; the gap is almost entirely middlegame judgement.

minority-attack.knowledge_type_note: A named plan with a specific structural precondition, and one whose point is easy to state and easy to execute badly.

attributions.note: POSSIBLY the source of the formulation that a numerical pawn minority can be a qualitative majority, given the freedom of those pawns to attack the base of the enemy chain. This base has NOT verified the attribution: it rests on a single university lecture note that credits him, and the claim was not found in his own text during this research. The relation is recorded as association rather than origin for that reason, and the plan itself is older than any individual credit for it.
The standard modern exponent, and the source of the caution against executing it mechanically.

history.notes: The Carlsbad structure is named for the 1923 tournament where it came to prominence. The Nimzowitsch attribution is UNVERIFIED — one lecture note credits him with the qualitative-majority formulation and this base did not find it in his own text. Treat the plan as having no established individual origin.

minority-attack.engine_era_note: Unremarkable to engines, which evaluate the resulting weakness directly. It has held up as a plan: the resulting structures are still assessed as pleasant for the attacker, and the modern refinement is about timing rather than about soundness.

preconditions: A Carlsbad-type structure: locked centre, each side with a half-open file
The attacker has fewer pawns on the wing being attacked
indicators_for: Rooks already on the c-file
The a-pawn left at home
b4-b5 achievable in a few moves
The defender's counterplay is slow
indicators_against: The defender is faster in the centre or on the other wing
b5 can be met by ...c5 or ...a6 favourably
The attacker's own king is exposed to the counter-attack
recognition.detector: proposed: Carlsbad structure recognition plus wing pawn counts (not yet written)
false_positive_traps: Advancing pawns on the wing where you have fewer is only right in this specific structure. Elsewhere it is simply weakening.
The plan is slow. Reporting it without checking the defender's counterplay recommends the form of the idea and not its content.
The goal is a fixed weakness, not space and not a passed pawn. A minority attack that gains space and creates no target has failed.

typical_plans: Rooks to the c-file, then b4-b5, then bxc6
Leave the a-pawn at home so it cannot become a target
Manoeuvre around c5 rather than forcing b5 through when the defender is ready
After the exchange, attack the fixed pawn with more pieces than can defend it
typical_moves: Rb1 and Rc1
bxc6
typical_pawn_structures: The Carlsbad structure from the Queen's Gambit Declined, Exchange Variation
typical_piece_arrangements: Doubled rooks on the c-file
strategic_consequences: Converts a nominal pawn deficit on a wing into a permanent structural target

exceptions: Where Black is faster in the centre the whole plan is too slow, which is its standard refutation.
Black can recapture on c6 with a piece instead, accepting a weak d5 pawn rather than a weak c6 pawn — the weakness moves rather than disappearing.
Karpov's practice: where b5 is well met, the correct plan is to manoeuvre instead, not to force it.
limitations: No detector exists for the Carlsbad structure, so this system cannot recognise the plan; the record is for explanation and vocabulary.
The Nimzowitsch attribution is second-hand and low confidence.
The master game cited verifies only for its first 46 plies; the source's later moves do not replay and are not used.
The Nimzowitsch attribution is unverified and is recorded as an association rather than an origin; do not repeat it as his formulation.
misconceptions: That you should always play where you have more pawns. This is the standard counterexample, and the reason is that the minority pawns are the mobile ones.
That the aim is a passed pawn. The aim is a fixed weakness on a half-open file.
That b4-b5 should be forced through. Its most successful practitioner routinely declined to.

conflicts.resolution: A minority attack deliberately gives up space on the wing it attacks — the advancing pawns are exchanged off. The two aims are incompatible and the structural target is the one worth having, because space on a wing with no target is not an advantage.

This base's own feature detector confirms the textbook result: Black now has three pawn islands and an isolated a7 pawn, White has a semi-open c-file with BOTH rooks already on it, and the b-file is open. FEN derived by replaying the game through the page's own move generator; the source's score fails to replay from Black's 24th move, so only the verified prefix is used.

The concept is a plan rather than a feature, so what the number establishes is modest and real: the plan's typical structure, with the attack under way, is worth about two pawns here.

This is the minority attack at its STARTING position rather than at its conclusion, and the evaluation is the honest reading of that: the plan has been chosen and has not yet achieved anything. counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-majority-advance-is-not-a-minority-attack`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A wing pawn advance against an enemy pawn group, aiming to create a weakness. That is the plan a minority attack executes, and the word 'minority' is the part readers drop. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "Advancing pawns on the wing where you have fewer is only right in this specific structure. Elsewhere it is simply weakening." White has THREE queenside pawns against Black's two. Advancing there is a majority attack, whose point is a passed pawn, and this record's third trap draws the line explicitly: "The goal is a fixed weakness, not space and not a passed pawn." WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing here, which is correct and is the whole content of the case: the concept turns on a COUNT that is trivial to make and trivial to skip. Three against two is a majority and two against three is a minority, and the same pawn move means opposite things in the two cases. This base has no minority-attack matcher, and this position is one reason - the plan is named by the count AND by the structure, and the record's second trap adds a third condition on top of both.

ambiguous_examples.note: Two queenside pawns against two. A wing advance here is neither a minority attack nor a majority one, because the count that names the plan is equal - and the plan's whole identity is that count. This record's first trap says 'advancing pawns on the wing where you have fewer is only right in this specific structure. Elsewhere it is simply weakening', and here there is no 'fewer'. Read against this record's registered false-positive case, which is the same board with three white pawns against two and is a MAJORITY advance: three positions, three names, and the only difference between them is one pawn. Filed as ambiguous rather than negative because a2-a4 and b2-b4 are both playable and the concept genuinely has nothing to say about which.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 22, settled at depth 1, with the pawn counts equal on both wings. The plan's name needs an asymmetry the position does not have.

by_level.beginner: Pushing your two pawns at their three, so that when they trade off, one of their pawns is left weak.
by_level.intermediate: The minority attack: b4-b5 and bxc6, which leaves Black a weak c-pawn on a file your rooks already own.
by_level.advanced: The minority is the mobile majority — your pawns can attack the base of their chain and their extra pawn cannot do anything. Leave your a-pawn at home.
by_level.master: It is slow, and Karpov's lesson is that it should be manoeuvred towards rather than forced through.

by_depth.short: Advancing fewer pawns against more, to leave a weakness behind.
by_depth.normal: A minority attack: advancing your two queenside pawns against their three, so that the exchange on c6 leaves them with a fixed weak pawn on a half-open file your rooks are already using. The aim is a target, not space.
by_depth.deep: The plan that looks like a mistake — you advance on the wing where you are outnumbered. Nimzowitsch's justification is that the minority is the QUALITATIVE majority, because those pawns are free to attack the base of the enemy chain while the defender's extra pawn does nothing. The mechanism is rooks to the c-file, then b4-b5 without moving the a-pawn, then bxc6, after which every recapture concedes something: with the b-pawn a fixed weakness on c6, with a piece a weakened d5 instead. Its real cost is time, which is why its most successful practitioner routinely declined to force b5 through and manoeuvred instead.

explanations.lesson: You are playing for a weakness, not for space. If the attack gains ground and leaves no target, it has failed.

beginner_words: pushing your pawns to make theirs weak
avoid: always attack where you have more pawns

audit_notes: 2026-09-01: first written with an originated-by attribution to Nimzowitsch at low confidence. The audit flagged it as an unhedged attribution, correctly — one lecture note is not grounds for crediting an origin. Downgraded to later-associated-with with the uncertainty stated.

minority-attack.definition_short: Advancing a pawn minority against an enemy pawn majority in order to force a weakness, not to win space.
minority-attack.definition_long:
The plan that looks like a mistake. On the queenside White has two pawns to Black's three, and advances them anyway — against the general advice to play where you are stronger.

NIMZOWITSCH'S JUSTIFICATION is that the numerical minority is a QUALITATIVE majority: White's pawns are free to advance and attack the base of Black's chain, while Black's extra pawn is not doing anything. The attack is not for space or for a passed pawn. It is for a WEAKNESS.

THE MECHANISM in the Carlsbad structure, which is where it lives: rooks to the c-file, then b4-b5 — usually WITHOUT moving the a-pawn, since a2-a4 would give Black a target — and finally bxc6. Black must then recapture, and every recapture concedes something. With the b-pawn, the c6 pawn becomes a fixed weakness on a half-open file with White's rooks already on it; with a piece, the d5 pawn is weakened instead. The point is that Black gets to choose which weakness, not whether to have one.

IT IS SLOW, and that is its real cost. Setting up b4-b5 takes several moves, and Black's counterplay in the centre or on the kingside runs on the same clock. The instruction most worth keeping is Karpov's: he never forced b4-b5 through mechanically, and often manoeuvred around c5 instead, because a plan pushed through against a prepared defence achieves the form of the idea and none of its content.

THE TARGETS ARE a7 AND c6, and this base's own feature detector confirms them in the master game recorded here: after the exchange on c6, Black has three pawn islands, an isolated a-pawn, and White has both rooks on the resulting semi-open c-file.

mixed-piece-endgames.knowledge_type_note: A record about a class whose defining property is that class-level principles do not apply to it.

history.notes: Not a tradition with an origin; a residual category in the endgame literature.

mixed-piece-endgames.engine_era_note: The class most transformed by tablebases, because the hardest mixed endings are small enough to solve and were previously matters of opinion. Several long-held evaluations of specific material balances have been overturned outright.

preconditions: Few pieces remain
The two sides hold different kinds of material
indicators_for: A passed pawn one side's material is suited to stopping
Pieces that defend one another against a piece that must work alone
recognition.detector: material in lib/features.js reports the counts; the imbalance is visible from them
false_positive_traps: The point count is least reliable exactly here, and this is where people rely on it most. This base holds a proven draw a bishop and a pawn up.
The 60% figure for bishops over knights in endings is a population statistic and says nothing about a particular position.
This class is under-researched in this base, and confidence should stay low regardless of how clean the material description looks.

typical_plans: Ask which side's material suits the pawn structure
Keep two minor pieces defending each other rather than operating separately
Use a knight to blockade a passer and a rook to chase one
Look for a fortress when material down
typical_pawn_structures: Pawns on both wings, which favours the bishop
A symmetrical structure on one wing, which favours the knight
strategic_consequences: Conversion is unusually hard, and fortresses are unusually common

exceptions: Fortresses defeat material reasoning entirely and are common in this class.
The bishop's statistical edge reverses when the pawns are all on one wing.
limitations: This base has not researched mixed-material endings in depth; the record is orientation and says so.
No tablebase-verified position of this class is held here beyond the wrong-rook-pawn and opposite-bishop cases already recorded.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION. The examples on this record are `tablebase-position`s, and for this family that is the stronger provenance rather than a substitute: the claims here are about what a class of ending can and cannot do, and a proof over every legal continuation settles that where a single game only illustrates it. What a master game would add is evidence that the principle GUIDED a strong player, which is a different claim, and this base has not yet found an annotated position making it for this family. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Arbakov-Kramnik, GMA-qual 1989, above.
misconceptions: That the point count settles unbalanced endings. It is least reliable precisely here.
That two minor pieces automatically beat a rook. They do when coordinated and lose when they are not.

examples.note: Rook and bishop against rook - the ending this record exists for, because material counting gives the wrong answer and nothing but knowledge of the specific ending gives the right one. An extra bishop is worth about three pawns everywhere else on the board and is worth nothing here with the defence set up correctly. The record's subject is precisely that: endings where the piece values stop applying and the position has to be known rather than calculated.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 26. The engine agrees with the tablebase here, which it does not always do in this ending - the drawn defensive positions are famously hard to find over the board and the winning attempts run past fifty moves.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0. A whole extra minor piece and a proven draw, established over every legal continuation rather than over a search. This is the sharpest available statement of what a mixed-piece ending is: the material table is a summary of the middlegame and it does not survive into here.

examples.note:
BOTH HALVES OF THE PRECONDITION, which is what separates this record from the three beside it. Few pieces remain - four - and the two sides hold DIFFERENT KINDS of material: White a rook and a bishop, Black a rook and a knight.

That asymmetry is the concept. A rook-and-bishop against rook-and-knight ending cannot be reasoned about with the rules for either of the pure endings, which is why the record exists separately from `rook-endgame-principles` and `knight-endgames`, and why it was the hardest of the three to find: the scan has to compare the two material signatures rather than read one.

WHAT IS CLAIMED AND WHAT IS NOT. The category is decided by the material, which is mechanically certain and needs no engine. Whether the position is INTERESTING, or who is better in it, is a different question and this record does not answer it - its own typical_confidence says as much. What the position establishes is that the class of ending this record is about occurs in master play and can be pointed at.

PROVENANCE. Found by reading the MATERIAL of every position in 330 replayed master games rather than by asking the API, which never reports this concept because it has no matcher. The move list replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `the-same-kinds-of-material-on-both-sides`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A rook and a knight each, kings on the board, no pawns. Four pieces, two kinds, and an ending that is neither a pure rook ending nor a pure knight ending. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's subject is endings where 'the two sides hold DIFFERENT kinds of material — rook against two minors, queen against rook and pieces, bishop against knight'. Here both sides hold the same kinds. There is no exchange-rate question to get wrong, which is the whole thing the record is about: the point count becomes unreliable exactly where the kinds differ. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Nd1. The API reports `open-file` and nothing else. The case is registered because 'mixed' is a word about the RELATION between two armies rather than about how many kinds of piece are present, and a detector counting piece types on a board would get this backwards — it would see two kinds and call the ending mixed, when what makes an ending mixed is the two sides holding different ones.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW, best move Nd1. Both sides hold the same kinds of material, so there is no exchange-rate question to get wrong - which is the only thing this record is about.

ambiguous_examples.note: Rook and bishop against rook - the SAME material as this record's positive example, and a PROVEN WIN in 15 rather than a proven draw. Two positions, one material balance, opposite results, and nothing in the point count distinguishes them: what does is where the defending king stands and whether the defence has been set up. That is this record's central claim - 'the point count becomes the least reliable guide exactly where people lean on it most' - and the pair is the claim rather than an illustration of it. Filed as ambiguous because the concept applies fully to both halves and tells a reader nothing about which one they are looking at.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 11 at depth 26, settled at depth 1, in the material the same record's positive example holds to a proven draw.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 7, mate in 15, best move Rg1. The positive example on this record is the same five men in a different arrangement and is a PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0.

by_level.beginner: Endings where each side has different pieces — a rook against two minor pieces, say. Counting points helps least here.
by_level.intermediate: What decides them is whether the pieces work together and whose material suits the pawn structure.
by_level.advanced: Bishops beat knights in about 60% of endings, and the more symmetrical the structure the better for the knight — a statistic, not a rule.
by_level.master: The class most rewritten by tablebases, and the one where principles help least.

by_depth.short: Endings with different material on each side.
by_depth.normal: Endings where the two sides hold different kinds of material. They are defined by not being one of the studied types, and the point count - already a rule of thumb - is least reliable exactly here.
by_depth.deep: The endings that are not a type. What decides them is coordination rather than count, since two minor pieces beat a rook when they work together and lose to it when they do not; which side's material suits the pawn structure, since a knight blockades superbly and chases badly while a rook does the reverse; and the presence of fortresses, which live in unbalanced material because a fortress is precisely a position where extra material cannot be converted. The commonest case has a real result behind it - bishops outperform knights in about 60% of endings, and symmetry favours the knight - but that is a statistic about a population and not a claim about any position.

explanations.hedge: Under-researched in this base and orientation rather than theory; where a position is small enough for a tablebase, the tablebase is the authority.
explanations.lesson: Ask whose pieces suit the pawns, not whose pieces add up to more.

mixed-piece-endgames.definition_short: Endings where the two sides hold different KINDS of material — rook against two minors, queen against rook and pieces, bishop against knight.
mixed-piece-endgames.definition_long:
The endings that are not a type. Rook-and-pawn endings have a body of theory and named positions; so do knight endings and queen endings. Mixed-material endings are defined by what they are not, and the practical consequence is that the point count — already a rule of thumb — becomes the least reliable guide exactly where people lean on it most.

WHAT ACTUALLY DECIDES THEM:
- COORDINATION over count. Two minor pieces beat a rook when they work together and lose to it when they do not, which is why these endings turn on whether the pieces defend each other and have squares.
- PASSED PAWNS, and specifically who can BLOCKADE. A knight blockades superbly and chases badly; a rook does the opposite. Mixed endings are usually decided by which side's material suits the pawn structure it is facing.
- KING ACTIVITY, as everywhere in the endgame.
- FORTRESSES. Unbalanced material is where fortresses live, because a fortress is precisely a position in which extra material cannot be converted. This base holds proven examples.

THE BISHOP-VERSUS-KNIGHT ENDING is the commonest mixed case and the one with a real result behind it: bishops are better than knights in the endgame roughly 60% of the time, and the more SYMMETRICAL the pawn structure the better for the knight. That is a statistic about a population, not a rule about a position, and this base records it as such.

THE HONEST POSITION on this class is that principles help less here than anywhere else in the endgame, and where a position is small enough for a tablebase the tablebase is the authority. This base has not researched the class in depth and says so.

modern-dynamic.knowledge_type_note: A description of how top-level play changed, and a thesis about why. The thesis is attributable and contestable.

attributions.note: Secrets of Modern Chess Strategy argues that concrete analysis over rule-based thinking is the core of modern strategy. Cited at second hand here, not read.
His own account attributes his progress to clear analysis of variations rather than to principles.

history.notes: A thesis rather than an event, and recorded at low confidence because the primary source was not read directly. The corroboration from the cognitive-psychology literature is independent of the chess literature, which is what makes it worth recording at all.

development.note: Play organised around principles and structural advantages.
Concrete analysis becomes the deciding method.
Engines reward and intensify concreteness, and make principles checkable.

modern-dynamic.engine_era_note: Engines are the extreme case of the tendency this concept describes: pure concrete calculation with no principles at all, willing to break every classical rule when a line supports it. They did not start the shift but they settled it.

preconditions: A position where a principle and a concrete line disagree
indicators_for: A move that breaks a classical rule and is supported by a line
Dynamic assets with an expiry date being spent rather than banked
false_positive_traps: This describes a historical tendency, not a property of a position, and must not be attached to a move.
'Modern play ignores principles' is an overstatement of the thesis. Principles remain the fastest route to a reasonable move; what changed is which has the final word.
A move breaking a classical rule is not thereby modern or good. It needs the concrete line that justifies it.

typical_plans: Check the principle against a concrete line before trusting it
Treat dynamic advantages as assets to be spent before they expire
strategic_consequences: Structural concessions are accepted far more readily than classical teaching allowed, when a line supports them

exceptions: In quiet positions with no concrete content the classical method is not merely adequate but correct.
Concrete analysis is expensive; below master level the principles do most of the work.
limitations: A thesis about a trend, argued by identifiable people rather than measured.
The primary source for the thesis was not read directly.
misconceptions: That modern play has abandoned principles. It has demoted them from deciders to orientation.
That engines caused the shift. It predates strong engines, which rewarded and settled it.

examples.note: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, 21...Kxh7 - Watson's thesis with a board under it. Every principle in the classical vocabulary says do not take that pawn: the king steps onto an open h-file in front of a bishop on g5, two rooks and a queen. The annotation is explicit that the decision was made by calculation rather than by judgement: 'Black sees no threats following either gxf7 or gxh7. His king may look exposed, but in actuality, there is no immediate danger to his king, and Garry knows that his attack is much stronger at the moment.' This base carries the same position as a `king-attack` NEGATIVE, because every mechanical sign of an attack is present and the attack is not real - which is the same fact read from the detector's side.
examples.attributed_by: corpus entry adams-kasparov-2005-21Kxh7-king-attack-negative

engine.verdict_note: +2.12 from Black's side, and the engine's own first move is 21...Kxh7. Two pawns' worth, for the move that every rule of thumb forbids. This is the largest number attached to any historical example in this base and it is attached to the record about preferring calculation to rules, which is a coincidence worth not over-reading - but the direction is not a coincidence.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-position-calculation-cannot-help`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A concrete position with an extra bishop and an extra pawn, exactly the kind of material edge modern play is supposed to convert by calculation rather than by rule. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: No amount of calculation changes it. The bishop is the wrong colour for the h-pawn's queening square and the defending king cannot be driven from the corner by any series of moves. This record's thesis is that concrete analysis has displaced principle; here principle — one sentence about bishop colour — settles the position and analysis adds nothing to it. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, over every legal continuation. The API reports `wrong-rook-pawn` at high confidence, which is the sentence that decides it, and says nothing about calculation. Worth keeping beside this: Stockfish 18 at depth 26 evaluates the same position at +0.92 — the engine, which is the instrument the modern school is built on, is WRONG here and the old rule is right. That is the sharpest available counterweight to this record's own thesis, and it is why the record is filed as a historical-teaching-principle rather than as a fact.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW over every legal continuation - and Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says +0.92. The engine, which is the instrument this record's thesis is built on, is wrong here and a one-sentence rule about bishop colour is right.

ambiguous_examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein, Berlin 1928, 22.Qxc6 - a move made by concrete calculation twenty years before the school this record dates. The annotation says it 'looks like a mistake' by every principle available at the time: it dissolves the isolated pawn Capablanca spent the game creating. He played it because of what he had calculated the resulting ending to be, which is this record's thesis - principles demoted to orientation, concrete analysis deciding - performed by the most classical player in the game's history. Filed as ambiguous because the record's own dividing line is historical and this position sits on the wrong side of it: either the thesis is about a style that predates the school, or the move is classical judgement that happens to look modern, and nothing on the board decides which.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-22Qxc6-transformation

engine.verdict_note: +0.34 and the engine's first choice at depth 22 - a move that looks like a concession and is best, which is the shape this record says principle-based judgement gets wrong and calculation gets right.

by_level.beginner: Modern players work out what actually happens in this position rather than following general rules.
by_level.intermediate: Concrete analysis over principle. Rules orient you; the line decides.
by_level.advanced: Dynamic factors — initiative, activity, compensation — are treated as real assets with expiry dates rather than as debts.
by_level.master: The shift predates engines and was settled by them; several measurements in this base are that check being carried out on individual principles.

by_depth.short: Concrete analysis over general rules.
by_depth.normal: The modern preference for working out the specific position over applying a principle to it, and for dynamic factors over static ones. Principles are demoted from deciding to orienting.
by_depth.deep: Classical strategy and the hypermodern reaction both worked by principle: find the feature, apply the rule, follow the plan. Modern high-level play works by concrete analysis with principles demoted to orientation, and Watson's thesis is that this is the real dividing line between classical and modern chess. The cognitive-psychology literature says the same thing independently, describing the rule-driven picture of the strong player as the outdated view and modern play as concrete. What 'dynamic' adds is the elevation of the temporary over the permanent - initiative and activity treated as assets to be spent before they expire. Engines did not start this and did settle it, being the purest concrete players there are.

explanations.hedge: A thesis about a historical trend, argued by identifiable writers rather than measured, and easy to overstate: the classical principles remain the fastest route to a reasonable move.
explanations.lesson: Let the principle suggest the move and the line decide it.

modern-dynamic.definition_short: The modern preference for concrete calculation over rule-based judgement, and for dynamic factors over static ones.
modern-dynamic.definition_long:
WHAT CHANGED. Classical strategy, and the hypermodern reaction to it, both worked by PRINCIPLE: identify the position's features, apply the rule that fits, follow the plan. Modern high-level play works by CONCRETE ANALYSIS of the position in front of you, with principles demoted to orientation. Watson's thesis is that this shift is the core of the modern Soviet school and the real dividing line between classical and modern chess.

THE COGNITIVE LITERATURE INDEPENDENTLY SAYS THE SAME THING, which is unusual corroboration. A study of time pressure notes that the picture of the strong player running on rules and pattern recognition corresponds to the OLD and 'somewhat outdated' view associated with Nimzowitsch, and that modern high-level play no longer relies on rule-oriented thinking but on concrete analysis. Kotov's own account agrees: the ability to analyse enough variations clearly was, he concluded, the basic condition for success.

WHAT 'DYNAMIC' MEANS HERE is the elevation of the temporary over the permanent — initiative, activity, the initiative's expiry date, compensation — against the classical preference for durable structural advantages. It is not that structure stopped mattering; it is that a temporary advantage is now treated as a real asset to be spent rather than a debt to be repaid.

THE ENGINE ERA INTENSIFIED IT rather than caused it. The shift predates strong engines, but engines rewarded it: they are the purest concrete players, they routinely violate the classical rules when a line supports it, and they made it possible to check whether a principle was true. Several of this base's own measurements are that check being carried out.

THE HONEST QUALIFICATION: this is a thesis about a trend, argued by identifiable people, not a measured fact. It is also easy to overstate — the classical principles remain the fastest way to reach a reasonable move, and the concrete method is expensive. What changed is which one has the final word.

history.notes: A meta-record summarising this base's own attribution findings; each individual claim is documented on its own concept.

named-strategic-concepts.engine_era_note: Engines settle whether a named rule is TRUE, which is a different question from who said it. Tarrasch's rule is the case where both were checked and both came back negative: the attribution is disputed and the rule is false as stated.

false_positive_traps: A name attached to a concept is a claim about history and needs a source like any other claim. This base's checked attributions came back wrong or disputed more often than they came back clean.
Popularising is not originating, and the schema separates them precisely because conflating them is how misattributions start.
An attribution being widespread is not evidence. The Lucena misattribution has been repeated since 1880.

Keep competing claims side by side rather than choosing
Say unknown where the trail runs out

Absence of a recorded dispute means this base has not found one, not that none exists.

It is an index over other concepts, and the conditions it states are conditions on how this system names and files things - not patterns a position can exhibit. by_level.intermediate: Named strategic ideas usually record who popularised them, not who found them.

by_depth.normal: Ideas that carry a person's name, and the finding that checking the name usually changes the story: the Lucena position is not in Lucena's book, the worst-piece rule has four different names, and Tarrasch's rook rule is both disputed and false as stated.
by_depth.deep: Chess attaches names to ideas readily and checks them rarely, and when this base checked, the attributions usually did not survive intact. The Lucena position is not in Lucena's 1497 book and the error is traceable to an 1880 handbook. The principle of two weaknesses is Nimzowitsch's idea under another word while the name travels through three other people. The worst-piece rule has four names, one of them after a player who never stated it. Why it happens is ordinary - names attach to whoever popularised an idea in a language, and citations get copied rather than checked - and it matters because repeating attributions confidently teaches things that are not true.

explanations.lesson: A name on an idea is a historical claim. Check it, or record it as unverified.

named-strategic-concepts.definition_short: Strategic ideas attached to a person's name — and the finding that the attribution is wrong or disputed more often than not.
named-strategic-concepts.definition_long:
Chess attaches names to strategic ideas readily and checks them rarely. This base checked, and the results are consistent enough to be worth stating as a general finding: WHEN AN ATTRIBUTION IS CHECKED IT USUALLY DOES NOT SURVIVE INTACT.

WHAT THE CHECKING FOUND, each recorded in full on its own concept:
- THE LUCENA POSITION is not in Lucena's 1497 book. Salvio credits Genovino in 1634, and the misattribution is traceable to Schwede's 1880 Handbuch.
- TARRASCH'S RULE about the rook behind the passed pawn is disputed between Tarrasch and Tartakower, and is DISPROVED as a general rule by this base's own Vancura pair.
- THE PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES is Nimzowitsch's idea under a different word — he has it as 'tacking' — while the NAME travels Belavenets to Dvoretsky to Shereshevsky.
- THE WORST-PIECE RULE has four names: Anderssen's, Makogonov's, Fischer's (from Botvinnik, though Fischer never stated it) and Dvoretsky's 'principle of the worst piece'.
- 'THE BEST WAY TO REFUTE A GAMBIT IS TO ACCEPT IT' drifts between 'gambit' and 'sacrifice' across sources and is doubtfully Steinitz's, who separately said declining is not cowardice.
- STEINITZ'S OWN THEORY may be Paulsen's in its key proposition, on one source's account.
- ZUGZWANG's coinage is 'alleged' to Max Lange, per Winter.

WHY IT HAPPENS is ordinary: names attach to whoever POPULARISED an idea in a given language, citations get copied rather than checked, and a memorable attribution outlives the correction. None of it is scandalous and all of it matters, because a base that repeats attributions confidently is teaching things that are not true.

THE PRACTICE THAT FOLLOWS: every attribution here carries a RELATION rather than a bare name — originated-by, first-documented-by, popularized-by, named-by, later-associated-with — plus a confidence, and competing claims are recorded side by side rather than resolved by preference. Where the trail runs out the record says unknown.
