notation.knowledge_type_note: Algebraic notation is defined by the FIDE Laws; the other systems here are conventions, and are labelled as such.

history.notes: Algebraic notation displaced descriptive notation in English-language literature during the 1970s and 1980s. FIDE recognises only algebraic for official play.

development.note: Descriptive notation standard in English-language chess literature.
Algebraic displaces it; FIDE recognises algebraic alone.
UCI, FEN and PGN become the machine-readable layer alongside it.

notation.engine_era_note: UCI and FEN exist because engines needed unambiguous, position-independent formats. They are additions rather than replacements.

preconditions: A move or position is being written down
false_positive_traps: SAN is contextual: the same text means different moves in different positions, and disambiguation depends on what else is on the board. It cannot be parsed without a position.
Descriptive notation named a square differently for each player, so a quotation converted from it can silently name the wrong square. Treat converted historical lines with care.
A FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position - it is a picture of one.

strategic_consequences: In blindfold play notation is the interface, not the record

exceptions: FIDE recognises algebraic only; the other systems are conventions, however universal.
PGN carries game metadata as well as moves and is a container format rather than a notation.
limitations: This record covers what the systems are, not how to teach reading them - the course in blind-chess.html does that.
misconceptions: That UCI and algebraic are the same thing written differently. UCI is position-independent and algebraic is not.
That a FEN is just the board. Half its fields are about rights and counters that the board cannot show.

examples.note: Two knights that can both reach d2, so the move must be written Nbd2 rather than Nd2. Algebraic notation names a move by its destination and adds only as much as is needed to make it unique, which means the NAME of a move depends on the whole position and not on the piece that makes it. The page's own toSAN is asked for both halves of this pair and returns Nbd2 here and Nd2 in the other.

counterexamples.note: The same knight making the same move on an otherwise identical board, written Nd2 - because the knight on f3 is not there and no other knight can reach the square. A reader who learns 'Nbd2' as the name of this move has learned something about the position rather than about the move, and would write it wrongly here.

Registered false-positive case `an-ambiguous-san-is-not-a-move`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: 'Nd2' looks like a complete move. There is a knight, there is a square, the square is empty and reachable. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "SAN is contextual: the same text means different moves in different positions, and disambiguation depends on what else is on the board." Two knights reach d2 here, so 'Nd2' names two moves and therefore none. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: This base's own toSAN() writes the three moves to d2 as Nfd2, Nbd2 and Kd2 — it disambiguates by file because it must, and it is the same function the game writes its move list with. The case exists because the failure here is silent: a reader, a database or a converted quotation that drops the disambiguating letter produces text that looks like notation and denotes nothing, and no error is raised anywhere.

by_level.beginner: Squares are named by file letter and rank number — e4, g8 — and pieces by a letter, so Nf3 means a knight to f3.
by_level.intermediate: Algebraic for reading, UCI for engines, FEN for positions. Algebraic needs a position to make sense of it; UCI does not.
by_level.advanced: A FEN's last four fields — castling, en passant, and the two clocks — are precisely the state a board cannot show.
by_level.master: Descriptive notation named squares from each player's own side, which is why converted historical quotations need checking.

by_depth.short: How moves and positions are written down.
by_depth.normal: Algebraic notation (Nf3) is the standard and the only one FIDE recognises; UCI (g1f3) gives the origin square too and is what engines speak; FEN records a whole position including castling and en passant rights.
by_depth.deep: Four systems answering different questions. Algebraic is written from the reader's side so a square has one name for both players, and is contextual - it needs a position to be interpreted, and disambiguation when two pieces can reach the square. UCI and long algebraic give the origin as well, so they are unambiguous without a position, at the cost of being unreadable as chess. FEN records a position rather than a move, and half its fields cover what a board cannot show: castling rights, en passant, and the clocks. Descriptive notation, used until the 1970s, named squares from each player's own side, so the same square had two names.

explanations.lesson: Algebraic needs a position to mean anything; UCI does not. Pick the one that matches what you have.

notation.definition_short: The systems for writing down a position or a move.
notation.definition_long:
Four systems matter, and they answer different questions.

ALGEBRAIC (SAN) is the only notation FIDE recognises for official play. Files a-h, ranks 1-8, pieces by an initial letter, and — the property that matters — it is written from the READER's point of view rather than a player's, so a square has one name for both sides. It is also CONTEXTUAL: Nf3 names a move only relative to a position, and needs disambiguation (Nbd2) when two pieces of a kind can reach the square.

LONG ALGEBRAIC and UCI give the origin square as well (e2e4), which makes them unambiguous without knowing the position. UCI is what engines speak, and adds a promotion letter (e7e8q). The trade is that a UCI move is unreadable as chess and a SAN move is unreadable without a board.

FEN records a POSITION rather than a move: piece placement, side to move, castling rights, en passant target, halfmove clock, fullmove number. Those last four fields are exactly the state a position cannot be reconstructed without, which is the same list that makes transposition work.

DESCRIPTIVE notation (P-K4) is historical and was written from each player's own side, so the same square had two names. Reading pre-1970s literature requires it, and this base flags quotations that may have passed through a conversion.

IN THIS CODEBASE all four appear: `toSAN` for display, `uciOf` for the engine and the wire protocol, `fenOf`/`stateFromFEN` for positions, and `parseMoveIn` for reading what a player types. That is not incidental — a blindfold game is played in notation, so notation IS the interface here rather than a way of recording it afterwards.

open-file.knowledge_type_note: Names a board feature. That rooks belong on open files is a related rule of thumb, not part of the definition.

attributions.note: My System devotes early chapters to the open file — its genesis, its purpose, obstacles to a file operation, and the outpost as its natural consequence.

history.notes: Rooks on open files were understood long before Nimzowitsch; what he supplied was systematic treatment and the link to the outpost. Not a claim of invention.

development.change: Systematic treatment; the file is tied to the outpost and to provoking pawn weaknesses.
Quantified: open-file bonuses of roughly 8-20 centipawns, with extra for doubling and for bearing on the enemy king.

open-file.engine_era_note: Uncontroversial and directly quantified in engine evaluation. The engine-era refinement is that the bonus is conditional — larger when the file bears on the enemy king, and worth little without an entry square.

preconditions: A file contains no pawns of either colour (open), or pawns of one colour only (half-open for the other side)
indicators_for: A safe entry square exists on the seventh or eighth rank, or on any rank the defender cannot cover
The file leads towards the enemy king
Rooks can be doubled on it, or a queen placed behind them
The opponent cannot contest the file, or contesting it costs them something
indicators_against: Every entry square on the file is defended — the rook stares and does nothing
The opponent can contest the file and trade all the rooks off
The file can be closed by a pawn advance
Occupying it costs a tempo the position cannot spare
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: open-file, implementing the record's entry-square and contested-file traps
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a file with no pawns is not automatically useful. Without an entry square, a rook on it accomplishes nothing.
Detecting 'no pawns on this file' is trivial and fires constantly. The reportable fact is the file PLUS a usable entry square.
Contested files where all rooks come off leave neither side with anything.
An open file is not an advantage on its own. In a proven test position with a rook of each colour on the open d-file, the evaluation is +0.02 - the file belongs to nobody.

typical_plans: Double rooks on the file, then invade on the seventh
Half-open file: pile onto the enemy pawn standing on it
Create the entry square first by exchanging its defender
Open a file deliberately with a pawn break aimed at the enemy king
typical_moves: Rook to the file, then doubling; a rook lift to the third rank and across
typical_pawn_structures: Half-open c-file in Sicilian structures
Half-open d-file in front of a backward d-pawn
typical_piece_arrangements: Doubled rooks, or queen behind rook, on one file
tactical_consequences: Invasion on the seventh rank; back-rank threats
strategic_consequences: Files are how heavy pieces enter a position at all

exceptions: A file with no entry squares is worth nothing.
A half-open file can be more valuable than a fully open one, because the enemy pawn on it is a fixed target and the file cannot be neutralised by a simple rook trade.
Nimzowitsch's usage of the term differs from the modern one.
limitations: The feature is trivially detectable and therefore trivially over-reportable. Usability is the whole question.

MEASURED 2026-09-01 and fixed: this record's REGISTERED false positive - 'a file with no pawns is not automatically useful; without an entry square, a rook on it accomplishes nothing' - had never been implemented. The matcher required a rook on the file, which took it from 61% to 55.7% of the 788 shipped positions and left it the second-broadest label in the base. Requiring the rook to be able to ENTER - a legal move down the file into the opponent's half after which static exchange evaluation does not win it - and then the third trap, that a file the enemy also has a rook or queen on is contested rather than entered, brings it to 35.5%. Both conditions were in the record and neither was in the code.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'an open file is not an advantage on its own. In a proven test position with a rook of each colour on the open d-file, the evaluation is +0.02' is the same condition as the registered false positive already built - a usable entry square is required, and a file both sides' rooks contest produces none. The measured effect of building it was 61% -> 35.5%.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the last of this record's indicators_against that a static scan can answer - 'the file can be closed by a pawn advance' - is now built, and it is near-inert: 35.5% -> 35.4%. That is a fact about open files rather than about the guard. A file is open precisely because both pawns have left it, so a pawn arriving from an adjacent file to shut it is rare. Built, measured, and reported as near-inert rather than dressed up.
misconceptions: That rooks belong on open files unconditionally. They belong on files they can invade down.
That an open file is better than a half-open one.

examples.note:
A QUIET position from a master game — after Rxe5, ply 60 — in which the c- and e-files are open, and White's rook on c1 and White's rook on e1 and Black's rook on e8 and Black's rook on e5 stand on it. Quiet here has a mechanical meaning: the side to move has no check and no capture that wins material, so the next move has to be chosen on positional grounds. That matters because this base's other corpus is 788 tactical puzzles, in which a positional feature cannot be isolated.

WHAT IS VERIFIED: the game replays legally end to end through the page's own move generator, so the FEN is derived rather than transcribed; and the feature is present by mechanical measurement in lib/features.js.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: that the concept decides this position, or that the players were thinking about it. Note also a limitation of method — the position was FOUND by this system's own Layer 4, so it demonstrates the concept and cannot by itself validate the matcher that found it. Other concepts licensed here: passed-pawn, isolated-queen-pawn, doubled-pawns, bishop-pair.

the e and f and g-file is open with White's rook on g7. The position is QUIET by mechanical test: the side to move has no check available and no capture that wins material, so the next move must be chosen on positional grounds. That is the property this base's tactical corpus almost never has. Found by tools/prospect.js, which searches 1576 real positions for a concept's feature and scores quiet positions far higher. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Quiet and close to balanced at -0.36, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

examples.note: A quiet position from a master game — after Kf2, ply 61 — where the c-file is open, and White's rook on c4 stands on it. Quiet has a mechanical meaning here: the side to move has no check and no capture that wins material, so the next move must be chosen positionally. VERIFIED: the game replays legally end to end through the page's own move generator, and the feature is measured by lib/features.js. NOT CLAIMED: that the concept decides this position, or that the players were thinking about it. Method note: the position was found by this system's own Layer 4, so it illustrates the concept and cannot by itself validate the matcher that found it. Other concepts licensed here: passed-pawn, doubled-pawns, weak-square, material-imbalance.

counterexamples.note: A symmetric position with the d-file open and a rook of each colour already on it. Constructed to isolate the file itself: if an open file were an advantage, occupying one could not leave the position dead level.

engine.verdict_note: Dead level at +0.02, with the best line trading the rooks off immediately. An open file is not an advantage in itself - it is an advantage only when one side can use it and the other cannot, and here both can equally. This is the position behind the open-file-not-useful false-positive case, and it is why this system reports a file as open rather than as good.

counterexamples.note: an open e-file that neither side has occupied — the file exists and nobody is using it. The position is QUIET by mechanical test: the side to move has no check available and no capture that wins material, so the next move must be chosen on positional grounds. That is the property this base's tactical corpus almost never has. Found by tools/prospect.js, which searches 1576 real positions for a concept's feature and scores quiet positions far higher. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

engine.verdict_note: Quiet and close to balanced at 2.44, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

ambiguous_examples.note: A BOTH-SIDES candidate where all three readings disagree. The base reports an open file for White and an open file for Black. Material says Black by 1150 centipawns. The engine says White mates in 3, beginning with Re4+. The open file is in fact what decides the position - the white rook on the e-file delivers the first move of the mate - and none of that is visible in a report that says both sides have one. An ambiguous example is not a position where the feature is absent; it is a position where the feature is present on both sides and being told so leaves the reader exactly where they started.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 3 for the side 1150 centipawns down on material, and the mate runs along the open file the concept named for both players.

by_level.beginner: There are no pawns on that file, so a rook there can see all the way down the board.
by_level.intermediate: The {file}-file is open. Before committing the rook, find the square you intend to invade on — a file with no entry point does nothing.
by_level.advanced: Open file with an entry square on {square}. Double, or place the queen behind, and check whether the opponent can contest and trade off.
by_level.master: File plus entry point, always. A half-open file with a fixed enemy pawn on it is frequently worth more than a fully open one, because it cannot be neutralised by an exchange of rooks.

by_depth.short: No pawns on the {file}-file.
by_depth.normal: The {file}-file is open. That matters because there is an entry square on {square} — a file a rook cannot invade down is not worth occupying.
by_depth.deep: A file with no pawns of either colour; half-open means pawns of one colour only, and is the natural file to attack down since the enemy pawn is a fixed target. Nimzowitsch treated the open file systematically and tied it to the outpost — the file supports a piece planted in enemy territory, and driving that piece off with a pawn is what damages the file in turn. The qualification that matters in practice is the entry square: engine evaluation gives a rook on an open file only about 8 to 20 centipawns, which is the right order of magnitude for the feature by itself. What makes a file decisive is somewhere to go.

explanations.lesson: An open file is a road. Before you drive down it, check there is somewhere to arrive.

beginner_words: the rook can see down the board

open-file.definition_short: A file with no pawns of either colour, which rooks and queens can use to exert pressure and invade.
open-file.definition_long:
A file with no pawns on it at all. A HALF-OPEN (or SEMI-OPEN) file has pawns of one colour only — half-open for the side without a pawn there, and the natural file to attack down, because the enemy pawn on it is a target.

The critical qualification, and the one most often left out: a file is worth having only if it offers an ENTRY SQUARE. A rook on an open file whose seventh and eighth ranks are all covered controls squares and achieves nothing. The plan is always file plus entry point, not file alone.

Nimzowitsch treated the open file as a subject in its own right and tied it to the outpost: the file is what supports a piece planted in enemy territory, and driving that piece away with a pawn is what damages the file. Note a terminology difference — he used '(semi) open file' even for rooks standing in front of their own pawn chain, which modern usage would not.

Engine evaluation gives a rook on an open file a bonus of roughly 8 to 20 centipawns, which is a useful calibration: real, worth having, and far smaller than a pawn.

opening-development.knowledge_type_note: Deliberately typed rule-of-thumb, not principle. The conventional five rules are teaching devices with well-known exceptions, and every one of them is broken routinely at master level. They carry mandatory hedging wording.

attributions.note: The modern school's treatment of development as an accountable resource rather than a matter of taste.
Conventionally credited with hardening the guidance into teachable rules; not verified here.

history.notes: The five-rule list has no single author and is a pedagogical convention. Both attributions are conventional and neither was verified against a primary text.

development.change: Development codified as rules; the centre is to be occupied by pawns.
Central occupation challenged — the centre may be controlled from a distance and invited to overextend.
Opening theory becomes concrete; many rule-breaking systems are vindicated, and the rules survive as scaffolding for players who cannot yet calculate the exception.

opening-development.engine_era_note: Engines break all five rules routinely when a concrete reason exists, and modern opening theory contains many respectable lines that violate them. What survives is the underlying accounting — tempo is real and finite. What does not survive is treating the rules as constraints rather than defaults.

preconditions: The game is in the opening — pieces are still undeveloped
indicators_for: Pieces remain on their starting squares while the opponent develops
A piece has moved twice with no capture, no escape and no clear gain
The king is uncastled past move ten with the centre open
The queen is out early and can be harassed with tempo
indicators_against: The repeated move captures something, escapes a threat, or reaches a decisively better square
The centre is closed, so the timetable is slower and the king is not in danger
The opening is a known system where the deviation is theory
A concrete tactic justifies the move
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: moving the same piece twice is not automatically wrong. Capturing, escaping and reaching a much better square all justify it, and this is the brief's own illustration of tactics overriding a principle.

REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: early queen development is not automatically wrong — the objection is that the queen can be harassed WITH TEMPO, so where no such harassment exists the objection does not apply.
Detecting a rule violation is easy and says almost nothing. Only the absence of a concrete justification makes it a criticism.
'The opening' has no fixed end. Applying opening rules at move 15 of a closed position is a category error.
A piece moving twice is not evidence of a mistake. Proven counterexample: 4.Ba4 in the Ruy Lopez is best by 0.34 over any move that leaves the bishop alone.

typical_plans: Develop minor pieces towards the centre, castle, then connect the rooks
Develop with threats where possible, so each move gains a tempo
Decide which side to castle by where the opponent cannot attack
typical_moves: Knights before bishops, as a default rather than a law
tactical_consequences: A lead in development converts into an initiative in open positions
strategic_consequences: Time spent in the opening cannot be recovered
The choice of castling side sets the character of the middlegame

exceptions: Moving a piece twice to capture, to escape, or to reach a decisively better square.
Early queen sorties that cannot be harassed — the Scandinavian's ...Qa5 is theory, not an error.
Delaying castling deliberately when the centre is closed, or when castling would walk into a prepared attack.
Hypermodern openings that decline to occupy the centre at all and invite overextension instead.
limitations: These are teaching heuristics. Every one has standard exceptions, and a violation is only a criticism when no concrete justification exists.
Not detectable in any useful sense: the rule violation is trivially detectable, the justification is not.
misconceptions: That the rules are rules. They are defaults for players who cannot yet judge the exception.
That moving a piece twice is a mistake.
That the queen must stay home until move 10.
That 'the opening' ends at a fixed move number. It ends when the pieces are developed.
That moving the same piece twice in the opening is an error. In the Ruy Lopez it is the best move, measured at +0.42 against +0.08 for the alternative.

examples.note: The Opera Game after 12.O-O-O. Every white piece is developed and the king is castled; Black has a queen on e7 that has been chased, a knight that had to come to d7 to block a check, a rook still on a8 and a bishop that has never moved. Morphy has spent twelve moves and used every one of them. The record's own trap is the one that matters here - 'counting developed pieces overstates a development lead. Count the moves each side still needs' - and by that count Black needs four moves to reach a normal position and does not have them: the game ends five plies later. -5.87 for Black in a position where MATERIAL IS LEVEL, which is the only honest way to say what a development lead is worth. counterexamples.note: The Ruy Lopez after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 - one of the most-played positions in chess. White's best move retreats the bishop that already moved on move three. Constructed-test: the FEN was built from the standard move sequence for this comparison.

engine.verdict_note: Refutes 'do not move the same piece twice' as a rule. 4.Ba4 - a SECOND move by the bishop - is best at +0.42, and by a wide margin: 4.Bxc6 is +0.08 and 4.Bc4 is +0.04. Moving the same piece again is not merely tolerable here but worth about a third of a pawn more than any alternative. The rule describes a typical cost, not a prohibition, and this base will not report a repeated piece move as an error.

ambiguous_examples.note: The Giuoco Piano after 3...Bc5. Both sides have developed two pieces, both have a bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal and a knight out, neither has castled, and the position is symmetric to the move. Every count this rule of thumb runs - pieces developed, tempi spent, centre occupied - comes out level, which is the case a development rule cannot speak about and is also the commonest case in the opening. This record's own trap is that 'counting developed pieces overstates a development lead. Count the moves each side still needs', and here both sides still need the same moves. Filed as ambiguous because the concept is fully applicable and completely uninformative, which is what a symmetric opening is.

by_level.beginner: Get your pieces out towards the middle, castle your king to safety, and try not to move the same piece twice — every move counts in the opening.
by_level.intermediate: Opening principles. Before criticising a move for breaking one, check whether it captures, escapes, or reaches a square worth two tempi.
by_level.advanced: Heuristics for spending tempi when calculation is unavailable. In a closed centre the timetable slackens and most of them relax with it.
by_level.master: Defaults, not constraints. The interesting question is always what concrete justification the deviation has.

by_depth.short: Get the pieces out and the king castled.
by_depth.normal: The conventional opening guidance: control the centre, develop, castle, avoid moving one piece twice, and keep the queen home early. They are about spending tempo well, and each has standard exceptions.
by_depth.deep: Five heuristics whose common currency is tempo: an opening move cannot be recovered, and moving one piece twice pays two moves for one working piece. Each has explicit exceptions. Moving a piece twice is justified by a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square. Early queen development is objectionable only where the queen can be harassed with tempo. Castling early is really a decision about the kind of game wanted — castling opposite converts it into a race where speed beats material and your own shield pawns become weapons. The hypermodern school rejected the central-occupation rule outright, and engines break all five routinely when a concrete reason exists.

explanations.hedge: These are teaching guidelines, not rules. Strong players break every one of them routinely when a concrete reason exists, and a move that violates one is only a mistake if it has no such justification.
explanations.lesson: Opening rules are for when you cannot see the exception yet. When you can see one, the exception wins.

avoid: never move the same piece twice
never bring the queen out early

opening-development.definition_short: Bring pieces off the back rank quickly, towards the centre, and get the king castled — the conventional opening guidance, with exceptions that matter.
opening-development.definition_long:
The standard five: control the centre, develop your pieces, castle early, do not move the same piece twice, and do not bring the queen out too early. They are excellent guidance for a player who does not yet know when to break them, and every one of them is broken constantly by strong players for concrete reasons.

The underlying quantity is TEMPO. Each opening move is a unit of time you cannot get back, and moving one piece twice means paying two moves for one working piece. The rules are heuristics for spending time well when you cannot yet calculate whether a specific deviation pays.

'DO NOT MOVE THE SAME PIECE TWICE' has explicit, standard exceptions, and this is the brief's own example of principle yielding to tactics. Capturing something is worth the move. Saving an attacked piece is not optional. Reaching a decisively better square can be worth two tempi. And the rule's scope is bounded — 'the opening' ends when the pieces are developed, not at a fixed move number.

'CASTLE EARLY' is really a decision about what kind of game you want, not only about safety. Castling opposite your opponent converts the game into a race in which speed beats material and the pawns in front of your own king become attacking units rather than shelter.

opening-repertoire.definition_short: The set of openings a player has chosen to know and play.
opening-repertoire.definition_long:
The openings a player has specialised in. A repertoire exists because the amount of theory is unbounded and a player's study time is not: choosing what NOT to learn is the substance of it.

The governing trade-off is between soundness and practicality. A repertoire's main lines should be sound enough to give playable positions against best defence, since an unsound line is a liability once opponents know it. Unsound gambits work as surprise weapons and fail as foundations.

The most useful modern advice is to organise a repertoire around PAWN STRUCTURES rather than move sequences. Every move-order trick an opponent tries still has to land in some structure, and understanding a handful of structures deeply generalises where memorised lines do not. Openings sharing structural characteristics also make preparation compound across lines.

A repertoire is expected to change. Lines effective against amateurs can be much less so at master level — the Benko Gambit is the standard illustration, where the activity that troubles club players is defused by stronger defenders who simply keep the pawn — and a repertoire that never evolves can hold a player back.

opposite-coloured-bishops.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept with unusually hard statistical backing, but still a concept rather than a proven result: whether a given position draws depends on the position.

history.notes: No coinage researched; the term is descriptive and standard. The earliest example in the ChessBase database is Paulsen-Anderssen 1862, which is a fact about the database rather than about the concept.

opposite-coloured-bishops.engine_era_note: Engines evaluate opposite-coloured-bishop endings poorly for the same reason they misjudge fortresses — the draw is a positional wall rather than a line — and this is a standard reason to consult tablebases. Their middlegame sharpness, by contrast, engines assess well.

preconditions: Each side has exactly one bishop
The bishops travel on opposite colours
indicators_for: An endgame with few or no other pieces — the drawish case
The defender can blockade the passed pawns on their own bishop's colour
The defender's pawns are on their own bishop's colour, so the bishop defends them
One of the pawns is a wrong rook pawn
indicators_against: Queens or rooks remain — winning chances rise sharply, and in the middlegame the bishops are an ATTACKING asset
The extra pawns are separated by three files or more
The defender cannot establish a blockade on their bishop's colour
The attacker's king can penetrate on the colour the defending bishop cannot cover
recognition.detector: materialPattern opposite-colour bishops — not yet written
false_positive_traps: The drawish reputation is an ENDGAME fact. In the middlegame with heavy pieces on, opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker, because the bishop operates where the defender's cannot answer. Announcing 'opposite bishops, drawn' with queens on the board is the standard error.
Detecting the material is trivial; whether a blockade is achievable is not.
Two extra pawns are often not enough — but three files of separation often are. The count of pawns is the wrong variable; their separation and the blockade are the right ones.

typical_plans: As the defender: blockade on your own bishop's colour, put your pawns there too, and accept a 'bad' bishop deliberately
As the attacker: put your pawns on the colour OPPOSITE your bishop, separate the passed pawns by at least three files, and keep heavy pieces on
As the attacker: aim for the colour complex the defending bishop cannot cover
typical_moves: A bishop sacrifice to gain the tempo needed for the king to reach a blockade square
typical_pawn_structures: Separated passed pawns — the attacker's best try
Blockaded connected pawns on the defender's bishop colour — the drawing setup
typical_piece_arrangements: Defending king and bishop sharing the blockade duties
tactical_consequences: Bishop sacrifices for a single tempo are a standard defensive resource
strategic_consequences: Material largely stops being the operative variable; position takes over
A standard way for a worse side to save a game is to steer into them

exceptions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.
A wrong rook pawn draws regardless of how far apart or how advanced the pawns are.
The defender's best practice is the opposite of normal: make your bishop bad on purpose.
limitations: The material pattern is trivially detectable; whether the position draws is not.
The published statistics apply to specific material counts and should not be generalised.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first trap - 'the drawish reputation is an ENDGAME fact. In the middlegame with heavy pieces on, opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker' - was not in the wording, which said one thing in every position. The phase and the heavy-piece count now decide which half is said. Saying 'drawish' with queens and rooks on the board is the commonest thing anyone says about this material and it is the error this record names.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: two traps here are about a judgement no static test makes. 'Detecting the material is trivial; whether a blockade is achievable is not', and 'two extra pawns are often not enough - but three files of separation often are. The count of pawns is the wrong variable; their separation and the blockade are.' Pawn separation IS measurable and pawn counts are not reported, so nothing here says 'two pawns up should win'; whether a blockade can be reached is not attempted and is recorded as such rather than approximated.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: this record says 'two extra pawns are often not enough - but THREE FILES OF SEPARATION often are. The count of pawns is the wrong variable; their separation and the blockade are' - and the base was reporting neither variable. Separation is now measured and named: a side a pawn up with its pawns three or more files apart is told that separation decides these endings, and one whose pawns are closer is told that one bishop covers that and the count is the wrong variable. The blockade half is not measurable and is left alone. The middlegame caveat still takes precedence, because with queens and rooks on this is not an ending at all.
misconceptions: That opposite-coloured bishops mean a draw. That is an endgame tendency, and the reverse is true in the middlegame.
That an extra pawn or two settles it. Two extra pawns frequently fail to win.
That a bad bishop is bad here. For the defender it is the correct setup.

conflicts.resolution: `two-weaknesses` lists opposite-coloured bishops as a case where the principle fails, and that is right: the defending bishop holds one colour complex however many targets exist, so stretching the defence does not work. Where the two meet, the bishop colour wins — unless the second weakness creates a breakthrough square on the defender's OWN colour, which is the one way through.

Direct inversion. `bad-bishop` treats pawns on the bishop's colour as a defect; here the DEFENDER should deliberately create that defect, because a bishop that defends its own pawns on its own colour is what builds the fortress. The general concept is right and this configuration is the standard exception to it.

by_level.beginner: The bishops move on different colours, so they can never meet or defend against each other. In endgames that usually makes it hard to win, even a pawn or two ahead — unless there are passed pawns on BOTH wings, because one bishop cannot guard two places at once.
by_level.intermediate: Opposite-coloured bishops. In the endgame they are the most drawish material in chess when the fight is on one wing: blockade the pawns on your own bishop's colour and even two extra pawns often fail. The exception is the one that decides games — passed pawns three or more files apart, which a single bishop cannot blockade at both ends.
by_level.advanced: Endgame: drawish while the play is confined to one wing, and the defender should deliberately make their bishop bad to build the fortress. Separation is what breaks it — roughly three files between passers, with a king marching to escort one of them. Middlegame: sharp, because your bishop operates where theirs cannot answer.
by_level.master: The operative variables are blockade feasibility and pawn separation, not the pawn count. Three files apart usually wins; a wrong rook pawn draws regardless.

by_depth.short: Bishops on different colours — usually hard to win, unless there are passers on both wings.
by_depth.normal: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.
by_depth.deep: The most drawish material configuration in the endgame — roughly half of bishop-and-four-pawns endings against an opposite bishop are drawn, against over 90% wins with same-coloured bishops. The defensive method inverts an ordinary principle: put your pawns on your own bishop's colour so the bishop defends them, deliberately creating a 'bad' bishop that is exactly what the fortress needs. Two other reversals: separated pawns beat connected ones, and zugzwang is much less available than usual. The drawish reputation belongs to the ENDGAME, though. With heavy pieces still on, opposite bishops favour the attacker, because a bishop attacking on a colour the defender cannot answer is an extra attacker.

explanations.lesson: Opposite bishops are drawish when the fight is on ONE wing, and dangerous in middlegames. Before announcing a draw, count what else is on the board and how far apart the passers can be made — three files usually wins.

opposite-coloured-bishops.definition_short: Each side has one bishop and they run on opposite colours. Strongly drawish in the endgame — two extra pawns often fail to win — and sharply attacking in the middlegame.
opposite-coloured-bishops.definition_long:
Because the bishops can never meet or contest the same squares, each side is effectively playing with a piece the other cannot answer on its own colour. That has two opposite consequences depending on phase.

IN THE ENDGAME they are the most drawish material configuration in chess. The numbers are stark: about HALF of endings with bishop and four pawns against a bishop on the opposite colour are drawn, against over 90% wins when the bishops are on the same colour. One extra pawn usually draws, and two extra pawns frequently do too, because the defender can blockade on the colour of their own bishop and the attacker's bishop can never challenge the blockade. Zugzwang, the usual tool for breaking such positions, is much less available than with same-coloured bishops.

The defensive method inverts an ordinary principle: the weaker side should DELIBERATELY make their bishop bad, putting their pawns on the bishop's own colour so it defends them, and building a fortress on that colour complex. The attacker should do the reverse.

Separated pawns beat connected ones here, which is also the reverse of the usual rule — with one file between the pawns it is normally a draw, with three files the attacker normally wins, because the defender must block one pawn with the king and the other with the bishop and then the attacking king wins the blockaded piece.

IN THE MIDDLEGAME the same feature makes them SHARP, not drawish, because a bishop attacking on a colour the opponent cannot defend is a genuine extra attacker. The drawish reputation belongs to the endgame and is routinely over-applied earlier.

opposition.knowledge_type_note: Typed tablebase-fact rather than positional-concept because the core claim is provable and has been proved here: the same position is a draw or a win purely according to who must move. That is not a heuristic.

attributions.note: Credited with the formulation that the opposition is a means to an end, the end being penetration to a key square.

history.notes: No coinage researched. The technique is ancient and anonymous; Averbakh's corrective is the attributable part and is second-hand here.

opposition.engine_era_note: Fully settled by tablebase, and the proof is a one-bit comparison. Nothing about the concept has been revised; what tablebases add is that the exceptions — positions where taking the opposition is the wrong move — can now be demonstrated rather than argued.

by_level.beginner: The two kings are facing each other with one square between. Whoever has to move must step aside, so you want it to be their turn, not yours.
by_level.intermediate: Direct opposition. The side NOT to move has it. Use it to force their king off the squares in front of your pawn.
by_level.advanced: Opposition, a special case of zugzwang. Remember Averbakh: it is a means to an end, and the end is a key square — sometimes marching there directly beats taking it.
by_level.master: Decidable. In king-and-pawn endings the opposition is exact, and the corresponding-squares framework generalises it for cluttered positions where simple opposition misleads.

by_depth.short: Kings face each other; whoever must move gives way.
by_depth.normal: The opposition: kings on the same line with one square between them. Because kings cannot touch, whoever is to move has to step aside — so the side NOT to move has the opposition and can force the other king off key squares.
by_depth.deep: A special case of zugzwang, and one of the few chess ideas that is exactly provable. In the basic king-and-pawn-versus-king position the same arrangement is a draw with one side to move and a win in 28 with the other — a full point turning on a single bit. Diagonal and distant opposition are variants, usually used as routes to the direct form. The corrective that matters is Averbakh's: the opposition is a means to an end and the end is penetration to a key square. Taking it is not automatically correct, and in some positions the king should simply march for the key squares instead.

explanations.lesson: In king-and-pawn endings, work out who has the opposition before you move — and then check that taking it actually gets your king somewhere it wants to be.

opposition.definition_short: Kings facing each other with one square between them on a rank or file. The side NOT to move has the opposition.
opposition.definition_long:
Two kings a knight's-jump-less apart — one empty square between them on a rank or file. Since kings may not stand adjacent, each blocks the other, and whoever must move has to give way. The player NOT on move is said to have the opposition.

It is a special case of zugzwang, and its effect is exact rather than approximate. In the basic king-and-pawn-versus-king position with White Ke5, pawn e4, Black Ke7, the tablebase gives a DRAW with White to move and a WIN for White (mate in 28) with Black to move. Same pieces, same squares; one bit of difference.

Variants: DIAGONAL opposition, kings on a diagonal with one square between; DISTANT opposition, kings on the same line with an odd number of squares between, where again the player not to move holds it. Both are usually routes to direct opposition.

AVERBAKH'S CORRECTIVE is the part most often missed: the opposition is a MEANS TO AN END, and the end is penetration to a KEY SQUARE. Taking the opposition is not automatically right. Wikipedia's own example makes the point — in one position 1.Ke2 taking the distant opposition wins, while in another taking the opposition with 1.Ke4 only draws and the king should simply march for the key squares instead.

outpost.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept. NOT a rule and not a proven result: whether occupying an outpost is good depends on the whole position. Recorded as positional-concept rather than strategic-principle because it names a board FEATURE, not a method of play.
outpost.definition_short: An advanced square, usually protected by a pawn, that no enemy pawn can attack — so a piece placed there cannot be driven away. Sources disagree on whether an open or half-open file behind it is part of the definition.
outpost.definition_long:
THE DEFINITION IS GENUINELY DISPUTED. This is not vagueness in the sources; it is a real divergence that a system using the word must handle explicitly.

NIMZOWITSCH (My System, 1925), who coined the term, requires the file. His words: 'by an outpost we mean one of our own pieces, (usually a knight), which is placed, being protected (by a pawn of course) and on an open file within enemy territory.' He is emphatic that the file is load-bearing: 'The outpost must be accompanied by the file behind and the pawn protecting it from one side', and 'The outpost does not draw its strength from its own resources, but much more from its open file and the protecting pawn.' For him the outpost has two purposes: (a) it is a base for new attacks, and (b) it PROVOKES a weakening — the opponent drives the knight away with a pawn, and that pawn move damages the file. He also held that a flank outpost belongs to a rook rather than a knight.

HOOPER & WHYLD (Oxford Companion, 1992) make the file optional: a square 'guarded by a pawn but cannot be attacked by an enemy pawn, especially such a square on an open file'.

MODERN COMMON USAGE drops the file entirely: an advanced square (4th-7th rank), defended by one's own pawn, unattackable by enemy pawns. Chess.com adds a third condition frequently omitted elsewhere and important in practice — no piece of equal value can easily challenge the occupant. The Chess Programming Wiki states the drift plainly: in the broad sense 'the half-open file and provocation aspect of the outpost is lost, though the evaluation term is still useful.'

IM Xavier Bedouin proposed a full nomenclature precisely because of this, distinguishing strong square, protected strong square, foothold (open file) and outpost (semi-open file), each absolute or relative. It is a coherent proposal, not established usage, and is recorded as such.

ROMANOVSKY supplies the condition that decides whether any of it matters: a square is a real weakness only when an enemy piece 'which it will not be possible to drive away or eliminate by an exchange' threatens to occupy it.

PRACTICAL POSITION FOR THIS SYSTEM: use the modern conditions for RECOGNITION, because they are what most readers will mean, but never assert an outpost without checking the exchangeability condition, and prefer the more specific wording ('a knight that cannot be driven away') over the contested label where the two would differ.

attributions.note: The underlying idea, via the 'hole': 'not alone the weakness on one single pawn but also that of one single square into which any hostile man can be planted with commanding effect'. Steinitz did not use the word outpost.
Coined 'outpost' (Vorposten) and gave the file-dependent definition quoted above.
Reference-work definition that relaxes the file requirement; the origin of much modern usage.
The 'eternal knight' condition: exploitability requires the occupant be neither dislodgeable nor exchangeable.

history.notes: Origin of the TERM is secure (Nimzowitsch, 1925). Origin of the IDEA is Steinitz's hole, 1886. What is disputed is not who coined it but what it means: the file condition was part of the original definition and has been dropped by most later usage. Bedouin notes the root cause — 'the problem goes back to Nimzowitsch himself. In My System he suggests various examples, but he doesn't give clear definitions.'
competing_claims: Nimzowitsch 1925: requires an open or half-open file behind the square.
Hooper & Whyld 1992: file is 'especially' relevant but not required.
Modern usage / engine evaluation terms: file dropped entirely.
Dorfman (The Method in Chess): a square on a half-open file in front of an enemy pawn, on the 6th rank.
Bedouin: 'outpost' should be reserved for semi-open files, with other cases renamed.

development.change: The idea, as the 'hole' — a square into which a hostile man can be planted with commanding effect.
Named, and tied to open-file play and provocation of a weakening pawn move.
File requirement relaxed in the standard reference work.
Reduced to a static evaluation term: pawn-protected, pawn-unattackable advanced square. Provocation aspect lost.

outpost.engine_era_note: Engines carry an outpost term in their evaluation, so the feature is real and worth points. What engine testing does NOT support is treating it as decisive. In the Chess Programming Wiki's own illustrative position for 'the mighty outpost Nd5', Stockfish 18 at depth 28 prefers Nb5 (+0.52) over Nd5 (+0.30). The outpost move is sound and second-best, not the point of the position. Any explanation that presents occupying an outpost as automatically the strongest move is overstating it.

preconditions: A square on the 4th rank or beyond, counted from the occupying side
No enemy pawn can ever attack the square — the pawns on both adjoining files have advanced past it, been exchanged, or do not exist
The square is defended by a friendly pawn (usual, and required by Nimzowitsch and Hooper & Whyld, but relaxed in some modern usage)
indicators_for: The occupant cannot be exchanged for a piece of equal value — Romanovsky's condition, and the one that most often decides whether the outpost matters
The defender's remaining bishop is of the wrong colour to challenge the square
The square is central (c/d/e/f files) and the occupant is a knight, whose short range benefits most
An open or half-open file leads to the square — required by Nimzowitsch, and the mechanism by which driving the knight away costs the defender a pawn weakness
The square sits in front of a backward or isolated enemy pawn
From the square the piece attacks something concrete or denies the enemy king and rooks key squares
indicators_against: An enemy pawn can still advance to challenge the square, and doing so costs the defender nothing
The occupant can be traded off by a knight or a same-coloured bishop with no compensation
The square is on the a/b/g/h files and the intended occupant is a knight — Nimzowitsch assigns flank outposts to rooks
The piece on the square attacks nothing and restricts nothing; it is safe but idle
Occupying costs a tempo the position cannot spare, or walks into a concrete tactic
false_positive_traps: A knight on d5 is not an outpost merely because it is on d5. If ...c6 or ...e6 is available, the knight is visiting.
A pawn-protected advanced square whose occupant can simply be exchanged is not an outpost in any useful sense — Romanovsky's condition fails.
A safe square that the piece does nothing from. Safety is a precondition, not the benefit.
In the engine test above, the archetypal 'outpost' move was second-best. Being a genuine outpost does not make occupying it the best move.

A centralised advanced knight is not an outpost. If an enemy pawn can still challenge the square, the piece is visiting. The detector in lib/features.js checks this and correctly refuses in the recorded counterexample.

typical_plans: Route a knight to the square by a path the defender cannot contest
Exchange the defender that could challenge the square, especially a same-coloured bishop
Occupy with a knight, then use the square as a base for a further attack — Nimzowitsch's point (a)
Invite the pawn advance that drives the knight away, because that advance is itself a concession — Nimzowitsch's point (b)
On a flank file, occupy with a rook rather than a knight
typical_moves: Nd5 / Nc5 / Ne5 and their mirrors, supported by a pawn
typical_pawn_structures: In front of a backward d-pawn on a half-open d-file
Isolated queen's pawn structures, where the squares beside the isolani are the natural outposts
After a fianchettoed bishop has been exchanged, on the resulting colour complex
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight on the square, pawn supporting it, rook behind on the same file
tactical_consequences: An unchallengeable knight near the king supports mating ideas and forks from a permanent base
strategic_consequences: Silman's estimate, reported by Chess.com: an established knight on the sixth rank is worth about a rook
The square denies the defender's own pieces access, shrinking their available squares
The advantage is durable because pawns cannot move backwards to repair it

exceptions: An outpost that can be neutralised by an equal exchange confers little. Check what can capture the occupant before naming it.
Occupying is not obligatory. The THREAT of occupying can bind the defender while the piece does something else.
Nimzowitsch's own counter-illustration: with the file behind it closed, the point largely goes. He asks the reader to imagine an extra white pawn on d3 — 'the capital would have run out'.
A flank outpost suits a rook, not a knight, because the rook exerts pressure along the whole rank.
A bishop on an outpost defends its own supporting pawn, so it cannot be undermined the way a knight can — a genuine asymmetry between the pieces.
limitations: The definition is contested; there is no authoritative wording to appeal to.

Not reliably engine-testable. Three separate controlled-pair designs failed to isolate the variable, because no pawn can be moved without altering several structural facts at once. See METHODOLOGY.md.
Recognition is heuristic. Detecting 'no enemy pawn can attack this square' is mechanical; deciding that the square MATTERS is not.

Safety is a precondition, not the benefit' - is now built, and it almost never binds: it refuses 1 of the 122 positions on the shipped corpus where the rest of the definition is satisfied. That is not a failure of the guard but a fact about the geometry - the outpost zone is the enemy's half, and a knight standing in it bears on something almost by construction. The shape it does catch is a bishop walled in by its own pawns. Rate 15.5% -> 15.4%, and saying it moved would overstate it.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'in the engine test above, the archetypal outpost move was second-best. Being a genuine outpost does not make occupying it the best move' is a claim about MOVES, and this matcher never recommends one. It reports that a piece already standing on such a square cannot be driven off and bears on the position behind it. Nothing in this base suggests playing a piece to an outpost.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the second indicator_against - 'the square is on the a/b/g/h files and the intended occupant is a knight; Nimzowitsch assigns flank outposts to rooks' - had been built only for the a- and h-files, and only because Capablanca-Tartakower 1924 forced it. Widened to b and g for knights: 15.4% -> 11.9% of the 788 shipped positions, leading 30 times instead of 43. That is more than it looks - a pawn-defended knight on b5 or g5 in the enemy half is not rare in a corpus of tactical puzzles, and every one was being called an outpost by a base whose own record assigns the square to a rook. The remaining two indicators are about tempo and about a trade with no compensation, both judgements.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first indicator_against - 'the occupant can be TRADED OFF by a knight or a same-coloured bishop with no compensation' - is now said rather than used to suppress. The square survives the trade and the piece does not, and the difference is worth a clause: the outpost is held on loan until the swap happens. A bishop of the opposite colour to the square does not count, which is what makes the condition worth testing rather than approximating.
misconceptions: That any advanced knight protected by a pawn is on an outpost.
That an outpost is automatically the best move available — the engine test above shows otherwise.
That outposts are only for knights. Bishops and rooks use them too, and Nimzowitsch specifically assigns flank outposts to rooks.
That the pawn protection is what makes it strong. Nimzowitsch says the strength comes from the file AND the pawn together; the modern reading keeps the pawn and forgets the file.

by_level.beginner: No pawn can ever attack this square, so a piece put there cannot be chased away. A knight is usually the best piece for the job.
by_level.intermediate: An outpost on {square}: protected by {pawn}, and no enemy pawn can reach it. Worth having here because {reason} — but check first whether the knight can simply be traded off.
by_level.advanced: Outpost in the modern sense. Nimzowitsch additionally required the half-open file behind it, both as support and because driving the knight off costs the defender a pawn weakness. Romanovsky's condition applies: it counts only if the occupant can be neither dislodged nor exchanged.
by_level.master: Note which sense is meant. If the file is closed this is a protected strong square rather than an outpost in Nimzowitsch's sense, and the provocation mechanism is absent. Evaluate exchangeability, what the piece actually does from the square, and whether the tempo spent getting there is affordable.

by_depth.short: No enemy pawn can ever attack {square}, so the knight there is permanent.
by_depth.normal: {square} is an outpost: your pawn defends it and no enemy pawn can attack it, so a knight there cannot be driven away. It matters here because it cannot be exchanged either, and from there it {does what}.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch coined 'outpost' in 1925 for a protected piece, usually a knight, on an OPEN FILE in enemy territory — the file being as load-bearing as the pawn, since driving the knight off with a pawn damages the file the attacker is working on. Later usage, following Hooper and Whyld, dropped the file requirement, and engine evaluation terms use the broad static sense. Whichever definition is used, Romanovsky's test decides whether it matters: the square is a real weakness only if a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged can occupy it. Engine testing supports the feature but not its primacy — in the standard illustrative position, the outpost move is only second-best.

explanations.lesson: Before calling a square an outpost, ask two questions: can a pawn ever attack it, and can the piece standing there be exchanged? If the answer to either is yes, it is just a square.

beginner_words: a square they can never attack with a pawn
a permanent home for your knight
avoid: always put a knight on an outpost
the knight is centralised, therefore an outpost

overloading.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Its relationship to the strategic principle of two weaknesses is a genuine structural link, not an analogy of convenience.
overloading.definition_short: A piece with two defensive jobs cannot do both; take one and the other collapses.
overloading.definition_long:
A single unit is the only defender of two things. The tactic exploits the fact that answering one threat abandons the other. It is listed as a category in the Encyclopedia of Chess Middlegames.

Overloading is the tactical form of the same logic that the PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES applies strategically: finite defensive resources stretched across more duties than they can cover. The difference is timescale — overloading resolves in a move or two, two weaknesses over dozens.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: One enemy unit is the sole defender of two distinct targets or duties
indicators_for: Removing or diverting that unit leaves both targets loose
The two duties require the piece to be on different squares
indicators_against: A second defender covers one of the duties
The piece can perform both duties from one square
Capturing the overloaded piece is answered by a recapture that restores the defence

exceptions: A defender that appears overloaded may be adequate if one 'duty' was never real.
limitations: Depends on enumerating duties, which is a functional judgement.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET. This concept has no matcher, so the scan that supplied master positions to eleven other records - five famous games replayed and analysed position by position - could not nominate one here: the API never reports the concept, so there is nothing for a scan to find. Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled.

examples.note: Adams-Torre, New Orleans 1920, 19.Qc4 - the first of five consecutive queen offers, none of which can be accepted. The state that makes them work is an overload: Black's queen is the only thing defending the rook on e8, and the rook on e8 is the only thing stopping Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8 mate. Every time White attacks the queen, the queen must both move and keep guarding e8, and it cannot do both. That is this record's definition exactly - one piece with two jobs - and it is why the game is the standard illustration. The engine's own line IS the game: Qc4 Qd7 Qc7 Qb5 a4 Qxa4 Re4. This base reports nothing about overloading here, correctly, because the concept has no matcher: whether a piece is asked to do both AT ONCE is a property of what the attacker can arrange rather than of the board. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator - 45 plies, every one legal. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

engine.verdict_note: +4.27 for the queen offer against +0.16 for a quiet move at depth 22 with two lines - four pawns of difference, and the engine's principal variation is the game continuation move for move. The overload is worth the whole advantage.

examples.note: Constructed. The rook on d8 has two jobs: it defends the knight on d5 down the file, and it is the only guard of the back rank. Rxd5 asks it to do both at once - if it recaptures it leaves e8, and Re8 is mate. The engine's own line is the demonstration: after Rxd5 it plays ...Rb8 rather than ...Rxd5, which is to say Black DECLINES the recapture and simply loses a knight. That is what overloading means, and it is why this base refuses to detect the motif mechanically: the geometry here is a rook on a file, and what makes it overloading is a mate on a different file that has not happened yet.

engine.verdict_note: +6.73 at depth 22, settled at depth 14, and the engine plays Rxd5. The size is the evidence: a knight plus the refused recapture, in a position where material was level before the move.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `two-defenders-for-two-duties`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A black rook on d8 defends the knight on d5 down the file, the black king is boxed in on the back rank, and White has rooks on d1 and e1. Every piece of the overloading picture is on the board, and it is this record's positive example with one man added. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The one man added is a second black rook, on e8. Overloading is a claim that ONE piece is asked to do two jobs at once; here there are two pieces and two jobs. After Rxd5 Rxd5, the rook on e8 still guards the back rank and there is no mate. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report overloading. Stockfish 18 says -4.30 at depth 22 and its first move is Rxe8+, trading into a position where Black is a knight up — so Rxd5, the move that works in the positive example, is simply a blunder here. Read against this record's positive at +6.73: one rook added to the defence and the same move goes from winning a knight to losing one. This record has no matcher, and the reason is on the record — an overload is a claim about being asked to do both at once, which is a property of what the attacker can arrange rather than of what is on the board.

ambiguous_examples.note: The overload configuration exactly: the rook on d8 defends the knight on d5 down the file AND is the only guard of the back rank, and White's rook is on d1 facing it. It does not work, because White has only one rook - Rxd5 is met by Rxd5 and the back-rank threat never arrives, so the black rook is asked to do one job at a time and can. The position is -0.01. Read against this record's positive example, which is the same picture with a SECOND white rook on e1: one piece added, and the rook on d8 goes from comfortable to unable to recapture. Filed as ambiguous because the configuration the concept names is fully present and the concept is not: an overload is a claim about being asked to do both at once, and nobody is asking.

by_level.beginner: That piece is guarding two things at once. Take one and it cannot keep guarding the other.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} is overloaded — it is the only defender of both {a} and {b}.
by_level.advanced: Overloading. The tactical counterpart of the principle of two weaknesses: the same finite-defence logic on a shorter timescale.

by_depth.short: A piece with two jobs cannot do both.
by_depth.normal: Overloading: one defender is holding two things at once. Attack either and it must choose — take one, and the other collapses. The claim is about a single piece being asked to do both, not about two pieces each doing one.
by_depth.deep: The distinction that decides it is a count. A back rank guarded by two rooks is not an overload; the same rank guarded by one is. This base's positive and its false-positive case differ by exactly one added rook, and the same move goes from winning a knight to losing one. Overloading and deflection are the same fact seen twice — the overload is the state, the deflection is the move that exploits it — which is why a spare defender destroys both. There is no matcher for it, because whether a piece is asked to do both AT ONCE is a property of what the attacker can arrange rather than of the board.

overprotection.knowledge_type_note: Typed historical-teaching-principle rather than strategic-principle deliberately: it is Nimzowitsch's own named innovation, it is taught as his, and it is the one idea of his that later practice has been most sceptical about. Mandatory hedging applies.

attributions.note: Verified against the primary text, where he describes it as 'my innovation of overprotection'.

history.notes: Directly self-attributed in the primary text, which has been read.

development.change: Introduced as a named innovation and given its own chapter.
Retained as vocabulary but treated with scepticism in practice; the least-adopted of his ideas.

overprotection.engine_era_note: The Nimzowitsch idea engines least support. They will defend a point as many times as a concrete line requires and no more, and they consistently prefer activity to redundant defence. Overprotection as a general policy does not survive; the underlying observation — that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed — does.

preconditions: A strategically important point is defended more times than it is attacked
indicators_for: The point is central and both sides want it
The overprotecting pieces are well placed for other reasons too
A blockading piece needs support from behind
indicators_against: The extra defenders have nothing else to do from those squares
The point is not under any real pressure
The tempo could be spent on something concrete
false_positive_traps: Counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing. Overprotection is a CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile, and that claim is often false.
This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well.

typical_plans: Support a blockading piece from behind
Contest a key central square with more force than the opponent
typical_piece_arrangements: Several pieces bearing on one central square
tactical_consequences: Wins the exchange sequence when the point is finally contested
strategic_consequences: Pieces in contact with a strong point are ready when lines open

exceptions: Defending an unattacked point is usually a waste of time, and modern practice says so.
Engines defend exactly as much as a line requires.
limitations: The weakest-supported concept in the Nimzowitsch cluster, and the record says so rather than presenting it at face value.
misconceptions: That overprotection is generally good practice. It is a named historical idea with limited modern support.
That more defenders is safer. Beyond what a concrete line needs, extra defenders are usually idle pieces.

examples.note: The position after 14.Nf3, annotated by Nimzowitsch himself: 'The blockading forces are to be reinforced by the knight.' This is overprotection as its author practised it — the e5 point is already held, and he adds a defender to it anyway, because the pieces that guard a strategically important square draw their own scope from doing so. Recorded here because a concept should where possible be illustrated by the player who formulated it, annotating his own move. The number matters more than its sign: overprotection is a claim about durability rather than about advantage, and a record whose only example evaluated in its favour would be evidence for the wrong proposition. What is established is that the position is playable and roughly balanced with the arrangement in place.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The pawn on d5 is defended by the bishop on e4 and the queen on d3 with a rook behind her — three units aimed at one square, which is Nimzowitsch's picture of an overprotected strong point. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second trap: "This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well." And its second indicator_against: "The point is not under any real pressure." Nothing attacks d5 at all. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports battery, center-control and passed-pawn here and does not report overprotection. That is the right set: the geometry really is a battery, the pawn really is passed, and the CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile is the one thing nobody can read off the board. This record's first trap says so in as many words — 'counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing' — and it is why there is no matcher.

Overprotection is a CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile, and that claim is often false', and its second says not to report it 'unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well'. Two of the three defenders here are on good squares anyway and one is behind the other. The engine says 0.00.
