by_level.beginner: Defending an important square more times than you strictly need to, so your pieces are ready when the fight for it comes.
by_level.intermediate: Overprotection — Nimzowitsch's idea that piling defenders on a key point is worthwhile. Treat it with care: extra defenders that do nothing else are slow moves.
by_level.advanced: His own named innovation, and the one that has aged least well. The defensible core is that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed anyway.
by_level.master: Recorded as historical teaching. Engines defend to the requirement of the line and no further.

by_depth.short: Defend a key square more times than needed.
by_depth.normal: Overprotection: Nimzowitsch's idea that defending an important point beyond necessity is worthwhile, because the defenders are well placed by their contact with a strong square and ready when it is contested.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch calls it 'my innovation' and gives it a chapter. He links it to the blockade — a blockading piece needs support from the rear — and to exchanges, since a point both sides want becomes the site of a mass liquidation the better-supported side wins. It is also the idea of his that wears worst: piling defenders onto an unattacked square looks like passivity and often is, and engines defend only as much as a concrete line requires. What survives is the narrower observation that pieces bearing on a strong central square tend to be well placed for other reasons too.

explanations.hedge: A historical teaching principle and the least-supported of Nimzowitsch's ideas. Modern practice is sceptical, and engines defend a point only as many times as a concrete line requires. Do not present it as general good practice.
explanations.lesson: The idea to keep is narrower than the name: pieces aimed at a strong central square are often well placed anyway. Defending an unattacked square for its own sake is a slow move.

beginner_words: defend it more than you need to

overprotection.definition_short: Defending a strategically important square or point with more pieces than are needed, so that those pieces draw strength from it.
overprotection.definition_long:
Nimzowitsch calls it 'my innovation' in My System, and it is the most contested of his ideas. The claim is that piling defenders onto a key point — typically a central square — is not wasted effort, because the overprotecting pieces are themselves well placed by virtue of their contact with a strong square, and are ready when the position opens.

He ties it directly to the blockade: 'The effectiveness of the blockade is increased by links to the rear (overprotection needed!)'. And to exchanges — a strong point both sides want becomes the site of what he calls a 'great blood-letting', so the side with more defenders wins the exchange sequence.

IT IS THE IDEA OF HIS THAT WEARS WORST. Piling pieces on a square that is not under attack looks, and often is, like passivity, and modern practice is much readier to call it a waste of time. It is recorded here as a historical teaching principle rather than a live technique, with the hedge that a system that recommends overprotection without a concrete reason is recommending slow moves.

passed-pawn.knowledge_type_note: A board feature, defined mechanically. That it is an ADVANTAGE is a separate judgement, and one that is wrong often enough to be worth separating.

attributions.note: The blockade doctrine and the much-quoted 'A passed pawn is a criminal which should be kept under lock and key. Mild measures, such as police surveillance, are not sufficient.' Widely attributed and cited by Wikipedia; the passage has NOT been located in the primary text during this research, so the quotation is recorded as attributed rather than verified.

The rule that rooks belong behind passed pawns is CONVENTIONALLY Tarrasch's. ATTRIBUTION DISPUTED: a second source consulted attributes it instead to TARTAKOWER. Neither was checked against a primary text. Do not state either as fact.

history.notes: Passed pawns are as old as chess and nobody coined the term. Both attached rules of thumb are attributed to Nimzowitsch and Tarrasch respectively by convention. Neither attribution has been checked against a primary text in this research, and the 'criminal' quotation in particular is exactly the kind of famous line the brief warns about. Confidence low, deliberately.
competing_claims: 'Rooks belong behind passed pawns' attributed to Siegbert Tarrasch (conventional).
The same rule attributed to Savielly Tartakower by another source. Unresolved.

development.change: The blockade is systematised: a passer must be stopped by a piece, and which piece matters.
Engines weigh passers by rank and by whether they are blockaded, and are markedly less impressed by a passer that ties down its own side.

passed-pawn.engine_era_note: Engines value passers strongly and by rank, but they are also the clearest demonstration of the exception: a securely blockaded passer often evaluates as no advantage at all. The engine does not share the human bias towards being impressed by one.

preconditions: No enemy pawn ahead on the pawn's own file
No enemy pawn ahead on either adjacent file
indicators_for: It is advanced — the further, the more it is worth
It is protected by a friendly pawn, or escorted by the king
It is outside, far from the other pawns, so it deflects the enemy king
It has a connected partner and the two can advance in tandem
The blockading square cannot be safely occupied by an enemy piece
indicators_against: It is securely blockaded by a piece that cannot be dislodged, especially a knight
Defending it ties down more of the owner's pieces than of the opponent's
It stands on a square where it is easily attacked
It was created by a pawn trade that also fixed it as a target
The position has no second front, so the blockader is never distracted
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a passed pawn is not automatically an advantage. A permanently blockaded passer that must be defended is a liability, and the blockading square is an excellent one for the defender.
Detecting a passer is trivial and fires constantly in endgames. Reporting one is only informative alongside whether it can actually advance.
A passer created from doubled pawns is often born weak.

typical_plans: Mobilise a healthy majority; the candidate pawn — the one with no direct opponent — leads
Escort it with the king in simplified positions
Put the rook behind it
Use it to deflect the enemy king while operating on the other wing
As the defender: blockade with a knight, and if possible make the blockade permanent
typical_moves: The breakthrough b6! in the classic trio structure
typical_pawn_structures: A healthy 3-vs-2 majority, which produces a passer almost by force
Outside passer against a symmetric kingside — the two-weaknesses mechanism
typical_piece_arrangements: Knight blockading on the square in front
Rook behind the pawn
tactical_consequences: The threat of promotion forces pieces into passive defence and creates deflection tactics
strategic_consequences: Often the single most important asset in an endgame
An outside passer wins by deflection rather than by promoting

exceptions: A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.
A passer pushed too early becomes a fixed target.
A passer created from doubled pawns is frequently weak from birth.
Even a blockaded passer retains value if there is a second front the blockader can be pulled towards — which is the principle of two weaknesses doing the work.

PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
limitations: The definition is mechanical and reliable; the evaluation is not.
Both attached rules of thumb (blockade, rook behind) are heuristics with well-known exceptions.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: three of this record's five indicators_against are judgements no static scan reaches - 'defending it ties down more of the owner's pieces than of the opponent's', 'it was created by a pawn trade that also fixed it as a target', and 'the position has no second front, so the blockader is never distracted'. The other two are built. 'Securely blockaded by a piece that cannot be dislodged' has been enforced since the Reshevsky-Petrosian correction: a passer with an enemy piece directly in front of it is not reported at all. 'It stands on a square where it is easily attacked' is now carried in the SENTENCE rather than used to suppress - a passer attacked more times than it is defended is named as a target rather than an asset, which is what the whole record is about. The firing rate is unchanged at 60.4%, and it would be the wrong claim to make about this change.
misconceptions: That a passed pawn is always an advantage.
That the aim is to promote it. Often the aim is to make the opponent spend pieces stopping it.
That any piece will do as a blockader. A knight loses nothing standing there; a queen loses almost everything.
That 'rook behind the passed pawn' is always right. It is a heuristic with a proven counterexample — see vancura-position.

conflicts.resolution: Not opposed but complementary, and the interaction is the interesting part: a blockaded passer is worthless alone but decisive when a second front exists, because the blockader cannot be in two places. The tablebase-proven pair in the two-weaknesses record is exactly an outside passer plus a second target.

Tarrasch's rule is a good default and a proven mistake in one specific configuration. Where the pawn is a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook already in front, the Vancura side-attack draws and the rule loses. Prefer the specific proven result over the general heuristic whenever the configuration matches.

by_level.beginner: No enemy pawn can stop that pawn — only their pieces can. If it gets far enough, they have to give up a piece for it.
by_level.intermediate: A passed pawn on {square}. What matters is whether it can advance: a passer that is permanently blockaded ties down your pieces rather than theirs.
by_level.advanced: Passer on {square}, {protected / outside / connected}. Blockade with a knight if defending; if attacking, ask whether the blockader can be distracted by a second front.
by_level.master: Value scales with rank and with whether the blockade is permanent. The decisive question is which side's pieces are tied down by it.

by_depth.short: Nothing can stop {square} except a piece.
by_depth.normal: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
by_depth.deep: Defined by three conditions: no enemy pawn ahead on its own file or either adjacent file. Adjacent files count because pawns capture diagonally. Value rises steeply with rank, and the named variants matter — protected, connected, outside. Nimzowitsch's blockade doctrine attaches: stop it with a piece, and prefer a knight, which loses none of its powers standing guard, over a queen, which loses almost all of hers. Tarrasch's rule attaches too: rooks belong behind passed pawns. Both are heuristics with real exceptions. The most important is that a securely blockaded passer achieves nothing while its owner defends it — unless a second front exists to pull the blockader away, which is where this concept and the principle of two weaknesses meet.

explanations.lesson: A passed pawn is only as good as its ability to move. Before counting it as an advantage, ask who is tied down by it.

passed-pawn.definition_short: A pawn with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own file or on either adjacent file, so only pieces can stop it.
passed-pawn.definition_long:
Three conditions, all necessary: no enemy pawn ahead on its own file, and none ahead on either adjacent file. Enemy pawns BEHIND it are irrelevant. The adjacent files matter because pawns capture diagonally — a pawn on an adjacent file ahead of the passer can always trade itself for it eventually.

Value scales sharply with advancement: a passer on the third rank is a long-term asset, one on the seventh is a crisis the opponent must solve now. Variants worth naming: a PROTECTED passed pawn is defended by a friendly pawn; CONNECTED passed pawns on adjacent files are very strong, and are best advanced in tandem on the same rank so they cannot be blockaded singly; an OUTSIDE passed pawn is separated by several files from the rest and wins by deflecting the enemy king — which is the mechanism behind the two-weaknesses controlled pair in this base.

Two standing rules of thumb attach to it. Nimzowitsch: every passed pawn must be blockaded, and the blockader should be a piece that keeps its powers while standing guard — the knight is the best, the queen the worst. Tarrasch: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, yours to push it and the enemy's to attack it.

THE IMPORTANT EXCEPTION. A passed pawn is not automatically good. A firmly blockaded passer that requires constant defence is a liability: you are guarding a pawn that generates no threats, while the blockading piece stands on an excellent square. The operative test is whether it ties down THEIR pieces or YOURS.

pawn-break.knowledge_type_note: A method rather than a tactic; it is kept separate from pawn-breakthrough, which is the sacrificial motif for forcing a passer.

history.notes: Standard vocabulary; no coinage traced.

pawn-break.engine_era_note: Engines time breaks far better than humans and are notably readier to delay one; the timing question the concept is about is exactly where they are strongest.

preconditions: A pawn advances into contact with an enemy pawn
indicators_for: Pieces already placed on the lines the break will open
The opponent must answer, committing their structure
A file or diagonal opens towards a target
indicators_against: The opponent is better developed and will use the opened lines first
The break opens a line towards your own king
Nothing of yours is placed to use what opens
recognition.detector: a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn, from lib/features.js and the move generator
false_positive_traps: Any pawn advance into contact is mechanically a break; whether it is a good one depends on who is placed to use the lines it opens, which the detector cannot see.
A break is not a pawn-breakthrough. This base keeps them separate: the breakthrough sacrifices to force a passer, the break challenges a structure.
The break's value is often as an unplayed THREAT, and a position where it is available but not played may be the concept working correctly.

typical_plans: Place the pieces on the lines the break will open, then break
Break to force the opponent's structure to commit
Hold the break in reserve as a standing threat
typical_moves: c4-c5 and d4-d5 in queen's pawn structures
f4-f5 and e4-e5 against a king's position
...c5 and ...f5 as the standard freeing breaks for Black
typical_pawn_structures: Any fixed structure — the break is how a fixed structure stops being fixed
typical_piece_arrangements: Rooks behind the pawn that is about to advance
tactical_consequences: The moment of the break is usually the sharpest moment of the game
strategic_consequences: Whoever chooses the moment of the break usually chooses the resulting structure

exceptions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.
limitations: Detecting a pawn advancing into contact is mechanical; judging whether it is right is not, and this record does not claim the detector does.
This base holds one master-game example and no counterexample of a break played too early.
misconceptions: That a break wins material. It changes the structure and opens lines; material is a separate question.
That you should break as soon as it is available. The threat is often worth more than the execution.
That a break and a breakthrough are the same thing.

conflicts.resolution: Opposite methods against a structure and both correct at different moments: restraint keeps the opponent's pawns where they are, a break forces them to move. The question is which side benefits from the structure changing, and the answer is usually whoever is better placed for the lines that open.

by_level.beginner: A pawn move that runs into an enemy pawn, so the structure has to change and lines open up.
by_level.intermediate: A pawn break. Get your pieces onto the lines it will open BEFORE you play it.
by_level.advanced: It is often played to make the OPPONENT commit rather than to gain anything directly.
by_level.master: The break's value is frequently as an unplayed threat; timing it is the whole skill.

by_depth.short: A pawn advance that forces the structure to change.
by_depth.normal: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
by_depth.deep: Pawn structures are stable because pawns cannot retreat, so a structure changes only when a pawn advances into contact — and whoever chooses when that happens usually chooses the terms. The break opens lines for both sides, so it favours whoever is better placed to use them, which is why breaking against a better-developed opponent is the standard misapplication. Its other and less obvious use is to force the opponent to commit: Fischer's 20.e4 against Spassky in 1972 was played not to gain material but to make one of two hanging pawns advance, so that the square it left could be occupied.

explanations.lesson: Put the pieces where the lines will open before you open them.

beginner_words: a pawn move that opens things up

pawn-break.definition_short: A pawn advance that challenges an enemy pawn, forcing the structure to change and opening lines the pieces behind it want.
pawn-break.definition_long:
The move that turns a static position into a decided one. Pawn structures are stable because pawns cannot retreat, so a structure only changes when a pawn advances into contact — and whoever chooses WHEN that happens usually chooses the terms.

IT IS NOT PLAYED TO WIN A PAWN. A break is played to open a file for the rooks, a diagonal for a bishop, or a square for a knight; or, in its other and less obvious use, to force the OPPONENT to commit — Fischer's 20.e4 against Spassky in 1972 is the model, played not to gain material but to make one of two hanging pawns advance so that the square it left could be occupied.

THE PIECES COME FIRST. A break opens lines for both sides, so it favours whoever is better placed to use them. Breaking while the opponent is better developed opens the position for them, which is the standard way the idea is misapplied.

TIMING IS THE WHOLE SKILL. The break exists as a threat before it is played, and the threat is often worth more than the execution — the opponent must keep guarding against it, which is a restraint on their own plans.

DISTINGUISH IT FROM A BREAKTHROUGH. A pawn BREAK challenges a structure and usually costs nothing; a pawn BREAKTHROUGH sacrifices material to force a passer past the defenders. This base keeps them as separate records because the second is a tactic with a calculation attached and the first is a strategic decision.

pawn-breakthrough.knowledge_type_note: A tactical motif rather than a strategic principle: it is a concrete forcing sequence whose correctness is settled by calculation, not judgement. It happens to occur in pawn structures, which is why it is often taught as strategy.

history.notes: The pattern is old and anonymous; it appears in endgame manuals long before any of the sources consulted here. No coiner is claimed and none was found.

pawn-breakthrough.engine_era_note: Wholly concrete, so engines settle it exactly. Nothing about the concept has been revised; what engines add is that the boundary conditions — how advanced the pawns must be, how far the king may stand — can now be checked in seconds rather than analysed.

preconditions: Opposing pawn groups face each other with no passer for either side
The attacker has at least as many pawns in the group and they are advanced
A pawn advance creates two levers simultaneously
indicators_for: A trio against a trio, the attacker's one rank further on
The defending king is outside the square of the prospective passer
The attacker has a space advantage in that pawn group
Whichever way the defender captures, a different pawn gets through
indicators_against: The defending king is close enough to catch the runner — check the rule of the square first
The attacking pawns are too far back; the same structure one rank earlier usually fails outright
The defender can decline the capture and hold
The attacker's own king is needed elsewhere and cannot support
false_positive_traps: A pawn sacrifice that creates a passer is not a breakthrough unless the passer actually cannot be stopped. The rule of the square decides this and is cheap to check.
The pattern is highly recognisable and therefore easy to play on autopilot in a position that is one rank short of it working.

typical_plans: Push the middle pawn to create two levers, then sacrifice again to deflect, then run
Combine with an outside passer to stretch the defending king
Prophylactically: prevent the lever structure from arising at all
typical_moves: b6! in the a5-b5-c5 against a7-b7-c7 structure
g6! and h6! and f6! in the kingside mirror (f5-g5-h5 against f7-g7-h7)
typical_pawn_structures: Trio against trio, one rank apart
Blocked majorities in king-and-pawn endings
typical_piece_arrangements: Typically none — this is usually a pure pawn ending
tactical_consequences: Produces an unstoppable passer by force
strategic_consequences: Makes a space advantage in a pawn group concrete
Turns apparently blocked and drawn endings into wins

exceptions: Fails outright without enough space. Moving the whole structure one rank back is the standard demonstration.
Fails if the defending king is inside the square of the resulting passer.
The defender can sometimes decline the first capture and hold.
limitations: Entirely concrete. It should be verified by calculation every time, not recognised and trusted.

SCOPE, stated rather than hidden: the detector runs only when nothing but kings and pawns is left, because the rule of the square - which the record's own false-positive trap names as the thing that decides - is a proof there and a guess anywhere else. In a middlegame the same pattern may be a breakthrough and this base cannot show that it is, so it says nothing.

It proves that ACCEPTING the offer loses. A defender who declines is answering a different question, and the matcher's wording says so. Over the 788 shipped puzzle positions it fires zero times, which is correct - none of them is a pawn ending - and means the 788 provide no evidence about its false-positive rate.

MEASURED 2026-09-01, and the number is the point. The shipped puzzle generator tags 86 of the 788 positions `pawnBreakthrough`; ZERO of those 86 is a pawn ending, and this base confirms a forced breakthrough in none of them. The two are not measuring the same thing and neither is wrong. The generator's test (tools/puzzle_rules.js) is: the first move is a non-capturing pawn move and after it the destination is winnable by static exchange evaluation OR the pawn is passed - a puzzle classification, which does not ask whether the passer can be stopped. That question is this concept's own registered false-positive trap. The consequence for a later session is that the 788 positions provide no evidence at all about this detector's false-positive rate, and a corpus of pawn endings would have to be built to get any.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, and it is the first measurement this detector has ever had. None of the 788 shipped positions is a pawn ending, so pawn-breakthrough fired on none of them and its 0.0% rate said nothing about its accuracy. tools/pawn_endings.js generates pawn endings through the page's own move generator; tools/verify_breakthrough.py checks each claim against Syzygy, where a pawn ending of seven men or fewer is DECIDED rather than estimated. The claim being checked is the narrow one the matcher makes - accepting the offer loses - so the position tested is the one after the offer and after a pawn capture of it. RESULT: 22 of 24 tablebase-decidable claims proved, 2 disproved. The detector fires on 6.1% of random pawn endings, so the old note that its 0.0% on the shipped corpus was 'scope, not rarity' is confirmed. TWO REAL BUGS were found and fixed. (1) A breakthrough is a move and cannot be played out of turn: pawnBreakthrough() read the moves of whoever was to move, so when features() asked it for the other side - which it does for both sides, every time - it claimed the OPPONENT'S pawn moves as the offer. (2) One king cannot be in two places: the rule of the square was applied to each enemy passer in turn, which quietly assumed one king could catch all of them. WHAT IS NOT A BUG, and is now recorded rather than claimed away: the rule of the square is NOT a proof in a multi-pawn ending. Promoting one move before the defender is not winning - Syzygy calls 8/8/2K4P/1p6/4p3/8/k4P2/8 w a draw after 1.f3 exf3 2.h7 f2 3.h8=Q f1=Q - so the enemy passer must be two tempi slower, not one; and a pawn that is not PASSED can still queen after an exchange, which is what the two remaining failures are. The matcher reports at MEDIUM and its sentence says 'an indication rather than a proof'. It used to say high, on the grounds that the rule of the square is a proof.
misconceptions: That the breakthrough always works in a trio-against-trio structure. Space and king distance decide it.
That it is a strategic idea. It is a forcing tactical sequence that happens to be made of pawns.

counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. IDENTICAL material and identical structure — three pawns against three, kings on the same squares — with White's trio moved one rank back to a4-b4-c4. This isolates the space-advantage condition and nothing else, and it tests pawnbreak.com's testable claim that 'move all pawns one row and the breakthrough does not work at all anymore'.

engine.verdict_note: The claim is confirmed exactly and the margin is enormous. The analogous breakthrough 1.b5 evaluates -5.86 and is NOT best; the quiet 1.a5 at -0.46 is. So the same pattern, with the pawns one rank further back, swings from +64.85 (winning by force) to -5.86 (losing) — a difference of over 70 pawns produced by one rank of space, with material and structure held identical. This is the cleanest confirmation in the base that a positional-sounding precondition can be exactly decisive, and it is why the concept is typed tactical-motif: it must be calculated, never recognised.

The tablebase's own first move is NOT the breakthrough: it is Ka2, a king move, because with the black king on d7 the pawn sacrifice lets the king in and the slow method does not. Filed as ambiguous because the concept is correctly present and correctly reported and is not what wins: the same structure with the defending king further away IS won by the breakthrough, and this record's positive example is that position. The two differ by where one king stands, which is the condition this record states as 'the attacker's own king is needed elsewhere and cannot support'.

by_level.beginner: White gives away two pawns so the third one can run all the way to the end, and the king is too far away to catch it.
by_level.intermediate: A breakthrough. The middle pawn goes first because it attacks two ways at once, so whichever way Black captures, a different pawn gets through.
by_level.advanced: Classic trio breakthrough. Two conditions to check: enough space, and the defending king outside the square of the runner. Both are calculable, so calculate them.
by_level.master: Concrete throughout. Verify both captures, the declined capture, and the full race before playing it — the same pattern one rank back is simply a lost pawn.

by_depth.short: Two pawns are given so the third cannot be stopped.
by_depth.normal: A pawn breakthrough: the middle pawn advances to create two levers at once, a second pawn is sacrificed to deflect the defender, and the third promotes. It works here because the pawns are far enough advanced and the king is outside the square.
by_depth.deep: The canonical form is a5-b5-c5 against a7-b7-c7: 1.b6! and either 1...axb6 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 or 1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6. The middle pawn leads because it creates two levers, so the defender's choice does not matter. Two conditions decide whether it works and both are concrete — enough space, and the defending king outside the square of the resulting passer. Move the same structure one rank back and it fails entirely, which is why this is a calculation rather than a pattern to trust.

explanations.lesson: When pawns face each other and nothing seems to be happening, check for the breakthrough — and then check the square rule before you play it.

beginner_words: giving up pawns so one can run
avoid: breakthroughs always work in this structure

audit_notes: Promoted to validated: both halves of a properly isolated controlled pair are engine-settled, and the space-advantage condition the sources state is confirmed with a 70-pawn swing.

2026-09-01 audit: source_confidence was 'high' with no source rated high — the sources are a programming wiki, two instructional sites and an encyclopedia. Downgraded to medium. The ENGINE evidence is strong and unaffected; it is the textual sourcing that is medium.

pawn-breakthrough.definition_short: Sacrificing one or two pawns to force through a passer the enemy king cannot catch.
pawn-breakthrough.definition_long:
A forcing pawn sacrifice that manufactures a passed pawn out of a blocked structure. The canonical pattern is three pawns against three, one rank apart — white a5, b5, c5 against black a7, b7, c7:

  1.b6! and now
     1...axb6 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 and the a-pawn queens; or
     1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6 and the c-pawn queens.

The middle pawn moves first because it creates two levers at once, so whichever way the defender captures, another pawn breaks through. The second sacrifice deflects the pawn that would have stopped the runner. Two pawns are given to promote the third.

IT IS CONCRETE, NOT GENERAL. Two conditions decide it and both are calculable. First, SPACE: the attacking pawns must be advanced enough. Move the whole structure one rank back and the breakthrough simply fails — a claim testable directly, and tested in this record. Second, KING DISTANCE: the defending king must be outside the square of the resulting passer, which the rule of the square settles at a glance.

Because both conditions are checkable, a breakthrough should never be played on general grounds. Verify both captures, the refusal to capture, and the full promotion race.

pawn-storm.knowledge_type_note: A method with a clear precondition — the pawns being advanced must not be your own king's shelter.

history.notes: Standard vocabulary; no coinage researched. The systematic treatment of opposite-side-castling races is attributable to the modern attacking literature rather than to any individual.

pawn-storm.engine_era_note: Engines storm readily with opposite-side castling and are notably reluctant to do so with same-side castling, which matches the precondition exactly. They also find the central counter-blow far faster than humans do, which has made premature storms harder to get away with.

preconditions: A group of pawns advancing towards the enemy king
Pieces available to use the lines that open
indicators_for: Opposite-side castling, so the storming pawns are not your own shelter
A hook — an advanced enemy shield pawn to attack
The centre is closed or under control
Rooks already placed on the files that will open
indicators_against: Same-side castling, so the storm exposes your own king
The centre is open or can be opened by the defender
No pieces can follow into the opened lines
The defender is faster in the race
false_positive_traps: Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow. Without that, it is a structural concession.
With same-side castling the same moves that attack also expose, and this is the commonest way a storm rebounds.
Counting the storm's speed without counting the defender's central break is how these positions are misjudged.

typical_plans: Count tempi to contact and start first
Attack a hook to force a file open
Combine the storm with prophylaxis against the counter-attack
typical_moves: h4-h5 and g4-g5
g6 as a breakthrough sacrifice
typical_pawn_structures: Opposite-side castling with pawn masses facing each other
A defender's h6 or g6 as a hook
typical_piece_arrangements: Rooks behind the advancing pawns
tactical_consequences: Sacrifices to open the last file are routine and often correct
strategic_consequences: A failed storm usually leaves the attacker structurally worse for the endgame

exceptions: With same-side castling the storm is a concession first and an attack second.
A central counter-blow refutes a premature storm — the standard antidote.
Against an intact shield with no hook, the storm may never force a file open at all.
limitations: Whether the storm arrives first is a concrete calculation, not a judgement.
misconceptions: That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. It is a way of making a road; without pieces it is a weakness.
That storms are always double-edged. With opposite-side castling they cost the attacker nothing.

conflicts.resolution: The same pawn moves attack and expose, and the resolution is which king they shelter. Opposite-side castling removes the conflict entirely; same-side castling makes it acute, and there king safety wins unless a concrete line says otherwise.

examples.note: The Yugoslav Attack setup: opposite-side castling, White's h- and g-pawns advancing at a fianchettoed king, and every white piece placed to follow them in - queen on d2, rook on d1, rook on h1, bishop on e3. That last part is the whole of the concept and the part the phrase leaves out. This record's counterexample is Letelier-Fischer 1960, four pawns advanced with every piece at home, and the difference between the two positions is not the pawns. The engine says -0.27 - level - and that is the honest reading: a storm is a PLAN and not an advantage, and both sides are attacking on opposite wings with everything still to play for.

engine.verdict_note: -0.27 at depth 20, settled at depth 9, and the engine's own first move is h4-h5 - it plays the storm and rates the position level. A plan that the engine adopts and that changes no evaluation is exactly what a middlegame plan is.

counterexamples.note: Letelier-Fischer, Leipzig Olympiad 1960, after 7.f4, and it is a NEGATIVE because the annotation names the concept and then says why it failed: 'His opponent decided to launch an early pawn storm against Black's King's Indian and delay his development. When central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target for the opponent.' Four pawns advanced, no pieces behind them, and Fischer answered with ...d6 and ...f6 and won in twenty-three moves. This record has no POSITIVE example yet, and that is recorded rather than filled with a constructed one: a storm that works is a storm whose pieces arrive, and choosing a position where that is true is a judgement this base has not yet found a human source for.

engine.verdict_note: -0.10 - level, from Black's side, with White's pawns on c4, d4, e5 and f4. The storm has gained no advantage at the moment it is complete, which is the negative claim stated as a number, and the engine's own first move begins dissolving it.

ambiguous_examples.note: Fischer-Spassky 1972, game 6, 30.h4 - a pawn advanced at the enemy king in a position where White is winning and attacking, which is what a storm looks like. The annotation calls it something else: '30.h4! Restricting the knight on h7 even further', and Havanur adds 'after this move neither the black queen nor the knight can use g5 as a springboard'. One pawn move, and the two readings are a storm gaining ground and a restraining move taking a square. This base already files it as `restraint`'s positive and `prophylaxis`' ambiguous; it is here a third time because the difference between the three is what the move is FOR, and the board is the same in all three readings.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase, 2022) - corpus entry fischer-spassky-1972-g6-30h4-restriction

engine.verdict_note: The annotated move is the engine's THIRD choice at +3.75 against +4.15 for 30.e6. If it were a storm it would be one the engine slightly prefers not to start; if it is restraint, forty centipawns is the price of the square.

by_level.beginner: Push your pawns at their king to open a line your rooks and queen can use.
by_level.intermediate: A pawn storm. It is nearly free when you have castled on the opposite side, and expensive when you have castled on the same side.
by_level.advanced: The pawns make the road; the pieces do the work. Look for a hook to attack, and check the centre before committing.
by_level.master: In opposite-castling races count tempi to contact, and combine the storm with prophylaxis rather than racing blind.

by_depth.short: Push pawns at their king to open a file.
by_depth.normal: A pawn storm: advancing pawns at the enemy king to trade off its shelter and open a line for your pieces. It costs nothing when you have castled on the other wing, and dismantles your own cover when you have not.
by_depth.deep: The pawns are the tool, not the attack — their job is to force a file open for the pieces behind them. The precondition is whose shelter they are: with opposite-side castling they are not yours, so the game becomes a race where one tempo decides; with same-side castling the same advance exposes you. A hook makes it work, since an advanced enemy shield pawn gives you something to attack; against an intact shield the file usually has to be forced with a sacrifice. The standard refutation is a central counter-blow, since a wing attack is only as sound as your control of the centre.

explanations.lesson: Before storming, ask two questions: are these pawns sheltering my own king, and can my pieces follow into the lines that open?

beginner_words: push the pawns at their king

pawn-storm.definition_short: Advancing a group of pawns at the enemy king to open a file for the pieces behind them.
pawn-storm.definition_long:
Pawns are a barrier, and the king is safe behind them; a storm's purpose is to trade that barrier away and open a line the heavy pieces can use. The pawns are not the attack — they are the tool that creates the road.

THE PRECONDITION is which pawns you are pushing. With OPPOSITE-SIDE CASTLING the g- and h-pawns are not your own king's shelter, so they can be thrown forward at no cost to your own safety, and the game becomes a race in which a single tempo decides. With SAME-SIDE CASTLING the same advance dismantles your own cover, and the burden of proof shifts entirely onto the attacker.

A HOOK makes it work. If the defender has advanced a shield pawn — ...h6, say — the attacker has something to attack with g4-g5, which forces the file open. Against an intact f7-g7-h7 there is nothing to bite on, and the storm has to force the exchange itself, usually with a sacrifice.

The standard refutation is a central counter-blow: a wing attack is only as sound as your control of the centre, and the classic punishment for a premature storm is ...d5 opening lines at the storming side's own king.

perpetual-check.knowledge_type_note: Terminology for a TECHNIQUE, emphatically NOT an official rule, and this is the single most common rules misconception in the area. A draw by perpetual check has not been a rule of chess for a long time. What actually ends the game is threefold repetition, the fifty-move rule, or agreement. Classifying this as `official-rule` would be exactly the error the epistemic typing exists to prevent.

history.notes: No coiner researched. The historically interesting question is when perpetual check ceased to be a separate rule in the Western codes, which has not been established here and is recorded as an open question rather than guessed at.

development.change: Treated in some rule sets as a distinct way to draw.
Not mentioned in the Laws at all; resolved through repetition or the fifty-move rule.
Shogi and xiangqi forbid it, with the checking side losing.

perpetual-check.engine_era_note: Engines evaluate a perpetual as exactly 0.00 and find them readily, which makes this one of the few defensive ideas that is trivially verifiable. A 0.00 evaluation with a repeating check sequence in the principal variation is as close to a mechanical confirmation as this knowledge base has.

preconditions: A sequence of checks exists that the defending king cannot escape
The checking side cannot improve on repeating, and the defender cannot deviate without becoming worse
indicators_for: The evaluation is exactly 0.00 with a repeating check sequence in the principal variation
The defending king has only two squares, both reachable by the same checking piece
The checking side is materially lost, so a draw is a success
A queen or a knight-plus-queen battery near an exposed king
indicators_against: The defender has an interposition that blocks the checks with gain
The king can step to a square outside the checking pattern
The checking side is BETTER, in which case the perpetual is a failure, not a resource
A check can be answered by a counter-check, or by capturing the checking piece
recognition.detector: puzzle_rules.js: checks >= 2 and final eval within 60cp of level
false_positive_traps: A series of checks that merely delays the end is not a perpetual. The test is whether the position REPEATS, not whether checks are available.

The repo's detector is a proxy — two or more checks and a near-level final evaluation — which will also fire on a position that is simply drawn after some checks. Treat the tag as a candidate, not a finding.
Reporting a perpetual as a good outcome for the side that was winning inverts the meaning entirely.

typical_plans: When lost, look for a check the king cannot escape before looking for anything else
When winning, spend a tempo removing the enemy queen's checking squares before converting
Sacrifice material to expose the enemy king enough that the checks never run out
typical_moves: A queen check on a square from which it can shuttle between two checking squares
typical_pawn_structures: A king whose pawn cover has been stripped, on an open file or diagonal
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen alone against an exposed king
Queen and knight cooperating
tactical_consequences: Converts a lost position into a draw
strategic_consequences: A standing reason not to strip your own king's cover even when attacking

exceptions: It is not a rule and cannot be claimed as one. The claimable rules are threefold repetition and the fifty-move rule.
For the side that stands better a perpetual is a failure, not a resource.
Other chess variants forbid it outright, so it is not a necessary feature of chess-like games.
limitations: The engine test (0.00 with repeating checks in the PV) is reliable; the repo's two-checks-and-level heuristic is not, and will over-report.
misconceptions: That perpetual check is a rule of chess. It is not, and has not been for a long time.
That you can 'claim a perpetual'. You claim threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule.
That any long series of checks is a perpetual.

examples.note: Real position from the shipped middlegame ladder (puzzle mi-5f4be05ec3). White is losing and saves the game with Qa8+. The engine's principal variation is the perpetual itself: Qa8+ Kg7, Ne8+ Kh8, Nf6 Kg7, Ne8+ — the position repeats and neither side can deviate.

engine.verdict_note: As clean as this concept gets. Qa8+ evaluates to exactly 0.00 and the PV contains the repeating check cycle. Every alternative tested is a forced loss for White — Ne6+ is mate in 13 against, Qg3 is mate in 3 against. So the perpetual converts a lost position into a draw, which is precisely the concept's claim. Settled from depth 1, i.e. the engine never changed its mind.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `checks-available-in-a-winning-position`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White's rook can check the black king along the eighth rank and follow it about indefinitely. A stream of checks the defender can never escape is what a perpetual is. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Two of this record's conditions fire at once. The first trap: "A series of checks that merely delays the end is not a perpetual. The test is whether the position REPEATS, not whether checks are available." And the third indicator_against: "The checking side is BETTER, in which case the perpetual is a failure, not a resource." White is a whole rook up. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report perpetual-check. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says +56.95: taking a draw by repetition here would be one of the worst decisions available on the board. This record's third trap is the one that matters most and it is about the reader rather than the detector - 'reporting a perpetual as a good outcome for the side that was winning inverts the meaning entirely' - which is why the concept must be reported with the side named or not at all.

by_level.beginner: White keeps checking and the black king can never get away, so the same position keeps happening and the game is a draw.
by_level.intermediate: Perpetual check. Note it is not a rule in itself — the checks force the position to repeat, and threefold repetition is what draws.
by_level.advanced: A perpetual: 0.00 with a repeating check cycle. Worth hunting for first whenever a position turns bad, and worth preventing before converting when you are the one winning.
by_level.master: Not a rule; a mechanism producing a claimable repetition. The practical corollary is prophylactic — before converting, spend the tempo that removes the enemy queen's checking squares.

by_depth.short: The checks never end, so the position repeats and the game is drawn.
by_depth.normal: Perpetual check: a sequence of checks the king cannot escape. Strictly it is not a drawing rule — it forces the same position to appear three times, and threefold repetition is the rule that ends the game. In practice players agree the draw long before that.
by_depth.deep: An unending series of checks. Widely believed to be a rule of chess, and it is not: FIDE's Laws do not mention it, and a perpetual reaches a draw through threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule. That its status is a choice rather than a necessity is clear from shogi and xiangqi, where giving perpetual check loses. Its value is asymmetric — for the defender it turns a loss into half a point, and for the attacker it is the thing to prevent before starting to convert. Engines make it unusually easy to confirm: exactly 0.00 with a repeating check cycle in the principal variation.

explanations.lesson: When your position collapses, look for a check the enemy king cannot escape before you look for anything else. And when you are winning, spend the tempo that takes those checks away.

avoid: draw by perpetual check (as a rule)

perpetual-check.definition_short: An unending series of checks the defender cannot escape. It is not itself a drawing rule — it forces a repetition, and the repetition is what draws.
perpetual-check.definition_long:
One side gives check after check, the enemy king can never escape the sequence, and neither side can profitably deviate. In practice this saves a lost position, and it is the commonest resource for the defending side in sharp middlegames.

THE RULES POSITION, which is widely misunderstood. Wikipedia states it plainly: 'A draw by perpetual check is no longer one of the rules of chess, but will eventually allow a draw claim by either threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule.' In practice players agree the draw long before either triggers. So a perpetual is a MECHANISM that produces a position covered by a rule; it is not a rule.

That the status is a rules CHOICE rather than a necessity is shown by other games: shogi and xiangqi forbid perpetual check, and giving it loses.

Its value is asymmetric. For the defender it converts a loss into a half point, which is why it is worth hunting for the instant a position turns bad. For the stronger side it is a danger to avoid, and a reason to keep the enemy queen off checking squares before starting to convert.

philidor-position.knowledge_type_note: A specific named position with a proven result; the defender's counterpart to the Lucena.

attributions.note: Analysed the position in 1777. The attribution here is secure, unlike the Lucena's.
Showed that Philidor's claim of uniqueness was not strictly correct; Johann Berger expanded on it.

history.notes: Better founded than the Lucena's naming. Recorded medium rather than high only because Philidor's own text was not consulted here.

development.change: The third-rank defence is analysed and presented as the drawing method.
Philidor's claim that it was the only drawing method is shown to be too strong.

philidor-position.engine_era_note: Tablebase-confirmed. Engines also make clear how narrow the alternatives are, which is why the third-rank defence remains the practical method.

preconditions: Rook and pawn against rook, defending side to hold
Defending king in front of the pawn
Pawn not yet on the defender's third rank
Defending rook on the defender's third rank
indicators_for: The attacking king cannot reach its sixth rank because the rook denies it
The defender's rook has the seventh and eighth ranks available for rear checks
indicators_against: The defending king is cut off from the pawn's file — likely a Lucena instead
The pawn has already reached the third rank while the rook is still on it
The defending rook has no safe far rank to drop to
false_positive_traps: The rook must leave the third rank at exactly the right moment — too early and the king comes in, too late and the pawn is past. Recognising the setup is not the same as executing it.
If the defending king is not in front of the pawn, this is not a Philidor and the position may be lost.

typical_plans: Hold the third rank; when the pawn advances to it, go to the far rank and check from behind
Accept a rook trade if offered on the third rank — the pawn ending is drawn
typical_moves: A waiting rook move along the third rank
Rook to the eighth rank once the pawn advances
strategic_consequences: The defensive target in most rook endings a pawn down

exceptions: Philidor's own claim of uniqueness is too strong: other defences draw, though they are harder.
With the pawn less advanced, the defending rook uses its FOURTH rank instead of the third and the king needs only to reach its second.
limitations: NO MASTER-GAME POSITION, and the reason is what this record IS. A named theoretical position is a position rather than a moment in a game: it is defined by its own geometry, it is reached from thousands of different games and from none in particular, and its authority is a tablebase rather than an annotator. The examples on this record carry `origin_kind: tablebase-position` for that reason and it is the correct provenance, not a weaker one - a Syzygy result is a statement about every continuation, which is more than any game can be. A famous game that REACHED this position would be a fact about that game and would add nothing to the claim.
misconceptions: That it is the only way to draw — Karstedt showed otherwise in 1897.
That passive defence works. It does not; the rook must switch to rear checks at the right moment.

examples.note: Philidor setup with colours reversed from the usual diagram: White is the DEFENDER, king on e1 in front of the pawn, rook on a3 holding the third rank. Black has king e5, pawn e4, rook b2.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw. The tablebase's best move is a waiting rook move along the rank, which is exactly the third-rank defence's first phase — hold the rank and do nothing until the pawn commits.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Ra1, engine 0.00 at depth 26. The Philidor defence holds, and it holds over every legal continuation rather than over the twenty the engine looked at. Note what this base has NOT been able to build: a verified counterexample. With the pawn on the fourth rank the defence draws from almost anywhere, so the position that would show the method failing has resisted three attempts and the record says so.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `philidor-without-the-philidor-rook`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Rook and pawn against rook, the pawn on the sixth, the attacking king in front of it, the defending king directly opposing on the queening file. Every visible ingredient of the Philidor defence is here. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The defending rook is on the seventh rank, in front of the pawn. Philidor's method is that the rook holds the rank in FRONT of the pawn only until the pawn reaches the sixth, and then drops to the eighth to check from behind. The pawn has reached the sixth and the rook has not dropped back, so the defence is not set up — and by then it is too late to set it up. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN WIN in 29, dtz 5, best move Kf6. The API does not report the Philidor position. This is the case this record has been missing: four earlier constructions with the pawon on the fourth rank all came back DRAWN, because there the defence holds from almost anywhere, and that finding is registered as this record's OPEN case. It is a different claim from this one. The open case asks for a position where the third-rank defence FAILS; this one shows a position where the defence is ABSENT and the ending is lost, which establishes that the method is necessary rather than that it is breakable.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 29, best move Kf6. The defending rook is on the seventh rather than the eighth and the pawn has already reached the sixth, so the Philidor defence is not set up and cannot be. This record's OPEN case is the complementary and still-unbuilt claim: a position where the defence IS set up and fails.

ambiguous_examples.note: A rook-and-pawn ending that any reader would call a Philidor position, and the Philidor defence is not what is holding it. The rank matters: Philidor's method is that the defending rook sits on the rank in front of the pawn until the pawn reaches the sixth, and then checks from behind. With the pawn on e5 the relevant rank is the sixth, and White's rook is on the third - so the defence being executed here is not Philidor's at all, and the position is drawn anyway, because the pawn is too far back and the defending king is in front of it. Filed as ambiguous because the name and the mechanism come apart: the arrangement is the one the name is attached to and the reason for the draw is a different one.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0, and this record's positive example - the same pieces with the pawn one rank further advanced, where the third-rank defence IS the reason - is also a proven draw. Two draws, one method, and only one of them is Philidor's.

by_level.beginner: Keep your king in front of their pawn and your rook across the third row so their king cannot come forward. When the pawn finally advances, drop your rook far back and check them from behind.
by_level.intermediate: The Philidor position — a draw. Two phases: hold the third rank, then check from behind once the pawn arrives on it. Getting the switch wrong is how the draw is lost.
by_level.advanced: Third-rank defence. Both attacking tries fail: pushing the pawn removes the king's screen, and interposing on the third rank allows a rook trade into a drawn pawn ending.
by_level.master: The defensive target in rook endings a pawn down. Note Philidor's uniqueness claim was disproved by Karstedt in 1897, though the alternatives are harder.

by_depth.short: King in front, rook on the third rank, then check from behind.
by_depth.normal: The Philidor position: the drawing method in rook and pawn against rook. Hold your rook on the third rank so their king cannot advance; when the pawn is pushed to that rank, swing the rook to the far end and check from behind.
by_depth.deep: The defender's counterpart to the Lucena, analysed by Philidor in 1777. Conditions: defending king in front of the pawn, pawn not yet on the defender's third rank, attacking king beyond it, defending rook on it. The method has two phases and the timing is everything — hold the rank until the pawn commits, then check from behind, where the attacking king has lost the screen its own pawn provided. Both attacking tries fail cleanly: pushing removes the cover, interposing allows a rook trade into a drawn pawn ending. Philidor believed it was the only drawing method; Karstedt showed in 1897 that it is not, though the alternatives are more complicated.

explanations.lesson: A pawn down in a rook ending, get your king in front of the pawn and your rook on the third rank. Then wait — and only switch to checking from behind when the pawn actually advances.

beginner_words: king in front of the pawn

philidor-position.definition_short: The drawing setup in rook and pawn against rook: defending king in front of the pawn, defending rook on the third rank, then checking from behind once the pawn advances.

validation_na.master_game: N/A rather than missing, and the argument is what this record IS. A named theoretical position is a POSITION rather than a moment in a game: it is defined by its own geometry, it is reached from thousands of games and from none in particular, and its authority is a tablebase. The examples here carry `origin_kind: tablebase-position`, which is the stronger provenance and not a weaker one - a Syzygy result is a statement about every legal continuation, and a game is a statement about one. A famous game that happened to REACH this position would be a fact about that game and would add nothing whatever to the claim the record makes.

piece-activity.knowledge_type_note: A property of a position that can be described concretely - what squares a piece reaches and what it bears on - even though measuring it is a judgement.

attributions.note: Piece placement and centralisation appear among the temporary advantages in the element lists descended from his theory.

history.notes: Ordinary vocabulary with no coinage; the classification as a temporary advantage is the traceable part.

piece-activity.engine_era_note: Engines weigh activity heavily and are markedly more willing than classical human teaching to give material for it, which has shifted practice - the modern preference for the active defence over the passive one owes a good deal to engine analysis.

preconditions: Pieces are on the board with differing scope
indicators_for: A piece bearing on enemy weaknesses
A rook on an open file or the seventh rank
A knight on a protected advanced square
Pieces with several useful squares available
indicators_against: A piece tied to defending something
A bishop shut in by its own pawns
A piece with moves available that accomplish nothing
false_positive_traps: Counting available squares is not measuring activity. A piece with many moves that bear on nothing is not active.
Active pieces do not guarantee compensation. The Halloween Gambit position in this base has genuinely active pieces and evaluates 1.75 worse.
Activity is generally a temporary advantage and must be converted; reporting it as though it were permanent overstates it.

typical_plans: Improve the least active piece
Trade passive pieces for the opponent's active ones
Open lines for pieces that would benefit
Tie enemy pieces to defence and keep your own free
typical_moves: Rook lifts to open files
Giving a pawn to activate a rook in an endgame
typical_pawn_structures: Open positions favouring long-range pieces
Closed structures favouring knights
typical_piece_arrangements: A rook chained to a pawn's defence
A knight on a supported outpost
tactical_consequences: Active pieces generate threats, and threats gain tempi
strategic_consequences: Activity is usually temporary and must be converted into something durable

exceptions: Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it.
Activity purchased with too much material is not compensation, as this base's gambit measurements show.
limitations: No reliable measure of activity exists in this system; the judgement is heuristic.
The concept is broad enough that it risks being applied to any move, which is exactly why the false-positive traps are stated.

MEASURED 2026-09-02 and fixed: the matcher counted LEGAL moves, which is exactly what this record's first false-positive trap forbids - 'counting available squares is not measuring activity. A piece with many moves that bear on nothing is not active.' It now counts ACTIVE moves: captures, moves into the opponent's half, and moves that attack an enemy man from where they land. The threshold is unchanged at a gap of eight; what changed is what is counted, and the firing rate went from 44.4% of the 788 shipped positions to 33.9%.

ARMY-LEVEL ONLY, and this base has a corpus entry failing on it. Keene on Reti-Capablanca 1924 writes that Capablanca 'is doing his utmost with his strongest piece' - a claim about ONE PIECE carrying a side, which this measure cannot express: Black's queen has a scope of 13 against its own next-best piece's 9, while White's army has 24 active moves to Black's 20. by_level.beginner: A piece is active if it is doing something - attacking, defending something important, or controlling squares the opponent wants.
by_level.intermediate: Piece activity. A rook chained to defending a pawn is worth far less than one free to make threats, whatever the material says.
by_level.advanced: Activity competes with material at a real exchange rate, and it is usually temporary - convert it before it expires.
by_level.master: Most positional concepts are special cases of this one: an outpost, a bad bishop and an open file are all statements about activity.

by_depth.short: How much a piece is actually doing.
by_depth.normal: Piece activity: the squares a piece controls and the targets it bears on. An active piece makes threats and chooses where to go; a passive one is tied to defence and loses material the moment it leaves.
by_depth.deep: The most general positional idea, and the one most others are special cases of - an outpost is a square that makes a knight active, a bad bishop is an inactive one, an open file is a rook's route to activity. It is not mobility alone: a piece with many available squares bearing on nothing is not active. It trades against material at a rate that can be measured, and this base has measured it - the Evans Gambit is a pawn down and evaluates exactly level, so that activity is worth precisely one pawn, while the Halloween Gambit produces real activity and a mobile centre and still evaluates 1.75 worse, because a knight is too much to pay. And it is usually temporary, so it has to be converted into something durable before it expires.

explanations.lesson: Ask what each piece is actually doing, not how many squares it can reach.

piece-activity.definition_short: How much a piece actually does: the squares it controls, the targets it bears on, and whether it is free to move at all.
piece-activity.definition_long:
The most general positional idea there is, and the one most other positional concepts are special cases of. An outpost is a square that makes a knight active; a bad bishop is an inactive one; an open file is a route to activity for a rook.

ACTIVITY IS NOT MOBILITY ALONE. A piece with many available squares that bear on nothing is not active in any useful sense. What counts is whether the squares it controls MATTER — whether it attacks something, defends something that needs defending, or controls squares the opponent wants.

THE SHARPEST FORM OF THE IDEA is the active-versus-passive contrast, clearest with rooks. An active rook makes threats and goes where it likes; a passive rook is chained to defending a pawn and loses material the moment it leaves. That asymmetry costs the passive side nothing in material and decides games, which is why giving a pawn to activate a rook is routinely correct in rook endings.

IT COMPETES WITH MATERIAL, and the exchange rate is the interesting part. A pawn for lasting activity is often a good trade; this base measured the Evans Gambit at exactly equal a pawn down, which is activity worth precisely one pawn. The same measurement showed the reverse: the Halloween Gambit produces genuinely active pieces and a mobile centre and still evaluates 1.75 worse, because a knight is too much to pay. Activity is real, measurable, and finite.

IT IS USUALLY TEMPORARY. In Steinitz's division, piece placement and centralisation are TEMPORARY advantages, which means activity must be converted into something durable — material, a weakness, a passed pawn — before it expires.

piece-coordination.knowledge_type_note: A property of a whole position rather than of any single piece, which is why it is the hardest positional concept to detect or attribute to a move.

attributions.note: The standard exemplar; sources consistently identify coordination and manoeuvring as the defining and least imitable feature of his play.
Devoted a book, Maneuvering: the Art of Piece Play, to finding the best squares for pieces when no forcing line or obvious plan exists. Known here from its description only, not read.

history.notes: Ordinary positional vocabulary with no coinage traced. The named associations are to exemplars and treatments rather than to an origin.

piece-coordination.engine_era_note: Engines coordinate pieces superbly and explain nothing about it, which makes this the concept where the gap between a correct move and an intelligible reason for it is widest. Translating an engine's quiet regrouping move into a human reason is close to the core problem this Education System exists to solve.

preconditions: Several pieces on the board with a shared or conflicting purpose
indicators_for: Pieces defending one another
Several pieces bearing on the same target or break
A move that vacates a square another piece wants
A regrouping that prepares a break requiring several pieces at once
indicators_against: Pieces obstructing each other
Pieces on opposite wings with unrelated purposes
A piece that must stay put to hold something together
false_positive_traps: This is the concept most easily misused as a label for any quiet move whose point is not understood. It must never be the default explanation when nothing else fits - saying nothing is better.
Individually well-placed pieces are not the same as coordinated pieces, and this is exactly the distinction the concept exists to make.
Coordination is a property of a position, so attributing it to a single move requires knowing what the move prepares - which usually requires the continuation, not the move alone.

typical_plans: Regroup so every piece supports the intended break
Move a piece off a square another piece needs more
Arrange the pieces harmoniously before committing to an operation
typical_moves: Knight retreats from an outpost that is no longer needed
Modest queen moves that free a file or diagonal
Rook transfers that connect two plans
typical_piece_arrangements: Pieces converging on one break or one target
tactical_consequences: Well-coordinated pieces generate tactics; uncoordinated ones are vulnerable to them
strategic_consequences: Coordination is what allows a plan to be executed at all

exceptions: In forcing positions coordination is subordinate to calculation.
A piece may correctly be left badly placed if moving it costs more than the disharmony does.
limitations: The least detectable concept in this base: no mechanical signature, and a claim about the whole position rather than a move.
One of its sources is known only from a publisher description and has not been read.
No engine or tablebase validation exists for this concept, and none is currently designed.

No detector, per the record's human-only classification, and the corpus entries for it are scored as 'absent by design'. Two annotated master positions are recorded as human ground truth so that a later session which builds one has something to test it against.

by_level.beginner: Your pieces should work together - defending each other and aiming at the same thing.
by_level.intermediate: Coordination. Every piece can be on a decent square and the position still be badly coordinated, because they are not helping each other.
by_level.advanced: The skill of quiet positions, where nobody has an active plan and whoever regroups better gets the advantage.
by_level.master: The characteristic coordinating move looks strange in isolation, because its point is what it frees or prepares for other pieces.

by_depth.short: Whether your pieces work together.
by_depth.normal: Piece coordination: how well the pieces support one another and one plan. It is a property of the whole army rather than of any piece, and a position can have every piece on a reasonable square and still be badly coordinated.
by_depth.deep: What distinguishes a good position from a collection of good squares. It is the skill of quiet positions - many middlegames reach an equilibrium where neither side has an active plan and the game turns on who regroups better - and it explains the class of move that looks wrong in isolation: a knight retreating from an outpost it no longer needs, a queen stepping to a modest square, correct because of what it frees or what it prepares. It is also the hardest concept here to detect, having no mechanical signature and being a claim about a whole position rather than about a move, which is why this record forbids using it as a default label for quiet moves whose point is not understood.

explanations.hedge: The least detectable concept in this base; it has no mechanical signature and must not be offered as a fallback explanation.
explanations.lesson: Ask what the move does for the other pieces, not what it does for itself.

piece-coordination.definition_short: How well the pieces work together - whether they support one plan and one another, rather than each being individually well placed.
piece-coordination.definition_long:
The property that distinguishes a good position from a collection of good squares. Coordination is about the army, not the piece: it asks whether the pieces defend each other, aim at the same targets, and leave each other room, and it is entirely possible for every piece to stand on a reasonable square while the position is badly coordinated.

IT IS THE SKILL OF QUIET POSITIONS. Many middlegames reach an equilibrium in which neither side has an active plan available; what remains is manoeuvring, and the player who regroups more skilfully gets the advantage. Karpov is the standard exemplar precisely because of this, and the quality repeatedly identified in his play is the ability to see each piece IN THE CONTEXT OF THE WHOLE ARMY rather than on its own merits.

IT EXPLAINS MOVES THAT LOOK WRONG. The characteristic coordinating move is one that appears strange or even retrograde in isolation — a knight retreating from an outpost it no longer needs, a queen stepping to a modest square — and is correct because it frees a square another piece wants, or prepares a break that needs three pieces at once. This is the class of move a single-move explanation handles worst, and naming coordination is often the only honest account of it.

IT IS CLOSELY TIED TO PROPHYLAXIS. Arranging one's pieces harmoniously before a decisive operation, and doing so in a way that also anticipates the opponent's plan, is the same activity seen from two sides.

THE HONEST LIMIT is that coordination is the least detectable concept in this base. It has no mechanical signature, it is a claim about a whole position, and it is easy to invoke as a post-hoc label for any quiet move that turned out well. This record therefore states plainly that it must not be used as a default explanation for moves the system cannot otherwise account for.

piece-exchanges.knowledge_type_note: Typed rule-of-thumb: the standard exchanging rules are useful defaults with well-known exceptions, and carry mandatory hedging.

attributions.note: Devotes attention to exchanges as an active weapon rather than a neutral simplification. Read in the primary text.

history.notes: The exchanging rules are common pedagogical property with no identifiable origin; only Nimzowitsch's treatment of exchanges as a weapon is attributable here.

piece-exchanges.engine_era_note: Engines make exchange decisions concretely and are notably less willing than club teaching to simplify when ahead — they will keep pieces on if the position calls for it and trade into a drawn ending never.

preconditions: A capture or trade is available and optional
indicators_for: Ahead in material with no drawn-ending risk
Cramped, with pieces obstructing one another
Under attack, and the trade removes an attacker
The trade damages their structure or improves yours
indicators_against: The resulting endgame is drawn — a wrong rook pawn, opposite bishops, or insufficient material
You hold space, which exchanges relieve
You hold the initiative, which exchanges dissipate
The trade gives up your better minor piece or breaks your bishop pair
false_positive_traps: 'Simplify when ahead' is the most over-applied rule in chess. Trading into a proven drawn ending is how won games are drawn, and this base holds tablebase-proven examples of exactly that.
The rule is about removing counterplay, not about removing pieces. If the opponent has no counterplay, there is no reason to trade at all.
Trading one bishop destroys a bishop pair worth half a pawn — a cost that a simple material count does not see.
A trade being available is not a reason to make it, and being ahead is not a reason either. Proven case: Rxh7+ draws where Rb8 mates in one.

typical_plans: Ahead in material: trade pieces, keep pawns, and check the resulting ending is not drawn
Cramped: trade to gain room
Under attack: trade the strongest attacker, ideally queens
With space or the initiative: keep pieces on
typical_moves: An offered queen trade as a defensive resource
strategic_consequences: Every trade changes what kind of position it is, which is usually a larger decision than the material

exceptions: Simplifying when ahead fails if the ending is drawn — wrong rook pawn, opposite bishops, insufficient material.
The side ahead in material should keep pawns, not trade them.
With a rook against two minor pieces, trade major pieces even when nominally behind, because major pieces are redundant.
limitations: The rules are defaults; almost every one has a named exception recorded elsewhere in this base.
misconceptions: That trading is good when ahead. It is good when it reduces counterplay and bad when it approaches a drawn ending.
That an even trade is positionally neutral. It changes the character of the position, which is usually the bigger consequence.
That capturing or trading is safe when you are winning. A proven position in this base has one available capture, which is also a check, and it converts mate in one into a draw.

conflicts.resolution: Directly opposed in the case that matters most: 'simplify when ahead' meets 'the defender is heading for a fortress'. The fortress wins the argument — trading into a wrong rook pawn or an opposite-bishop blockade converts a win into a proven draw. Always check the resulting ending before simplifying.

Recorded as the positive case beside this record's tablebase counterexample where a capture throws away mate in one: exchanging is a method, and which position you exchange INTO is the whole of it.

Every question this concept asks - who does the exchange favour, does it simplify towards a won or a drawn ending, is the resulting structure better for one side - has the same answer here, which is that it does not matter. The engine says 0.00. Filed as ambiguous because the concept is fully applicable and produces no information: a trade that changes nothing is neither a good exchange nor a bad one, and a system that had to say which would be inventing a difference. This record's positive example is the opposite case - Capablanca trading into a specific ending he had judged - and its counterexample is a capture that throws away mate in one.
