by_level.beginner: When you are ahead, trading pieces usually helps. When you are cramped, trading gives you room. When you are behind, avoid trades.
by_level.intermediate: Before any trade, ask what the position becomes. Ahead in material, trade pieces but keep pawns — and check the ending is not one of the drawn ones.
by_level.advanced: Exchanges are the main lever on the character of a position. Trading is about reducing counterplay, not about reducing pieces.
by_level.master: Also a weapon in Nimzowitsch's sense — exchanges can force an opponent out of a strong post, and weak squares tend to be traded off against each other.

by_depth.short: Trade when ahead or cramped; keep pieces when behind or attacking.
by_depth.normal: Exchanges: trade when you are ahead in material, cramped, or under attack; avoid trading when behind, when you hold space, or when you have the initiative. Ahead in material, trade pieces but keep pawns.
by_depth.deep: The standard defaults are sound but heavily over-applied. 'Simplify when ahead' is really about reducing counterplay, and it fails outright when the resulting ending is drawn — a wrong rook pawn, an opposite-coloured-bishop blockade, or insufficient material, all of which this base holds tablebase-proven examples of. The classical refinement is to trade pieces but not pawns when ahead, and pawns but not pieces when behind. Nimzowitsch adds that exchanges are an active weapon: they can force an opponent out of a strong position, and weak squares tend to get traded off against each other.

explanations.hedge: These are defaults, not rules. Almost every one has a named exception, and the most damaging error in the area is simplifying automatically when ahead into an ending that is drawn.
explanations.lesson: Before you trade, picture the position afterwards and ask whether you would want it. 'I am ahead so I should trade' is how won games become draws.

piece-exchanges.definition_short: Deciding what to trade. The defaults: exchange when ahead in material or cramped; avoid exchanges when behind, or when you hold space or the initiative.
piece-exchanges.definition_long:
Every capture is a decision about what the position becomes, and the standard guidance is a set of defaults rather than rules.

TRADE WHEN: ahead in material, since fewer pieces makes the advantage easier to convert; cramped, since fewer pieces need fewer squares; under attack, since trading the attackers defuses it — and trading queens is the single strongest defensive resource; or when the trade improves your structure or worsens theirs.

AVOID TRADING WHEN: behind in material; holding space, since exchanges relieve your opponent's cramp; holding the initiative, since it needs pieces to sustain it; or when the trade removes your better minor piece.

The classical refinement is that when ahead in material you should trade PIECES but not PAWNS, and when behind you should trade pawns but not pieces — because the materially superior side wants pawns left to promote, and the inferior side wants to head towards drawn endings.

THE STANDARD OVERCORRECTION is simplifying automatically when ahead. It is not true that simplification always helps: trading into a drawn ending, a wrong-rook-pawn fortress or an opposite-coloured-bishop blockade throws the win away, and this base contains proven examples of each. The rule is about reducing counterplay, not about reducing pieces.

Nimzowitsch's angle, from My System, is that exchanges are a WEAPON: they can be used to force an opponent out of a strong position, and weak squares tend to be traded off in what he calls an exchange of prisoners of war.

Stop using it when the position has a concrete feature the count cannot see

The count is a static measure and says nothing about activity, structure or king safety.

by_level.intermediate: They are averages, not facts. A bishop is better in open positions and a knight in closed ones or on an outpost.
by_level.advanced: The half-pawn bonus belongs to the bishop PAIR, not to a bishop — the pair works because the two cover different colours.
by_level.master: Their own authorities disagree by half a pawn on bishop versus knight, and a proven draw in this base is a bishop and pawn up.

by_depth.deep: The first thing anyone learns and the thing most often mistaken for a fact. The values are disputed among their own authorities: Fischer at bishop 3.25 to knight 3, Kaufman's statistics at 3.5 each with the bonus attaching to the pair, and GM Studer holding that individual bishop superiority is unevidenced. What the numbers compress away is what usually decides: a bishop is a half-board piece and a knight reaches everywhere; the bishop wants open lines and the knight closed ones and outposts; and with all the pawns on one wing the ordering reverses. And a count says nothing about a position — this base holds a proven draw in which one side is a bishop and a pawn ahead.

piece-properties.definition_short: The conventional numeric values of the pieces, and the properties those numbers compress away.
piece-properties.definition_long:
The first thing anyone learns and the thing most often mistaken for a fact.

THE CONVENTIONAL COUNT is pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9, king priceless. It is a good enough approximation to decide most exchanges and is not more than that.

THE NUMBERS ARE DISPUTED, and the clearest case is the bishop against the knight, recorded in full on its own concept: Fischer put the bishop at 3.25 against a knight's 3; Kaufman's statistics put both at 3.5 — EQUAL — with the half-pawn attaching to the PAIR rather than to the bishop; and GM Studer says the claim of individual bishop superiority 'is not funded with evidence'. Three authorities, three positions, and this base records the dispute rather than picking a winner.

WHAT THE NUMBERS COMPRESS AWAY is what actually decides positions:
- COLOUR-BOUNDEDNESS. A bishop is a half-board piece; a knight reaches every square.
- RANGE VERSUS REACH. A bishop's value rises with open lines; a knight's with closed ones and with outposts. With all the pawns on one wing the knight is stronger, which is the reversal people find most surprising.
- THE PAIR. Two bishops complement each other because they cover different colours; two knights are redundant because they want the same squares. The bonus attaches to the asymmetry.
- THE EXCHANGE. Rook for minor piece is nominally +2 and is routinely given up for lasting compensation, which is a whole named concept here.

AND THE COUNT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT POSITIONS. This base holds a tablebase-proven draw in which one side is a bishop AND a pawn ahead. A point count reads that as roughly +4; the truth is a dead draw, because the pawn is a rook pawn whose promotion square the bishop cannot control.

pin.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), mechanically detectable. The interaction with FIDE Art. 3.9.1 makes it a rules matter as well.
pin.definition_short: A line piece attacks through a less valuable enemy unit to a more valuable one behind it, so moving the front unit is illegal or costly.
pin.definition_long:
Only bishops, rooks and queens can pin, because a pin needs a line. The pinned unit stands between the pinning piece and a target behind it.

An ABSOLUTE pin is against the king: moving the pinned piece is illegal. A RELATIVE pin is against any other piece: moving is legal but loses material.

Two consequences follow. First, a pinned piece is a poor defender — it may be attacked again and cannot run. Second, and routinely misunderstood: a pinned piece STILL GIVES CHECK and still controls the squares it attacks. FIDE Art. 3.9.1 is explicit that a king is in check 'even if such pieces are constrained from moving to the square occupied by the king because they would then leave or place their own king in check.' A pinned knight defending a square does not defend it against the king, but it does defend it against everything else.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly line piece, an enemy unit, and a more valuable enemy unit are collinear, in that order, with no other piece between
indicators_for: The target behind is the king (absolute pin)
The pinned unit is currently defending something
The pinned unit can be attacked again to win it
indicators_against: The pinned piece can capture the pinner
The defender can interpose a third unit on the line
The target behind can simply step off the line
The 'pinned' piece is worth more than the piece behind it — that is a skewer, not a pin

typical_plans: Attack the pinned piece again with a pawn or a minor piece
Prevent the pin from being broken before adding attackers

exceptions: A pinned piece still delivers check and still guards squares against non-king units.
A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.
Pinning is not automatically good: a pin can be dissolved and the pinning piece can end up misplaced.
limitations: Detecting alignment is mechanical; deciding whether the pin is exploitable is not.

Engine agreement does not establish that a pin explains a move. In a controlled test the same move (d4-d5) was best both with and without the pin; only the margin over alternatives distinguished the two (1.57 vs 0.28).

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

Verified 2026-09-02 by reading blind-chess.html's findMotifs() directly, which is where this concept is detected: the tag arrives from the page and Layer 4 translates it. tools/trap_audit.js reads lib/matchers.js and lib/features.js and cannot see that function, so a condition honoured there reads as unread. This note is the reading. "The 'pinned' piece is worth more than the piece behind it - that is a skewer, not a pin" is ENFORCED, and it is the branch that decides which tag is emitted: `if (VAL[l.backP.t] > VAL[l.frontP.t]) pins.push(...) else if (VAL[l.frontP.t] > VAL[l.backP.t]) skewers.push(...)`. Worth noting what falls between: when the two are worth the SAME, neither tag is emitted, so a rook lined up in front of a rook is reported as nothing rather than as the wrong one of the two. The other two indicators_against - interposition, and the rear unit stepping off the line - are not built, and both are properties of the DEFENDER'S next move rather than of the position, which is the class of condition this base has consistently declined to guess at.

examples.note: Nimzowitsch-Capablanca, St Petersburg 1914, 22...Reb8 - Capablanca doubling on the b-file, and the detector's reading of what that achieves is a pin: 'the pawn on b2 is pinned to the rook behind it and cannot step aside'. The annotation is about the file rather than the pin - 'his extremely active pieces and PLAY ON THE OPEN B-FILE more than compensate for the structural weakness' - and the pin is what the play on the file consists of. A pin against a ROOK rather than a king is the relative kind, and it is the commoner kind in real games, which is why this is a better master example than a mating-net pin would be. PROVENANCE. The position is a corpus entry - a master game with a verified move list and a named annotator - and the annotator named a DIFFERENT concept there. So this grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one: the motif is what this base's own detector reads off the board, and the game is what makes the board real. `attributed_by` is deliberately absent.

ALSO VERIFIED: Bb3 is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. counterexamples.note: THE SAME THREE MEN WITH TWO OF THEM SWAPPED. On the d-file a rook, a knight and a king: with the knight in front it is a PIN and the knight cannot legally move; with the KING in front - this position - it is a skewer, the king must move, and the knight falls behind it. Nothing else on the board changes and the name of the motif does. The page's own findMotifs tags the first `pin` and this one `skewer`, and this base does not second-guess it.

Registered false-positive case `a-pin-the-pinned-piece-dissolves-by-capture`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: After Rxe8, White's rook on e8 attacks the black rook on f8 with the black king behind it on g8. Line piece, enemy unit, more valuable enemy unit, collinear, nothing between — the record's precondition, word for word. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first indicator_against: "The pinned piece can capture the pinner." The rook on f8 does exactly that, and comes out even. The detector's sentence — "the rook on f8 is pinned to the king behind it and cannot step aside" — is true and misleads, because a reader takes 'cannot step aside' to mean the rook is stuck. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Reported at HIGH confidence until a guard was written. The geometry is genuinely there, which is why findMotifs() is right to see it; whether it MEANS anything is the concept record's question and the record answers it. The guard reads the pinned square out of the detector's own sentence rather than re-deriving the pin — two implementations of one motif are how the two start to disagree — and suppresses the report when the pinned piece has a legal capture of the pinner that SEE does not punish. It fails open: if the position cannot be rebuilt or the sentence is not in that shape, the motif is reported, because a guard that cannot run has no standing to overrule the detector. Rate: pin fell to 9.0% of the 788 shipped puzzles.

engine.verdict_note: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE RESULT. d5 is STILL the best move here (+5.40) — the pin is not what makes it best. What changes is (a) the value of the move, +7.26 vs +5.40, and (b) how clearly best it is: a 1.57 margin over the runner-up with the pin, only 0.28 without it. So 'the engine picked this move' is NOT evidence that the pin concept applies; using best-move agreement as the test would produce a false positive here. Reliable signals are the margin over alternatives and the paired eval delta.

by_level.beginner: That piece cannot move, because moving it would expose the more valuable piece behind it.
by_level.intermediate: A pin. The pinned piece is stuck and makes a poor defender, so you can pile up on it.
by_level.advanced: Absolute pin against the king (illegal to move) or relative pin (legal but costly). Remember a pinned piece still gives check.

by_depth.short: That piece cannot move without exposing something more valuable.
by_depth.normal: A pin: the {piece} on {square} is stuck, because moving it would expose the {target} behind it. A pinned piece is a poor defender, so it can often be attacked again.
by_depth.deep: A line piece attacks through a less valuable enemy unit to a more valuable one behind it. Absolute against the king, where moving is illegal; relative against anything else, where moving is legal but costly. Two consequences follow, and the second is routinely misunderstood: a pinned piece makes a poor defender and can be piled on, but it STILL GIVES CHECK and still controls its squares against everything except the king — FIDE Art. 3.9.1 is explicit about this. Note also that engine testing showed a pin does not necessarily change which move is best, only how clearly best it is.

planning.knowledge_type_note: Advice on how to decide what to aim at. Frameworks for it are numerous and none is authoritative.

attributions.note: Planning in the modern sense is usually traced to his doctrine that play should follow the position's features rather than a search for attacks. This is an association rather than a coinage: no source consulted here credits him with originating planning as such, and the connection is this base's inference from his theory, not a claim found in the literature.

history.notes: No coinage and no clear origin. The Steinitz link is recorded as an association at low confidence, not an attribution - the named historical contributions are to positional evaluation, from which planning follows. The modern frameworks are recent instructional material with no scholarly standing.

planning.engine_era_note: An area where engines are least helpful to humans. An engine supplies the move and the number but not the objective, and its plans are frequently not expressible as a human plan at all. Explaining what an engine is aiming at is a translation problem, and it is precisely what this Education System exists to do.

preconditions: No forced sequence demands attention
The position has identifiable features
indicators_for: A fixed enemy weakness that cannot run away
A pawn majority capable of producing a passer
A recognisable pawn structure with known plans
An enemy piece with no good squares
indicators_against: A concrete threat must be met first
The position is too forcing for planning to be relevant
false_positive_traps: A plan that names nothing cannot be verified, followed or abandoned, and is not a plan.
A plan that ignores the opponent's counterplay is the standard way good-looking moves lose games.
This system cannot know a player's plan and must not attribute one to a move without evidence.

typical_plans: Attack a fixed weakness that cannot be defended by moving it
Mobilise a pawn majority into a passed pawn
Create a second weakness once the first is tied down
Prevent the opponent's plan rather than pursue your own
Improve the worst-placed piece when nothing else is asking to be done
typical_pawn_structures: Structures with known associated plans, such as the isolated queen's pawn or a queenside majority
tactical_consequences: Tactics generally appear in service of a plan rather than instead of one

exceptions: Forcing positions need calculation, not planning.
Shereshevsky's 'thinking in schemes' inverts the usual order in endgames: decide the target arrangement first, then find the route to it.
limitations: No planning framework has scholarly standing; they are instructional scaffolding and this base treats them as such.
This system observes moves, not intentions, and cannot verify that a player had a plan.

misconceptions: That a plan is a sequence of moves. The opponent gets to move too; a plan is an objective and an arrangement.
That having any plan beats having none. A bad plan pursued rigidly is worse than responding to the position.
That abandoning a plan is weakness. Recognising that circumstances changed is a skill in itself.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-quiet-move-called-a-plan`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kd1 in a fully locked position. Any quiet move can be described afterwards as part of a plan — improving the king, preparing to bring it to the queenside, waiting for the opponent to commit. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: A plan is a sequence with a goal, and this position has no goal available to anybody: every file is rammed shut and no piece can enter. Describing the move as planful names an intention the board does not contain. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing at all here — not planning, not prophylaxis, not restraint — and the engine says 0.00 with both kings walking about on the kingside. The three concepts share this position as a registered case for the same reason: each is a claim about what a move is FOR, and this base reports what is on the board. A position where every word of three records is true and none of the three concepts is present is the sharpest available test of that discipline.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 24, and the engine's line is both kings walking about on the kingside. There is no plan in the position for either side, which is the point: three other records - `prophylaxis`, `restraint` and `middlegame-principles` - carry this same board for the same reason, because each is a claim about what a move is FOR and there is nothing for a move to be for.

by_level.beginner: Pick something to aim at - a weak pawn, a square, a file - and bring your pieces towards it.
by_level.intermediate: A plan is an objective, not a move sequence. It should follow from the position's features and name something specific.
by_level.advanced: Read the plan off the pawn structure, check the opponent's counterplay, and be willing to abandon it when the position changes.
by_level.master: In endgames invert it: choose the arrangement you want to reach, then work out the route.

by_depth.short: Pick a concrete objective the position points at.
by_depth.normal: Planning: choosing an objective that follows from the position's features and arranging your pieces to achieve it. A plan is not a sequence of moves, since the opponent moves too - it is a target and a set-up.
by_depth.deep: What to do when nothing is forced. The plan is read off the position rather than invented: a fixed enemy weakness makes the plan about that weakness, a pawn majority makes it about mobilising the majority. It has to name something, because 'improve my position' cannot be verified, followed or abandoned. The pawn structure governs what is available, which is why recognising a structure and recalling its plans beats deriving one from scratch. Three failures recur - a plan too vague to direct anything, a plan that ignores the opponent's counterplay, and a plan held after the position that justified it has changed.

explanations.hedge: Planning frameworks are instructional scaffolding rather than established method; they agree broadly on what to look at and none is authoritative.
explanations.lesson: If your plan does not name a square, a pawn, a file or a piece, it is not yet a plan.

avoid: a plan is a series of moves

planning.definition_short: Choosing a concrete objective that follows from the position's features, and arranging your pieces to achieve it.
planning.definition_long:
What to do when no move is forced. A plan is not a sequence of moves — the opponent has a vote — but an OBJECTIVE together with the arrangement of pieces that serves it.

IT FOLLOWS FROM THE ASSESSMENT, and this is the part most often skipped. The plan is not invented; it is read off the position's features. If the opponent has a weak pawn, the plan concerns that pawn. If you have a majority on one wing, the plan is to mobilise it. The standard sequence is assess, choose the objective the assessment points at, verify it with concrete calculation, and revise when the position changes.

IT MUST NAME SOMETHING. 'Improve my position' and 'create pressure' are not plans, because they give no direction and cannot be verified or abandoned. A plan should point at a specific square, pawn, file or piece.

WHAT THE POSITION ALLOWS depends on the pawn structure above all, because the pawns decide which squares the pieces can use and which breaks exist. Recognising a structure and recalling the plans that belong to it is much more efficient than deriving a plan from scratch, and it is why studying structures generalises where studying variations does not.

THE THREE COMMON FAILURES are worth naming: a plan too vague to direct anything; a plan that ignores the opponent's counterplay; and a plan held rigidly after the position that justified it has changed. Knowing when to abandon a plan is a real skill and is not the same as lacking one.

FRAMEWORKS EXIST IN QUANTITY — question lists, staged procedures, mnemonics — and this base records them as scaffolding rather than method. They agree on substance: look at both sides' weaknesses, where you are strong, which piece is worst placed, what to trade, and what the opponent intends.

positional-evaluation.knowledge_type_note: A method for assessing positions, originating in a specific theoretical claim about how chess games are won.

attributions.note: Changed his style from romantic to classical in 1873 and formulated the theory the elements serve.
The seven numbered propositions as commonly quoted come from Hooper's article in the British Chess Magazine.
His maxim 'no combination without a considerable plus, no considerable plus without a combination' states the same doctrine from the tactical side.

Credited by the Exeter Chess Club with FIRST indicating proposition 4 - that an attack from an equal position can be refuted by correct defence - and described there as the progenitor of the fully formed theory of Steinitz. He declared, unfashionably for the time, that all gambits can be defended, and played that way. Recorded because the theory is normally credited wholly to Steinitz; the claim rests on a single club source and is not verified further.

history.notes: The element lists as circulated are explicitly a REFINED version rather than Steinitz's own words - one source consulted here says so directly - so this record credits Steinitz with the theory and treats the itemised lists as a later tidying. Hooper's propositions were quoted at second hand through the Exeter page, not read in the British Chess Magazine. A single source consulted here credits Louis Paulsen with first indicating the fourth proposition, making him the theory's progenitor rather than Steinitz alone. That is recorded at low confidence because only one source states it.

development.note: Steinitz turns from the romantic style to positional assessment.
Hooper's seven-proposition summary becomes the standard formulation.
Evaluation becomes a number, and the elements survive as the vocabulary for explaining it.

positional-evaluation.engine_era_note: Engines evaluate positions numerically without decomposing them into named elements, and the modern neural-network evaluation is not element-based at all. The elements survive as the language humans use to EXPLAIN an evaluation rather than as the means of producing one - which is exactly the role they play in this system. Steinitz's central claim has aged well: engine analysis of the initial position supports equilibrium and games decided by error rather than by winning attacks.

preconditions: A position to be assessed
false_positive_traps: Listing elements is not evaluating. A position with several observations attached and no judgement about which dominates has not been assessed.
The permanent/temporary division is about durability, not importance. A temporary advantage can be decisive precisely because it is about to expire.
This system should use the elements to explain an engine's number, never to argue against it.

typical_plans: Assess before planning, and let the plan follow from the assessment
Attack where you are strongest or the opponent is weakest
Convert temporary advantages before they expire; bank permanent ones
tactical_consequences: Steinitz's rule that a combination requires a pre-existing advantage, which Lasker restated
strategic_consequences: Small advantages accumulate into decisive ones

exceptions: The theory's claim that attacks cannot succeed against correct defence in an equal position is a statement about correct defence, not about practical play, where unsound attacks win regularly.
The element lists are a later refinement and not Steinitz's own enumeration.
limitations: The elements organise a search; they do not weigh the results, and the weighing is the skill.
Hooper's propositions were consulted at second hand.
This base has not tested any element list against engine evaluation, and does not claim the lists are complete or correctly weighted.
misconceptions: That positional evaluation means counting material and adding adjustments. King safety and threats can make material irrelevant.
That Steinitz's lists are his own words. What circulates is a later refinement.
That an advantage can be accumulated indefinitely. Steinitz's seventh proposition says a sufficient advantage must be acted on or it dissipates.

examples.note: Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz 1908 at move 20, and it is here because the corpus annotation is itself a worked positional evaluation rather than a comment on a move: 'The bishop on e6 is bad, blocked by its own pawns. The knight was already traded off. The rooks have no open files. The queen is being chased. Black is completely passive.' Five features named, none of them material, and a verdict drawn from them. That is the method the record describes, performed by an annotator on a real board. The engine's number is the check on it: material is level and the position is not.
examples.attributed_by: corpus entry rubinstein-salwe-1908-20-bad-bishop

engine.verdict_note: +0.34 with material level. The evaluation the annotator reached from five static features and the evaluation the engine reaches from a twenty-two-ply search point the same way, which is the modest claim this record can make: the method is sound, and it is not precise.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-position-a-feature-scan-cannot-read`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: An ordinary middlegame with pieces developed, a queen on d4, bishops on b2 and d5, and no obvious weakness on either side. A positional evaluation would count the features and report a roughly balanced position with a small pull. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The position is decided by a single move. Bxb7+ uncovers a check and wins on the spot: +4.67 at depth 22, first choice by nearly four pawns. Nothing in the static features carries that; the concept's method — identify durable features, weigh them, draw a verdict — is the wrong instrument for a position whose answer is one move deep. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Shipped puzzle mi-f2e1be14e7. The API reports `battery`, `bad-bishop`, `king-safety` and `center-control` — a perfectly reasonable feature scan — and does not claim to have evaluated the position. That separation is the point: this record has no matcher, and the reason on the record is that a positional evaluation is a JUDGEMENT assembled from features rather than a feature, so reporting the features is the honest half of it. This base's ambiguous example for the same record is the opposite failure, Adams-Kasparov, where the features say one thing and the truth is +2.12 the other way.

ambiguous_examples.note: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005. Every static feature a positional evaluation would count says Black is in trouble: the king is about to step onto an open h-file in front of a bishop on g5, two rooks and a queen; White has a pawn on h7 and one on h5; the black king's cover is being dismantled. The evaluation is +2.12 FOR BLACK, and the engine's own first move is taking the pawn. The annotation says the decision was made by calculation rather than by judgement - 'his king may look exposed, but in actuality, there is no immediate danger.' Filed as ambiguous because this record's method is not wrong in general and is wrong here, and the position gives no way to tell which case you are in from the features alone. This base carries the same board as `king-attack`'s NEGATIVE and `modern-dynamic`'s POSITIVE.

by_level.beginner: Judge a position by more than material: is the king safe, are the pawns healthy, are the pieces doing anything?
by_level.intermediate: Assess in order - king safety, material, threats, activity, pawn structure, space - because the first two can make the rest irrelevant.
by_level.advanced: Separate permanent advantages from temporary ones. Temporary advantages must be used before they expire.
by_level.master: Steinitz's point was theoretical, not procedural: equilibrium holds until someone errs, so an attack without a pre-existing advantage should fail.

by_depth.short: Judge a position by its elements, not by material.
by_depth.normal: Positional evaluation: assessing a position by breaking it into elements - king safety, material, threats, piece activity, pawn structure and open lines, space - and dividing the advantages found into permanent ones, which can be banked, and temporary ones, which must be used before they expire.
by_depth.deep: The method began as a theory rather than a checklist. Steinitz's propositions start from equilibrium and reach a striking conclusion: correct play maintains it and draws, so a player wins only through an opponent's error and there is no such thing as a winning move. An attack on a position still in equilibrium must fail and leave the attacker worse for trying, so one should not attack without an advantage - and, the proposition that stops this being mere caution, once a sufficient advantage exists one MUST attack or it dissipates. The elements serve that argument, divided by durability into permanent advantages such as material, weak enemy pawns and the bishop pair, and temporary ones such as development, centralisation and space. What the method does not supply is priority, and priority is the skill.

explanations.lesson: Assess before you plan, and decide which single factor dominates - the list organises the search, it does not answer it.

positional-evaluation.definition_short: Judging a position by breaking it into elements - king safety, material, pawn structure, piece activity, space - rather than by counting material.
positional-evaluation.definition_long:
The method that turned chess from a game of attacks into a game of assessment, and it began as a theory rather than a checklist.

STEINITZ'S ACCUMULATION THEORY, in Hooper's seven propositions, is the argument the elements serve. It begins with equilibrium at the start of the game and reaches a startling conclusion: correct play by both sides maintains that equilibrium and draws, so a player can win only as a consequence of an error — 'there is no such thing as a winning move'. An attack against a position still in equilibrium must fail against correct defence and leave the attacker worse for having tried. Therefore one must not attack until an advantage exists, and — the proposition that stops the theory being merely cautious — once a sufficient advantage HAS been obtained, one MUST attack, or it dissipates.

THE ELEMENTS follow from that, and are divided by durability. PERMANENT advantages: material, a bad enemy king position, passed pawns, weak enemy pawns, strong and weak squares, pawn islands, a strong pawn centre, control of a file, rank or diagonal, and the bishop pair. TEMPORARY advantages: bad piece placement, inharmonious pieces, a lead in development, centralisation, and space. The division is the same one this base records as static versus dynamic, and it carries the same practical consequence: temporary advantages must be used before they expire, permanent ones can be banked.

THE MODERN WORKING ORDER is a short list applied consistently: king safety, material, threats, piece activity, pawn structure and the open lines it creates, and space. The order matters more than the contents, because king safety and immediate threats can make everything below them irrelevant.

WHAT EVALUATION DOES NOT SUPPLY is priority. A position usually contains several valid observations at once, and knowing which one dominates is the skill; the element list organises the search rather than answering it.

positional-sacrifice.knowledge_type_note: A strategic method rather than terminology, because it prescribes a way of playing — convert material into a static asset — rather than merely naming a move type. NOTE a genuine terminological collision: Spielmann uses 'positional sacrifice' for a SHAM sacrifice that regains material with an improved position, while modern usage means a REAL sacrifice for long-term static compensation. These are near-opposite meanings.

attributions.note: Used the phrase, but for a sham sacrifice with forced material recovery — not the modern meaning.
Made the positional exchange sacrifice a standing strategic method; devoted a chapter of one of his books to it.

history.notes: Disputed not about who used the phrase but about what it means. Spielmann's sense (sham, material returns) and the modern sense (real, material does not return) are close to opposites, and both are current. Do not attribute the modern concept to Spielmann.
competing_claims: Spielmann 1935: a sham sacrifice in which recovering the material is an essential characteristic.
Modern usage: a real sacrifice for static compensation, with no forced recovery.

development.change: Phrase used for temporary material investment with forced return.
Reframed as permanent investment for static assets; the exchange sacrifice becomes a positional instrument.

positional-sacrifice.engine_era_note: The class most changed by modern engines and by neural-network evaluation, which values long-term compensation far more highly than earlier material-weighted search did. Sacrifices that classical engines called simply bad are now often endorsed. That is a genuine revision in understanding rather than a change in the concept.

preconditions: Material is given up
No forced sequence recovers it
No mating attack follows
indicators_for: The compensation is static: structure, a permanent square, a colour complex, the bishop pair
The opponent's extra material has no active role — a rook with no open file, a bishop biting on granite
The resulting position would still be pleasant after further exchanges
The sacrifice removes the piece that was defending a complex
indicators_against: The compensation is described but not visible on the board
The opponent can return the material to liquidate into a good endgame
The asset gained is temporary and the material deficit is not
false_positive_traps: Calling any unclear sacrifice positional. If the point is an attack, it is not a positional sacrifice.
Asserting compensation that cannot be named. 'Positional compensation' with no named asset is the vaguest claim in chess writing and must not be produced by this system.
Spielmann's sense and the modern sense are opposite; using the phrase without saying which is meant is itself a false positive.

typical_plans: Exchange for the defender of a colour complex, then occupy it
Accept a material deficit to obtain a permanent outpost for a knight
Wreck the enemy structure permanently and play against the fixed weaknesses
Defensively: give material to remove the key attacking piece or reach a fortress
typical_moves: ...Rxc3 in Sicilian structures, wrecking the queenside and taking the dark squares
...Rxe4 giving the exchange for a pawn, the bishop pair and a better structure
typical_pawn_structures: Sicilian structures where ...Rxc3 doubles the c-pawns
Structures where one side's bishop is the sole guardian of a colour complex
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight established where no pawn can challenge it, bought with the exchange
strategic_consequences: The material deficit never expresses itself because the extra piece has no role
Assets survive into the endgame, unlike an attack

exceptions: The compensation must survive simplification. An asset that evaporates when queens come off is not positional compensation.
The opponent can often return the material at a good moment to reach a favourable endgame; a positional sacrifice must account for that resource.
Defensive positional sacrifices are a real and under-taught category.
limitations: Recognition confidence is LOW. Nothing forces the payoff, so the judgement cannot be checked by a short line.
The word is used in two near-opposite senses.
misconceptions: That a positional sacrifice is a slower attacking sacrifice. It is not an attack at all.
That Petrosian invented the term. He is associated with the modern practice; the phrase is older and meant something different.

examples.note: Petrosian's 25...Re6, offered for static compensation rather than for an attack or a forced recovery of material: a permanent blockading square for the knight on d5, and a bishop with no opposite number. This is the case the concept is built around — material given for factors that do not expire, with no combination attached.

engine.verdict_note: +0.97 at depth 22, and the engine's own first move is Bxe6 - the sacrifice itself. Both concepts filed against this position are claims about that one move, and the engine plays it: the material goes and the evaluation stays about a pawn in favour of the side giving it up, which is what compensation means stated as a number rather than asserted.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-sacrifice-whose-point-is-mate`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Rxd5 gives up a rook for a knight and gets no material back. Material invested for something other than material is what a positional sacrifice is. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "Calling any unclear sacrifice positional. If the point is an attack, it is not a positional sacrifice." Nothing is invested here at all — the rook cannot be recaptured, because Rxd5 would allow Re8 mate. The 'compensation' is a mate in two. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report positional-sacrifice. It reports back-rank-mate, hanging-piece and sacrifice, and the engine's line — Rxd5 followed by ...Rb8 rather than ...Rxd5 — shows what the move actually is: Black declines and is simply a knight down, +6.73. This record's second trap is the reason it has no matcher: 'asserting compensation that cannot be named. Positional compensation with no named asset is the vaguest claim in chess writing and must not be produced by this system.' The same position is `exchange-sacrifice`'s registered case and `overloading`'s positive example — three records reading one board, and only one of them is entitled to it.

ambiguous_examples.note: The Evans Gambit accepted. A pawn given for a tempo, the c3 and d4 squares and a half-open b-file - no attack yet, no forced line, and nothing material coming back. Whether that is a POSITIONAL sacrifice is precisely what this record refuses to settle, and its third trap says why: 'Spielmann's sense and the modern sense are opposite; using the phrase without saying which is meant is itself a false positive.' In Spielmann's vocabulary a sacrifice for lasting positional assets with no calculable return is the real sacrifice; in the modern one a gambit whose compensation is measurable is not a sacrifice at all. The engine measures it at -0.10 - full compensation exactly - which is the reading that satisfies both senses and settles neither.

engine.verdict_note: -0.10 at depth 24, a pawn down. The same position is `compensation`'s ambiguous example, and the two records disagree about what to call it while agreeing entirely about the board.

by_level.beginner: This gives up material not to attack, but to get something that lasts — a better pawn structure, or a square their pieces can never take back.
by_level.intermediate: A positional sacrifice: material for a lasting asset rather than an attack. The test is whether the compensation would still be worth something after more pieces come off.
by_level.advanced: Static compensation, no forced return. Name the asset — structure, colour complex, an eternal outpost — and check it survives simplification, because nothing forces the payoff.
by_level.master: Petrosian's instrument. The question is whether the opponent's extra material has a role: an exchange given for a knight that cannot be challenged and a structure that cannot be repaired is not a deficit in any operative sense.

by_depth.short: Material given up for a lasting positional asset, not an attack.
by_depth.normal: A positional sacrifice — material for static compensation such as {asset}, with no attack and no forced way to win the material back. It has to be judged rather than calculated, and the compensation must be durable enough to survive into an endgame.
by_depth.deep: Material converted into assets that do not expire: structure, squares, a colour complex, an unassailable outpost. Associated above all with Petrosian and the exchange sacrifice, whose point was never a mating attack but a permanent asset that made the opponent's extra material irrelevant. Note a terminological trap: Spielmann used 'positional sacrifice' for a SHAM sacrifice in which recovering the material was essential, which is close to the opposite of the modern meaning. Modern engines, especially neural-network evaluation, value this kind of compensation far more highly than older search did, and have rehabilitated a number of sacrifices previously called unsound.

explanations.lesson: If you cannot name the asset you are buying, and say why it will still matter after further exchanges, you are not making a positional sacrifice.

beginner_words: giving up material for something that lasts

positional-sacrifice.definition_short: Giving up material for long-term static compensation — structure, squares, a permanent outpost, the bishop pair — with no attack and no forced return.
positional-sacrifice.definition_long:
Material converted into assets that do not expire. Not an attack: the payoff is a better structure, an unassailable square, a colour complex, a crippled enemy majority, or the bishop pair. Because nothing forces the payoff, the compensation has to be strong enough to survive into any endgame, which is what makes these the hardest sacrifices to play.

TERMINOLOGY WARNING. Spielmann uses the phrase for something else — a SHAM sacrifice whose 'recapture of the material given up is an essential characteristic', i.e. material is lent and returned with a better position. Modern usage means the opposite: a REAL sacrifice where the material does not come back. Both usages are attested; a record or explanation must not silently pick one.

Tigran Petrosian is the player most associated with the modern sense, above all through the exchange sacrifice. The point of his sacrifices was not a mating attack but assets — an untouchable knight, a dark-square grip — and the material deficit simply never expressed itself.

It also works defensively, which most treatments omit: giving material to defuse an attack, remove a key attacking piece, or reach a fortress.

practical-principles.knowledge_type_note: Advice about playing a game rather than about a position; the distinction is enforced because this system explains positions.

attributions.note: Quoted for the stance that the practical question is the best move rather than the correct assessment.

history.notes: No single tradition; this record collects the practical stance from several sources already held.

practical-principles.engine_era_note: Engines sharpened the objective/practical distinction by making the objective half settleable. Before that the two were routinely argued as one thing.

preconditions: A game is being played by people
false_positive_traps: Practical advice is not a property of a position and must never be offered as the reason a move is good. This system sees a board, not a player, a clock or a tournament table.
A line being a good practical try is not a claim that it is sound, and the two must be reported separately.

typical_plans: Ask what the best move is rather than who stands better
Choose complexity or simplification according to who benefits from a mistake
Report objective soundness and practical value as two separate things

exceptions: In correspondence or analysis, where time and reference are unlimited, practical considerations largely disappear and only the objective claim remains.
limitations: Most circulating practical advice is untested, and this record deliberately excludes what it cannot support.
This system has no access to the clock, the opponent or the standings, and can give no practical advice at all.

by_level.intermediate: Practical advice depends on who is playing; objective advice does not. Keep them apart.
by_level.advanced: Purdy: the question that matters is what your best move is, not who has the theoretical advantage.
by_level.master: An engine verdict is the ceiling of a line's soundness and practical results are its floor; report both rather than blending them.

by_depth.short: Advice about playing a game, as distinct from the position.
by_depth.normal: Guidance that depends on the players, the clock and the situation rather than on the board. It is kept separate from objective claims on purpose, because a system that explains positions can see the board and cannot see any of the rest.
by_depth.deep: A deliberately small record, because most practical chess advice is untested and this base carries only what it can support. The organising distinction is that an objective claim is about the position and holds regardless of who is playing, while a practical claim is about the game. What is actually supported comes from the research on the neighbouring concepts: spend the clock where the position is unclear, expect risk aversion when short of time and over-reach after an error, and prefer a fast move to a good slow one under real time pressure. The standing caveat is that an engine verdict is the ceiling of a line's soundness and practical results are its floor.

explanations.lesson: Keep the two claims apart: what is true of the position, and what is wise for a person playing it.

practical-principles.definition_short: Guidance about how to play a game — the clock, the opponent, your own error patterns — as distinct from what is true of the position.
practical-principles.definition_long:
A deliberately small record, because most of what circulates as practical chess advice is untested and this base carries only what it can support.

THE ONE ORGANISING DISTINCTION: an OBJECTIVE claim is about the position and is true regardless of who is playing; a PRACTICAL claim is about the game and depends on the players, the clock and the tournament situation. Both are legitimate, and confusing them is how a system explaining a move ends up asserting something it cannot see. This system explains positions, so practical advice is recorded here for vocabulary and is never attached to a move.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY SUPPORTED, from the research recorded on the neighbouring concepts:
- Spend the clock in the middlegame and where the position is unclear, because that is where errors compound rather than add.
- Expect risk aversion when short of time, and expect over-reach immediately after a mistake.
- Under severe time pressure a fast move beats a good slow one — measurably.

PURDY'S POINT is worth keeping as the practical stance: 'the question that matters to you in actual play is simply, What is my best move?, and if you can decide without being sure who has the theoretical advantage, so much the better.' Assessment serves the move; it is not the product.

AND THE ENGINE-ERA CAVEAT that runs through this base: an engine verdict is the CEILING of a line's soundness and practical results are its floor. A gambit refuted only by a narrow computer defence is a poor objective choice and can be an excellent practical one, because the refutation has to be found at the board. This base states the objective verdict and flags where the practical value diverges, rather than blurring the two.

practical-psychology.knowledge_type_note: Restricted deliberately to effects that have been MEASURED. Chess psychology is full of confident folklore, and this record carries only what a study supports.

attributions.note: Established that masters do not search more widely, which is the foundation the later work builds on.

history.notes: A research literature rather than a chess tradition. Several results are recent and thinly replicated.

development.note: De Groot and then Chase and Simon establish pattern recognition and its limits.
Time-pressure studies show quality degrading for strong and weak players alike, more so for the weak.
Large-sample game analysis becomes possible, and engine benchmarks make move quality measurable.

practical-psychology.engine_era_note: The engine is what made this field possible: every modern result here depends on scoring human moves against an engine benchmark. Before that, claims about psychology at the board could not be checked at all.

preconditions: A human is playing
false_positive_traps: None of this is a property of a position and none of it may be attached to a move.
Chess psychology is unusually rich in confident unevidenced claims. This record holds only measured effects and names what it is leaving out.

by_level.beginner: When you are short of time you will play more cautiously than you should, especially when you are already worse.
by_level.intermediate: Errors are not random — they cluster where you are short of time AND the position is unclear.
by_level.advanced: Expect risk aversion under time pressure and over-reaching just after a mistake; both are measured tendencies, not character flaws.
by_level.master: Deliberation remains essential at world-champion level, which is not what a purely intuitive account of expertise would predict.

by_depth.short: The measured ways players depart from just playing the position.
by_depth.normal: The parts of chess psychology that have actually been measured: players become more risk-averse when short of time and most so in bad positions, take more risk just after an error, and blunder where low time and an unclear position coincide.
by_depth.deep: Chess writing about psychology is mostly assertion, so this record carries only measured effects. Professionals become more risk-averse as thinking time falls, most strongly in the bad positions where risk is most needed, and take more risk immediately after a mistake. Blunders cluster rather than scatter, concentrating where time pressure and positional ambiguity coincide and amplifying rather than adding. And deliberation remains central even for grandmasters and world champions, whose accuracy degrades under time pressure - which is not what a purely intuitive account of mastery would predict. What is deliberately absent is everything about intimidation, tilt and playing the opponent: possibly real, and not measured here.

explanations.hedge: Only measured effects are recorded, from population studies of many games; they describe tendencies rather than what any player should do in a given position.
explanations.lesson: Know where your errors cluster. That is more useful than resolving to make fewer.

practical-psychology.definition_short: The measured, non-obvious ways human decision-making at the board departs from simply choosing the best move.
practical-psychology.definition_long:
Chess writing about psychology is mostly assertion. This record holds the parts that have been measured, and says so where a claim is popular but unevidenced.

RISK AVERSION UNDER PRESSURE. Analysis of FIDE World Cups from 2013 to 2023 found that less thinking time consistently pushes professionals towards MORE RISK-AVERSE moves — and that the effect is strongest in bad positions, which is precisely where risk is most needed. The same study found correlational evidence of the opposite tendency after a mistake: players take more risk having just erred. Both are departures from playing the position in front of you.

ERRORS CLUSTER. Blunders are not scattered randomly through a game; they concentrate where low time and an unclear position coincide, and the two amplify each other rather than adding. Knowing WHERE your errors are likely is more useful than resolving to make fewer.

DELIBERATION IS NOT OPTIONAL, EVEN FOR EXPERTS. A study of twenty grandmasters and seven world champions found that time pressure hurt both their speed and their accuracy, and concluded that deliberate calculation remains central at the highest level. The popular picture of the master who simply sees the right move is not what the data shows; what elite players actually do is decide well WHEN to intuit and when to calculate.

PATTERN RECOGNITION IS REAL BUT NARROWER THAN CLAIMED. Masters recall real positions almost perfectly and random ones no better than novices, so the advantage is in meaningful structure rather than memory. And experts search slightly DEEPER than weaker players but not WIDER — the difference is in which moves they look at.

WHAT THIS RECORD DELIBERATELY OMITS: claims about intimidation, playing the opponent rather than the board, tilt, and confidence effects. They may well be real. This base has not found measurements for them, and a system that explains moves has no business asserting them.

promotion.knowledge_type_note: Official rule. Underpromotion is a consequence of the rule, not a separate rule.
promotion.definition_short: A pawn reaching the far rank is replaced, as part of the same move, by a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour.
promotion.definition_long:
A pawn reaching the eighth rank (first rank for Black) must be exchanged, as part of the same move, for a new queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour. The choice is not restricted to pieces already captured, and there is no limit on how many of a kind may be on the board.

FIDE Art. 4.6 governs the physical act: 'the pawn does not have to be placed on the square of arrival', the order of removing pawn and placing piece does not matter, and 'if an opponent's piece stands on the square of promotion, it must be captured.' Art. 4.4.4: the choice is finalised when the new piece touches the promotion square.

Choosing something other than a queen is UNDERPROMOTION, and is correct when a queen would stalemate, or when a knight's move is what the position needs (a check or fork a queen cannot give).

preconditions: A pawn is moving to the eighth rank (White) or first rank (Black)

exceptions: Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

examples.note: a pawn can promote on this move (f8=Q+). This is a DEFINITIONAL example: the feature is present by the rules of chess and by the page's own move generator, which is the whole of what needs verifying. No engine was consulted, because no engine is needed to establish that a legal move exists. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

counterexamples.note: A white pawn on the seventh rank and it can never promote. The enemy king stands on the queening square, nothing sits on d8 or f8 to capture, and no white piece can drive the king away - so the pawn is one square from the eighth rank for ever. The rule is not in doubt here and its PRECONDITION is: promotion happens when a pawn REACHES the far rank, and reaching it is a separate question the rule says nothing about. This base's positive example is the rule; this is the condition under it.

by_level.beginner: A pawn reaching the far end of the board turns into another piece — almost always a queen.
by_level.intermediate: Promotion. A queen is right nearly always, but check for stalemate, and check whether a knight would give a decisive check or fork.
by_level.advanced: Art. 3.7.5 / 4.6. Underpromotion is justified by stalemate avoidance or by knight geometry.

by_depth.short: A pawn reaching the far rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour.
by_depth.normal: Promotion: a pawn arriving on the eighth rank is replaced immediately, as part of the same move, by a piece of its own colour. The choice is free and unlimited — a side may have several queens — and it is not confined to pieces already captured.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 3.7.5 with Art. 4.6 on completing the move. Underpromotion has exactly two standard justifications and both are geometric rather than material: a rook instead of a queen because the queen would stalemate, and a knight because the knight reaches squares no queen does, most often with check. Everything else is a queen. The rule is also what makes a passed pawn worth calculating rather than counting.

prophylaxis.knowledge_type_note: A strategic principle and a method of THINKING rather than a board feature. It prescribes a question to ask, not a pattern to detect, which is why its detectability is human-only.

attributions.note: Verified against the primary text: he presents it as his own conception of positional play, explicitly ranking it above the accumulation of advantages.
Conventionally regarded as the great practitioner of prophylactic play. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED against a primary source.

history.notes: Unusually well founded: Nimzowitsch's own words were read in the full text of My System, and he claims the conception explicitly rather than being credited with it by others.

development.change: Introduced as the central idea of positional play, above accumulation.
Becomes standard technique, associated above all with Petrosian.
Vindicated in an unexpected way: engines routinely play quiet preventive moves that improve nothing directly, which is exactly what prophylaxis describes.

prophylaxis.engine_era_note: Strongly vindicated. Engines constantly prefer quiet moves that deny an opponent's resource over moves that improve their own position, and human commentators reach for the word 'prophylactic' to explain them. If anything the concept is more useful now than when it was coined, because engines demonstrate how often it is correct.

preconditions: A move that prevents an opponent's idea rather than advancing one's own
indicators_for: The opponent has a specific concrete resource, and the move removes it
The move improves nothing of the mover's own position
The opponent's plan was the only source of counterplay
A pawn move that denies a square before an enemy piece can reach it
indicators_against: The threat being prevented is not real
The prevention costs more than the threat was worth
The move is simply slow, and the opponent had nothing
false_positive_traps: Any quiet move can be called prophylactic after the fact. The claim requires naming the specific idea prevented — if you cannot name it, the move was just quiet.
Preventing a threat that does not exist is not prophylaxis, it is a wasted move.
This is not detectable from a static position. It is a property of what the move DENIES, which requires knowing what the opponent intended.

typical_plans: Before choosing a move, ask what the opponent would play if it were their turn
Deny the square, file or break the opponent's plan depends on
Internal prophylaxis: forestall the weaknesses your own plan would create
typical_moves: A quiet pawn move denying a square to an enemy knight
Kh1 or ...Kh8 stepping off a diagonal before it matters
An exchange that removes the opponent's best piece before it becomes active
tactical_consequences: Removes the tactical resource the opponent's position was resting on
strategic_consequences: Leaves the opponent without a plan, which is often decisive by itself

exceptions: Prevention has a cost. If the opponent's idea was not dangerous, the tempo is simply lost.
In sharp positions, speed can outweigh prevention — a prophylactic move in a race loses the race.
Nimzowitsch's ranking of prophylaxis above accumulation is a claim about emphasis and was polemical; the two are complementary.
limitations: Not detectable from a position, and this is intrinsic: prophylaxis is defined by what a move prevents, so recognising it requires modelling the opponent's intention.
The easiest concept in the base to assert falsely, because any quiet move can be described this way afterwards.
misconceptions: That prophylaxis means passive or defensive play. Nimzowitsch explicitly says it is neither attack nor defence.
That it only concerns the opponent. He distinguishes external from internal prophylaxis, the latter aimed at one's own position.
That it is a modern refinement. It is his stated central conception of positional play, from 1925.

conflicts.resolution: Genuine tension. The initiative must be used before it expires, and a prophylactic move spends a tempo on prevention rather than pressure. Which applies depends on whether the opponent actually has a resource worth denying: with the initiative and a concrete continuation, press; without one, prevention is usually the better use of the move.

examples.note: Classified by GM Naroditsky as the PROPHYLACTIC exchange sacrifice: its first purpose is to stop something. Petrosian saw White's plan — h4 provoking a kingside weakness, then the bishop back to c1 with an attack, supported by a mobile centre — and spent the exchange to make the plan impossible rather than to meet it move by move. Recorded here because prophylaxis is normally illustrated with a quiet defensive move, and the concept is about preventing a specific idea, whatever it costs.

engine.verdict_note: +0.97 at depth 22, and the engine's own first move is Bxe6 - the sacrifice itself. Both concepts filed against this position are claims about that one move, and the engine plays it: the material goes and the evaluation stays about a pawn in favour of the side giving it up, which is what compensation means stated as a number rather than asserted.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-quiet-move-preventing-nothing`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kd1 in a locked position: a quiet, non-committal move that loses nothing and can be described afterwards as restraining Black's plans. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "Any quiet move can be called prophylactic after the fact. The claim requires naming the specific idea prevented — if you cannot name it, the move was just quiet." Nothing is prevented here; the structure prevents everything by itself, and did so before the move. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports nothing at all here — not prophylaxis, not restraint, not anything. That is the correct answer and it is the one a keyword rule would fail: every word in the record about quiet moves in blocked positions is true of this position, and the concept is absent. This record's third trap is why there is no matcher for it: prophylaxis is a property of what a move DENIES, which requires knowing what the opponent intended, and this base does not guess at intentions.

ambiguous_examples.note: Fischer-Spassky 1972, game 6, 30.h4 - and the ambiguity is which concept it belongs to. This base carries it as `restraint`'s positive example, on the annotation '30.h4! Restricting the knight on h7 even further'. But Havanur's wording names a SPECIFIC idea being prevented: 'after this move neither the black queen nor the knight can use g5 as a springboard.' Naming the specific idea is exactly what this record demands before a prophylaxis claim can be made - its first trap is 'the claim requires naming the specific idea prevented' - and a named annotator has named it. The two concepts are separated in this base on the general-versus-specific line, and this move is on the line. The engine adds a second layer: it is the THIRD choice at +3.75 against +4.15 for 30.e6, so the restraining move is good and not best.

engine.verdict_note: The annotated move is the engine's THIRD choice at +3.75, against +4.15 for 30.e6, at depth 22 with three lines. Partial agreement, and the gap is 40 centipawns - small enough that the move is not refuted and large enough that it is not endorsed either.

by_level.beginner: Instead of asking what you want to do, ask what they want to do — and stop it.
by_level.intermediate: A prophylactic move. It does not improve your position; it removes the resource their position depended on.
by_level.advanced: Prophylaxis in Nimzowitsch's sense, and note he distinguishes external — aimed at the opponent's moves — from internal, aimed at weaknesses your own plan would create.
by_level.master: He ranked it above the accumulation of advantages, which was a deliberate shot at the classical school. Engines have largely vindicated the emphasis.

by_depth.short: This stops their idea before it happens.
by_depth.normal: Prophylaxis: preventing the opponent's plan rather than pursuing your own. The move often improves nothing of yours, which is why it is hard to find — the value is entirely in what it denies.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch's central conception of positional play, and he put it above Steinitz's accumulation of small advantages: 'neither attack nor defence are what is essential... what is needed is a far more energetic and targeted prophylaxis.' He divides it into external prophylaxis, directed at the opponent's moves, and internal, directed at the weaknesses one's own plans would create — a distinction most modern summaries drop. The method is a question rather than a pattern: before moving, ask what the opponent would play if it were their turn. Engines have vindicated the emphasis, since they constantly prefer quiet preventive moves over moves that improve anything.

explanations.lesson: Before you choose a move, spend one moment on their position: if it were their turn, what would they play? Quite often stopping that is worth more than anything you had planned.

beginner_words: what do they want to do?

prophylaxis.definition_short: Preventing the opponent's ideas before they materialise — asking what they want to do, and stopping it, rather than only pursuing your own plan.
prophylaxis.definition_long:
Nimzowitsch's own statement of it, from My System, is stronger than the way it is usually reported: 'The well-known accumulation of tiny advantages is only the second (or perhaps third) most important thing; what is far more significant is prophylaxis (anticipation of problems)... neither attack nor defence are what is essential, in my opinion, in positional play; what is needed is a far more energetic and targeted prophylaxis. What is important above all is to head off certain positionally undesirable possibilities before they materialise.'

That is a direct challenge to the classical school. Steinitz's doctrine was the accumulation of small advantages; Nimzowitsch demotes it to second or third place and puts prevention first.

HE SPLITS IT IN TWO, and modern summaries usually lose the distinction. EXTERNAL prophylaxis is directed at the opponent's moves — seeing what they intend and denying it. INTERNAL prophylaxis is directed at one's OWN position — anticipating the weaknesses one's own plans would create and forestalling them. The second is the less obvious and the more characteristic.

In practice the method is a question rather than a pattern: before choosing a move, ask what the opponent would play if it were their turn, and whether preventing it is worth more than your own plan. A prophylactic move often improves nothing of yours — which is exactly why it is hard to find and easy to under-value.

queen-activity.knowledge_type_note: Observations about how the most valuable piece behaves, which is mostly a story about what it cannot afford to do.

history.notes: No coinage; ordinary observations about the piece.

queen-activity.engine_era_note: Engines are far more willing than classical teaching to bring the queen out early when concrete lines support it, which has softened the rule without removing its basis - the tempo cost is real and measurable.

preconditions: A queen is on the board
indicators_for: Weaknesses on both square colours
An exposed enemy king
A passed pawn the queen can escort
indicators_against: The queen can be attacked by cheaper pieces with tempo
The queen is tied to defending a single point
false_positive_traps: An advanced queen is not an active queen. It is often a queen about to be chased, and the chasing moves develop the opponent.
This base measured the early-queen cost at about 0.68 in the standard case - real, and much smaller than the usual teaching tone.

typical_plans: Bring the queen in after the minor pieces, not before
Use it against positions weak on both colours
Escort a passed pawn with it in the endgame
Decide deliberately whether to allow the queen trade
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen behind a rook or bishop in a battery, rather than in front
Queen and knight together
tactical_consequences: The queen is the piece most vulnerable to forks and skewers, precisely because of its value
strategic_consequences: Trading queens changes the phase and with it what the king is for

exceptions: In endgames the queen leads perfectly well, since there is nothing cheap left to chase it.
Some openings bring the queen out early by design and pay a measured, affordable price.
limitations: The queen-and-knight claim is recorded from the literature and has not been tested here.
Most of this record is about what the queen should not do, which reflects the sources rather than a bias.

Named 2026-09-02 as the concept that fits a corpus position `piece-activity` cannot: Keene's note on Reti-Capablanca 1924 that Capablanca 'is doing his utmost with his strongest piece'. A single-piece activity claim needs a single-piece detector, and this concept has none.
misconceptions: That the strongest piece should attack first. Its value is exactly why it should not.
That an advanced queen is doing something. It is usually about to be attacked.

counterexamples.note: After 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 - the most-played illustration in existence of this record's first trap: 'An advanced queen is not an active queen. It is often a queen about to be chased, and the chasing moves develop the opponent.' What makes this a good counterexample rather than a cheap one is the SIZE of the effect. The engine says +0.39 for White, which is an ordinary opening edge, and this base has measured the early-queen cost at about 0.68 in the standard case. The move is not a blunder, and the teaching tone around it is louder than the number. The record says that too, and this position is why it says it.

engine.verdict_note: +0.39 at depth 24, and the engine's own line is ...Nc6 and ...g6 with Qf3 - the queen driven back to a square it could have reached in one move, having developed two black pieces on the way. The trap's mechanism is visible in the principal variation rather than in the number.

ambiguous_examples.note: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924, 27...Qe5, annotated by Raymond Keene: 'Capablanca is really doing his utmost on the fourth rank with his strongest piece, but the queen is no match for White's heavily centralised knights and rooks.' This record's limitations already named this position as the one it exists to cover; this is it, on the record. It is ambiguous in the strict sense - the queen genuinely IS the most active piece on the board, a titled annotator says so in as many words, and it is worth nothing: Keene's own verdict is that Black had to give up the exchange with 27...Rxe3 instead. Corpus entries `reti-capablanca-1924-27Qe5-initiative-negative` and `reti-capablanca-1924-27Qe5-piece-activity-ambiguous` are the same position read for two neighbouring concepts.
