engine.verdict_note: The engine prefers the exchange sacrifice Keene recommends over the queen move that was played: the annotation and the engine agree that one active queen is not the resource here. Depth 22, multipv 3, carried over from the corpus entry.

by_level.beginner: The queen is the strongest piece, which is why it should not go first — everything can chase it.
by_level.intermediate: Bring the queen in behind the other pieces. In front, it gets attacked and driven back with tempo.
by_level.advanced: It is strongest where its rook and bishop movements combine rather than duplicate — weaknesses on both colours, or an exposed king.
by_level.master: Whether to allow the queen trade is often the whole strategic question, because it changes what the king is for.

by_depth.short: The strongest piece, and the wrong one to attack with first.
by_depth.normal: The queen moves as rook and bishop together, and is worth more than anything that can attack it - so it must retreat from every threat. That is why it should not lead an attack or come out early, and why tying it to defending one point wastes it.
by_depth.deep: Almost everything true about queen play follows from its value: it must retreat from any threat, so a queen that arrives first is driven back with tempo by cheaper pieces, and a queen tied to one defensive job is a nine-point piece doing a one-point task. It is strongest where its two movements combine rather than duplicate - against weaknesses on both colours, against an exposed king, and escorting a passed pawn it can shepherd alone. Queen and knight complement each other where queen and rook duplicate lines, which is a real asymmetry though an untested one here. And the queen trade is often the most consequential exchange available, because it changes what the king is for.

explanations.lesson: The queen goes in last, and the decision to trade it is usually bigger than it looks.

queen-activity.definition_short: The queen combines rook and bishop movement, which makes it the strongest piece and the worst attacker to lead with.
queen-activity.definition_long:
THE QUEEN'S PROBLEM IS ITS VALUE. It moves like a rook and a bishop together and is therefore worth more than any piece that can attack it, so it must retreat from every threat. That single fact generates most of what is true about queen play:

- IT SHOULD NOT LEAD AN ATTACK. A queen arriving first is attacked by cheaper pieces and driven off with tempo. It belongs behind the attack, arriving when the defenders are already committed.
- IT SHOULD NOT COME OUT EARLY, for the same reason, which this base has measured at about two thirds of a pawn in the standard case.
- IT IS A POOR BLOCKADER and a poor defender of a single point, because tying a nine-point piece to one job wastes most of it.

WHERE IT IS STRONGEST is where its two movements combine rather than duplicate: against a position with weaknesses on both colours, against an exposed king where checks come from everywhere, and in endgames with a passed pawn it can escort alone.

THE QUEEN AND KNIGHT PAIRING is a genuine observation worth keeping: the two complement each other because the knight covers the squares the queen cannot reach in one move, while queen and rook duplicate lines. It is a real asymmetry rather than a saying, though this base has not tested it and records it as sourced rather than demonstrated.

THE EXCHANGE OF QUEENS is often the most consequential trade on the board, because it converts the position into one where the king is a piece rather than a liability. Deciding whether to allow it is frequently the whole strategic question.

queen-endgames.knowledge_type_note: A principle-level record; the concrete theory of these endings largely resisted human analysis and is now tablebase territory.

history.notes: No individual attribution traced. The historically notable fact is negative: the theory of queen and pawn versus queen was not completed by human analysis, and tablebases settled it.

development.note: Queen and pawn versus queen resisted complete human analysis.
Solved exhaustively; the class is now looked up rather than derived.

queen-endgames.engine_era_note: The clearest case in the endgame domain of a class that humans could not finish and machines simply solved. Queen endings are also where engine defence most often finds perpetual checks that human analysis had missed.

preconditions: Queens and pawns only, or nearly so
indicators_for: A far-advanced passed pawn
An exposed king on either side
A king that can be sheltered from checks
false_positive_traps: Counting pawns is a poor guide here: an advanced passed pawn outweighs a numerical deficit, because a queen can escort it alone.
An extra pawn is much less often decisive than in a rook ending, and this class wins less frequently than the rook equivalent.
Reasoning from principle is weak in queen endings. Where the position is small enough for a tablebase, look it up.

typical_plans: Advance a passed pawn with the queen behind or beside it
Find shelter for your own king so the checks run out
As the defender, start checking before the enemy king finds shelter
Meet a check with a check
typical_moves: Centralising queen moves that shield the king and support the pawn
typical_pawn_structures: A far-advanced passed pawn
typical_piece_arrangements: The queen placed to block checks on the file or diagonal the enemy queen wants
tactical_consequences: Perpetual check is the defence and must be calculated, not estimated
strategic_consequences: Material counting is unusually unreliable in this class

exceptions: Where the defending king is exposed, the usual perpetual-check defence may fail and ordinary material logic returns.
Fortresses exist in queen endings and defeat material reasoning entirely.
limitations: This base holds no tablebase-verified queen-ending positions yet; the record is orientation rather than theory.
The class is large and mostly concrete; principles help less here than anywhere else in the endgame.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION. The examples on this record are `tablebase-position`s, and for this family that is the stronger provenance rather than a substitute: the claims here are about what a class of ending can and cannot do, and a proof over every legal continuation settles that where a single game only illustrates it. What a master game would add is evidence that the principle GUIDED a strong player, which is a different claim, and this base has not yet found an annotated position making it for this family. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Capablanca-Marshall, USA match 1909, above.
misconceptions: That an extra pawn should win. Queen endings convert less often than rook endings, which are themselves notoriously drawish.
That perpetual check is a lucky escape. It is the defender's standard plan and should be expected.

examples.note: Constructed. Queen and pawn against queen, and the whole ending turns on one thing this record names: the checks. The defending queen can check almost anywhere, so the attacker wins only by finding shelter for his king, and the shelter here is the pawn itself - the white king stands on c7 in front of it, where a whole family of checking lines is blocked by his own pawn. That is why the win exists at all, and why the same material with the king anywhere else is usually drawn.

The record's claim is that an advanced passed pawn outweighs extra material here and that the defender's standing resource is perpetual check, and the position has the ingredients: Black's c4 pawn is passed and two squares from queening, and both kings are in the open where a queen can check them from anywhere.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT CAME WITH IT. A first scan of 100,106 positions from 1,320 replayed master games found NO queen ending at all, and the reason is not master play: this base's own `phaseOf()` calls a queen-and-pawns-against-queen-and-pawns position a MIDDLEGAME. Two queens is more material than its endgame threshold allows, which is right for most purposes and wrong for this record. Dropping the phase gate and asking the material directly found 372, every one of them classified `middlegame`. The limitation is recorded in state/research-state.json.

WHAT IS CLAIMED. The category, which the material decides mechanically. Not who is better - that is a different question and this record's own typical_confidence says so.

PROVENANCE. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The claim has 'advanced' in it and the pawn is on the third rank. The mechanism the record describes is that a queen can escort a passer to promotion alone, without the king; a pawn five squares from queening gives the defending queen five moves to arrange checks, and the material count decides after all. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN LOSS for the side with the passer, dtz -9, mate in 20 against. The API reports `passed-pawn` and `king-activation` and says nothing about queen endings, which have no matcher. What makes the case worth registering is that the record's own sentence contains the condition and the condition is the whole claim: read without the word 'advanced', the sentence says a passed pawn beats a queen, and this position is what that would mean.

What makes this ambiguous rather than simply an exception is that the record cannot say which way it cuts - the same sentence that predicts material will fail also predicts that an advanced passer outweighs the count, and both are operating here on opposite sides. The file of the pawn decides, and no principle on this record names files.

by_level.beginner: Queens and pawns. Watch for endless checks — they save a lot of these positions.
by_level.intermediate: An advanced passed pawn matters more than an extra pawn, because the queen can escort it alone. The defence is perpetual check.
by_level.advanced: Shelter your king so the checks run out, and remember you can answer a check with a check.
by_level.master: Human analysis never finished queen and pawn versus queen; it was tablebases that did. Treat the class as reference material.

by_depth.short: Advanced passed pawns decide; perpetual check saves.
by_depth.normal: Endings of queens and pawns. Because a queen can escort a passed pawn to promotion unaided, how far advanced a passer is outweighs how many pawns each side has - and the defender's constant resource is perpetual check, which makes converting an extra pawn hard.
by_depth.deep: The sharpest and longest of the common endings, and where material arithmetic breaks down most completely. A queen escorts a passed pawn alone, so advancement outweighs number, and the defence is always perpetual check in principle - so the attacker's real task is finding shelter for their own king, sometimes behind their own pawns and sometimes behind the enemy king, with the characteristic winning trick being to answer a check with a check. The class is very long and very concrete: queen and pawn against queen is the second most common piece-and-pawn ending, it wins less often than the rook equivalent, and human analysts never completed its analysis before tablebases did.

explanations.lesson: Count how far the pawn has come, not how many pawns there are - and expect to be checked.

queen-endgames.definition_short: Endings with queens and pawns, where an advanced passed pawn outweighs extra material and the defender's standing resource is perpetual check.
queen-endgames.definition_long:
The sharpest and longest of the common endings, and the one where the usual arithmetic of material breaks down most completely.

THE PASSED PAWN OUTWEIGHS THE COUNT. A queen can escort a passed pawn to promotion ALONE, without help from the king, so how far advanced a passer is matters more than how many pawns each side has. Kasparov versus the World is the standard illustration: Kasparov won with fewer pawns because his was further advanced.

PERPETUAL CHECK IS THE DEFENCE, and it is always available in principle, which is why converting an extra pawn is so hard. The defender is not trying to hold a position but to reach an endless sequence of checks before the attacker's pawn arrives.

THE TECHNIQUE FOLLOWS FROM THAT. The attacker's task is to find shelter for their own king — often using their own pawns, sometimes using the enemy king — so that checks run out; and the characteristic winning trick is to answer a check WITH a check, which no other ending offers so readily. Centralising the queen and placing it to shield the king while supporting the pawn is the standard winning arrangement.

THESE ENDINGS ARE VERY LONG, and that is a fact about the theory, not the players: queen and pawn against queen is the second most common piece-and-pawn ending after rook and pawn against rook, and human analysts could not complete its analysis at all before endgame tablebases. It also wins less often than the corresponding rook ending.

THIS BASE THEREFORE TREATS QUEEN ENDINGS AS A PLACE TO LOOK THINGS UP rather than to reason about. Where a position is small enough for a tablebase, the tablebase is the authority, and the principles above are for orientation.

ranks-files-diagonals.knowledge_type_note: Vocabulary for the board's lines, and the observation that the lines are what long-range pieces actually fight over.

history.notes: Elementary vocabulary defined in the Laws of Chess.

preconditions: A board
recognition.detector: fileState / sliderLines in lib/features.js and blind-chess.html
false_positive_traps: A line being open is a fact; its being useful is not. This base holds a tested position where an open file with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing.

typical_plans: Open a file for the rooks with a pawn break
Fianchetto to take a long diagonal
Keep the pawns off the colour your bishop travels on
tactical_consequences: Pins, skewers, x-rays and batteries all require a line
strategic_consequences: Pawn moves are the only way to open or close a file, which is why structure governs activity

exceptions: Knights ignore lines entirely, which is what makes them the right piece for closed positions.
limitations: Vocabulary. It names what the pieces fight over; it does not say who wins the fight.
Rests on the Laws of Chess for the definitions and one encyclopedia article for the rest, with no evidence of this base's own; the source confidence is medium accordingly.
misconceptions: That a rook belongs on any open file. It belongs on one with a square to invade.
That diagonals are secondary to files. The long diagonals are the longest lines on the board.

examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein, Berlin 1928, 23.Re7 - a RANK rather than a file, which is why it is the right positive for this record. The three kinds of line are not interchangeable in value: a file is a road, a diagonal is a road with a colour, and the seventh rank is a road that runs behind the enemy pawns. Van Der Nat: 'he plays 23.Re7 and seizes the seventh rank. A rook planted on the seventh, behind the enemy pawns, attacks everything on that rank and hunts any pawn that dares advance.' Read against this record's registered false-positive case, an open FILE that leads to an empty corner and is worth exactly nothing: the same geometric fact, and the difference is entirely what the line arrives at.
examples.attributed_by: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM) - corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-23Re7-rook-on-the-seventh

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `an-open-file-worth-nothing`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The a-file is open — no pawn of either colour on it — and a white rook stands on it. Open files are what rooks are for, and the line is a fact anyone can read off the board. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own trap, and it names this position type: "A line being open is a fact; its being useful is not. This base holds a tested position where an open file with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing." Here it is worth nothing: the file leads to an empty corner, there is no entry square, and material is symmetric. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `open-file` — which is true and is a statement about the pawns — and refuses `piece-activity`, which would be the claim that the file is doing something. Stockfish 18 at depth 28: 0.00, and its own first move puts the rook on the sixth, where it also achieves nothing. The same position is `piece-activity`'s registered false-positive case; it is registered here as well because the two records make different claims about it and both have to be right at once — the geometry is real and its value is separate.

by_level.beginner: Rows are ranks, columns are files, slants are diagonals.
by_level.intermediate: Long-range pieces fight over lines rather than squares — a rook is worth what its file is worth.
by_level.advanced: Only pawns can open or close a file, which is the mechanical link between structure and activity.
by_level.master: The long diagonals are the longest lines on the board and run through the centre, which is the whole case for the fianchetto.

by_depth.short: Ranks are rows, files are columns, diagonals are slants.
by_depth.normal: The board's three kinds of line. They matter because long-range pieces fight over lines rather than squares: a rook's strength is a property of its file, a bishop's of its diagonal.
by_depth.deep: Ranks run across, files up and down, diagonals at a slant, and the vocabulary earns its place because the long-range pieces contest lines rather than squares. Pins, skewers, x-rays and batteries exist only along one. Pawns decide which lines exist, since they are the only pieces that cannot move sideways — a file is opened by a pawn move and by nothing else — which is the mechanical reason pawn structure governs piece activity and is treated as the more permanent of the two.

explanations.lesson: Ask what line a piece is on before asking what square it is on.

avoid: diagonals are less important than files

ranks-files-diagonals.definition_short: The three kinds of straight line on the board: rows, columns and slants.
ranks-files-diagonals.definition_long:
RANKS are the rows, numbered 1 to 8 from White's side. FILES are the columns, lettered a to h from White's left. DIAGONALS are the slants, named by their end squares (the a1-h8 diagonal).

WHY THE VOCABULARY MATTERS is that the long-range pieces do not fight over squares so much as over LINES. A rook's power is a function of the file it stands on; a bishop's is a function of the diagonal. This is why so many positional concepts in this base are stated as facts about lines — open and semi-open files, the seventh rank, the long diagonal, batteries, pins and skewers, which exist only along a line.

PAWNS DECIDE THE LINES. Pawns are the only pieces that cannot move sideways, so a file is opened or closed by pawn moves and by nothing else, and a diagonal is blocked by whichever pawns sit on its colour. That is the mechanical link between pawn structure and piece activity, and it is why structure is treated as the more permanent of the two.

THE LONG DIAGONALS (a1-h8 and h1-a8) are singled out because they are the longest lines on the board and pass through the centre, which is what makes a fianchettoed bishop a strategic asset rather than a developed piece.

removing-the-defender.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). The three defender-removal ideas (removal, deflection, overloading) shade into each other and sources draw the lines differently.
removing-the-defender.definition_short: Capturing or driving off the piece that defends a target, so the target can then be taken.
removing-the-defender.definition_long:
The most direct of the defender-removal ideas: instead of attacking the target, attack what holds it. Informant theme a, 'Annihilation of Defence'. UNDERMINING is the same idea applied to a pawn that supports a piece or a key square.

It differs from deflection in that the defender is destroyed or driven off rather than lured into abandoning its post, and from overloading in that the defender may have only one job — it is simply removed.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A target is defended
The defender can be captured or driven away
indicators_for: The defender is the only one
Capturing it is at worst an even trade
indicators_against: A second defender exists
Removing the defender costs more than the target
recognition.detector: proposed, and deliberately unclaimed (not yet written)

exceptions: Fails against a second defender, or when the removal costs more than it wins.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE YET, and four constructions were tried and thrown away. Each failed the same way: a position where removing the defender is available and WRONG turns out, on inspection, to be one where the removal simply wins - taking a knight with a rook and then collecting the target is worth doing far more often than not, so the material arithmetic that would make the concept ambiguous is hard to arrange. The nearest attempt, two rooks against a rook and knight with the defender capturable, evaluates at +5.66 for the removal against +0.19 for the alternative, which is a positive example rather than an ambiguous one. Recorded so the next attempt does not start over.

examples.note: The Opera Game, 13.Rxd7 - the first of the two removals that make the finish work. The knight on d7 is holding the d-file together and Morphy gives a rook for it; three moves later he gives the bishop for the replacement knight, and four moves later the queen for the third defender. The concept's two preconditions are satisfied at every step: a target is defended, and the defender can be captured. What makes this the master-game example rather than a constructed one is that the same idea is executed three times in a row against three different pieces, which is not something a made-up position shows. PROVENANCE, stated plainly. The game is famous and the move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js - 33 plies, every one legal, which is what makes the FEN trustworthy rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and NOT the human-grounded one: it is evidence that the concept occurs in master play, and not evidence that a person named it here. The validation ladder already draws that line for eleven other concepts and it is drawn again here.
examples.game: Morphy-Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858 (the Opera Game)

Bxf6 then Rxd5. What makes this the clean case rather than a fork is that the bishop's capture wins nothing by itself - the knight is worth more than the pawn that follows - so the move only makes sense as removal of a guard.

engine.verdict_note: +4.81, settled at depth 1. The engine plays the removal and then takes on d5 in its own line.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `removing-one-of-two-defenders`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Bxd5 captures a defended pawn and removes a unit that was guarding it. Capturing what defends the target is the concept's second precondition, word for word. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: The first precondition is that the target IS defended after the removal, and here the d5 pawn has two defenders — the pawns on c6 and e6. Taking one leaves the other, so nothing has been removed in the sense the concept means: the whole idea is that the target becomes takeable, and it does not. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report removing-the-defender. This record's positive example is the same shape with ONE defender — a knight on f6 guarding d5, a bishop on g5 to take it, +4.81 — and the two differ by a single pawn. The concept is a counting claim before it is a tactical one, which is why the positive example's note says what makes it clean: the bishop's capture wins nothing by itself, so the move only makes sense as removal of a guard.

by_level.beginner: Take the piece that was guarding it, and then the guarded piece falls too.
by_level.intermediate: Removing the defender. Count defenders first — this only works if it is the last one.
by_level.advanced: Annihilation of defence (Informant theme a). Undermining is the pawn-support version.

by_depth.short: Capture or drive off the guard, and the guarded piece falls.
by_depth.normal: Removing the defender: the target is defended, the defender can be captured or chased away, and once it is gone the target is takeable. The move that removes the guard often wins nothing by itself, which is what marks it out from an ordinary capture.
by_depth.deep: It is a counting claim before it is a tactical one, and the count is how many defenders there are: taking one of two removes nothing. Morphy does it three times in a row in the Opera Game — a rook for the knight on d7, then a bishop for the knight that replaces it, then the queen for the third defender — which is not something a constructed position shows. The exchange also has to be worth making: capturing a guard worth more than the target it guards is a different move with a different name.

restraint.knowledge_type_note: A strategic method: it prescribes a way of playing — reduce what the opponent can do — rather than naming a board feature.

attributions.note: The formula and the surrounding theory are his, and the maxim was verified verbatim in the primary text.

history.notes: Verified in the full text of My System, where the formula appears twice, once as the motto of an illustrative game.

restraint.engine_era_note: Engines play restraining moves constantly, and human commentary reaches for this vocabulary to explain them. The concept is unrevised.

preconditions: A move that reduces the opponent's options rather than advancing one's own plan
indicators_for: An enemy pawn break is prevented or made costly
An enemy piece is denied its best square before it gets there
The opponent's pawn mass is fixed and can no longer expand
indicators_against: The advance being restrained was not something the opponent wanted anyway
Restraining costs more than permitting
The position demands speed
false_positive_traps: Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours.
Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.

typical_plans: Fix the enemy pawn mass before attacking it
Deny the square an enemy piece needs
Restrain, blockade, destroy — in that order
typical_pawn_structures: Fixed enemy pawn chains
strategic_consequences: Reduces the opponent to waiting, which is often decisive by itself

exceptions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.
limitations: Not detectable from a static position: it is defined by what a move prevents.

MEASURED 2026-09-02, against the record's own second trap: 'like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.' This base does NOT name the advance. Its matcher measures the change in the opponent's SAFE destination squares across the move, which is a count and not a name, and reports the count. Naming the prevented advance needs a model of what the opponent intended, which nothing here has. The count is the honest half and it is what is reported; the record's instruction is not met and is recorded here rather than looking unnoticed.
misconceptions: That restraint is defensive. Nimzowitsch treats it as the first stage of an attacking plan.
That it is the same as the blockade. The blockade is restraint made permanent by a piece.

examples.note: Black's e6 pawn cannot advance and the whole position is built to keep it that way — Nimzowitsch's note four moves earlier reads 'The immobility of the e-pawn is now greater than ever.' Restraint rather than prophylaxis: nothing specific is being prevented, the opponent's general mobility is being reduced, which is the distinction this record exists to preserve. FEN verified by replay.

engine.verdict_note: -0.47 at depth 22. Restraint is not an advantage claim and this record's own trap says so - 'restraint is not the same as passivity' - so the useful reading is that the restrained side is not better despite the material being level, which is the effect the concept names.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-quiet-move-that-restrains-nothing`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kd1 in a fully locked position is a quiet, non-committal move that does not lose anything. Quiet moves in blocked positions are the shape prophylaxis and restraint are usually claimed about. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's traps, both of them: "Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours." And: "Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented." No advance is being prevented — the structure prevents them all by itself, and it did so before the move. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API is silent on restraint. The matcher asks whether the move reduces the opponent's safe destinations rather than whether it is quiet, which is the first trap built rather than quoted; and it is move-based, so it cannot be asserted after the fact about the position. This is the case that a keyword rule would fail: every word in the record about quiet moves in blocked positions is present here and the concept is absent.

This is the negative half: the position is fully locked, nothing is being restrained because nothing can advance in the first place, and the evaluation confirms that no advantage attaches to the quiet move that was played.

ambiguous_examples.note: Nominated by tools/mine_ambiguous.js on its fourth ground, NOT-THE-MOVE: the concept fires on a legal move that is not the solution of a shipped puzzle. The first three grounds ask about a POSITION and could not reach a move-based or motif concept at all - this concept and eleven others reported NONE until the tool learned to supply a move. What makes the case ambiguous rather than false is that nothing reported is absent: b3-b4 genuinely reduces Black's safe destinations - it takes c5 from the knight on a6 and from the pieces behind it, which is what this base measures rather than 'total piece scope'. It is also a move made while a whole bishop is hanging on f8. This record's third indicator_against says it out loud - 'the position demands speed' - and this position is that sentence with a number: +0.24 for the restraining move, +4.37 for taking the rook.

engine.verdict_note: b4 scores +0.24 and Bxa3, the solution, scores +4.37. Restraint is a slow idea and this is a position with no time in it, which is exactly the condition the record states and the matcher cannot test.

by_level.beginner: Stop their pawns from moving forward before you try to win them.
by_level.intermediate: Restraint: reduce what they can do. It is the first step of restrain, blockade, destroy — stop the pawn, then block it, then take it.
by_level.advanced: The general case of the blockade. Distinguish it from prophylaxis: prophylaxis prevents a specific idea, restraint reduces general mobility.
by_level.master: Nimzowitsch's Hemmungstheorie. The cost is the same as prophylaxis's — the move does nothing for you, so what it prevents must be worth preventing.

by_depth.short: Stop them expanding before you attack.
by_depth.normal: Restraint: preventing enemy pawns and pieces from advancing, as progress in its own right. It is the first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula — first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
by_depth.deep: The idea that reducing the opponent's options counts as progress even when it improves nothing of yours. The formula is in My System verbatim, and the ORDER is its content: a pawn is stopped from advancing, then physically blocked, and only then attacked. Restraint is the general case and the blockade the concrete one. It sits close to prophylaxis, and the distinction worth keeping is that prophylaxis prevents a specific idea while restraint reduces general mobility — Nimzowitsch's own term for the wider strategy was Hemmungstheorie, inhibition strategy.

explanations.lesson: Before attacking something, stop it moving. A pawn you have fixed is a pawn you can attack at leisure.

restraint.definition_short: Stopping enemy pawns and pieces from advancing before doing anything else. The first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula: first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
restraint.definition_long:
Restraint is the idea that preventing your opponent's expansion counts as PROGRESS, even though it improves nothing of yours. Nimzowitsch's formula appears verbatim in My System: 'First restrain, then blockade and finally destroy!' — and the order is the content. A pawn is first stopped from advancing, then physically blocked, and only then attacked.

It is the general case of which the blockade is the concrete one. Restraint may be exercised by control of a square, by pressure that makes an advance costly, or by fixing a pawn so that moving it loses something. The blockade is restraint made permanent by putting a piece in the way.

The idea is close to prophylaxis and the two are often conflated. The useful distinction: prophylaxis prevents a specific IDEA the opponent has, while restraint reduces their general MOBILITY. Nimzowitsch's own term for the broader strategy was Hemmungstheorie, usually rendered as inhibition strategy.

Its cost is the same as prophylaxis's: a restraining move often does nothing for you, so it is only worth the tempo if what it prevents was worth preventing.

rook-endgame-principles.knowledge_type_note: Typed a principle rather than a rule, and hedged hard, because this is the endgame type in which general rules most often fail - a claim this base can support with proofs rather than assert.

attributions.note: The rule of placing the rook behind the passed pawn is conventionally attributed to him; this base records the attribution as DISPUTED, with Tartakower a competing claimant, on the passed-pawn concept.

history.notes: No single origin. The named drawing positions carry their own histories, including the Lucena position's well-documented misattribution, recorded on its own concept.

rook-endgame-principles.engine_era_note: Tablebases have been harder on rook-endgame folklore than on any other area, because rook endings are small enough to solve and numerous enough in practice for the difference to matter. Several rules of thumb are now known to be wrong as stated rather than merely approximate.

preconditions: Rooks and pawns only, or nearly so
indicators_for: An activity difference between the rooks
A passed pawn on either side
A known drawing set-up available to the defender
false_positive_traps: This is the endgame type where general rules are least trustworthy, and this base holds proofs against three of them: Tarrasch's rule, king centralisation, and the value of a check.
A pawn advantage is much weaker evidence here than elsewhere, because the defensive constructions are so numerous.
Recognising the material as a rook ending says almost nothing. The concrete configuration decides.

typical_plans: Activate the rook, giving a pawn for it if necessary
Cut the enemy king off from the pawn along a rank or file
Tie the enemy rook to defence and then open a second front
As the defender, aim for a known drawing set-up rather than counting material
typical_pawn_structures: A single passed pawn against a lone rook
typical_piece_arrangements: A rook cut off from the action
A rook chained to a pawn's defence
tactical_consequences: Giving a pawn to activate the rook is frequently correct
strategic_consequences: An extra pawn is often insufficient, so conversion technique matters more than acquisition

exceptions: Tarrasch's rule fails in the Vancura configuration, proven in this base.
King centralisation fails in some rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate.
Passive defence is sometimes correct, in defiance of the activity principle, when a known drawing set-up requires it.
limitations: This record is deliberately an umbrella of caveats; the load-bearing knowledge lives in the named positions - Lucena, Philidor, Vancura - each of which is validated here against tablebase.
This base has not systematically covered rook-endgame technique; only the positions it has proven.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION. The examples on this record are `tablebase-position`s, and for this family that is the stronger provenance rather than a substitute: the claims here are about what a class of ending can and cannot do, and a proof over every legal continuation settles that where a single game only illustrates it. What a master game would add is evidence that the principle GUIDED a strong player, which is a different claim, and this base has not yet found an annotated position making it for this family. Recorded rather than filled. RESOLVED: Botvinnik-Shebarshin, Leningrad 1926, above.
misconceptions: That an extra pawn wins a rook ending. A great many such positions are drawn, because of how many defensive constructions exist.
That the rook belongs behind the passed pawn. It often does, and this base holds a proof that as a general rule it is false.
That rook endings can be played on principle. They are the type most resistant to that.

conflicts.resolution: Rook endings are the recorded exception to king centralisation. Where the two collide, the concrete line decides and the general principle yields - which is Shereshevsky's own position, not a hedge invented here.

examples.note: The Philidor position, and the reason it belongs to a principles record rather than only to a named-position one: the third-rank defence is the single most-taught rule in rook endgames, and it is a rule with a condition attached - it works while the enemy pawn has not reached the sixth. The defending rook sits on the third rank keeping the enemy king out; when the pawn advances to the sixth the rook drops to the eighth and checks from behind. Both halves are one idea and it holds by force.

Note what this base has not managed to build beside it: a verified counterexample. With the pawn on the fourth rank the defence draws from almost anywhere, so the position that would show the method failing has resisted three attempts, and the record says so rather than shipping a wrong one.

examples.note:
ROOKS AND PAWNS ONLY - the most common ending there is, and the one this record calls the least rule-governed. Rook and passed a-pawn against rook, with a kingside pawn each.

The record's first claim is that activity outweighs material, and the position is that claim in miniature: material is level, White's rook is on the sixth cutting the black king off, and White's a-pawn is one square from the eighth rank. Nothing about the material count says anything about who is winning.

WHAT IS CLAIMED AND WHAT IS NOT. The category is decided by the material, which is mechanically certain and needs no engine. Whether the position is INTERESTING, or who is better in it, is a different question and this record does not answer it - its own typical_confidence says as much. What the position establishes is that the class of ending this record is about occurs in master play and can be pointed at.

PROVENANCE. Found by reading the MATERIAL of every position in 330 replayed master games rather than by asking the API, which never reports this concept because it has no matcher. The move list replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `rooks-on-the-board-is-not-a-rook-ending`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Both sides have two rooks and pawns. Rooks are the most common piece to reach an ending with, and this record is 'the most common and least rule-governed endings'. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Both sides also have a bishop, and every principle on this record is about what rooks do when there is nothing else — an active rook makes threats and goes where it likes, a passive one is chained to a pawn, and giving a pawn to activate a rook is routinely correct. None of that survives a minor piece being on the board to defend with and to trade against. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `opposite-coloured-bishops` — which is the concept that DOES apply here — and nothing about rook endings. +0.12 at depth 20 in a symmetric position. The case is registered because 'rook ending' is a claim about what is left rather than about what is present, and a detector reading the piece list would find two rooks each and stop there.

ambiguous_examples.note: The defending rook is behind the passed pawn, which is the most-quoted rule in rook endings - Tarrasch's, and repeated everywhere since - and Black is PROVEN LOST in 63. The same position with that rook on f6 instead, in front of nothing and beside everything, is a proven draw: the Vancura defence. So the rule and its exception are one rook move apart, and the record's own opening sentence is the honest reading of that - these are 'the most common and least rule-governed endings: activity outweighs material, and almost every general rule has proven exceptions'. Filed as ambiguous because the rule is correctly applied here and loses, and a system that reported it would be quoting Tarrasch at somebody in a position where Tarrasch is wrong.

by_level.beginner: Keep your rook active. A rook stuck defending a pawn is worth much less than one that can attack.
by_level.intermediate: Activity beats material in rook endings - giving a pawn to free your rook is often right. And many rook endings a pawn down are drawn.
by_level.advanced: Learn the drawing positions. The defence has more resources here than in any other ending, and the general rules are least reliable.
by_level.master: Three standard rules have proven counterexamples in this base alone: the rook behind the passed pawn, king centralisation, and the value of a check.

by_depth.short: Activity beats material; learn the drawing positions.
by_depth.normal: Rook endings are the commonest in practice and the least governed by rules. An active rook is worth more than a pawn, so giving a pawn to activate one is routinely right, and the defence has so many known drawing set-ups that an extra pawn frequently wins nothing.
by_depth.deep: The commonest endings and the ones where general principles are least reliable. Activity over material is the idea that survives everywhere - a passive rook chained to a pawn loses material the moment it moves, and that asymmetry decides more rook endings than a pawn does. What makes the type distinctive is the depth of the defensive resources: named drawing constructions hold positions that material counting calls lost, which is why so many rook endings a pawn down are drawn. And the general rules fail here demonstrably rather than arguably - Tarrasch's rule about the rook behind the passed pawn is disproved by a proven pair in this base, king centralisation is documented as sometimes wrong by its own advocate, and one check can draw while another loses in the same position.

explanations.hedge: Rook endings are the endgame type in which general rules are least trustworthy; prefer a known position to a principle wherever one applies.
explanations.lesson: Reach for a known position before reaching for a rule.

beginner_words: a rook stuck defending is nearly useless
avoid: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn

rook-endgame-principles.definition_short: The most common and least rule-governed endings: activity outweighs material, and almost every general rule has proven exceptions.
rook-endgame-principles.definition_long:
The commonest endings in practice, and the ones where general principles are least reliable.

ACTIVITY OVER MATERIAL is the one idea that survives everywhere. An active rook makes threats and goes where it likes; a passive rook is chained to a pawn and loses material the moment it moves. That asymmetry decides rook endings more often than a pawn does, which is why giving a pawn to activate a rook is routinely correct — a trade that would be absurd in most other endings.

THE DEFENDER'S RESOURCES ARE UNUSUALLY DEEP, and this is what makes the type distinctive. Rook endings are full of specific drawing set-ups — Philidor, Vancura — which hold positions that material counting says are lost. The practical consequence is the old observation that a great many rook endings a pawn down are drawn, and it is not a joke about laziness: it is a statement about how many defensive constructions exist.

WHY GENERAL RULES FAIL HERE, with evidence rather than assertion:
- TARRASCH'S RULE, to put the rook behind the passed pawn, is DISPROVED as a general rule by this base's Vancura pair: same material, one rook moved, and the result changes from a proven draw to a proven loss in 63.
- CENTRALISING THE KING, elsewhere almost never wrong, is documented by Shereshevsky himself as sometimes outright incorrect in rook endings, which he attributes to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
- A CHECK is not even weak evidence: this base holds a rook ending where one check draws and another loses.

The honest summary is that rook endings are learned as concrete positions and techniques rather than derived from principles, and that a system explaining them should reach for a known position before reaching for a rule.

rook-on-the-seventh.knowledge_type_note: A piece-placement concept. That it is decisive is a common overstatement and is handled in the exceptions.

attributions.note: Devoted a chapter of My System to the seventh rank and drew the absolute/relative distinction.
Credited by Naroditsky with introducing 'pigs on the seventh' in the Winning Chess series. Attribution is second-hand and not verified against Seirawan's books.

history.notes: The power of the seventh rank was known long before Nimzowitsch; the absolute/relative distinction is his contribution. The 'pigs' nickname attribution rests on a single secondary source and is recorded as medium.

development.change: Systematised; absolute versus relative seventh introduced.
Corrective: two rooks on the seventh rarely mate against a defended eighth rank; the advantage is usually transitional and must be converted.

rook-on-the-seventh.engine_era_note: Engines are markedly less impressed by a rook on the seventh than club instruction is. They value it when it attacks something and restricts the king, and price it near zero when the pawns on the rank have moved and the king is free.

preconditions: A rook occupies the opponent's seventh rank (second for Black)
indicators_for: The enemy king is confined to the eighth rank — the ABSOLUTE seventh
Two or more enemy pawns still stand on the seventh and can be attacked sideways
A second rook can be brought to the rank, or a passed pawn supports it
The rook cannot be evicted with tempo
indicators_against: The enemy king has escaped to the sixth rank or beyond
The pawns on the seventh have already advanced, so there is nothing to attack
The rook can be challenged and traded off, or driven away with gain
The eighth rank is defended, so the mating dimension of a second rook is absent
Reaching the seventh costs a tempo the position cannot spare
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a rook arriving on the seventh is not automatically important. With the pawns advanced and the king free, it attacks nothing and confines nobody.
Two rooks on the seventh do NOT generally mate a king whose eighth rank is defended. Explaining them as a mating attack is usually wrong.
Detecting 'rook on rank 7' is trivial and fires often; the reportable facts are what it attacks and whether the king is trapped.
A rook reaching the seventh is not decisive by itself. With an empty seventh rank and an enemy king that has luft, a tested position evaluates level at -0.04.

typical_plans: Establish the rook, then bring a second one to the rank
Support the rook with a pawn advancing to the sixth, which the defender often cannot allow
Convert the transitional advantage into material or a favourable trade rather than hunting a mate
Combine an absolute seventh with a passed pawn
typical_moves: Rd7 / Re7 after winning a file
A rook lift to the third rank and across
typical_pawn_structures: Enemy pawns still on their starting squares on the seventh
typical_piece_arrangements: Doubled rooks on the seventh; rook on the seventh plus a passed pawn
tactical_consequences: Back-rank threats when the king is confined
Sideways attacks the pawns cannot answer
strategic_consequences: Restricts the enemy king and pieces even when it wins nothing directly
Frequently a transitional advantage to be transformed, not a final one

exceptions: The king escaping forward removes most of the value at a stroke.
Two rooks on the seventh rarely mate against a defended eighth rank.
A rook on the seventh with nothing to attack is just a rook on a rank.
It can be a liability if it can be trapped there.
limitations: Trivially detectable and therefore easy to over-report. Usefulness depends entirely on targets and on the king.

MEASURED 2026-09-02 and fixed: the matcher reported the geometry and nothing else, which is this record's own third trap - 'detecting rook on rank 7 is trivial and fires often; the reportable facts are what it ATTACKS and whether the KING is trapped.' One of those two is now required, and the sentence says which. 12.8% -> 10.7% of the 788 shipped positions, and the corpus's annotated instance - Capablanca-Rubinstein 1928, 23.Re7 - still leads.

RECORDED FAILURE, 2026-09-02. This record's indicators_against say 'the rook can be challenged and traded off, or driven away with gain' and its indicators_for say 'the rook cannot be evicted with tempo'. Neither is built. Karpov-Polgar, Linares 2001 is in the corpus as a failing negative: Black's rook is on a2, attacks g2 and h2, and the white king is on its back rank - the ABSOLUTE seventh this record calls decisive - and Stockfish has White at +0.83, playing Karpov's 24.Kc1 as its first choice with the Nb5-c3 eviction in the principal variation. Jan Markos: 'Polgar's rook is a beast... Yet Karpov nicely shows that the rook lacks sufficient support.' A one-ply eviction test was written and measured: it fixes that position and BREAKS Capablanca-Rubinstein 1928, this corpus's own annotated instance, where ...Rd7 challenges the rook and ...Ng6 attacks it with a lesser piece and the concept is right anyway. Karpov's eviction takes four preparatory king moves and no one-ply test can see it. The failure is recorded rather than fitted around.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: two more of this record's conditions are now in the SENTENCE rather than absent. The central distinction - Nimzowitsch's ABSOLUTE seventh, with the enemy king confined to the eighth behind the rook, against the RELATIVE seventh once it has slipped out - was a fact the matcher already had and a word the sentence did not use; a reader was told the rook was on the seventh and not which kind. And Naroditsky's correction, which this record quotes in full: 'with the eighth rank defended by a rook or queen, two rooks on the seventh can ALMOST NEVER checkmate by themselves. Their power is mobility and restriction, not mate.' The pigs-on-the-seventh picture is the most over-taught image in the concept and this base was drawing it without the condition that makes it wrong. Neither changes the firing rate; both change what is said.
misconceptions: That a rook on the seventh is automatically winning.
That two rooks on the seventh mean mate. Usually they mean material.
That the aim is the rank. The aim is the pawns on it and the king behind it.

by_level.beginner: The rook has got behind their pawns, where they cannot defend themselves, and the king cannot come out past it.
by_level.intermediate: A rook on the seventh. It matters here because {the king is stuck on the back rank / it attacks {n} pawns} — check both before valuing it.
by_level.advanced: Absolute seventh, with the king confined. That is the version worth investing in; a relative seventh, with the king out, is a good rook rather than a winning one.
by_level.master: Treat it as transitional. Two rooks on the seventh will not mate a defended eighth rank, so plan the conversion — material, or a favourable trade — rather than a mating attack.

by_depth.short: The rook is behind their pawns and cutting off the king.
by_depth.normal: A rook on the seventh rank: it attacks pawns from a side they cannot defend and confines the king. It is decisive mainly when the king is trapped on the eighth behind it — if the king is out, the rook is good rather than winning.
by_depth.deep: Nimzowitsch's distinction is the operative one. The seventh is held absolutely when the enemy king is confined behind it, at which point every threat carries mating undertones and he rated an absolute seventh plus a passed pawn as usually decisive. It is held only relatively when the king has escaped forward, and then the rook eats pawns but nothing more. The famous 'pigs on the seventh' need a corrective: with the eighth rank defended, two rooks on the seventh can almost never mate by themselves, and their real power is restriction and mobility. Treat the configuration as a transitional advantage to convert, not as a mating attack.

explanations.lesson: Before you spend anything getting to the seventh rank, look at their king. If it is trapped behind you, pay whatever it costs. If it is not, pay less.

beginner_words: the king is stuck on the back row
avoid: a rook on the seventh wins
two rooks on the seventh is mate

rook-on-the-seventh.definition_short: A rook on the opponent's second rank, attacking unmoved pawns from the side and confining the king — decisive mainly when the king is trapped behind it.
rook-on-the-seventh.definition_long:
A rook reaching the seventh attacks the pawns that have not moved, from a direction they cannot defend against, and simultaneously cuts the king off from the rest of the board.

NIMZOWITSCH'S DISTINCTION is the one that makes the concept usable. The seventh is held ABSOLUTELY when the enemy king is confined to the eighth rank behind the rook: every threat then carries mating undertones, and a second attacker arriving creates immediate mate threats. He rated the absolute seventh plus a passed pawn as usually decisive on its own. The rank is held only RELATIVELY when the king has escaped forward — the rook still eats pawns sideways, but the mating dimension is gone and the defender can often afford to shed a pawn to get active.

The practical use: before spending moves or material to reach the seventh, look at the enemy king. If the rook will trap it on the back rank, the investment almost always pays. If the king slips out, you are buying a good rook, not a winning one, and should pay less.

TWO ROOKS ON THE SEVENTH ('pigs on the seventh', a nickname Naroditsky attributes to Seirawan) are famous, and famously misunderstood. Naroditsky's corrective is worth quoting in substance: with the eighth rank defended by a rook or queen, two rooks on the seventh can ALMOST NEVER checkmate by themselves. Their power is mobility and restriction, not mate, and they are often best treated as a transitional advantage to be converted into something more tangible — a favourable rook trade, or material.

sacrifice.knowledge_type_note: Terminology for a class of move, not a motif and not a principle. There is no rule that says 'sacrifice here'. The record's real content is Spielmann's CLASSIFICATION, which is what makes the word usable.

attributions.note: The Art of Sacrifice in Chess was the first systematic attempt to classify sacrifices; the sham/real division is his and remains standard.

history.notes: Sacrifices are as old as the game and no one coined the word. What is securely attributable is the CLASSIFICATION, which is Spielmann's and is read here from his own text rather than from summaries. Note he did not claim the taxonomy was objective — of the real-sacrifice subdivisions he wrote 'I have had to adopt a subjective point of view again and to proceed at times by instinct.'

development.change: Sacrificial attack treated as the natural style of play; soundness secondary.
First systematic classification: sham vs real, active vs passive, and subtypes by object.
The positional sacrifice, especially of the exchange, is developed into a standing strategic method rather than an attacking device.
Speculative sacrifices are checkable after the fact; some famous ones are refuted, and some long-doubted ones are confirmed. Practical value at the board is unaffected by either.

sacrifice.engine_era_note: Engines settle soundness for sham sacrifices completely and retrospectively for real ones. What they do not settle is whether a sacrifice was a good PRACTICAL decision: a line refuted by weeks of analysis was never going to be refuted by a defender under a clock. An explanation should distinguish 'objectively unsound' from 'a bad decision', which are not the same claim.

preconditions: A move gives up material that static exchange evaluation says was takeable
The material is offered anyway
indicators_for: The opponent must accept, or is much worse for declining
Concrete compensation is nameable: lines opened at the king, tempi, a structural wound, a square
The line is forcing, so the consequences can be calculated

by_level.beginner: This gives away material on purpose, to get something else — usually an attack on the king or a piece that cannot be stopped.
by_level.intermediate: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
by_level.advanced: Spielmann's division applies: sham if the material returns by force or mate follows, real if it does not. The two are checked by different faculties — calculation and judgement — and mixing them is the standard error.
by_level.master: Name the compensation in the currency actually obtained: tempi, king exposure, structure, squares, coordination. Note the floor as well as the ceiling — a sacrifice with a mating ceiling and a drawing floor is a different proposition from one that mates or loses.

by_depth.short: Material given up for {compensation}.
by_depth.normal: A sacrifice: {n} points of material given up for {compensation}. The material {does / does not} come back by force, so this is a {sham / real} sacrifice.
by_depth.deep: Spielmann classified sacrifices in 1935 and the frame still holds. A sham sacrifice regains the material by force or ends in mate — no risk, and 'properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' A real sacrifice cannot be calculated out; the player relies on judgement, and 'the risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice.' The practical point is that the two are verified differently, calculation against judgement, and confusing them goes wrong in both directions. A second axis is whether the offer must be accepted or may be declined.

explanations.lesson: Before you sacrifice, ask one question first: does the material come back by force? If yes, calculate to the end and trust nothing else. If no, name what you are buying — and if you cannot name it, the move is a blunder rather than a sacrifice.

avoid: the engine refuted it so it was a mistake

sacrifice.definition_short: Deliberately giving up material for compensation in another currency — time, king exposure, structure, squares, or mate.
sacrifice.definition_long:
The voluntary surrender of material for something not measured in material. What makes the word worth having is Spielmann's division, which is still the standard frame ninety years on.

SHAM (pseudo, temporary) — the material comes back by force, with interest, or the line ends in mate. Spielmann is blunt: 'Properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' He subdivides these into positional sacrifices, sacrifices for gain, and mating sacrifices. There is no risk, because the consequences were foreseen from the first.

REAL — the player 'gives up material, but is unable to calculate the consequences with accuracy; he has to rely on his judgment.' Compensation is dynamic and must be realised gradually. Spielmann's own summary: 'the risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice.'

The division matters because THE TWO ARE CHECKED BY DIFFERENT FACULTIES. A sham sacrifice is settled by calculation and nothing else; a real one by judgement. Confusing them goes wrong in both directions — trying to calculate a real sacrifice to exhaustion, or 'judging' a sham one on intuition when a variation would have settled it.

Spielmann's second axis is ACTIVE versus PASSIVE: an active sacrifice must be accepted, a passive one may be declined without the declining side being worse. He notes the active form is 'by far the more powerful'. Wikipedia renders the same distinction as forced/non-forced, and adds that failing to notice when an offer can simply be declined is a common error.

Compensation, concretely, is some mix of: time (the initiative), king exposure, structure, squares and domination, and the destruction of the opponent's coordination.

SHAM AND REAL, which is Spielmann's classification and the standard one. He splits sacrifices by whether the consequences were calculable at the moment of offering: 'sham sacrifices involve losses of material only for a definable amount of time; in the case of real sacrifices, the amount of time required for recovering the material is not clear.' A sham sacrifice 'involves no risk. After a series of forced moves, the player either recovers the invested material with advantage, or else even mates his opponent. The consequences of the sacrifice were foreseen from the first. Properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' Sham divides into positional sacrifices, sacrifices for gain and mating sacrifices; real ones are the rest, and 'risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice'.

This matters here for a specific reason: the SEE test this base uses detects that material was OFFERED, which is the definition it was written to, and it cannot tell sham from real, because that turns on whether the consequences could be calculated. Capablanca's 24.Qg8+ against Mattison is mate in two and is therefore a mating sacrifice - sham, and 'properly speaking, no sacrifice' - while Chernev and the whole literature call it a queen sacrifice. Both are right about different questions, and this base reports the material fact and does not adjudicate between them.

semi-open-file.knowledge_type_note: An observable feature of the pawn structure, with the usual gap between the feature being present and its being worth anything.

history.notes: Standard vocabulary; Nimzowitsch's treatment of files is the classical source but the term is not his coinage.

semi-open-file.engine_era_note: Unremarkable to engines, which evaluate the resulting pressure directly. The concept survives as the explanation for why the pressure exists.

preconditions: A file carrying an enemy pawn and none of your own
indicators_for: The enemy pawn on it is backward or otherwise fixed
You can bring more pieces to bear than can defend it
A rook already stands on the file
indicators_against: The pawn can simply advance
Another enemy pawn can defend it
The file has no entry square beyond the pawn

false_positive_traps: A semi-open file is a fact about pawns; whether it produces pressure depends on whether the target is fixed and whether you can attack it more times than it can be defended.
Both sides can have semi-open files, usually on opposite wings, and each will be attacking on their own. Reporting only one side's is half the position.

typical_plans: Double rooks against the pawn on the file
Fix the target first so it cannot advance out of the pressure
Trade off its defenders rather than adding attackers
typical_pawn_structures: A backward pawn on a semi-open file
Sicilian and French structures, which are largely arguments about which files each side gets
typical_piece_arrangements: Doubled rooks on the file
strategic_consequences: The file usually outlives the pieces currently on it, so it is a durable asset

exceptions: A semi-open file with no entry square and a defensible pawn achieves nothing.
Where the enemy pawn can advance freely, the file is a route rather than a lever.
limitations: Detecting the file is mechanical; judging whether the target is fixed is not.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: this record's first trap states the whole test - 'whether it produces pressure depends on whether the TARGET IS FIXED and whether you can ATTACK IT MORE TIMES THAN IT CAN BE DEFENDED' - and the matcher quoted it and built neither half. A comment in it claimed a rook on the file was 'the half a static scan can answer', which was a claim nobody had checked: both halves are answerable. The enemy pawn on the file must have no safe advance, and it must be attacked at least as many times as it is defended. 39.5% -> 16.4% of the 788 shipped positions, and the sentence now names the pawn being bear down on.

CORRECTED 2026-09-02, by a human-grounded position. The 'target is fixed' half of this record's first trap was built as 'the pawn cannot advance safely', and that is wrong for a FILE concept: a pawn that advances is still on the same file. Nimzowitsch-Capablanca 1914 settled it - the annotators name 'play on the open b-file' and say the b2 pawn falls six moves later, and the first version dropped the b-file entirely because b2-b3 is a perfectly safe move. It is, and the pawn is still on b3, still on the file, still outnumbered. The escape is now defined as arriving somewhere it is no longer attacked at least as often as it is defended. The second half is also softened, deliberately and with a measurement. The record says 'attack it MORE TIMES THAN IT CAN BE DEFENDED', which is the condition for WINNING the pawn; reporting only that measures 8.6% and again loses the b-file in the annotated position, where the count is 1-1. At parity the pawn is not falling and the file is not nothing - the defence is committed to it - so both are reported and the sentence says which. 39.5% -> 24.5%.

That the file is the asset. The fixed pawn on it is the asset.

by_level.beginner: A file where you have no pawn and they do — so your rook is already pointing at something.
by_level.intermediate: A semi-open file. Better than an open one for attacking, because it comes with a target that cannot step aside.
by_level.advanced: Fix the pawn first. A target that can advance out of the pressure is not a target.

by_depth.normal: A semi-open file: no pawn of your own, one of the opponent's. It is often more useful than a fully open file, because it is asymmetric - the enemy pawn is a target that cannot move sideways, and you can usually attack it more times than it can be defended.
by_depth.deep: The asymmetric half of the open-file idea. An open file is a road both sides can use, and this base holds a tested position where one with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing; a semi-open file comes with a target built in. It is created by the pawn structure rather than chosen, which is why so many openings are arguments about which files each side gets. And the target is worth having only when it is fixed: a backward pawn on a semi-open file is the classic pairing, because it can neither advance out of the pressure nor be defended by its neighbours.

semi-open-file.definition_short: A file with none of your own pawns on it but one of the opponent's — so your rook looks straight at a pawn that cannot run away sideways.
semi-open-file.definition_long:
The more useful half of the open-file idea, and the one that supplies targets rather than merely space.

WHY IT IS OFTEN BETTER THAN AN OPEN FILE: an open file is a road both sides can use, and this base holds a tested position where an open file with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing. A semi-open file is asymmetric by construction. The enemy pawn on it is a TARGET that cannot step sideways out of the way, and pressure against it can be built with more pieces than can defend it.

IT IS CREATED BY THE STRUCTURE, not chosen. Every pawn capture that leaves one side with a pawn on a file and the other without makes one, which is why so many openings are really arguments about which files each side gets. The Sicilian's whole character comes from Black's semi-open c-file, the French's from the same on the other wing.

THE TARGET IS BEST WHEN IT IS FIXED. A backward pawn on a semi-open file is the classic combination, because the pawn cannot advance to escape and its own neighbours cannot defend it. Where the pawn can simply advance or be defended by another pawn, the file is a route rather than a lever.

seventy-five-move-rule.definition_short: After 75 moves by each player with no capture and no pawn move, the game is drawn automatically.
seventy-five-move-rule.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 9.6.2: the game is drawn if 'any series of at least 75 moves have been made by each player without the movement of any pawn and without any capture. If the last move resulted in checkmate, that shall take precedence.'

The automatic counterpart to the claimable fifty-move rule. The checkmate proviso is the interesting part: a move that simultaneously completes the 75 and delivers mate is a win, not a draw.

preconditions: 150 ply have elapsed with no capture and no pawn move
indicators_against: The final move delivers checkmate — mate takes precedence
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: seventy-five-move-rule, over the halfmove clock

exceptions: Checkmate on the 75th move takes precedence over the draw.
limitations: Reported from 130 ply. Unlike the fifty-move rule this needs no claim, which is the difference the wording carries.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

The halfmove clock reads 149; the rule is 75 moves by each player without a capture or a pawn move, which is 150 halfmoves, and it is the ARBITER'S rule rather than a claim: unlike the fifty-move rule nobody has to invoke it, the game is drawn automatically. The material is deliberately a rook ending White wins with correct play - the rule does not care, and that is what distinguishes it from `dead-position` and from `insufficient-material`.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The halfmove clock reads 149. One more move with no capture and no pawn move and the arbiter ends the game as a draw, whatever the position looks like. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's only indicator_against: "The final move delivers checkmate — mate takes precedence." The move that reaches 150 is Ra8, and it is mate. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The move generator settles it: the only mate in one here is a1a8, and it is a rook move that captures nothing and moves no pawn, so it is precisely the move that would otherwise trigger the rule. FIDE 9.6.2 makes mate take precedence, and this base does not need a guard for that because the rule and the exception are decided by the same function — a position with no legal moves and the king in check is checkmate before anything else is asked about it.

by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 9.6.2, and the clause that matters is the exception: if the move that completes the count delivers checkmate, the mate stands. So the rule never converts a win into a draw on the final move. This base's registered case is exactly that position — halfmove clock at 149, and the move that would reach 150 is mate. skewer.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), mechanically detectable, defined purely by the value ordering along a line.
skewer.definition_short: A line attack where the MORE valuable piece is in front; when it moves, the lesser piece behind it is captured.
skewer.definition_long:
The pin's mirror image. A bishop, rook or queen attacks a valuable enemy unit that has a lesser unit directly behind it on the same line. The front piece must move — by force if it is the king — and the piece behind falls.

Skewers are ABSOLUTE when the front piece is the king (the move is compelled) and RELATIVE otherwise (the defender may prefer to lose the exchange, counter-attack, or defend the rear piece).

Skewers are most common in endgames, where kings are exposed on open lines and there are few pieces to interpose.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly line piece attacks an enemy unit with a second enemy unit directly behind it on the same line
The front unit is worth more than the one behind, or is the king
indicators_for: The front unit is the king, so the move is forced
The rear unit is undefended once exposed
indicators_against: The front unit can capture the skewering piece
A third unit can interpose
The front unit can move so that it still defends the rear unit
The rear unit is defended and the exchange is not favourable

exceptions: If the front piece moves along the same line it may keep defending the piece behind.
limitations: Same as the pin: geometry is mechanical, profitability is not.

examples.note: The skewer proper: the king is in front, must move out of check, and the knight behind it is taken. Paired with the identical men in the other order, which is a pin.

counterexamples.note: The mirror of `pin`'s counterexample and the other half of one controlled pair: the same rook, knight and king on the d-file with the knight in front instead of the king. That is a pin, not a skewer - the piece behind is the more valuable one, which is the whole distinction between the two motifs and the commonest thing a learner gets backwards.

Registered false-positive case `a-skewer-the-front-unit-eats`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Rb1 attacks the black queen on b5 with the rook on b8 directly behind it. More valuable unit in front, less valuable behind, nothing between — the geometry of a skewer, and the detector says so: 'The queen on b5 has to move, and the rook on b8 behind it falls.' WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first indicator_against: "The front unit can capture the skewering piece." The queen is not obliged to move at all; she takes the rook, which is undefended. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Reported at HIGH confidence until a guard was written. Syzygy settles it without an opinion: after Rb1 the position is a WIN FOR BLACK, dtz 1, mate in 7, and the tablebase's own best move is Qxb1+. The guard is one step wider than the record's wording — it asks whether ANY capture of the skewering piece is profitable rather than only the front unit's — and that is deliberate, because a skewering piece somebody else eats is not a skewer either. skewer fell from 11.4% to 7.6% of the 788 shipped puzzles.

tablebase.note: PROVEN, from the mover's side: after Rb1 White is LOST in 7, and the tablebase's best move is Qxb1+. The front unit does not move; it eats.

ambiguous_examples.note: Nominated by tools/mine_ambiguous.js on its fourth ground, NOT-THE-MOVE: the concept fires on a legal move that is not the solution of a shipped puzzle. The first three grounds ask about a POSITION and could not reach a move-based or motif concept at all - this concept and eleven others reported NONE until the tool learned to supply a move. What makes the case ambiguous rather than false is that nothing reported is absent: the skewer is real geometry and the move loses by six pawns. ...Qf6 scores -5.48 against ...Nxf6 at +0.78, a gap of 626 centipawns, and the reason is on the board rather than in the motif: after dxc6 the position collapses. A motif detector reports what is geometrically true of the move it is given, and being given the wrong move is not something it can notice.

by_level.intermediate: A skewer — the pin turned around, with the bigger piece in front.

by_depth.short: The valuable piece in front must move, and the one behind it falls.
by_depth.normal: A skewer: a line attack with the MORE valuable unit in front. It moves, and what stands behind it is taken. The inverse of a pin, and it wins material immediately rather than paralysing.
by_depth.deep: Three conditions separate a skewer from a line of pieces, and all three are commonly skipped. The front unit must not simply capture the skewering piece. The rear unit must be worth taking once it is exposed — a piece skewered to a defended PAWN is a line and not a skewer, and this base's guard removes most reported skewers on that test alone. And the front unit must not be able to step aside and keep defending the rear one, which it often can along the same line. Where the two units are worth the SAME, this base reports neither pin nor skewer rather than guessing which.
