smothered-mate.knowledge_type_note: Named mating pattern (D). Philidor's Legacy names the specific queen-sacrifice delivery, not every smothered mate; sources sometimes use the terms interchangeably.
smothered-mate.definition_short: A knight mates a king that is completely surrounded by its own pieces.
smothered-mate.definition_long:
The king is hemmed in on every side by its own men, so only a knight — which jumps — can reach it. The classic delivery, known as Philidor's Legacy, runs Qg8+ (a queen sacrifice on g8 or b8 forcing the rook to capture) followed by Nf7#, with the rook now blocking the last flight square.

The mechanism depends on DOUBLE CHECK earlier in the sequence: the knight checks from f7 or h6 with the queen also checking, so the defender cannot capture or interpose and must move the king into the corner.

history.notes: Descriptive pattern name of long, largely anonymous usage.

preconditions: The enemy king's flight squares are all occupied by its own pieces
A friendly knight can reach a square giving check
indicators_for: The king is in the corner with rook and pawns adjacent
A queen sacrifice is available to fill the last escape square
indicators_against: A flight square is empty or can be vacated
The knight's square is defended

exceptions: If any surrounding piece can move away with tempo, the mate evaporates.
limitations: Reported only on an actual mate. The pattern without the mate is a king that happens to be surrounded, which is a description rather than a mating pattern. Fires on none of the 788 shipped positions and on the constructed Philidor pattern.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

Verified 2026-09-02. Both of this record's indicators_against - "A flight square is empty or can be vacated" and "The knight's square is defended" - describe positions that are not mate, and the detector only speaks when the position IS mate: findMotifs() computes `const mated = !theirMoves.length && inCheck(after, them)` from the move generator's own reply list. If a flight square existed, theirMoves would not be empty; if the knight could be taken, the same. Both conditions are unreachable rather than unguarded, which is a different and better answer than a guard would be.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET, and the search that failed is worth recording. Five famous games were replayed through this base's own move generator and scanned position by position with the API - the Opera Game, the Evergreen, the Immortal, the Game of the Century and Legall's Mate, 225 plies between them - and this concept was not reported in any of them. That is not evidence the motif is rare; it is evidence that the five games this base can currently verify do not contain a clean instance of it, and that adding one means adding a game rather than looking harder at these. tools/replay_game.js is the instrument: a move list that is wrong is refused rather than guessed at.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION, and this record now has a MEASUREMENT rather than an excuse. tools/mine_master_motifs.js replayed 35,648 games from 22 world-champion and grandmaster collections through the page's own move generator - 2,822,256 positions, 492 games rejected as unplayable and skipped rather than patched - and asked at every ply the test this concept's own matcher asks: a knight gives check, it is mate, and every flight square is blocked by the king's OWN men. It found ZERO. That is not a failure of the search; it is the concept. A smothered mate is forced two or three moves before it lands, and a master resigns into it rather than allowing it to be played, so the mate itself is missing from the score even where the combination was the reason the game ended. The famous instances - Philidor's legacy, Lucena, the Polerio game - are compositions or pre-modern games outside these collections. The rung stays MISSING rather than N/A: a master game containing one certainly exists and the search that would find it is a search for the position two moves BEFORE the mate, which is a different test than the one this base's matcher makes and would have to be written and argued for on its own.

Paired with the identical position with the h-pawn on h6, where Nf7 is a check and the king has h7.

Nf7+ is a check and nothing more. Paired with the identical position with the pawn on h7, which is mate in the classical picture.

by_level.beginner: The king is boxed in by its own pieces, so the knight — the only piece that can jump — delivers mate.
by_level.intermediate: Smothered mate: every escape square is occupied by the king's own men.
by_level.advanced: Smothered mate. The Philidor's Legacy delivery uses a double check and a queen sacrifice to fill the last flight square.

by_depth.short: A knight mates a king hemmed in by its own pieces.
by_depth.normal: Smothered mate: the king's flight squares are all occupied by its own men, so a knight — the only piece that can jump — delivers a check nothing can answer. It cannot be blocked, and if the knight cannot be captured it is mate.
by_depth.deep: Philidor's Legacy is the standard delivery and it is a manufactured version of the pattern: a queen sacrifice on g8 or b1 forces a rook to fill the last flight square, a double check drives the king into the corner, and the knight mates. What makes the pattern hard to detect honestly is that the precondition — a king boxed in by its own men — is common and worth nothing without a knight that can reach the square. This base holds the two positions one pawn apart: with the h-pawn on h7 the knight move is mate in one, and with it on h6 the same move leaves the mating side PROVEN LOST in thirty-eight.

soviet-school.knowledge_type_note: A historical school whose central claims — the primacy of the initiative and the acceptability of structural concessions for dynamic play — are teaching principles rather than laws.

attributions.note: Associated above all with the professionalised preparation the school is known for. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED in detail; the sources describe the school rather than assigning this to him individually.

Credited with the King's Indian and Sicilian treatments that embody the school's willingness to concede structure for counterplay. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: this is one encyclopedia's characterisation, not a documented claim of origination, and no primary source was consulted.

history.notes: Weakly sourced compared with the other schools: one encyclopedia summary and one community wikibook. The individual attributions in particular are the sources' characterisations rather than documented claims, and no Soviet primary text was consulted. This area deserves dedicated research.

development.change: The school forms; preparation becomes systematic and professional.
Dominance of the world championship; the initiative elevated above static factors.
Synthesis: all three schools treated as partially correct.
Further erosion of classical piece dogma — bishops traded for knights on slight compensation, good bishops exchanged and bad ones kept.

soviet-school.engine_era_note: The school engines vindicated most clearly. Modern engines value the initiative and concrete dynamic play very highly and are entirely willing to accept structural damage for it, which is the Soviet position stated computationally.

preconditions: A plan that prefers concrete activity to structural soundness
indicators_for: Structural concessions accepted for counterplay
Counterattack preferred to passive defence
Deep opening preparation as a weapon
indicators_against: The activity gained is temporary and the structural damage permanent, with nothing concrete to show
false_positive_traps: Accepting a bad structure is not Soviet-school play unless something concrete is obtained for it. The school's claim is that dynamics can OUTWEIGH structure, not that structure is unimportant.
This record is weakly sourced and should not be leaned on for historical claims until it has had dedicated research.

typical_plans: Seek the initiative even at structural cost
Defend by counterattacking rather than by consolidating
Prepare openings deeply enough that the concrete lines are known in advance
typical_pawn_structures: Boleslavsky's Sicilian hole on d5
King's Indian structures conceding the centre
strategic_consequences: Made dynamic evaluation respectable alongside static evaluation

exceptions: Structural concessions still have to be paid for. The school's contribution was that the price could be worth it, not that it was free.
Its own defensive preference for counterattack is not universal — some positions require consolidation.
limitations: This record's history is weakly sourced and flagged as needing dedicated research.
'School' is a loose grouping covering several decades and many distinct players.
misconceptions: That the Soviet school abandoned positional chess. It subordinated static factors to dynamic ones; it did not discard them.
That it replaced the earlier schools. Fischer's summary — that all three were correct in their own way — is the standard modern view.

examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik, World Championship 1954, game 1, 6.b4 - and it illustrates two of the four features Britannica uses to define this school at once. PREPARATION: the annotation says the sacrifice was 'recommended by Alekhine in the book of the New York international tournament of 1924', so a world-championship game opens with a thirty-year-old published recommendation, which is the professionalised preparation the record describes. MATERIAL: a pawn is given for the initiative, which is the 'new appreciation of differences in material' and the elevation of dynamic over static. The same game supplies this base's `initiative` positive at 20...Qc7, where the annotator writes 'the turning point of the game - the initiative now passes to Black'.

The number establishes that b4 does not throw the advantage away; it does not establish that Alekhine was right.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A piece sacrificed in the opening for a big centre and fast development, with every white piece pointing at the black king. A willingness to give material for the initiative is the first thing Britannica lists about this school. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Britannica lists four features and this position has one of them wearing the others' clothes. The Halloween Gambit is not prepared, not sound, and not a considered appreciation of material — it is a piece for two tempi. This record's positive example is a world-championship game opening with a thirty-year-old published recommendation of Alekhine's, which is what the school's word for preparation means. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `center-control` and `blockade` and says nothing about any school. Stockfish 18 at depth 22: +1.71 from Black's side — the same figure the `compensation` record quotes for this position and the same one that record's trap names, 'the Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse'. Activity, material given, an initiative of a kind, and none of it is the thing the school is named for.

ambiguous_examples.note: Smyslov-Botvinnik, World Championship 1954, game 1, after 21.Nc5 - and it is the Soviet school's own preference producing a piece that is badly placed. Britannica's first distinguishing feature of the school is a high priority on the INITIATIVE, and the annotation says the knight 'has to be placed on c5, where it does not stand safely'; fifteen moves later the same annotator notes the exchange that removes it, 'the knight was insecurely placed on c5'. The dynamic choice was forced by the dynamic play, and the position is level. Filed as ambiguous because the school's central claim is operating and the result is neither a vindication nor a refutation of it: the same game supplies this base's `initiative` positive nine moves earlier.

by_level.beginner: The Soviet players cared most about making threats and keeping the pressure on, even if it meant accepting weaknesses in their own position.
by_level.intermediate: The Soviet school: the initiative above all, structural concessions accepted for counterplay, and openings prepared in depth.
by_level.advanced: The subordination of static evaluation to dynamic play. Boleslavsky's Sicilian — a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn for use of the c-file — is the emblem.
by_level.master: The third term after classical evaluation and hypermodern correction, and the one engines most clearly vindicate.

by_depth.short: The initiative first; structure is negotiable.
by_depth.normal: The Soviet school, dominant from 1948: the initiative valued above static factors, pawn structures accepted that earlier schools called bad, and opening preparation treated as a professional discipline.
by_depth.deep: Britannica identifies four features: priority on the initiative, willingness to accept structures Lasker considered bad, a new appreciation of material differences, and concentrated pre-game preparation. The theoretical move is the elevation of dynamic factors over static ones — and in defence, a preference for counterattack over the solid passivity of Steinitz and Tarrasch. Its emblems are Bronstein and Boleslavsky's King's Indian treatment, allowing White a free hand in the centre in return for counterplay, and Boleslavsky's Sicilian, accepting a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn for the c-file and pressure on e4. Both are surrenders of the centre that Tarrasch would simply have called bad. Fischer's summary is the usual modern position: a dose of all three schools is correct.

explanations.hedge: A historical school, and this record is more weakly sourced than the others here — one encyclopedia summary and one community reference, with no Soviet primary text consulted. Treat its specific historical claims as provisional.
explanations.lesson: The lasting contribution is that a structural concession can be worth paying — provided you can name what you got for it.

avoid: the Soviet school ignored positional chess

soviet-school.definition_short: The school that dominated from 1948, valuing the initiative above static considerations, accepting structures earlier schools called bad, and professionalising preparation.
soviet-school.definition_long:
The generation that emerged in the 1930s and dominated the world championship from 1948 to 1972. Britannica identifies four distinguishing features: a high priority on gaining the INITIATIVE, a willingness to accept pawn structures even Lasker considered bad, a new appreciation of differences in material, and a concentrated approach to pre-game preparation.

The theoretical move is the elevation of DYNAMIC over STATIC factors. Where the classical school accumulated durable advantages and the hypermoderns argued about the centre, the Soviets asked what could be forced — and were willing to pay in structure for it. When defending they rejected the solid passivity of Steinitz and Tarrasch in favour of counterattack.

The concrete results are the openings that still define modern practice. Bronstein and Boleslavsky showed in the King's Indian that White could be allowed a free hand in the centre provided Black obtained counterplay; Boleslavsky's Sicilian treatment accepted a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn in return for use of the c-file and pressure on e4. Both are surrenders of the centre that Tarrasch would have called simply bad.

It is best understood as the third term in a sequence rather than a fourth rival: classical evaluation, hypermodern correction, and then the subordination of both to concrete dynamic play. Fischer's position — that a dose of all three schools is correct — is the usual modern summary.

space.knowledge_type_note: A board feature, mechanically countable, whose VALUE is conditional on being able to use it.

attributions.note: Treats space as one of the primary imbalances and stresses the entry-point requirement. Full text consulted.

history.notes: Space is standard vocabulary with no identifiable coiner; only its treatment as a named imbalance is attributable, and weakly.

space.engine_era_note: Engines carry space and mobility terms and value them, but considerably less than club instruction implies. They will concede space readily for concrete play, which is closer to the hypermodern position than the classical one.

preconditions: One side controls more squares behind its pawn front
indicators_for: The opponent's pieces have few squares and obstruct one another
An entry square exists or can be created
The extra space spans both wings, so the opponent cannot defend both
The opponent cannot trade pieces off
indicators_against: No entry point exists, so the territory buys nothing
The advanced pawns are fixed targets rather than a front
The cramped side can liquidate with exchanges
The space was gained by overextension the opponent can undermine
recognition.detector: pawnSpace + entrySquares in lib/features.js; the `space` matcher in lib/matchers.js
false_positive_traps: Counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing.
Advanced pawns are not automatically a space advantage — they may simply be weak and fixed.
The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary.

typical_plans: Avoid exchanges, improve pieces behind the front, then open a second front
Create an entry square before advancing further
As the cramped side: exchange pieces, and look for a freeing pawn break
typical_moves: A space-gaining pawn advance supported by pieces
A freeing break such as ...c5 or ...f6 by the cramped side
typical_pawn_structures: Advanced pawn chains
Maroczy Bind and similar space-clamping structures
strategic_consequences: Enables switching wings faster than the defender
Combines directly with the principle of two weaknesses, which needs exactly that ability

exceptions: Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.
The cramped side exchanging pieces is the standard and effective antidote.
limitations: Countable but conditional: the count says nothing about usability.

TRAP 3 IS NOT IMPLEMENTED AND CANNOT BE, MECHANICALLY. 'The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary' is a claim about what the position will BECOME, and no static feature answers it. The other two traps are built: an entry square is required (53.3% -> 34.6% of the 788 shipped positions), and a territory made entirely of weak, blocked pawns is refused (a further 1 position — it almost never binds, because a side with a real space advantage rarely has EVERY space-creating pawn weak, and the rate is recorded rather than talked up).

HUMAN-GROUNDED NEGATIVE ADDED 2026-09-02, and it is a live test of the entry-square guard rather than a vacuous one. Torre-Karpov, Bad Lauterberg 1977, move 26: White's pawns control NINE squares in Black's half against zero - as unambiguous a territorial advantage as this corpus contains, and six times the matcher's own threshold - and there is no entry square at all. Until this session the concept would have been reported here with confidence, in a position Stockfish scores at -3.01 after the move actually played. The annotators introduce the game as 'a great example of how not to play when you have space advantage'.
misconceptions: That more space is simply better. It is better if you can enter.
That advancing pawns gains space safely. It also fixes them and leaves holes behind them.

conflicts.resolution: The hypermodern position is precisely that space gained by pawn advance can be a liability, since the pawns become targets. Both are right conditionally: supported and expanded on time, space wins; static and overextended, it is a target. The deciding variable is whether the pawn front can be supported, not the amount of territory.

by_level.beginner: You control more squares, so your pieces have room and theirs are bumping into each other.
by_level.intermediate: A space advantage. Avoid trades, improve your pieces, and find the square you intend to invade on — space with no way in achieves nothing.
by_level.advanced: The value is the mobility difference and the ability to switch wings faster than the defender. Watch the cost: advanced pawns are fixed and leave holes.
by_level.master: Space combines directly with the two-weaknesses method, because that method needs exactly the ability to operate on both wings faster than the defence can follow.

by_depth.short: More room for your pieces, less for theirs.
by_depth.normal: A space advantage: you control more squares behind your pawn front. The value is mobility — their pieces get in each other's way. Avoid exchanges, and find an entry square, because space without a way in wins nothing.
by_depth.deep: Territory behind the pawn front, whose worth is the mobility difference rather than the squares themselves. Two corollaries matter more than the count: the cramped side should exchange pieces, since fewer pieces need fewer squares, and space must be usable — a big advantage almost certainly wins if a way can be found into enemy territory, which puts the emphasis on the entry point. The cost is real: advancing pawns fixes them and permanently uncovers the squares behind them, and space gained by overextension is a liability. That is exactly the hypermodern critique of the classical pawn centre.

explanations.lesson: Space is only worth what you can enter with. Before pushing another pawn, ask which square you intend to invade on.

space.definition_short: More squares controlled behind your own pawns, which gives your pieces room to manoeuvre and denies the opponent room to do the same.
space.definition_long:
Space is territory: the squares behind your pawn front, which your pieces can use and the opponent's cannot. Its value is not the territory itself but the MOBILITY difference — a cramped side's pieces get in each other's way and cannot be regrouped quickly, and the side with space can switch wings faster than the defender can follow.

Two standing corollaries follow, and both are more useful than the raw count. First, the cramped side should EXCHANGE PIECES: fewer pieces need fewer squares, and every trade relieves the cramp. Correspondingly, the side with space should avoid trades. Second, space must be USABLE — Silman's framing is that a big space advantage almost certainly wins if a way can be found to break into enemy territory, which puts the emphasis on the entry point rather than on the territory.

The cost side is real and easy to forget. Advancing pawns to gain space also fixes them, leaves squares behind them permanently uncovered, and can leave the advanced pawns as targets in an endgame. Space gained by overextension is a liability, which is precisely the hypermodern critique of the classical pawn centre.

stalemate.knowledge_type_note: Official rule. Its status as a draw rather than a win is a rule choice, not a logical necessity — some historical and regional variants scored it differently.
stalemate.definition_short: The side to move has no legal move and is NOT in check. The game is drawn immediately.
stalemate.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 5.2.1: 'The game is drawn when the player to move has no legal move and his/her king is not in check. The game is said to end in stalemate. This immediately ends the game...'

The absence of check is what separates stalemate from checkmate, and it is a draw regardless of material. A player a queen ahead who stalemates has drawn. This makes stalemate a defensive RESOURCE, not merely an accident, and one of the main reasons endgame technique requires care rather than force.

history.notes: The rule that stalemate is a draw was not universal historically; it has been scored as a win and as a loss in various times and places. Not yet researched for this record.

preconditions: The side to move has zero legal moves
That side's king is not in check
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: stalemate, over legalMoves and inCheck

limitations: Being drawn regardless of material makes it a deliberate defensive device; an explanation should treat a stalemate trick as a resource, not a blunder by the winner.
Fires on none of the 788 shipped positions, which is correct - a puzzle whose answer is stalemate is a stalemate RESOURCE, and the position offered is not itself stalemate.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

The queen on g6 covers g7, g8 and h7 and does not attack h8, which is the whole trick - one square further and it is mate, one square back and Black has a move.

counterexamples.note: THE CLASSIC CONFUSION, as a controlled pair: the same three men, the queen one square over. On f7 it is stalemate and the game is drawn; on g7 it is checkmate. A king with no legal move is not stalemate - a king with no legal move AND NOT IN CHECK is. Building this pair found that the base could say 'this position is stalemate' about a board and could not say 'this position is checkmate' about the same board, because checkmate was reachable only through the MOVE; a structural arm was added for it.

by_level.beginner: The player to move has no legal move at all, but is not in check. That is stalemate, and the game is a draw — no matter who was winning.
by_level.intermediate: Stalemate: no legal move and no check, so the game is drawn. Watch for it whenever you are converting a large material advantage.
by_level.advanced: Art. 5.2.1. A standing defensive resource in simplified endings.

by_depth.short: No legal move and no check. The game is drawn however lopsided the position.
by_depth.normal: Stalemate: the side to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is drawn immediately, whoever was winning and by however much — which is what makes it the defender's standing resource in simplified endings.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 5.2.1, and the exact complement of checkmate: empty reply list, no check. The pair matters more than either half. This base's stalemate example has a queen covering three of the king's four squares and deliberately not the fourth; one square further and it is mate, one square back and the defender has a move. Underpromotion to a rook rather than a queen is the standard practical answer, and it exists entirely because of this rule.

static-vs-dynamic.knowledge_type_note: A framework for classifying other advantages rather than an advantage itself. Its practical content is a rule about TIMING.

attributions.note: His enumeration of advantages divides them into permanent and temporary, which is the origin of the distinction. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: taken from a community study of his list rather than from The Modern Chess Instructor itself.
Re-weighted the framework decisively towards dynamic factors.

history.notes: The framework is universally used and weakly sourced here; the Steinitz attribution is conventional and unverified.

development.change: Advantages classified as permanent or temporary.
Dynamic factors elevated; structural concessions accepted for activity.
Engines weigh dynamic factors very highly and will accept large static damage for concrete play, which vindicates the Soviet re-weighting.

static-vs-dynamic.engine_era_note: Engines have shifted the balance further towards the dynamic side than any human school did, accepting structural damage that classical theory would have called simply bad whenever concrete play justifies it. The FRAMEWORK is unaffected — it is the weighting that moved.

preconditions: An advantage exists and its durability is being assessed
indicators_for: STATIC: pawn structure, weak squares, the bishop pair, a permanent outpost — all survive exchanges
DYNAMIC: the initiative, a development lead, an exposed king, a temporarily awkward enemy piece — all decay
indicators_against: The advantage is being described without asking whether it survives simplification
false_positive_traps: The classification is not a property of the feature alone. A passed pawn is static if it can be held and dynamic if it must run now.
'Dynamic' is often used loosely to mean 'sharp'. Here it means specifically that the advantage expires.

typical_plans: Static: improve every piece, do not hurry, trade into an endgame
Dynamic: force matters immediately, avoid trades, convert into something permanent before it fades
Ask which kind you hold before choosing a tempo
tactical_consequences: Dynamic advantages are what justify sacrifices; static ones rarely do
strategic_consequences: Determines whether to accelerate or slow down, which is the most common strategic decision

exceptions: The same feature can be either, depending on whether it can be maintained.
A dynamic advantage can be converted into a static one, which is usually the correct plan.
Modern practice weights dynamics more heavily than the classical framework implied.
limitations: A classification framework rather than a technique; its value is entirely in the timing decision it drives.

No detector, and the record's own first false-positive trap says why: the classification is not a property of the feature alone. The same isolated pawn is dynamic on move 15 of Capablanca-Rubinstein 1928 and static on move 30, and no reading of one position can tell them apart.
misconceptions: That static means good and dynamic means risky. They are different clocks, not different qualities.
That an advantage is permanently one or the other.

conflicts.resolution: Not a conflict but the framework that resolves several others. The two-weaknesses method is the correct handling of a STATIC advantage — fix, improve, do not hurry. Applying it while holding a dynamic advantage loses the advantage, and that is exactly the tension recorded on the initiative concept.

What Black holds is dynamic - space, an advanced pawn, open lines for the pieces - and it expires as pieces come off. This one is held permanently, by a queen standing directly in front of it, and it will never move again. by_level.beginner: Some advantages last and some run out. If yours will still be there in twenty moves, take your time. If it will not, you have to use it now.
by_level.intermediate: Static or dynamic? Structure and squares last; initiative and development leads expire. That decides how fast you should be playing.
by_level.advanced: The classification drives tempo. Playing a dynamic edge slowly loses it; hurrying a static one throws it away — and that mismatch is the commonest strategic error.
by_level.master: Also the framework for judging a sacrifice: static compensation must survive simplification, dynamic compensation must be cashed before it does.

by_depth.short: Does your advantage last, or does it expire?
by_depth.normal: Static advantages — structure, weak squares, the bishop pair — persist and reward patience. Dynamic ones — the initiative, a development lead, an exposed king — expire and must be used at once. Which you hold decides your speed.
by_depth.deep: Steinitz's separation of permanent from temporary advantages, and the most useful classification in positional chess because it converts an evaluation into an instruction about tempo. Static advantages often grow as pieces come off, so the method is the slow one: improve everything, do not hurry, trade towards an endgame. Dynamic advantages decay, so they must be converted into something permanent before they fade, and exchanges work against you. Most strategic errors below master level are a mismatch between the kind of advantage held and the speed played. The Soviet contribution was a re-weighting towards the dynamic side, and engines have pushed it further still — they accept structural damage classical theory called simply bad whenever concrete play justifies it.

explanations.lesson: Before choosing a plan, ask one question: will this advantage still be here in twenty moves? The answer tells you whether to hurry.

static-vs-dynamic.definition_short: Static advantages are durable and can be built on slowly; dynamic ones expire and must be used at once. Which kind you hold decides how fast you must play.
static-vs-dynamic.definition_long:
The division goes back to Steinitz's separation of permanent from temporary advantages, and it is the most useful single classification in positional chess because it converts an evaluation into an instruction about TEMPO.

STATIC advantages persist and often grow as pieces come off: a superior pawn structure, a weak square, the bishop pair, a permanent outpost, a better minor piece. They reward patience, and the correct method is the slow one — improve every piece, do not hurry, and let exchanges work for you.

DYNAMIC advantages decay: the initiative, a lead in development, an exposed enemy king, a temporary piece placement. They must be converted into something permanent before they expire, and exchanges usually work against you.

The practical rule is therefore: identify which kind you hold, and let it set your speed. Playing a dynamic advantage slowly loses it; playing a static advantage in a hurry throws it away. Most strategic errors below master level are this mismatch rather than a wrong plan.

The whole Soviet contribution can be read as a re-weighting of this framework — they were willing to accept static damage for dynamic gain far more readily than the classical school, and modern engines agree with them.

strong-square.knowledge_type_note: The mirror of a weak square, seen from the side that gets to use it.

attributions.note: My System treats strong points and their overprotection as a central strategic device.

history.notes: The vocabulary of weak and strong squares is older and anonymous; Nimzowitsch's contribution is the systematic treatment and the overprotection idea.

strong-square.engine_era_note: Engines value control of such squares implicitly and are markedly less impressed than classical teaching by occupying one when a concrete alternative exists.

preconditions: A square no enemy pawn can attack
A friendly pawn able to defend it
indicators_for: The square is in or adjacent to the enemy camp
A knight can reach it in a move or two
It sits on a file your rooks can use
indicators_against: The square can only be held by pieces, not pawns
Nothing useful can reach it
Occupying it achieves nothing concrete
recognition.detector: holesFor in lib/features.js, from the occupying side
false_positive_traps: A square being safe is not a reason to put a piece on it. This base's outpost testing found the textbook outpost move to be only second best in the textbook outpost position.
A strong square held by pieces rather than by a pawn is expensive, and the cost can exceed what the square is worth.

typical_plans: Manoeuvre a knight towards it
Overprotect it so the defenders gain scope from doing so
Trade off the enemy piece that could contest it, usually a knight or a same-coloured bishop
typical_pawn_structures: Structures where an enemy pawn has advanced past the square
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight on the square, defended by a pawn
strategic_consequences: A strong square is permanent in a way a piece placement is not, because it is a property of the pawns

exceptions: A strong square is worth nothing if nothing valuable can reach it.
Occupying is not the only use: controlling the square may matter more than standing on it.
limitations: The geometry is mechanical; the value is not, and this base has failed three times to isolate outpost value in a controlled test.

DELIBERATELY HAS NO MATCHER, and the measurement is why. A detector written to this record's preconditions - a square no enemy pawn can attack, with a friendly pawn able to defend it - fires on 80.1% of the 788 shipped positions, which is the `semi-open-file` failure this project has already made once. It is also a third name for a fact this base already reports twice: `weak-square` is the same square seen from the defender's side and `outpost` is the same square with a piece on it. This record's own note says an outpost and a strong point are really the same thing. Written, measured, and removed rather than shipped.

Identifying an instance in a master game means reading the game, which is research rather than tooling, and it has not been done. Recorded rather than filled. misconceptions: That a strong square must be occupied. Controlling it can be worth more, and occupying it can be second best.
That the centre has the strong squares. They are wherever the enemy pawns have gone past.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. Both of this record's preconditions and nothing else: no enemy pawn can ever attack d5 (Black's c-pawn is gone, and the e5 pawn captures towards d4 and f4, never backwards), and a friendly pawn on e4 defends it. The knight on d5 is therefore permanent AND cheap, which is the second condition doing the work this record says it does - 'the first makes a piece there permanent; the second makes it cheap, because the piece is not tying down other pieces to hold it'. What this base actually reports here is `outpost` for White and `weak-square` for Black; `strong-square` has no matcher of its own, and saying so is more useful than pretending the neighbouring concept is this one.

White's c- and e-pawns are the only pawns that could ever challenge it and both have gone past - c4 and e5 - so d4 cannot be attacked by a pawn for the rest of the game. Black's c5 pawn defends it.

A matcher was written for it exactly to the two preconditions its record states, and it fired on 80.1% of the 788 shipped positions. A concept true of three quarters of all boards cannot be the most informative thing about any of them, so the matcher was thrown away and the record kept. The API therefore never reports `strong-square` and no scan that reads the API could nominate a position for it. Layer 3 still computes the feature, and that is what found this one - the outposts list, restricted to the central files, in positions where there is exactly ONE of them. That restriction is doing the work the discarded matcher could not: it is not a definition of the concept, it is a way of finding the positions where the concept is the striking fact rather than one of five.

PROVENANCE. 330 replayed master games, read through Layer 3 rather than through the API. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator. No annotator read.

by_level.beginner: A square in their half that their pawns can never attack and one of yours can defend.
by_level.intermediate: A strong square. Get a knight there — but check that being there actually does something.
by_level.advanced: Two conditions: no enemy pawn can attack it, and one of your pawns can defend it. The second is what makes it cheap.
by_level.master: Nimzowitsch's move is to overprotect it, on the grounds that the defenders gain scope from bearing on a square that matters.

by_depth.short: A square their pawns cannot attack and yours can defend.
by_depth.normal: A strong square: the mirror of a weak one, seen from the side that gets to use it. It needs both conditions - no enemy pawn able to attack it, and a friendly pawn able to defend it - because the first makes a piece there permanent and the second makes it cheap.
by_depth.deep: The same geometry as a weak square, from the other side. What makes it strong rather than merely reachable is the pair of conditions: no enemy pawn can attack it, so a piece there cannot be driven away, and one of your own pawns can defend it, so holding it does not tie down other pieces. Nimzowitsch's contribution was overprotection - defending such a point beyond necessity, on the reasoning that the defenders gain their own scope from bearing on a square that matters. The outpost is the special case where a minor piece actually occupies it, and this base's own engine testing is the standing warning that occupying is not automatically best.

explanations.lesson: Ask whether a pawn can defend it. That is what separates a strong square from a square you can reach.

beginner_words: a safe square in their half

strong-square.definition_short: A square in or near the enemy position that your pawns can defend and theirs cannot attack.
strong-square.definition_long:
The same geometry as a weak square, described from the other side of the board. A square is weak FOR the player who can no longer cover it with a pawn, and strong FOR the opponent who can.

TWO CONDITIONS make it strong rather than merely reachable: no enemy pawn can attack it, and one of your own pawns can defend it. The first makes a piece there permanent; the second makes it cheap, because the piece is not tying down other pieces to hold it. A piece on a strong square that has to be defended by two pieces is a liability wearing a good square's clothes.

NIMZOWITSCH'S CONTRIBUTION was to treat such a point as something to be OVERPROTECTED — defended beyond necessity — on the reasoning that the defenders gain their own scope from bearing on a square that matters, so the overprotection costs less than it appears to. That is the constructive form of the idea, and it is recorded on its own concept.

THE OUTPOST IS THE SPECIAL CASE: a strong square actually occupied by a minor piece, usually a knight. The strong square is the real estate; the outpost is what gets built on it. And this base's engine testing on outposts is the standing warning that occupying one is not automatically the best move.

tabiya.knowledge_type_note: A term for a class of position, used mainly in opening literature.

history.notes: The Arabic derivation (ta'biya, battle array) is well attested and consistent across sources. One community answer instead traces the word through Sanskrit and Old Persian; that chain is not corroborated here and the two accounts are not reconciled, so the etymology is recorded at low confidence. The count of sixteen named ta'biyat in 9th-10th century shatranj manuscripts comes from a community answer and has NOT been verified against a scholarly source such as Murray.

competing_claims.note: Consistent with the standard literature on shatranj.

competing_claims.claim: From Sanskrit, passing into Old Persian

tabiya.engine_era_note: Tabiyas have been pushed deeper. Where preparation once ended around the tabiya, elite games now frequently follow analysis well past it.

preconditions: A position reached by a standardised sequence
Several distinct plans available from it

The branching continuations embody different strategic ideas

by_level.beginner: The standard position an opening always seems to reach, where the real choices begin.
by_level.intermediate: A tabiya - the position where an opening's theory starts, after the near-automatic moves are done.
by_level.advanced: What makes it a tabiya is that different plans, not merely different move orders, branch from it.
by_level.master: The natural unit of opening study, though preparation now routinely runs well past it.

by_depth.short: The standard starting position of an opening's real theory.
by_depth.normal: A tabiya: a position reached after a heavily standardised sequence, from which several genuinely different plans branch. The moves leading to it are played quickly and by convention; the choices that matter start there.
by_depth.deep: The point where an opening's theory actually begins. What distinguishes it from any other frequently seen position is that its continuations represent different plans rather than different routes to the same one. Depth varies widely, from eight or nine moves in some openings to seventeen in others. The word is Arabic - ta'biya, a battle array - and comes from shatranj, where the pieces moved so slowly that the approach phase was nearly uncontested and the named formations were themselves the body of opening theory.

explanations.hedge: The etymology and the count of documented shatranj formations are recorded at low confidence and were not verified against a scholarly history.
explanations.lesson: Study the plans that branch from the standard position, not the moves that lead to it.

tabiya.definition_short: A standard position reached after a heavily established sequence, from which several genuinely different plans branch.
tabiya.definition_long:
The position where an opening's theory really begins. The moves leading to it are more or less forced by convention rather than by force — strong players reach it quickly and without much thought — and the branching that matters starts there.

The distinguishing feature is that the continuations from a tabiya represent DIFFERENT PLANS, not merely different move orders aiming at the same thing. That is what separates a tabiya from any other well-known position.

How deep a tabiya sits varies enormously by opening: some are reached in eight or nine moves, others as many as seventeen. The word is Arabic, ta'biya, meaning a battle formation or array. In shatranj — the medieval Arabic game — the pieces moved so slowly that the approach phase was nearly uncontested, and the named ta'biyat were the formal body of opening theory; sixteen of them are documented in ninth- and tenth-century manuscripts. The modern usage is a direct descendant of that meaning.

What the engine era did change is the standing of individual famous combinations, many of which turn out to have been unsound and to have worked because the defence was hard rather than impossible.

preconditions: A forcing sequence exists
It has an identifiable goal
indicators_for: The opponent's replies are compelled at every step
Material is offered as part of the sequence
The resulting position is materially or positionally decided
indicators_against: The opponent has real choices at some point, which makes it a plan rather than a combination

A forcing sequence without a sacrifice is a manoeuvre on Botvinnik's account and a combination on Romanovsky's. Reporting it either way takes a side in an open argument.
Length and forcing-ness do not make a combination; there has to be a goal it reaches.

Search forcing moves first, since a combination is by definition made of them

strategic_consequences: Lasker's dictum ties combinations to a pre-existing advantage: no combination without a considerable plus

Both primary definitions were consulted through secondary accounts rather than in the original.

examples.note: Anderssen-Dufresne 1852, from 21.Qxd7+ - and it is here because it is a combination on BOTH of the contested definitions at once, which is what this record needs and rarely gets. Botvinnik requires a sacrifice: there is one, a queen. Romanovsky requires only a forced sequence reaching a goal: every move to the end is a check and the goal is mate in four. The record's rule is that this system must not assert either version as the definition, and an example that satisfies both is the way to have a positive without taking a side. The third trap is satisfied too - 'length and forcing-ness do not make a combination; there has to be a goal it reaches' - and the goal is 24.Bxe7 mate.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 4 at depth 20, settled at depth 1. Qxd7+ Kxd7, Bf5+ Ke8, Bd7+ Kf8, Bxe7 mate - a queen given and every reply forced.

THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: A forced sequence of checks running nineteen moves to mate, with the defender's replies determined throughout. A long forcing line ending in mate is what most players mean by a combination. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second trap: "A forcing sequence without a sacrifice is a manoeuvre on Botvinnik's account and a combination on Romanovsky's. Reporting it either way takes a side in a live disagreement." Nothing is sacrificed here at any point. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports double-check and does not report a combination. Syzygy: PROVEN WIN, dtz 17, mate in 19 — so the sequence really is forced and really does reach a goal, which is the third trap's requirement ('length and forcing-ness do not make a combination; there has to be a goal it reaches'). What it does not have is a sacrifice, and this record's FIRST trap forbids the system from deciding whether that matters: 'whether a sacrifice is REQUIRED is contested by named authorities, so this system must not assert either version as the definition.' Not reporting is the only answer that does not take a side.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 17, mate in 19. The sequence really is forced and really does reach a goal, which is what this record's third trap requires of a combination. What it does not contain is a sacrifice, and the record's first trap forbids the system from deciding whether that matters.

by_level.beginner: A forced sequence of moves that achieves something concrete — often starting with a sacrifice.
by_level.intermediate: A combination. Note that whether it must involve a sacrifice is genuinely disputed among strong authorities.
by_level.advanced: Botvinnik: a forced variation with a sacrifice, and a forced variation without one is a manoeuvre. Romanovsky and Lasker did not require the sacrifice.
by_level.master: A 1952 discussion in Chess in the USSR failed to settle it, and Averbakh argued both sides four years apart.

by_depth.short: A forced sequence of moves with a concrete goal.
by_depth.normal: A combination: a forcing sequence with a specific goal, grounded in tactics. Whether it must contain a sacrifice is contested — Botvinnik said always, Romanovsky and Lasker did not require one, and the Oxford Companion reports the disagreement rather than settling it.
by_depth.deep: One of the few places where the definition is itself the open question. Botvinnik's 1939 formulation - a forced variation with a sacrifice, as against a forced manoeuvre without one - became the majority view from the mid-1960s, but Romanovsky had defined it in 1929 without any sacrifice requirement, Lasker treated it as a net of forcing variations, and the Oxford Companion adds surprise as the essential property while explicitly declining to settle the sacrifice question. A formal discussion in Chess in the USSR in 1952 reached no consensus and was never summarised, and Averbakh argued for the sacrifice requirement in 1976 and against it in 1980. What every version agrees on is that the sequence is forcing and has a goal.

explanations.hedge: The definition is contested among named authorities and this base adopts none of them; only 'forcing' and 'has a goal' are common to every version.
explanations.lesson: Everyone agrees a combination is forcing and gets somewhere. Whether it must give something up has been argued for eighty years.

beginner_words: a forced sequence that wins something
avoid: a combination always involves a sacrifice

tactical-combinations.definition_short: A forced sequence of moves with a specific goal — and, according to some authorities but not others, necessarily involving a sacrifice.
tactical-combinations.definition_long:
One of the few concepts in this base where the DEFINITION is the open question, and the argument is documented well enough to record properly.

BOTVINNIK (1939), in Chess in the USSR and later as an appendix to One Hundred Selected Games: 'A combination is a forced variation with sacrifice.' He drew the line explicitly — 'a forced manoeuvre is a forced variation WITHOUT sacrifice' — and illustrated it with two of his own endgame examples, calling the one with a two-pawn sacrifice a combination and the one without a manoeuvre.

ROMANOVSKY (Mittelshpiel, 1929), earlier and without the sacrifice requirement: 'a variation (or group of variations) during which both sides make forced moves and which ends with an objective advantage for the active side.'

LASKER, earlier still, treats it as a net of variations: where a player can find a forcing line to a desirable outcome, 'the totality of these variations and their logical connections, their structure, are named a combination'.

HOOPER AND WHYLD, in the Oxford Companion, decline to settle it and say so: 'a sequence of forcing moves with a specific goal, and grounded in tactics. A sacrifice is LIKELY to be present and Botvinnik, among others, says is ALWAYS present.' They add the property the others leave out — SURPRISE, the line differing in form from what would normally be expected.

THE ARGUMENT HAS A HISTORY AND NO ENDING. Chess in the USSR ran a formal discussion in 1952 that reached no consensus and whose results were never summarised. The 1964 Chess Dictionary followed Romanovsky. Opinion swung to Botvinnik after Bondarevsky's Combinations in the Middlegame (1965) — Kotov switched sides by 1975, and Averbakh and Beilin wrote in 1976 that sacrifices made for an advantage simply ARE combinations. Then in 1980 Averbakh reversed himself, arguing the sacrifice requirement was too narrow and proposing a definition based on the transformation of relationships between pieces instead.

THIS BASE ADOPTS NONE OF THEM. What all versions agree on is FORCING and a GOAL, so those are what the record treats as the concept; the sacrifice requirement is recorded as contested.

tempo.knowledge_type_note: A unit of measurement, not a principle. It is what initiative is counted in.

history.notes: Ordinary chess vocabulary of long standing; no coinage researched or claimed.

tempo.engine_era_note: Engines handle time implicitly through search rather than as a term, and they are notably less impressed by tempo-counting than opening books are — a 'lost tempo' that produces a better structure is often simply the right move.

preconditions: A move is being assessed for what it costs or gains in time
indicators_for: The move develops or improves a piece AND forces a reply
The opponent's forced reply does nothing for them
A piece is being moved twice in the opening without compensation — a lost tempo
indicators_against: The 'threat' forcing the reply is not real, so no tempo is gained
The forced reply actually improves the opponent's position — a common trap
The position is closed, where time matters little
false_positive_traps: Chasing a piece with a threat it WANTED to answer is not gaining a tempo — the classic case is driving a piece to a better square with an attack.
Counting tempi in a closed position, where they may be worth nothing.
Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square all justify it.

typical_plans: Develop with threats so each move does two jobs
In the endgame, keep a spare pawn move in reserve as a tempo
Triangulate to lose a tempo deliberately
typical_moves: A developing move that attacks something
A spare pawn move held back in a pawn ending
strategic_consequences: Accumulated tempi become a lead in development and then the initiative

exceptions: 'Losing a tempo' is a virtue in the endgame, where triangulation aims at exactly that.
A tempo has no fixed value; the three-tempi-per-pawn heuristic is an opening rule of thumb only.
Moving the same piece twice is not automatically a lost tempo.
limitations: Not mechanically detectable. Whether a move 'gains a tempo' depends on whether the threat is real and whether the reply helps the opponent.
misconceptions: That a tempo is worth a third of a pawn. It has no fixed value.
That gaining tempi is always good — driving an enemy piece to a better square costs you more than it gains.
That tempo and initiative are the same thing.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `the-same-piece-moved-twice`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White's bishop has gone b5 then a4: the same piece moved twice in the opening, and Black has developed a piece in between. By the rule as it is usually taught, White has lost a tempo. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's third trap, and it is the one the record itself says is registered: "Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square are all reasons to move it again." Here it is an escape — Black played ...a6 to attack the bishop — and the tempo Black spent attacking it is the same tempo White spent retreating. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: WRITTEN BECAUSE THE RECORD CLAIMED IT ALREADY EXISTED. The `tempo` record said 'this is a registered false-positive case' and no case with that concept was in this file — a claim the file did not back, which is the same defect class as an `implements` string claiming what the code does not do. A test now asserts that any record using that phrase has a case. The position is the Ruy Lopez after 4.Ba4, the most-played opening in the history of the game; Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says -0.43 from Black's side, an ordinary opening edge for White. The API reports nothing about tempo here, correctly: this base has no tempo matcher, because counting tempi requires knowing whether the forced reply was one the opponent wanted, and that is not on the board.

by_level.beginner: A tempo is one move's worth of time. You gain one when your move improves your position and forces them to answer with a move that does nothing for them.
by_level.intermediate: A tempo. Check the threat is real and that answering it does not actually help them — that is where tempo-counting usually goes wrong.
by_level.advanced: One unit of time. Note the sign flips in the endgame: losing a tempo by triangulation is the goal there, not a cost.
by_level.master: Tempi are only meaningful relative to the position's sharpness. In a locked structure they are close to worthless; in an open one a single move decides.

by_depth.short: One move's worth of time.
by_depth.normal: A tempo is one move considered as time. Gaining one means your move improves your position while forcing a reply that does not improve theirs — the move has to do two jobs.
by_depth.deep: The unit initiative is counted in. Gaining a tempo requires a move that both improves your position and compels a reply that does nothing for the opponent; the common error is 'gaining' a tempo by driving an enemy piece somewhere it preferred to be. The word is also used with the opposite sign in the endgame, where triangulation is described as losing a move on purpose in order to return the same position with the opponent to play. There is no fixed exchange rate with material: the familiar three-tempi-per-pawn figure is an opening heuristic, and in a closed position tempi may be worth nothing at all.

explanations.lesson: A move gains a tempo only if the reply it forces is one your opponent did not want to make. Check that before congratulating yourself.

avoid: a tempo is worth a third of a pawn

tempo.definition_short: One move, considered as a unit of time. To 'gain a tempo' is to improve your position while forcing a reply that does not.
tempo.definition_long:
A single move regarded as a unit of time. Gaining a tempo means making a move that does two jobs at once — it improves your position AND compels a reply that does not improve theirs. Losing a tempo means spending a move that achieves nothing, or moving the same piece twice for no gain.

The relationship to INITIATIVE is the thing to keep straight, and the two are constantly conflated: a tempo is one unit, the initiative is the sustained state built out of them. Tempi are the coins; the initiative is what you have when you keep spending them profitably.

Confusingly, 'losing a tempo' is also used APPROVINGLY in the endgame, where triangulation is described as losing a move on purpose in order to hand the same position back with the opponent to play. The two usages are opposite in sign and both are standard.

A tempo has NO fixed value. The common rule of thumb that three tempi are worth a pawn is a rough opening heuristic and nothing more: in a sharp position one move decides the game, and in a locked position several are worth nothing at all.

theoretical-novelty.knowledge_type_note: A term of art about the state of published theory, not a judgement about a move's quality.

history.notes: Standard vocabulary of tournament practice; the abbreviation TN is common in game annotation.

theoretical-novelty.engine_era_note: The most heavily changed item in this domain. Novelties at elite level are now predominantly engine-generated and essentially all engine-checked, which shifts the skill from finding a new move to choosing which of many engine-approved moves poses the most practical problems. The depth of preparation has grown to the point where opening lines are contested fifteen and more moves in with both sides following home analysis.

preconditions: An opening move with no precedent in the reference database
indicators_for: The move departs from established theory at a known branching point
indicators_against: The move is merely rare rather than unprecedented
The position is already outside the opening
false_positive_traps: Novelty is relative to a particular database. A move absent from one corpus may be well known in another, so the label is only as good as the reference used.
A novelty is not automatically good. The term describes the literature, not the move's merit, and this base will not report one as an improvement without evidence.
Not detectable by this system: identifying this requires an opening database, which the Education System does not have.

typical_plans: Prepare a new move at home and keep it for a chosen opponent
Depart from theory early to leave a better-prepared opponent on their own
strategic_consequences: Transfers the burden of solving the position from the preparer to the opponent, and with it the clock time

exceptions: A novelty played by accident carries none of the preparation value that gives the term its point.
limitations: This system has no opening database, so it cannot identify novelties and does not attempt to.
The claim 'never played before' is unverifiable without a defined corpus, and should be stated with the corpus named.

A case in tests/false_positive_cases.json is a POSITION where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is not, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This record's `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`: what it describes is something a player does rather than something a board contains, so there is no surface pattern for a position to carry and nothing for the system to decline. The conditions this record states are read and answered in `limitations` and in the trap audit instead. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item.
misconceptions: That a novelty is by definition a strong move. It is by definition an unplayed one.
That novelties are found by human insight alone. At the top level they are overwhelmingly engine-generated now.

by_level.beginner: A move in the opening that has not been played before.
by_level.intermediate: A theoretical novelty - a new move in a known opening. New does not mean good.
by_level.advanced: A novelty kept back deliberately is a prepared variation; its value is that the opponent must solve at the board what you solved at home.
by_level.master: The scarce resource is no longer the new move but the choice of which engine-approved line sets the hardest practical problems.

by_depth.short: A new move in a known opening.
by_depth.normal: A theoretical novelty: an opening move with no precedent in the recorded body of theory. The term describes the state of the literature rather than the quality of the move - a novelty can be an improvement, an error, or simply something nobody had tried.
by_depth.deep: A move without precedent in the recorded corpus, which makes the label bibliographic rather than evaluative. Its competitive value appears when it is found in advance and withheld - a prepared variation - because then the opponent must solve at the board, on the clock, what the preparer solved at home with unlimited time and an engine. The value is spent on first use: after the game the move is theory. In the engine era the skill has shifted, since novelties at the top are now overwhelmingly machine-generated and universally machine-checked, so the difficulty lies in choosing which sound line poses the most practical problems rather than in finding a new move at all.

explanations.hedge: This system has no opening database and therefore cannot tell whether a move is a novelty; the concept is recorded for vocabulary and explanation, not for detection.
explanations.lesson: New is a fact about the books, not about the move.

theoretical-novelty.definition_short: A new move in the opening — one not previously played in the recorded body of theory.
theoretical-novelty.definition_long:
A sequence of opening moves that has not appeared before in the recorded corpus. The term says something about the LITERATURE, not about the move: a novelty may be an improvement, a mistake, or simply a move nobody had bothered to play. Calling a move a novelty is a bibliographic claim.

When a novelty is found in advance and deliberately withheld until a chosen game, it is a PREPARED VARIATION, and that is where its competitive value lies. The point is not that the move is unknown to theory but that it is unknown to the opponent, who must solve at the board what the player solved at home with unlimited time.

The concept has a defined shelf life. A novelty is novel exactly once; after the game it enters theory, and its value as a surprise is spent even if its value as a move is permanent.

threefold-repetition.knowledge_type_note: Official rule. The claim/automatic distinction against Art. 9.6.1 is explicit.
threefold-repetition.definition_short: A player to move may CLAIM a draw when the same position is about to appear, or has just appeared, for the third time.
threefold-repetition.definition_long:
FIDE Art. 9.2: 'The game is drawn, upon a correct claim by a player having the move, when the same position for at least the third time (not necessarily by a repetition of moves)' either is about to appear (announced in advance) or has just appeared.

It is a CLAIM, not automatic — play continues if nobody claims. The repetitions need not be consecutive and need not come from repeating moves.

Art. 9.2.3 defines position identity precisely: 'Positions are considered the same if and only if the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy the same squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the same.' Two riders follow: positions differ if at the start of the sequence a pawn could have been captured en passant (9.2.3.1), and if a king had castling rights with an unmoved rook but forfeited them afterwards (9.2.3.2).

preconditions: The same position, by the Art. 9.2.3 test, has occurred three times

exceptions: Not automatic — without a claim the game continues.
Side to move, castling rights and en-passant availability are all part of the position; ignoring any of them produces false repetitions.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

examples.pgn: 1. Ra2 Kd8 2. Ra1 Ke8 3. Ra2 Kd8 4. Ra1 Ke8 5. Ra2 Kd8 6. Ra1 Ke8
examples.note: A position is not enough for this concept and the example says so by being a SEQUENCE. Threefold repetition is a claim about history: the same position, the same side to move, the same castling and en-passant rights, three times. The line above was replayed through this base's own move generator move by move - every one legal, no capture, no pawn move - and the starting position recurs FIVE times in it. The count is what the generator reports, not what the notation looks like.

counterexamples.note: Constructed, and it is a SEQUENCE because the rule is about history. From r3k2r/8/8/8/8/8/8/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1 both sides move a rook out and back: 1.Rg1 Rg8 2.Rh1 Rh8. Every man is on the square it started on and the position has NOT repeated, because both sides have lost the right to castle kingside - the FEN reads `w Qq - 4 3` where it read `w KQkq - 0 1`. FIDE Art. 9.2.3 includes castling rights in the definition of the same position, so a diagram that looks identical is a different position and no claim exists. This is the exact error the `notation` record's third trap names: a FEN without the castling, en-passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one. The four moves were played through this base's own move generator, which emitted both FENs.

by_level.beginner: The same position has now happened three times, so either player whose turn it is may claim a draw.
by_level.intermediate: Threefold repetition. Remember it is a claim, and that castling rights and en-passant possibilities are part of what makes a position 'the same'.
by_level.advanced: Art. 9.2, with position identity defined at 9.2.3 including the en-passant and castling-rights riders.

by_depth.short: The same position three times, with the same side to move, is claimable as a draw.
by_depth.normal: Threefold repetition: a player to move may CLAIM a draw when the same position is about to appear, or has just appeared, for the third time. Positions need not be consecutive, and the claim is a right rather than an automatic result.
by_depth.deep: FIDE Art. 9.2, and 'the same position' is a term of art defined at 9.2.3: the same men on the same squares, the same side to move, the same castling rights, and the same en-passant possibility. Two of those four are invisible on a diagram, which is why this base's example for the rule is a SEQUENCE rather than a position — sixteen plies replayed through the move generator, in which the starting position recurs five times.

validation_na.false_positive_test: N/A rather than missing. A registered false-positive case is a position where the concept's surface pattern is present and the concept is absent, replayed as an assertion so the system can be shown declining the error. This concept is DECIDED BY THE MOVE GENERATOR - the same function that decides it in a game - so there is no judgement to get wrong and no surface pattern that can be present without the thing itself. The nearest genuine risk is a PATTERN NAME attached to a position that is check and not mate, and that risk belongs to `back-rank-mate` and `smothered-mate`, both of which carry a registered case for it.

time-management.knowledge_type_note: Unusually well evidenced for practical advice: the claims here come from large-sample studies of real games rather than from received wisdom.

history.notes: A research literature rather than a tradition; the findings here are from 2007-2026 and several are recent enough that replication is thin.

competing_claims.claim: faster decisions are associated with HIGHER quality even controlling for complexity
competing_claims.note: A separate study reports this, which sits awkwardly beside the time-pressure findings and is recorded rather than reconciled.

time-management.engine_era_note: This whole literature exists because engines made move quality measurable. Every study cited here scores human moves against an engine benchmark, which is what turned clock advice from anecdote into measurement.

preconditions: A game played with a clock
false_positive_traps: This is advice to a player about a clock, not an observation about a position, and must never be attached to a move as an explanation of it.
The evidence is about populations. It does not establish what any individual should do on any given move.
One study in this set reports faster decisions correlating with HIGHER quality, which does not obviously sit with the time-pressure findings. Both are recorded; neither is presented as settled.

typical_plans: Move quickly in the opening and in simplified endings
Spend the time in the middlegame, where the options genuinely multiply
Spend most where the position is unclear, since that is where errors compound
In severe time trouble prefer a fast move to a good slow one
strategic_consequences: Varying the spend matters more than the average spend; flexibility is the measured hallmark of strength

exceptions: A forced sequence needs no time regardless of phase.
An endgame that is theoretically critical deserves time even though endgames are generally played fast.
limitations: The studies measure populations of games, not individual decisions.
Several results are recent and thinly replicated; the blitz error-amplification study is from 2026.
This system cannot see a clock and can give no advice about one.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and a FEN is not the right kind of evidence for one here. An ambiguous example in this base is a POSITION where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - the pattern is on the board and the reading of it is not. This record's subject is not on the board: its `recognition.detectability` is `human-only`, and what it describes is something a player does at the board rather than something the board contains.
