misconceptions: That strong players think longer. They think longer in the middlegame and shorter elsewhere, and vary more.
That mastery is intuition and time pressure therefore costs experts little. Grandmasters and world champions show strong adverse effects.
That time trouble simply makes you play worse. It makes you play worse SPECIFICALLY where the position is also unclear, and the two combine nonlinearly.

by_level.beginner: Play the opening quickly and think in the middlegame, where the position gets complicated.
by_level.intermediate: Strong players spend less time than weak ones on openings and endings and more on middlegames — and vary their spend far more.
by_level.advanced: Spend where the position is unclear: blunders rise nonlinearly when low time and an ambiguous position coincide.
by_level.master: In severe time trouble the clock becomes material — at 20 to 30 seconds in a blitz game, eight seconds was worth about a knight.

by_depth.short: Think in the middlegame; move fast elsewhere.
by_depth.normal: How to spend the clock, with unusually good evidence behind it. Across 91,000 games, strong players spend LESS time than weak players on openings and endings and significantly more on middlegames, and vary their spend far more — flexibility rather than sheer thinking time is the measured hallmark.
by_depth.deep: One of the few practical areas with real evidence. Everyone plays openings and endings faster than middlegames, and strong players exaggerate the pattern while varying their spend much more widely. The middlegame genuinely is harder - the number of reasonable options grows roughly linearly for twenty moves - but complexity stays high into the endgame while players speed up anyway, so the late speed-up is a chosen trade-off rather than a response to simplicity. Under real time pressure the clock becomes material: at 20 to 30 seconds in a three-minute game, eight seconds was worth about an extra knight. And time pressure degrades even world champions, who remain dependent on deliberation and are simply strategic about when to spend it.

explanations.hedge: These are findings about populations of games, measured against engine benchmarks; they do not determine what any individual should do on a particular move, and one study in the set points the other way.
explanations.lesson: Spend your time where the position is genuinely unclear. That is where errors multiply rather than add.

beginner_words: don't use all your time early

time-management.definition_short: How to spend the clock — and the finding that strong players spend it very differently from weak ones.
time-management.definition_long:
One of the few practical areas where there is real evidence rather than folklore.

WHERE THE TIME ACTUALLY GOES. An analysis of over 91,000 games found that everyone plays openings and endgames faster than middlegames — but that STRONG PLAYERS EXAGGERATE THE PATTERN. Players rated above 1900 spend even less time than weak players on the opening and the ending, and significantly more on middlegame moves. Their time distribution is also wider: the hallmark is not spending more time but VARYING it more, matching the spend to the position.

WHY THE MIDDLEGAME COSTS MOST is measurable. The number of reasonable options grows roughly linearly over the first twenty moves, so decisions genuinely get harder. But the same study found complexity stays high into the endgame while players speed up anyway — so the late speed-up is a deliberate shift in the speed-accuracy trade-off, not a response to a simpler position.

TIME BECOMES MATERIAL. The most striking single result: as the clock runs down, the factor determining the outcome shifts from position to time. In three-minute games with 20-30 seconds left, an eight-second advantage on the clock was worth about as much as an extra knight. Under real time pressure a fast move beats a good move that costs time.

TIME PRESSURE DEGRADES EVERYONE, including the very best. A study of twenty grandmasters and seven world champions found strong adverse effects on both speed and blunder rate, and concluded that elite players remain dependent on DELIBERATION — they are simply strategic about when to spend it. That cuts against the popular idea that mastery is mostly intuition. Consistent with it, once players are forced to play fast their normal-time rating becomes markedly less predictive of results, an effect strong at blitz and weak at rapid.

AND ERRORS CLUSTER RATHER THAN SCATTER. In a study of nearly 40,000 blitz positions, blunder probability rose NONLINEARLY when low time and an unclear position coincided — the combination is worse than the sum of its parts. The practical reading is that the moment to spend time is when the position is genuinely unclear, and the moment to move fast is when it is not.

transformation-of-advantages.knowledge_type_note: A method for converting advantages, and one whose own authors record an internal tension with the principles it sits beside.

attributions.note: Technique in Chess sets out the four golden principles with the transformation of an advantage as a named section.
The standard exemplar, on the strength of his games rather than any formulation of his own.

history.notes: The idea is older than the formulation and no coinage is traced. Two definitions of 'technique' are recorded alongside it from the same discussion: Zaitsev's 'technique is an art from the past', and Gligoric's plainer 'technique is the skilful application of the laws of strategy and tactics'.

transformation-of-advantages.engine_era_note: Engines transform advantages constantly and without sentiment, releasing binds and returning material whenever a more convertible advantage results. Watching an engine do this is one of the clearest ways the concept can now be studied, and it exposes how reluctant human players are to give up an advantage they can see for one they must first believe in.

preconditions: One side holds an advantage of some kind
A conversion of that advantage into another form is available
indicators_for: The current advantage has stopped growing
A concrete line converts the edge into material or a won ending
The opponent's only counterplay can be removed by a transformation
indicators_against: The advantage is still increasing by simple improvement
The transformation surrenders more than it obtains
false_positive_traps: A transforming move often looks like a concession and can be reported as an error by anything judging moves on what they give up rather than what they get.
Not every exchange of one advantage for another is a transformation; it must be for a MORE convertible advantage, and this base cannot judge that without concrete evidence.
The concept describes a player's intention. This system observes moves, not intentions, and must not attribute a transformation to a move without evidence.

typical_plans: Convert a positional bind into won material
Convert a material edge into a technically winning endgame
Trade an expiring dynamic advantage for a permanent structural one
Remove all counterplay first, then look for the concrete path
typical_moves: Returning sacrificed material at the moment it buys a won ending
Exchanging into an endgame that is winning rather than merely better
tactical_consequences: The concrete phase generally requires exact calculation rather than judgement
strategic_consequences: An advantage that is never transformed usually dissipates

exceptions: Where an advantage can be converted directly, no transformation is needed.
The authors themselves note that concrete play runs contrary to the patient principles, so the method contains a real internal tension rather than a smooth procedure.
limitations: Recognising the turning point is the whole difficulty and no source offers a test for it.
This base has not validated any transformation example against an engine, so the concept currently rests on textual authority alone.

No detector, per the record's human-only classification. The concept describes an intention and this base observes moves; the corpus entry records the one position where a named annotator, the game's continuation and the engine all agree what the intention was.
misconceptions: That an advantage should be held onto. Advantages are usually converted through several intermediate forms, and holding one unchanged is how it dissipates.
That giving something up means conceding. A transformation is judged by what is obtained.
That technique means playing safely. Its authors describe the decisive phase as precise calculation, not patient manoeuvring.

conflicts.resolution: A tension the source itself names: patient improvement and forcing calculation pull against each other, and the skill is knowing when the first has run out. This base records the authors' framing and the published objection to it, and does not choose.

examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein, Berlin 1928, Qxc6. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM). Corpus entry `capablanca-rubinstein-1928-22Qxc6-transformation`, which carries the full annotation, the alternates the annotator rejected, and the engine's verdict. A transforming move gives something up, and that is precisely what makes it hard to recognise and easy to mislabel. Twenty moves of pressure on d4 are abandoned in one move; the reader who is following the plan sees a concession. The concept record names this as its first false-positive trap in reverse - 'a transforming move often looks like a concession and can be reported as an error by anything

engine.verdict_note: fully. 22.Qxc6 is the engine's first choice at depth 22 (+0.34), ahead of 22.Bb4 (+0.09) and 22.Re2 (+0.05), and its principal variation continues 22...bxc6 23.Kf1 - it likes the resulting ending for the same structural reason the annotation gives. A quarter-pawn gap is small in absolute terms and decisive in kind: the two runners-up are moves that keep the attack on d4, and the engine puts the move that abandons it first.

examples.attributed_by: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM) — corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-22Qxc6-transformation

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `material-given-and-nothing-obtained`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Bxh7+ gives up a bishop for a pawn — one advantage, the bishop pair and the extra piece, exchanged for another, an exposed king. Trading one kind of advantage for another is the concept, word for word. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Nothing is obtained. The record's second trap says a transformation must be for a MORE convertible advantage; here the knight on f6 simply takes on h7 and White has given a piece for a pawn. A transformation that acquires nothing is not a transformation, it is a blunder, and this record's first trap warns of the mirror error — that a real transforming move 'often looks like a concession'. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report a transformation. It reports `sacrifice` at medium with the record's caution attached, `pin` and `trapped-piece` — all true of the move, none of them claiming it is good. Stockfish 18: the position is 0.00 with a normal move and Bxh7+ scores -3.89, and the refutation is Nxh7 rather than Kxh7. This record has no matcher and its third trap says why: 'the concept describes a player's INTENTION. This system observes moves, not intentions, and must not attribute a transformation to a move without evidence of what it obtained.'

ambiguous_examples.note: Capablanca-Rubinstein 1928, 22.Qxc6 - which this base already carries as this record's POSITIVE example, and it is here a second time for the half the positive cannot say. The annotation is explicit that the move looks like a mistake: 'at first glance this looks like a mistake, because after 22...bxc6 Black's pawns are united and his once-isolated pawn is no longer isolated at all. Capablanca has apparently thrown away the very weakness he spent the whole game creating.' This record's own first trap is that a transforming move 'often looks like a concession and can be reported as an error by anything judging moves on what they give up'. Filed as ambiguous because the concept requires knowing that the new advantage is MORE convertible than the old one, and the record's second trap says outright that this base cannot judge that - so the same position is both the concept's best instance and the proof that the base cannot recognise it.
ambiguous_examples.attributed_by: corpus entry capablanca-rubinstein-1928-22Qxc6-transformation

engine.verdict_note: +0.34 and the engine's first choice at depth 22 with three lines, so the move is objectively best - which settles that it is not an error and settles nothing about whether it is a TRANSFORMATION. That distinction is the record's third trap: the concept describes a player's intention, and this system observes moves.

by_level.beginner: Trade the advantage you have for one that is easier to win with - a better position for extra material, extra material for a won ending.
by_level.intermediate: Transformation of an advantage. Judge the move by what you get, not by what you give up.
by_level.advanced: Remove counterplay, improve everything, and then find the concrete path - the difficulty is recognising when patient play has run out.
by_level.master: Miss the turning point and the advantage survives but may become unconvertible.

by_depth.short: Trade one advantage for a more convertible one.
by_depth.normal: Transformation of an advantage: converting the edge you have into a different kind that is easier to cash - a bind into material, material into a winning endgame, activity into a lasting weakness. Advantages are rarely converted directly; they are usually transformed several times first.
by_depth.deep: The step most often missing between having an advantage and winning with it. It sits inside a larger method - do not allow counterplay, do not hurry, two weaknesses, correct exchanging - and is the operation those principles create the conditions for. The hard part is the turning point: once everything extractable by patient improvement has been extracted, the player must switch from manoeuvring to exact calculation, and missing that moment leaves the advantage intact but much harder to convert, or unconvertible. Transforming moves are difficult to see because they look like concessions - releasing a bind, giving up the bishop pair, returning material - and are judged by what is obtained rather than what is surrendered.

explanations.lesson: Judge the move by what it obtains, not by what it gives up - and notice when patient improvement has stopped paying.

transformation-of-advantages.definition_short: Exchanging one kind of advantage for another that is easier to convert - a space edge for a material one, activity for a structural weakness, a better position for a won ending.
transformation-of-advantages.definition_long:
The step most often missing between having an advantage and winning with it. An advantage is not usually cashed directly; it is TRANSFORMED, often several times, into a form that can finally be converted — a positional bind into won material, material into a winning endgame, activity into a permanent weakness in the opponent's camp.

IT SITS INSIDE A LARGER METHOD. Dvoretsky and Yusupov give four golden principles of technique: DO NOT ALLOW COUNTERPLAY, DO NOT HURRY, THE PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES, and CORRECT EXCHANGING. Transformation is the operation those principles create the conditions for.

THE HARD PART IS THE TURNING POINT, and the authors are unusually direct about it. At some stage everything extractable by patient improvement has been extracted, and the player must switch from manoeuvring to precise calculation and find the concrete path. Miss that moment and the advantage does not vanish, but converting it becomes 'considerably more complicated, delayed, or even impossible'. The difficulty is not knowing the principles; it is recognising when they have run out.

THE AUTHORS' OWN TENSION, recorded here because it is real: they describe concrete play as 'to some extent contrary' to their golden principles, since patient improvement and forcing calculation pull in different directions. At least one reviewer disputes that framing, arguing concrete play is simply accuracy and is required whether one wins by attack or by technique. This base records the disagreement rather than resolving it.

WHY IT IS HARD TO SEE is that a transforming move often LOOKS like a concession — releasing a bind, giving up the bishop pair, allowing a structural change, returning material. It is assessed by what is obtained, not by what is surrendered.

transposition.knowledge_type_note: A fact about how chess positions are identified, not a piece of advice. It follows from the rules, so it is not disputable.

history.notes: Standard technical vocabulary of opening theory; no coinage researched. The claim that a position remembers only castling rights, en passant availability and repetition count is verified against the FIDE Laws (Article 9.2.2 defines position identity for repetition, including castling and en passant rights), not taken from the instructional sources.

transposition.engine_era_note: Unaffected as a fact, but far more heavily exploited in practice. Engine and database preparation is organised around positions rather than move sequences, which is why searching by position rather than by opening name is the professional habit.

preconditions: Two different move sequences reaching one position
indicators_for: The piece placement matches a known position exactly
Castling rights and en passant rights also match
indicators_against: A piece stands on a different square, however similar the position looks
Castling rights differ, which makes it a different position in law as well as in fact
false_positive_traps: Nearly the same is not the same. One pawn move inserted for both sides makes a different position, and treating it as the canonical one is the commonest opening disaster at club level.
Castling rights are invisible on the board but are part of the position. Two arrangements that look identical are not transpositions if one side has lost the right to castle.

typical_plans: Choose a move order that denies the opponent a line you do not want to face
Use a flexible first move to keep several destinations available
Reach a familiar structure from an unfamiliar opening
typical_moves: Flexible first moves such as 1.Nf3 and 1.c4 that can enter several systems
strategic_consequences: Repertoire size can be reduced by funnelling many openings into one structure

exceptions: Castling rights, en passant availability and repetition count are remembered, so positions matching in piece placement alone may still differ.
limitations: Whether a given move order is safe is a concrete question about the extra options it concedes, not something the concept itself answers.
misconceptions: That a transposition is a kind of repetition. Repetition is one game revisiting a position; transposition is different routes reaching a position once.
That reaching the same opening name means reaching the same position. Names index move sequences, positions do not.

examples.note: Two move orders reaching one position, both replayed through this base's own move generator: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 and 1.c4 e6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3. The men stand identically, the side to move is the same, the castling rights are the same, and neither carries an en-passant possibility - which is the FIDE Art. 9.2.3 definition of the same position, in full. THE FEN STRINGS DIFFER: the halfmove clocks read 1 and 2. That is the finding worth keeping. Position identity under the Law does not include the halfmove clock, so two different FENs can be the same position, and a system comparing FEN strings would report a transposition as a difference. This base's registered false-positive case for this record is the complementary error, where the boards match and the en-passant field does not.

engine.verdict_note: An ordinary opening position at about a third of a pawn. The evaluation is not the evidence here - the move generator is, and it produced both orders and reported both final positions.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `the-same-board-is-not-the-same-position`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Two diagrams, piece for piece identical: kings on e1 and e8, rooks on a1, h1, a8 and h8, nothing else on the board. Any comparison that reads the squares alone calls them the same position. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second trap: "Castling rights are invisible on the board but are part of the position. Two arrangements that look identical are not transpositions if one side has lost the right to castle." WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Settled by counting moves. With the rights present this base's move generator produces 26 legal moves including e1g1 and e1c1; with them absent it produces 24 and no castling. Same men, same squares, two legal positions, and the difference is in a FEN field rather than on the board. The `notation` record's third trap is the same fact from the other side — 'a FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one' — and `en-passant`'s registered case is the third member of that family.

Registered false-positive case `the-same-board-a-move-order-apart`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 and 1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.d4 put every man on the same square, with the same side to move and the same castling rights. Any comparison that reads the diagram calls them the same position and the move orders a transposition. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second trap: "Castling rights are invisible on the board but are part of the position." The same is true of the en-passant possibility, and it is what differs here. In the second order White's last move was d2-d4, so the position carries an en-passant target on d3; in the first it carries none. FIDE Art. 9.2.3 includes that possibility in the definition of the same position, so these are two positions and not one. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Both move orders were replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js and it emitted the two FENs: `... b KQkq - 1 3` and `... b KQkq d3 0 3`. The boards are identical and the fourth field is not. This record's positive example is the complementary case and is the more surprising one — 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 against 1.c4 e6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 reach FENs that differ in the HALFMOVE CLOCK, 1 against 2, and are the SAME position, because Art. 9.2.3 does not include the clock. So a FEN string is neither necessary nor sufficient for position identity: two identical positions can have different FENs, and two different positions can differ only in a field a reader skips.

by_level.beginner: The same position reached by playing the moves in a different order.
by_level.intermediate: A transposition. Once the pieces stand on the same squares, everything known about that position applies however you got there.
by_level.advanced: Positions remember only castling rights, en passant, and repetitions. Everything else about the route is forgotten, which is what makes move order a tool.
by_level.master: Move orders are asymmetric: pick the route whose junctions deny the opponent what you least want to face.

by_depth.short: The same position by a different move order.
by_depth.normal: A transposition: two different sequences of moves reaching one and the same position. Because a position is defined by where the pieces stand, all the theory about it applies no matter which route produced it.
by_depth.deep: A position has no memory of the moves that made it, with exactly three exceptions - castling rights, en passant availability, and the repetition count - which is why theory attaches to positions rather than to move orders. What makes this a weapon rather than a curiosity is that routes are asymmetric: two orders reaching the same destination pass different junctions, so choosing an order decides which positions the opponent may steer into. The matching hazard is the transposition trap, where an apparently equivalent order concedes one extra option or spends a commitment the canonical version keeps in reserve.

explanations.lesson: Compare the position you are entering with the standard version piece by piece, and treat any difference as a new position until you have checked it is harmless.

transposition.definition_short: Reaching the same position by a different order of moves.
transposition.definition_long:
A position is defined by where the pieces stand, not by the path taken to get there. Two games that open completely differently can arrive at an identical position, and at that moment every piece of theory about that position applies to both, regardless of route.

THE EXCEPTIONS ARE EXACTLY THREE, and they are the only things a chess position remembers about its own history: castling rights, en passant availability, and the count of previous repetitions. Everything else is forgotten. This is not a convention — it is visible in the FEN record, which stores precisely those items and nothing else about the past.

Transposition matters because move orders are ASYMMETRIC. Two routes to the same destination pass different junctions along the way, so choosing a move order decides which positions the opponent is allowed to steer into. This is what makes it a weapon rather than a curiosity: the destination can be identical while one route deletes an option the opponent wanted.

The corresponding hazard is the TRANSPOSITION TRAP — a move order that looks equivalent to the main road but concedes one extra option, or quietly spends a commitment that the canonical version keeps in reserve. A piece already developed to a square is a piece that can no longer go anywhere else.

trapped-piece.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Detection needs mobility counting rather than line geometry, so it is a different kind of detector from the pin/skewer family.
trapped-piece.definition_short: A piece with no safe square is attacked and lost, even though it is not currently pinned or forked.
trapped-piece.definition_long:
Material is won not by a geometric double attack but by taking away every retreat first. Common victims: a queen that has grabbed a pawn deep in enemy territory, a bishop that has run out of diagonal after ...h6 and ...g5, and a knight on the rim.

ECM lists 'Trapping a piece' as a category. It is worth distinguishing from a fork because the winning move often attacks only ONE piece — the tactic is in the absence of squares, not in the presence of a second target.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: An enemy piece has no safe square available
It can be attacked by a unit it cannot capture or evade
indicators_for: The piece is deep in enemy territory or on the rim
Its own pawns block its retreat
Every flight square is covered
indicators_against: A counter-sacrifice frees it
It has a desperado capture that recovers the material
Trapping it costs more material than it is worth

exceptions: A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.
limitations: TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

A counter-sacrifice frees it: not built, and not buildable at this layer. The record states it as an indicator_against, and a version of it existed briefly - it iterated the defender's captures and then let the trapped piece move as well, which is the defender playing two moves in a row, and it suppressed 34 of the 110 trappedPiece motifs on the 788 shipped positions on that basis. The honest form is three plies deep: the sacrifice, the trapper's answer to it, and only then the escape - and whether the answer is good is a judgement no static test makes. The other indicator_against, 'trapping it costs more material than it is worth', IS built, netted against what the trapping move itself captured.

examples.note: Legall's Mate, Paris 1750, after 5...Bxd1 - and the trapped piece is the bishop that has just taken the queen. The detector: 'the bishop on d1 is trapped - every square it can reach loses it.' That is true and it is beside the point, which is what makes it the right master example for this record: White is not going to collect the bishop, White is going to mate in two with 6.Bxf7+ Ke7 7.Nd5#. A piece can be trapped and irrelevant at the same time, and a system that reported the trapped bishop as the news would be describing the least important thing on the board. PROVENANCE. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js, which refuses a wrong list rather than guessing, so the FEN is verified rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.
examples.game: Legall de Kermeur - Saint Brie, Paris 1750

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 2 at depth 20 - the trapped bishop is never taken, and the position is decided by a mating net that has nothing to do with it.

examples.note: A clean instance: the detector reports trappedPiece and nothing else, for the move Nf4+. Two things are verified here and a third is not. VERIFIED: findMotifs() in blind-chess.html reports the motif — and that detector, not this system, is the authority on whether a motif is present. ALSO VERIFIED: Nf4+ is the recorded solution of a shipped puzzle, and tools/generate_puzzles.js only admits a position when one move is objectively best by a wide margin at confirmation depth, so the move carries engine backing by construction rather than by a separate search here. NOT claimed: that the motif is the whole reason the move wins. Provenance: the puzzle corpus is engine self-play — a real position from a real game between engines, not a master game.

The move is therefore engine-verified as best without this base running its own search. examples.note: The bishop went pawn-grabbing to a7 and ...b6 shuts the door: the a7 bishop has no square that is not covered, which is the oldest trap in the opening repertoire.

counterexamples.note: The identical pawn move with the bishop on a6 instead of a7. It has b7 and b5 and the rest of the diagonal, and ...b6 traps nothing. One square of difference between a piece that is lost and a piece that is merely awkward.

Shipped puzzle, and a registered false-positive case `a-trapped-rook-with-a-desperado`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: After Qxf8+, the detector reports 'The rook on c8 is trapped — every square it can reach loses it.' Every square it can reach does lose it. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second indicator_against: "It has a desperado capture that recovers the material." One of the squares it can reach is f8, where the white queen is standing. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: This is not a constructed position. It is shipped puzzle mi-9f06a55404, and the puzzle's OWN SOLUTION LINE is the refutation of the label: h6f8, c8f8, e7f8q — the second move of the answer is the trapped rook taking the queen. A rook that is lost is trapped; a rook that is lost after eating a queen is a trade. The scan that found it read all 788 shipped puzzles and asked, of every trapped-piece report, whether any capture available to the piece breaks even after recapture: 8 of them do, and all 8 were being reported. The guard implements the condition and trapped-piece fell to 12.9%.

ambiguous_examples.note: Nominated by tools/mine_ambiguous.js on its fourth ground, NOT-THE-MOVE: the concept fires on a legal move that is not the solution of a shipped puzzle. The first three grounds ask about a POSITION and could not reach a move-based or motif concept at all - this concept and eleven others reported NONE until the tool learned to supply a move. What makes the case ambiguous rather than false is that nothing reported is absent: after Qxf7+ Kxf7 something of White's really is trapped, and the detector is right that it is. What the detector cannot see is that White gave a queen for a pawn to arrange it. The solution is Bb5 at +0.80; the move that produces the trapped-piece report is -5.63. This is the sharpest illustration in this base of why a motif tag is not a recommendation.

engine.verdict_note: Qxf7+ scores -5.63 and Bb5, the solution, scores +0.80 - a gap of 643 centipawns. The motif is present in the worse move and absent from the better one.

by_level.beginner: That piece has nowhere safe to go, so attacking it wins it.
by_level.intermediate: The {piece} is trapped — every retreat square is covered.
by_level.advanced: Trapped piece. Check for desperado resources and counter-threats before committing material to the hunt.

by_depth.short: A piece with no safe square, attacked and lost.
by_depth.normal: A trapped piece: every square it can reach loses it just the same, so attacking it wins it. Not a pin and not a fork — the piece is free to move and has nowhere to go.
by_depth.deep: Two things stop this being as simple as it sounds. A desperado capture that recovers the material means the piece is not lost, only traded, and eight of the 788 puzzles in this repository carried a trapped-piece report that the piece's own capture refuted — in one of them the puzzle's solution line IS the refutation. And a trapped piece can be entirely beside the point: in Legall's Mate the bishop that has just taken the queen is trapped on d1 and is never collected, because White mates in two. Reporting it as the news would name the least important thing on the board.

triangulation.knowledge_type_note: A technique whose effect is exact: it returns the same position with the other side to move. Whether that wins is then decidable, so this is a proven result rather than a heuristic.

attributions.note: The British master analysed a king-and-rook-versus-king position giving a manoeuvre that returned to the initial position with the inferior side to move, describing it as 'throwing the move upon Black'. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED against a primary text; taken from a secondary source.

history.notes: No coinage established. Walker's description is the earliest use found in the sources consulted, and it is second-hand.

triangulation.engine_era_note: Exact, and now decidable: a tablebase settles whether the triangulated position is actually better, and — as the example in this record shows — whether triangulation was the best way to get there at all.

preconditions: The same position with the opponent to move would be better
One side's piece has a three-square route back to its square; the opponent's has only two
indicators_for: A mutual-zugzwang position where whoever moves must concede
The opposing king is confined to two squares by its defensive duties
No pawn tempo is available to either side
indicators_against: A spare pawn move exists, which is a cheaper way to lose a tempo
The defender has the same number of squares and can mirror the manoeuvre
A direct route wins faster — check before triangulating
The piece is a knight, which cannot triangulate at all
false_positive_traps: MEASURED: the standard textbook position for triangulation does not require it. Every king move wins there and a direct pawn move wins fastest. Do not report triangulation as necessary without checking that the alternatives fail.
A spare pawn tempo achieves the same thing more cheaply and is usually available.
A knight cannot triangulate; asserting it can is a geometric error.

typical_plans: Identify the corresponding squares, then use the extra square you have and the defender does not
Verify the target position is actually winning with the opponent to move before spending the moves
typical_moves: A king triangle such as d5-e5-d4-d5
typical_pawn_structures: Blocked structures where no pawn tempo remains
typical_piece_arrangements: Kings in a corresponding-squares relationship
tactical_consequences: Imposes zugzwang without any threat being made
strategic_consequences: Converts a drawn-looking opposition standoff into a win

exceptions: A knight cannot triangulate — it cannot return to a square in an odd number of moves.
A spare pawn move does the same job more cheaply.
The textbook example does not require triangulation; several moves win and a direct one wins faster.
limitations: Recognising the opportunity requires the corresponding-squares relationship, which is a judgement outside tablebase range.
Instructional sources overstate its necessity; verify before asserting it.

NO POSITIVE EXAMPLE, and eight constructions were tried and thrown away. A triangulation position needs a RECIPROCAL zugzwang - the same board won with one side to move and drawn or lost with the other - plus a three-square king route for the winning side that the defender cannot mirror. Symmetric blocked structures are drawn with either side to move, which Syzygy confirmed for four of them; the asymmetric ones either gave the winning side a spare PAWN tempo, which removes the need to triangulate at all, or turned out to be illegal with one side to move because a pawn was checking the king. The ambiguous example on this record is a proven win whose first move is a pawn break rather than a king manoeuvre, which is the same difficulty seen from the other side. Recorded so the next attempt does not repeat these eight.
misconceptions: That triangulation is the only way to lose a tempo. A spare pawn move is usually available and simpler.
That any king manoeuvre returning to the same square is triangulation. It must return the position with the OTHER side to move.
That a knight can do it.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-knight-cannot-lose-a-tempo`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Two kings and a knight in an endgame, with the side to move wanting to hand the move back. Triangulation is the standard way to do that, and the knight looks like a piece with spare moves to make. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: A knight cannot lose a single tempo: every knight move changes the colour of the square it stands on, so returning to the same square always takes an even number of moves. Triangulation is precisely the technique of reaching the same position with the OTHER side to move, and a knight can never contribute one. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report triangulation. Syzygy: 3 pieces, draw, dtz 0 — the position is drawn whoever moves, so there is no tempo worth losing in it either. The geometric fact is the interesting half and it is not evaluative at all: a king triangulates because it can reach a square in two moves or three, and a knight's parity forbids the equivalent. This is why the technique belongs to king-and-pawn endings and to bishops, and why a knight ending is the standard example of a position where zugzwang cannot be manufactured.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0. The position is drawn whoever moves, so there is no tempo worth losing in it - which is the second half of why triangulation does not apply. The first half is geometric and not evaluative at all: every knight move changes square colour, so a knight can never return to its square in an odd number of moves.

ambiguous_examples.note: The standard textbook triangulation position: White Kd5 with pawns b5 and c5, Black Kd7 with a pawn on b7. The instructional line is 1.Ke5! Kc6 2.Kd4 Kd7 3.Kd5, returning the same position with Black to move. Included as the concept's principal caveat, not as a clean positive.

tablebase.note: PROVEN, and it corrects the teaching. Every legal move was checked. The direct 1.b6 wins in 22; the triangulating 1.Ke5 wins in 46; Kc4, Kd4 and Ke4 all win in 48. Only 1.c6+ is a draw. So the position genuinely teaches 'do not push the pawn', and it does NOT establish that triangulation was necessary — it is one of five winning moves and the slowest of them. Recorded as ambiguous because it supports the technique's existence while contradicting the necessity the source implies.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 1, mate in 23, best move b6 - and the engine agrees at mate in 14. Filed as AMBIGUOUS because what is in doubt is not the result but whether triangulation is what achieves it: the tablebase's own first move is a pawn break rather than a king manoeuvre, so the position wins and this concept may not be the reason.

by_level.beginner: The king walks around a little triangle and comes back to the same square, having used one more move than the other king can. Now it is their turn in a position where they did not want it to be.
by_level.intermediate: Triangulation: lose a move on purpose so the same position comes back with your opponent to play. Useful only when that position is mutual zugzwang.
by_level.advanced: Losing a tempo via a three-square route the defender cannot mirror. Check first whether a spare pawn move does it more cheaply, and whether a direct win exists.
by_level.master: The corresponding-squares relationship is what makes it work — you have an extra square from which the relationship holds and the defender does not. Verify the target position before spending the moves.

by_depth.short: Walk the king round a triangle to hand the move back.
by_depth.normal: Triangulation: manoeuvre so the identical position arises with your opponent to move. It works when they have only two squares to your three, and it decides mutual-zugzwang positions.
by_depth.deep: A method of losing a tempo deliberately. The king takes a three-square route home while the defending king has only two, so the same position returns with the other side to play — decisive in mutual zugzwang. Queens, rooks and bishops can do it; a knight cannot, since its move always changes square colour. Worth a caution: the standard textbook example does not actually require the technique. Checked against tablebase, every king move there wins and the direct pawn advance wins fastest, with only one move throwing the win away. Triangulation is a real technique that instructional sources routinely present as more necessary than it is.

explanations.lesson: Before triangulating, check two things: that the position you are aiming for is actually won, and that a spare pawn move or a direct route does not do the job faster.

beginner_words: walking the king around to waste a move

triangulation.definition_short: Manoeuvring a piece around three squares to return to the start having spent an extra move, so the same position arises with the opponent to play.
triangulation.definition_long:
A way of losing a tempo on purpose. A king that can reach its square by a three-square route while the opposing king has only two available returns to the identical position with the opponent to move — which, in a mutual-zugzwang position, is decisive.

The mechanism depends on CORRESPONDING SQUARES: the triangulating king has more squares from which it maintains the relationship than the defender does, so the defender runs out first.

A queen, rook or bishop can also triangulate. A KNIGHT CANNOT — its move always changes square colour, so it can never return to a square in an odd number of moves.

IMPORTANT AND MEASURED CAVEAT. The technique is real, but instructional sources routinely present positions as REQUIRING it when they do not. In the standard textbook example — White Kd5 with pawns b5 and c5, Black Kd7 with a pawn on b7 — the tablebase says every king move wins and the direct 1.b6 wins fastest at mate in 22, against mate in 46 for the triangulating 1.Ke5. Only 1.c6+ throws the win away. So the position teaches the idea, and it does not establish that the idea was necessary. Recorded because presenting a demonstration as a necessity is the standard way instructional material overstates.

two-weaknesses.knowledge_type_note: A strategic principle, not a theorem and not merely a rule of thumb. It is stronger than a rule of thumb because a controlled engine test shows the mechanism is real and can be decisive (a dead draw becomes a forced mate purely by adding a distant second target). It is weaker than a proven result because well-documented classes of position defeat it entirely - fortresses, opposite-coloured bishops, and targets close enough for one king to cover both.
two-weaknesses.definition_short: A single weakness can usually be defended, because the defender can concentrate every piece on it. Creating a second target far from the first stretches the defence past what it can cover, and something falls.
two-weaknesses.definition_long:
When one side has a lasting positional advantage but no immediate tactic, attacking the opponent's single weak point normally fails: the defender parks enough force beside it and waits. The method is to fix that first weakness so it cannot be advanced, exchanged or otherwise repaired, tie the defending pieces to it, improve every one of your own pieces while the opponent has no active move, and only then open a second front far enough away that the defenders cannot cover both. Play then alternates between the two targets, attacking whichever is less defended. The defence cracks not because either target is indefensible but because finite pieces cannot be in two places at once.

The distance between the targets is what does the work. Rooks and queens change wings in one or two moves; kings and minor pieces do not. When the defending king can shuttle between both targets, the mechanism largely fails - which is why the principle belongs above all to the endgame, where the defender has least counterplay, and why sources pair it with 'do not hurry': the second front should be opened only after the first weakness is permanent and every piece is already at its best square.

history.notes:
The substance and the name have different origins, and secondary sources conflate them.

SUBSTANCE: present in Nimzowitsch's My System, chapter 'Manoeuvring' (Ch. 5/VI; Ch. 14 in the New in Chess edition). Verified against the full text. He writes: 'an opposing weakness can be attacked in at least two ways, but each of these attacks will meet a satisfactory defence. So to seize the opposing weak point, our attack alternates between the methods (manoeuvring is like a sailing boat tacking)'. Section 2(b) is headed 'Two pawn weaknesses, in this case c3 and h3' and speaks of 'the logical connection between the two separate battlefields'; section 3 is 'Combining play on both wings, when for the moment the weaknesses either do not exist or are hidden'.

NAME: Nimzowitsch never calls it the principle of two weaknesses. The phrase comes from the Soviet training tradition. Shereshevsky's Endgame Strategy (1985) has it as a named chapter and credits the formulations to an article by Sergey Belavenets; Dvoretsky separately describes his own notebook 'General Principles of Endgame Play', says Shereshevsky built the book from it, and says he was himself prompted by reading Belavenets. GM Alex Fishbein, editing My System (Fast Track Edition), retitled Nimzowitsch's 'changing tack' chapter to 'playing against two weaknesses' because 'that is basically what it is' - which is the bridge between the two traditions.

Sources asserting 'Nimzowitsch formulated the principle of two weaknesses in My System, 1925' are therefore right about the idea and wrong about the name. Certainty is marked 'disputed' for the naming, not for the substance.
competing_claims: Nimzowitsch, My System, 1925 - widely repeated; correct as to substance, wrong as to name
Sergey Belavenets - credited by Shereshevsky as the source of the formulation
Mark Dvoretsky - transmitted it as a training principle; Shereshevsky built his chapter from Dvoretsky's notes
Mikhail Shereshevsky, Endgame Strategy, 1985 - where it becomes a named, taught principle

two-weaknesses.engine_era_note: The mechanism survives engine scrutiny and is provable by tablebase in simple material. What engines revise is the RHETORIC around it. Shereshevsky's 'the position would be drawn' with the kings centralised is +0.75, not 0.00. Dvoretsky's necessary/inaccurate marks in Kotov-Pachman separate two moves by 0.05 pawns at depth 32. The principle is a sound method of conversion whose classical statements overstate how forced its consequences are.

preconditions: The position is materially level or the stronger side is ahead, with no forcing tactic available
The defender has at least one durable target: a backward, isolated or doubled pawn, a fixed pawn on the colour of its own bishop, an exposed king, or a piece tied to defence
The attacker has at least one piece that can change wings faster than the defender can follow (rook or queen against king or minor piece)
The attacker's own king is safe and the attacker has no weakness of comparable value
indicators_for: Two distinct targets at least three files apart
At least one defending piece has no move that does not abandon a target
The attacker has an unopposed pawn break, space gain or king entry square on the far wing
The defender's rook is passive (tied to a pawn) while the attacker's is active
The first weakness is fixed: it cannot advance, and it cannot be exchanged off
indicators_against: The two targets are within two files of each other, so one defending king covers both
Opposite-coloured bishops with no breakthrough square - the defending bishop holds one colour complex regardless of how many targets exist
The defender can reach a known fortress
Opening the second front concedes counterplay, a passed pawn, or an open line towards the attacker's own king
The first weakness can be liquidated by a pawn break or a favourable exchange
The defending king already stands between the two targets
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: two-weaknesses, implementing three preconditions that had been written and not built
false_positive_traps: Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.

Any position has several imperfections. Calling any two of them 'two weaknesses' is the commonest misuse — they must require DIFFERENT defensive resources and be far enough apart that the defence cannot cover both.

The principle describes a method of conversion, not an evaluation. A position with two weaknesses is not thereby winning, and Kotov-Pachman shows the gap: the moves annotators mark necessary and inaccurate differ by 0.05 pawns.
Against opposite-coloured bishops or a reachable fortress, the count of weaknesses is simply not the operative variable.

A pawn that is structurally weak can be the position's KEY DEFENSIVE ASSET, and no pawn-skeleton test tells the two apart. Shirov-Kramnik, Linares 2000, move 20: this base lists Black's f4 among the weaknesses White should play against, and Jan Markos calls the same pawn, together with b4, the cage that 'guards all the roads to d5'. Both readings follow from the skeleton and only one is true of the position.

typical_plans: Fix the first weakness, then improve every piece before touching the second wing
Provoke a pawn advance on the far wing and fix the resulting pawn as the second target
Advance a rook-file or knight-file pawn to create a second front by force
Activate the king towards a second entry square while the defender is tied to the first target
Alternate threats between the two targets to induce zugzwang or a decisive concession
typical_moves: A quiet flank pawn move that forces the defender to create a second isolated pawn (Capablanca's 31...a5 against Lasker, 1921)
A space-gaining advance such as h4-h5 or g4-g5 that fixes an enemy pawn as a target
A rook swing from the blockaded wing to the opposite wing once the defence is committed
Declining to capture the first weakness in order to keep the defender tied to it
tactical_consequences: Defending pieces become overloaded, so a tactic against one target wins the other
Zugzwang becomes available once every defensive piece has a fixed job
A defender forced to guard both wings often loses to a decoy or deflection
strategic_consequences: Converts a static positional edge into material or a passed pawn
Turns an equal-looking endgame into a one-sided practical struggle
Justifies keeping pieces on: fewer pieces means fewer overloads to exploit

exceptions: Fortresses: once the defender reaches a fortress the number of weaknesses stops mattering, since none of them can be converted.

Opposite-coloured bishops: extra material and multiple targets are routinely insufficient, because the defending bishop guards one colour complex indefinitely. A second weakness helps only if it creates a breakthrough square or drags the bishop off its blockade.

Targets too close together: if the defending king can shuttle between both, the mechanism largely fails. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending - moving the kings from g1/g8 to d3/d6 drops the evaluation from +1.74 to +0.75.
Self-weakening: pushing pawns to open a second front can create new targets in the attacker's own camp, or hand the defender a passed pawn.
Winning the first weakness may be wrong even when possible, if the capture activates the defender's pieces. The fixed pawn can be worth more as a permanent burden than as material.
limitations: It describes a method of conversion, not an evaluation. A position with two weaknesses is not thereby winning.

Its effect is often practical rather than objective. In Kotov-Pachman 1950 the moves annotators mark as necessary and inaccurate differ by 0.05 pawns at depth 32; the second weakness made the defence hard to find over the board, and the game was decided by a later error.
It presupposes the attacker has time. Against active counterplay the slow improving phase is unavailable.
Recognition is heuristic, not mechanical: 'a target' and 'far enough apart' are judgements, and the detector for this concept is not yet written.

MEASURED 2026-09-01 and fixed: three of this record's four preconditions were written down and never implemented, and the matcher fired on 72.5% of the 788 shipped positions - which is this record's own second trap, 'any position has several imperfections; calling any two of them two weaknesses is the commonest misuse'. Adding the heavy piece that can switch wings, the first trap's requirement that the defending king not stand between the targets, and a comparison of the two sides' weakness counts brings it to 38.6%.

'The attacker has no weakness of comparable value' cannot be measured by counting, and the attempt to do so produced a false negative on the textbook game. After 9.Nxc6 bxc6 in Rubinstein-Salwe 1908, White's b2 and e2 count the same as Black's a7 and c6 - one pair a fixed target complex on half-open files, the other two pawns on their original squares on move nine. The test is therefore only that the attacker is not MORE weak than the defender, and the rest of the precondition is recorded here rather than pretended.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the SECOND half of precondition 1 - 'with no forcing tactic available' - is still not implemented, and it was tried. Layer 3 already answers it (quietness.quiet), and requiring it would remove this concept from the corpus's own textbook instance: Rubinstein-Salwe 1908 at move 24, the moment the SECOND weakness is created and the entry this base annotates as two-weaknesses, is not quiet. So the same thing happened as with 'no weakness of comparable value' - the precondition as written cannot be implemented without losing the game it was written about, and it is recorded here rather than pretended. What the attempt did produce is worth keeping: the 788 shipped positions are TACTICAL puzzles, every one of which has a forcing solution by construction, so any quietness-gated rate on that corpus measures the corpus. tools/firing_rates.js --quiet restricts to the quiet ones, where this concept fires on 28.6% rather than 38.6%. RE-MEASURED 2026-09-02 after quietness() was found to be broken - it had been counting no winning captures at all, so 172 of the 788 looked quiet where 98 are; the conclusion is unchanged, and BOTH Rubinstein-Salwe entries are non-quiet under the fixed test rather than one.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the fourth trap - 'against opposite-coloured bishops or a reachable fortress, the count of weaknesses is simply not the operative variable' - is now built for the half this base can see. With one bishop each on opposite colours the concept is not reported at all, whatever the count says, because the defender holds a whole colour complex. 38.6% -> 33.8%. The fortress half is not detectable and is not attempted.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the fifth trap, added the same day from Shirov-Kramnik, is recorded and NOT implemented on purpose - 'a pawn that is structurally weak can be the position's KEY DEFENSIVE ASSET, and no pawn-skeleton test tells the two apart'. Markos calls Black's b4 and f4 the cage guarding the roads to d5; this base lists f4 among the weaknesses White should play against. Both readings follow from the skeleton and only one is true of the position. Dropping f4 would not change the claim, which also names f7 and d6.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: 'the first weakness can be LIQUIDATED by a pawn break or a favourable exchange' is now SAID rather than enforced, and two measurements decided that. Requiring both weaknesses to be unable to advance safely scores 23.1% and deletes Rubinstein-Salwe 1908; requiring one scores 29.4% and deletes it as well. At the moment the annotator marks - 9.Nxc6 bxc6, where the weaknesses are CREATED - both a7 and c6 can still advance, and Rubinstein's entire game is about preventing ...c5. The annotation marks the creation; this record's method describes what is done afterwards. A matcher that fires only once the fixing is done cannot report the game the concept is named for, so the sentence names what still has to be fixed instead. Three of the remaining indicators - a fortress, counterplay conceded by opening the second front, and a favourable EXCHANGE liquidating the weakness - are judgements about a future position and are not attempted.

KNOWN FALSE NEGATIVE, kept visible. The matcher reads 'two weaknesses' as two structural pawn weaknesses of the defender, far enough apart, with the defending king not between them, and an attacker able to switch wings faster than the defence. The classic ENDGAME instance is often none of that: an outside passed pawn decoys the defending king to one wing while the attacking king eats the other, and neither front is a structural weakness at all. This record's own tablebase-proven positive example (8/8/3k1pp1/8/P2K4/5PP1/8/8 b, mate in 23 by Syzygy) is exactly that shape and the matcher is silent on it. Widening the matcher to catch it was tried and measured at 58.5% of generated pawn endings, which is a detector that means nothing; the false negative is the better of the two errors, and it is recorded here rather than papered over.
misconceptions: That two weaknesses make a position winning. They make it convertible, not won; the tablebase pair shows the mechanism can be decisive, and the Kotov-Pachman example shows it often is not.
That the second weakness must be another weak pawn. An exposed king, an invasion square or a passive piece serve equally.
That the first weakness should be captured as soon as possible. Holding it fixed often binds more defenders than taking it wins material.

conflicts.resolution: Not a true conflict but a scale difference: overloading is the same finite-defence logic resolving in a move or two, this is the same logic over dozens. If a concrete overload exists now, explain the tactic; reach for the strategic principle only when no forcing line exists.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. Symmetric f+g pawns, kings in opposition, plus one distant White a-pawn. The a-pawn decoys the black king and the white king eats the kingside. Paired with the counterexample below, which is identical except that the a-pawn is absent.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 23 for White. The paired position without the a-pawn is 0.00. The only difference between them is the presence of a second, distant target, so the mechanism is isolated from every other factor. Strongest single piece of evidence for this concept.

tablebase.note: PROVEN, not evaluated. Result is from the side to move (Black), so this is a forced win for White. Supersedes the earlier Stockfish 'mate in 23': within tablebase reach the theoretical status is a fact and no search is needed.

examples.matcher_blind_reason: The matcher does not report two-weaknesses here, and the example stays anyway. This position is a proven instance of the PRINCIPLE and not an instance of what the detector reads. Layer 3's weakSpread finds Black's weak pawns and there are none: f6 and g6 defend each other, neither is isolated, backward or doubled. The second front here is White's outside a-pawn - a passed pawn of the ATTACKER, not a structural weakness of the defender - and the detector has no notion of that. Measured, not assumed: the relaxation that would report it was written and then thrown away, because dropping the heavy-piece requirement in pawn endings fired on 58.5% of 4000 generated pawn endings (tools/pawn_endings.js --n 4000 --seed 11) and still did not report this position. A guard that admits half of all pawn endings to catch one proven example is a worse detector, so the false negative is kept and written down instead.

examples.note: Lasker-Capablanca, World Championship game 10, after 35.axb3. Capablanca has manufactured a second isolated pawn on b3 to go with White's weak d4, and the white rook cannot defend both. He called his play from move 24 on one of his best efforts; Lasker called it 'enchanting'.
examples.game: Emanuel Lasker - Jose Raul Capablanca, World Championship (10), Havana 1921

engine.verdict_note: +1.74 for Black in a materially level rook-and-knight ending. The engine's own first move, 35...Rb6, is Capablanca's move, and its continuation 36.Rd3 Ra6 follows the game exactly - the rook goes behind the pawns and both weaknesses are attacked.

counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. Identical to the positive example except the White a-pawn is removed, leaving one front. With a single area of operations the defending king holds everything.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00. Establishes the necessity half of the claim: the same structure with one target is a dead draw, so the win in the paired position is attributable to the second target and nothing else.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw. Together with the paired position this establishes the concept's core claim as a theoretical fact in this material: identical kings and identical kingside structure, one distant second target, win vs draw.

White fixes h7 and g6 as a second front. Included as a case where the concept is practically decisive but objectively almost neutral.

engine.verdict_note: Dvoretsky and British Chess News mark 42...h5 as necessary and 42...Kf6 as an inaccuracy. At depth 32 the gap is 0.05 pawns (-0.11 vs -0.16) - objectively nothing. Both hold. The second weakness created a defensive task Pachman failed thirteen moves later, not a lost position. Recorded as ambiguous deliberately: it supports the concept's PRACTICAL force and contradicts any claim that a second weakness is objectively decisive.

ambiguous_examples.note: Shereshevsky's hypothetical on the Lasker-Capablanca position: the same material and structure, but with the kings on d3 and d6 instead of g1 and g8. He states it 'would be drawn', because the defending king stands between the two weaknesses. This is the concept's central exception, stated by a source that teaches the concept.

engine.verdict_note: +0.75, against +1.74 for the real position. Shereshevsky's mechanism is confirmed and large - centralising the defending king removes over half the advantage - but his absolute claim of a draw is not supported at depth 30. Recorded as the exception being real and the wording being overstated.

by_level.beginner: Your opponent can defend one weak point, because every piece can gather around it. Give them a second thing to worry about on the other side of the board, and they cannot guard both.
by_level.intermediate: One weakness is usually holdable. Fix it so it cannot run away, improve your pieces while your opponent has nothing to do, then open a second front on the far wing. Attack whichever target is less defended - the defence breaks in transit, not at either target.
by_level.advanced: The first weakness is a magnet, not a meal: its value is the defensive commitment it forces, which is often worth more than the pawn. Convert by fixing it, restricting counterplay, bringing every piece to its best square, and only then creating a second target far enough away that the defending king cannot cover both. Distance between targets is the operative variable.
by_level.master: Price the tempo, not the target. The method costs time - fix, restrain, improve every piece, and only then open the second front - and that is exactly what a player holding a dynamic advantage cannot spend, which is why this and the initiative are recorded as being in direct tension. The operative variable is the DISTANCE between the two targets against the defending king's speed, not the count of them: two weaknesses the king can cover from one square are one weakness. Against a fortress it fails outright, and no amount of alternating will find the entry that is not there.

by_depth.short: One weakness can be defended. Create a second one far away and the defence breaks.
by_depth.normal: A single weak point is holdable because every defender can gather around it. Fix it so it cannot be repaired, improve your own pieces while the opponent has nothing to do, then open a second front on the far wing. The defence cracks in transit between the two, not at either one.
by_depth.deep: Method of conversion attributed in substance to Nimzowitsch (as 'tacking') and named in the Soviet training line Belavenets - Dvoretsky - Shereshevsky. Procedure: fix the first weakness, deny counterplay, improve every piece, create a second target far enough that the defending king cannot cover both, then alternate. Distance between targets is the operative variable — moving the kings from g1/g8 to d3/d6 in the Lasker-Capablanca ending costs the attacker over half the advantage. Fails against fortresses and opposite-coloured bishops regardless of how many targets exist.

explanations.hedge: This is a method for converting an advantage, not a law. It fails against fortresses and against opposite-coloured bishops, and it fails when the two targets are close enough for one king to guard both.
explanations.lesson: When your opponent is holding a weak point comfortably, stop attacking it harder. Fix it, improve everything, and go make a second problem somewhere they cannot reach quickly.
