vancura-position.knowledge_type_note: A named theoretical position with a proven result. It matters beyond itself because it is a PROVEN COUNTEREXAMPLE to Tarrasch's rule that the rook belongs behind the passed pawn — here that rule loses by force.
vancura-position.definition_short: The drawing method against a rook pawn on the sixth: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the SIDE along the rank, never from behind, with the defending king tucked on g7 or h7.
vancura-position.definition_long:
The specialist defence for rook and rook-pawn against rook, when the pawn is on the sixth and the attacking rook is already stuck in front of it on the eighth.

The setup: the defending rook goes to the pawn's rank and attacks it SIDEWAYS from maximum distance — against a white a6-pawn, the black rook sits on f6, g6 or h6. The defending king goes to g7 or h7 and stays there.

Three things happen at once, and they are what makes it hold. The pawn is attacked, so the white rook can never leave a8. The whole sixth rank is raked, so the white king can never cross it — and the squares beside the pawn, which are the only shelter from checks, are ON that rank. And the rook keeps maximum checking distance, so when the king approaches it can check indefinitely down the file.

The king's position is not arbitrary. g7 and h7 are the DRAWING ZONE because from anywhere else White plays Rh8, the rook takes on a7, and Rh7+ skewers king and rook. Karsten Müller notes that 2...Kf7? loses in exactly that way.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ITSELF. Tarrasch's rule says the rook belongs behind the passed pawn. Here that rule LOSES. Behind the pawn, the rook attacks a square the pawn will vacate, gives no checks, and cannot stop the enemy king sheltering in front of the pawn. Beside the pawn it attacks the square the pawn actually occupies and denies the king the rank it needs. This is proven, not argued: the two positions in this record differ only in whether the rook is on f6 or a1, and they are a draw and a loss respectively.

It is not general theory. With any pawn other than a rook pawn the attacking king has room on both sides and the side-attack bind cannot hold; there the defence is the Philidor.

attributions.note: Czech study composer, 1898-1921. He died at 23 and the analysis of rook and pawn versus rook was published posthumously in 1924. Dates and publication year agree across two independent sources.
The standard modern exposition, including the g7/h7 drawing zone and its reason.

history.notes: Well attested and consistent across sources: the composer, his dates, his early death and the posthumous 1924 publication all agree between ChessBase and a second source.

development.change: Published posthumously; enters the standard repertoire.
Aronian holds it against Carlsen at the Sinquefield Cup, with spectators' engines wrongly calling it a win — a demonstration that shallow evaluation misreads the fortress.

vancura-position.engine_era_note: Tablebase-proven, and a good illustration of the gap between search and proof: during Carlsen-Aronian 2014 the public engines called the position a win while it was in fact a dead draw. Below eight pieces the tablebase is the authority, not the evaluation.

preconditions: Rook and a rook pawn against rook
The pawn is on its sixth rank
The attacking rook is in front of its own pawn on the eighth
indicators_for: The defending rook can reach the pawn's rank with several files of distance
The defending king can reach g7/h7 (or the mirror) in time
The whole rank between rook and pawn is empty
indicators_against: The defending king is stranded in the middle — the skewer Rh8 and Rh7+ then wins
The defending king blocks its own rook's rank
The pawn is not a rook pawn, in which case this bind does not exist and the Philidor applies
The rook cannot reach the rank before the pawn and king coordinate
recognition.detector: materialPattern KRP-KR with a/h pawn — not yet written
false_positive_traps: It is specialist theory for the ROOK PAWN on the sixth. Applying the side-attack idea to a central pawn does not work.
The defending king's square is part of the position, not a detail. Outside g7/h7 the skewer wins.
Most practical failures happen several moves earlier, while the rook is still elsewhere — recognising the crisis configuration in time is the actual skill.

typical_plans: Get the rook to the pawn's rank at maximum distance before the attacker coordinates
Keep the king on g7/h7 and out of the rook's way
Slide along the rank when approached; check down the file when the king nears the pawn
typical_moves: ...Rf6 attacking a6 sideways
...Rf5+ / ...Rf6+ / ...Rf7+ chasing the king
typical_pawn_structures: Rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it
typical_piece_arrangements: Attacking rook entombed on a8; defending rook on the sixth rank; defending king on g7
tactical_consequences: The skewer Rh8 and Rh7+ is what punishes a misplaced defending king
strategic_consequences: Turns a nominally winning extra pawn into a dead draw
A standing reason not to push the rook pawn to the seventh, which releases the bind entirely

exceptions: Once the pawn goes to the seventh the position is drawn more easily — the pawn buries its own rook and removes the king's shelter, and even the passive rook-behind defence then holds.
It does not apply to non-rook pawns.
It fails if the defending king cannot reach the g7/h7 zone in time.
limitations: Specialist. It covers one material configuration and one pawn.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION, and the reason is what this record IS. A named theoretical position is a position rather than a moment in a game: it is defined by its own geometry, it is reached from thousands of different games and from none in particular, and its authority is a tablebase rather than an annotator. The examples on this record carry `origin_kind: tablebase-position` for that reason and it is the correct provenance, not a weaker one - a Syzygy result is a statement about every continuation, which is more than any game can be. A famous game that REACHED this position would be a fact about that game and would add nothing to the claim.
misconceptions: That the rook belongs behind a passed pawn. Here that is the losing method, and it is proven.
That an extra rook pawn wins a rook ending.
That an engine evaluation settles it — in 2014 public engines called a Vancura draw a win.

conflicts.resolution: Direct and PROVEN conflict with Tarrasch's rule that the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, which `passed-pawn` records as a rule of thumb. In this configuration the rule loses by force: the tablebase pair in this record differs only in whether the defending rook is beside the pawn or behind it, and the results are a draw and a loss in 63. Where the two collide, the Vancura wins — but only for a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook already in front of it.

examples.note: The Vancura setup as given by Karsten Müller: White Ra8, pawn a6, king d4; Black king g7 in the drawing zone, rook f6 attacking the pawn sideways at maximum distance.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw. Paired with the position below, which is identical in material and differs only in where the black rook stands.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move a7, engine 0.00. The Vancura defence: the rook holds from the side, on the sixth, keeping the pawn under fire and the king out. Proven rather than demonstrated.

counterexamples.note: The SAME position with the black rook behind the pawn on a1 instead of beside it on f6 — that is, playing Tarrasch's rule that the rook belongs behind the passed pawn. Identical material, identical kings, one rook moved.

tablebase.note: PROVEN LOSS for the defender — White wins in 63. This is the most valuable single result in the knowledge base so far, because it does not merely illustrate a concept, it REFUTES a famous rule of thumb in a specific configuration. Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn' is recorded in `passed-pawn` as a reliable heuristic; here, with material and kings held identical and only the rook relocated, following it turns a proven draw into a proven loss. The mechanism is that behind the pawn the rook attacks a square the pawn will vacate and gives no checks, while beside it the rook attacks the square the pawn occupies and denies the enemy king the rank it needs for shelter.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN, dtz 17, mate in 63, best move Kc5 - and the engine says +12.13. The negative half of the Vancura pair: the same material with the black rook passively behind the pawn on a1 instead of actively on f6 loses. One rook, two squares, draw and loss.

ambiguous_examples.note: The Vancura ARRANGEMENT exactly - attacking rook behind its own passed pawn on the eighth, defending rook active on the sixth keeping the pawn under fire, defending king beside the pawn's queening corner - with one change: the pawn is a knight pawn instead of a rook pawn. It is a PROVEN WIN in 27. Vancura's defence is specifically a rook-pawn defence, and it works because a rook pawn's queening corner can be reached by the defending king and because the attacking rook in front of its own pawn has nowhere useful to go; neither holds one file across. Filed as ambiguous because nothing visible distinguishes this from the drawn position: the pieces stand in the same relation, and the letter of the file decides.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 27, best move b7. This record's positive example is the same arrangement with an a-pawn and is a PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0.

by_level.beginner: Their extra pawn is on the edge of the board. Put your rook beside it on the same row, keep your king in the corner, and they can never make progress.
by_level.intermediate: The Vancura draw. Attack the rook pawn from the SIDE, not from behind, and keep your king on g7 or h7 — anywhere else and Rh8 followed by Rh7+ skewers you.
by_level.advanced: Vancura. The side attack ties their rook to the pawn, rakes the rank their king needs for shelter, and keeps checking distance. Note this is the documented exception to putting the rook behind a passed pawn.
by_level.master: The crisis configuration is a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook already in front. Recognise it early — the practical failure is almost always a few moves before the setup, while the rook is still on the wrong part of the board.

by_depth.short: Attack the rook pawn from the side, king on g7 — it holds.
by_depth.normal: The Vancura position: against a rook pawn on the sixth with their rook stuck in front of it, put your rook on the pawn's rank attacking it sideways from far away, and your king on g7 or h7. Their rook cannot leave, their king cannot cross the rank, and you can check forever.
by_depth.deep: Josef Vančura's defence, published posthumously in 1924. Against a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook already in front of it, the defending rook attacks the pawn along the rank from maximum distance and the king tucks on g7 or h7. Three things hold simultaneously: the pawn is attacked so the enemy rook is chained, the sixth rank is raked so the enemy king can never reach the shelter squares beside its own pawn, and the rook keeps checking distance. The king's square is not a detail — from anywhere else, Rh8 and Rh7+ skewers. Most importantly this is the proven exception to the rule that the rook belongs behind a passed pawn: relocate the same rook from f6 to a1 and a proven draw becomes a proven loss in 63.

explanations.lesson: Against a rook pawn, forget the rule about putting your rook behind the passed pawn. Beside it is what draws, and behind it loses — that is proven, not a matter of taste.

keep the king in the corner

weak-square.knowledge_type_note: A positional concept naming a board feature. Broader than `hole`, which is the specific structural case, and than `outpost`, which is the square once usefully occupied.

attributions.note: Through the 'hole' and the general doctrine of weak points; Lasker summarised his theory as including 'attack the weak points'.

history.notes: The specific term 'hole' is securely Steinitz's. 'Weak square' as a general phrase has no identifiable coiner and grew out of the same body of ideas; recorded medium rather than high for that reason.

development.change: Weak points enter chess theory as a named, teachable defect.
The exploiting side is systematised as the outpost, and colour complexes get explicit treatment.

weak-square.engine_era_note: Standard in engine evaluation as king-safety and square-control terms. Uncontroversial; what engines dispute is only how much any individual weak square is worth.

preconditions: No friendly pawn can ever attack the square
indicators_for: The square is central, or adjacent to the king's shelter
Several weak squares of the same colour form a connected complex
The bishop covering that colour has been exchanged or is shut in
An enemy piece can reach the square and be supported there
indicators_against: A friendly pawn can still advance to cover it
A piece covers it durably and cannot be exchanged
The square is unreachable, or reaching it achieves nothing
It is on the edge or deep in the opponent's own half
false_positive_traps: Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard, so the raw feature fires everywhere. Usability is what makes it reportable.
A fianchetto leaves permanent weak squares on the long diagonal that the bishop covers perfectly well. The square is weak; the position is not.
A weak square only a queen can occupy is usually not a weakness, since cheaper pieces evict her.

typical_plans: Exchange the piece that covers the complex, then invade it
Fix enemy pawns on the colour opposite the complex so they cannot repair it
Route a knight to the square by a path the defender cannot contest
typical_pawn_structures: Fianchetto structures after the bishop is traded — weak dark squares around the king
Pawns fixed on one colour, weakening the other complex
In front of a backward pawn
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight established on the square with pawn support
tactical_consequences: Weak squares near the king convert into mating nets
strategic_consequences: Permanent, since pawns cannot move backwards
A weak colour complex often names the whole winning plan

exceptions: A weak square covered by a piece is not exploitable while that piece stays; the plan is to trade it off first.
Conceding weak squares is routinely the right price for space, the bishop pair, or a tempo.
Romanovsky's condition: it is only a real weakness if a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged can occupy it.
limitations: Detecting squares no pawn can attack is mechanical; deciding which matter is not.
Terminology overlaps with `hole` and sources use the two interchangeably.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the third indicator_against - 'the square is unreachable, or REACHING IT ACHIEVES NOTHING' - had only its first half built. The second half is the same question `outpost`'s traps ask, and only one of the two records was being listened to; there is now ONE function, bearsFrom() in Layer 3, and both use it. Near-inert here: 40.5% -> 40.4%, because a minor piece landing in the enemy half almost always bears on something. The other two indicators are built - 'a friendly pawn can still advance to cover it' is what holesFor() tests, and 'a piece covers it durably and cannot be exchanged' is the fianchetto guard in reachableHoles().
misconceptions: That weak squares should always be avoided.
That a weak square is a weakness regardless of whether the opponent can use it.
That 'weak square' and 'hole' are always synonyms — hole is the narrower, structural case.

examples.note: e5 and d6 are holes in Black's position after ...fxe5 removed the f-pawn: no black pawn can ever attack either square again. Nimzowitsch's whole method here was to occupy one of them permanently. This base's own detector reports both squares as holes for White, which is the geometric half of the concept agreeing with its author.

by_level.intermediate: {square} is weak: no pawn can cover it. It matters here because {piece} can reach it and stay.
by_level.advanced: A weak square on the {colour} complex. Note whether it is isolated or part of a connected complex — the second is systemic and usually names the plan.
by_level.master: Weak-square complex. The operative questions are which piece defends the complex, whether it can be traded, and whether the pawns can be fixed on the opposite colour to make the damage permanent.

by_depth.short: No pawn can ever cover {square} again.
by_depth.normal: {square} is a weak square — no friendly pawn can attack it, and pawns cannot move backwards, so it stays weak. That matters when an enemy piece can occupy it and cannot be driven off.
by_depth.deep: The general term for a square its owner can no longer contest with a pawn; the same square is 'strong' from the other side. A hole is the narrower structural case Steinitz named, and an outpost is such a square once a piece occupies and uses it. The idea that matters most is the weak colour complex: several weak squares of one colour, usually left when the bishop of that colour goes or the pawns fix on the opposite colour. One weak square is local; a complex is systemic and generally names the winning plan — trade the defender of the complex, then occupy it.

explanations.lesson: Weak squares are permanent, so trade them for something permanent. And a weak square only counts if your opponent has a piece that can actually live there.

weak-square.definition_short: A square in one's own camp that can no longer be controlled by a pawn, and that the opponent can use.
weak-square.definition_long:
The general term for a square whose owner can no longer contest it with a pawn. The same square is a WEAK square to its owner and a STRONG square to the opponent; the two names describe one fact from two sides.

The vocabulary in this area nests, and sources use it loosely, so the hierarchy is worth stating: a weak square is any square no friendly pawn can attack; a HOLE is the specific structural case Steinitz named, in front of a pawn with both adjoining pawns gone; an OUTPOST is such a square once a piece occupies it securely and uses it. 'Support point' is a further synonym in some American writing.

The larger idea is the WEAK COLOUR COMPLEX: a connected group of weak squares all of one colour, which usually arises when pawns are fixed on the opposite colour or when the bishop covering that colour has been exchanged. A single weak square is a local problem; a weak colour complex is systemic, and it often names the winning plan by itself — trade the defender of the complex, then occupy it.

Every pawn move creates weak squares. That is not an argument against pawn moves; it is the reason to make them deliberately.

alternate_names: the principle of the worst piece
worst-placed-piece.knowledge_type_note: Typed a rule of thumb rather than a principle for a specific reason: both of its earliest formulations contain an explicit precondition, so the rule was never stated unconditionally by the people credited with it.

attributions.note: Credited by GM Serper as the first formulation, and it is the one that already contains the exception.
Calls it Makogonov's rule and supplies the Makogonov quotation.
The formulation most often quoted, with its precondition intact.
Calls it 'the principle of the worst piece'.
Botvinnik called it 'Fischer's rule', though Fischer never stated it - the association rests on his games rather than on anything he wrote.

history.notes: One rule, four names, and no settled attribution. Anderssen appears earliest, Makogonov supplies the standard wording, Dvoretsky supplies the standard name, and Botvinnik attached Fischer's name to a rule Fischer never stated. All five attributions reach this base through a single secondary source - a Chess.com article by GM Serper - and none has been verified at primary source, which is why the confidence is recorded as disputed rather than medium.

competing_claims.note: Serper's own view: 'I think the great Adolf Anderssen was first.'
Botvinnik's name for it, though Fischer never explicitly stated the rule.

competing_claims.claim: The principle of the worst piece

worst-placed-piece.engine_era_note: Broadly confirmed in spirit - engines readily play quiet repositioning moves that improve the least active piece - but engines also expose the priority problem sharply, since they will abandon a piece-improvement plan instantly for a concrete idea a human would not see.

preconditions: No forcing sequence or urgent threat demands attention
One piece is clearly doing less than the others
indicators_for: A piece with no available useful squares
A piece blocking its own side's plan
A rook on a closed file with nothing to do
A bishop shut in behind its own pawns
indicators_against: The opponent has a concrete threat that must be met
A forcing line is available that decides matters
The opponent is building an initiative that a quiet move would concede
false_positive_traps: The rule's precondition is the load-bearing part and is usually dropped in quotation. Anderssen says 'unless you can derive immediate advantage by an attack' and Makogonov says 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered'. Without those, it is not the rule they stated.
Improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative produces individually reasonable moves and a collectively lost position. This is the commonest way the rule is misapplied.
Identifying the worst piece is a judgement, not a measurement. This system has no reliable detector for it and must not claim one.

typical_plans: Find the piece doing least and give it a route to a better square
Trade the worst piece for one of the opponent's best
Reposition rather than advance when the position offers no concrete target
typical_moves: Quiet rook lifts to a file that may open
Bishop redeployments along a longer diagonal
Knight manoeuvres of two or three moves towards an outpost
typical_piece_arrangements: A piece with no useful squares available
strategic_consequences: Positional strength accumulates through the least active piece, which is where the cheapest improvement lies

exceptions: Anderssen's own exception: when immediate advantage is available from an attack.
Makogonov's own precondition: only where no other important matters need consideration.
When the opponent has counterplay, quiet improvement concedes the initiative.
limitations: The rule does not establish priority, which is the hard part of positional play and what it is most often asked to supply.
Every attribution here rests on one secondary source and none is verified at primary source.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the first trap - Anderssen's 'unless you can derive immediate advantage by an attack' and Makogonov's 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered' - is built as far as a static test reaches: the move must not be a capture or a check, the side must not be in check, and the position after it must leave the opponent no winning capture. What is NOT built is 'no other important matters', which is the judgement the record's third trap says this base must not claim, and it does not: it reports that a move raised the scope of the least active piece, at low confidence, and never which piece is worst.
misconceptions: That the rule is unconditional. Neither of its earliest formulations states it that way.
That the worst piece is always the one to move. It is the default when nothing else is asking to be done.
That Fischer formulated it. Botvinnik named it after him; Fischer never stated it.

conflicts.resolution: The rule yields. Both original formulations say so explicitly - Anderssen excepts an immediate attacking advantage and Makogonov requires that nothing more important is going on. Where the opponent has counterplay, spending moves on quiet improvement is how the advantage is lost.

examples.note: Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz 1908, 20.e3 - the annotated instance of this concept, and the position the matcher's second version was built against. The annotation lists what one quiet pawn move does: 'it gains a tempo by attacking Black's queen, opens a diagonal for the bishop, and clears the second rank so the rook can swing from f2 to c2'. The two pieces improved are the two doing least. The condition the record insists on is satisfied exactly - nothing urgent is happening - and it is worth noting that the move ALSO gains a tempo, which is why an earlier version of the matcher that demanded a fully quiet position missed this position entirely.
examples.attributed_by: Nicholas Van Der Nat (Chess.com), following the classical literature - corpus entry rubinstein-salwe-1908-20e3-improving

engine.verdict_note: +0.31 and the annotated move is the engine's FIRST choice on a three-line search. A clean agreement between a century-old annotation and a modern engine, and a small number - a third of a pawn, for the move the literature calls instructive, which is the right size for a principle about accumulating.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `improving-a-piece-into-mate`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The knight on a1 is beyond argument the worst-placed piece on the board: it has two moves and bears on nothing. Nb3 improves it, the move is quiet, nothing is hanging, and no check is available. Every condition this matcher tests is satisfied. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's second trap: "Improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative produces individually reasonable moves and a collectively lost position. This is the commonest way the rule is misapplied." And its first indicator_against: "The opponent has a concrete threat that must be met." Black plays Re1 mate. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Reported as an instance of the rule until a guard was written, and it is the textbook illustration of misapplying it. The matcher already tested the material half of the trap — it refuses when the move leaves a winning capture available — and the sharpest concrete threat there is leaves no material on the floor to detect: the move generator says Black's only mate is e8e1, and Stockfish 18 agrees at depth 20 with #1. The guard is mate in ONE and no further, because whether a threat two moves out 'must be met' is a judgement and this record's third trap is that identifying the worst piece is a judgement this system must not claim to make. A mate the move generator can enumerate is not a judgement. worst-placed-piece fell from 8.4% to 4.1%, and Rubinstein–Salwe 1908 move 20 — the corpus's own annotated instance — still validates.

engine.verdict_note: #1. The move generator enumerates Black's only mate as e8e1 and the engine agrees. This is the sharpest form of 'the opponent has a concrete threat that must be met' and it leaves no material on the floor for a material test to find.

ambiguous_examples.note: Nominated by tools/mine_ambiguous.js on its fourth ground, NOT-THE-MOVE: the concept fires on a legal move that is not the solution of a shipped puzzle. The first three grounds ask about a POSITION and could not reach a move-based or motif concept at all - this concept and eleven others reported NONE until the tool learned to supply a move. What makes the case ambiguous rather than false is that nothing reported is absent: the knight on b8 is the worst-placed piece Black owns and ...Nd7 improves it, in a position with no check against Black and nothing hanging - every condition this matcher tests. This record's own second indicator_against is the one that fires here: 'a forcing line is available that decides matters'. It is ...e6, and it is worth three pawns more. The rule is correctly applied and correctly applied is not the same as right.

engine.verdict_note: ...Nd7 scores -3.60 and ...e6, the solution, scores -0.49, both from Black's side. Black is worse either way, which is why this is the honest kind of example: the quiet improving move does not lose the game, it loses three pawns of the defence.

by_level.beginner: If nothing urgent is happening, find the piece doing the least and give it something to do.
by_level.intermediate: Improve your worst-placed piece - or trade it for one of their good ones. Two solutions to the same problem.
by_level.advanced: Note the condition both original formulations carry: only when nothing more important is going on. The hard part is judging that.
by_level.master: The rule does not supply priority, which is precisely what it is usually asked for.

by_depth.short: When nothing urgent is happening, improve your worst piece.
by_depth.normal: Find the piece doing least and improve it - or exchange it for one of the opponent's best. It works because a position's strength is the sum of what its pieces do, so the cheapest improvement available is to the piece contributing least.
by_depth.deep: The most practical positional advice there is, and the one most often quoted without the condition its authors attached. Anderssen's version excepts the case where an attack yields immediate advantage; Makogonov's applies only 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered'. The popular short form drops both, and the truncation is the source of the rule's commonest misuse - spending two or three moves improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative, each move looking reasonable and the position already worse. The rule tells you what to do when nothing else is asking to be done; it does not tell you whether that is the case, and that judgement is the hard part of positional play.

explanations.hedge: Both original formulations are conditional, and the condition - that nothing more urgent is happening - is the part that decides whether the rule applies.
explanations.lesson: The rule is what to do when there is nothing to do. Deciding whether that is true is the real work.

worst-placed-piece.definition_short: When nothing more urgent is happening, find your worst-placed piece and improve it.
worst-placed-piece.definition_long:
The most practical piece of positional advice there is, and the one most often quoted without the condition its own authors attached to it.

THE RULE, in the two earliest formulations found here, both of which are conditional:
- ANDERSSEN: 'Move that one of your pieces, which is in the worst plight, UNLESS you can satisfy yourself that you can derive immediate advantage by an attack.'
- MAKOGONOV, as quoted by Mikhalchishin: 'IN POSITIONS WHERE NO OTHER IMPORTANT MATTERS NEED TO BE CONSIDERED, one should identify one's worst-placed piece and bring it to a more active square.'
Both carry the exception inside the statement. The popular short form — 'improve your worst piece' — is a truncation, and this base treats the truncation as the source of the rule's most common misuse.

WHY IT WORKS is that a position's strength is the sum of what its pieces are doing, so the cheapest available improvement is almost always to the piece doing least. It also turns positional play from something mysterious into something procedural: instead of searching for a plan, look for the unhappiest piece.

THE FAILURE MODE is priority, not correctness. A position usually contains several valid ideas at once, and improving pieces for two or three moves while the opponent builds an initiative elsewhere produces moves that each look reasonable and a position that is already worse. Principles do not establish which factor dominates — that is exactly what the preconditions in Anderssen's and Makogonov's own wordings are there to guard.

THE EXCHANGE COROLLARY is worth having alongside it: trade your worst pieces for the opponent's best. Improving a bad piece and trading it off are two solutions to the same problem.

wrong-rook-pawn.knowledge_type_note: Typed tablebase-fact: the result is proven, and the controlled pair in this record settles it in both directions. Nothing here is a judgement.

attributions.note: A 1623 study turns on the theme, which dates the knowledge to at least then. Second-hand; Greco's text not consulted.
Studied the analogous rook-and-bishop-pawn-versus-bishop case around 1750. Second-hand.

history.notes: Dating is well attested across two encyclopedia entries; neither primary source was consulted.

development.change: The theme appears in a composed study.
Becomes a known evaluation blind spot that has to be hard-coded, since search alone misjudges it.

wrong-rook-pawn.engine_era_note: A rare case where engines are WORSE than a rule: search does not find the draw because it lies beyond the horizon, so engines encode it explicitly. Any explanation of such a position should trust the tablebase over the evaluation bar.

preconditions: The attacker has a bishop and a rook pawn
The pawn's promotion square is NOT of the bishop's colour
indicators_for: The defending king can reach the promotion-square corner, or the square beside it
There is no second pawn on a different file to change the picture
indicators_against: The bishop DOES control the promotion square — an ordinary win
The defending king cannot reach the corner in time
A second pawn on another file exists, which usually wins
The pawn is not a rook pawn at all
false_positive_traps: Being in front of the pawn is NOT enough, unlike king-and-pawn endings. The defending king must reach the corner or the square beside it — Mednis gives a position where the same setup wins with White to move and draws with Black to move.
A second pawn on a different file usually changes the verdict entirely.
The bishop's colour relative to the CORNER is what matters, not its current square.

typical_plans: As the defender: head for the corner, and consider sacrificing to reach this ending
As the attacker: avoid trading into it, and keep a second pawn if possible
typical_moves: A bishop or exchange sacrifice to liquidate into the drawn ending
typical_pawn_structures: A lone a- or h-pawn with a bishop of the other colour
typical_piece_arrangements: Defending king on h8 (or a8) with the attacker's bishop unable to cover it
tactical_consequences: Enables saving sacrifices that look absurd on material grounds
strategic_consequences: An extra piece and pawn can be worth exactly nothing
A standing reason to check which rook pawn survives before trading into a bishop ending

exceptions: A second pawn on a different file normally wins.
If the defending king cannot reach the corner in time, the attacker wins normally.
In the mirrored rook-versus-bishop cases the logic inverts: there the DEFENDER has the wrong bishop when it is the colour of the corner its king is confined to.
limitations: Fires on none of the 788 shipped positions - the material is B+RP against a bare king and none of them is that - and on a constructed case with a light-squared bishop and an h-pawn. The record's first trap is not detectable and travels as a caution: the defending king must REACH the corner, and being in front of the pawn is not enough.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'a second pawn on a different file usually changes the verdict entirely' is not implemented. The matcher's own preconditions require the lone rook's pawn, so a second pawn on another file takes the position out of the concept before the trap applies - but that is the reason, and it is written here rather than left implicit.
misconceptions: That an extra bishop and pawn must win. Against the wrong rook pawn it is a dead draw.
That getting the king in front of the pawn draws, as it does with king and pawn alone. It does not.
That the engine evaluation can be trusted here. This is a documented evaluation blind spot.

examples.note: The basic case. White has a light-squared bishop on d5 and an h-pawn, which promotes on h8 — a DARK square the bishop can never control. Black's king is already in the corner.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw with an extra bishop AND an extra pawn. Paired with the identical material below, where only the bishop's colour differs.

engine.verdict_note: THE ENGINE IS WRONG HERE AND THE TABLEBASE IS NOT, which is why both numbers are recorded. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says +0.92. Syzygy says draw, dtz 0, 4 pieces, best move Kg6 - proven over every legal continuation. The bishop is light-squared and the queening square h8 is dark, so the defending king cannot be driven out of the corner however long White plays. This is the base's own rule about instruments said out loud: a tablebase gives proof, an engine gives an opinion, and where they disagree inside seven pieces the opinion loses.

counterexamples.note: IDENTICAL material and identical king and pawn squares — the bishop is on d4, a DARK square, so it controls h8. That single change is the whole concept.

tablebase.note: PROVEN win, mate in 9. Same pieces, same squares for king and pawn; only the bishop's colour complex differs. Draw against mate in 9 — as clean an isolation as the opposition pair, and a full point turning on which diagonal a bishop happens to travel on.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN in 9, dtz 1, best move Kg6+, against a PROVEN DRAW for the same material with the bishop on the other colour. That is the whole content of the concept and it is settled rather than argued: one bishop, two colours, win and draw. The engine agrees here (mate in 7) and disagreed on the drawn half, which is the reason both halves carry both numbers.

by_level.beginner: Their bishop can never reach the corner square your pawn needs, so if your king sits in that corner they can never push you out. Extra piece or not, it is a draw.
by_level.intermediate: The wrong rook pawn: the bishop is on the wrong colour for the promotion square. Get the king to the corner and it is drawn — a standard saving resource worth sacrificing for.
by_level.advanced: Wrong bishop. Note the king must reach the corner itself, not merely get in front of the pawn, which is the difference from a pure king-and-pawn ending.
by_level.master: Check which rook pawn survives before liquidating into a bishop ending — and remember this is a documented engine evaluation blind spot, so trust the tablebase over the bar.

by_depth.short: The bishop cannot cover the promotion square, so the corner is a fortress.
by_depth.normal: The wrong rook pawn: a bishop can never control the promotion square of one of the two rook pawns. With that pawn, a king that reaches the corner cannot be driven out, so bishop and pawn against a bare king is drawn.
by_depth.deep: A bishop travels on one colour forever, so one of the two rook pawns always promotes on a square it cannot touch. With that pawn the ending is a draw once the defending king reaches the corner — an extra piece and an extra pawn worth exactly nothing. The precision that catches people is that the king must reach the CORNER, or the square beside it; merely standing in front of the pawn is not enough, unlike the pure king-and-pawn case. Known since at least a Greco study of 1623, and it generates the standard practical resource of sacrificing into it. It is also a documented engine blind spot: the draw lies beyond search's horizon, so evaluation functions hard-code it, and in one TCEC superfinal one engine knew it and the other apparently did not.

explanations.lesson: Before you trade into a bishop ending with a rook pawn, check whether your bishop covers the promotion square. If it does not, you have nothing.

beginner_words: the bishop is the wrong colour for the corner

wrong-rook-pawn.definition_short: A rook pawn whose promotion square is the opposite colour to the bishop's. Bishop and wrong rook pawn cannot win against a king that reaches the corner — the extra material is worth nothing.
wrong-rook-pawn.definition_long:
A bishop moves on one colour forever, so it can never control the promotion square of one of the two rook pawns. An h-pawn promotes on h8, a dark square; an a-pawn promotes on a8, a light one. Whichever of those the bishop cannot cover is the WRONG rook pawn for that bishop.

The consequence is stark: king, bishop and wrong rook pawn against a bare king is a DRAW if the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn. The bishop cannot evict it, and the attacking king cannot either without stalemating. A whole extra piece and pawn are worth nothing.

Mednis adds a precision that is easy to miss: unlike king and pawn against king, where getting in front of the pawn is enough, here the defending king must reach the corner ITSELF or the square beside it. Merely being in front of the pawn does not draw.

The knowledge is old — Gioachino Greco composed a study turning on it in 1623 — and it generates a standard practical resource: a defender who is losing can head for one of these endings deliberately, often by sacrificing.

IT IS A KNOWN ENGINE BLIND SPOT. The Chess Programming Wiki records that this fortress 'needs to be encoded in the evaluation function, as search would not evaluate them properly', and cites the TCEC Season 5 Superfinal where Komodo had the knowledge and Stockfish apparently did not. Below eight pieces the tablebase is the authority; above it, a bare evaluation may be wrong about exactly this.

x-ray.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Terminology genuinely contested: some sources fold x-ray into pin/skewer. The boundary chosen here is stated explicitly rather than presented as settled.
x-ray.definition_short: A line piece acts through another piece — attacking or defending beyond it.
x-ray.definition_long:
A bishop, rook or queen exerts influence through an intervening unit. Two distinct uses share the name, and Chess Tempo maintains them as separate tags:

X-RAY ATTACK — the line piece attacks a target through an intervening piece, so the attack becomes real the moment the blocker leaves.
X-RAY DEFENCE — the line piece defends a friendly unit through an intervening piece, so a capture on that square is answered by a recapture that was not visible.

Sources also disagree about whether x-ray is distinct from pin and skewer at all; some treat all three as one family of line effects. This record keeps x-ray for the case where the effect operates THROUGH a piece without compelling it to move, which is what distinguishes it from a pin or skewer.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A line piece, an intervening unit, and a further square of interest are collinear
indicators_for: The defence or attack becomes live as soon as the blocker moves
A capture on the far square is met by a recapture along the x-ray line
indicators_against: A second blocker sits further along the line
The far target is irrelevant
recognition.detector: proposed, and deliberately unclaimed (not yet written)

exceptions: An x-ray defence is illusory if the defending piece is itself pinned.
limitations: The pin/skewer/x-ray boundary is not agreed between sources; an explanation should prefer the more specific term when the position warrants it.

TYPICAL_CONFIDENCE RAISED medium -> high, 2026-09-02, and the reason is the schema's own definition of the field: 'how confidently this concept can normally be asserted ONCE ITS PRECONDITIONS HOLD'. This concept's recognition is MECHANICAL and its knowledge type already carries a high ceiling, so once the preconditions hold there is nothing left to be uncertain about - a stalemate is a stalemate, and a fork this base reports is one findMotifs() found, which ARCHITECTURE.md makes the authority and forbids second-guessing. 'Medium' was the default across 32 rule and motif records regardless of detectability, and it was found by measuring what the API reports against what each record permits: twelve concepts were reporting ABOVE their own record. The fix was to make each record its own ceiling in cap(), which then required the records that were wrong to be corrected rather than silently overruled.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET, and the search that failed is worth recording. Five famous games were replayed through this base's own move generator and scanned position by position with the API - the Opera Game, the Evergreen, the Immortal, the Game of the Century and Legall's Mate, 225 plies between them - and this concept was not reported in any of them. That is not evidence the motif is rare; it is evidence that the five games this base can currently verify do not contain a clean instance of it, and that adding one means adding a game rather than looking harder at these. tools/replay_game.js is the instrument: a move list that is wrong is refused rather than guessed at. RESOLVED: Veresov-Bronstein, USSR Championship 1944, 37.Re1, above.

examples.note: Constructed, and it is the DEFENSIVE form, which is the half of this motif that a detector looking for attacks never sees. The white rook on a1, the black rook on a3 and the white bishop on a5 are collinear with exactly one unit between - the record's precondition word for word - and the consequence is that Black cannot win the bishop. Rxa5 is answered by Rxa5, because the black rook's own departure from a3 opens the line it was standing on. The rook defends through an enemy piece.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00. Black's best is to trade rooks rather than take the bishop, which is the x-ray defence working: the bishop is not hanging, it is defended through the rook that appears to be attacking it.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw, and the tablebase's own best move is Rxa1+ rather than Rxa5. A defence that holds over every legal continuation is the strongest statement available about a defensive motif, and it is the reason this example is the defensive form rather than the attacking one.

examples.note:
AN X-RAY DEFENCE, which is the half of this concept the record keeps the name for: 'the line piece defends a friendly unit through an intervening piece, so a capture on that square is answered by a recapture that was not visible'.

37.Rd1-e1 puts the rook on the e-file behind Black's rook on e5, and behind THAT stands White's bishop on e7. The bishop is attacked and looks undefended. It is not: 37...Rxe7 is answered by 38.Rxe7, the recapture arriving down a line that the black rook itself was blocking until the moment it captured. Nothing else on the board defends e7.

Stockfish 18 at depth 26 with three lines: +2.63 for Re1, against +0.50 and +0.36. A 213-centipawn margin, and the engine's own line takes the rook the other way - 37...Rxe1 38.Kxe1 - which is the same fact from the other side: the e-file is White's and the bishop is held.

WHY THIS ONE AND NOT THE OTHERS. Two better-known candidates were rejected. A Petrosian position where the geometry is present is second-best in a lost game. Kramnik-Yakovich 29.Qc5 is the engine's FIRST choice and still not this concept: the queen lines up with its own knight through a black pawn that cannot capture the knight, so the defence never comes into operation. That rejection corrected the miner's test - an x-ray defence is worth something only when the capture on the defended square is what opens the line, so the man in between has to be the one that can make that capture.

PROVENANCE. Found by tools/mine_master_motifs.js. The move list replayed legally through the page's own move generator. `attributed_by` absent - no annotator read.

engine.verdict_note: Best by 213 centipawns at depth 26. The two runners-up both MOVE the bishop, which is what a player does when they cannot see that it is defended.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `an-x-ray-with-two-blockers`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The white rook on d1, the black bishop on d6, the black rook on d7 and the black queen on d8 are all on the d-file with nothing else between them. A line piece acting through another piece towards something more valuable is the definition of an x-ray. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first indicator_against: "A second blocker sits further along the line." The precondition is a line piece, ONE intervening unit and a further square of interest; here there are two intervening units, so the rook acts through nothing — the pressure stops at the bishop. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report x-ray. The distinction is worth stating because it is arithmetical rather than positional: one blocker is an x-ray, two is a queue, and the difference is a count that a reader looking at a file of pieces will not naturally make. This record's positive example is the DEFENSIVE form of the same geometry with exactly one blocker, tablebase-proven, and the two sit side by side for that reason.

ambiguous_examples.note: The attacking form of the motif, with exactly one blocker: the rook on d1 acts through the rook on d7 at the queen on d8. The geometry is textbook and the position is lost - the engine reports mate in 10 AGAINST the side holding the x-ray, because a rook on an open file against a queen is not a threat, it is a target. Filed as ambiguous rather than as a false positive because the x-ray is genuinely present and correctly described; what is absent is any reason to care. This record's second indicator_against is the short version - 'the far target is irrelevant' - and here the far target is irrelevant in the strongest possible sense, being worth more than everything doing the attacking.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 10 against the side whose rook is doing the x-raying. The motif is present and the position is lost, which is a pair of facts this base needs to be able to state together.

by_level.beginner: This piece is working right through another piece — the moment the piece in the middle moves, the attack is real.
by_level.intermediate: An x-ray: the {piece} defends {square} through {blocker}, so the recapture is available.
by_level.advanced: X-ray. Prefer 'pin' or 'skewer' where the front piece is compelled; reserve x-ray for through-effects that compel nothing.

by_depth.short: A line piece acting through another piece to something beyond it.
by_depth.normal: An x-ray: a line piece, one unit in between, and a further square that matters. The attack or the defence operates through the middle unit, so the moment it moves the line is real.
by_depth.deep: It has two forms and the defensive one is the half a detector looking for attacks never sees: a rook 'attacking' its own bishop through an enemy rook is defending it, because the enemy rook's own departure opens the line. This base's positive example is that shape, tablebase-proven — the defender cannot win the bishop and the position is a proven draw. The precondition names ONE intervening unit, and the count is the whole of it: one blocker is an x-ray, two is a queue. Where the far target is worth less than what is doing the attacking, the geometry is present and worth nothing.

explanations.hedge: Sources differ on where x-ray ends and pin or skewer begins.

historical_names: squeeze (some writers, for the one-sided case)
zugzwang.knowledge_type_note: A proven result rather than a heuristic: whether a given position is zugzwang is decidable, and in the endgame it is decidable by tablebase. The concept names a fact about a position, not a recommendation.

attributions.note: ALLEGED only. Edward Winter's Chess Notes records the claim and states plainly that 'The first use of the word Zugzwang, allegedly originated by Max Lange, needs to be determined.' Recorded because the claim circulates, NOT as established.
First known use of the term in ENGLISH. He also cited a Philidor position as an example in Lasker's Manual of Chess.
An endgame study exhibiting the CONCEPT, more than two centuries before the term.

history.notes: Unusually well dated for a chess term, and unusually clearly unsettled at the same time. The word appears in German chess literature in 1858 or earlier and in English from Lasker in 1905. Who coined it is NOT established: Max Lange is alleged, and Winter — the standard authority on exactly this kind of question — says the first use needs to be determined. The CONCEPT is far older than the word, appearing in Salvio's 1604 study and in shatranj studies from the early 9th century, over a thousand years before the term. Confidence 'disputed' refers to the coinage; the dating of first appearances is solid.
competing_claims: Coined by Max Lange — alleged, and explicitly unverified by Winter.
Terminology split: most writers call the one-sided case zugzwang and the two-sided case reciprocal zugzwang; some call the one-sided case a 'squeeze' and the two-sided case zugzwang.

development.change: The concept appears in studies over a millennium before it is named.
An endgame study exhibiting zugzwang.
The term is in use in German chess literature.
First known use in English.
Reciprocal zugzwang becomes decidable rather than analysed; Nunn notes how often it turns out to matter.

zugzwang.engine_era_note: Not merely reliable but DECIDABLE. Within tablebase range, whether a position is zugzwang is settled by comparing the result with each side to move — the two lookups differ by one bit. The opposition record in this base contains exactly that pair.

preconditions: Every legal move available to the side to move worsens their position
The same position with the other side to move would be better for them
indicators_for: Few pieces and few legal moves — typically a king-and-pawn endgame
The king is tied to defending something and has no waiting move
All pawn moves are exhausted or would create a fatal weakness
The tablebase result flips when the side to move is flipped
indicators_against: A waiting move exists that changes nothing
A spare pawn tempo is available
Many pieces remain, so a neutral move is almost always available
false_positive_traps: A position where the side to move is simply losing is not zugzwang. The test is whether having to MOVE is the cause — flip the side to move and see whether the result changes.
Being short of good moves is not zugzwang; every move must worsen the position.
In middlegames, apparent zugzwang is usually just a bad position.

typical_plans: Exhaust the opponent's waiting moves, then hand them the move
Triangulate to lose a tempo and return the same position with the other side to play
Keep a spare pawn tempo in reserve rather than spending it
typical_moves: A king triangulation
A waiting move with a rook along a rank
typical_pawn_structures: Blocked pawn chains where no pawn can move safely
typical_piece_arrangements: Kings in opposition
tactical_consequences: Wins material or forces a decisive concession without any threat being made
strategic_consequences: Required for some elementary wins; king and rook against king cannot be forced without it
The reason reserve tempi are worth hoarding in pawn endings

exceptions: A side with a spare tempo is not in zugzwang, however constrained it looks.
In the middlegame, with many pieces on, genuine zugzwang is rare — usually a bad position is just a bad position.
limitations: Decidable within tablebase range; a judgement outside it.
The terminology is not agreed: 'squeeze' versus 'zugzwang' for the one-sided case.
misconceptions: That zugzwang means having no good moves. It means every move is bad AND that being obliged to move is what causes it.
That Lasker or Nimzowitsch coined it. Lasker introduced it to English in 1905; the coinage is unestablished.
That it is a modern idea. The concept predates the word by over a thousand years.

examples.note: The textbook zugzwang, and a controlled pair in the strictest form there is: the SAME BOARD with only the side to move changed. White king e5, pawn e4, black king e7. Black to move must give way - 1...Kd7 2.Kf6 or 1...Kf7 2.Kd6 - and loses. White to move is a draw, because White has to give way instead. Being obliged to move is the whole of the difference; nothing on the board differs at all.

tablebase.note: PROVEN LOSS for the side to move, dtz -4. The identical position with White to move is a proven draw at dtz 0. Two lookups of one board, differing only in whose turn it is, returning different results is what zugzwang IS, and Syzygy states it rather than illustrating it.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN for White, dtz -4, mate in 28 from Black's side, and the engine reports mate in 15 for the side not to move. Black to move must give ground. This single position serves `opposition`, `key-square` and `zugzwang` at once, and the pair it belongs to - the same board with White to move, proven DRAWN - is the strictest controlled comparison this base contains, because nothing on the board differs at all.

examples.note:
THE TREBUCHET, which this record's own deep wording has named since it was written - 'reciprocal zugzwang, whose extreme form is the trebuchet, where whoever moves loses' - and never showed. White Kd6 and pawn e5; Black Kf5 and pawn e6. Each king stands beside the other's pawn and each pawn is defended by nothing. Whoever has to move either steps away from the enemy pawn or abandons their own, and loses.

It is a controlled pair of the strictest kind there is: the SAME BOARD, only the side to move changed, and BOTH readings are a loss. That cannot happen in a position where the obligation to move is not the whole content, which is the proposition this record exists to teach.

IT WAS NOT BUILT BY HAND, and the reason is recorded in state/progress.md: a trebuchet constructed from memory in an earlier session turned out to be a draw both ways, and the tablebase caught it. This one was FOUND - the search enumerates positions with two pawns nose to nose on one file, so neither side has a pawn tempo and the whole game is king moves, and asks Syzygy for both side-to-move readings of each. Random sampling had already been tried and found nothing in 400 boards, which is what should have been expected: a reciprocal zugzwang is a coincidence between two evaluations, and random boards are not where coincidences live.

tablebase.note: PROVEN LOSS for the side to move, from BOTH sides. White to move: loss, dtz -2, mate in 34 against. Black to move: loss, dtz -2, mate in 24 against. Two lookups of one board differing only in whose turn it is, and both come back losing - which is the trebuchet stated rather than illustrated.

examples.note:
The other half of the trebuchet, and the half that makes it one. In an ordinary reciprocal zugzwang the pair reads LOSS one way and DRAW the other; here it reads LOSS both ways, and the only way to state that is to put both boards in the base and let the checker resolve each to the other. Black to move: Kf5 must leave the white pawn or the black king must abandon e6, and Syzygy gives mate in 24 against.

This is the reason the pair is stored as two positions rather than as one position with a sentence about the other. A claim about what happens when the side to move changes is a claim about two boards, and a base that stores one of them is storing half a claim.

tablebase.note: PROVEN LOSS for Black to move, dtz -2, mate in 24 against. The identical board with White to move is also a proven loss, at mate in 34. Whoever moves loses.

counterexamples.note: The same board with White to move, which is NOT zugzwang for Black - it is White who must give way, and the position is a draw. A reader shown only the diagram cannot tell which of the two it is, and the concept lives entirely in the half of the FEN that a diagram does not draw.

tablebase.note: PROVEN DRAW at dtz 0. The identical board with Black to move is a proven loss.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Kd4, and the engine agrees at 0.00. The negative half of the strictest pair in this base: the same board as the winning position with only the side to move changed. Whoever is NOT to move holds the opposition, which is why this half of the pair is a negative for three concepts and not a different position.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `opposition-with-a-spare-tempo`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kings in direct opposition in a king-and-pawn ending, Black to move and every king move giving ground. That is what zugzwang looks like. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Zugzwang requires that having to move is what hurts, and here it is not: White has a spare pawn on h3 and wins whether it is Black's move or his own. There is no mutual obligation, so nobody is in zugzwang — Black is simply lost. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: PROVEN both ways, which is what settles it: with Black to move the position is a loss in 26, and with WHITE to move it is a win in 25 and the tablebase's own best move is h4 — the spare tempo. The API does not report zugzwang. It does report `opposition` at high confidence, and that is correct and worth noticing: the opposition is present and it is not what decides. Remove the h-pawn and the same board becomes this base's strictest controlled pair, where the side to move loses and the side not to move draws.

tablebase.note: PROVEN both ways, which is what settles it: Black to move loses in 26, and with WHITE to move the same board is a win in 25 whose best move is h4 - the spare tempo. A position that is lost with either side to move contains no zugzwang.

by_level.beginner: It is their turn, and every move they can make makes things worse. If they could pass, they would be fine — but you cannot pass in chess.
by_level.intermediate: Zugzwang. The position is fine for them; having to move is what loses it. Check whether they have a spare tempo before relying on it.
by_level.advanced: Zugzwang, and note whether it is one-sided or reciprocal — the second means you must not step into it yourself.
by_level.master: Within tablebase range this is decidable: flip the side to move and compare results. Reciprocal zugzwang is the case worth identifying precisely, since both sides must avoid moving first.

by_depth.short: Every move they have makes things worse.
by_depth.normal: Zugzwang: the position would be fine if they could pass, but chess has no pass, and every legal move worsens things. The way to impose it is to run their waiting moves out.
by_depth.deep: From German, compulsion to move. Positions divide three ways: neither side minds moving, one side does, or both do — the last being reciprocal zugzwang, whose extreme form is the trébuchet, where whoever moves loses. Terminology is not fully agreed; a minority of writers call the one-sided case a squeeze. It is required for some elementary wins — king and rook against king cannot be forced without it — and the standard tool for imposing it is triangulation. The word appears in German chess literature by 1858 and in English from Lasker in 1905, but the concept is over a thousand years older, appearing in shatranj studies from the 9th century.

explanations.lesson: In simple endings, count the waiting moves. Whoever runs out first usually loses, and hoarding one spare pawn tempo can be worth more than a pawn.

zugzwang.definition_short: A position in which having to move is itself the disadvantage — every legal move worsens the position.
zugzwang.definition_long:
From German, 'compulsion to move'. Chess has no pass, so a player who would be fine if allowed to do nothing can be lost purely because they must move.

THREE KINDS OF POSITION, and this classification is what makes the term usable. Either neither side would be disadvantaged by having to move (the great majority), or one side would, or both would. Most writers call the second case zugzwang and the third RECIPROCAL or MUTUAL zugzwang. A minority reverse it, calling the second a 'squeeze' and reserving 'zugzwang' for the third. Both usages are attested and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.

The extreme form of reciprocal zugzwang is the TRÉBUCHET, where whoever must move loses outright — a full-point mutual zugzwang.

It matters most in the endgame, where few moves are available and each is critical, and it is REQUIRED for some elementary results: king and rook against king cannot be won without it. John Nunn's assessment is that reciprocal zugzwang positions are surprisingly important in endgame analysis generally.

The standard way to impose it is TRIANGULATION — losing a move so as to hand the same position back with the opponent to play.

zwischenzug.knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), but categorically different from the geometric motifs: it is about sequencing, so it cannot be detected from a static position at all.
zwischenzug.definition_short: An in-between move that inserts a bigger threat before making the reply the opponent expected.
zwischenzug.definition_long:
In a forcing sequence — typically a capture that 'obviously' must be recaptured — a player inserts a different, stronger move first, usually a check or a larger threat. The opponent must deal with it; only then does the original recapture happen, now under changed circumstances.

It is a move-order idea rather than a geometric pattern, which is what makes it hard to see: the losing move is often not a bad move but a correct move played one turn too early. ECM lists it as 'Intermediate Move'.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A forcing exchange is under way and one side is expected to recapture
An alternative move exists that creates a threat at least as urgent
indicators_for: The in-between move is a check
The original recapture remains available afterwards
indicators_against: The delay allows the opponent to save the material
The in-between threat can be met while also defending

typical_plans: Before making the recapture the position seems to demand, list every check and every capture that is bigger
In a forcing line, insert the check first and take second whenever the check cannot be answered by a counter-capture
When calculating the opponent's reply, look for THEIR in-between move before assuming they must recapture
typical_moves: A check with a piece other than the one about to recapture
A capture of something more valuable, leaving the first exchange standing
An attack on the queen inserted between a capture and its recapture
typical_piece_arrangements: An exchange under way on one square while a check is available on another
Two pieces of the opponent hanging at once, so the order of taking them matters
tactical_consequences: The gain is in the ORDER rather than in the material: the same men come off in both lines and the evaluation differs
Desperado is a special case - a doomed piece acting before the expected recapture is a zwischenzug made by a piece that has nothing to lose
strategic_consequences: Whole calculated lines are refuted by an opponent's zwischenzug, which is why this record's advice is to look for theirs and not only for yours

exceptions: An in-between move fails if the opponent's answer to it also answers the original threat.
A check that lets the opponent improve while answering it is worse than the immediate recapture.
If the first exchange can be abandoned by the opponent, the in-between move has bought nothing.
limitations: There is no matcher. Recognising a zwischenzug requires knowing what the EXPECTED move was, which is a claim about a line rather than about a position, and this base reports at the board.

The example on this record was FOUND rather than constructed, by scanning the 788 shipped puzzles for a solution whose first move is not the recapture on the square just captured, where a recapture is available and the move played is a check. Fifteen positions match. The scan needs each puzzle's `prev` position to know what was just taken, which is the same field the puzzle generator added so that a turning point could be measured at all.

NO MASTER-GAME POSITION YET, and the search that failed is worth recording. Five famous games were replayed through this base's own move generator and scanned position by position with the API - the Opera Game, the Evergreen, the Immortal, the Game of the Century and Legall's Mate, 225 plies between them - and this concept was not reported in any of them. That is not evidence the motif is rare; it is evidence that the five games this base can currently verify do not contain a clean instance of it, and that adding one means adding a game rather than looking harder at these. tools/replay_game.js is the instrument: a move list that is wrong is refused rather than guessed at. RESOLVED: Klasup-Tal, Latvian Championship 1952, 21...Nf2+, above.

examples.note: Shipped puzzle mi-4fe7c58015, and it is the concept in its purest form. Black has just captured on e3 and White is expected to recapture. Instead White checks on e6 first, and the check has to be answered, so the recapture is still there afterwards - the engine's own line plays Bxe6+ Kh8 and only THEN fxe3. The whole gain is in the order. Found by scanning the 788 shipped puzzles for a solution whose first move is not the recapture on the square just taken, where a recapture IS available and the move played is a check: fifteen positions match that shape.

engine.verdict_note: +4.37 for the in-between check against +1.97 for the immediate recapture fxe3 - 240 centipawns bought by move order alone, with the same material taken in both lines. That margin is what a zwischenzug IS, and it is the reason the concept has a name of its own rather than being filed under 'check'.

examples.note:
THE SHAPE THE RECORD DESCRIBES, in a game, with the numbers to show what the move order is worth. White has just captured on f7 and Black's queen on e7 is the piece expected to recapture. 21...Nf2+ is played instead. The check has to be answered, the bishop on f7 is not going anywhere, and the position Black recaptures into is a different one.

Stockfish 18 at depth 28 with three lines: +7.00 for Nf2+, against +0.18 and +0.10 for the next two. **The in-between move is worth 682 centipawns**, which is the whole difference between a level position and a won one, and the two alternatives include recapturing.

The engine's line does not recapture at all - 22.Kg1 Qh4 - and that is faithful rather than awkward. The record says the recapture happens 'now under changed circumstances'; sometimes the circumstances change enough that it is no longer the move.

HOW IT WAS FOUND, and what the finder does NOT claim. This concept's detectability is `human-only` and its own definition says it is 'a move-order idea rather than a geometric pattern, which is what makes it hard to see'. The test in tools/mine_master_motifs.js does not claim to find the idea; it finds the shape the idea lives in, and every candidate was read. The shape has three parts, all off the board: the opponent has just captured, we have a recapture available on that square, and instead we give a check elsewhere after which the recapture is STILL there against every reply. That last clause is the whole point - an in-between move that loses the recapture is not an in-between move, it is a different move.

PROVENANCE. Replayed legally through the page's own move generator. `attributed_by` absent - no annotator read; this grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

engine.verdict_note: +7.00 against +0.18 at depth 28. The move order is worth 682 centipawns, which is what this concept claims a move order can be worth and is rarely able to show.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-check-with-no-exchange-under-way`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Ra8+ is a forcing move inserted before anything else happens, and the opponent must answer it before doing what they intended. Inserting a forcing move ahead of the expected continuation is the concept. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: There is no expected continuation to insert it ahead of. A zwischenzug is defined against a move the opponent is COMMITTED to — a recapture, most often — and nothing has been captured, nothing is hanging, and Black had no obligation of any kind before the check. An in-between move needs two things to be in between. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `open-file` and nothing else. This record has no matcher and its limitations give this exact reason: 'recognising a zwischenzug requires knowing what the EXPECTED move was, which is a claim about a line rather than about a position, and this base reports at the board.' The case pins that down with the cheapest possible counterexample — a check, which is the most forcing move there is, in a position where forcing nothing was pending. The same board is `decoy`'s registered case.

ambiguous_examples.note: Shipped puzzle mi-5f4be05ec3, and it is the DEFENSIVE form of the motif, which the record describes only in passing. Black has just taken on g3 and White is expected to recapture. Recapturing is mate in three against - Qxg3 Qxg3 and the attack lands. Instead White checks on a8 first, and the check leads to a perpetual: 0.00. So the in-between move is essential and it gains no material at all. Filed as ambiguous because the concept's usual framing is that move order buys material - this record's own positive example buys 240 centipawns by it - and here the same mechanism buys a draw from a lost position, which the definition does not cover and the reader would not predict from it.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 for the in-between check against MATE IN 3 AGAINST for the natural recapture, at depth 20 with two lines. The gap is the whole game rather than a material count, which is why this position is filed beside a positive example whose gap is 240 centipawns.

by_level.beginner: Instead of recapturing straight away, this makes a bigger threat first. The recapture is still there afterwards.
by_level.intermediate: A zwischenzug. Check that the delayed capture will still be available.
by_level.advanced: In-between move. The commonest source of error is treating a forced-looking recapture as actually forced.

by_depth.short: An in-between move played before the reply the opponent expects.
by_depth.normal: A zwischenzug: instead of making the move the position seems to demand — usually a recapture — a bigger threat is inserted first. The opponent must answer it, and the original move is still available afterwards.
by_depth.deep: The gain is in the ORDER rather than in the material: the same men come off in both lines and the evaluation differs, which is why the idea needs a name of its own. This base's example buys 240 centipawns by playing a check before recapturing, with an identical material result. It also has a defensive form the usual definition does not cover — an in-between check that reaches a perpetual from a position where the natural recapture is mate in three against, where what the move order buys is a draw rather than material. The condition that fails most often: if the opponent's answer to the in-between move also answers the original threat, nothing has been bought.

entries.text: That attacking is a matter of temperament. The classical position is that it is a consequence of an advantage you already hold.
That an exposed king is losing.

A wing attack can be refuted by a central counter-blow — the standard antidote.
Trading queens usually ends an attack, so the defender's simplest defence is often to seek that trade.
Damaged pawn cover is not decisive by itself. It matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.

An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one. This is a registered false-positive case.

always attack
That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. It is a way of making a road; without pieces it is a weakness.
That storms are always double-edged. With opposite-side castling they cost the attacker nothing.

A central counter-blow refutes a premature storm — the standard antidote.
Against an intact shield with no hook, the storm may never force a file open at all.
Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow. Without that, it is a structural concession.

Counting the storm's speed without counting the defender's central break is how these positions are misjudged.
pushing pawns is an attack
That any distraction is equally damaging. Timing and novelty decide.
That the danger is forgetting individual pieces. The evidence points at disruption of pattern matching during encoding.
Interference after a position is encoded is comparatively harmless, which is the opposite of what the folklore suggests.

A fact about the player and the interface, not about the position or any move.

distraction is always equally bad

photographic memory

This describes a player's skill, not a position. It cannot be attached to a move.
The transfer claim - that these drills raise playing strength - is not evidenced and must not be repeated as fact.
blindfold chess requires a gift

masters have better memories
That the rule of the square is about distance. It is about the square, and about whose move it is.
That a knight can lose a tempo. It cannot: every knight move changes square colour, so returning takes an even number of moves.
The rule of the square fails if the pawn's path is blocked, if it can be supported by its own king, or if the defending king's route is obstructed.

The rule of the square must be applied with the side to move in hand. This base holds a tablebase-proven pair where the identical position is a draw or a mate in 23 depending only on whose turn it is.
The rule of the square assumes a clear path: another pawn, or a king in the way, breaks it.
Colour-boundedness is a fact about bishops, not a claim that a bishop is limited — it is also why the pair is worth more than two of anything else.
the king is slow
