That the point values are facts. They are averages, and their authors disagree.
That being ahead on material means being better. A proven draw in this base is a bishop and pawn up.
That a bishop is worth more than a knight. That is one position in a live dispute, not a settled value.
Fortresses and wrong-coloured-bishop draws are proven counterexamples to the count.
With all pawns on one wing the knight is generally stronger than the bishop, reversing the usual ordering.
The exchange (rook for minor) is given up often enough that treating it as a fixed +2 is a mistake.
Counting material is not evaluating a position. This base holds a PROVEN DRAW a bishop and a pawn up.
The values are disputed among their own authorities, and the bishop-versus-knight disagreement is a full half-pawn wide.
The pair bonus attaches to having two bishops, not to each bishop. Reporting a lone bishop as worth more than a knight asserts the disputed claim.
a bishop is worth more than a knight
the piece values are
That a rook belongs on any open file. It belongs on one with a square to invade.
That diagonals are secondary to files. The long diagonals are the longest lines on the board.
Knights ignore lines entirely, which is what makes them the right piece for closed positions.
A line being open is a fact; its being useful is not. This base holds a tested position where an open file with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing.
diagonals are less important than files
That stronger players calculate more deeply and widely. De Groot found they do not search more, and may search less.
That calculation can replace judgement. A variation is worth only what the position at its end is worth.
That calculating further is always better. Ideas at the start of a line matter more than refinements at the end.
Many positions are decided by judgement and require almost no calculation.
In defence the emphasis shifts: pare the candidates down harder and examine the most critical first, since there is little point exploring suspect lines.
A description of how a player thinks, not a feature of the position. It cannot be offered as the reason a move is good.
That a move requires calculation is not evidence that it is correct.
strong players calculate deeper
That Kotov's tree describes how strong players actually think. It does not, on the testimony of several grandmasters including one who checked Kotov's own analysis.
That revisiting a line is a lack of discipline. It is how the comparison between lines is made, and the ideas found in one line frequently belong in another.
That a longer candidate list is better. Breadth is for generating; the work is done by going deep on the critical one.
Positions with one forced line need no list; the tree is a single branch.
Nunn's goal-seeking case: moves that only make sense as part of a larger operation will not appear in any candidate list, and must be found another way.
Tisdall argues the candidate list should not be the primary task at all, and that leaning on an instinctive first choice engages intuition and starts the abstract assessment.
This is a technique for the player, not a property of the position, and must never be presented as an explanation of why a move is good.
The one-pass tree must not be taught as current best practice. Nunn, Dvoretsky, Tisdall and Leitao all reject it, and this base records the rejection as the consensus.

Some strong moves are unreachable by candidate generation at all. Nunn's example is a move that 'makes absolutely no sense except as part of the whole tactical operation' and so never enters a candidate list.
analyse each line only once
never go back in a variation
That a plan is a sequence of moves. The opponent gets to move too; a plan is an objective and an arrangement.
That having any plan beats having none. A bad plan pursued rigidly is worse than responding to the position.
That abandoning a plan is weakness. Recognising that circumstances changed is a skill in itself.
Forcing positions need calculation, not planning.
Shereshevsky's 'thinking in schemes' inverts the usual order in endgames: decide the target arrangement first, then find the route to it.
A plan that names nothing cannot be verified, followed or abandoned, and is not a plan.
A plan that ignores the opponent's counterplay is the standard way good-looking moves lose games.
This system cannot know a player's plan and must not attribute one to a move without evidence.
improve my position
create pressure
a plan is a series of moves
That any piece will do. The choice of blockader is most of the concept.
That blockading is free. It commits a piece, and Nimzowitsch says so.
A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.
The pawn must not be allowed too far forward before the blockade is established — Nimzowitsch's own caveat.
A piece standing in front of a pawn is not necessarily blockading it usefully. The test is whether the piece keeps its powers there — a queen on a blockading square is doing a knight's chore.
A blockade becomes a weakness when it ties down a piece needed elsewhere, which is the standard cost and is easy to omit.
A pawn stopped by an enemy PAWN is a ram, not a blockade, and no piece is being spent.
blockade with anything
That defence means making passive moves and waiting. It is an active discipline with its own techniques.
That a worse position should be simplified. That is right when the position is holdable and wrong when it is lost.
That attacks succeed because attack is stronger than defence. The classical claim is the reverse: attacks from equal positions should fail, and succeed largely because defence is played badly.
Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it - Polugaevsky gives an example where the outwardly more active move loses.
Against a lost position, objectively bad moves that complicate can be the best practical choice.
Polugaevsky is explicit that modern success rests on offensive play, and that seeking defence contrary to the position's demands is as punishable as any other error.
Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle.
The simplify-versus-complicate advice is genuinely contradictory in the sources and must not be reported as settled. Which applies depends on whether the position is holdable or lost.
A concession that was not forced is not a defensive move. Conceding early and conceding more than necessary are the two ways defences collapse.
defence means waiting
always simplify when worse
That overprotection is generally good practice. It is a named historical idea with limited modern support.
That more defenders is safer. Beyond what a concrete line needs, extra defenders are usually idle pieces.
Defending an unattacked point is usually a waste of time, and modern practice says so.
Engines defend exactly as much as a line requires.
Counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing. Overprotection is a CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile, and that claim is often false.
This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well.
always overprotect the centre
That prophylaxis means passive or defensive play. Nimzowitsch explicitly says it is neither attack nor defence.
That it only concerns the opponent. He distinguishes external from internal prophylaxis, the latter aimed at one's own position.
That it is a modern refinement. It is his stated central conception of positional play, from 1925.
Prevention has a cost. If the opponent's idea was not dangerous, the tempo is simply lost.
In sharp positions, speed can outweigh prevention — a prophylactic move in a race loses the race.
Nimzowitsch's ranking of prophylaxis above accumulation is a claim about emphasis and was polemical; the two are complementary.
Any quiet move can be called prophylactic after the fact. The claim requires naming the specific idea prevented — if you cannot name it, the move was just quiet.
Preventing a threat that does not exist is not prophylaxis, it is a wasted move.
This is not detectable from a static position. It is a property of what the move DENIES, which requires knowing what the opponent intended.
prophylaxis means playing passively
any quiet move is prophylactic
That restraint is defensive. Nimzowitsch treats it as the first stage of an attacking plan.
That it is the same as the blockade. The blockade is restraint made permanent by a piece.
Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.
Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours.
Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.
restraint is passive play
That controlling the centre means putting pawns there.
That the hypermoderns thought the centre was unimportant — they thought it was too important to commit to early.
That one school won. Textbooks treat hypermodernism as an extension of classical theory, not a replacement.
Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.
In the endgame the logic inverts: the centre matters for king activity rather than for restriction.
Counting pawns on central squares measures occupation, not control. A fianchettoed bishop controls e4 without standing anywhere near it.
A big pawn centre is not automatically an advantage. Whether it is an asset or a target is a question of timing and support, and that cannot be read off the structure.
Central pieces are only strong while they cannot be kicked; a piece on a central square a pawn can attack is visiting.

A rook or queen whose line to a central square runs through one of its own men counts as an attacker and should not be read as a piece fighting for the square. The move-based arm measures pawns and minors for this reason.
always occupy the centre with pawns
the centre does not matter
That the initiative is the same as being better. A worse position can hold the initiative, and often that is the only reason it survives.
That checks and captures create an initiative. They create forcing moves, which is not the same thing.
That it is White's by right.
It expires. An initiative that is not converted into something permanent is worth nothing afterwards.
A series of forcing moves is not an initiative if the replies help the opponent.
Black can hold it. It is not White's by right of the first move.
A series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them.
Having more active pieces is not the same as having the initiative — the test is whether they must answer you.
The initiative is invisible to a static feature scan, so it cannot be detected from the board alone; it is a property of the sequence.
the initiative means you are better
White always has the initiative
That the rules are rules. They are defaults for players who cannot yet judge the exception.
That moving a piece twice is a mistake.
That the queen must stay home until move 10.
That 'the opening' ends at a fixed move number. It ends when the pieces are developed.
That moving the same piece twice in the opening is an error. In the Ruy Lopez it is the best move, measured at +0.42 against +0.08 for the alternative.
Moving a piece twice to capture, to escape, or to reach a decisively better square.
Early queen sorties that cannot be harassed — the Scandinavian's ...Qa5 is theory, not an error.
Delaying castling deliberately when the centre is closed, or when castling would walk into a prepared attack.
Hypermodern openings that decline to occupy the centre at all and invite overextension instead.

REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: moving the same piece twice is not automatically wrong. Capturing, escaping and reaching a much better square all justify it, and this is the brief's own illustration of tactics overriding a principle.

REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: early queen development is not automatically wrong — the objection is that the queen can be harassed WITH TEMPO, so where no such harassment exists the objection does not apply.
Detecting a rule violation is easy and says almost nothing. Only the absence of a concrete justification makes it a criticism.
'The opening' has no fixed end. Applying opening rules at move 15 of a closed position is a category error.
A piece moving twice is not evidence of a mistake. Proven counterexample: 4.Ba4 in the Ruy Lopez is best by 0.34 over any move that leaves the bishop alone.
never move the same piece twice
never bring the queen out early
That more space is simply better. It is better if you can enter.
That advancing pawns gains space safely. It also fixes them and leaves holes behind them.
Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.
The cramped side exchanging pieces is the standard and effective antidote.
Counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing.
Advanced pawns are not automatically a space advantage — they may simply be weak and fixed.
The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary.
more space is always better
That a tempo is worth a third of a pawn. It has no fixed value.
That gaining tempi is always good — driving an enemy piece to a better square costs you more than it gains.
That tempo and initiative are the same thing.
'Losing a tempo' is a virtue in the endgame, where triangulation aims at exactly that.
A tempo has no fixed value; the three-tempi-per-pawn heuristic is an opening rule of thumb only.
Moving the same piece twice is not automatically a lost tempo.
Chasing a piece with a threat it WANTED to answer is not gaining a tempo — the classic case is driving a piece to a better square with an attack.
Counting tempi in a closed position, where they may be worth nothing.
Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square all justify it.
a tempo is worth a third of a pawn
That it is a more complicated version of the opposition. It is the general theory; the opposition is its simplest case.
That it applies broadly. It applies to blocked king-and-pawn endings and almost nowhere else.
Any spare pawn tempo dissolves the correspondence.
Where opposition suffices, the extra machinery adds nothing.
The framework is only needed where opposition fails. Invoking it where simple opposition answers the question is unhelpful precision.
Correspondences break the moment a pawn tempo becomes available.
This is an expert-level tool. Reporting it to a player who has not yet mastered the opposition explains nothing.
corresponding squares are just the opposition
That endgames are simple because few pieces remain. They are the most exact phase, which is the opposite of forgiving.
That trading into an endgame is safe when ahead. Which endgame is reached decides, and several are proven draws a piece down.
Do not hurry does not apply against a concrete threat or in a race, where a single tempo decides.
Centralisation of the king has documented failures in rook endings, recorded on its own concept.
Simplification, the other common endgame reflex, can convert a proven win into a proven draw - this base holds tablebase proofs of exactly that.
The boundary is not sharp. A queenless position with many pieces may still be a middlegame, and treating it as an endgame is how kings get mated.
These are organising ideas, not a substitute for calculation. Every one of them has recorded exceptions, several proven by tablebase in this base.
endgames are simple
always trade when ahead
That a fortress is any stubborn defence. It is the impossibility of progress.
That the engine bar settles it. This is the clearest case where it does not.
That being material down means losing. A fortress makes the material count irrelevant.
A fortress that can be broken by a sacrifice was never a fortress.
Many apparent fortresses fail to zugzwang once the defender's waiting moves run out.
Within tablebase range the question is not a judgement at all — look it up.
A position that is merely HARD to break is not a fortress. The test is that no progress is possible at all, and that is a strong claim.
Claiming a fortress on the basis of an engine evaluation being stuck is backwards — engines misjudge these in BOTH directions.
A defender with a limited number of waiting moves does not have a fortress; they have a position that loses to zugzwang.
The commonest error is the reverse one: declaring a real fortress lost because the material count says so.
the engine says +3 so it is winning
That the opposition is the goal. The key square is the goal; the opposition is a means.
That key squares are the same for every pawn. They depend on the pawn's rank and file.
Rook pawns have their own, much more restrictive key squares and are often drawn.
Reaching a key square by the direct route is sometimes impossible while a route around the pawn works.
Key squares are only meaningful in king-and-pawn endings. Reporting them with pieces on the board is a category error.
For a rook pawn the usual rules do not apply and the ending is frequently drawn regardless.
Reaching a key square is the goal; taking the opposition is only one way of getting there and is sometimes the wrong one.
always take the opposition
That the king should be kept safe in the endgame as it is earlier. The change in the king's role is what defines the phase.
That centralisation is always correct. Its own advocate documents rook endings where it is not.
Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.
Races, where a centralising move may simply be too slow.

The single most important trap is rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate: Shereshevsky found centralisation there to be not merely untimely but sometimes simply wrong, and warns against automatic centralising moves.
A king moving towards the centre is not automatically doing the right thing; the move still has to survive checks. His example has 1...Ke5? losing to 2.Rd5+ while the retreat 1...Kc5! draws.
Centralisation with queens still on is a different matter entirely and this concept does not apply.
Never recommend centralising a king while the opponent has a queen, whatever the piece count says. The phase test in lib/features.js is material-based and can call a queens-on position an endgame.
always centralise the king
keep the king safe in the endgame
That a knight ending is a pawn ending. It is one for the purposes of several techniques and is not one when the knights start forking.
That knights are good blockaders and good chasers. They are excellent at the first and poor at the second.
Knight against knight and pawn is explicitly outside the principles: the standard reference says there are none operative for many such positions.
The knight is poor at catching a passed pawn, so the pawn-ending intuition about races does not transfer.
Rook pawns suit the knight badly.

Botvinnik's formula is a guide to which techniques transfer, not a claim that the ending IS a pawn ending. The knight's ability to fork and check reintroduces tempo, and knight against knight and pawn has no operative principles at all on the standard reference's own account.
A knight cannot lose a tempo, so triangulation and other tempo-losing methods that work with other pieces are unavailable to it.
a knight ending is a pawn ending (unqualified)
That the point count settles unbalanced endings. It is least reliable precisely here.
That two minor pieces automatically beat a rook. They do when coordinated and lose when they are not.
Fortresses defeat material reasoning entirely and are common in this class.
The bishop's statistical edge reverses when the pawns are all on one wing.
The point count is least reliable exactly here, and this is where people rely on it most. This base holds a proven draw a bishop and a pawn up.
The 60% figure for bishops over knights in endings is a population statistic and says nothing about a particular position.
This class is under-researched in this base, and confidence should stay low regardless of how clean the material description looks.
two minors beat a rook
count the material
That opposite-coloured bishops mean a draw. That is an endgame tendency, and the reverse is true in the middlegame.
That an extra pawn or two settles it. Two extra pawns frequently fail to win.
That a bad bishop is bad here. For the defender it is the correct setup.
The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.
A wrong rook pawn draws regardless of how far apart or how advanced the pawns are.
The defender's best practice is the opposite of normal: make your bishop bad on purpose.

The drawish reputation is an ENDGAME fact. In the middlegame with heavy pieces on, opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker, because the bishop operates where the defender's cannot answer. Announcing 'opposite bishops, drawn' with queens on the board is the standard error.
Detecting the material is trivial; whether a blockade is achievable is not.
Two extra pawns are often not enough — but three files of separation often are. The count of pawns is the wrong variable; their separation and the blockade are the right ones.
opposite bishops means a draw
That having the opposition means it is your move. It means the opposite — the side NOT to move has it.
That taking the opposition is always right.
That it is a rule of thumb. In king-and-pawn endings it is provably exact.
Taking the opposition is not always best. Averbakh: it is a means to an end, and if it does not lead to a key square, marching the king there directly may be correct.
A spare pawn tempo neutralises it entirely.
In positions decided by a pawn race, king geometry may be irrelevant.
Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides.
Taking the opposition is not always correct. In some positions the king should ignore it and head for a key square directly — this is Averbakh's corrective and it is the standard error.
A spare pawn tempo makes the opposition irrelevant, since it can simply be handed back.
I have the opposition because it is my move
always take the opposition
That perpetual check is a rule of chess. It is not, and has not been for a long time.
That you can 'claim a perpetual'. You claim threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule.
That any long series of checks is a perpetual.
It is not a rule and cannot be claimed as one. The claimable rules are threefold repetition and the fifty-move rule.
For the side that stands better a perpetual is a failure, not a resource.
Other chess variants forbid it outright, so it is not a necessary feature of chess-like games.
A series of checks that merely delays the end is not a perpetual. The test is whether the position REPEATS, not whether checks are available.

The repo's detector is a proxy — two or more checks and a near-level final evaluation — which will also fire on a position that is simply drawn after some checks. Treat the tag as a candidate, not a finding.
Reporting a perpetual as a good outcome for the side that was winning inverts the meaning entirely.
draw by perpetual check (as a rule)
claim a perpetual
That an extra pawn should win. Queen endings convert less often than rook endings, which are themselves notoriously drawish.
That perpetual check is a lucky escape. It is the defender's standard plan and should be expected.
Where the defending king is exposed, the usual perpetual-check defence may fail and ordinary material logic returns.
Fortresses exist in queen endings and defeat material reasoning entirely.
Counting pawns is a poor guide here: an advanced passed pawn outweighs a numerical deficit, because a queen can escort it alone.
An extra pawn is much less often decisive than in a rook ending, and this class wins less frequently than the rook equivalent.
Reasoning from principle is weak in queen endings. Where the position is small enough for a tablebase, look it up.
an extra pawn wins
That an extra pawn wins a rook ending. A great many such positions are drawn, because of how many defensive constructions exist.
That the rook belongs behind the passed pawn. It often does, and this base holds a proof that as a general rule it is false.
That rook endings can be played on principle. They are the type most resistant to that.
Tarrasch's rule fails in the Vancura configuration, proven in this base.
King centralisation fails in some rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate.
Passive defence is sometimes correct, in defiance of the activity principle, when a known drawing set-up requires it.
This is the endgame type where general rules are least trustworthy, and this base holds proofs against three of them: Tarrasch's rule, king centralisation, and the value of a check.
A pawn advantage is much weaker evidence here than elsewhere, because the defensive constructions are so numerous.
Recognising the material as a rook ending says almost nothing. The concrete configuration decides.
the rook belongs behind the passed pawn
an extra pawn wins
That triangulation is the only way to lose a tempo. A spare pawn move is usually available and simpler.
That any king manoeuvre returning to the same square is triangulation. It must return the position with the OTHER side to move.
That a knight can do it.
A knight cannot triangulate — it cannot return to a square in an odd number of moves.
A spare pawn move does the same job more cheaply.
The textbook example does not require triangulation; several moves win and a direct one wins faster.

MEASURED: the standard textbook position for triangulation does not require it. Every king move wins there and a direct pawn move wins fastest. Do not report triangulation as necessary without checking that the alternatives fail.
A spare pawn tempo achieves the same thing more cheaply and is usually available.
A knight cannot triangulate; asserting it can is a geometric error.
you must triangulate here
That an extra bishop and pawn must win. Against the wrong rook pawn it is a dead draw.
That getting the king in front of the pawn draws, as it does with king and pawn alone. It does not.
That the engine evaluation can be trusted here. This is a documented evaluation blind spot.
A second pawn on a different file normally wins.
If the defending king cannot reach the corner in time, the attacker wins normally.
In the mirrored rook-versus-bishop cases the logic inverts: there the DEFENDER has the wrong bishop when it is the colour of the corner its king is confined to.

Being in front of the pawn is NOT enough, unlike king-and-pawn endings. The defending king must reach the corner or the square beside it — Mednis gives a position where the same setup wins with White to move and draws with Black to move.
A second pawn on a different file usually changes the verdict entirely.
The bishop's colour relative to the CORNER is what matters, not its current square.
an extra piece always wins
That zugzwang means having no good moves. It means every move is bad AND that being obliged to move is what causes it.
That Lasker or Nimzowitsch coined it. Lasker introduced it to English in 1905; the coinage is unestablished.
That it is a modern idea. The concept predates the word by over a thousand years.
A side with a spare tempo is not in zugzwang, however constrained it looks.
In the middlegame, with many pieces on, genuine zugzwang is rare — usually a bad position is just a bad position.
A position where the side to move is simply losing is not zugzwang. The test is whether having to MOVE is the cause — flip the side to move and see whether the result changes.
Being short of good moves is not zugzwang; every move must worsen the position.
In middlegames, apparent zugzwang is usually just a bad position.
zugzwang means no good moves
That advanced concepts are more useful. They are more dependent, which is a different thing and often makes them less usable.

Advanced concepts are the ones this system detects least reliably, because they rest on other concepts rather than on board features. Confidence should be low here even when the reasoning looks clean.
Reaching for an advanced concept because no simple one fits is the standard failure. Saying nothing is better.
advanced players know
That a list of misconceptions means the underlying rules are worthless. Most are useful with their conditions restored.
That avoiding a misconception means asserting its opposite. The correct response is usually to say something narrower and specific to the position.
The rules behind these misconceptions are mostly sound in their conditional form; the index targets the unconditional statement, not the underlying idea.
The index records beliefs that are FALSE AS STATED, not beliefs that are always wrong. Doubled pawns are frequently a real weakness; the misconception is that they are one by definition.
This record must not be used to contradict a rule in a position where the rule holds. It exists to prevent unconditional assertion, not to invert it.
always
never
the rule is
That a principle with many exceptions is a bad principle. It may simply be a well-studied one.
That listing exceptions is hedging. It is the part that makes the rule applicable.
Official rules of chess and proven results have no exceptions, and are typed so that the test suite does not demand any.
Mechanical tactical motifs have conditions rather than exceptions - a fork either exists on the board or does not.
An exception existing does not make a rule useless. Most of these rules are correct in the large majority of positions.
The absence of a recorded exception means this base has not found one, not that none exists.
this rule is absolute
That difficulty means how hard the idea is to play. It means how much context is needed to state it without lying.
Difficulty describes the concept, not the reader. An intermediate concept still needs beginner wording when a beginner meets it, which is what explanations.by_level is for.
The tier is an editorial judgement made when the record was written, not a measured property.
intermediate players should
That LPDO means you should defend every piece.
That Nunn coined it — the better-sourced account is that Mike Cook did and Nunn popularised it.
That any lost undefended piece illustrates LPDO. It illustrates it only when being undefended is why the tactic worked.
Strong players leave pieces loose deliberately, having calculated that nothing reaches them.
Defending everything is a real error in the other direction: it wastes tempi and produces passive pieces.
The heuristic describes a tendency across many games, not a property of any one position.
A piece being undefended is not a mistake, and calling it one teaches a habit of pointless defending.

Not every loss of a loose piece is an LPDO instance. A ChessBase reader demonstrated that the article's own headline example was not: the piece did not fall because it was loose but because a square had become a forking square. If the tactic would work against a defended piece too, LPDO is not the explanation.
always defend your pieces
LPDO is a rule
Nunn coined LPDO
That the top tier holds the most important concepts. It holds the ones that break if stated approximately.
The tier is for concepts that need specific theory to state truthfully, not for concepts that are impressive. Marking something master-level to signal importance destroys what the field is for.
Most master-level chess knowledge is concrete rather than conceptual and does not belong in a concept record at all.
master-level (as praise)
That the classical school was refuted. Its evaluation framework is the basis of modern positional chess and of engine evaluation.
That Steinitz and Tarrasch held the same views with the same rigidity.
That 'classical' was what they called themselves — they were the Modern school.
Tarrasch's dogmatic form is widely and correctly broken; the underlying evaluation framework is not.
'Do not attack without an advantage' remains sound, but 'advantage' turned out to include dynamic factors the classical school undervalued.
Do not conflate Steinitz with Tarrasch. Steinitz's evaluation framework survived; Tarrasch's dogmatic rules did not, and the hypermodern attack was aimed at the second.
The school was called 'Modern' in its own time, which makes contemporary quotations easy to misread.
the classical school was refuted
That engines have refuted classical chess strategy. They have mostly measured it and found it directionally right and overstated.
That a principle stated by a world champion has been checked. Several in this base had not been until now.
Some principles have survived checking unqualified, particularly the geometric facts and the rules of the game itself.
An old principle being qualified does not make it worthless; most are right in direction and overstated in strength, which is why they are kept rather than deleted.
Quoting a principle in its popular form usually drops the condition its author attached. Prefer the author's own wording where this base holds it.
That a principle is old is not evidence against it, and that it is modern is not evidence for it.
engines disproved classical chess
the old masters were wrong
That hypermodernism beat classical theory. Textbooks present it as an extension of it.
That hypermoderns thought the centre unimportant.
That fianchetto equals hypermodern.
The school's own central claim fails as a rule: cede the centre against proper support and you lose to space.
It did not replace classical theory and was absorbed into it within a decade.
Several of its ideas predate it in nineteenth-century practice.
A fianchetto is not by itself hypermodern. The school's claim is about the centre, and a fianchetto with no plan against a central pawn mass is just a bishop on a long diagonal.
Ceding the centre without a break is not hypermodern; it is the failure mode the school itself warned about.
Attributing every modern positional idea to hypermodernism. Several were understood by Staunton's generation.
hypermodernism replaced classical chess
the centre does not matter
That modern play has abandoned principles. It has demoted them from deciders to orientation.
That engines caused the shift. It predates strong engines, which rewarded and settled it.
In quiet positions with no concrete content the classical method is not merely adequate but correct.
Concrete analysis is expensive; below master level the principles do most of the work.
This describes a historical tendency, not a property of a position, and must not be attached to a move.

A move breaking a classical rule is not thereby modern or good. It needs the concrete line that justifies it.

That a name on a chess idea records who thought of it. It usually records who popularised it in a particular language.
That widely repeated attributions have been checked. The Lucena misattribution dates from 1880 and is still repeated.
Some attributions are solid: the gambit etymology traces to Ruy Lopez in 1561 with Lopez's own derivation quoted, and Nimzowitsch's prophylaxis and overprotection are his beyond dispute.
A name attached to a concept is a claim about history and needs a source like any other claim. This base's checked attributions came back wrong or disputed more often than they came back clean.

An attribution being widespread is not evidence. The Lucena misattribution has been repeated since 1880.

That the Soviet school abandoned positional chess. It subordinated static factors to dynamic ones; it did not discard them.
That it replaced the earlier schools. Fischer's summary — that all three were correct in their own way — is the standard modern view.
Structural concessions still have to be paid for. The school's contribution was that the price could be worth it, not that it was free.
Its own defensive preference for counterattack is not universal — some positions require consolidation.
Accepting a bad structure is not Soviet-school play unless something concrete is obtained for it. The school's claim is that dynamics can OUTWEIGH structure, not that structure is unimportant.
This record is weakly sourced and should not be leaned on for historical claims until it has had dedicated research.
the Soviet school ignored positional chess
That castling makes the king safe.
That an exposed king is losing.
That pushing a pawn to chase an enemy piece away from your king is a defensive move. It usually creates a hook and the piece just steps aside.
That material compensates for king danger. It does not — checkmate ends the game regardless.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.
An uncastled king in a closed position can be safer than a castled one.
Castling into an oncoming pawn storm gives the attacker a fixed address; sometimes delaying or castling the other way is correct.
h3 or ...h6 is useful luft in a quiet position and a hook against an opponent who can storm. The same move, opposite meanings.
REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: an exposed king is not automatically losing. With the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often simply an active one — and in the endgame that is the goal.
Castling does not establish safety and failing to castle does not establish danger. A closed centre changes both.
Counting attacking pieces linearly overstates one or two and understates four. The relationship is S-shaped, and it is not worth reporting an attack below three attackers.

Against a queenside-castled opponent, luft is a hook and usually a concession.
With no heavy pieces left, back-rank mate is not a threat and luft is a wasted move.
Making luft is not automatically prudent. The same move is a hook against an opponent who can storm, and this is the standard error.
Luft is unnecessary when the back rank is adequately defended or when no heavy pieces remain.

That rooks belong on open files unconditionally. They belong on files they can invade down.
That an open file is better than a half-open one.
A file with no entry squares is worth nothing.

Nimzowitsch's usage of the term differs from the modern one.
REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a file with no pawns is not automatically useful. Without an entry square, a rook on it accomplishes nothing.

Contested files where all rooks come off leave neither side with anything.
An open file is not an advantage on its own. In a proven test position with a rook of each colour on the open d-file, the evaluation is +0.02 - the file belongs to nobody.

Where the enemy pawn can advance freely, the file is a route rather than a lever.
A semi-open file is a fact about pawns; whether it produces pressure depends on whether the target is fixed and whether you can attack it more times than it can be defended.
Both sides can have semi-open files, usually on opposite wings, and each will be attacking on their own. Reporting only one side's is half the position.

That a plan should be found before the position is assessed. The plan is supposed to follow from the assessment.
Sharp theoretical positions are played from preparation rather than from principle.
Forcing positions require calculation and the procedure above does not apply.

This is an umbrella record. Attaching it to a move explains nothing; the specific concept under it is what carries content.

Luft defeats it outright: one pawn move can turn mate into nothing.
A defended back rank is not weak; count defenders before claiming the pattern.
If any surrounding piece can move away with tempo, the mate evaporates.
That any rook move on the fourth rank builds a bridge. The order matters — drive the king back first.
Does not work with a rook pawn in general.
Fails if the defending rook denies the bridge rank, though other wins usually exist.
Interposing before the enemy king is driven back is the standard error and can allow perpetual check or a stalemate trick.
The fifth rank is the wrong bridge rank in general, and there is a known line where building there loses the rook to a capture and draws.

That any rook-and-pawn-on-the-seventh position is a Lucena.
That it works with a rook pawn.
Does not apply to rook pawns.
Fails if the defending rook can stop the attacking rook reaching the bridge rank — though other wins usually exist.
The short-side defence draws if the defending king is on the side with fewer files and the rook has at least three files of checking distance.
A rook pawn is NOT a Lucena. The mechanism needs room on both sides of the pawn, and rook-pawn endings are frequently drawn — see the Vancura position.

The name does not tell you who discovered it, and a record that repeats the attribution as fact is wrong.

That an extra rook pawn wins a rook ending.

It is specialist theory for the ROOK PAWN on the sixth. Applying the side-attack idea to a central pawn does not work.
The defending king's square is part of the position, not a detail. Outside g7/h7 the skewer wins.

That compensation means attacking chances. Structural damage and the bishop pair are compensation too, and they last longer.
That the defender should hold the extra material. The standard technique is to return it at the right moment.
That a gambit's name tells you whether compensation exists. It has to be measured.

Where the material given is more than a pawn, tempo compensation alone is rarely enough.
Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse.
Counting developed pieces overstates a development lead. Count the moves each side still needs.
An evaluation near zero while a pawn down means full compensation NOW; it says nothing about whether it survives the next ten moves.

That an early queen move loses material or the game. In the measured case it costs about two thirds of a pawn.
That the danger is to the queen herself. The queen is rarely trapped; the cost is time.
That the rule is absolute. Several sound openings violate it by design.
That openings which break the rule escape its cost. The Scandinavian pays about 0.46 for its early queen move and is a good opening anyway.

Queen moves that create a threat the opponent must answer, which reverses who is gaining tempi.
Positions where no minor piece can attack the queen usefully.

Many sound openings move the queen early. The Scandinavian's main line brings Black's queen out on move two and is entirely respectable, so the bare fact of an early queen move must never be reported as an error.
The rule is about being attacked with tempo, not about the queen being 'exposed'. If nothing attacks her profitably, there is no penalty.
The measured cost is about 0.68 pawns. Reporting an early queen move in the language of a blunder overstates the evidence.

That gambits are unsound in general. The Evans measures at exactly equal, which is not the same as bad.
Openings called gambits where the material cannot actually be held, such as the Queen's Gambit.
Gambits whose compensation is structural rather than dynamic - the Benko is the standard case, where the pressure on the a- and b-files persists into the endgame instead of expiring.

That memorising lines is what a repertoire is. Memorised lines without understanding are exactly what move-order tricks punish.
At elite level, narrow specialisation is increasingly impractical against engine-assisted preparation.

That it is simply a common position. The branching into different plans is the defining part.

Which positions count is a matter of editorial convention, so the label is softer than it sounds.

That a novelty is by definition a strong move. It is by definition an unplayed one.
That novelties are found by human insight alone. At the top level they are overwhelmingly engine-generated now.
A novelty played by accident carries none of the preparation value that gives the term its point.
Novelty is relative to a particular database. A move absent from one corpus may be well known in another, so the label is only as good as the reference used.

That every backward pawn is a weakness.
That the pawn is the target. The square in front of it is usually worth more.
Not a weakness if it cannot be attacked, or if the freeing break is always available.
Accepting one for space or activity is routine modern practice.
The square in front is often the real asset; winning the pawn can be the lesser goal.
A pawn that is merely behind its neighbours but CAN advance safely is not backward in the operative sense.

Reporting the pawn and not the square in front of it usually misses the more important half.

That doubled pawns are a weakness. They are a concession with a price attached, and the price is often worth paying.
That the Capablanca quotation about doubled pawns and the seventh rank is verified. It is not.
That they matter equally in middlegame and endgame. They mainly bite in the endgame.
That doubled pawns are a weakness. Measured here: inflicting them cost the inflicting side 0.34, and the side that accepted them is exactly equal.

The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.
The recapture-towards-the-centre guideline has three standard exceptions: king shelter, a more useful file, and creating a chronic target.

That they are two isolated pawns. They defend the squares in front of each other, which an isolani has nobody to do.

Where the pair can advance profitably, they are a space-gaining asset rather than a weakness.
With enough piece activity the structure is fully sound; the 'weak by nature' framing is a starting assessment, not a verdict.
Hanging pawns are not automatically weak. The structure is dynamic, and the same pair that loses one game wins the next depending on where the pieces are.

hanging pawns are weak
That every square a pawn cannot guard is a hole worth naming. Most are not.
That holes are always bad. They are a structural cost that is frequently worth paying.
That a hole is created by moving a pawn. It is created by moving BOTH adjoining pawns, or by their exchange.
A hole is only a weakness if it can be occupied usefully. Romanovsky: the square becomes a real weakness when a piece that cannot be driven away or exchanged threatens to take it up.
Creating a hole is often the correct price for something else — space, the bishop pair, or a tempo. Steinitz's own example (1.e4 e5 2.c4) is a playable opening, not a mistake.
A hole covered by a well-placed piece is not exploitable while that piece remains; the plan is to exchange the defender first.

That the aim is to promote it. Often the aim is to make the opponent spend pieces stopping it.

That an advanced queen is doing something. It is usually about to be attacked.
In endgames the queen leads perfectly well, since there is nothing cheap left to chase it.
Some openings bring the queen out early by design and pay a measured, affordable price.
An advanced queen is not an active queen. It is often a queen about to be chased, and the chasing moves develop the opponent.
This base measured the early-queen cost at about 0.68 in the standard case - real, and much smaller than the usual teaching tone.
attack with the queen
an advanced queen is active
That a rook on the seventh is automatically winning.
That two rooks on the seventh mean mate. Usually they mean material.
That the aim is the rank. The aim is the pawns on it and the king behind it.
The king escaping forward removes most of the value at a stroke.
Two rooks on the seventh rarely mate against a defended eighth rank.
A rook on the seventh with nothing to attack is just a rook on a rank.
It can be a liability if it can be trapped there.
REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: a rook arriving on the seventh is not automatically important. With the pawns advanced and the king free, it attacks nothing and confines nobody.
Two rooks on the seventh do NOT generally mate a king whose eighth rank is defended. Explaining them as a mating attack is usually wrong.
Detecting 'rook on rank 7' is trivial and fires often; the reportable facts are what it attacks and whether the king is trapped.
A rook reaching the seventh is not decisive by itself. With an empty seventh rank and an enemy king that has luft, a tested position evaluates level at -0.04.
a rook on the seventh wins
two rooks on the seventh is mate
That an exchange sacrifice is always positional. It is frequently just a mating combination.
That Petrosian invented it. He popularised its positional use.
That the exchange is worth a fixed amount. Its value depends on whether the rook would have had a file.
In open positions with files available, a rook is worth more than the nominal margin and the sacrifice is correspondingly worse.
Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.
An exchange sacrifice inside a forced mate is not a positional sacrifice at all, whatever it is tagged.

THE MAIN ONE: a rook given up inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice, not a positional exchange sacrifice, even though the material given is identical. The engine test on puzzle mi-bb512d9713 in this record is exactly that case — tagged exchangeSacrifice, actually mate in 2.
Detecting 'rook for minor piece' is mechanical; deciding it was POSITIONAL requires that no forced return exists, which the material test cannot see.
In an open position with files for the rooks, the same trade can simply be bad.
the exchange is worth 1.5 pawns (as a fixed fact)
That the piece-value scale evaluates positions. It counts material, which is a different thing.
That two rooks beat a queen. The database says the opposite.
That the bishop pair is worth nothing measurable — it is about half a pawn, and that is quantified.
That the side ahead in material should always trade. With a rook against two minors the reverse is true.
Values shift with the amount of material: minor pieces are worth more pawns with a full board, rooks more with an empty one.
The redundancy of major pieces reverses the usual exchanging rule for the side with a lone rook against two minors.
Queen against two rooks favours the queen in practice, against the standard teaching.
An exposed king shifts everything towards the queen.
REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: the 1/3/3/5/9 count is not an evaluation. Being 'ahead on material' by that scale says very little once the material is of different kinds.
Detecting the imbalance is mechanical and trivial; saying who it favours is not, and depends on open files, king safety and how much else remains.
Statistical values are averages. They tell you what to expect across many games, not what is true in this one.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: a knight against a bishop is not an imbalance by this record's own preferred numbers - Kaufman puts a knight and an UNPAIRED bishop at the same 3.5 - and the matcher fired on every such swap, 42.1% of the 788 shipped positions. It is a third name for a fact `bishop-pair` and `bad-bishop` already report. The exception is the pair itself, which Kaufman does separate (7.5 against 7.0), so two bishops against two knights is still reported. 42.1% -> 35.5%.
a rook is worth five points
two rooks beat a queen
That trading is good when ahead. It is good when it reduces counterplay and bad when it approaches a drawn ending.
That an even trade is positionally neutral. It changes the character of the position, which is usually the bigger consequence.
That capturing or trading is safe when you are winning. A proven position in this base has one available capture, which is also a check, and it converts mate in one into a draw.
Simplifying when ahead fails if the ending is drawn — wrong rook pawn, opposite bishops, insufficient material.
The side ahead in material should keep pawns, not trade them.
With a rook against two minor pieces, trade major pieces even when nominally behind, because major pieces are redundant.
'Simplify when ahead' is the most over-applied rule in chess. Trading into a proven drawn ending is how won games are drawn, and this base holds tablebase-proven examples of exactly that.
The rule is about removing counterplay, not about removing pieces. If the opponent has no counterplay, there is no reason to trade at all.
Trading one bishop destroys a bishop pair worth half a pawn — a cost that a simple material count does not see.
A trade being available is not a reason to make it, and being ahead is not a reason either. Proven case: Rxh7+ draws where Rb8 mates in one.
always simplify when ahead
That positional evaluation means counting material and adding adjustments. King safety and threats can make material irrelevant.
That Steinitz's lists are his own words. What circulates is a later refinement.
That an advantage can be accumulated indefinitely. Steinitz's seventh proposition says a sufficient advantage must be acted on or it dissipates.
The theory's claim that attacks cannot succeed against correct defence in an equal position is a statement about correct defence, not about practical play, where unsound attacks win regularly.
The element lists are a later refinement and not Steinitz's own enumeration.
Listing elements is not evaluating. A position with several observations attached and no judgement about which dominates has not been assessed.
The permanent/temporary division is about durability, not importance. A temporary advantage can be decisive precisely because it is about to expire.
This system should use the elements to explain an engine's number, never to argue against it.
evaluation means counting material
That a positional sacrifice is a slower attacking sacrifice. It is not an attack at all.
That Petrosian invented the term. He is associated with the modern practice; the phrase is older and meant something different.
The compensation must survive simplification. An asset that evaporates when queens come off is not positional compensation.
The opponent can often return the material at a good moment to reach a favourable endgame; a positional sacrifice must account for that resource.
Defensive positional sacrifices are a real and under-taught category.
Calling any unclear sacrifice positional. If the point is an attack, it is not a positional sacrifice.
Asserting compensation that cannot be named. 'Positional compensation' with no named asset is the vaguest claim in chess writing and must not be produced by this system.
Spielmann's sense and the modern sense are opposite; using the phrase without saying which is meant is itself a false positive.
positional compensation (with no named asset)
unclear but probably good
That every material give-up is a sacrifice — a blunder gives up material for nothing.
That sacrifices are inherently risky. Sham sacrifices carry no risk at all; that is what makes them sham.
That a sacrifice refuted by an engine was a mistake to play. Objective soundness and practical merit are different questions.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.
A passive sacrifice can simply be declined. Not noticing that is a standard error.
An objectively unsound sacrifice can be the best practical decision against a human on a clock. Those are different claims and should not be merged.
A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
An even trade is not a sacrifice.
Calling a blunder a sacrifice. The difference is whether the compensation is real and nameable — annotators decide between '!' and '?' on exactly that.

Spielmann's distinction is invisible to a material test. A forced mating sacrifice and a speculative one give up the same material and are different things; 'risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice', and risk is not a property of the position, it is a property of what could be calculated from it.
sacrifices are always risky
the engine refuted it so it was a mistake
That static means good and dynamic means risky. They are different clocks, not different qualities.
That an advantage is permanently one or the other.
The same feature can be either, depending on whether it can be maintained.
A dynamic advantage can be converted into a static one, which is usually the correct plan.
Modern practice weights dynamics more heavily than the classical framework implied.
The classification is not a property of the feature alone. A passed pawn is static if it can be held and dynamic if it must run now.
'Dynamic' is often used loosely to mean 'sharp'. Here it means specifically that the advantage expires.
dynamic means risky
That an advantage should be held onto. Advantages are usually converted through several intermediate forms, and holding one unchanged is how it dissipates.
That giving something up means conceding. A transformation is judged by what is obtained.
That technique means playing safely. Its authors describe the decisive phase as precise calculation, not patient manoeuvring.
Where an advantage can be converted directly, no transformation is needed.
The authors themselves note that concrete play runs contrary to the patient principles, so the method contains a real internal tension rather than a smooth procedure.
A transforming move often looks like a concession and can be reported as an error by anything judging moves on what they give up rather than what they get.
Not every exchange of one advantage for another is a transformation; it must be for a MORE convertible advantage, and this base cannot judge that without concrete evidence.
The concept describes a player's intention. This system observes moves, not intentions, and must not attribute a transformation to a move without evidence.
hold on to your advantage
never give anything back
That two weaknesses make a position winning. They make it convertible, not won; the tablebase pair shows the mechanism can be decisive, and the Kotov-Pachman example shows it often is not.
That the second weakness must be another weak pawn. An exposed king, an invasion square or a passive piece serve equally.
That the first weakness should be captured as soon as possible. Holding it fixed often binds more defenders than taking it wins material.
Fortresses: once the defender reaches a fortress the number of weaknesses stops mattering, since none of them can be converted.

Opposite-coloured bishops: extra material and multiple targets are routinely insufficient, because the defending bishop guards one colour complex indefinitely. A second weakness helps only if it creates a breakthrough square or drags the bishop off its blockade.

Targets too close together: if the defending king can shuttle between both, the mechanism largely fails. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending - moving the kings from g1/g8 to d3/d6 drops the evaluation from +1.74 to +0.75.
Self-weakening: pushing pawns to open a second front can create new targets in the attacker's own camp, or hand the defender a passed pawn.
Winning the first weakness may be wrong even when possible, if the capture activates the defender's pieces. The fixed pawn can be worth more as a permanent burden than as material.

Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.

Any position has several imperfections. Calling any two of them 'two weaknesses' is the commonest misuse — they must require DIFFERENT defensive resources and be far enough apart that the defence cannot cover both.

The principle describes a method of conversion, not an evaluation. A position with two weaknesses is not thereby winning, and Kotov-Pachman shows the gap: the moves annotators mark necessary and inaccurate differ by 0.05 pawns.
Against opposite-coloured bishops or a reachable fortress, the count of weaknesses is simply not the operative variable.

A pawn that is structurally weak can be the position's KEY DEFENSIVE ASSET, and no pawn-skeleton test tells the two apart. Shirov-Kramnik, Linares 2000, move 20: this base lists Black's f4 among the weaknesses White should play against, and Jan Markos calls the same pawn, together with b4, the cage that 'guards all the roads to d5'. Both readings follow from the skeleton and only one is true of the position.

That the rule is unconditional. Neither of its earliest formulations states it that way.
That the worst piece is always the one to move. It is the default when nothing else is asking to be done.
That Fischer formulated it. Botvinnik named it after him; Fischer never stated it.
Anderssen's own exception: when immediate advantage is available from an attack.
Makogonov's own precondition: only where no other important matters need consideration.
When the opponent has counterplay, quiet improvement concedes the initiative.

The rule's precondition is the load-bearing part and is usually dropped in quotation. Anderssen says 'unless you can derive immediate advantage by an attack' and Makogonov says 'in positions where no other important matters need to be considered'. Without those, it is not the rule they stated.
Improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative produces individually reasonable moves and a collectively lost position. This is the commonest way the rule is misapplied.
Identifying the worst piece is a judgement, not a measurement. This system has no reliable detector for it and must not claim one.
always improve your worst piece
Fischer's rule
That practical and objective advice are the same kind of claim. One depends on who is playing and the other does not.
That a practically effective line is thereby sound. The engine verdict is the ceiling and practical results are the floor.
In correspondence or analysis, where time and reference are unlimited, practical considerations largely disappear and only the objective claim remains.
Practical advice is not a property of a position and must never be offered as the reason a move is good. This system sees a board, not a player, a clock or a tournament table.
A line being a good practical try is not a claim that it is sound, and the two must be reported separately.
objectively best (as a practical recommendation)
That masters play mostly on intuition. Time pressure degrades grandmasters and world champions substantially, which it should not if intuition were doing the work.
That masters have better memories. On random positions they do not.
That blunders are random accidents. They concentrate where time pressure and positional ambiguity coincide.
These are tendencies across many games, and any individual game may run against all of them.
None of this is a property of a position and none of it may be attached to a move.
Chess psychology is unusually rich in confident unevidenced claims. This record holds only measured effects and names what it is leaving out.
Population effects do not license statements about an individual player.
masters see the right move
play the opponent, not the board
That strong players think longer. They think longer in the middlegame and shorter elsewhere, and vary more.
That mastery is intuition and time pressure therefore costs experts little. Grandmasters and world champions show strong adverse effects.
That time trouble simply makes you play worse. It makes you play worse SPECIFICALLY where the position is also unclear, and the two combine nonlinearly.
A forced sequence needs no time regardless of phase.
An endgame that is theoretically critical deserves time even though endgames are generally played fast.
This is advice to a player about a clock, not an observation about a position, and must never be attached to a move as an explanation of it.
The evidence is about populations. It does not establish what any individual should do on any given move.
One study in this set reports faster decisions correlating with HIGHER quality, which does not obviously sit with the time-pressure findings. Both are recorded; neither is presented as settled.
strong players think longer
masters play on intuition
The ROOK may be attacked, and in queenside castling the b1/b8 square the rook crosses may be attacked — only the king's three squares matter.
Rights once lost never return, even if the piece goes back to its original square.
you must castle early
That a check is a good move because it forces a reply. In the Vancura position one check draws and another loses.
A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.
A check being available is not a reason to play it. Proven case: Ra7+ draws and Rg8+ loses in the same position.
check is always good
That every chess idea has a name. Many do not, and inventing one is worse than describing the idea.
That a term appearing in many articles makes it established. Several widely repeated terms have no canonical definition behind them.
Where no recognised name exists, describing the thing plainly is correct and is not a failure.
A descriptive phrase must never be presented as an established term. The schema records which is which precisely so this cannot happen by accident.
Do not create a concept because a detector needed a label. positionalTactic is the standing example of a pipeline tag that is not a chess idea.

Deflection, decoy, overloading, interference and double attack are deliberately unclaimed here. Adding a detector for them without criteria that survive false-positive testing would reintroduce exactly the wrong-label problem.
the technical term is
K+N+N vs K is a draw in practice but is NOT a dead position: mate is legally reachable with cooperation, so the game does not end automatically.
A completely blocked position with full material can be a dead position even though material is ample.
insufficient material (when the FIDE rule is meant)
Cannot be deferred: the right is lost if not exercised immediately.
Like any move, it is illegal if it leaves or places one's own king in check.
Not automatic — it must be claimed.
Some endgames proven winnable by tablebase require more than 50 moves and are therefore drawn under the Laws. The rule and the theoretical truth genuinely diverge here.
Implementations differ on K+N+N vs K and on K+B vs K+N; do not state a universal rule.
Blocked positions with full material are dead under the Laws but are not caught by this test.
the rules say insufficient material
That UCI and algebraic are the same thing written differently. UCI is position-independent and algebraic is not.
That a FEN is just the board. Half its fields are about rights and counters that the board cannot show.
FIDE recognises algebraic only; the other systems are conventions, however universal.
PGN carries game metadata as well as moves and is a container format rather than a notation.
SAN is contextual: the same text means different moves in different positions, and disambiguation depends on what else is on the board. It cannot be parsed without a position.
Descriptive notation named a square differently for each player, so a quotation converted from it can silently name the wrong square. Treat converted historical lines with care.
A FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position - it is a picture of one.
notation is just shorthand
Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.
always promote to a queen
Checkmate on the 75th move takes precedence over the draw.
Not automatic — without a claim the game continues.
Side to move, castling rights and en-passant availability are all part of the position; ignoring any of them produces false repetitions.
same moves three times
Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.
A clearance sacrifice fails if the follow-up is a tempo too slow — the whole idea depends on forcing continuations.
Clearing a line for a piece that is then driven off achieves nothing; the arriving piece must be able to stay.
A clearance that also opens a line towards your own king is a different move from the one you calculated.
A decoy fails outright if the sacrifice can be declined.
A decoy that lands the enemy king on a square where the follow-up needs one more move than the defender has is not a decoy, it is a lost piece.
Decoying a defender onto a square where it still defends is the commonest miscalculation in this motif.
A deflection fails if the deflected piece can answer the threat and keep its duty, which is the commonest miscalculation in the motif.
Deflecting a defender that has a second defender behind it achieves nothing.
If the opponent can decline, it is not a deflection — the whole idea rests on the reply being forced.
The whole idea rests on the piece being genuinely unsaveable. Verify that first.
A desperado that gives the opponent a tempo they needed is worse than losing the piece quietly.
If the piece can be saved by a counter-threat rather than by moving, it is not doomed and the desperado is a blunder.
A discovery is worthless if the unmasked line hits nothing of value.
In a discovered check the moving piece may stand en prise with impunity — normal safety reasoning does not apply to it.
If the discovered check can be met by a capture of the checking piece, the free move is not free.
A single move can sometimes answer both threats — an interposition that also defends, or a counter-check.
A double check is not automatically strong: if the king simply steps aside safely, the attacker may have given away material for nothing.
That forcing moves are usually best. They are usually cheapest to check.
That checking first means checking always. A check spends a resource and can be the losing move.
Quiet positions may contain no useful forcing move at all, and the search then has to be conducted differently.
Nunn's goal-seeking case: some strong moves make no sense except as part of a whole operation and will never appear in a forcing-move scan.
Forcing is not the same as good, and this is the trap that matters. This base holds a proven position in which one check draws and another loses.
The rule is about search order, not move choice. Reporting 'it is forcing' as a reason a move is strong misuses it entirely.
Applying it only to your own moves is how calculated lines get refuted; the opponent's forcing replies are the ones that overturn analysis.
forcing moves are strong
always check first
A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.
forks always win material
That Bxh7+ works whenever the bishop can reach h7.
That the name's origin is settled. Two incompatible derivations circulate and neither is verified here.
That Kxh7 is forced. Declining is sometimes better, and that possibility has to be checked too.
Vukovic's conditions are necessary but not sufficient. Every instance still has to be calculated.
If g5 is defended, the sacrifice is refuted outright — a bishop for a pawn.
The king walking to g6 rather than retreating is the standard tricky defence and must be checked separately.
The mirrored Black version (...Bxh2+) is the same pattern with the same conditions.
The pattern is extremely recognisable, which is exactly why it is played in positions where it does not work. Vukovic's conditions are necessary, NOT sufficient.
The commonest single error is not checking whether g5 is defended. The controlled pair in this record isolates that one variable.
Bxh7+ 'looks like' the Greek gift whenever a bishop eyes h7; without the knight and queen in range it is just a lost bishop.
Bxh7+ always works when the bishop eyes h7
That a piece with a defender cannot be hanging. It can — if the defender is pinned or overloaded, or if it is attacked twice and defended once.
That every hanging piece should be taken.
A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.
A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange.
A nominal defender that is pinned does not defend. SEE catches this; a naive defender count does not.
Material already loose before the move is not this move's doing — reporting it makes the move look worse than it was.
hanging always means undefended
Fails if the interposed unit can be captured by a piece that does not itself have a duty.
That a knight fork always wins material. The landing square's safety decides it.
That the family and royal fork are distinct motifs. They are the same motif with more expensive targets.
A knight fork on a guarded square wins nothing.
Only another knight can attack a knight back without moving, which is why knight-versus-knight forks behave differently.
The landing square must be safe. This base's fork controlled pair shows the same knight move at +7.39 and at +0.57 depending only on whether one bishop guards the square.
A knight attacking two defended pawns is not a fork worth reporting.
a knight fork always wins material
That every piece should be defended.
That a loose piece is a blunder. It is a standing risk.
Strong players leave pieces loose constantly and correctly, when no forcing move can exploit it.
Spending tempi to defend a piece nothing attacks is a real cost and often the worse choice.
Being loose is not being bad. Reporting every undefended piece would flag most positions and teach nothing.
It only matters when a forcing move can reach it. A loose rook in a locked position is not a weakness.
loose means hanging
A defender that appears overloaded may be adequate if one 'duty' was never real.
A pinned piece still delivers check and still guards squares against non-king units.
A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.
Pinning is not automatically good: a pin can be dissolved and the pinning piece can end up misplaced.
a pinned piece cannot do anything
Fails against a second defender, or when the removal costs more than it wins.
If the front piece moves along the same line it may keep defending the piece behind.
That 'combination' has an agreed definition. It has at least four, from named authorities, and a formal 1952 discussion failed to reconcile them.
That a combination must sacrifice. That is Botvinnik's position, and Romanovsky's, Lasker's and Averbakh's later view all disagree.
On Botvinnik's definition a forcing line with no sacrifice is a manoeuvre and not a combination at all.
Whether a sacrifice is REQUIRED is contested by named authorities, so this system must not assert either version as the definition.
A forcing sequence without a sacrifice is a manoeuvre on Botvinnik's account and a combination on Romanovsky's. Reporting it either way takes a side in an open argument.
Length and forcing-ness do not make a combination; there has to be a goal it reaches.
a combination always involves a sacrifice
by definition a combination
A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.
An x-ray defence is illusory if the defending piece is itself pinned.
An in-between move fails if the opponent's answer to it also answers the original threat.
A check that lets the opponent improve while answering it is worse than the immediate recapture.
If the first exchange can be abandoned by the opponent, the in-between move has bought nothing.
